title: Charles’s rebuttal of Earl Spencer’s claim about Diana offers rare glimpse into palace thinking | Monarchy | The Guardian
description: From ‘there were three of us in this marriage’ to ‘recollections may vary’, a lot can be conveyed with a carefully worded phrase
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: From ‘there were three of us in this marriage’ to ‘recollections may vary’, a lot can be conveyed with a carefully worded phrase
Content: Buckingham Palace rarely responds to the claims made in books on royalty, adhering to its ‘never complain, never explain’ mantra.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersView image in fullscreenBuckingham Palace rarely responds to the claims made in books on royalty, adhering to its ‘never complain, never explain’ mantra.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersMonarchyCharles’s rebuttal of Earl Spencer’s claim about Diana offers rare glimpse into palace thinkingFrom ‘there were three of us in this marriage’ to ‘recollections may vary’, a lot can be conveyed with a carefully worded phraseCaroline DaviesThu 17 Sep 2026 10.47 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs denials go,King Charles’s response to Earl Spencer’s allegationsthat Charles said after Diana’s death, “We’ll forget her soon enough”, was a masterclass in the diplomatic royal rebuke.Rarely has Buckingham Palace responded to claims in countless books on royalty. But it was straight out of the block on this one.Little over an hour after the Daily Mail, which is serialising Spencer’s memoir Swan Song about his sister, the lateDiana, Princess of Wales, had published its first extract online, a statement was issued.Charles, the headline claimed, had told Spencer days after Diana’s death and during a heated row over funeral arrangements: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough.”The king’s swift countering, that “the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss”, will enter the canon of carefully constructed regal pushbacks.View image in fullscreenCharles’s swift rebuke suggests the palace acknowledged the damage Spencer’s claim could do and needed to set the record straight.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersAs rebukes go, it is up there withthe late Queen Elizabeth II’s “some recollections may vary”in response to a torrent of allegations from the Duke and Duchess of Sussex in their Oprah Winfrey interview.Senior courtiers are often drawn from the diplomatic service and thus highly-skilled in couching the passive-aggressive denial. Deploying delicate language to devastating effect is a stock in trade at the Foreign Office.But it is a weapon to be used sparingly. The royal mantra is, usually, “never complain, never explain”.However, Charles’s former communications secretary Julian Payne said: “This is a much more personal situation, given its author, and therefore has a greater ability to do harm.”That is why the palace “felt the need to set the record straight and deny these remarks have been made”, Payne told the BBC’s Today programme. Given the amount of things the palace don’t comment on, “you can imagine the strength of feeling”, he added.Payne remains close to the king and was due to be sitting alongside him at Thursday’s AI summit just hours later, so the fact he felt able to speak so freely suggests his robust defence of Charles came with official sanction.What is said behind palace doors usually remains private. The language may be less sensitive. But a carefully chosen phrase in public pulls back the privacy screen.When Diana, in her highly controversial Panorama interview, said “there were three of us in this marriage, so it was a bit crowded”, she reaped public revenge on her then husband and Camilla.In return, Diana found herself on the sharp end of Elizabeth’s ire weeks later. After Diana failed to respond to the queen’s request that the couple divorce, a palace spokesperson issued a statement: “After considering the present situation, the queen wrote to both the prince and princess earlier this week and gave them her view, supported by the Duke of Edinburgh, that an early divorce is desirable.” The matter was now, officially, out of Diana’s hands.View image in fullscreenHarry and Meghan during their interview with Oprah in 2021, which led to the late queen’s ‘recollections may vary’ statement.Photograph: ReutersWhite fury was behind the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s statement in February 2021: “We can all live a life of service. Service is universal.” It was read as a succinct and direct challenge to the late queen’s insistence they could not keep their public service roles after stepping down as working royals.Meghan was less direct in a 2019 interview with ITV’s Tom Bradby in which he asked her if she was OK juggling life as a royal with a newborn, Prince Archie. “Thank you for asking, because not many people have asked if I’m OK,” she replied. Was it directed at the palace and the institution? A huge number of the claims the Sussexes later made, in TV interviews and in Harry’s memoir Spare, were that the duchess had been unsupported throughout her time as a working royal.One royal famously deficient in the art of the diplomatic royal rebuke, however, was the late Duke of Edinburgh. Philip was renowned for his gaffes. When a BBC journalist politely asked the queen at a banquet at the Élysée Palace if she was enjoying her stay in Paris in 2006, Philip dispensed with tact to snap: “Damn fool question!”Explore more on these topicsMonarchyDiana, Princess of WalesKing Charles IIIQueen Elizabeth IIMeghan, the Duchess of SussexPrince HarrynewsShareReuse this content

title: With Kemi’s new shadow chancellor, the Tories must hope for a bout of public amnesia | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Andrew Griffith is keen on clearing red tape. Good job he wasn’t part of a Treasury team that abolished the Office for Tax Simplification
Author: John Crace
Headline: Andrew Griffith is keen on clearing red tape. Good job he wasn’t part of a Treasury team that abolished the Office for Tax Simplification
Content: ‘Looking like you’ve been locked in the boiler room by the college principal isn’t the best of looks.’ Andrew Griffith delivering a speech at Capital City College Group in London.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreen‘Looking like you’ve been locked in the boiler room by the college principal isn’t the best of looks.’ Andrew Griffith delivering a speech at Capital City College Group in London.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAThe politics sketchConservativesWith Kemi’s new shadow chancellor, the Tories must hope for a bout of public amnesiaJohn CraceAndrew Griffith is keen on clearing red tape. Good job he wasn’t part of a Treasury team that abolished the Office for Tax SimplificationThu 17 Sep 2026 13.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTShareOn days like this, it’s not hard to be overwhelmed by existential futility. At the current rate of progress, the UK looks on course to wipe itself out far sooner than it would with any interference from AI. Everything feels hopeless. Years of minimal growth and a cost of living crisis. The tech bros and the bankers may be getting richer. The rest of us? Not so much.And there’s no end in sight. Andy Burnham may offer better vibes, but he is fighting a losing battle against global forces – wars, energy prices, borrowing costs – that he can’t control. You can feel the hope drain out of him as each day passes. Mr Congeniality is not quite so congenial as he once was. All the economic forecasts suggest things are going to get even worse in the next year.Even Labour allies are preparing the ground for a tough budget next month. The chancellor, John Healey, has been making it known that even he is surprised by just how bad things are. Can’t think why. The rest of us have known for a while, and he’s had the benefit of sitting at the Cabinet table with Rachel Reeves for the past two years. Perhaps he dozed off while she was speaking. He wouldn’t have been the first.Still, the government does have one thing going for it. There is currently no one better. That might not be much comfort to some people, but it helps Labour sleep a little easier. Reform members seem determined to take themselves down. If not by financial scandals then by their own stupidity.That’s why Richard Tice has such a prominent role within the party. Only on Wednesday, Dicky was at it again. Responding to the news that Healey had made the TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, a non-executive director of the Bank of England, Motormouth Dicky immediately declared Britain had descended into a socialist hell. Were he better informed, he would have known it’s been a tradition for the last 40 years or so that the TUC head honcho gets a gig at the Bank. One started by that well-known Commie apparatchik Margaret Thatcher. But why let that get in the way of an ill-thought through social media clip.Usually, Dicky is in a league of his own in the competition to be the dimmest and least competent MP in Westminster. But this timeKemi Badenochwas keen to join in with a similar post. As much to remind everyone that the Tory party was still not ready to be taken seriously or forgiven for its 14 years of unmanaged decline as anything else. And where Kemi led, Andrew Griffith followed with his own statement insisting the unions would soon be running the country. You’d have thought that a shadow chancellor, with experience as a junior minister in the Treasury, would have inside knowledge of the Bank of England’s conventions.There again, Andrew will be Andrew. Living proof of Kemi’s currently insurmountable problem. She can say all she wants that she has changed the party, but all the country sees is more or less the same faces promising that this time everything will be different. Something that’s more or less inevitable when you have a party of fewer than 120 MPs. It takes some cheek to appoint a backer of Liz Truss’s mini-budget as your shadow chancellor. Two fingers to everyone.Right now, Griffith’s main function appears to be to make people yearn for the return of Mel Stride. The Melster may have been a bit useless, but he always looked as if he was trying to be decent. The Tories have set a lot of store by the fact that Andrew made a lot of money in the private sector before becoming an MP. Yet there is no sign that he can translate those skills into the public sphere. In Westminster, he is most noted forhaving loanedhis £9.5m house to Boris Johnson’s leadership campaign team, for declaring that Elon Musk had saved humanity by buying Twitter and that too many Lib Dems were vegans.On Thursday, Griffith chose to make his debut speech as shadow chancellor at a college in north London. He can only hope that not many people were listening because it rapidly became apparent that he didn’t have much to say. And what he did say was – not to put too fine a point on it – half-arsed and intellectually dishonest.Where to start? The optics weren’t great. Looking like you’ve been locked in the boiler room by the college principal isn’t the best of looks. Though maybe it would have been better if he had been. There were no apologies, no acknowldgement of the Tories’ part in the current economic state of the country. It was as though July 2024 had been year zero. Everything had been just fine until then and Labour had ruined everything.“The chancellor must rule out raising taxes,” he said. Something he, himself, is unwilling to do. The Tories have committed to keeping the current tax thresholds until 2028, a stealth tax that raises billions more for the Treasury each year. It was breathtaking. But there was more. Griffith was determined to simplify tax regulation and red tape. Another astonishing feat of amnesia. It had been Andrew who played a key role in the Treasury abolishing the Office for Tax Simplification while in office. He must think we’re stupid.Surprisingly, he had nothing to say on the one tax cut that Kemi has actually committed to exploring. The abolition of inheritance tax. A proposal that would benefit the wealthiest 5%. So much for being the party of small business and the self-employed. Sometimes, it feels as if the current iteration of the Tories just can’t help themselves. They are their own burial ground.There was just time for Griffith to reiterate that Nowak’s appointment to the Bank of England was a death knell for the country – you’d have thought he might have wanted to rethink this after a night’s sleep – before he brought the event to a close. Astonishingly, he thought it had all gone brilliantly.Explore more on these topicsConservativesThe politics sketchKemi BadenochConservative leadershipEconomic policyTax and spendingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Beck: ‘What does a devil’s haircut look like? Anything with a lot of architecture and wild flights of fancy’ | Beck | The Guardian
description: The genre-fluid singer answers your questions on being funky v lonesome, his infamous MTV interview with Thurston Moore and why he said yes to performing with a chain-smoking alcoholic robot
Author: Kate Solomon
Headline: The genre-fluid singer answers your questions on being funky v lonesome, his infamous MTV interview with Thurston Moore and why he said yes to performing with a chain-smoking alcoholic robot
Content: ‘I don’t think anybody’s mentioned Odelay to me in years’ … Beck.Photograph: Autumn De WildeView image in fullscreen‘I don’t think anybody’s mentioned Odelay to me in years’ … Beck.Photograph: Autumn De WildeFilm & Music reader interviewBeckInterviewBeck: ‘What does a devil’s haircut look like? Anything with a lot of architecture and wild flights of fancy’As told toKate SolomonThe genre-fluid singer answers your questions on being funky v lonesome, his infamous MTV interview with Thurston Moore and why he said yes to performing with a chain-smoking alcoholic robotRead Alexis Petridis’s 5* review of new album Ride LonesomeThu 17 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 13.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou’ve been performing since the late 80s. What keeps you going?AmongstTheWavesIt’s a good question. I don’t really know any other life. I’ve spent a lot of my time trying to create a body of work, and out of that, maybe there’s a few songs at the end that are not bad. So I just keep going down into the mine, trying to come back with a couple of things worth keeping. It’s a lot of digging. If I had to stop and get a job painting houses or something, I would still make songs just for myself, because that’s how it started.You tend to alternate between styles from album to album. What do you feel is closer to your intrinsic self, funky Beck orlonesome Beck?MazziniProbably lonesome. But the other side of things gets me out of my shell, stops me from being a little too ponderous, which I’m apt to do. The other side of what I do – Loser or Odelay – was more of a fluke. At the time that was what people liked. Now it’s kind of reversed – they prefer the more introspective, quiet songs, and stuff that’s a little more genreless. I don’t have any songs that they play at weddings, like Uptown Funk. I remember telling Mark Ronson, “Hey, you made a wedding song.” He was like, “Yeah, finally.” That’s a very elite category of song.Your interview withThurston Moore on MTV in 1994is one of the most gloriously ramshackle interviews ever. Were you both doing a bit?LoftyDogWe filmed a bunch of things they wouldn’t air because they thought they would get in trouble or get sued by people. I’d brought an old-fashioned telephone and at one point we pulled out some baseball bats and destroyed the phone. I don’t remember what the bit was – who was calling us? Whatever it was, we decided to smash the phone in reaction to a call. We were kind of doing performance art. I met a lot of resistance and ridicule for being like that on my first album. I would do interviews and say wild things because so much of it was boring, just rote questions – and I thought if my friends are reading this, they’d be bored to death.A lot of the things on TV were just going through the motions. As a kid, every once in a while I’d see something that jarred me. Like, wow, there was a glitch in the system and something real broke through. Something genuine that reminded us that this is all a construct, this smooth oiled machine that provides content for us. It was a very youthfully exuberant attempt to try to disrupt everything that was very pre-programmed and uninteresting. Thurston and I both came from underground art backgrounds, so it was preposterous to be allowed on mainstream TV. We were like, let’s seize the moment and do something.View image in fullscreen‘Let’s seize the moment’ … Beck at the Troubadour in West Hollywood in 1994.Photograph: Lindsay Brice/Getty ImagesGiven how productive you were right from the start of your career, how did you feel about being tagged with the “slacker rock” label?SalfordianBlueI thought it was a reductive term. There was this influx of all this underground music that had been bubbling through the 80s and early 90s, and it all hit the mainstream at once. One day it was Vanilla Ice and hair metal and Whitney Houston, and then the next day it was Nirvana and all the stuff that you would see at your local dive bar. The 80s had been very curated and airbrushed and brightly coloured – I remember the first time I went to a record label, they told me I looked messy and rough, and it would never work. Whoever that was missed the point. We were reacting to how cleaned up everything was, and going back to something a little more raw and real.To many, Loser felt like a classic one-hit wonder. Did you always have faith that you’d have a long career in music?StayPositiveI never had any expectations. I think the thing that supersedes everything is whether you are writing good songs. The people I came up with who wrote good songs – they’re the ones that are still around and playing arenas and stadiums. And it was tricky when I was coming up, writing a catchy song was frowned upon. If you had anything that was too poppy or catchy, you were selling out, it wasn’t real art. What’s funny is the catchiest, poppiest songs from that time are the ones that everybody loves now.What would a devil’s haircut look like, and have you ever seen someone sporting one?StayPositiveBeck: Devils Haircut – ideoIt’d probably have a little bit of a rockabilly edge. Somebody showed me a video once of these proto-punk type people in Australia called sharpies, and they had a bizarre version of a mullet. It was really short bangs and kind of draped in the back. Something like that, maybe. I have a book of hairstyle photos that they would use in 80s hair salons – there are a lot of devil’s haircuts. I think any haircut that has a lot of architecture to it, with wild flights of fancy.In their1998hitYou Get What You Give the New Radicalsthreatened tokick the asses of Hanson, Courtney Love, Marilyn Manson – and Beck. Did they ever catch up with you?Dave_RowlinsonI ran into [New Radicals songwriter Gregg Alexander] in an Erewhon [health food supermarket] at the time, and he said: “I’m a big fan. We should write together.” And I just looked at him like, “What do you …? What’s happening here?” I thought the song was a little corny at the time, but it’s probably a classic now. It’s pretty catchy. I think the chords, to me, were a little too fancy for the aesthetic of the time.View image in fullscreen‘If you had anything that was too poppy or catchy, you were selling out’ … performing at the John Anson Ford Amphitheatre, LA in 2017.Photograph: Chris Pizzello/Invision/APAre you still in touch with [producer duo]the Dust Brothers? You’re one of the last artistswho worked with them, onGueroin2005, before they vanished into thin air. I genuinely wonder what happened to them!CoopertapesI did actually see them about a year ago. I see them from time to time. We have unfinished records that were never put out, so who knows? Maybe there’ll be something down the road. I’ve never asked, but I’m guessing they don’t really need to work in music, they’re doing other things. They worked with Hanson right after Odelay – people thought we were related [Beck’s surname is Hansen]. I remember they were working on that, the Rolling Stones and the Fight Club soundtrack. So that’s why my next two albums were not fully produced by the Dust Brothers, after the success of Odelay they became too busy.View image in fullscreen‘You have to do it!’ … Beck in Futurama.Photograph: 20th Century FoxLooking to the future, do you see yourself sharing the stage with a chain-smoking alcoholic robot? AKA how did you come to be a guest star on Futurama?vammypThey wrote a script and sent it to me, and I said no. Through that whole era, I said no to pretty much everything. I was asked to do the theme for Austin Powers 2 and 3, and Shrek, and I was even saying no to, like, Amores Perros and Y Tu Mamá También and Run Lola Run, all these classic movies. They wanted me to act in High Fidelity and Ghost World, and I just decided that I didn’t want to “go Hollywood”.They sent me this cartoon and I thought, well, if I did something like this it would be The Simpsons – a lot of people have done that, Sonic Youth have done that. The script was sitting on the tour bus, and my band got a hold of it on a long drive and said, “What is this?” And I said, “Oh, it’s this show, Futurama. I’ve never heard of it, but they want me to do this ridiculous thing.” And they said, “You have to do it!” They all ganged up on me so I did it.‘Our computer sampler cost more than a house!’: how the Korgis made Everybody’s Got to Learn SometimeRead moreBeercanis my go-to “shake your ass” number. What is yours?TeeDubyaBeeI would say anything from the early 80s funk era. Anything Sly Stone, James Brown – and early 80s Prince era, Talking Heads. Classics.Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mindis one of my favourite films, and your recording ofEverybody’s Got toLearn Sometimeis a sublime part of it. How did you get involved with the film, and why that song in particular?CybillserviceI did a music video withMichel Gondry, the director, and we became pals. I was having dinner over at his house one night, and he described this convoluted plot that I couldn’t quite follow. I said, “I don’t totally understand what this is, but when you make it, I want to see it.” Three or four years later, he called me up and said, “I made the movie.” My buddy Jon Brion was doing the score. It’s one of the only things, again, that I said yes to. But it was because it was a personal relationship. It’s become one of my songs that people love the most. I had just done Sea Change, which I think is one of the reasons they called me. That album had met so much shock from my fans that I swore to never make a record like that again. And now it’s beloved. It’s probably the main thing that people care about. I don’t think anybody’s mentioned Odelay to me in years, it’s all Sea Change and Midnite Vultures.Beck’s new album Ride Lonesome is released 18 September via Iliad/CapitolExplore more on these topicsBeckFilm & Music reader interviewPop and rockMichel GondryThurston MoorefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Amazing community’: how people are making new friends and connections as adults | Loneliness | The Guardian
description: As concern about loneliness and social isolation grows, we spoke to people who have joined groups and set up activities
Author: Nicola Slawson
Headline: As concern about loneliness and social isolation grows, we spoke to people who have joined groups and set up activities
Content: ‘Even though you’re doing an exercise class, there’s that informal aspect where you are having a bit of a joke and a laugh.’Photograph: Thomas Barwick/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Even though you’re doing an exercise class, there’s that informal aspect where you are having a bit of a joke and a laugh.’Photograph: Thomas Barwick/Getty ImagesLoneliness‘Amazing community’: how people are making new friends and connections as adultsAs concern about loneliness and social isolation grows, we spoke to people who have joined groups and set up activitiesNicola SlawsonandJane ClintonThu 17 Sep 2026 09.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 10.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmid growing concern about loneliness and social isolation, new research from the Institute for Public Policy Research found the number of young people in England withno close friends has risen fivefold since 2014, with one in 20 now reporting having none at all.Making new friends as an adult is not always easy. We spoke to people who have taken deliberate steps to make new connections about what worked for them.‘If I was in trouble in some way, I’ve now got people I could actually call’View image in fullscreenRhiannon with one of her creations that she made at Yarners.Photograph: Rhiannon D’AvercFor Rhiannon, a 35-year-old ghostwriter from East Sussex, joining a local knitting and crochet group has become “a lifeline” after separating from her husband and moving a few towns away, and finding connections harder to maintain.In February, she joined the Yarners, a weekly group in Mayfield. Having only started crocheting a month earlier, she was “absolutely terrified” they would judge her for being a beginner. “But they didn’t care.”The group quickly became an important part of her life. “No matter what is happening at home, I know for two hours a week I can just sit in a calm and supportive space with people who share my hobby. It’s more than just a group. It’s a real community.”Having local friends to rely on is one of the biggest perks. “If I needed something, if I was in trouble in some way, I’ve now got people I could actually call and say: ‘Hey, can you help me?’”‘It just blew up. There are 70 people in the group now’View image in fullscreenRia started a club to bring people together over coffee.Photograph: Ria VaghelaRia, 27, moved from Mumbai to London five years ago, but after later moving to Reading, she found it harder to maintain the friendships she had made in the capital.“I faced acute loneliness,” says Ria, who now works in mergers and acquisitions in London. “When people move away from their home, it gets tough at this age to make friends.”In May, she created a WhatsApp group to bring her London friends together. It soon expanded through friends of friends and Instagram. “It just blew up. There are 70 people in the group now.”The London Coffee Club holds meetups in cafes for groups of five to 10. “I’m slightly introverted, so I don’t prefer big groups. It’s a relaxed vibe. There’s no agenda.”‘She’s helping me and I’m helping her’View image in fullscreenRebecca missed informal office conversations.Photograph: RebeccaWorking from home left Rebecca, a 31-year-old NHS project support officer in Bristol, missing everyday social interaction. “I completely underestimated how much I would miss face-to-face contact, even informal conversations such as: ‘How was your weekend?’”A few months ago, she joined exercise classes at her local leisure centre “as a way to make friends”. Although “absolutely terrified” at first, she now attends pilates, weights and body conditioning classes about three times a week.“Even though you’re doing an exercise class, there’s that informal aspect where you are having a bit of a joke and a laugh. Working from home, you don’t get that sort of office banter. To me, this is my new equivalent.”Rebecca has also met a new friend through Bristol Girls, a local Facebook group, and encouraged her to join the classes. “She’s helping me, and I’m helping her,” she says.‘I have met some of my closest friends here’View image in fullscreenBen and a co-star in a production of Private Lives in 2023.Photograph: Paul HoodAfter leaving his job as a primary school teacher Ben, 35, suddenly had more free time so thought he would use it to “meet new people” and get back into stage performance.“It was something I loved at school and at university,” says Ben, who lives in Gateshead and works in education.In 2017, he joined the People’s Theatre in Newcastle upon Tyne, a non-professional community theatre company, and has since performed in about 20 productions.“The first year was non-stop as I jumped from play to play and met so many fantastic people,” he says. “It’s been nearly a decade, and I count some people, even people I only met less than a year ago, as some of my closest friends.”The friendships now extend well beyond rehearsals and performances, with regular social gatherings.“It’s a huge community, and everyone involved, whether it’s performing, set building, or costume design, does it for the love of it,” he says. “It’s so inspiring.”‘It’s vital for people to have a safe third space’View image in fullscreenChris is enjoying revisiting his hobby in a friendly environment.Photograph: Chris/Guardian CommunityChris, 32, says a combination of growing older, the isolation of Covid and having no similarly aged peers at work led to a point where he “essentially had no local friends any more”.The systems manager from Kent decided to revive his interest in board and card games and found a local games shop holding £3-a-session games evenings. Although “terrified” before his first event, he “couldn’t have asked for a better environment”.“I feel like it’s not the impossible feat I thought it was to make new friends as an adult on your own,” he says. “The joy it brings me to be able to take part in a fun activity while getting to know people and enjoying good humour is priceless.“I think it’s vital for mental health for people to have a safe third space where they can develop relationships, skills and experiences without being dependent on work or partners to fill that void.”‘It’s brought me this amazing community’View image in fullscreenThe Girls Collective (co-founded by Chloe, holding the phone) recently hosted a pilates event.Photograph: The Girls Collective/GuardianWhen Chloe, 27, moved back to Hertfordshire after living in the Midlands, the change left her feeling lonely.View image in fullscreenSarah (left) and Chloe created the Girls Collective.Photograph: The Girls Collective/GuardianBut instead of joining a group, she created one.“All I wanted was just a friend to go for coffee or go to the cinema with,” she says. “I thought: there’s nothing for local women to make local friends. It’s so important to have that community.”With this in mind, Chloe, a content creator, and her friend Sarah, 30, a nail technician, created the Girls Collective, organising activities where women can meet while trying something new, from keyring making to line dancing.To drum up interest, they posted content on social media which caught people’s attention.“We had 65 people for our first event just from our TikTok videos,” she says.Engaging in an activity, Chloe and Sarah believe, helps to cut through any nerves and awkwardness.View image in fullscreenA pottery painting event hosted by the Girls Collective.Photograph: The Girls Collective/Guardian CommunityThe group now has 500 women in its community chat, and more than 250 have attended events. “They’ve made their own friendships and hang out outside of us [too], which is brilliant,” says Sarah.Chloe adds: “I had thought having to move back was the worst thing. But now I’m like, no, because it’s brought me this amazing community.”Explore more on these topicsLonelinessYoung peopleFriendshipCommunitiesMental healthHobbiesEnglandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Open AI and the million-dollar maths problem - video | Science | The Guardian
description: In early September, OpenAI announced it had solved a major mathematics problem that has stumped humans for nearly a century. The news left mathematicians reeling, and many expressed concern over what will be left for humans as AI becomes ever more adept at unravelling complex problems. Now 25 recipients of the Fields medal – often called the Nobel prize for maths – have signed an open letter expressing their fears of a ‘severe misalignment’ between AI companies and their field. To find out how AI is likely to upend maths – and how mathematicians might respond – Ian Sample speaks to Colva Roney-Dougal, professor of pure mathematics at the University of St Andrews

To find out how AI is likely to upend maths – and how mathematicians might respond – Ian Sample speaks to Colva Roney-Dougal, professor of pure mathematics at the University of St AndrewsPresented byIan Sample, produced byEllie SansandJacob Liebenberg, graphics byNatalie Gegan, the executive producer wasEllie Bury,Source: The GuardianThu 17 Sep 2026 09.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 11.10 EDTShareExplore more on these topicsScienceScience Weekly video episodesMathematicsAI (artificial intelligence)Computing

title: I’m nearly 30, a virgin and feel lonely. The manosphere is trying to draw me in – where else can I seek assurance? | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: The manosphere says this type of suffering is targeted neglect, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. But your suffering gives you the ability to make your part of the world better.
Author: Eleanor Gordon-Smith
Headline: The manosphere says this type of suffering is targeted neglect, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. But your suffering gives you the ability to make your part of the world better.
Content: ‘You know what it is to feel overwhelmed, adrift, unsure of yourself,’ writes Eleanor Gordon-Smith. ‘That means you can give other people what you yourself are looking for: understanding and acknowledgment.’ Painting: A Musician’s Reverie by John Pettie.Photograph: Heritage Image Partnership Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘You know what it is to feel overwhelmed, adrift, unsure of yourself,’ writes Eleanor Gordon-Smith. ‘That means you can give other people what you yourself are looking for: understanding and acknowledgment.’ Painting: A Musician’s Reverie by John Pettie.Photograph: Heritage Image Partnership Ltd/AlamyLeading questionsAustralian lifestyleI’m nearly 30, a virgin and feel lonely. The manosphere is trying to draw me in – where else can I seek assurance?The manosphere says this type of suffering is targeted neglect, writes advice columnistEleanor Gordon-Smith. But your suffering gives you the ability to make your part of the world better.Read moreLeading questionsEleanor Gordon-SmithThu 17 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 20.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m approaching 30 and I’m still a kissless virgin.I’ve suffered with depression and anxiety since childhood and my family isn’t the most functional or supportive. I don’t really have friends either, as I find it hard to connect with others due to being bullied and feeling that I’m not worthwhile or wanted. I was also homeschooled from 14 and moved to a different part of the country at 15 and a few more times since then, so I feel quite rootless and alienated.I attended university but struggled to cope, and my time coincided with Covid – after which I never returned to live in my university’s city.I have tried dating very tentatively in the past but I feel like an impostor andas if I need to be perfect.I don’t feel attractive and I tend to feel invisible.I’mworking in a job which I enjoy and I get on with my colleagues, although I am often riddled with thoughts that they secretly dislike me. The town where I live is also starting to decline and I’m deeply worried about the future.My mother-in-law buys overly girly clothes for my daughter. I try to be gracious but it kills me – do I tell her to stop?Read moreI’ve managed to avoid most of the manosphere but I have been gravitationally drawn into it in my search for guidance and advice, as well as to soothe my need for certainty and assurance. I abhor it but I don’t knowhow to go forward as a misfit man.My question is mainly how do I manage with all this? Am I missing something? And should I forget about meeting someone and accept I might be one of those people who’ll never find anyone?Eleanor says:Here’s the validating part: this is an awful lot to bear. You have lived through a terrible period of loneliness and isolation, and your depression and anxiety are as serious and potentially debilitating as any physical ailment (and, it goes without saying, as deserving – and requiring – of ongoing treatment).Now for the tough part. It’s not thatyou alonelack certainty and assurance. There’s not a party that only you were uninvited from. It is hard for so many people right now.The manosphere tells us this suffering is unique, targeted neglect, contrary to your entitlements. It positions you as the temporarily embarrassed fortunate. It tries to restore one group’s position in the pecking order, rather than asking why anyone has to lose. To the extent that it positions itself as a movement interested in wellbeing and loneliness, it is telling that it has complete disinterest in other people’s suffering or other kinds of loneliness. It is not a desire that these things be fixed. It is a desire that it does not happento me.That’s a mistake that would forfeit one of the greatest gifts available to you. Suffering like yours gives you understanding. Life made you purchase that understanding at great cost, but you now know what it’s like to be lonely. You know what it is to feel overwhelmed, adrift, unsure of yourself. That means you can give other people what you yourself are looking for: understanding and acknowledgment.My dad died suddenly with no will. Am I morally obliged to share his estate with my estranged half-sibling? | Leading questionsRead moreMany of the most beautiful souls in the world did not become that way by having great family, an easy ride and no anxiety.Being a good person is often about ratio – what-did-you-endure to what-did-you-pass-on. What-were-you-handed: what-did-you-make. Some people are handed two mothballs and a piece of string, and make things better in their corner of the universe.Your suffering and your anxiety gives you the ability to make your part of the world better, partly by seeing and meeting other souls, sometimes at their most vulnerable: at their most scared, most lonely, least sure of what’s going to happen.Admittedly, that kind of connection is not the same as getting numbers at bars. The fact that you are kind and thoughtful and responsible may not show up in digital spaces that prioritise facial structure or banter. So you might be down a few smooches. Smooches are great, don’t get me wrong – but compared to the depth of possible human connection, they are ultimately flotsam.But for that deeper connection, you don’t want to be attractive topeoplewrit large. You want to be attractive to the handful of peoplewith whom you’d be a good match.I can’t take away your uncertainty about whether you’ll find that person, I wish I could. But if you find them, you’ll find them in the spaces organised around your interests, and you’ll find them by beingyouon purpose, not by being a pastiche of other people’s ideas about a “man”, or a collage of your fears about yourself. You want to be loved foryou.You have been dealt a hard hand. It’s no wonder that you – like so many people right now – feel adrift and hungry for certainty.But it’s not about finding assurance and certainty. It’s about learning to live and make things better for other people, even without it.The reader’s letter has been edited for length and clarity.Ask Eleanor a questionShare your questionTell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.NameWhat is your question for Eleanor?Email addressYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.By submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreExplore more on these topicsAustralian lifestyleLeading questionsLonelinessHealth & wellbeingMenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Outright racist’ activist Daniel Thomas will face ‘full force of law’ over any crimes, says home secretary | Far right | The Guardian
description: Shabana Mahmood says she wants to distinguish between far-right extremism and legitimate local concerns over asylum sites
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Shabana Mahmood says she wants to distinguish between far-right extremism and legitimate local concerns over asylum sites
Content: Shabana Mahmood referred to ‘the far right and outright racists like Danny Thomas’ (above) whose behaviour was ‘completely unacceptable’.Photograph: Theo Shaw/PAView image in fullscreenShabana Mahmood referred to ‘the far right and outright racists like Danny Thomas’ (above) whose behaviour was ‘completely unacceptable’.Photograph: Theo Shaw/PAFar right‘Outright racist’ activist Daniel Thomas will face ‘full force of law’ over any crimes, says home secretaryShabana Mahmood says she wants to distinguish between far-right extremism and legitimate local concerns over asylum sitesRajeev SyalHome affairs editorThu 17 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShabana Mahmood has described the anti-asylum activist Daniel Thomas as “a far-right and outright racist” who will feel “the full force of the law” if his organisation commits crimes near contested asylum sites such as Piddington.In an interview with the Guardian, the home secretary also “wanted to reassure” concerned villagers that asylum seekers due to move in to a neighbouring former defence site would not “put pressure” on local resources because they would be given “self-contained facilities”.Her intervention came after Thomas, a convicted criminal known as “Danny Tommo” and the co-founder ofthe Patriot Platform, said thousands of his masked followers could descend “for days” on to the Oxfordshire village to prevent male asylum seekers being moved in.At the launch of a crackdown on knife crime inBirminghamon Thursday, Mahmood said she wanted to distinguish between legitimate concerns felt by Piddington residents over a large-scale asylum centre and extremists who were “hijacking” community concerns.“I understand the anxiety of local people when they’re about to see a change to their community. But it is important to distinguish that anxiety, where reasonable people can have a conversation, and the far right and outright racists like Danny Thomas walking into town, hijacking an issue and then using that to divide our communities,” she said.“Their behaviour is completely unacceptable. And where they break the law, they will face the full force of the law.”View image in fullscreenResidents of Piddington, Oxfordshire, voted overwhelmingly to become an independent state in a symbolic ‘referendum’.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAPiddington’s local populationregistered their oppositionto the proposed asylum facility on Wednesday, casting 285 votes against 26 in a symbolic ballot to leave the UK and seek self-determination.The parish has been approached by hundreds of other town and village councillors and residents for advice on replicating the campaign, which was backed by the Conservatives, Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats.Thomas visited Piddington the day after the vote. He was dressed in a grey suit and white shirt and was not accompanied by people wearing balaclavas.Joe Marshall, a parish councillor, said it was a private visit and Thomas was due to be given a tour of the village and a cup of tea by a resident.“It is a closed meeting. We will engage with them and walk them around the village and have a cup of tea,” he said. “We have also had an open invitation to Reform, Labour, Conservatives and Restore to visit.”Marshall said it was not clear that villagers would want security assistance from men in balaclavas, if it were offered. “This is a mild-mannered place,” he said.View image in fullscreenPiddington, Oxfordshire; MoD Bicester, the proposed site for the asylum camp, can be seen in the background.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAThomas visited the village hall briefly and later visited the entrance to the Ministry of Justice camp where the asylum seekers are scheduled to be housed. In an interview broadcast on YouTube with Dan Wootton, he said he had spoken to three residents.“The people we are meeting are just normal mothers, normal grandmothers, normal men,” Thomas said. “We have to start somewhere. Right now there are no men in that camp. We are going to put a legal, lawful plan in place to help this community in a way that has never been done before.”Asked how she would respond to Piddington residents after the vote, Mahmood said: “I want to reassure the residents of Piddington that actually our experience from other large sites where we already have, asylum seekers accommodated, whether that’s inWethersfieldorCrowborough, is that putting all facilities on to one site is actually the best way to manage pressures for local communities.“Our experience of other large sites where we are housing asylum seekers is that we’re able to put on that site more of the facilities that asylum seekers need. It’s a relatively self-contained facility, and the knock-on pressure to those local areas, I don’t think we’re going to see.”Mahmood said she understood the anxiety of people in the countryside towards large groups of asylum seekers, but she pointed out that many people in inner-city areas such as her Birmingham constituency had similar concerns.“I do understand the anxiety that people feel, when they’re about to see a change in their community or they are reading misinformation on the internet, or when they’re just concerned that a village is about to have a facility nearby that maybe they think may pose them some challenges,” she said.“I also hear that concern from communities such as mine, where there are large numbers of HMOs [houses of multiple occupation] and accommodation in which asylum seekers are held as well. There is concern across every type of community. Not just in the countryside or in those sorts of areas, but in inner-city areas as well.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenShabana Mahmood said she understood ‘the anxiety of local people when they’re about to see a change to their community’.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAWhat is Patriot Platform, the far-right group that descended on Dover and Portsmouth?Read moreThomas and his supportersrecently coordinateddisruptive protests in Dover and Portsmouth, where masked supporters blocked roads and attempted to intercept newly arrived people.On Thursday, Mahmood summoned police chiefs and urged them to improve their intelligence gathering and use all powers at their disposal, including new laws that allow for a blanket ban on face coverings at a designated location.Hampshire police then sought to impose the ban on Saturday asan anti-asylum demonstrationtook place in Thomas’s home town of Portsmouth. Thomas urged his supporters to stay away.A former bodyguard for Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known asTommy Robinson, Thomas established his anti-immigration movement after serving a prison sentence for attempted kidnapping.In an interview with Robinson, broadcast on Friday night, he said: “How powerful would it be if 5,000 men … surround the [Piddington] camp. We take tents. We sit there for days and we don’t let them [the asylum seekers] get in. And then we reinforce [the blockade] with members from the north, from Scotland, from Ireland.”In the interview, Thomas said he was not racist and welcomed people of other nationalities into his organisation. “Racism within our organisation is just not acceptable. That is the stance we have. We are not a white nationalist movement. I have friends that are black.”Thomas has been approached for comment.Mahmood made her comments as she launched an anti-knife crime programme. More than 230 areas affected by knife crime will share £26.25m to pay for police patrols, CCTV and early-prevention work as part of a knife-crime crackdown across 27 police forces in England and Wales.Each area, roughly the size of 10 football pitches, will receive more police patrols, alongside programmes designed for young people most at risk of being a victim or a perpetrator of knife crime. Action in small, targeted areas was the most effective way of driving down knife crime, the Home Office said.Mahmood launched the initiative at the Acocks Green boxing gym in south Birmingham, which plays a role in the local area in supporting vulnerable young people to stay away from crime. She was joined by the anti-knife campaignersLynne Baird, Lorraine Jones Burrell andPooja Kanda. Each has lost a child to knife crime.Additional reporting byAmelia GentlemanExplore more on these topicsFar rightShabana MahmoodImmigration and asylumOxfordshireBirminghamTommy RobinsonKnife crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Suspect in ‘Putney pusher’ case told family that investigation was ‘murdering him’ | London | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Sisters of Nicholas Brandram recount 44-year-old’s deteriorating mental health in days before he took his life
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Exclusive: Sisters of Nicholas Brandram recount 44-year-old’s deteriorating mental health in days before he took his life
Content: Brandram was arrested in June on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm, nine years after a jogger shoved a woman into the path of a bus in London.Photograph: Family handout/PAView image in fullscreenBrandram was arrested in June on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm, nine years after a jogger shoved a woman into the path of a bus in London.Photograph: Family handout/PALondonSuspect in ‘Putney pusher’ case told family that investigation was ‘murdering him’Exclusive: Sisters of Nicholas Brandram recount 44-year-old’s deteriorating mental health in days before he took his lifeEmine SinmazThu 17 Sep 2026 16.33 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 18.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDays before Nicholas Brandram, the man suspected of being the “Putney pusher”, killed himself, he told his family that the police investigation was “murdering him”.He had “no fight left” in him, he told his sisters, Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker, and could not see an end to the Metropolitan police investigation, or the online abuse.Brandram’s lawyers warned the Met last week that his mental health had deteriorated and he was receiving treatment in a psychiatric hospital after renewed press reporting that he had been released under investigation.“He said a couple of days ago that this investigation was murdering him. Day by day, he was slowly being murdered,” Hicks, 40, said through tears.“He saw no end to this investigation,” added Voelcker, 45. “My sister and I were keeping a close eye on him because he was telling us he couldn’t go on. He said it more than once in the week before, that he couldn’t keep going. All we could do was just reassure him. We had faith in the system, we had faith in the police, and they neglected him. They failed in their duty of care to him, to the wider family, and we do not want to see another family going through this.”The pair insisted that Brandram, 44,was not the “Putney pusher”and that he died thinking no one would believe in his innocence.He was arrested on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm on 15 June, nine years after a jogger shoved a woman headfirst into the path of an oncoming bus on Putney Bridge in south-west London.The case attracted considerable media attention but appeared to elude detectives, who wound down their investigation in 2018, after interviewing 50 men and arresting three suspects.But there was renewed interest in the case after Brandram’s arrest, which his family described as heavy-handed and disproportionate. A number of officers in body armour reportedly swooped on his home address, his sisters said, while a reporter who had been tipped off about the arrest filmed the ordeal.Although Brandram’s name was not published in the media because he had not been charged, his family said that biographical information in reports made him easily identifiable. He was described as a wealthy banker who lived in a £1.4m west London home and an army veteran with links to royalty. Brandram was the grandson of Princess Katherine of Greece, who was a great-granddaughter of Queen Victoria.View image in fullscreenFrom left to right: Nicholas Brandram, Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker as children.Photograph: Family handoutWhile in police custody in June over the Putney Bridge incident, he was also arrested on suspicion of possession of class A and class B drugs.His sisters said there was no forensic evidence linking Brandram to the Putney incident and that he had a prominent military tattoo and a withered calf which, they said, distinguished him from the man in footage of the attack on 5 May 2017.That morning, Brandram had walked from his home in Notting Hill Gate to his office in Bond Street and sent his sisters an email from his work account, which they said he could only access from his workplace. They said that evidence was passed on to the police.They added that Brandram had volunteered to take part in an identification parade and provided his DNA for comparison with a sample recovered at the time of the incident. Hicks said detectives told Brandram just days ago that they still did not know when the DNA analysis would be completed.“Our brother willingly provided DNA in an attempt to obviously help clear his name and to complete the investigation, and for weeks now we’ve been asking the police just to complete the DNA test,” Voelcker said.“We’ve always maintained that he’s innocent. He always maintained he was innocent. We just needed the police to complete their inquiry, and it just felt particularly egregious that they were just hanging this DNA test over him.”Hicks said as details of the case kept being reported in the press, her brother became preoccupied by online abuse on forums such as Reddit.“His reputation within a couple of days was in tatters. People saying he’s the alleged pusher, and you can imagine the vitriol that was coming out online,” Voelcker said.“You can imagine what people might say about somebody they think tried to push a woman in front of a bus. There was a lot of people had a lot of views about our brother, about his background, about where he worked.”“And the problem was he was reading it all every day,” Hicks said. “The vitriol is still there and that’s what’s so heartbreaking for us, is that when he took his own life he died thinking that effectively everyone hated him and thought he’d done something awful and that no one would see that he was innocent and he knew that his family were behind him but it wasn’t enough.”The sisters said Brandram had stayed with them in recent days after his mental health deteriorated following the publication of an update about the case that said he had been released under investigation.“He was really talking about ending his life and ending things. And he was very low and said he felt like he had no fight left in him. He couldn’t see the end,” Voelcker said.Brandram was admitted to a psychiatric hospital for six days before being discharged on Sunday.His family insisted the Met police were warned about his mental health.Voelcker tried to boost his mood on Tuesday by telling him it was a beautiful day and that he had many friends and his family supporting him. He wasfound dead at his home in Chiswick, west London,later that day.The family said their priority was to clear their brother’s name and “to ensure another family does not have to go through what we have as a result of the police delays and leaks to the media”.Hicks said: “Nick was really very loving, enthusiastic. He had an infectious character to be around, very funny. He was an extrovert, so he loved people. He was a much-loved father and uncle.”Voelcker added: “He spent a long time in the army before going into the city. And his reputation was important. He was a proud man. I think that’s the thing and even the fact that he needed to seek help from a psychiatric hospital was a big deal for him.”Ch Supt Dan Knowles, in charge of policing for south-west London, said: “Our thoughts are with Mr Brandram’s family and friends at this deeply distressing time. We recognise the significant impact his death will have on those who knew and loved him. We also understand the strain that being subject to a police investigation can place on individuals and their families.“The investigation remains ongoing. Following Mr Brandram’s release under investigation, it was made clear that inquiries would continue while officers progressed outstanding lines of inquiry and forensic examinations. This remains the position, and further investigative work is ongoing.“Investigations of this nature, particularly those involving complex evidential and forensic work, can take a number of months to complete as officers gather and assess all available evidence.”He added that the force had made a mandatory referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct on 16 September.In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsLondonMetropolitan policePolicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham: UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050 | Greenhouse gas emissions | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: PM, who is facing pressure over whether to approve North Sea oil and gasfields, makes strongest comments yet on issue
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Exclusive: PM, who is facing pressure over whether to approve North Sea oil and gasfields, makes strongest comments yet on issue
Content: Burnham: ‘I want Britain to believe in itself again.’Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenBurnham: ‘I want Britain to believe in itself again.’Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAGreenhouse gas emissionsAndy Burnham: UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050Exclusive: PM, who is facing pressure over whether to approve North Sea oil and gasfields, makes strongest comments yet on issueBritish people understand the climate crisis threat. Today I’m empowering them to tackle itUK politics live – latest updatesPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentThu 17 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 18.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050,Andy Burnhamhas argued in his strongest comments yet on the issue, saying it is no longer possible for Britons to believe they are not already affected by a changing climate.Writing for the Guardianabout new plans for a mass of community-led local green energy projects, the prime minister said the UK must “believe in itself”, and set out his determination to reach net zero targets, which have been rejected by the Conservatives and Reform UK.British people understand the climate crisis threat. Today I’m empowering them to tackle itRead moreThe tone marks a contrast to the summer, when Burnhamfaced criticismfor a seemingly muted response to the heatwaves, droughts and wildfires that affected the UK, with his main initiative being a ban on portable barbecues.“I am determined that we meet the commitment on whichLabourwas elected and reach net zero by 2050,” Burnham said. “I want Britain to believe in itself again.”Saying he wanted to connect local communities to green power projects – to reach net zero targets and make energy more affordable – Burnham said: “I am acutely aware that our changing climate is a major concern for many Britons, not least because we have just emerged from our hottest summer on record.”He went on: “Punishing heatwaves left nurses collapsing on hospital wards and bus drivers working in 40C cabs. Wildfires destroyed homes, leaving families with nothing. And more extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead.“The climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is here and with us now. The British people are no longer insulated from the consequences, and they do not want to be excluded from the solutions. They are looking for ways to do their bit. Community energy gives them that chance.”The issue is still a tricky one for Burnham, who is facing significant pressure from both sides over whether to approve the Jackdaw gasfield and Rosebank oilfield in the North Sea.A number of Labour MPs believe approving the projects would send a negative signal on climate efforts, and would provide a boost to the Greens, who argue that Labour is insufficiently serious in tackling the climate emergency.A seemingly imminent decision to approve Jackdawhas been delayeduntil later this autumn, prompting the Greens to accuse Labour of wanting to bury the issue before the high-profileHolborn and St Pancras byelection, where Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales, is challenging for the seat vacated by Keir Starmer.Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, had been poised to give her recommendation toapprove the field off the coast of Aberdeen, but it has been put off. Consultations on Jackdaw and Rosebank closed last month, with Fahnbulleh since considering her response.Approving either or both projects would place renewed pressure on Burnham over his commitment to net zero.No 10 officials point out that Burnham discussed the climate emergency in his first Commons statement as prime minister at the start of the month, andwhen he visitedStourbridge in the West Midlands in August after fires there. But in August, a series of climate organisationsaccused himof being silent about the subject during the heatwave.In his Guardian article, Burnham tied net zero plans to devolution, setting out funding for so-called people’s power projects, where communities will have a stake in local green energy projects, such as solar panels, windfarms and hydro schemes.He wrote: “Across Britain, people are taking back control of the things that matter to them: their pubs, their libraries, their leisure centres. Some have already done the same with energy. There are fine examples in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland of community energy schemes, which keep the lights on, the local economy moving and the benefits close to home.“These projects work and we want to take them nationwide … The climate crisis presents us with an enormous challenge and possibility. In the coming years, we need to change the way we travel, the way we build homes and the way we produce energy. I have long seen the green transition as the best chance we will ever have to reindustrialise Britain.”Explore more on these topicsGreenhouse gas emissionsAndy BurnhamOilFossil fuelsEnvironment policyEnergyClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Find a credible plan for British Steel, ministers told as ‘startling’ costs soar | British Steel | The Guardian
description: Government spending watchdog warns of ‘startling’ price of keeping publicly owned firm in business
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Government spending watchdog warns of ‘startling’ price of keeping publicly owned firm in business
Content: British Steel was taken into public ownership in July.Photograph: Darren Staples/ReutersView image in fullscreenBritish Steel was taken into public ownership in July.Photograph: Darren Staples/ReutersBritish SteelFind a credible plan for British Steel, ministers told as ‘startling’ costs soarGovernment spending watchdog warns of price of keeping publicly owned firm in businessAlex DanielThu 17 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLabour has been urged to lay out a credible plan for the future ofBritish Steel, as the government spending watchdog warned of the “startling” costs of keeping the struggling manufacturer in business with no end in sight.British Steel was taken into public ownership in July to protect “the future of steel production”, 15 months after the government stepped in to prevent the closure of its steelworks in Scunthorpe and the loss of 4,000 jobs.But it is costing £1.3m a day to keep the company running, with the total estimated cost reaching as much as £1.5bn by 2028. By mid-June, the government had spent £555m paying workers’ salaries and buying raw materials, excluding the cost of external advisers.The public accounts committee of MPs said on Friday that ministers were still “unable to articulate what business model” would put the company on a sustainable footing, nearly ayear and a half after taking control at Scunthorpe.It added that the Department for Business and Trade had not given “even indicative estimates” of how much British Steel would ultimately cost taxpayers or how long the situation would continue.Afternationalising British Steel,the government appointed new bosses to focus on stabilising the business.Clive Betts, the committee’s deputy chair, said the move to save the company was “all well and good”, but added: “This was just the beginning. Having brought British Steel onto the taxpayers’ books, it is now up to government to explain its plan for its future.“Unfortunately, beyond simply propping up the company with public money, the government was not able to outline such a plan to our inquiry. The reality is that British Steel is unable to wash its own face, and government is now in charge of making sure it gets on to a sustainable financial footing for the future.“We also require assurances that the startling levels of funding British Steel is currently receiving do not come at the expense of the wider sector.”The criticism came days after Labour alsonationalised Britain’s third-biggest producer of the metal,the Yorkshire-based Speciality Steel UK, in an attempt to protect 1,300 jobs.Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said at the time that the government did not “intervene in private companies lightly” but that the move was important to safeguard heavy industry.The public accounts committee said it showed the government could not “spend all its money supporting British Steel, when clearly there will be a need to support other parts of the industry”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt added: “[Taxpayers] remain exposed to significant and growing costs and uncertainty – it is not clear whether the money will ever be recovered.”The government should publish a plan for the company that included “options and analysis for the intended future production model and the role of British Steel in the UK economy; the preferred decarbonisation pathway; how the company will become financially sustainable; and the expected costs, funding sources and timetable”, the committee’s report said.The former owner Jingye has separately argued that British Steel owed it almost £1bn when it was nationalised and has started a formal process under an international treaty to win compensation from the government.The move has also put pressure on UK-Chinese relations, with China’s governmentsaying it is “strongly dissatisfied”with the situation.Explore more on these topicsBritish SteelSteel industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Addison Lee founder owes £20.5m in tax after UK tribunal ruling | HMRC | The Guardian
description: HMRC wins challenge over John Griffin’s claim to be non-dom despite having lived in England since childhood
Author: Patrick Daly
Headline: HMRC wins challenge over John Griffin’s claim to be non-dom despite having lived in England since childhood
Content: John Griffin pictured in 2012. He was born to Irish parents in 1942 and briefly lived there until he moved to London at the age of nine.Photograph: Felix ClayView image in fullscreenJohn Griffin pictured in 2012. He was born to Irish parents in 1942 and briefly lived there until he moved to London at the age of nine.Photograph: Felix ClayHMRCAddison Lee founder owes £20.5m in tax after UK tribunal rulingHMRC wins challenge over John Griffin’s claim to be non-dom despite having lived in England since childhoodPatrick DalyThu 17 Sep 2026 17.04 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 17.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe founder of Addison Lee owes £20.5m in tax after a tribunal dismissed a claim that he should be treated as a nom-dom despite living in the UK since childhood.John Griffin had argued he should be treated as a nom-dom due to his connection toIreland, saying: “I was and am besotted with Ireland, infatuated with Ireland. I believe that I have always been and am Irish.”HM Revenue and Customs challenged the domicile status on Griffin’s self-assessment tax returns from 2013 to 2020, which would have allowed the 84-year-old to not pay UK tax rates on foreign earnings kept outside the country.This week, a London tribunal ruled in the tax authority’s favour.Billionaire Chris Rokos, who paid £330m in tax last year, to quit UKRead moreGriffin was born to Irish parents in 1942 and briefly lived there until he moved to London at the age of nine, according to tribunal documents.HMRC argued thatEnglandshould be considered Griffin’s home, with the businessman raising a family in Hertfordshire and building his London-based taxi empire, having founded Addison Lee in 1975.Tribunal judge Michaela Snelders and tribunal member Gill Hunter said: “We are satisfied that by 5 April 2013, Sir John had settled in England in every meaningful sense.”“England was where he had established his home, raised his family, built his business, accumulated his wealth and organised his personal, social and professional life.“Although he retained a powerful emotional attachment to Ireland and a genuine hope that he might one day spend more time there, those sentiments never crystallised into a sufficiently definite intention to make Ireland his permanent home.”View image in fullscreenThe ruling reflects the period after John Griffin sold Addison Lee to a private equity firm in 2013. The business was reported to be worth £300m at the time.Photograph: Felix ClayThe tax chamber tribunal was told Griffin spent eight nights in Ireland in 2015, one of the years he claimed to be domiciled there, which the chamber ruled was “inconsistent with someone seriously preparing for permanent relocation”.As part of his appeal against HMRC’s stance, Griffin had argued that his domicile should be the same as his father, Jack, who had come to England from Ireland in search of work in 1935. Under UK law, a child’s domicile is the same as their father’s if the parents were married at the time of their birth.Legal counsel for HMRC, however, said Griffin’s domicile status under UK law would have changed when his father’s domicile of choice became England. They argued it had done so some time before Griffin reached adulthood at the age of 21 in 1963. The tribunal agreed with HMRC’s stance.The ruling caps off a long-running inquiry into Griffin’s tax affairs and reflects the period after hesold Addison Leeto private equity firm the Carlyle Group in 2013. The business was reported to be worth £300m at the time.Having Irish domicile would have potentially allowed Griffin to avoid being taxed on earnings made outside the UK, a legal benefit of being classified as a nom-dom. The tribunal’s ruling makes his worldwide income from the period subject to UK tax rules, with HMRC calculating that he owes an additional £20.5m covering the seven-year period.Nom-dom status was scrapped by the Labour UK government in April 2025, after a promise a year earlier by Rishi Sunak’s Conservative administration to do the same.Griffin, knighted in 2024 for services to business and charity, did not give evidence in person to the tribunal after HMRC accepted he was not medically fit to do so due to “cognitive decline”.Explore more on these topicsHMRCIrelandSelf-assessment taxEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: US passenger duct-taped to plane seat says: ‘I don’t remember any of it’ | Baltimore | The Guardian
description: After being read charges, Layne Lundeen said: ‘I assaulted a police officer? Is that what it says? I don’t have my glasses’
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: After being read charges, Layne Lundeen said: ‘I assaulted a police officer? Is that what it says? I don’t have my glasses’
Content: Layne Arthur Lundeen was secured to his seat with duct tape.Photograph: Courtesy Richard O'LenickView image in fullscreenLayne Arthur Lundeen was secured to his seat with duct tape.Photograph: Courtesy Richard O'LenickBaltimoreUS passenger duct-taped to plane seat says: ‘I don’t remember any of it’After being read charges, Layne Lundeen said: ‘I assaulted a police officer? Is that what it says? I don’t have my glasses’Maya YangThu 17 Sep 2026 12.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 14.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn American Airlines passenger who was duct-taped to his seat following an alleged outburst including racial and homophobic slurs said that he does not recall the incident.On 3 September, 67-year old Layne Lundeen was restrained in his first-class seat with duct tape and zip ties over alleged unruly behavior. The American Airline Flight 618 was originally traveling from Dallas,Texas, to Newark,New Jersey, and was diverted to the Baltimore/Washington Thurgood Marshall airport in an emergency landing.Upon landing, authorities arrested Lundeen and charged him with second-degree assault and disorderly conduct.US real estate agent duct-taped and zip-tied to plane seat after ‘racial slurs’ is firedRead moreIn a court hearing the following day, Lundeen said, “I don’t remember any of what happened,” according to a recordingrecently reviewedby the Baltimore Banner.The outlet added that after being read his charges, Lundeen said: “I assaulted a police officer? Is that what it says? I don’t have my glasses.”He added: “Oh my god, what a mess … I don’t remember any of it.”The Guardian has reached out to Lundeen’s lawyer for comment.Speaking to ABC following the incident, Juan Mejia, a former law enforcement officer and one of the flight’s passengers who helped restrain Lundeen,saidthat he had allegedly “made derogatory remarks to the staff of American Airlines and other passengers – racial slurs, vulgar language, very offensive to the women.”Another passenger, Richard Olenick,toldCNN that Lundeen had allegedly also tried to hit the passenger next to him, as well as a woman who tried to intervene. Olenick, who also helped restrain Lundeen in his seat using duct tape, told the outlet: “Physically it lessened his ability to move for sure, but it did not solve the issue. He was still pushing and resisting and trying to get up.”American Airlines has also issued a statement,saying: “The safety ​and ​security ​of our customers ​and team members ​is our top ​priority and ​we ​do not ​tolerate violence. We thank our ​team members for ​their ​professionalism ​and ​our customers ​for ​their ​understanding.”Meanwhile, Lundeen’s former employer, Long Realty in Tucson, Arizona, said in a Facebook statement that it had “ended its affiliation” with him.“Long Realty is aware of reports concerning criminal charges filed against a former affiliated real estate agent arising from an incident that allegedly occurred during a commercial flight. Upon learning of the incident, Long Realty promptly ended its affiliation with the individual. The individual is no longer associated with or authorized to represent Long Realty in any capacity,” the companysaid.Explore more on these topicsBaltimoreAir transportTexasNew JerseyMarylandUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Charles sounded ‘giddily elated’ after Diana’s death, claims Earl Spencer  | Monarchy | The Guardian
description: In latest extracts from upcoming memoir, Diana’s brother suggests some in Buckingham Palace were ‘relieved’ at her death
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: In latest extracts from upcoming memoir, Diana’s brother suggests some in Buckingham Palace were ‘relieved’ at her death
Content: Earl Spencer claims Buckingham Palace wanted William, Harry and himself to walk behind Diana’s coffin to protect Charles from potential abuse.Photograph: Fiona Hanson/PAView image in fullscreenEarl Spencer claims Buckingham Palace wanted William, Harry and himself to walk behind Diana’s coffin to protect Charles from potential abuse.Photograph: Fiona Hanson/PAMonarchyCharles sounded ‘giddily elated’ after Diana’s death, claims Earl SpencerIn latest extracts from upcoming memoir, Diana’s brother suggests some in Buckingham Palace were ‘relieved’ at her deathCaroline DaviesThu 17 Sep 2026 14.47 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe brother of the lateDiana, Princess of Wales, has claimed in published extracts of his new memoir that King Charles sounded “giddily elated – like a lottery winner” in a phone call to him immediately after her death.Earl Spencer also says he believed Buckingham Palace wanted William and Harry and himself to walk behind Diana’s coffin because the then prince was “adamant” he was going to walk and palace officials feared “members of the public might shout abuse at him”.By getting Diana’s sons to walk, “that would surely guarantee against insults flying”, he wrote.View image in fullscreenCharles Spencer’s book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published next week.Photograph: Penguin Random House/ReutersThe memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, due to be published next week, has already madeheadlines, with Spencer alleging that during a heated phone call before Diana’s funeral, the king remarked: “rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough.”Buckingham Palace issued a robust rebuttal on Wednesday evening, saying in a statement: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”In new extracts, published on Thursday on the website of theDaily Mail, which is serialising the book, Spencer suggests that some inside Buckingham Palace were “relieved – indeed pleased” at Diana’s death in a Paris car crash. It was his suspicion that Charles’s first reaction must have been to think how he could now marry Camilla Parker Bowles.According to Spencer, Diana had confided in a friend that days before their wedding, Charles had told her “she needed to know he was very happy to marry her, but he was not actually in love with her”, and she was certain he was “entering their marriage with his heart elsewhere”.View image in fullscreenDiana and Charles pictured in March 1981, before they got married.Photograph: PADiana tried to break off the engagement after finding a bracelet Charles had bought for Camilla, who is now the queen, he writes.
