But their father was “appalled”, telling her “it was impossible to pull out of such an enormous commitment at that point”.Spencer says in the book that he also believes Charles may have contributed to the princess’s eating disorder, saying Diana’s waist shrank from 29in to 23.5in between the engagement and wedding after she was “devastated” at her fiance squeezing her waist and saying: “Oh, a bit chubby here, aren’t we?”He was also convinced Diana had ADHD and, like himself, suffered from Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria. He writes: “It is a sad fact that, in her later years, Diana drove herself more than once to Beachy Head, the highest chalk sea cliff in England, while contemplating ending it all. Her love for her sons stopped her from going further.”The excerpt goes on to say that Diana told him she was going to get divorced and that “my husband is in love with his valet”.Spencer, 62, has said he wrote the memoir to correct “untruths” told about his elder sister.The row over the book overshadowed a busy day for the royal family, with the Duke of Sussex also entering the mix with an engagement of his own.Harry, who it is understood was aware of his uncle’s book in advance but not its contents, arrived at the inaugural Invictus Spirit awards in London on Thursday evening in his first appearance since returning to the UK from the US last month.Harry was joined by, among others, the comedian James Corden, singers Jess Glynne and Sonique, rugby star James Haskell and actor Ross Kemp for the champagne reception and fundraiser at the Old Naval College in Greenwich, south London.The evening was to recognise those who have beaten the odds, supported others in their recovery, advanced sport and rehabilitation or made an outstanding contribution to the wider Invictus community.Giving a speech at the awards, Harry recalled how Invictus had begun.He said: “In 2008, flying home from Afghanistan, I travelled alongside three seriously injured British servicemen and the coffin of a Danish soldier.“That flight stayed with me because it helped me begin to understand two things about the military that would shape the rest of my life: it gives you purpose, identity, belonging, a team; and, in a matter of seconds, injury or illness can take it all away.“Years later, after seeing the Warrior Games in America, we brought an idea back to London. In September 2014, more than 400 competitors from 13 nations came together for the first ever Invictus games. Now, 12 years later, thousands have benefited. We have 26 nations in our community, and the games are coming home.”View image in fullscreenAmid the row over his uncle’s book, the Duke of Sussex made his first public appearance since returning to the UK from the US last month.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAThe Prince and Princess of Wales were on their first official trip to the Isle of Bute off the west coast of Scotland. The couple, who hold the titles of Duke and Duchess of Rothesay in Scotland, visited the namesake town of Rothesay, dropped in at a shinty club and stopped at a pub while meeting community leaders and volunteers.Charles, meanwhile, was appearing in public for the first time since Spencer’s allegations were aired, at an AI summit he had convened at Dumfries House, in Ayrshire. Addressing global tech leaders, he warned of the “existential dangers” of AI systems falling into the wrong hands.As those who have created these technologies had warned, AI risked “developing darker capacities – perhaps even to take life”, he said. The king spoke of the need for reassurance that “our humanity remains sacred” and “that we will not lose control of our destiny, or our souls”.Explore more on these topicsMonarchyDiana, Princess of WalesKing Charles IIIPrince HarryAutobiography and memoirDaily MailnewsShareReuse this content

title: New cat species identified for first time in more than a century in Bolivia | Bolivia | The Guardian
description: New species of wild cat was discovered in Bolivia’s Yungas forest and is smaller than the average domestic ⁠cat
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: New species of wild cat was discovered in Bolivia’s Yungas forest and is smaller than the average domestic ⁠cat
Content: Researcher Paola Nogales Ascarrunz observes the cat at an animal refuge in the Yungas region in Bolivia on 1 September 2026.Photograph: Fernando Faciole/National Geographic/ReutersView image in fullscreenResearcher Paola Nogales Ascarrunz observes the cat at an animal refuge in the Yungas region in Bolivia on 1 September 2026.Photograph: Fernando Faciole/National Geographic/ReutersBoliviaNew cat species identified for first time in more than a century in BoliviaNew species of wild feline was discovered in Bolivia’s Yungas forest that is smaller than the average domestic ⁠catReutersThu 17 Sep 2026 16.43 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 18.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia’s ⁠cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living feline species has been formally named and described in more than a century.The cat, called tilcayo by local communities, is part of a group called tiger ⁠cats found across much of South ⁠America. It was found in Bolivia’s ​lush Yungas forest, a mountainous region where forests are often covered by clouds and surrounded by high humidity, according to researchers. It measures about 18in (46cm) long and weighs about 3lb (1.4kg), making it smaller than the average domestic ⁠cat.Researchers used genetic data to confirm that the cat is a new species, and gave it the scientific nameLeopardus tilcayo, retaining its local name.View image in fullscreenALeopardus tilcayocat at the Senda Verde animal refuge in the Yungas region of Bolivia on 1 September 2026.Photograph: Fernando Faciole/National Geographic/Reuters“Its fur is light brown … with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body,” said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer and one of the authors ⁠of the study describing the newly identified species published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology.Little is yet known about the cat’s biology and lifestyle. Remains of small rodents in scat ​samples suggest they may form part of its diet, while camera-trap evidence indicates it ‌could be more active at night, Nogales-Ascarrunz said.Tiger ‌cats are so-called cryptic species, meaning they cannot easily be distinguished merely by appearance, said evolutionary biologist and study co-lead author Jonas Lescroart of the University of Antwerp in Belgium.Tiger ‌cats previously had been considered a single species, but genetic studies decades ago suggested the existence of multiple species.View image in fullscreenA tilcayo cat, the only known individual of the newly identified species living in protective captivity.Photograph: Fernando Faciole/National Geographic/ReutersReferring to the new species, Lescroart said: “Our information at this moment is limited to the two live individuals that we examined, and a small number of camera-trap records.”One of the live cats is a 10-year-old male that now lives in the Senda Verde wildlife sanctuary in Bolivia after being kept by a local family in their home.Observing the Bolivian cat drew interest because “its characteristics did not match the descriptions, most of them based on Brazilian cats”, Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “This made us wonder: what tiger cat do we actually have in Bolivia?”The team analysed DNA from 38 cats sampled across several South ‌American countries, including eight museum specimens. The study found that tiger cats are in fact five genetically distinct species.“We never expected this Bolivian tiger cat to be a separate species, and no one had ever proposed it as a different animal, subspecies or otherwise,” Lescroart said.Genetic analysis suggested ​that the tilcayo lineage separated from other tiger cats about 1.4m years ago.“The more differences in their DNA, the longer the time that we estimate those lineages to have been physically separated,” Lescroart said, adding that such a gap is generally considered a species-level divide in cats.The research team also described a new tiger cat subspecies in Peru’s Yungas region, naming itLeopardus tigrinus antisuyoafter Antisuyu, the region of the old Inca empire that included the area it inhabits.The International Union forConservationof Nature (IUCN) red list tracking the status of species currently treats ⁠tiger cats as two “vulnerable” species with declining populations.The researchers have shared their findings with the IUCN, whose upcoming review will assess ​the five lineages separately. That could give a more accurate picture ​of risk, Lescroart said, and species such as the tilcayo ​could be considered endangered when assessed on their own.The need for a clearer assessment is particularly acute in the Yungas, one of the ​region’s most threatened ecosystems.The mountain forests ‌face growing pressure from deforestation, agricultural ​expansion, human-caused fires and mining, Nogales-Ascarrunz said. ​Restoring forest patches damaged by fires, protecting remaining native forest and maintaining connections between habitats are urgent priorities, she added.“Showing the general public that even in a flagship group such as cats … there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message,” said Eduardo Eizirik, an evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil and senior author of the study. “There are many undiscovered species out there in the world, and they are at risk of disappearing before we even discover them.”Explore more on these topicsBoliviaWildlifeEndangered speciesIUCN red list of endangered speciesPeruBiodiversityConservationnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Forcing a reckoning’: How Asia is preparing for a ‘supersized’ El Niño | El Niño southern oscillation | The Guardian
description: From Sri Lanka to South Korea, governments are preparing for droughts, wildfires, typhoons and floods – with climate plans facing their biggest challenge to date
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: From Sri Lanka to South Korea, governments are preparing for droughts, wildfires, typhoons and floods – with climate plans facing their biggest challenge to date
Content: Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to hit a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027.Photograph: Aditya Aji/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to hit a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027.Photograph: Aditya Aji/AFP/Getty ImagesEl Niño southern oscillation‘Forcing a reckoning’: How Asia is preparing for a ‘supersized’ El NiñoFrom Sri Lanka to South Korea, governments are preparing for droughts, wildfires, typhoons and floods – with climate plans facing their biggest challenge to dateOliver Holmes,Hannah Ellis-Petersenin Delhi,Raphael Rashidin Seoul,Justin McCurryin Tokyo, andDanny Vincentin Hong KongThu 17 Sep 2026 19.57 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 20.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAsian governments are rushing preparations for the most severe El Niño weather event on record, with hundreds of millions of people bracing for multiple crises at once as extreme heat, heavy rain and food shortages hit the region.Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to grow to a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027.The World Food Programme has warned that about 50 million people will probably be pushedinto acute hungerdue to the exceptionally intenseweather system, while UN secretary-general António Guterressaidthis month that El Niño was “being supersized before our eyes”.Here are the steps countries in Asia are taking to prepare for El Niño:‘Climate risk maps’ in ChinaView image in fullscreenA man sits in the shade to avoid the heat in Seoul, South Korea.Photograph: Lee Jin-man/APInHong Kong, authorities have already been forced to revise workplace policies, after the city experienced its hottest day on record on 9 August. During times of extreme heat, companies are expected to reschedule work, provide cooling equipment and rest breaks for their employees.Employers in the international financial hub could even face prosecution if they fail to provide staff with support at times of sweltering heat.In mainlandChinaa 100-day campaign has been launched to prepare for extreme weather and help safeguard harvests against the opposing extremes of drought and intense rainfall.Beijing has plans to upgrade early warning monitoring systems, and in July, it launched a national plan encouraging cities to draw up ‘climate risk maps’ to help identify areas most vulnerable to flooding and severe heat.View image in fullscreenPedestrians shield under umbrellas as they cross the street under scorching heat in Taipei, Taiwan.Photograph: Ritchie B Tongo/EPATaiwan, meanwhile, is treating the predicted extreme weather as an emergency situation, and preparing using methods similar to what it would do to train for a terrorist attack or earthquake. In early September, the island nation held a mass exercise simulating three consecutive days of temperatures above 40C. Hundreds of people took part in the field exercises, which simulated power and water disruption, rail problems, air conditioner failure and mass heatstroke.The government has also been testing its “Cool Map” online platform, which helps to direct vulnerable people to airconditioned and cool spaces.Sri Lanka plans to process salterwaterEl Niño is already wreaking havoc across south Asia; in parts ofIndiathere has been a shortfall of monsoon rainfall of almost 50% in September, with knock-on effects on key crops such as rice, pulses, cotton and maize. Concerns are mounting that there could be a diminished harvest in the coming months, likely driving up food prices – already crippling for poor and lower middle class families.View image in fullscreenKashmiri farmers work in a paddy field during the harvest season on the outskirts of Srinagar, the summer capital of Indian Kashmir.Photograph: Farooq Khan/EPAThe Indian government has taken a hyper-vigilant approach to establish what the agriculture minister, Shivraj Singh Chouhan, described as a “protective shield for farmers”.In more than 350 vulnerable districts authorities are boosting water conservation infrastructure and water harvesting, and are encouraging farmers to plant low-water, short duration crops – such as pulses and millets.But the most intense impact of El Niño in the area is inSri Lanka, where the absence of rainfall and high temperatures have become so severe that the country is experiencing its worst drought in a decade. More than 160,000 people are now facing a drinking water shortage as several key reservoirs run dry.Officials have been forced to close the tourist areas of the Yala national park, home to leopards, elephants, crocodiles and spotted deer, and have been bringing in tankers of water to fill the ponds to make sure the animals do not die. In Mullaithivu lagoon, in the north-east of Sri Lanka, thousands of fish were found dead due to the lack of fresh water.View image in fullscreenA villager digs a hole in a dried-out riverbed to collect water to take a bath in Ampara district, Sri Lanka.Photograph: Priyanshu Singh/ReutersThe country’s disaster management centre is preparing for a situation in which freshwater supplies could vanish. “If water sources dry up, there will be no alternative means of obtaining water,” an official said. Colombo would then be forced to process salt water from the sea, although relying on the country’s one desalination plant is not considered workable.How El Niño shifts weather patterns across AsiaTackling an agriculture crisis in south-east AsiaIn south-east Asia, El Niño is compounded by a series of ongoing crises. The Iran war has already disrupted global energy and supply chains and inflated fertiliser costs,disproportionately hitting the region. At the same time, severe haze from seasonal fires across Malaysia and Indonesia has choked cities and is damaging plants and trees.During the 2023–2024 El Niño, south-east Asian governments successfully cushioned agricultural impacts by adjusting planting calendars and managing water, but those strategies will be insufficient to deal with the scale of the crisis, experts warn. Regional rice yields are already projected to fall by 8 to 10%.View image in fullscreenA forest fire breaks out on Mount Bromo in East Java, Indonesia.Photograph: Ali Lutfi/NurPhoto/Shutterstock“We can’t just assume that this El Niño is going to be the same as the last because there are so many challenges that have been stacking on top of each other,” says Elyssa Kaur Ludher, a climate and food security expert based in Singapore.The Philippines, Malaysia andIndonesiaare particularly vulnerable to food price changes, says Kaur Ludher, a visiting fellow with the Climate Change for Southeast Asia Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.“In Singapore, most of our income is not spent on food. It’s under 10%. But for Indonesians, it can be up to 50% or even more as a proportion of income spent on food. So any price rise affects them disproportionately.”With the potential for price rises to leave people desperate and angry, Kaur Ludher has argued for food security to be reframed as a national security issue. In Indonesia and the Philippines in particular, she said, social stability depends a lot on food prices. “Rice is a lifeline to this region,” she says.View image in fullscreenAn Indonesian firefighter works to extinguish wildfires in South Sumatra, Indonesia.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesTo prepare, south-east Asian governments and farmer cooperatives are promoting regenerative agriculture and shifting toward biofertilisers.“We have come to a stage where climate change is putting so much pressure on us – on our existing, already crumbling or structurally unsound, systems,” say Kaur Ludher. “Nature will force us to have a reckoning.”South Korea overhauls its heatwave alert systemSouth Korea saw the driest July on record in the country’s south-east. Weeks later came a freak reversal, as a weakening storm system dragged in a deluge that dumped some of the heaviest rainfall ever recorded at a Korean weather station. The heat was so intense that farmers described spoilt potatoesas being “boiled” in the ground.The country’s weather agency has overhauled its heatwave alert system for the first time in 18 years, adding a top tier that triggers official guidance to stop non-emergency outdoor work once feels-like temperatures hit 38C. Nationwide, phones have buzzed for weeks with government alerts urging people to stay indoors during the hottest hours.View image in fullscreenA weather forecast map of the temperatures across South Korea is shown by an officer from the Korea Meteorological Administration in Seoul.Photograph: Lee Jin-man/APOfficials are watching out for a rough autumn, with seas around the Korean peninsula remaining unusually warm for the season and forecasters expecting the north-west Pacific to produce far more powerful storms than usual this year, since a strengthening El Niño is weakening the high pressure that has so far kept them away.Japan prepares for ‘cruelly’ hot days and typhoonsJapan is also bracing for the arrival of so-called super-typhoons, which experts attribute to a combination of El Niño and human-induced global heating.El Niño was once associated with slightly cooler summers in Japan. But rising sea surface temperatures mean it is having the opposite effect, blanketing many parts of the country in record-breaking heat and humidity in 2023-4, the last time the weather pattern materialised.Japanrecorded its first official “cruelly hot day”– orkokushobi– in July, just after the start of the current El Niño event. The Japanese term, introduced in April to underscore the threat to health posed by rising temperatures, refers to days when the mercury exceeds 40C.Now, as the summer heat dissipates, the country is bracing for the arrival of potentially destructive typhoons.View image in fullscreenPeople carry umbrellas to shield themselves from the sun as they walk across an intersection in Tokyo.Photograph: Kiichiro Sato/APThe public is encouraged to take measures to protect themselves and their homes, such as heeding official evacuation warnings and stocking up on food and water. People living in apartments are urged to secure or bring inside flower pots and furniture – anything that could become a dangerous flying object during a storm.This month the infrastructure ministry said it had identified several high-risk underpasses on national highways that would be closed preemptively during heavy rain. Underpasses – which allow cars to travel beneath other roads or railway lines – became a focus of concern last month after two trapped motorists drownedduring record-breaking rainin Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo.Yu-chen Li contributed to this articleExplore more on these topicsEl Niño southern oscillationExtreme weatherSouth and central AsiaIndonesiaAsia PacificClimate crisisSri LankafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Balletic hits and bicycle kicks: Teqball comes of age at the Asian Games | Sport | The Guardian
description: Invented a little over a decade ago in Hungary, teqball is a combination between soccer and ping pong
Author: Natasha May
Headline: Invented a little over a decade ago in Hungary, teqball is a combination between soccer and ping pong
Content: Suphawadi Wongkhamchan (L) kicks the ball with an acrobatic gesture during Teqball World Series Madrid at Plaza de España on 26 May, 2024 in Madrid, Spain.Photograph: Eurasia Sport Images/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSuphawadi Wongkhamchan (L) kicks the ball with an acrobatic gesture during Teqball World Series Madrid at Plaza de España on 26 May, 2024 in Madrid, Spain.Photograph: Eurasia Sport Images/Getty ImagesSportBalletic hits and bicycle kicks: Teqball comes of age at the Asian GamesInvented a little over a decade ago in Hungary, teqball is a combination of football and ping pongNatasha Mayin BangkokThu 17 Sep 2026 19.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 20.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn Bangkok’s Sports Science Centre, Jutatip Kuntatong is airborne, executing a gravity-defying bicycle kick that slams the ball on to the curved table with a force that echoes throughout the gym.She is preparing to representThailandat the Asian Games, which start on Saturday, but six years ago she had never even heard of teqball, the sport of which she is now the world champion.“I had no idea at all what sport is this,” the 28-year-old says on the sidelines of the team’s training session. “I just said yes.”After taking out the singles and doubles titles at the most recent world championships in Transylvania in December, she is now the No 1-ranked woman in the world in the nascent sport.Winning Teqball shots“It feels like a dream because everything happened so fast,” Jutatip says. However, it is not just her 151cm stature which helps her achieve the acrobatic feats that have powered her success. Many of her signature moves come from a centuries-old south-east Asian sport that has given the Thai team its edge: Sepak takraw, often called “foot volleyball”, which has long been popular in south-east AsiaTeqball was invented a little over a decade ago in Hungary, when two friends started playing football on a ping pong table, before going on to create the signature curved table the game is played on.The new sport is quickly entering the mainstream. This weekend it will debut at the Asian Games in Japan, after its historic inclusion at the European and African games, with ambitions to be an Olympic sport by 2032.Teams from 16 nations will be competing at the competition, which will also debut padel and virtual taekwondo,a non-contact sport using virtual reality headsets.View image in fullscreenFor feature on the new sport “Teqball”. The Thai national team are the strongest country in the sport at the moment. Jutatip Kuntatong -  No. 1 ranked woman Teqball player, 2025 World Champion for both women’s single and doubles category.Photograph: Natasha May/The GuardianTeqball is scored like ping pong – with matches made up of singles or doubles games. Players may hit a standard soccer ball with any part of their body except their hands. They are allowed a maximum of three touches before returning the ball to the opponent, with no player allowed to use the same body part consecutively.The rule banning use of the same body part makes the sport “very intricate”, says László Vajda, the secretary general of the International Teqball Federation.Vajda says that of the 147 national federations around the world, Thailand is the strongest nation at the moment.The Hungarian inventors of teqball introduced it as a mix of table tennis and football, but Thai audiences see in the game an entirely different sport.View image in fullscreenMyanmar athletes warm up during the Teqball event on day three of the 6th Asian Beach Games on April 25, 2026 in Sanya, China.Photograph: Lintao Zhang/Getty Images“We reckon that it’s not football – the skills and the way you use the moves is more like sepak takraw, says association secretariat of the Teqball Association of Thailand major general Piyapat Jarunpong.Like teqball, sepak takraw is played without the use of hands or arms – relying heavily on leg strength and controlling the ball through kicks.So when Thailand decided to take up the new sport, they called upon players like Jutatip who had been training for years in sepak takraw.Somsak “Joe” Duangmuang, the national Teqball team’s coach, was a sepak takraw coach for over 20 years, and a former national sepak takraw team player himself.“It’s quite exciting for me, that I see an opportunity to bring a new challenge to our athletes. It’s expanded a new area of training with the skills that we have,” Somsak says.An extended Teqball rallyLike most sports, different styles are emerging based on national features, László Vajda says.“In Brazil, it’s a lot of chest and head. In central Europe – especially Romania, Hungary, Poland – because of local sports, it’s a lot of side smashes,” he says.“In Asia, especially south-east Asia, because of sepak takraw, you have a lot of bicycle kick when they jump up backwards, and they smash with their feet up.View image in fullscreenThe Thai national team are the strongest in the sport. Jutatip Kuntatong (L) and Suphawadi Wongkhamchan (R). Together they won the 2025 World Teqball Championship’s women’s doubles category.Photograph: Natasha May/The Guardian“Africa and the Middle East it’s very athletic – amazing jumps and very technical, very football-ish.“It’s quite amazing to see when for example there is a Brazil/Thailand, or a Serbia/Thailand game very, very different styles clash,” Vajda says.The Thai association hopes the Asian Games will present an opportunity for more people in the region to learn about the sport, which will aid the association’s goal to get recruit more younger players.Piyapat says: “It’s quite a big step forward. It’s a huge leap, to be honest.”Explore more on these topicsSportThailandAsia PacificfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Bank of England is shaking up its bond sales – why does it matter? | Quantitative easing | The Guardian
description: The UK central bank has announced shakeup of its bond sales programme as it unwinds massive balance sheet
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: The UK central bank has announced shakeup of its bond sales programme as it unwinds massive balance sheet
Content: The Bank is selling off hundreds of billions of pounds worth of government bonds it bought via the emergency policy of quantitative easing during the financial crises and Covid.Photograph: Bank of England/PAView image in fullscreenThe Bank is selling off hundreds of billions of pounds worth of government bonds it bought via the emergency policy of quantitative easing during the financial crises and Covid.Photograph: Bank of England/PAQuantitative easingExplainerThe Bank of England is shaking up its bond sales – why does it matter?What the plan to sell £146bn in gilts back to the Treasury means for the public financesBank of England holds interest ratesBurnham’s talk of ‘breathing space’ at odds with reality of future rate risesHeather StewartEconomics editorThu 17 Sep 2026 11.45 EDTFirst published on Thu 17 Sep 2026 11.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMixed in with the Bank of England’s decision on Thursday tohold interest rates at 3.75%was a surprise announcement that it was shaking up its programme of quantitative tightening.So why is this apparently arcane change to QT important, and what does it mean for the public finances?What is QT?It is the Bank of England’s controversial process of selling off hundreds of billions of pounds worth of government bonds that it bought via the emergency policy of quantitative easing (QE) during the financial crises of 2008 and Covid.The Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) sees QT as the necessary unwinding of the massive balance sheet it built up. Its stockpile of bonds, known as gilts, has already been reduced from a peak of £895bn in February 2022, to £488bn.But critics on the right and left have complained that selling off significant quantities of government bonds costs the Treasury, as they are being sold at a loss.There have also been concerns that ina febrile bond market, large-scale sell-offs risk depressing prices – and thus driving up the yield, or interest rate, the government has to pay to borrow.What is the Bank looking to change?Instead of looking for private-sector buyers for its stock of gilts, the Bank plans to sell them directly to the Treasury instead.The Treasury’s debt management office (DMO), which has the job of doing the government’s borrowing for it, will then issue new bonds to cover the costs of those it has bought from the Bank.The Treasury sees this as simplifying what can be a messy process. As the chancellor, John Healey, put it in a letter to the Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey, on Thursday: “This sales model … would see a return to a single public-sector supplier of gilts to the market.”It also has the advantage of allowing the DMO to tailor gilt sales to market demand, which currently favour gilts that mature over a shorter period, rather than the Bank having to sell off the 20- and 30-year dated gilts it still has on its books, for which there is less investor appetite.The yield, effectively the interest rate, on 30-year gilts dropped sharply on Thursday after the decision was announced, to 5.745% – and was on course for its biggest drop since 2020.No final decision has been made, however, despite the fact the Treasury, Bank and DMO have apparently been discussing the idea for a year. Healey has promised to make a final ruling in April – and until then, QT will be paused.Wasn’t QT already being slowed down?Yes. The Bank has run down its stock of giltsby £70bn this year. That included £20bn of actual sales; and another £50bn worth that reached their maturity date.Over the coming years, it plans to sell off £20bn of government bonds annually, alongside retiring gilts that reach maturity.That’s because the Bank is keen to avoid the risks of exacerbatingalready-fragile bond markets. The minutes of the MPC meeting revealed that members discussed offloading bonds at a faster rate; but “at a time when bond markets globally had been volatile, this risked destabilising markets”.The Bank also announced it would set aside about £120bn of the longest-dated government bonds it holds, as these are used to back the issuance of the UK’s bank notes.In total, the Bank expects to sell a total of £146bn of gilts between now and 2034 – at a steady pace of £20bn a year – back to the government, if Healey gives the plan the thumbs up.What’s the impact for the public finances?Analysts expect it to be modest. The Treasury may be able to finance its borrowing a bit more cheaply when the Bank is not selling a slew of long-dated bonds into the market. As analysts at the investment bank Jefferies put it: “Taken together, the changes imply a materially lower future supply burden, particularly for [long-dated gilts].”And to the extent that the pace of sales is slowing, the losses on those bonds, which is borne by the Treasury, will crystallise more slowly – another marginal upside.Jefferies also suggested that, by making its future plans clear, the MPC’s decision could “ease some of the pressure that had been building for changes to the Bank’s QT approach”.Explore more on these topicsQuantitative easingBank of EnglandBondsGiltsGovernment borrowingEconomic policyEconomicsexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story review – it’s like Ryan Murphy’s new series was written by adolescent boys | Television | The Guardian
description: The latest Monster instalment, about the 1892 Borden axe murders, is packed with periods and beheadings, and feels like it was made up as they went along
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: The latest Monster instalment, about the 1892 Borden axe murders, is packed with periods and beheadings, and feels like it was made up as they went along
Content: ‘Full of great performances’ … Ella Beatty in Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story.Photograph: NetflixView image in fullscreen‘Full of great performances’ … Ella Beatty in Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story.Photograph: NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewMonster: The Lizzie Borden Story review – it’s like Ryan Murphy’s new series was written by adolescent boysThe latest Monster instalment, about the 1892 Borden axe murders, is packed with periods and beheadings, and feels like it was made up as they went alongLucy ManganThu 17 Sep 2026 11.42 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 12.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOkaaay – here’s what I think must have happened. Some time in the past year or two,Ryan Murphydiscovered that women menstruate. Incredulous but enthralled, he rushed off to share the news with his soon equally incredulous and enthralled little friends. After confirming the basics they all looked at each other for a moment in silence as they contemplated this crazy, secret habit of the wimminz. And then Ryan said: “You guys? We have got to make a show about this!” The others nodded in fervent agreement and off they all ran.The result is the utterly bonkers, blood-soaked, borderline-fetishistic fever dream that is The Lizzie Borden Story – the latest entry in Murphy’s popular anthology series Monster. This one is written by Ian Brennan and directed in the main by Max Winkler, the pairing responsible for the series’ previous offering, last year’s lamentable The Ed Gein Story. As, I presume, a gesture to the sex of this one’s subject, there is a female director for two of the Lizzie Borden episodes – Sarah Adina Smith – but it doesn’t really dent the vibe. Think: the gleeful disgust of a roomful of adolescent boys being taught about the female reproductive system in PSHE. It is now an eight-hour miniseries starringRebecca Hall. We live in strange times.So, then, to late 19th-century Massachusetts where the world’s most famous axe murder is, as we open, taking place in an affluent but otherwise unremarkable household in Fall River. Lizzie (Ella Beatty) gives her stepmother Abby (Hall) then father Andrew (Charlie Hunnam, who previously played the eponymous Ed Gein) multiple whacks and we then rewind to four months earlier to find out why.View image in fullscreenOliver Spenceman as Stephen and Charlie Hunnam as coffin-maker Andrew Borden.Photograph: NetflixNow, in real life, the why (even if you agree on the who, and there are those who point the finger at other Borden relatives nearby) was endlessly disputed. Some think she was angry about various property disposals Andrew had made to family members that she deemed unfair. Others think she had long-harboured resentment towards the victims for usurping and betraying her late mother (Andrew remarried quickly, and Lizzie and her sister Emma always referred to Abby as “Mrs Borden”, not “Mother”). Later theories include possible abuse in the family or a relationship with a suitor Andrew didn’t like and so on, but Messrs Brennan and Winkler have a simpler take: women be crazy!Especially women who menstruate! Most of the first episode centres on Lizzie’s heavy periods. I actually looked at the credits to see if her womb got separate billing. First Lizzie loses a suitor by clutching at her cramping parts, then enrages Abby by bleeding all over her precious mulberry silk fainting couch. A new maid, Bridget (Vicky Krieps), is hired, whose duties include dealing with Lizzie’s bloody problems. “We keep her on a bed of wooden planks and muslin sheets she’s free to befoul with her putrid clots,” says Abby, presumably while Hall is mentally firing her agent. Bridget tells Lizzie that blood is good (“It means no man’s seed has taken hold”), hands her a hand-cranked vibrator she picked up in Amsterdam for the relief of cramping and reads her stories about multiple murderer the Countess of Báthory who used to bathe in the blood of her servant girls to preserve her youth. The vibrator is later upgraded to a Chattanooga medical massager when Bridget diagnoses an unbroken hymen as part of Lizzie’s menstrual torments. Which suggests that either Brennan wasn’t listening very attentively in PSHE class or that he saw the phrase “Chattanooga medical massager” somewhere and worked backward from there.Unlike the team behind The Lizzie Borden Story, I have not made any of the above up, and it only gets madder from there. Bridget soon sets up a sex-for-lesbianism-in-the-miniseries relationship with Lizzie and a sex-for-money-for-keeping-the-many-axes-in-your-axe-cupboard-in-good-nick relationship with Andrew (a coffin-maker, who uses them to trim down corpses to a standard casket size, in case you were wondering). An avenue of cherry trees leading to a dovecote is mined for all the symbolism it’s worth, and soon the episodes are wall-to-wall decapitations (from birds to Báthory maidens, no one is safe), good sex (mostly between lesbians in the dovecote), bad sex (“the same ballbag slapping against you forever”), poisoned dinners, neighbours chatting genteelly over tea about “bitchcocks and pearly showers”, abortifacients, cameos from Sarah Paulson as Aileen Wuornos and much, much more. As I believe the Chattanooga medical massager ads used to say: I don’t know quite how they fit it all in.Bonkers, as I say. Stylish – it has an almost Wes Anderson feel at times – and it’s got brio, energy and is absolutely full of great performances, especially from Hall in one of those roles that an actor shouldn’t have touched with a bargepole, despite being the only one who could possibly have carried it off. But the latest Monster has nothing to say about Borden, the times that shaped her or the prejudices most think helped secure a not guilty verdict in the end – all of which remain interesting and pertinent to the modern era, and which might have made it an illuminating companion piece to Murphy’s flagship show The People v OJ Simpson. It’s a bunch of boys on a dare who should have been called back after class and made to get down to some real work.Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story is on NetflixExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewRyan MurphyHistorical drama (TV)Rebecca HallTV crime dramareviewsShareReuse this content
