title: Human harps, massive bananas and dogging: the 20 best Busby Berkeley dance routines – ranked! | Movies | The Guardian
description: To mark 50 years since the director and choreographer’s death, we count down his best fantastical, kaleidoscopic numbers, from erotic silhouettes to sinister tap dancers
Author: Anne Billson
Headline: To mark 50 years since the director and choreographer’s death, we count down his best fantastical, kaleidoscopic numbers, from erotic silhouettes to sinister tap dancers
Content: On the hoof … The Gang’s All Here, 1943.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreenOn the hoof … The Gang’s All Here, 1943.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyRankedMoviesHuman harps, massive bananas and dogging: the 20 best Busby Berkeley dance routines – ranked!To mark 50 years since the director and choreographer’s death, we count down his best fantastical, kaleidoscopic numbers, from erotic silhouettes to sinister tap dancersAnne BillsonThu 17 Sep 2026 07.48 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 14.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. Sittin’ on a Back Yard Fence from Footlight Parade (1933)So you thought Cats (2019) was tacky? Wait until you see Ruby Keeler (AKA Mrs Al Jolson) gambolling around as a fluffy white feline, being wooed by an ogling tomcat, or chasing Billy Barty, a child actor with dwarfism, costumed as a mouse.19.The Girl at the Ironing Boardfrom Dames (1934)Joan Blondell (seven months pregnant during filming) livens up workaday laundry tasks by fantasising about the men whose underwear she hangs out to dry. And the underwear flirts right back. Who cares if you can see the wires?18.Fascinating Rhythmfrom Lady Be Good (1941)If this were a tap dancing Top 20, Eleanor Powell would be at No 1, but Berkeley wisely stands back and showcases her epic skills with minimal fuss. All the tricksiness took place out of frame, where stagehands were pushing grand pianos out of her way.17.The Lady in the Tutti Frutti Hatfrom The Gang’s All Here (1943)View image in fullscreen‘Some people say I dress too gay, but every day I feel so gay!’Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyBerkeley’s first colour film as both director and choreographer stars “Brazilian Bombshell” Carmen Miranda in her signature fruit-laden headdress. The fruity motif continues in a musical number set on a fake tropical island where chorus girls wield giant bananas. Nothing salacious to see here, move along.16.Young and Healthyfrom 42nd Street (1933)This quintessential backstage musical was a huge hit and established Berkeley’s approach to choreography. An initially stagebound song with innuendo-laden lyrics, belted out by lecherous Dick Powell, blossoms into revolving geometric formations of young women shot from every conceivable angle, culminating in a travelling shot through their spread legs. This is cinema!15. Spin a Little Web of Dreams from Fashions of 1934 (1934)“Mr Berkeley, I’m not raising my daughter to be a human harp!” was one critic’s reaction to a vision of chorus girls plucking at harps fashioned from other chorus girls. Just before theHays Codebanished navels from Hollywood, blond-wigged beauties flaunt their belly buttons while performing the ultimate ostrich feather fan dance.14. Honeymoon Hotel from Footlight Parade (1933)Before Dick Powell went all film noir as Philip Marlowe in Farewell, My Lovely (1944), he and Keeler regularly played sweethearts in Berkeley’s musicals. The camera glides around what is essentially a sex hotel, as attempts to consummate their hasty marriage are hampered by other guests, interfering relatives and an unnaturally precocious child.13. Oh, Lady Be Good! from Lady Be Good (1941)Once again, Berkeley the choreographer stands back and lets Eleanor Powell work her magic. MGM failed to come up with a suitable dog to partner her for this number, so Powell bought a terrier mix called Buttons and trained it herself.12. Dames from Dames (1934)“What do you go for, go see a show for?” The answer is dames (male gaze, sorry) and here they are, not as scantily clad as in pre-code days, but forming a wide range of pleasing kaleidoscopic configurations and Bridget Riley-esque patterns until Dick Powell’s head bursts through their tableaux.11.Shuffle Off to Buffalofrom 42nd Street (1933)Keeler once again tries to consummate a marriage (to Clarence Nordstrom), this time on a sleeper train to Niagara Falls. Other passengers leer salaciously out of their curtained compartments, while worldly Una Merkel and Ginger Rogers predict the ingenue will soon be on a train to Reno for a quickie divorce.10. Shadow Waltz from Gold Diggers of 1933 (1933)Chorus girls, wired up to neon-tubed violins, twirl around on vertiginous walkways. Then the lights go out so all you can see are the violins, which rearrange themselves into the shape of one massive violin. So many ways this could have gone horribly wrong – and indeed, a 6.4 earthquake hit Los Angeles during filming, and some of the violins short-circuited.9.The Polka Dot Polkafrom The Gang’s All Here (1943)One minute Alice Faye is singing as normal, surrounded by dancing children who are only marginally weird. The next, we are plunged into a Technicolor hallucination of neon hoops, more dots than DC’s Polka-Dot Man could dream of, and psychedelic effects that will have you wondering if you accidentally ingested LSD.8.We’re in the Moneyfrom Gold Diggers of 1933 (1933)Before teaming up with Fred Astaire in the first of their 10 musical collaborations, Ginger Rogers played a golden-hearted broad in Berkeley’s first two backstage musicals. Heading a chorus line draped in silver dollars, she belts out an upbeat ode to capitalism, including one verse inPig Latin.7.42nd Streetfrom 42nd Street (1933)View image in fullscreenJust an ordinary day in NYC … 42nd Street.Photograph: Moviestore Collection/AlamyOnce again, a musical number opens out into an entire panorama that could not possibly be physically contained in a theatre. Keeler’s effortful hoofing (she’s no Eleanor Powell, but we love her anyway) gives way to rhythmic travelling shots of New Yorkers going about their business: traffic, newspaper sellers, hairdressers and, adding a touch of dirty realism, a murder.6.Pettin’ in the Parkfrom Gold Diggers of 1933 (1933)Dick Powell is trying to get into Keeler’s knickers in an outrageously nudge-nudge number featuring snowball fights, erotic silhouettes, roller-skating cops and stocking tops galore, before she finally stymies her beau with a onesie made of metal. Enter leering child actor Billy Barty, with a can opener.5. I Only Have Eyes for You from Dames (1934)Powell loves Keeler so much he keeps seeing her everywhere. And so do we, thanks to lookalike chorus girls in Keeler masks, holding up cut-outs of her face, or pulling their skirts over their heads to form one gigantic Keelertifo, all set to a Harry Warren-Al Dubin earworm that quickly became a standard.4. Shanghai Lil from Footlight Parade (1933)After The Public Enemy, James Cagney was keen to avoid being typecast as a gangster and draws on his vaudeville roots to give us a tap dance that almost makes up for Keeler in yellowface. Get an eyeful of Hollywood orientalism in all its pre-code horror, complete with sex workers, opium smokers and half the US Navy on manoeuvres.3.Remember My Forgotten Manfrom Gold Diggers of 1933 (1933)Audiences of the 1930s went to the cinema to escape the Great Depression, but numbers like this assured them that their pain wasn’t being ignored. Joan Blondell, with a sort ofsprechgesang, and contralto Etta Moten lament the treatment of poverty-stricken veterans of the first world war. As the chorus swells, the number segues from a theatrical street into montages of men marching to war and limping home to the breadline and a treadmill of silhouettes. Lump in throat time.2.By a Waterfallfrom Footlight Parade (1933)Dick Powell and Keeler celebrate “love in a natural setting”. Berkeley illustrates this early 1930s ode to dogging with an astonishing aquatic ballet of 100 synchronised swimmers forming flowers, snake shapes and a human fountain, shot from all angles in a glass-walled pool that filled an entire soundstage. None of this, of course, would be visible to the theatre audience glimpsed at the start of the number.1. Lullaby of Broadway from Gold Diggers of 1935 (1935)You ain’t heard nothing until you’ve heard 200 feet stomping out a time step in unison. Of all the musical numbers he directed, Berkeley’s personal favourite was this 13-minute expressionist nightmare in which a young woman’s nightclubbing gets out of hand. From Wini Shaw’s disembodied head turning into the Manhattan skyline, to the most sinister phalanx of tap-dancers this side of Leni Riefenstahl, to the frankly rather shocking ending, it’s an intoxicating masterpiece. “Come and dance!”Explore more on these topicsFilmRankedDancefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Margaret Busby: ‘My friend Bonnie Greer fearlessly spoke out and forged connections’ | Books | The Guardian
description: The writer and editor shares memories of a creative powerhouse who was generous with her time and expertise
Author: Margaret Busby
Headline: The writer and editor shares memories of a creative powerhouse who was generous with her time and expertise
Content: Greer died on Tuesday following a brief illness.Photograph: Lorenzo Dalberto/AlamyView image in fullscreenGreer died on Tuesday following a brief illness.Photograph: Lorenzo Dalberto/AlamyBooksMargaret Busby: ‘My friend Bonnie Greer fearlessly spoke out and forged connections’Margaret BusbyThe writer and editor shares memories of a creative powerhouse who was generous with her time and expertiseBonnie Greer, writer and cultural commentator, dies aged 77Thu 17 Sep 2026 09.12 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 09.20 EDTShareBonnie Greer personified courage, humour, principle and generosity. Before knowing her in person, I met her work. Her 1994 debut novel Hanging by Her Teeth – about a Black American woman travelling through the US and Europe in search of her father – was sent to me for endorsement by its publisher, and I commented unhesitatingly: “Writing with sharpness, wit and poignancy,Bonnie Greergathers the sequestered memories behind one Black woman’s bitter-sweet blues.”The scope of Bonnie’s own life is beyond anything fictional, encompassing highs and lows, triumphs and challenges, her trajectory starting in the West Side of Chicago and ending up navigating iconic areas of London – whether Holland Park or Covent Garden or Soho – as if to the manor born. It was an honour to become her friend, sharing many a good time, offering a consoling shoulder if needed. An added bonus was to meet her husband David Hutchins. What a wonderful mutually supportive team they made.Bonnie’s activism marched side by side with her creativity and powers of persuasion. Friendship, support, empathy and behind-the-scenes involvement were all part of who she was. She could be effervescently sociable. There was an era when she relished get-togethers of a sort of ladies-who-lunch club that she would organise, where we might chat for hours, exchanging memories, planning dreamy never-to-be-fulfilled projects. I recall one gathering that took place at the House of Commons – with Diane Abbott, Verna Wilkins, Maya Jaggi and Nana Ayebia Clarke – when Bonnie suddenly made us all pause to reflect on the fact we were all sitting there, with a view of the Thames and London’s landscape, given where we had come from.Seemingly ready to re-invent herself, she was perhaps defying anyone to easily label her. She could be public intellectual, television pundit, dramatist, librettist, academic. Her repertoire was wide-ranging and ever-expanding, with fresh ideas emerging at every opportunity. She fearlessly spoke out, forged new connections, took on weighty burdens.She lent expertise to numerous national cultural institutions – including on the boards of the British Museum, the Royal Opera House and the London Film School, and as vice president of the Shaw Society and chancellor of Kingston University London. She shared her vision with such ventures as the Black Theatre Co-operative and Talawa Theatre Company (where, during her stint as artistic director, she mooted an ambitious dramatisation of my 1,000-plus-page anthology, Daughters of Africa). We were both patrons of the SI Leeds Literary Prize for unpublished fiction by Black and Asian women in the UK.It was pure delight to accompany her anywhere to experience music, art, drama, film or anything intellectually stimulating.In June 2019, we went to a lecture by Lonnie Bunch III at the British Library – then newly appointed to secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, the first African American and first historian appointed to do so, whorecently announced his intention to retire at the end of 2026. Dr Bunch’s recent communication with me echoes my own feelings: “I have been made better by my interactions with Bonnie. She was generous with her time, with her contacts and with her friendship. Her passing is an immeasurable loss. I am crying but also smiling because of her impact on so many. She was simply amazing. Her ability to speak truth to power made her such a unique voice in both the UK and the US.”We will all miss her.Explore more on these topicsBooksBonnie GreerPublishingcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Songwriting instead of doomscrolling’: project inspires Welsh valleys towns to tune into their heritage | Wales | The Guardian
description: Community groups and schools work with Wales’s folk arts organisation to set stories of the area’s people to music
Author: Bethan McKernan
Headline: Community groups and schools work with Wales’s folk arts organisation to set stories of the area’s people to music
Content: The original songs are being professionally recorded for an album, including a composition created by Llwyncelyn primary school.Photograph: Nia Medi Evans/Medi Public RelationsView image in fullscreenThe original songs are being professionally recorded for an album, including a composition created by Llwyncelyn primary school.Photograph: Nia Medi Evans/Medi Public RelationsWales‘Songwriting instead of doomscrolling’: project inspires Welsh valleys towns to tune into their heritageCommunity groups and schools work with Wales’s folk arts organisation to set  stories of the area’s people to musicBethan McKernanWales correspondentThu 17 Sep 2026 09.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 15.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGrowing up inWales, Liz Puleston-Jones was familiar with the country’s rich heritage of storytelling and traditional music, but none of it ever seemed to have much of a connection to her life in Swansea.Researching the history of the area as part of Cân y Cymoedd (When Valleys Sing), a project in nearby Port Talbot, she came across the story of Isabel Thomas, a 14-year-old girl in the 1940s who left school and lied about her age to work in a tin plate works to support her family.“Her story really spoke to me,” said Puleston-Jones. “Before I did this, I didn’t really have a connection to the history and storytelling aspect of folk music, and how much it’s about community and telling the stories of normal people … Anyone can be part of a tune, and write a tune, and share it.”Thomas’s story has now been celebrated in song form as part of the project from Wales’s national folk arts organisation, Trac Cymru. At Cân y Cymoedd community and school workshops, musicians, historians and volunteers have helped each group uncover stories at local heritage sites and museums, and channelled their findings into the creation of two dozen new compositions about local life in Rhondda Cynon Taf and Neath Port Talbot.For many participants, the workshops have rekindled a sense of cultural pride and belonging in the community.Jenny Pope, who took part in the sessions in Port Talbot, said: “For me, it made the Port Talbot area feel like a real beacon of folk music – somewhere people might once have just driven past but now feels full of life and culture. Creating something we can pass on to the next generation has been amazing.”View image in fullscreenLiz Puleston-Jones: ‘Anyone can be part of a tune, and write a tune, and share it.’Photograph: Nia Medi Evans/Medi Public RelationsPuleston-Jones added: “I was terrified at the idea of having to write or produce something on my own but it was a collaborative experience. Now instead of watching rubbish TV or doomscrolling I’m being drawn to songwriting and playing my violin after years and years. It feels much healthier.”At Llwyncelyn primary school in Porth, in the Rhondda valley, a year 6 class has been busy learning the song about their village composed by last year’s cohort with the help of a fiddle player, Aneirin Jones, before recording a music video at RhonddaHeritagePark, a former colliery.Their song, Ein Cân Fach Ni (Our Little Song), references the area’s mountains, mines and chapels, as well as the activities and places that make up the children’s day-to-day lives, such as the recycling centre and the playground.View image in fullscreenAt Llwyncelyn primary school in Porth, a year 6 class has been busy learning the song about their village.Photograph: Nia Medi Evans/Medi Public RelationsIfan, 10, said: “I knewCwm Rhonddabefore but I didn’t really know anything else about folk music before this, it’s been really fun. My sister is annoyed because her class wrote the song but my class is going to make the video!”The original songs are being professionally recorded for an album Trac Cymru hopes will be accessible to a wider audience and become a resource for future generations.The project manager, Antwn Owen-Hicks, said: “Cân y Cymoedd is about making sure that traditions continue to evolve. Magic happens when people explore all of this and begin to see where they’re from in a different light. It doesn’t matter what musical level you’re at or what language you speak. If you’ve got a story, you can write a song, and we help you do this.”Explore more on these topicsWalesHeritageFolk musicnewsShareReuse this content

title: Faster! Louder! Brighter! How the attention economy overwhelmed children’s TV | Children | The Guardian
description: Does your child’s favourite show give them a chance to reflect, or does it move too quickly for its lessons to sink in?
Author: Natalia Kucirkova
Headline: Does your child’s favourite show give them a chance to reflect, or does it move too quickly for its lessons to sink in?
Content: Photograph: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Netflix/Fantorangen/Ludo Studio/Zach Hyman/ ZUMA Press, Inc./Apple TVDoes your child’s favourite show give them a chance to reflect, or does it move too quickly for its lessons to sink in?A version of this piece was originally published onAeonasThe bombarding of childhoodByNatalia KucirkovaThu 17 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIam at the airport gate waiting to depart, watching passengers hurry past with rolling suitcases and paper cups of coffee. A small boy sits very still beside his mother. He holds an iPad close to his chest, almost in a cramp, clutching the screen as if it might otherwise run away. I hear loud clapping hands and squeaking children’s voices. I lean over and see a cartoon character in green snatch a toy from another character in pink. The pink character begins to cry, tears splashing like sprinkles from its enormous eyes. The green character shouts sorry. Instantly, the tears stop and a wide smile replaces them before I have blinked. And, before I have even worked out whether the characters are speaking English or Arabic (as the mother does to the boy), the scene has changed and the two characters are rowing a boat with a random song in the background. The boy’s eyes dart on the screen from right to left, centre, down. His body is still but his attention is being hurried from cue to cue.This is the problem I have come to think of as the pace of children’s media.Children’s media is usuallyjudged by its content and quality: how many minutes watched and whether it was educational, age-appropriate, diverse, prosocial, commercial and safe. These questions matter and, with my colleagues, I have studied them through experiments and contributed to guidelines, regulations and toolkits for designers. But we have been missing a bigger design feature that may be just as consequential: the time a medium gives a child to make meaning. A programme or app can contain good lessons and still move too quickly for those lessons to settle. For instance, in the US animated educational series Ask the StoryBots, the subject matter may be genuinely rich – why the sky is blue, how eyes work and where planets come from – but the explanation unfolds through rapid jokes, songs, visual shifts and sudden changes in style. Before a child has time to sit with one image or idea, the scene has moved on to the next, with a burst of information.Different media have different temporal demands: a digital picture book, a game, a television episode and an app each ask a child to attend differently. But, across these media, the important question is whether the pace suits the experience that the narrative claims to support. Does it give children time to follow a story, grasp a concept, identify with a character, regulate emotion or share attention with another person? Or does it continually hurry them toward the next cue, the next reward, the next burst of stimulation?When media moves too quickly, the layers of experience collapse into one another. A child may laugh at someone slipping on a banana peel but imitate only the visible silliness, missing the anticipation and reversal that make the joke work. A character may comfort a friend, but if the scene moves on too quickly, the child has little time to recognise the repair, or imagine doing the same in the kindergarten room. To develop empathy in the early years, a child must notice that another person feels something different. That small act of crossing over takes time.In this sense, pace is not a minor stylistic feature of children’s media. It is one of the ways media imagines the child. Is the child a consumer to be retained, a nervous system to be stimulated, a vessel to be filled with educational content – or a person whose attention is still forming, and who therefore needs time to arrive?People who worry about children and screens tend to worry about violent content, advertising or whether a phonics app calling itself “educational” truly supports phonics. These are reasonable worries and I share them. But spend five minutes watching what many young children watch, and you will see how fast, loud and bright everything on the screen has become. It does not matter whether the child is watching on a smartphone in the car or on a TV at home. The screen has inherited the adult logic of media design.That logic is, for the most part, the logic of theattention economy. It overwhelms and overshouts, making it easier for the screen to steer the viewer. The attention economy has introduced a host of small design features for shortening time. The “like” button is faster than writing an appreciative comment. A progress bar tells us how many minutes remain in an article before we have decided whether to read to the end. Increasingly, AI appears beside long documents with an offer that sounds helpful but carries a philosophy: this text is long; would you like a quick summary?There are, of course, features that work in the opposite direction. The delay-email function and the pop-up that asks “Are you sure you want to delete this?” are two examples. Such features interrupt automatic action and return a modicum of judgment to the user. A nature documentary with linearity and the interpretive presence of an adult voice is a great model for children’s media; for example, in the TV show Prehistoric Planet, David Attenborough’s voiceover and the camera’s zoom-ins encourage children to look closely and wonder about unfamiliar life. But these are exceptions within a larger system where speed is treated as the default.When learning is crowded with content that keeps jumping ahead – a crisis appears, a mission begins, a spaceship launches, a door opens – the child’s attention is restarted as each problem is introduced and immediately solved. Such media may gesture at teamwork or perseverance, but the speed of the format leaves little time for those lessons to sink in. In the animated TV series Paw Patrol, for instance, a rescue is clear and reassuring: someone is in trouble, pups assemble, each uses a skill and order is restored. Yet the movement from problem to rescue to resolution is often so efficient that the child is swept along by urgency rather than invited to dwell on responsibility or care for the other. Similarly, in the app-based game Hot Wheels Unlimited, building tracks and racing cars may suggest creativity and problem-solving, but the dominant rhythm is acceleration: boost, race, crash, win, unlock, repeat.View image in fullscreenSesame Street … a great example of TV that supports learning.Photograph: Zach Hyman/NetflixResearch has told us many useful things about children’s media. We know that some educational television (such as Sesame Street)can support learning. We know that some apps arebetter designed than others. We know thatinteractive features in digital bookscan help when they serve the story, and distract when they do not. We know that characters and narrativesshape children’s ideasabout identity, gender and social life. Pace cuts across all of these questions as the condition under which content becomes experience.Screen time can run fast or slow. This is partly why merely clocking “screen time” is too crude a measure. Two children may each watch 20 minutes of media and have entirely different encounters with time. In one case, the child is moved through a coherent story with pauses, repetitions and recognisable emotional beats. In another, she is pulled through 10 clips, 30 characters, flashing colours, sudden songs and rewards that arrive before thought has had time to form. The clock records the same duration but the child does not live the same time.And parents are rightly worried: a four-year-old does not come to media with adult reserves of self-regulation. She is still learning how to stay with a feeling, how to wait for a story to unfold, how to connect one event to another, how to notice that a character’s sadness matters before the joke wipes it away. If a programme moves too quickly, it may encourage a child to expect information to arrive in rapid, constantly shifting bursts, making slower, more sustained forms of attention harder to tolerate. Stopping this vicious cycle starts by asking what exactly makes children’s media fast or slow.Don’t get me wrong, I am not saying that slow is always good or better than fast media. Some lively children’s media can be excellent; some slow media can be dull, inert or badly made. The point is that good children’s media gives a child time to complete an act of attention. Bad media keeps interrupting that act before it can become a memory or be turned into play.When my research group compared children’s shows, apps and digital stories, we saw that pace can become a set of design choices. A story can move in a way that helps a child anticipate what comes next, or it can jump so quickly between scenes that cause and effect become blurred. A screen can guide the eye toward one important object, or fill the frame with competing movement.This is why the familiar adult language of “engagement” is so poor for children. A child can look intensely engaged while being given very little time to think. In the Kids’ Slow Media Project, we have therefore tried tomake these differences visible. We evaluate children’s media by looking at how it organises time. We ask whether the narrative is coherent enough to follow; whether the sensory field overwhelms meaning-making at specific age junctures; whether the design builds in stopping points, where the story can be digested before it goes on. Does a piece of media allow learning to develop through meaningful repetition? And does a story or piece create openings for a child and adult, or two children, to notice something together?When in March 2026 the UK Department for Educationadvised parents of children under fiveto choose “slow-paced, age-appropriate” content, without saying what slow-paced actually is, our group sought to make the term concrete.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long ReadLose yourself in a great story: from politics to psychology, food to technology, culture to crimeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat makes a show slow or fast for a given child? It depends.Childrendiffer by age, temperament, language, sensory sensitivity and circumstance; thus, without testing their responses, it is impossible to provide a firm recommendation: a show that suits one four-year-old may overwhelm another. We therefore give ratings only to provide a map for adult judgment. The ratings are illustrations, inviting parents to check whether their child is being given enough time to complete an act of attention.The shows scoring highest on the slow rubric are those that leave room around the characters’ actions and allow the child to recognise the actions. Often there is a face, a puppet, a song, a greeting, a familiar body on screen that treats attention as a relationship. Indeed, the power of programmes such as the US show Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, the Norwegian series Fantorangen and the British shows In the Night Garden … and Teletubbies lies in their ability to build a rapport with the child and then repeat a theme or a segment, almost as in a ritual. Here, small acts and greetings or songs provide a familiar frame, like a safety net, within which new concepts can be introduced. In the Australian animated series Bluey, an episode often begins with an ordinary family situation that develops into imaginative games involving parents, siblings and friends; the pace can be lively, but it tends to return the child to pretend play, negotiation and emotional understanding. In the animated TV series The Adventures of Paddington – a British-French co-production – gentle mishaps are usually held inside a world of curiosity, politeness, family and repair, so comedy becomes a route into perseverance or social understanding. Such programmes are slow because they leave openings through which the story can travel back into meaning and play.Conversations between characters are another way in which higher-ranked shows convey new concepts with appropriate pace. When introduced with context, a new word or idea might not be immediately clear, but the child can notice and infer. Over time, the child arrives at understanding, and this slow, even arduous process helps the concept stick. For example, in one episode of Daniel Tiger’s Neighbourhood – based on Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood – Daniel is nervous about trying the swing. The scene allows that feeling to be acknowledged, sung through and gradually transformed into confidence, with support from Daniel’s friend Jodi Platypus and her grandmother. Similarly, in the Sesame Street-based game app Elmo Loves ABCs, a letter is traced, sounded, repeated, connected to words and encountered through touch and play.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Robert Nickelsberg/Getty ImagesThe lowest-scoring media is that in which the child’s attention is kept in motion by a manipulative rhythm that continuously restarts attention with the next tune, next bright image, next comic beat, next loop of familiarity or personalised nudge. Instead of allowing the child to settle into the story, such shows repeatedly pull attention back; the same is true of many preschool game apps built around loops of reward and progression.Evaluating children’s popular media taught me that pace is a revealing measure of quality but also a proxy for a deeper question about the child’s agency, their own sense of self. The real distinction is whether a medium leaves room for the child’s own attention or continually redirects it. When every pause is filled, every uncertainty immediately resolved and every wandering thought pulled back by a brighter cue, waiting and reflection can begin to feel intolerable. The child learns to reach for the next stimulus before the previous one has had time to settle. To give space for a child’s attention to drift inward, to reflect, is therefore to leave room for the child’s inner life. Slow media changes the relation between screen and child by saying: you may arrive at your own pace.Some critics may dismiss slow media as nostalgia: a longing for the children’s television of the previous generation, or a privilege available only to parents with time and large bookshelves and big houses with quiet rooms. But that is a notion we should refuse. Theattention economyhas trained us to treat a child’s pause as a problem, a wandering gaze as lost engagement and an unfilled moment as wasted time. The opposite is true: slow time gives children the space to perceive, process, respond and make meaning – and it can be designed into children’s media.Unboxing, bad baby and evil Santa: how YouTube got swamped with creepy content for kidsRead moreLike energy drinks, fast media promises more capacity than the child actually has: more attention is supposed to lead to better performance. Fast media feels like an extension of the child’s energy, but the bargain is unsustainable and unhealthy. What looks like support can become dependency, and what promises engagement and learning is actually compulsion.Children need media that doesn’t merely occupy them, instruct them or keep them quiet. They benefit and grow from stories and shows that preserve their capacity for inwardness and their relation to others. In fast media, the child’s attention is continually propped up by the next stimulus. Slow media insists on the opposite. In the end, the aim is not to withdraw children from the digital world, but to make that world more worthy of them.Listen to our podcastshereand sign up to the long read weekly emailhere.Explore more on these topicsThe long readChildrenTelevisionChildren's TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: British people understand the climate crisis threat. Today I’m empowering them to tackle it  | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: With nearly £30m of funding, I’m giving communities power over local energy. They know the gravity of global heating, and they want to be part of the solution, says UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Author: Andy Burnham
Headline: With nearly £30m of funding, I’m giving communities power over local energy. They know the gravity of global heating, and they want to be part of the solution, says UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Content: Solar panels being fitted on a roof in Wales.Photograph: Chris Howes/Wild Places Photography/AlamyView image in fullscreenSolar panels being fitted on a roof in Wales.Photograph: Chris Howes/Wild Places Photography/AlamyOpinionEnergyBritish people understand the climate crisis threat. Today I’m empowering them to tackle itAndy BurnhamWith nearly £30m of funding, I’m giving communities power over local energy. They know the gravity of global heating, and they want to be part of the solutionAndy Burnham: UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050Thu 17 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 15.59 EDTShareOn the day I became prime minister,I pledged to bring power to every postcode. Today, we begin to make good on that promise in the most literal sense. With nearly £30m of funding for People’s Power projects, communities across every nation of the UK will soon have the chance to build and control their own clean energy supply.This investment means villages, towns and cities can harness the natural resources around them with solar panels on libraries, publicly owned windfarms, hydro schemes in their rivers, or whatever else works for them. The purpose is to put money back in people’s pockets while giving them a direct role in tackling the climate crisis.Every council and community group awarded funding will have at least part-ownership in its renewable energy projects. That means, in the years ahead, more and more communities in Britain will do more than simply host solar panels and wind turbines. They will own a stake in them and retain a share of the wealth they create.Today’s announcement is part of this government’s sustained effort to make energy more affordable. In my first week in office,I said I would remove VAT from household electricity bills. From the beginning of October, that policy kicks in, giving families some much-needed breathing room. But the only lasting way to bring down bills is to produce more of our own clean, renewable energy at home, which People’s Power will achieve.I am acutely aware that our changing climate is a major concern for many Britons, not least because we have just emerged fromour hottest summer on record. Punishing heatwaves left nurses collapsing on hospital wards and bus drivers working in 40C cabs.Wildfires destroyed homes, leaving families with nothing. Andmore extreme weatheris forecast in the months ahead. The climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is here and with us now. The British people are no longer insulated from the consequences, and they do not want to be excluded from the solutions. They are looking for ways to do their bit. Community energy gives them that chance.Across Britain, people are taking back control of the things that matter to them: their pubs, their libraries, their leisure centres. Some have already done the same with energy. There are fine examples across the UK of community energy schemes that keep the lights on, the local economy moving and the benefits close to home.These projects work and we want to take them nationwide. Today’s investment is the first down payment on a £1bn Great BritishEnergyprogramme, the biggest investment in community energy ever, which will eventually fund more than 1,000 People’s Power projects.The climate crisis presents us with an enormous challenge and possibility. In the coming years, we need to change the way we travel, build homes and produce energy. I have long seen the green transition as the best chance we will ever have to reindustrialise Britain.With this in mind, I believe there are two routes we can follow. There’s the traditional Whitehall way: make people pay for the change with more regulation and higher costs, and allow private companies to reap the rewards. Or we can pursue a different route: help people make the change by creating jobs, lowering bills and bringing power back to them.That is the approach I took as mayor of Greater Manchester. When we brought the buses back under public control, we capped fares and made the fleet cleaner. The result was a transport system designed around the needs of the people who pay for it and rely on it. We are applying the same principle to community energy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI am determined that we meet the commitment on which Labour was elected and reach net zero by 2050. I want Britain to believe in itself again. That will not happen by asking people to stand still while the world spins around them. Everyone should have a say and a stake in their future. That is whatNo 10 Northis all about. It is what today is about – it is community power in every sense. Power owned by local people, power generated by local projects and power returned to every postcode.Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United KingdomExplore more on these topicsEnergyOpinionClimate crisisLabourCommunitiesRenewable energySolar powerWind powercommentShareReuse this content

title: Dear Ed Sheeran, fence-sitting is so last century: musicians can no longer opt out of politics | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: It’s all very 2026: with a stadium owner on one side and angry support acts on the other, the cornered star will have to pick a side, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: It’s all very 2026: with a stadium owner on one side and angry support acts on the other, the cornered star will have to pick a side, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Content: Ed Sheeran performing at BBC1’s Big Weekend festival in Sefton Park, Liverpool, 24 May 2025.Photograph: Andy Von Pip/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEd Sheeran performing at BBC1’s Big Weekend festival in Sefton Park, Liverpool, 24 May 2025.Photograph: Andy Von Pip/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionEd SheeranDear Ed Sheeran, fence-sitting is so last century: musicians can no longer opt out of politicsZoe WilliamsIt’s all very 2026: with a stadium owner on one side and angry support acts on the other, the cornered star will have to pick a sideThu 17 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 08.18 EDTShareEd Sheeran, seeking to stay out of politics, has become, in this moment, the most political artist in the world. And in trying to leave himself room to manoeuvre, he has backed himself into a corner. Since the rapper Macklemore was dropped as a support act on Sheeran’s Loop tour on Monday,every other opening acthas pulled out. Finneas O’Connellkept it briefon Tuesday: “Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed. I stand with Palestine and its people.” Aaron Rowewas already out, saying: “I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence … rightful voices.”Beoga, Sheeran’s actual backing band,then pulled out, along with the Danish band Lukas Graham, who probably made the mildest statement, managing to not even mention any countries: “We should be able to speak about war, about civilians being killed, about children who deserve to grow up. Wherever they live. Whatever flag flies over them.”Sheeran said thedecision to dropMacklemore was entirely down to venue owners and promoters, adding that there was a reason he didn’t talk about politics on stage: “My audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds.” Both statements sound weak, but more importantly, it is not true that Sheeran doesn’t take political stances. He hastaken part in a fundraising gigfor Ukrainians, telling them, “I love you, I stand with you”; in 2017 he outed himself as a “Corbynista fanboy” (TM the Sun), and has been a vocal supporter of LGBTQI+ rights, on stage and off, throughout his career. More specifically, it seems unlikely he didn’t know the views of his support acts when he chose them: Macklemore had asong about Hind Rajab, the five-year-old killed by the IDF in 2024, on his set list; Beoga arefounding membersof Irish Artists for Palestine.To try to psychoanalyse Sheeran, and say definitively whether he was trying to borrow the spirit of these artists while distancing himself from their beliefs, or in fact shares their views, would be premature; ultimately, he’s bound to declare himself. So far hehas simply saidhe was “appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine” and that the “suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy”. Just because he didn’t choose to speak publicly, he said, “doesn’t mean I don’t care”.This omertà won’t hold. But what we can say for certain now is that the idea of keeping politics out of entertainment, music, or art, is last century’s fantasy. Censorship is swift – but often not as overt as in this case. It is simply a fact that if artists don’t studiously avoid voicing certain opinions, they will get caught up in politics. It’s unclear whether it’s possible to create art – at least art that will be seen by a mass public – in those conditions.At thevanguard of the moveto jettison Macklemore from the tour was the Israeli-American Council, whose chief executive, Elan Carr,told the Today programmeon Wednesday that the rapper had “put forth a blood libel against the state of Israel and, by connection, the Jewish people”. He was pressed by Justin Webb on what Macklemore actually said: “The words free Palestine don’t necessarily mean … that anything awful should happen to Jewish people or indeed to the state of Israel.” “Free Palestine absolutely is a call for the extermination of the state of Israel and the Jewish people,” Carr replied.So what kind ofPalestineis it acceptable to want? The other difficult strand of Carr’s argument was that a concert audience was “captive … people have paid to be there”. If you’ve paid money to be somewhere, the logic runs, you shouldn’t be subjected to politics of any kind. Yet billionaires have no qualms about having a political agenda. Macklemore, both onstage and in his own statement, has rebuffed the argument that voicing support for Palestinians and criticising Israel and its actions in Gaza and the West Bank is antisemitic. (In 2014, he apologised for a costume he wore on stage, which critics said was antisemitic, saying: “I respect all cultures and all people.”)The concern of many of the artists was that they were facing not justcensorship, but censorship by billionaires: specifically Robert Kraft, who demanded Macklemore’s removal withthe threat of axingthe whole show from his Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts. Kraft has so far not commented onAlexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s chargethat he put pressure on other stadiums to follow suit. In his own statement, he insisted his decision to ban Macklemore from Gillette was “not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf”, but that such advocacy,“should not … obscure the responsibility of Hamas”.What next,Ocasio-Cortezasked an interviewer, rhetorically: “It could be speaking out about AI … you can now just get a handful of stadium owners to ensure that an entire person’s career can be jeopardised.”Ultimately, now, the only acceptable thing to say is nothing: there is no statement mild enough aboutIsraeland Palestine that can be made on a stage to a general audience. Even to wish for a world in which children aren’t killed is too political, and even the Sheeran fix – that there’s a lot of pain on both sides – which might or might not have been devised to soothe billionaire interests, does not meet their preference. They would simply prefer that everyone pretend the situation doesn’t exist, that they’ve never heard of it, that nothing has happened, and if anything ever had, they wouldn’t be able to find it on a map. The slippery slope argument, that an enforced public silence could spread to protests against datacentres next, is plausible but unnecessary: we don’t need this censorship to get worse before we take it seriously.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionZoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsEd SheeranOpinionPalestineIsraelIsrael-Gaza warMiddle East and north AfricaAlexandria Ocasio-CortezcommentShareReuse this content

title: Watching NAZA was like peering through a window – and seeing the machinery of killing in Gaza  | Mahmoud Mushtaha | The Guardian
description: I now know that the only difference between life and death may have been an AI algorithm, says Mahmoud Mushtaha, a Palestinian journalist from Gaza
Author: Mahmoud Mushtaha
Headline: I now know that the only difference between life and death may have been an AI algorithm, says Mahmoud Mushtaha, a Palestinian journalist from Gaza
Content: Palestinians search for missing people under the rubble of a destroyed house following Israeli air strikes on Deir Al Balah, 22 February 2024.Photograph: Mohammed Saber/EPAView image in fullscreenPalestinians search for missing people under the rubble of a destroyed house following Israeli air strikes on Deir Al Balah, 22 February 2024.Photograph: Mohammed Saber/EPAOpinionNAZAWatching NAZA was like peering through a window – and seeing the machinery of killing in GazaMahmoud MushtahaFor so long I wondered why I survived while family and friends were killed. Now I know the only difference between life and death may have been an AI algorithmThu 17 Sep 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 14.15 EDTShareThe lights go down, and for a moment I forget I’m watching a screen. It fills with a rooftop in Tel Aviv at night, black and grey. The camera pans down. Through windows, we see people watching screens of their own – couples holding each other close, following the news, eating food. They appear absorbed in their own worlds, and why wouldn’t they be?That’s the thing I can’t get past as a Palestinian journalist fromGaza, watching this apparent tranquillity: this must be it – this must be what safety actually looks like. Just an evening uninterrupted, with no military aircraft flying overhead or drones buzzing incessantly. Meanwhile, men and women on the rooftop above them calmly talk about how they decided how many Palestinian civilians would die on any given night.These are the soldiers, mostly intelligence officers, who helped Israel carry out its destruction of Gaza. Theirtestimonies form the basis of NAZA, a documentary whose title comes from an Israeli military acronym used to indicatehow many civilians are likely to die in an airstrike on the territory.What surprised me in the film wasn’t the massive scale of the killing, or even the coldness of it, but the proficiency of the soldiers who coolly described destroying people’s lives as if they were discussing a routine errand. One described the work simply as a “mission”, while another compared it to a “video game”.One soldier described knowing exactly what some of the people were doing in the moments before he killed them. He recalled hearing a man talking to his wife in bed. A baby crying. The sound of the TV. Despite taking all that humanity in, he quickly gave permission to drop the bomb.The soldier explained how he would then go out with friends in the evening, and come back the next morning to do it all over again. For these Israeli soldiers, killing Palestinians was simply a task that could be paused and repeated.There was no hesitation in their voices, no sense that they were describing something that should be difficult to say aloud. They spoke with the ease of people who had learned how to do this, how to talk about it and how to carry on afterward – as one of them put it, with “zero” consideration for the lives they annihilated.NAZA makes visible the targeting systems and planning decisions that precede a strike. But this is only part of the story.Some of the perpetrators were on the ground in Gaza, where the same violence became much more immediate as they moved through Palestinian neighbourhoods, entering homes, setting them on fire and enforcing “kill zones”.Yet for every act shown on film, there are many others that were never recorded and so will never be reckoned with – the constant surveillance, the restrictions on movement, the displacement of entire populations. NAZA opens a small window into the machinery of killing in Gaza, but it is something much larger than any film can capture.View image in fullscreenA scene from NAZA, a documentary produced by the Guardian and directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.Photograph: The GuardianThroughout the screening, I could not stop myself from putting names back into the places where the film placed numbers. When one soldier described how Israeli forces massacred Palestinians at aid distribution sites, I thought of my cousin, 35-year-old Raed Majed Mushtaha, killed in the “Flour Massacre” in early 2024 as he searched for food for his family. I remembered my friend Youssef Maher Dawas, killed in the first week of the genocide, whose body was later found beneath rubble.Other soldiers described how the army authorised the killing of 20 civilians in pursuit of a single junior target, and as many as 500 in pursuit of a senior target. These targets, however, had predominantly been “incriminated” by an AI system that, the soldiers admit, was known to err in about 15% of cases – yet they killed them anyway, along with their whole families.I felt stuck on that. I thought about my uncle, Hisham Zafer Mushtaha, his wife, Hanan, their sons, Basel and Mohammed, and their four grandchildren, Raged, Hisham, Lana and Abdrahman, aged between three and 12 years old. I imagined them being killed because an AI algorithm assumed there might be a target there.For the soldiers, these moments are merely part of a daily “mission”. But Raed, Youssef, Hisham, Hanan, Basel, Mohammed, Raged, Hisham, Lana and Abdrahman were people I knew and loved, whose calls I waited for, whose absence will for ever be felt.For so long, I had asked how these people I knew were killed. Watching the film, my mind kept returning to the opposite question: how did I survive? I had spent so much of my life in Gaza thinking that, because I did not belong to any faction, I would be safe. I believed that if Israel was justifying its killings to the world by portraying those it killed as military targets, then I would make it out alive, because I was not one of them.But the difference between me and the people I’ve lost may have been nothing more than what an AI algorithm flagged, and what someone decided, through a screen in Tel Aviv, would be an acceptable amount of NAZA. I realised, perhaps for the first time, that there was no precaution that I could have taken that would have guaranteed my survival. The fact that I did survive was completely random. And when I think about that, my heart sinks.What I want, watching this, is not catharsis. I have had enough of that. I want to attach names to the soldiers themselves – the ones who said it was “fun” to destroy Gaza, who viewed Palestinians in Gaza as mere data points. This is the only way that the “systematic” nature of Israel’s killing machine stops functioning as a shield, one that allows those responsible to feel as if they were mere cogs.When the film ended, I called my family in Gaza, as I do every night. I have rung them often to tell them where to move and which road to avoid, hoping to keep them safe amid the ongoing senseless destruction. But having watched the film, I kept thinking about surveillance and systems that track their movements and could turn them into targets.But sitting there after the film, a new thought took over: what if the soldiers watching them know more about where my family are than I do? What if they can see what I cannot? My family might be sitting together, drinking tea, laughing at something one of my brothers said, while, somewhere far away, those same moments could already be data on a screen.And as I spoke to them that night, for a moment I forgot everything I had seen in the film. I did not hear coordinates, or surveillance, or AI. I heard my family. A familiar voice. A breath. And I understood, in that moment, what these systems can never account for: that each person on the screen is an entire world unto themselves.After its screening at the Venice film festival,the film received a 25-minute standing ovation– an indictment, I couldn’t help thinking, of a western media that spent three years treating Palestinian journalists as unreliable narrators of our own deaths. A room rose to its feet, but that has not stopped the machine: the bombing hasn’t stopped, the machine on screen is still running even as the credits roll.I’m glad the testimony exists; glad it’s believed now. But belief this late, costing us this much, is not safety. My people do not feel safer because a film about their killers received applause in a theatre they will never sit in.Mahmoud Mushtaha is a Palestinian journalist from Gaza, and the author of Sobrevivir al genocidio en Gaza (Surviving the Genocide in Gaza). title: How’s your apocalypse stockpiling coming on? Three weeks in, mine has hit a few snags | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: Cans of tuna, sparkling water and an old torch – if the end of the world came for me now I’d struggle, but it’s hard to know how to prepare for an unknown threat, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: Cans of tuna, sparkling water and an old torch – if the end of the world came for me now I’d struggle, but it’s hard to know how to prepare for an unknown threat, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Content: ‘I’m not really prepared, and the biggest deficit in my unpreparedness is, evidently, my attitude.’Photograph: Lucy Ray/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘I’m not really prepared, and the biggest deficit in my unpreparedness is, evidently, my attitude.’Photograph: Lucy Ray/AlamyOpinionEmergency planningHow’s your apocalypse stockpiling coming on? Three weeks in, mine has hit a few snagsEmma BrockesCans of tuna, sparkling water and an old torch – if the end of the world came for me now I’d struggle, but it’s hard to know how to prepare for an unknown threatThu 17 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 10.46 EDTShareIt’s been three weeks since the government advisory urging us to startstockpiling in case of emergency– how’s your prep coming along? The Prepare campaign, backed by Wes Streeting, who one imagines gliding through the apocalypse, quiff undisturbed, listed nine essential items, among them wet wipes, first-aid kits and batteries. The World Health Organization, meanwhile, suggests budgeting for15 litres of waterper person per day, so a family of four will need to store upwards of 180 litres to cover the recommended period of three days. The chances of this actually happening seem to me, intuitively, to be considerably lower than the disaster they’re supposed to forestall. But hope springs, so let’s see.The first step towards stockpiling is stocktaking. This is where I’m at: one mega-torch (uncharged), which I bought in prepper mode after surviving the terrifying New York blackout of 2019 when for about an hour we couldn’t charge our phones; lots of very large sticking plasters and a handful of small round ones, the normal sizes having long been used up; two cans of tuna, which will go down to one after lunch; two litres of sparkling water, so for the first hour or so after a nuclear strike, assuming it happens this afternoon, we’ll at least be able to enjoy some bubbles; and three OxyContin saved from my c-section almost 12 years ago, which are probably less powerful than homeopathy at this point but I retain a vague hope I can use for barter when money breaks down.In other words, I’m not really prepared and the biggest deficit in my unpreparedness is, evidently, my attitude. On the evidence of what appeared to be a collective shrug, recently, when we wereinformed of the threats posed by AI, it’s an attitude problem that’s widely shared. It’s not that we don’t care, perhaps, but that it is hard to know what to do. By which I mean, it’s hard to know what to do that doesn’t involve giving over precious closet space to 40 two-litre bottles of water or disrupting our thought patterns to accommodate large, uncomfortable truths.In other words, if this is a collective failure of imagination, then what’s needed is some rigorous thought experiments that address our inability to imagine the worst. It’s wild that this should be necessary six years after a global pandemic, but of course, if there’s one thing to be said about humankind, it’s our ability to go scorched earth on recent trauma and pretend like nothing ever happened. This is called resilience – and there are, I’m sure, good evolutionary reasons for it, yet in this case it’s unhelpful. From scratch, then, we must develop what the government calls “household resilience”, which in my house means learning not to go into meltdown when someone can’t find their favourite hoodie or we run out of Nutella, or the Russians aim a missile towards our area.With this in mind, I would recommend browsing something called thelocal resilience forum, made up of regional lists of potential threats starting with “nuclear attack by a state on the UK mainland”, working down through pandemics, biblical droughts, floods, and the collapse of the National Grid, all the way to the threat posed by “space weather”. It’s very When the Wind Blows, and if it’s hard to square with real world scenarios, I suspect it’s because when you put something in local government language and stick it in a table, any sense of threat collapses beneath the sheer weight of boredom.For real imaginative engagement, we must turn to the fiction writers. The scene I go to in my head is the opening pages of Emily St John Mandel’s Station Eleven, in which a character called Jeevan, tipped off by a doctor friend that a pandemic is coming that will kill 99% of the world’s population, runs to a supermarket, shackles seven big shopping carts together and buys enough food and water to barricade himself in his apartment for 58 days, until the first panic has passed.So, as long as Tesco is open and I can beat the rush, perhaps things will work out just fine? I know there are some walnuts at the back of the cupboard. We could take the batteries out of the remote to use in the torch. Per The Day After Tomorrow, I have plenty of books for firewood, and worst-case scenario, can wear the cats for extra warmth. And while water is a problem, I think about that couple whosurvived in a tiny boatin the middle of the Pacific for 118 days, and imagine we will figure it out. I can catch the drips from the freezer as it defrosts and suck the gel from the aloe vera. See? Already thinking like a survivor. We’ve got this!skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEmma Brockes is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsEmergency planningOpinionFoodcommentShareReuse this content

title: Raheem Sterling’s bleak tale a reminder of absurd path young footballers face | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The winger was one of the first big-money academy transfers, part of a child labour market that has barely been questioned
Author: Jonathan Liew
Headline: The winger was one of the first big-money academy transfers, part of a child labour market that has barely been questioned
Content: Raheem Sterling’s sporting career may have come to a hard stop at the age of 31.Photograph: Pro Shots/AlamyView image in fullscreenRaheem Sterling’s sporting career may have come to a hard stop at the age of 31.Photograph: Pro Shots/AlamySoccerRaheem Sterling’s bleak tale a reminder of absurd path young footballers faceJonathan LiewWinger was one of the first big-money academy transfers, part of a  child labour market that has barely been questionedThu 17 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTShare“What’s your name?”“Raheem.”“What’s your surname?”“Sterling.”This is how a story ends. At 9.13 on a glorious May morning, by the side of the A327, sitting in the passenger seat of a wrecked Lamborghini, feverishly stashing canisters of nitrous oxide into the back, having to recite one’s name from scratch. A police officer asks him who was driving the car at the time it smashed into a metal pole on a country road in Hampshire. Sterling says nothing. There’s nobody sitting in the driver’s seat.As it transpired in court in Basingstoke this week, Sterling had been up driving all night by the time police started getting calls from members of the public concerned that someone was bobbing and weaving up the M3 in an unpredictable, uncontrollable manner. And of course there is an acrid and tasteless irony in the fact that this was exactly what Sterling was known for on the pitch: weaving in and out of traffic, no order or reason to it, following a logic that existed only in his own head.We can, and we should, and the district judge did, take an extremely dim view of the serious and life-threatening crime to which Sterling has admitted. We can also acknowledge that football is the one and only reason any of this remotely registered on our radar. You are not angry at the other dangerous drivers, whose names you do not know and will never look up. You are angry at this one in particular, a £50m footballer four years ago, nowfacing the possibility of prisonand a sporting career that may just have come to a hard stop at the age of 31.View image in fullscreen‘The end of Sterling as a going concern really happened much earlier, about the time his Arsenal loan deal ended.’Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersYep: younger than Kepa Arrizabalaga, younger than Solly March, younger than Ariana Grande. And let’s be real, the end of Sterling as a going concern really happened much earlier, about the time his Arsenal loan deal ended and Enzo Maresca made clear he had no further use for him at Chelsea and he was made to train on his own after 8pm despite having young children, and Maresca said this was no big deal, because people in the fishing industry also work hard hours.In a way, Sterling became a victim of the cycle he helped to catalyse. At the age of 15, he became one of the first big-money academy transfers when he moved from Queens Park Rangers to Liverpool for a fee of up to £2m. More than a decade on, the increasing emphasis on one‑on‑one duels, on straight-line speed and dynamic dribbling, on unpredictable and unmapped movement, has generated a kind of fetish for unscarred teenage footballers, a self-perpetuating market in child labour that nobody has ever really begun to question, much less challenge.The Premier League’s centre of gravity has been shifting younger for years, to the point where last season half its players were 25 or younger. The three youngest Premier League debuts (Jeremy Monga,Max Dowman, Ethan Nwaneri) have taken place since 2022. Farther afield players such as Lamine Yamal (La Liga debut at 15) andCavan Sullivan(Major League Soccer debut at 14) have begun to normalise the trope of the child footballer, the athlete propelled to global superstardom before they can legally buy a vape.This week it has been widely reported that JJ Gabriel, a talented and highly coveted 15-year-old attacking midfielder,has demanded to leave the Manchester United academy. Let’s assume for the sake of argument that Gabriel didn’t walk into the offices of the Daily Telegraph and plant this story himself. So what we really have here, in essence, is an entire locus of gossip – briefings, counter-briefings, whispers, internet spume, back-page splashes – centred on a child.View image in fullscreenIt has been widely reported that JJ Gabriel has demanded to leave Manchester United.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAAnd before we even get into the myriad safeguarding issues, it’s worth reflecting on the financial incentives involved here. As scouting networks broaden and deepen, as clubs increasingly remodel themselves as trading vehicles, the premium on exclusive young talent has become unignorable. Should Gabriel leave United he will undoubtedly have his pick of Europe’s top clubs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPlayers and their representatives have also begun to recognise their rarefied value in this market. In a previous era Michael Carrick might have had the luxury of integrating Gabriel gradually into the United first team, taking a long-term view of his development, much as Mikel Arteta has done withDowman at Arsenal. But of course if Lamine Yamal is playing first-team football at 15, then why not JJ Gabriel? If every big club in Europe is looking for the next big star, then who ultimately holds the power in this relationship: the kid or one of the biggest football clubs in the world?And this is absurd, and it is intentionally absurd, and it is no defence of Sterling’s subsequent actions to point out that this is basically a ridiculous path upon which to dispatch a human being: festooned with unimaginable riches as a teenager, placed at the very centre of things, cast on to the scrap heap by 29. This is an unbelievably weird life, one that starts so wildly and violently beyond the boundaries of normative society that it’s a wonder anyone manages to stay remotely sane within it.The life-changing money, the scrutiny, the lack of privacy, the intermediaries and handlers, the winnowing of trust, the noise beyond the windows, the strangers demanding a piece of you, at a time when – remember –you are still a childand this entire lifestyle has been sold to you as the ultimate aspiration. Remember, you’re supporting the whole family now. Gabriel’s original surname, taken from his father and agent, was reportedly changed from O’Cearuill to Gabriel because it was easier to pronounce and therefore more marketable.I guess the point here is that nobody has as much agency over their career as they might like. The young modern footballer exists at the mercy of forces barely within their control. Their job is contingent on so many others: the coaches who train their skills, the medical staff who manage their workload, the teammates who pass to them, the support network that might just dissuade them from getting into a car with a load of nitrous oxide balloons in the early hours of the morning.And by any measure, Sterling is one of the lucky ones. The teenager who made it, who scaled the peaks, won 82 international caps, four league titles, worked under one of the greatest managers of all time, who tasted the manna even if it eventually choked him. How many other thousands of lives you will never see have been fruitlessly and callously bent and twisted towards this world: skills you will never witness, names you will never hear? How much humanity are we prepared to fling into this machine in order for it to provide us with entertainment?Perhaps in the post-Ronaldo/Messi era we are beginning to shake the idea that great individual players can bend the arc of history to their will, a fallacy we may as well call the Ballon d’Or Industrial Complex. Injuries, circumstance, tactical trends, physical shifts, the inevitability of time and tide: these are the handmaidens of talent, its trade winds, its lucky charms. Gaze at any footballing prodigy from afar and you’ll see a seductive blur of gift and privilege. But look closely enough and you’ll notice that the driver’s seat is empty.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Take good care of your tailbone. I didn’t – and my derriere has never been the same since | Adrian Chiles | The Guardian
description: My coccyx still hurts from an extreme cycling challenge almost two decades ago. Is there anything it’s good for, asks Adrian Chiles
Author: Adrian Chiles
Headline: My coccyx still hurts from an extreme cycling challenge almost two decades ago. Is there anything it’s good for, asks Adrian Chiles
Content: ‘There’s a long list of aches, pains and assorted maladies about which to mutter.’Photograph: RealPeopleGroup/Getty Images (posed by a model)View image in fullscreen‘There’s a long list of aches, pains and assorted maladies about which to mutter.’Photograph: RealPeopleGroup/Getty Images (posed by a model)OpinionHealth & wellbeingTake good care of your tailbone. I didn’t – and my derriere has never been the same sinceAdrian ChilesMy coccyx still hurts from an extreme cycling challenge almost two decades ago. Is there anything it’s good for?Thu 17 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 06.18 EDTShare‘Welcome to middle age.” This is what my GP said to me 10 years ago when I asked her why I needed this pill or that. Being then just shy of 50, that hit home. Now being just shy of 60, I mutter those words to myself at least once a day. There’s a long list of aches, pains and assorted maladies about which to mutter. High up on that list are my shoulders. Bloody agony, both of them. Picking something off a high shelf or fishing for something on the back seat of the car have had to become planned events to be undertaken only if absolutely necessary.I interviewed Prof Alice Roberts this week. A writer, broadcaster, academic, anatomist, archaeologist and sometime medical doctor, she knows her bones, and no mistake. I noted with interest that her PhD thesis was titled “Rotator cuff disease in humans and apes: a palaeopathological and evolutionary perspective on shoulder pathology”. I’ve rarely felt so connected with my ancestors, so human, and indeed so ape-like. In an instant my shoulder pain became easier to bear, as I felt at one with a caveman wincing as he reached up to apply the finishing touches to some wall art.After the radio show I was full of regret that I didn’t get time to ask her about another bone with which I’ve had my troubles: the coccyx. Mine has not been the same since I did some extreme cycling for Sport Relief with Alan Shearer 18 years ago. To this day, every so often if I sit wrong, I get a very nasty kind of electric shock shooting up from my derriere.When I asked Roberts later about matters of the coccyx, she didn’t disappoint. As it happens, she, too, has had coccyx problems, damaging hers when she fell off a table on which she was dancing. Impressive. As, predictably, is her knowledge of this area. She told me the coccyx consists of tiny, fused vertebrae that finish off your vertebral column at the bottom, or rather,inthe bottom. Given that this remnant of a tailbone can’t be wagged, you may wonder if there’s any point to this little pointy thing. Well, without it there would be nothing to attach the pelvic floor muscles to, at the back. And that, she said, would result in your pelvic viscera falling out, which sounds awful. So look after your coccyx, at all costs.Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
