But maybe it’s slightly weaker than the one that’s attached. But it’s a weird one: you can still run and I haven’t missed any training the last three weeks. I’ve just had to alter my approach.”View image in fullscreenHodgkinson has taken confidence from good performances this season despite injury struggles.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAHodgkinson can still look on her 800m season with pride, having broken the indoor world record in February, won the world indoor title in March, and then set a personal best outdoors in June.“Obviously I would have loved to tick every goal that I wanted to do this year, but I’m 24,” said Hodgkinson.Asked why she had decided to run at the Ultimate Championships in Budapest and at Athlos, despite having done little speed work, Hodgkinson replied that she wanted to prove to herself she could compete in far from ideal circumstances.“What if it happened in an Olympic year? I’m not saying it will and, touch wood, it doesn’t. But I know that I can do this, regardless of if stuff goes right or wrong, and I can still perform with the best in the world. That’s given me confidence.”Hodgkinson is one of the headline actsat the all-female Athlos meeting, which also includes the Paris 2024 200m gold medallist Gabby Thomas and the former world 100m champion Sha’Carri Richardson.Athlos’ acting president, Kayla Green, said that with the event having a red carpet, multiple celebrities in attendance, and DJ Trauma on the decks, it would feel different to a typical athletics meeting.“Fans are going to walk away and say the competition and athleticism on the track was second to none, but the experience itself was something that made them really have a great time,” she said. “It will also be epic to watch on TV.”Explore more on these topicsKeely HodgkinsonAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Aaron Rai shrugs off early nerves to outshine playing partner Rory McIlroy | Golf | The Guardian
description: For all the talk of Rory McIlroy shooting 60 in a pro-am, his playing partner Aaron Rai’s first-round 66 put the Masters champion in the shade at Wentworth
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: For all the talk of Rory McIlroy shooting 60 in a pro-am, his playing partner Aaron Rai’s first-round 66 put the Masters champion in the shade at Wentworth
Content: Aaron Rai said he felt ‘really nervous’ about partnering Rory McIlroy but outscored the Masters champion by three.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAView image in fullscreenAaron Rai said he felt ‘really nervous’ about partnering Rory McIlroy but outscored the Masters champion by three.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAGolfAaron Rai shrugs off early nerves to outshine playing partner Rory McIlroyUS PGA champion shoots 66 to share lead with LagergrenPair lead by one from Gerard and Scott at WentworthEwan Murrayat WentworthThu 17 Sep 2026 12.10 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat do you get for shooting 60 in a pro-am? Just ask Rory ­McIlroy. ­“Nothing,” said the Masters ­champion. “Besides a social media post I didn’t want.” McIlroy was laughing but the underlying ­sentiment was obvious: exceptional rounds are best saved for the real stuff.News that McIlroy had taken only 60 shots around Wentworth’s West Course while in the company of ­celebrities was a hot topic of ­conversation going in to this PGA Championship. ­McIlroy shrugged off the score as something he ­produces fairly regularly. “It doesn’t mean anything,” he added. “My ­playing partners were happy, they won something.”Top golfers to get no favours for PGA Tour return after LIV bankruptcyRead moreHowever, this would have done nothing to improve the state of mind of Aaron Rai. The 31-year-old may be a major champion on account of ­heroics inthis year’s US PGA ­Championshipbut he ­admitted to trepidation about playing in ­McIlroy’s company at Wentworth. Not that Rai displayed any sense of fear; his 66 outscored McIlroy by three. Ryan Fox, the other member of this illustrious group, signed for a 68. Day one honours belonged to the popular Rai.“I felt really nervous,” said Rai. “I can’t remember feeling that ­nervous on a Thursday. It’s an amazing ­experience to be playing with the likes of Rory.“I definitely thought about it before we started today, a bit this morning and a bit the last couple of days when I found out what the draw was. Obviously it’s really amazing to be out there with Ryan and Rory. I am just really pleased that I got into the round pretty fast and that I continued to play well.“It’s a place that I’ve enjoyed before I even competed in the event here. I used to come here as a junior and watch the event and absolutely love it. I’ve started to play really well here over the last three or four years or so. So it’s a place that I enjoy and it’s always good coming here.” Indeed, Rai’s score tied the early lead with Joakim Lagergren. The lead is one from Ryan Gerard and Adam Scott.McIlroy remains in the middle of technical changes as he seeks to remove bad habits from his swing. “It definitely still looks better on the range than it does when I get out there on the course,” said the Northern Irishman. “But over time, if I just keep to what I’m doing, it will hopefully start to bed in.” McIlroy had been five under inside 10 holes before having to settle for minus three.View image in fullscreenRory McIlroy has been remodelling his swing.Photograph: Matthew Childs/ReutersPatrick Reed’s 68 was significant as he looks to hold off McIlroy in the DP World Tour’s season-long order of merit. Reed and McIlroy have jousted in plenty of environments before, yet on this occasion the American insists it is not personal.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Any time I get to go play against Rory, it’s always fun because that means you get to play some ­amazing golf,” Reed said. “With his record and the résumé that he has, he’s a ­champion. He’s been a champion a ton of times and he’s one of those guys that if you go up against the best, you’re going to have to take him and Scottie [Scheffler] on. To have the opportunity to take him on throughout the whole rest of the year is going to be fun.” Reed said if he denies McIlroy what would be a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title, he will only be delaying the inevitable.McIlroy has no fears about ­ending the DP World Tour’s ­season in the United Arab ­Emirates. Matt ­Fitzpatrick admitted on ­Wednesdayhe is not comfortablewith ­participating in events in Abu Dhabi and Dubai amid the ongoing Middle East ­conflict. “If the local governments feel like it’s safe to put on these events, they are not going to put their citizens or people ­visiting in harm’s way,” said McIlroy. “I love the Middle East. I have a lot of friends there and I’m looking forward to going back for sure.”Explore more on these topicsGolfRory McIlroyAaron RainewsShareReuse this content

title: Nato head: Britain must show ‘credible path’ of annual defence budget increases | Nato | The Guardian
description: Mark Rutte said Britain will need to steadily increase defence spending to meet Nato target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Mark Rutte said Britain will need to steadily increase defence spending to meet Nato target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035
Content: Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, spoke with the Press Association following meetings with Ed Miliband and Wes StreetingPhotograph: The Ditchley Foundation/PAView image in fullscreenNato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, spoke with the Press Association following meetings with Ed Miliband and Wes StreetingPhotograph: The Ditchley Foundation/PANatoNato head: Britain must show ‘credible path’ of annual defence budget increasesMark Rutte said Britain will need to steadily increase defence spending to meet Nato target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035Dan SabbaghDefence and security editorThu 17 Sep 2026 15.29 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain needs to show “a credible path” of annual increases in its defence budgets to meet aNatotarget of spending nearly £30bn more on the military by the middle of the next decade, the head of the alliance said on Thursday.Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, said that Britain could not wait until just before 2035 to lift defence spending to 3.5% of GDP, in an unusually pointed intervention a day after he met prime ministerAndy Burnham.In an interview with the Press Association, he said: “And that is why you need a credible path towards that 3.5%, and yearly increments.”The alliance’s secretary general, a former Dutch prime minister, made similar remarks to the BBC, where he said that the UK understood that the target could not be met “in one go in 2034” and that it would have to be achieved gradually.Earlier on Thursday, Rutte met withWes Streeting, the defence secretary, and Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary. He saw Burnham on Wednesday, at a business park in Didcot, and also met representatives from the defence industry.Keir Starmer signed the UK up to a Nato-wide target of increasing defence spending to 3.5% of GDP in the summer of 2025, under pressure from the US president, Donald Trump. The figure has since been endorsed by Burnham and his chancellor, former defence secretary John Healey.Current spending plans, covering until 2028/9, show defence spending levelling off at 2.7%, nearly £30bn below the ultimate target, raising the question of how it would be achieved after the next general election. It is unclear if taxes or borrowing would have to rise, or other government spending cuts.Healey resigned as defence minister in June because Starmer would not commit to lifting defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. At the time Healey said Labour needed to set “a clear path” to meet the Nato commitment, similar language to that used by Rutte in his interviews.But since then Healey and Burnham have avoided committing to the 3% by the end of the decade. Decisions on future spending are likely to be left to the next government spending review due next year, prompting the Nato leader to engage in public lobbying on his trip to Britain.Rutte said he was certain the Burnham government remained behind the ultimate goal and the need to increase defence spending gradually. “I am absolutely confident that when it comes to the yearly increments, they totally take it and accept it, that they have to be there,” he told the BBC.“There has to be a credible path. What that credible path exactly will be, we will see with the spending review next year,” Rutte added.A day earlier, Rutte gave a speech toat Ditchley Park in Oxfordshire, in which he warned that the 32 country military alliance faced “the most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation” with wars in Ukraine, the Middle East coming at time of rising state competition.Nato needed “more UK and more Europe”, he added, to take up the slack as the US reduces its military commitment to the alliance. Trump has long argued that the UK and Europe should match US levels of defence spending and take the lead in defending the continent from Russia aggression.Explore more on these topicsNatoMark RutteAndy BurnhamEd MilibandWes StreetingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Greens urge Zack Polanski to take stance on proposed policy declaring ‘Zionism is racism’ | Zack Polanski | The Guardian
description: The Green leader has not spoken publicly about the motion, which is likely to be debated at the party’s conference in October
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: The Green leader has not spoken publicly about the motion, which is likely to be debated at the party’s conference in October
Content: A senior member of the Green party said the proposal put Polanski ‘in a difficult position’.Photograph: Aldo Ciarrocchi/AlamyView image in fullscreenA senior member of the Green party said the proposal put Polanski ‘in a difficult position’.Photograph: Aldo Ciarrocchi/AlamyZack PolanskiGreens urge Zack Polanski to take stance on proposed policy declaring ‘Zionism is racism’Exclusive: The Green leader has not spoken publicly about the motion, which is likely to be debated at the party’s conference in OctoberPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentThu 17 Sep 2026 13.06 EDTFirst published on Thu 17 Sep 2026 12.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Greens are pushingZack Polanskito take a stance on a potential party policy stating “Zionism is racism”, with some fearing it could alienate Jewish supporters if it was passed.Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales, has not spoken publicly about the motion, which came top of a members’ vote of policy motions to be debated at the party conference in Brighton at the start of October, and is thus almost certain to feature.The Greens make party policy by member votes at conferences. If passed, the motion would equate Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – with racism, would call for a single Palestinian state, and would risk members who supported Zionism being disciplined for racism.While Polanski is believed to have reservations about the motion, some in the party believe he is wary of speaking out publicly to avoid angering left-leaning members who have joined the Greens in large numbers under his leadership, a number of whom have strong views on Gaza and Israel.“Zack can try to be everything to everyone, and that doesn’t always work in politics,” one senior Green said. “But he is in a difficult position. Some of the supporters of the motion can be quite aggressive.”A motion with the same title was submitted to the Greens’ spring conference but was never debated due to time constraints.If the motion had been debated, it is understood that the party’s MPs and Polanski would have opposed it.Polanski has not given a view yet this time but is understood to have concerns about any motion that could leave Jewish members feeling unwelcome in the party, or which could be seen as not helping a peace process.Some in the party view the coming weeks, and whether Polanski takes a stance or not, as a test of his leadership, and whether he is willing to challenge some of the new Green members, particularly those who were formerly in Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGreens just four points behind Labour in urban areas, poll revealsRead moreThe motion calls for “a single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital, equal rights for all, and the right of return for Palestinians and their descendants”, and says the Palestinian people have the full right to “resistance and liberation from Israeli occupation, domination and subjugation” within international law.If passed, Zionism “will be treated as any other form of racism” by the party, it adds.Two amendments to tone down the motion have been tabled, which one Green source said Polanski appeared to support.A Green official said that many activists loyal to the party’s leadership might not be at the autumn conference because it takes place a week before voting in theHolborn and St Pancras byelection, in which Polanski hopes to take Keir Starmer’s old seatfrom Labour, potentially leaving more scope for others to push through the motion.“The risk is that if it passes as it is we are alienating ourselves from the Jewish community in the UK, a lot of whom are not big fans of the current Israeli government,” a Green source said.There was, they added, a parallel worry about internal splits, with some Green activistsin leakedWhatsApp chats warning that Polanski was “struggling to overcome Zionist indoctrination”.They said: “In the past, even highly contested policy debates in the Greens have always been conducted in a mature and sensible way, even [a] boring way. Now it’s changed.”Explore more on these topicsZack PolanskiGreen partyAntisemitismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sway, Mobo-winning British rapper, dies aged 44 | Music | The Guardian
description: Rapper won prestigious award as an unsigned artist before breaking UK Top 10 and nurturing artists including KSI
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Rapper won prestigious award as an unsigned artist before breaking UK Top 10 and nurturing artists including KSI
Content: Sway in 2005.Photograph: Tony Buckingham/RedfernsView image in fullscreenSway in 2005.Photograph: Tony Buckingham/RedfernsMusicSway, Mobo-winning British rapper, dies aged 44Rapper won prestigious award as an unsigned artist before breaking UK Top 10 and nurturing artists including KSIBen Beaumont-ThomasThu 17 Sep 2026 12.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 13.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British rapper Sway, who proved inspirational to a generation of Black British musicians thanks to his independence and frank, dextrous storytelling, has died aged 44.The news was announced by the Mobo awards, with whom Sway won best hip-hop act in 2005, the first unsigned act to do so. “Proud to have him as part of our history. Our love goes out to his family, loved ones and fans,” the statement read.It was confirmed to the Guardian via a close friend, who said he died at his home in Ghana. No cause of death has been announced.Born Derek Safo, and later known as Sway Dasafo, he was born in Hornsey, north London, to Ghanaian parents, and as well as training as a producer, he honed a versatile rap flow that could be deployed on high-tempo grime and club tracks as well as thoughtful hip-hop leaning material.That versatility meant that he didn’t fit into any one scene: “UK garage was big at this time but I just couldn’t do it because I never felt the vibe of the scene suited me,” he said. “British hip-hop was just so dry and grey, hiplife was a no-no ‘cause I couldn’t rap in Twi, drum’n’bass just hurts my head sometimes and I can’t sing good so R&B was out the question! I never felt at home anywhere.”He started out in the groups Phynix Crew and One, before going solo and releasing a series of mixtapes. Breakout single Up Your Speed was a minor hit, but follow-up Little Derek – a manifesto for his own greatness, celebrating how “he ended up in HMV instead of HMP” – broke the UK Top 40 in 2006.It became a cornerstone track of his debut album This Is My Demo, which accrued critical acclaim – includinga four-star reviewin the Guardian – and his Mobo award, where he beat the much more established likes of 50 Cent and the Game. The album was also nominated for the Mercury prize, losing out to the Arctic Monkeys’ debut.Safo continued to release via his own Dcypha Productions label but entered into a partnership with Konvict Music, the label from Senegalese-American pop star Akon, who was one of the guests on the next Sway album, 2008’s The Signature LP.View image in fullscreenSway performing in 2008.Photograph: Jim Dyson/Getty ImagesHe later admitted difficulties as his fame grew, citing “ego, too many lights, and too much confusion” around the time of The Signature LP, but continued to embrace a more commercial sound and generated his biggest chart successes: the Ride on Time-sampling Still Speedin’ became his first Top 20 hit in 2011 (and featured a guest verse from Kano), then was outdone by Level Up, produced by dubstep star Flux Pavilion, which reached No 8 the following year.Safo also collaborated with Riz Ahmed, appearing on the Riz MC track Shifty; Ed Sheeran, appearing on his No 5 Collaborations Project EP; was courted for tracks by the US rappers Lupe Fiasco and Chamillionaire; and worked with other British rappers including Tinchy Stryder, Akala, Mitchell Brothers and Donae’o. He also crossed into other genres, guesting on Kaiser Chiefs’ third album Off With Their Heads.He nurtured artists on his own label and was instrumental in developing the career of KSI, who went on to have huge success as a YouTuber and musician. Safo and KSI had a minor hit together in 2013, No Sleep, featuring another young charge of Safo’s, the rapper Tiggs Da Author.He and his wife Helen married in 2013, and had four children: Jalil, AJ, Inaya and Imara. In a recent social media post Safo described himself as a single father.Explore more on these topicsMusicRapHip-hopMobosnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m genuinely sorry’: Australian Hyrox athlete who soiled herself apologises to China and rivals | Australia sport | The Guardian
description: Joanna Wietrzyk posts that she regrets her decision to keep racing but has decided to forfeit her win in the Beijing race
Author: Martin Farrer
Headline: Joanna Wietrzyk posts that she regrets her decision to keep racing but has decided to forfeit her win in the Beijing race
Content: Joanna Wietrzyk of Australia competes in the Hyrox event in Beijing.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJoanna Wietrzyk of Australia competes in the Hyrox event in Beijing.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesAustralia sport‘I’m genuinely sorry’: Australian Hyrox athlete who soiled herself apologises to China and rivalsJoanna Wietrzyk ‘regrets’ decision to keep racingShe forfeits points from her win in the Beijing raceMartin FarrerThu 17 Sep 2026 14.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 18.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Australian athlete who caused a storm by winning a Hyrox event in China despite soiling herself during the race has apologised to the “people of China” and rival athletes in a statement online.Posting on Instagram, Joanna Wietrzyk offered a “sincere apology” to the “people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the Hyrox organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing”.Footage of Wietrzyk, a world record-holder,went viralafter it showed her competing in – and winning – Saturday’s event with demanding exercises and using communal equipment, despite having faecal matter running down her legs.But she admitted in her post on Thursday night that she should have “stepped off the track” and that there was “more to life than racing”.Hyrox changes rules and apologises for allowing Australian athlete who soiled herself to continueRead more“I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness,” Wietrzyk wrote.“Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognise that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused.”She said she would forfeit the points from winning the event.“I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected. I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away. On reflection, I have decided to retroactively withdraw from the race and forfeit the points I earned.”Hyrox, an increasingly popular fitness competition launched in Germany in 2017, is now held in locations across the world. It made its debut in mainland China in late 2024.In each race, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises at shared high-intensity stations – including a rowing machine, sled pushes, burpee jumps, medicine ball throws and lunges while carrying a sandbag.Hyrox earlier this week apologised and pledged immediate rule changes after Wietrzyk was allowed to finish and win the Beijing event.Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste apologised in astatementon Instagram to everyone affected “directly or indirectly”.“Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race. In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents – and I did not,” Fürste said.He added that Hyrox had made “rulebook changes immediately”.“As of this moment, there are new rules and procedures in place to prevent situations like this from happening again.”Before the weekend’s incident, event rules penalised athletes for minor infractions such as littering on the course, or spitting or clearing their nose on the floor. But they contained no immediate protocol for faecal matter.Ending her Thursday statement, Wietrzyk said: “Thank you to those standing by me, both as an athlete and as a person, during this time, and to everyone who has reached out with kindness and support. It means more to me than I can properly express right now. I will be taking some time to recover, reflect and look after myself and my family away from the noise.”Explore more on these topicsAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump officials move to dismantle key protection for US endangered species | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Fish and Wildlife Service memo calls for change in what it means to ‘take’ an endangered species
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Fish and Wildlife Service memo calls for change in what it means to ‘take’ an endangered species
Content: Bowhead whales in shallow water in the Sea of Okhotsk.Photograph: Nature Picture Library/AlamyView image in fullscreenBowhead whales in shallow water in the Sea of Okhotsk.Photograph: Nature Picture Library/AlamyTrump administrationTrump officials move to dismantle key protection for US endangered speciesFish and Wildlife Service memo calls for change in what it means to ‘take’ an endangered speciesMaya YangThu 17 Sep 2026 17.28 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 20.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 1,600 critically imperiled species protected under the US Endangered Species Act (ESA) face losing further federal protections following a new reinterpretation of the 1973 law by the DonaldTrump administration.A September 14 memo distributed to Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) field offices by FWS director Brian Nesvik calls for a reinterpretation of what it means to “take” an endangered species.Under the ESA, “take” is defined as “to harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, or collect, or to attempt to engage in any such conduct”.Thememo, obtained and shared by the Center for Biological Diversity, reinterprets the law to mean that harming or killing an endangered animal would no longer be considered illegal unless the action was specifically intended to cause harm or death.“A vessel that inadvertently strikes a whale has not taken it, because the vessel’s course was not set against the whale,” the memo said, adding: “Felling a tree is not a take of the bats roosting in it unless the tree is felled for the purpose of killing or capturing them.”The reinterpretation effectively excludes economic activities such as logging, mining and industrial development from the ESA’s prohibition on “take” when those activities foreseeably kill or injure wildlife without intentionally targeting them.The memo follows the Trump administration’srepealin July of the ESA’s definition of prohibited “harm,” which was defined as “an act which actually kills or injures wildlife,” including acts that “may include significant habitat modification or degradation”.Interior secretary Doug Burgum justified the repeal in July bysaying: “For years, federal agencies abused the ESA to obstruct lawful land use and burden American families and businesses.”Earlier this month, 20 states and Washington DCsuedthe Trump administrationover its decisionto redefine “harm,” including removing “modification or degradation” of habitat from conduct that can constitute a prohibited take.In a statement on Thursday to the Guardian about the administration’s reinterpretation of “take,” the interior department, which oversees the FWS, said: “As outlined in the final rule, the department determined that the previous regulatory definition of ‘harm’ expanded the Endangered Species Act’s prohibition on ‘take’ beyond the text Congress enacted. The final rule restores that interpretation while maintaining the ESA’s core protections for listed species.”The memo has drawn swift backlash from environmental advocacy organizations. The Center for Biological Diversity pointed to the supreme court’s1995 6-3 decisionin Babbitt v Sweet Home Chapter of Communities for a Great Oregon, in which the majority rejected the argument that “take” is limited to actions deliberately directed against endangered species.“If you chop down a tree full of endangered birds or race a huge ship through a pod of endangered whales, you should be held accountable for your destructive acts,” Brett Hartl, the Center for Biological Diversity’s government affairs director,said.“But this administration wants to give wildlife killers a get out of jail free card. Imposing new limitations on the entire definition of take is a flagrant and illegal attempt to rewrite the Endangered Species Act via unilateral fiat. This would drive imperiled species over the cliff to extinction,” he added.Similarly, the environmental law nonprofit Earthjustice told the Guardian: “The government’s new legal position is a prescription for extinction. It says that as long as you claim you didn’t mean to kill an endangered species, the law can’t and won’t stop you. That’s ridiculous.“The supreme court decided this issue in the Sweet Home case and its ruling still represents the best reading of the Endangered Species Act. We’ll see the Trump administration in court about this.”The Trump administration’s reinterpretation of the ESA is the latest in a series of environmental rollbacks. Since returning to office last January, Trump has moved toweaken federal protectionsfor old-growth forests,potentially jeopardizing habitatfor 400 endangered species across the US;scrapped drilling restrictionsnear a world heritage site in New Mexico; and directed his administration toconsiderthe delisting of gray wolves from the ESA.During the signing ceremony for the latter, Trump asked: “You can shoot them as of today?” Agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins replied that Burgum “has to do a little magic, but yes”.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationShareReuse this content

title: ‘It bloody works’: why the world’s oldest cheddar-maker uses a ‘milk-source’ heat pump | Environment | The Guardian
description: Barber’s Farmhouse Cheesemakers can draw enough heat from cows’ fresh milk to bring water close to the boil, slashing carbon emissions
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Barber’s Farmhouse Cheesemakers can draw enough heat from cows’ fresh milk to bring water close to the boil, slashing carbon emissions
Content: Milk-source heat pumps have been described as ‘a slam-dunk opportunity’. Photograph: Peter Dean/AlamyBarber’s Farmhouse Cheesemakers can draw enough heat from cows’ fresh milk to bring water close to the boil, slashing carbon emissionsByAlison F TakemuraThu 17 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn many ways, the world’s oldest cheddar-maker hews to tradition. Since 1833, Barber’s Farmhouse Cheesemakers has operated from the rolling green pastures of south-west England, milking grass-fed cows and fermenting the milk with microbial starters passed down for generations. That heritage has led to award-winning cheese, now popular across continents.But when it comes to reducing its planet-warming emissions,Barber’sis on the cutting edge. In 2024, the company began to use new ultra-efficient heat pumps from the UK startupArkaya Energy. The devices quickly cool milk to keep it fresh, and simultaneously heat water used in milking operations, replacing conventional chillers and electric-resistance heaters.By cutting electricity use in half, the heat pumps are saving Barber’s about £70,000 a year – a ​“huge reduction,” said Alfie Barber, a seventh-generation cheesemaker and farm manager. At the same time, they are cutting carbon pollution by nearly 66 tons a year. The family has had these heat pumps installed at three of its seven milking parlours.“It is just a wonderful feeling … when we can save energy, save on the bottom line, and reduce our carbon footprint,” said Chris Barber, Alfie’s father and the farm director.All-electricindustrial heat pumps, which move heat rather than generating it from fossil fuels or running an electric current through a filament, are an ideal fit for decarbonising food production, asmost processesneed only low or medium temperatures, which the tech can readily provide. But food manufacturers have not exactly flocked to heat pumps. The appliances are an unfamiliar technology with a price premium, and rising electricity costsmake companies waryabout using them to replace fossil fuel options.View image in fullscreenHolstein friesian cattle in North Yorkshire. Farmers need hot water to wash udders, milk tanks, suction cups and other equipment.Photograph: John Bentley/AlamyBarber’s experience shows that early adopters can reap big payoffs – thanks largely to new advances in heat-pump technology.Almost allheat pumpsfall into three categories: air source, ground source and water source. Arkaya’s innovation is to draw heat not from the air or ground or a body of water, but from fresh milk, which comes out of the cow warm. It is ​“a predictable energy source whenever milking takes place”, said Arkaya’s founder, Kumo Sharma. The company calls its product a “milk-source heat pump”.Arkaya’s machines do the double duty of chilling milk to as low as 1.6C (35F) and diverting the waste heat to bring water to 92C (198F), close to a boil. Farmers need this hot water to wash udders, milk tanks, suction cups and other equipment to keep operations clean.For Barber’s, the payback on its heat pumps is less than two years – a welcome departure from the norm. ​“There’s not many investments that have [even] five-year paybacks,” Alfie said. ​“Every penny counts in our game.”The heat-recovery system Barber’s replaced had for years been considered the gold standard in the UK, Sharma said: an ice bank for cooling with a heat-recovery system that pre-warms water for washing up. However, it doesn’t get the job done on its own; it requires a boost from an electric-resistance or fossil-fuel-fired boiler to reach the necessary high temperatures.The milk-source heat pump ​“does that all combined in one system”, Sharma said. He declined to divulge some of the tech’s details, including what refrigerant it uses to move heat from milk to water.Arkaya, which began selling its heat pumps in 2024, has installed 27 to date and expects to deploy 34 more by the end of this year. The four-employee startup is, for now, focused on the UK market, home to nearly 7,000 dairy farms, and aims to increase its manufacturing capacity and grow its network of partner installers.Chris thinks Arkaya’s heat pump, whichwonthe Royal Association of British Dairy Farmers’ 2026 innovation award, could become a major player in the industry.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenArkaya Energy installed this milk-source heat pump (silver box, left), and water tanks that serve as thermal reservoirs, at one of Barber’s dairy farms in 2025.Photograph: Kumo Sharma/Arkaya EnergySharma said Arkaya planned to gradually expand into other countries, starting with Ireland and then the broader European market. The US would be a logical future target, too, he said, given the size of its dairy industry – nearly 25,000 dairy herds in 2024.Milking was one of the best applications for heat pumps, because dairy farmers had heating and cooling needs on site, said Ruth Checknoff, senior director at theRenewable Thermal Collaborative, a nonprofit working to decarbonise industrial heat. ​“This is like a slam-dunk opportunity.”Arkaya could find the field stateside wide open. While there are a number of firms offering other industrial heat-pump products for the dairy industry, including GEA, Frick and Tetra Pak, their tech appears to be geared toward processing dairy products at the factory rather than serving the needs of a humble milking parlour, according to Checknoff.“I haven’t run into anyone in the US that has a heat pump that will do all the final water heatings,” said Steve Koski, lead research engineer for industrial heat pumps atCascade Energy. Europe was likely ahead on heat-pump adoption because ​“they don’t have as cheap natural gas”, he said.Koski said that most new milking parlours in the US were being outfitted with money-saving heat-recovery systems, but these setups still needed additional heaters that used electric resistance, propane or, less commonly,fossil gas.Back in England, the Barbers are going all in on Arkaya’s heat pumps. They plan to convert their remaining milking parlours by 2028.“We’ve come across a technology that will be, possibly, the future of our dairy industry,” Chris said. ​“It bloody works.”A version of this article wasoriginally publishedin Canary Media and has been republished in the Guardian as part of ourClimateDeskpartnership.Explore more on these topicsThe alternativesCheeseFoodClimate crisisCattleFarmingShareReuse this content

title: 2025 was among driest years on record for world’s rivers, study finds | Environment | The Guardian
description: Analysis of global resources reveals depletion in world’s water savings bank to 42% below normal levels last year
Author: Sandra Laville
Headline: Analysis of global resources reveals depletion in world’s water savings bank to 42% below normal levels last year
Content: Usually submerged areas of the Danube were exposed in Rasova, Romania, in August amid exceptionally low water levels.Photograph: Robert Ghement/EPAView image in fullscreenUsually submerged areas of the Danube were exposed in Rasova, Romania, in August amid exceptionally low water levels.Photograph: Robert Ghement/EPAOur riversEnvironment2025 was among driest years on record for world’s rivers, study findsAnalysis of global resources reveals depletion in world’s water savings bank to 42% below normal levels last yearSandra LavilleandCarmen Aguilar GarcíaThu 17 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRivers across the world experienced one of their driest years in more than three decades in 2025, a comprehensive study of global water resources has found.The assessment of the global water cycle by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) reveals a depletion in the world’s water savings bank: the amount of freshwater held on or under the ground, including groundwater, lakes, rivers, snow, ice moisture in the soil and inside plants and trees, was 42% below normal across the world last year.The impacts of the climate crisis on extreme weather and the creation of so-called weather whiplash events are driving a more erratic and unpredictable water cycle. From melting glaciers to extreme droughts and flash flooding, the world’s rivers are swinging between having too much and too little water.Microplastics in soil pose global threat by acting like ‘Trojan horse’ to deliver toxinsRead moreThe last seven years have seen the fewest rivers around the world with “normal” flows since 1991. In 2025, one of the warmest years on record, only about a third of rivers were in the normal range, while 36% of the global river basin area had river flows below or well below normal, and 21% were above- and much-above-normal flows, according to the WMO study, using simulations from 13 global hydrological models, driven by observed weather data.Celeste Saulo, secretary general of the WMO, said: “We are depleting that savings account. Global terrestrial water storage has shown a declining trend since 2014–16 – a persistent, decade-long signal.”Last year, for the fourth year in a row, each of the world’s 19 major glacial regions lost ice mass. Glaciers have seen their greatest losses of ice mass since the 1990s, and the largest losses are the most recent. In 2025 alone the ice mass loss was 400 gigatons, which adds 1.1mm to global sea levels.Graphic showing river discharge conditions by regionThe analysis is a comprehensive, science-based assessment of the entire water cycle loop, including river flows, groundwater, evaporation and transpiration, land water storage, and snow and ice. Wayne Jenkinson, director of hydrology at the WMO, said the research was a call to action in the face of a continuing global picture of declining water resources.“We need to redouble our efforts to improve our understanding of water resources globally,” he said. “This requires increased data collection and sharing; that is how we increase understanding and protection for people’s lives and wellbeing.”The study is published as rivers across the world struggle against multiple threats caused by climate crisis-induced droughts, pollution and overexploitation.And the impact on our river systems has direct knock-on impacts for people, their wellbeing and the global economy.River discharge conditions by river basinThis summer record-low water levels on the Danube created an unprecedented energy crisis in Hungary and Romania, afterall but one of their nuclear reactors had to shut down because the river was too low to provide water to cool them.The Mississippi, which is the primary source of water for 50 US municipalities, is threatened by chemical pollution that has created hypoxic dead zones in the Gulf of Mexico, sea level rise that is hastening wetland loss andsaltwater intrusion, as well as intermittent droughts. Major African rivers such as the Nile, Niger and Zambezi face significant threats from severe pollution and climate-induced droughts that reduce water levels and harm local ecosystems.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn England not one river is in good overall ecological and chemical health. They are suffering from a toxic combination of sewage pollution, agricultural pollution, the impact offorever chemicalsand overabstraction.Record heatwaves bring Britain’s second-best butterfly season in 16 yearsRead moreThe WMO research shows the threat to rivers is continuing and, in some cases, accelerating. In 2025, for the seventh year in a row, the number of river basins with “normal” conditions was in a clear minority: ranging between 34 and 38%, compared with the average of 46% at normal conditions between 1991 and 2020, according to the report.Across the five years the WMO analysis has taken place, from 2021-25, repeated below-normal river flows were seen in major parts of the Amazon and La Plata basins, North America, central and east Africa, central Asia and the Middle East.View image in fullscreenA chemical plant on the Mississippi River upstream from the Quad Cities.Photograph: E. Jason Wambsgans/Chicago Tribune/Getty ImagesBelow-normal to much-below-normal river flows affected much of North America, the La Plata and São Francisco basins of South America, eastern European basins, the Middle East and central Asia.In each of the past five years, national meteorological and hydrological services around the globe reported record-breaking floods and droughts. Some places have had no recovery time between events.Over the next year, ina series called Our Rivers,the Guardian will focuson the environmental challenges facing the world’s rivers, looking at the waterways around the planetthat are overengineered or suffocating and drying up, and thosethat are being opened up again and given new lifeExplore more on these topicsEnvironmentOur riversRiversClimate crisisDroughtFloodingExtreme weatherMeteorologynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s beautiful when it’s clean’: the Argentine neighbourhood saving a contaminated river  | Environment | The Guardian
description: Sewage, dog carcasses and industrial waste clog Argentina’s second most-polluted river. Meet the activists cleaning it up
Author: Facundo Iglesia
Headline: Sewage, dog carcasses and industrial waste clog Argentina’s second most-polluted river. Meet the activists cleaning it up
Content: The workers’ cooperative cleans the Reconquista from Monday to Friday. But, says founder María Monges, ‘every day we will find rubbish.’Sewage, dog carcasses and industrial waste clog Argentina’s second most-polluted river. Meet the activists cleaning it upByFacundo IglesiaandCarmen Aguilar García; photographs by Anita Pouchard SerraThu 17 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwenty-three years ago, María Monges looked around her flooded neighbourhood and knew something had to be done.Founded in 1998 in Buenos Aires province’s San Martín district, the community of Costa Esperanza sits on the banks of the Reconquista, Argentina’s second most-polluted river and owes its name to the fictional location of a hit Argentine youth telenovela of the time, Verano del 98. But the real place is very different from the idyllic coastal city where the protagonists of Argentina’s answer to Dawson’s Creek met their first loves or sang around bonfires.View image in fullscreenA private truck loading waste in José León Suárez, Buenos Aires province, Argentina.“You don’t know what it was like – when we started cleaning up, all the streams were blocked up everywhere: rubbish, dead dogs … a bit of everything. It was unsanitary, but we carried on working anyway,” says Monges, now 61. She started knocking on doors, getting people out to work with her, and in 2005 got the provincial administration to give them tools, uniforms and training. Now Monges leads 9 de julio, a workers’ cooperative that, from Monday to Friday, cleans up streams flowing from the river. “Every day, we will find rubbish,” says Monges. “It’s like people don’t understand.”The Reconquista is 51 miles (82km) long, located in the north-east of the province of Buenos Aires and flows through 18 municipalities. About 4-5 million people live in its basin. It flows into the Luján River, which then connects with the Río de la Plata estuary.View image in fullscreenRubbish in the streets of José León Suárez.Since at least the 1970s, the river has been a dumping ground for untreated sewage, industrial waste and landfill leachate. It has the state sewage company on its banks, along with homes that lack adequate infrastructure, residents connecting their drainpipes so that waste is discharged directly into the water. Several factories located in the district of San Martín, known as “the Industrial Capital”, also throw their waste into the river.“All of this not only pollutes the water, but also the soil and the air. In this area there’s no access to drinking water … all the aquifers are contaminated,” says Natalia Gavazzo, an anthropologist and researcher at the National Scientific and Technical Research Council. Gavazzo directs the Migrantas en Reconquista project, which conducts research and carries out initiatives in the region to strengthen the socio-environmental strategies employed by women in the neighbourhoods of the Reconquista river basin. She adds that the environmental activism in Costa Esperanza is carried out primarily by women. “They are not just victims,” she says. “They are also the key agents of mitigation and adaptation; they possess a wealth of knowledge that is central to the survival of their communities.”But the Reconquista is just one of the troubled rivers in La Plata, the giant system that connects multiple waterways across Uruguay and Argentina. According to the World Meteorological Organization State of Global Water Resources report, out on Thursday, major parts of La Plata river basins have experienced recurring below-normal water levels between 2021 and 2025, caused by persistent multi-year drought conditions.La Plata basin includes the Paraguay River, which has consistently recorded water levels at their lowest since 2020. Analysis of WMO data shows that the Paraguay River’s water levels have been consistently below normal for the last six years, with its 25 driest months since 1991 registered after 2020.Graph showing Paraguay River water levelsThe drought and pollution issues plaguing La Plata and the Reconquista are affecting many more of the world’s rivers. As Gavazzo puts it, “climate change has an uneven impact around the world – the north produces the emissions, but we in the south foot the bill.” For the anthropologist, the same is true at a local scale. “People in gated communities throw out rubbish, but it ends up here,” she added.Juan Borús, who recently retired from the National Water Institute and is one of the country’s leading hydrologists, says that governments should “tackle every one of these sources of pollution individually, which is an extremely costly, painstaking task that requires regulation”, but that “companies that discharge complex effluents evade the rules … They’ve been doing it all their lives.”View image in fullscreenThe Reconquista, Argentina’s second most-polluted river.In 2001, the Buenos Aires province created the Reconquista River Basin Committee (Comirec) to clean it up, but it had limited impact, and parts of the river where Costa Esperanza is located still exhibit “severe deterioration”, according to its early 2026 reports. High levels of E coli (a bacterium that indicates the presence of fecal matter) and low levels of oxygen make it “not a suitable environment for aquatic life” and “a risk to the population”, according to Patricio Carmona, a biochemist specialising in environmental analysis.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLorena Batista, seen here in the organic community garden El Ceibo, says the smell of the Reconquista is ‘like an acid’.“The smell is like an acid,” says Lorena Batista, 47, a neighbour who works at the National Institute of Industrial Technology. “It is nauseating,” adds Zulma Monges, María’s daughter. The stench, they agree, becomes unbearable in summer, and when the wind blows they have to close their windows. It is not only the smell – neighbours have suffered from skin conditions such as hives, rashes, sores and scars, respiratory and lung problems, and gastrointestinal diseases, although Zulma says the skin conditions have become somewhat rarer since her mother’s community squad started picking up the rubbish.View image in fullscreenRosa Valencia at her grocery shop.Once a month, residents meet to discuss problems and contact representatives from the local government, to whom they address their concerns – accumulated rubbish or water cuts, for example. “It’s very much a part of our lives; it’s already become an integral part of the neighbourhood’s culture,” says grocer Rosa Valencia in her shop, laden with coconuts, plantains and yerba mate.And there are other efforts under way to clean up the river. The San Martín University’s School of Habitat and Sustainability is developing artificial wetlands – a nature-inspired method that could be installed on site to help filter out persistent pollutants and restore the area’s biodiversity. A group of several local organisations, Foro por la Recuperación del Río Reconquista, is campaigning for the creation of an ecological preserve. “Many years ago, before the landfill was built, that area was a large marshland with beaches,” they claim in their petition.View image in fullscreenZulma Monge works in the El Ceibo organic community garden in José León Suárez.“Older folks used to tell us: ‘we’d go fishing there, we’d spend our weekends there; there were always, always, always lots of animals’,” says Zulma Monges. The area, she says, is overpopulated, and “the few green spaces we do have, we’re maintaining them as a community”. Then she pulls out her phone and shows a picture of one of the streams, just after it was cleaned by her mother’s squad.“It’s beautiful when it’s clean,” she says. “The thing is, you have to stop the rubbish from reaching the neighbourhood. But this whole area … look, it’s beautiful.”Over the next year, in the Our Rivers series, we’ll be focusing on the environmental challenges facing the world’s rivers, looking at the waterways around the planetthat are overengineered or suffocating and drying up, and thosethat are being opened up again and given new life.Explore more on these topicsOur riversArgentinaAmericasfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Baby found wrapped in 1910 newspaper was killed with twine, UK inquest concludes | North of England | The Guardian
description: ‘Terrible thing’ happened to infant boy found under the floorboards at a house in Bishop Auckland, says coroner
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: ‘Terrible thing’ happened to infant boy found under the floorboards at a house in Bishop Auckland, says coroner
Content: Baby Auckland was laid to rest at Bishop Auckland cemetery in April.Photograph: Raoul Dixon/North News/North News & Pictures LtdView image in fullscreenBaby Auckland was laid to rest at Bishop Auckland cemetery in April.Photograph: Raoul Dixon/North News/North News & Pictures LtdNorth of EnglandBaby found wrapped in 1910 newspaper was killed with twine, UK inquest concludes‘Terrible thing’ happened to infant boy found under the floorboards at a house in Bishop Auckland, says coronerMark BrownNorth of England correspondentThu 17 Sep 2026 10.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 11.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA baby boy who was found with twine looped and knotted round his neck and wrapped in a116-year-old newspaperwas unlawfully killed, a coroner has concluded.Crispin Oliver on Thursday said the child, known only as Baby Auckland, had been garotted by an unknown person.He said it was an “unusual case, legally and evidentially”. The whole story, he added, was “very sad and singular”.Oliver said: “Clearly, this was a terrible thing that happened to a defenceless infant. It happened in our community. But it happened over a century ago, and it is heartwarming how the public and individuals in this community have stepped up to do the right thing by Baby Auckland.”The inquest heard that the skeletal remains of the baby had been found during renovations on the second floor of a late 19th-century house in Bishop Auckland, County Durham, on 29 July 2024.They were found by the house owner, Peter Moody, while he was laying a new floor. In a statement he said he had made the discovery when he lifted up a floorboard. He contacted the county council, unsure of whether he needed to call the police.DCI Mel Sutherland told the inquest he had been on duty in Bishop Auckland when he was alerted to the discovery of skeletal remains in a town centre house.After they were confirmed as human, he supervised the sealing of the house to keep it forensically sterile, while a forensic anthropologist was contacted. That scientist, Dr Micol Zuppello, travelled up that evening and spent two days at the house investigating.The baby’s skeleton was mostly complete, the inquest in Crook heard, bar a missing toe tip. The remains were partly mummified. Carbon dating could conclusively establish only that the baby died between the 17th century and 1955.A postmortem of the skeleton was carried out by Zupello and Dr Louise Mulcahy, a Home Office pathologist for north-east England based at the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle.Mulcahy said the baby had been 38-40 weeks, with no signs of traumatic injury, and had twine looped around his neck. She said it had been looped around the neck three times, knotted, and then looped again.View image in fullscreenPCSOs and a forensics officer outside the building in Bishop Auckland in 2024, after the discovery was made.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAIt was not possible to say, she added, if it had been tight or loose. The medical cause of death, she said, was “unascertained”.The skeleton was too old to be able to confirm or refute the presence of natural disease, she said. In the absence of soft tissue it was not possible, the inquest heard, to say if there had been any assault or trauma. Equally, it was not possible to say with any certainty if the baby had been stillborn or not.Oliver said police had “had to think laterally” during their investigation. He praised Sutherland for “leaving no stone unturned”.Sutherland described some of the techniques they had used to investigate further, including DNA testing. All were inconclusive.He said the newspaper was very brown, but articles could be seen. It was called The Umpire and dated June 1910.Sutherland said that in 1911 census data, the building was described as dining rooms, meaning “a cafe-type establishment”.A public appeal was made for people who thought they might be related to come forward. Two sisters came forward who believed they were related to a servant at the house, but DNA testing revealed no match.During the whole investigation, Sutherland said, there had been “very little to go on”.Oliver asked if the twine might have been used for a religious artefact, but nothing like that had been found, Sutherland said. There was also no evidence to suggest any link to midwifery practices of the time.A knot specialist could not be used, the inquest heard, because the nearest person was in the Netherlands and would have been too expensive for this type of investigation.Baby Aucklandwas laid to restat Bishop Auckland cemetery in April this year, with professionals involved giving their services for free.Sutherland said it had been two years of investigating, “challenging and frustrating at times, but heartwarming to see the send-off he got at the end”.Explore more on these topicsNorth of EnglandCounty DurhamForensic scienceCrimeEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lifeboat station in Portsmouth forced to temporarily shut after far-right action | RNLI | The Guardian
description: RNLI facility had been targeted by activists trying to stop asylum seekers landing in boats from the Channel
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: RNLI facility had been targeted by activists trying to stop asylum seekers landing in boats from the Channel
Content: Police outside the RNLI Portsmouth lifeboat station at Eastney in Hampshire.Photograph: Simon Czapp/Solent News & Photo Agency/Solent NewsView image in fullscreenPolice outside the RNLI Portsmouth lifeboat station at Eastney in Hampshire.Photograph: Simon Czapp/Solent News & Photo Agency/Solent NewsProtests from prisonRNLILifeboat station in Portsmouth forced to temporarily shut after far-right actionRNLI facility had been targeted by activists trying to stop asylum seekers landing in boats from the ChannelSteven MorrisThu 17 Sep 2026 08.14 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA lifeboat station on the south coast of England near the spot where far-right activists tried to stop asylum seekers landing has been forced to temporarily close, it has emerged.The station inPortsmouthshut after it and other sites run by the RNLI were targeted by people objecting to the lifeboat charity going to the aid of people trying to get to the UK on small boats.Jacqui Irons, the head of the south-east region of the RNL, said: “Portsmouth lifeboat station has been temporarily off-service since 7 September. We have a duty of care to our people. We therefore took the decision to pause activity at the station to review crew safety and wellbeing, and to support those involved in the incident on 6 September.”The charity said it did not mean there had been a lack of cover around Portsmouth, one of the busiest maritime areas in the UK.AnRNLIspokesperson said: “Search and rescue cover continues to be provided through established contingency arrangements, including flank RNLI stations and other declared assets.“At times, it is not unusual for lifeboat stations around the UK and Ireland to be temporarily unavailable due to maintenance or other operational requirements.“In such circumstances, established contingency arrangements are put in place to ensure continued search and rescue cover.”On Sunday 6 September two RNLI crewshelped bring a dinghy carrying 120 asylum seekersto Eastney in Portsmouth, a few hundred metres from the lifeboat station.Far-right activists were among those who tried to blockade the road leading to the landing spot, and police officers were injured.In the days after, lifeboat crew members were called traitors and protests took place against the charity, includingat the RNLI headquarters in nearby Poole.A museum in Poole telling the story of the RNLIalso closed temporarily, and Portsmouth lifeboat station took down its Facebook page.RNLI volunteers across the UK were told that they should consider not wearing RNLI branded clothing if they felt this could put them at risk. They have also been advised that they should feel empoweredto close shops or lifeboat stations if they feel in danger.The RNLI has defended its work in the Channel, saying that for more than 200 years it rescued people without judgment, fear or favour. It said rumours that the RNLI housed asylum seekers on its premises, or that there were RNLI missions to move migrants to secret locations, were “completely baseless and untrue”.The charity saidRNLI lifeboats launched 9,058 times in 2025 but that only 109 of those callouts were to small boats in the Channel, representing 1.2% of its rescue work.Separately, the first person to be arrested over the protest at Eastney has appeared in court.Del Somerville, 42, from Portsmouth, admitted violent disorder. He has also been charged with assaulting a police officer but did not enter a plea to that allegation.Philip Allman, prosecuting, asked for an adjournment so that a community impact statement could be prepared. The defendant was remanded in custody.Explore more on these topicsRNLIProtests from prisonPortsmouthImmigration and asylumEmergency servicesFar rightProtestShareReuse this content

title: Father of Noah, three, thanks those who searched for his son as village reels from loss | Suffolk | The Guardian
description: Rhys Woods says there are ‘no words’ for his family’s pain after Noah’s body was found in pond near Suffolk playground
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Rhys Woods says there are ‘no words’ for his family’s pain after Noah’s body was found in pond near Suffolk playground
Content: The small village of Brantham mobilised when Noah went missing from a playground on Tuesday afternoon.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe small village of Brantham mobilised when Noah went missing from a playground on Tuesday afternoon.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianSuffolkFather of Noah, three, thanks those who searched for his son as village reels from lossRhys Woods says there are ‘no words’ for family’s pain after Noah’s body was found in pond near Suffolk playgroundHelena HortonThu 17 Sep 2026 09.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 15.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe father of Noah, the three-year-old boy whowas found dead after going missing from a playground,has spoken of his heartbreak and thanked the community who launched a tireless search for his son.Rhys Woods said there were “no words to describe the pain of this loss”, adding that the family was “absolutely heartbroken”.The small village of Brantham, inSuffolk, had mobilised on Tuesday, when Noah went missing after becoming separated from a relative at 2.37pm. He is thought to have gone down a woodland path towards the pond where his body was found.View image in fullscreenMore than 1,300 people scoured the woodlands and fields around the area to search for Noah.Photograph: Suffolk PoliceMore than 1,300 people from the village and beyond descended on the area to search for Noah. They scoured the woodlands and fields around the area close to the River Stour on the Essex border as helicopters flew overhead. On Wednesday afternoon, a body was discovered at the pond, a short walk from the playground.Map of BranthamWoods said: “Noah was the sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give, and we are going to miss him so very much. It seems he has made an impact across the whole nation.“The compassion shown by all of you will never be forgotten by us, and brought us comfort and strength at the darkest time of our lives.”On Thursday, the normally busy playground from which Noah disappeared was silent, save for the crying of people leaving bunches of flowers, which lined the length of the wooden fence surrounding the park.View image in fullscreenThe playground from which Noah disappeared is surrounded by flowers propped up against the fence.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian“We didn’t know you, but we helped to find you,” read one note propped up against the fence. Another read: “We are sorry we couldn’t get to you sooner.” One person from the village wrote: “Little Noah, may you rest in eternal peace. You will remain in the hearts of the village and of all your friends.”The mood on Thursday morning was muted. The leisure centre had been turned into a makeshift community hub, with a response centre consisting of councillors, local police and volunteers having meetings in the adjacent village hall.View image in fullscreenSo many people turned out to help look for Noah that the police ran out of hi-vis vests.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianGoldie, who did not want to give her surname, was volunteering to help run the community hub, where a handful of people chatted quietly. She said: “We’re providing a place for people to gather, and we’ve made a tribute book. Tributes are pouring in online, but for the family there is frankly some abuse online so we want them to have something to look at while avoiding that. The community is reeling.“It’s a small village, and 1,300 people came to volunteer. If there was a chance for him to be found he would have been. Everyone did their very best. Obviously, we are all very upset today.”The police ran out of hi-vis vests because so many people turned out to help find Noah, and the force was not entirely prepared for the logistics of a huge search party descending on the small area.View image in fullscreenThe village Co-op ran out of flowers on Thursday, while the shop in nearby Manningtree was also running low.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianSgt Claire Connick told the Guardian: “I feel so grateful for the community. The way people pulled together was just phenomenal. A man explained to me that he had been up all night until 4am searching. We even had people volunteering to control the traffic. The traffic and parking was something we didn’t factor in, just the volume of people asking how they could help.”The love for the family and sorrow at the loss was evident. The local Co-op ran out of flowers, and the branch in the next town over, Manningtree, was also running low.Noah apparently loved the cartoon dog Bluey, and was wearing a T-shirt depicting the character when he went missing. At the playground people had left stuffed toys depicting Bluey, and flowers with Bluey stickers on the cellophane.View image in fullscreenA fundraiser gathering donations to support the family stands at £21,000 so far.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianCandles had been lit, but the drizzle had snuffed many of them out. A fundraiser gathering donations to support the family stands at £21,000, and Ipswich Town football club arranged to lay a wreath at the playground.Specialist police officers were supporting Noah’s parents, who had to identify their son’s body on Wednesday night. Connick said: “The nurses and doctors lined up to walk the family into hospital which was a wonderful thing. There really has been so much support for the family.” She added that there would be an increased police presence in the area to help support the community.View image in fullscreenThe manager of the local leisure centre said the village had ‘witnessed something extraordinary’ in the number of people who helped try to find Noah.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianLouise Madley, the manager of Brantham leisure centre, said: “There are far too many people to name individually, but to every single person who searched, donated, organised, sent messages of support, delivered supplies, supported the emergency services or helped in any way, thank you so much. Brantham, over the last 24 hours, we have witnessed something truly extraordinary in our village. Something I will, and I am sure others will, never forget. Noah, your memory will forever live on.”Wood added: “This was the most heartbreaking outcome for us. We were just hoping that he would be hiding somewhere obvious where someone could find him, that’s what we kept telling ourselves the whole time. With our love and deepest gratitude, from his daddy and mummy and little brother, Noah you will be loved forever, you will never be forgotten and we miss you so so much. It has been a privilege to be your parents and be able to have packed so much love in the short three years you were with us.”Explore more on these topicsSuffolkEnglandCommunitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bank of England holds interest rates at 3.75% but warns war could force future rises | Interest rates | The Guardian
description: Central bank announces surprise plan to sell billions of pounds in government bonds back to the Treasury
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: Central bank announces surprise plan to sell billions of pounds in government bonds back to the Treasury
Content: Financial markets expected the Bank of England would keep interest rates unchanged.Photograph: Corey Rudy/ReutersView image in fullscreenFinancial markets expected the Bank of England would keep interest rates unchanged.Photograph: Corey Rudy/ReutersInterest ratesBank of England holds interest rates at 3.75% but warns war could force future risesCentral bank announces surprise plan to sell billions of pounds in government bonds back to the TreasuryBurnham’s talk of ‘breathing space’ at odds with reality of future rate risesThe Bank is shaking up its bond sales – why does it matter?Business live – latest updatesRichard PartingtonSenior economics correspondentThu 17 Sep 2026 08.04 EDTFirst published on Thu 17 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheBank of Englandhas kept interest rates on hold as it warned a continuation of the bitter fighting in the Middle East could force it to raise borrowing costs amid mounting fears over inflation.It also announced a surprise plan to sell billions of pounds in UK government bonds back to the Treasury to avoid fuelling turbulence in the gilt market, a decision that could have consequences for the public finances before next month’s budget.As the fallout from war in the Middle East fuels a rise in energy prices, the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) voted by a majority of six to three to keep its base rate unchanged at 3.75%.Bank of England to slow bond-selling QT programme and leaves UK interest rates on hold – business liveRead moreHowever, the Bank said the increasingly probable prospect of a lengthy war fanning intense volatility in global markets had dramatically raised the chance of it putting up borrowing costs in future.Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, said: “So far higher global energy costs have had a limited effect on price and wage setting in the UK.“But the longer this volatility persists, the bigger the impact it will have on inflation, and the more likely it is we will need to raise [the] Bank rate to ensure that inflation falls back to our 2% target.”With Threadneedle Street under pressure to guard against high rates of inflation becoming entrenched, City traders predict a quarter-point rise in borrowing costs from as early as November with three more increases to 4.75% likely to happen next year.The sharp rise in global energy prices prompted the US Federal Reserveto raise interest rateson Wednesday for the first time since 2023, after a decision last week by the European Central Bankto raise eurozone borrowing costs.The Bank said inflation was on track to reach 4% by early next year, as the war-driven rise in energy prices hits households.Official figures on Wednesday showed inflationrose to 3.1%last month from 2.9% in July as the escalating hostilities in the Middle East drove up the average price of petrol and diesel by almost a quarter.It came after Andy Burnham said he wasprepared to take “difficult decisions”to tackle high inflation and keep the economy on track and would take action at next month’s budget on the cost of living.However, the MPC said the economy was showing signs of resilience and there was not yet a need to take action on borrowing costs because there had been “little evidence so far of material second-round effects” – when inflationary pressures push businesses and workers to demand higher prices and pay settlements.There were also signs of weaker food price inflation despite the surge in energy prices triggered by the Iran war, it added.Against a volatile backdrop in global financial markets, Threadneedle Street also announced updated proposals for the winding down of itsfinancial crisis-era quantitative easing programme, which had involved the buying of £895bn of UK government bonds at its peak.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn a surprise move, the Bank said it planned to sell £146bn of bonds to the Treasury, at a pace of about £20bn a year until 2034, in a plan that would require signoff from the chancellor, John Healey, next April. The Treasury’s Debt Management Office (DMO) would then sell bonds to cover the government’s financing commitments, including this buyback.The rationale is that the Bank holds long-term bonds where investor demand is dwindling, whereas the DMO would have the capacity to cover the buyback by issuing shorter-term debt.The process will be used to complete Threadneedle Street’s“quantitative tightening” programme– which has involved the sale of gilts held on its books since 2022, which has reduced its holdings to about £488bn.The Bank said it would retain about £120bn of bonds, which were needed to back the issuance of notes and coins circulating in the economy.Leaving about £222bn of bonds, it said this amount would be disposed of by allowing maturing debts to expire, and through active sales to the state if a deal was agreed. The Bank said it would pause its QT programme until a deal was finalised and that it would resume sales to City investors if an agreement could not be reached.In a letter to the chancellor, Bailey said the arrangement preserved “the independence of monetary policy” and would “maximise value for money by minimising cost and risk over the lifetime” of the QT programme.It came as the Office for National Statistics alsoupgraded its estimates for the UK’s productivity growth, in a boost for Healey as he prepares for the budget.The UK government’s borrowing costs and the pound fell slightly on Thursday after the decision. The central bank added that it would halt sales of long-dated gilts entirely. The 10-year gilt yield fell by six basis points to 5.243%, the lowest level in a week.Explore more on these topicsInterest ratesBank of EnglandEconomicsBondsnewsShareReuse this content

title: New lawsuit alleges Epstein possessed ‘child sexual abuse material of countless children’ | Jeffrey Epstein | The Guardian
description: Two women who filed suit against Epstein estate ask court to order program to notify potential victims
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: Two women who filed suit against Epstein estate ask court to order program to notify potential victims
Content: Jeffrey Epstein in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on 8 September 2004.Photograph: Rick Friedman/Corbis via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJeffrey Epstein in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on 8 September 2004.Photograph: Rick Friedman/Corbis via Getty ImagesJeffrey EpsteinNew lawsuit alleges Epstein possessed ‘child sexual abuse material of countless children’Two women who filed suit against Epstein estate ask court to order program to notify potential victimsAnna BettsThu 17 Sep 2026 12.22 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 14.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJeffrey Epstein’s estate is facing a new lawsuit filed by two women who allege that Epstein possessed child sexual abuse material (CSAM) of them. They want a judge to order that a program be set up to identify and notify all individuals whose “unlawful sexualized images” might have been in Epstein’s collection, and are also seeking monetary damages.The complaint was filed this week in the US district court for the southern district of New York on behalf of two plaintiffs, who are anonymous in the filing but described as survivors of Epstein’s CSAM crimes. The lawsuit was filed against Epstein’s former lawyerDarren Indykeand Epstein’s former accountantRichard Kahn, who are being sued in their capacities as co-executors of Epstein’s estate. Attorneys for Indyke and Kahn, who have both said that they hadno knowledge of Epstein’s crimesduring their employment, did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the complaint on Wednesday.The complaint claims that for more than two decades, Epstein, whodiedin a Manhattan jail in 2019 while awaiting trial onfederal sex-trafficking charges, possessed, transported, produced and distributed “child pornography and/or child sexual abuse material of countless children”. It alleges that Epstein “acquired by theft” nude or partly nude images of the first plaintiff, referred to in the document as Jane Doe, and that he transported the material across state lines and retained it.Woman pleads guilty to fraudulently obtaining $750,000 from Epstein victims fundRead moreThe lawsuit argues that many of those depicted in the CSAM that they say was possessed by Epstein have never been identified or notified through the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children’s victim-identification program.With regard to the second plaintiff, identified in the complaint under the pseudonym “Amy”, the lawsuit alleges that “upon information and belief, Epstein acquired CSAM images” of her.The complaint alleges that beginning in the 1990s, Epstein “created and kept” in his locked safe in his New York City home a “‘modeling book’ of sexualized images of children”. It further alleges that beginning in “at least in the 2000s, Epstein had his assistant take nude, sexualized photographs of multiple children, paid them for the images, and then used those photographs for his own sexual gratification and perhaps that of others”.Jane Doe alleges that she was around 12 years old when Epstein stole photographs of her partly nude, which the complaint claims had originally been taken “as part of an artist study for and catalogued, numbered and maintained by the artist in a lockbox”.The lawsuit alleges that Epstein also “stole nude or partially nude photos of another minor” and transported these images across state lines.
