The complaint also alleges that “despite contemporaneous reports made to law enforcement, specifically alerting law enforcement that Epstein had obtained these photos of Jane Doe, and similar photos of another minor, no one in law enforcement took action to prosecute anyone or even investigate these reports”.It adds that “upon learning that Epstein had possessed sexualized images of her as a child, Jane Doe suffered and continues to suffer severe emotional distress”.“Amy” alleges in the complaint that she is a victim of “actively traded CSAM which has been in distribution since the late 1990s to present day”. The lawsuit alleges that “on information and belief” images of her are contained within the CSAM collection seized from Epstein’s properties.In a statement to the Guardian, one of the lawyers representing the plaintiffs, Margaret Mabie, of Marsh Law, said that according to the released files, a report completed on Epstein’s collection identified 15 or more hits of known series like Amy’s and that “to our knowledge, none of the victims identified in that report, or in any other CSAM discovered in Epstein’s collection, have ever received notice”.The complaint also alleges that other people, “including Epstein’s employees and/or coconspirators, had access to, viewed, or otherwise received from Epstein, the CSAM images in his possession, including images of Jane Doe and ‘Amy’”.The two plaintiffs are bringing the lawsuit both individually and on behalf of a proposed class of other survivors they seek to represent, who are described as “all persons who were under the age of 18 at the time they appeared in any visual depiction of child pornography, including CSAM, contained within any image, video, or electronic media collections seized from properties or devices controlled by Jeffrey E Epstein, including the media identified in the Epstein Files Transparency Act productions and the materials described in the July 6, 2026, FBI and [justice department] memorandum”.In a statement this week, Hillary Nappi, of AWK Survivor Advocate Attorneys, said that their goal with the lawsuit “is accountability and identification”.“We want the estate to preserve and account for everything seized from Epstein’s properties, and we want a real, court supervised process to identify and notify every survivor depicted in that collection,” Nappi said. “Many of them have no idea their images exist in his files, and they deserve to know, and they deserve the chance to seek justice.“Survivors have waited years for accountability, and this case opens the door for others depicted in his collection who don’t even know they’re in it,” Nappi added.Explore more on these topicsJeffrey EpsteinUS crimeUS justice systemnewsShareReuse this content

title: Accused Oregon serial killer indicted in connection with death of sixth woman | Oregon | The Guardian
description: Grand jury indicts Jesse Calhoun on a charge of first-degree manslaughter in the death of Elizabeth Gibson
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: Grand jury indicts Jesse Calhoun on a charge of first-degree manslaughter in the death of Elizabeth Gibson
Content: Jesse Lee Calhoun in Multnomah county circuit court for his arraignment on 6 June 2024 in Portland, Oregon.Photograph: Dave Killen/APView image in fullscreenJesse Lee Calhoun in Multnomah county circuit court for his arraignment on 6 June 2024 in Portland, Oregon.Photograph: Dave Killen/APOregonAccused Oregon serial killer indicted in connection with death of sixth womanGrand jury indicts Jesse Calhoun, 41, on charge of first-degree manslaughter in the death of Elizabeth GibsonDani AnguianoThu 17 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 20.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnOregonman accused of killing five women has been indicted in connection with the death of a sixth woman, officials announced this week.Jesse Calhoun was indicted by a grand jury on a charge of first-degree manslaughter in the death of Elizabeth “Libby” Gibson, said the Multnomah county district attorney on Wednesday. Calhoun is accused of causing Gibson’s death and acting “unlawfully and recklessly under circumstances manifesting extreme indifference to the value of human life”.Gibson, who lived inPortland, was 32 when she was last seen in 2022 and reported missing the following year. Officials believe she was killed on or around 18 November 2022 but have not found her body.Ohio mother of 16 children rescued from ‘deplorable’ conditions pleads not guilty to child neglectRead moreCalhoun, 41, hasalready been chargedin the killings of Ashley Real, 22; Kristin Smith, 22; Charity Perry, 24; Bridget Webster, 31; and Joanna Speaks, 32, between 2022 and 2023. He has pleaded not guilty to five counts of second-degree murder and four counts of abuse of a corpse.“We will not stop. We will do everything in our power to hold him accountable and see that justice is done for each and every one of these victims. We remain committed to these families for as long as it takes,” Nathan Vasquez, the Multnomah county district attorney, said in a statement.Prosecutors said earlier this year that they plan to try Calhoun for all murders in one trial rather than holding separate proceedings.Calhoun was previously incarcerated for assaulting a police officer, trying to strangle a police dog, burglary and other charges. He was released early in 2021 for helping fight wildfires through a prison program, but Oregon’s governor’s reversed the decision in 2023 when he came under investigation for the deaths.Gibson’s family said in a statement that they were “grateful that a definitive step toward justice is finally being taken”.“Libby was kind, creative, and silly. She welcomed everyone with love and acceptance. Her future was tragically taken from her way too soon,” her siblings said in the statement.“We are deeply appreciative of the tireless work and dedication of the law enforcement officers and the district attorney’s office whose efforts have helped bring us to this point.”Melissa Marrero, the senior deputy district attorney, said the scope of the investigation had been “enormous”.“But all information is useful. And to the extent that individuals have been willing to come forward in the past and provide information to us, no matter how small, that information has led us to where we are here today,” she said in a statement.Explore more on these topicsOregonUS crimePortlandWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Revolut reportedly facing $3m ransom demand after hackers steal hundreds of customers’ data | Revolut | The Guardian
description: Europe’s largest financial technology company confirmed it had fallen victim to an impersonation scam last week
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Europe’s largest financial technology company confirmed it had fallen victim to an impersonation scam last week
Content: The data breach has reportedly impacted about 680 of Revolut’s customers, targeting those with suspected cryptocurrency holdings.Photograph: Corey Rudy/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe data breach has reportedly impacted about 680 of Revolut’s customers, targeting those with suspected cryptocurrency holdings.Photograph: Corey Rudy/ReutersRevolutRevolut reportedly facing $3m ransom demand after hackers steal hundreds of customers’ dataEurope’s largest financial technology company confirmed it had fallen victim to an impersonation scam last weekKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentThu 17 Sep 2026 11.58 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRevolut is facing a reported $3m (£2.2m) ransom demand after hackers posing as government officials accessed the data of hundreds of the bank’s cryptocurrency customers, including one victim who says he fears for his safety.Europe’s largest financial technology company confirmed last weekend that it had fallen victim to an impersonation scam in which hackers compromised an Italian government email system to contact Revolut staff and request personal customer details.While the data breach only affected about 680 of Revolut’s 80 million global customers, it is believed to have targeted customers with suspected cryptocurrency holdings.It is not clear how the scandal might affect Revolut’s much-anticipated stock market debut, with Revolut’s founder, Nik Storonsky,telling Les Echoes on Thursdaythat there were plans for a dual listing in both London and New York.One of the alleged hackers has reportedly threatened to publish the customer data unless Revolut pays a $3m ransom, according to the Financial Times, which has been speaking to the purported hacker. A Revolut spokesperson said the bank “has not received any direct contact or demand from the individuals or group making these claims”.But some victims have said they fear they could end up being forced to face ransoms.The former chief executive of failed bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox, Mark Karpelès, said he was one of the victims of the data breach and is now worried about his family’s safety. “I have kids, we’re living together. My address is in those files, so of course I’m worried about this,” he told the Guardian.He has since contacted law enforcement in Tokyo, where he lives, after saying in an X post earlier this week that he feared he could be “kidnapped or dead” by the time Revolut gave him more substantial information about the breach.Karpelès said he was relieved that Japanese officials were taking the threat seriously, “but I might still have to travel overseas or be in places that may not be as safe”.The French businessman, who has been a Revolut customer since 2023, said that hackers may have mistakenly targeted his account, thinking he was wealthier than he actually is. He said he was forced to declare bankruptcy in the wake of a high-profile court case in Japan.Karpelès is a controversial figure in the crypto world.He was charged, but later acquitted, of embezzlementby Japanese courts, following the collapse of the crypto exchange platform in 2014. He was found guilty of falsifying data.Karpelès said he has joined a victim chat group on X in the wake of the data breach, where customers having been sharing information and support. “We’re all in the same situation, which is: we don’t know exactly what happened, or how it happened, so we’re trying to get as much information as possible,” he said. He added that one of the victims got in touch with the purported hacker, who showed they had the victim’s personal details on hand.The hacker then said they would delete the information, but only if they were sent $50,000, Karpelès said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhile Karpelès was frustrated with Revolut, which was valued at $115bn in a secondary share sale earlier this summer, he does not believe the bank should pay the $3m ransom, which ultimately gives no guarantee that the data will be deleted.It is still not clear how many hackers are involved, and requests for the ransom to be paid through a platform known as Monero, meaning there would be no evidence or receipt of payment, allowing the hacker to claim they never received the money in the first place.Karpelès hopes Revolut will share more information about the breach.“This is very, very damaging [for the Revolut brand] because I do believe a lot of Revolut customers are more likely to be privacy sensitive,” he said, noting that this was usually a high priority among people invested in cryptocurrencies.A Revolut spokesperson said:“Revolut recently identified a sophisticated external impersonation scam where an unauthorised third party utilised a legitimate government agency domain email to submit fraudulent requests for information.“Upon detection, we immediately blocked the address and alerted the relevant government agency as well as enforcement agencies, data protection, and financial regulators. Revolut systems and customer funds are unaffected. We have contacted the limited number of impacted individuals directly to inform them and provide support.”Explore more on these topicsRevolutFinancial sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Meta ordered to remove UK deepfakes as oversight board criticises ‘inadequate’ safeguards | Meta | The Guardian
description: Facebook told it was wrong in leaving up AI-generated videos of a Labour councillor and Muslim campaigner, amid calls to curb fakes
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Facebook told it was wrong in leaving up AI-generated videos of a Labour councillor and Muslim campaigner, amid calls to curb fakes
Content: Meta has had policy changes recommended to it, including demoting ‘high risk’ content, making it less likely to appear in users’ feeds.Photograph: Daniel Cole/ReutersView image in fullscreenMeta has had policy changes recommended to it, including demoting ‘high risk’ content, making it less likely to appear in users’ feeds.Photograph: Daniel Cole/ReutersMetaMeta ordered to remove UK deepfakes as oversight board criticises ‘inadequate’ safeguardsFacebook told it was wrong in leaving up AI-generated videos of a Labour councillor and Muslim campaigner, amid calls to curb fakesDan MilmoGlobal technology editorThu 17 Sep 2026 10.43 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 14.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMeta’s “supreme court” has ordered the tech company to take down deepfake videos of a UK politician and a young Muslim woman from Facebook and do more to tackleAI-generated fake imagery.A fake video showing a Labour party councillor in Scotland making inflammatory comments about refugees should not have been left up byFacebook, the board said. It also ruled that an AI-generated video of a Muslim campaign volunteer should have been removed after it falsely depicted her offering health advice while carrying out absurd exercises or eating junk food.The board said Meta’s safeguards were “consistently and fundamentally inadequate” to address the rapid rise of AI deepfakes.“From politicians to private citizens, AI-generated deepfakes are increasingly being used to harass and silence women from engaging in public discourse,” said Pamela San Martin, an oversight board co-chair.“These cases demonstrate a broader, troubling pattern in which women who engage publicly on issues are disproportionately subjected to harassment and misinformation. Meta and other social media platforms need more robust policies to address the proliferation of deepfakes.”In the Scotland clip, the councillor is falsely represented as saying: “Refugees are welcome here, even if they rape our women, because white people do that too.”The oversight board, a quasi-independent body whose decisions are binding, said the video of the councillor appeared to be AI-generated, as indicated by the audio not being fully synchronised to the unnamed councillor’s facial movements.Even when raised directly with the company by the board, Meta decided the video did not violate its content policies and did not merit an AI label.In a blogpost published on Thursday, the board said the post should have been removed because it violated Meta’s rules on hateful conduct by alleging criminal and predatory sexual behaviour by refugees as an entire group and not as individuals. The video should also have received a “high risk AI” label, said the board, as it called for tougher measures on deepfakes.“The majority [of the board] finds that Meta needs more robust policies on deepfakes, including expanding the situations when ‘high risk’ labels can be applied, more measures to reduce the spread of deceptive AI content, increasing the penalties for accounts that repeatedly share it, and more transparency on data around when AI labels are applied,” it said.The board recommended nine policy changes at Meta, including ensuring algorithms demote content labelled “high risk”, making such posts less likely to appear in users’ feeds. It also recommended that Meta makes it more difficult for users to view AI-generated content by, for instance, introducing a warning screen that requires a click-through before viewing the content.In a separate ruling, the board also ordered Meta to take down from Facebook an AI-generated video mocking a young Muslim woman in Europe taking part in a campaign to improve menstrual health education and reduce stigma around health conditions for women and girls from ethnic minority backgrounds. AI-manipulated videos and images mocking the woman had tens of millions of views online, including on Meta platforms.The board singled out one of the videos – showing the woman exercising absurdly and eating junk food – as a breach of the company’s bullying and harassment policy. It recommended the post be removed and made three policy recommendations, including changing its definition of “unwanted manipulated imagery” to cover deepfakes of a private individual saying or doing things they did not say or do.The board was set up by Meta in 2020 to serve as a referee for content on its platforms. Meta has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsMetaSocial mediaDigital mediaFacebookDeepfakeAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Thousands of Barclays staff revolt over return-to-office mandate | Barclays | The Guardian
description: Union calls for payouts to help cover travel costs and exemption for those living more than 40 minutes away
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Union calls for payouts to help cover travel costs and exemption for those living more than 40 minutes away
Content: Unite represents nearly 80% of Barclays’ 45,000 staff.Photograph: Simon Dawson/ReutersView image in fullscreenUnite represents nearly 80% of Barclays’ 45,000 staff.Photograph: Simon Dawson/ReutersBarclaysThousands of Barclays staff revolt over return-to-office mandateUnion calls for payouts to help cover travel costs and exemption for those living more than 40 minutes awayBusiness live – latest updatesKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentThu 17 Sep 2026 05.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBarclays is facing a growing backlash over return-to-office plans, with thousands of staff calling for payouts to help cover travel costs and an exemption for those living more than 40 minutes from work.Unionised staff represented by Unite are pushing back against plans announced by the bank earlier this summer to get staff back into the office at least three days a week from October, with more senior employees expected to come in at least four days a week.The current policy requires full-time Barclays staff to be in at least two days a week.Barclaycard sent me a bill for someone else’s accountRead moreUnite, which represents nearly 80% of Barclays’ 45,000 UK staff, says thousands of employees have now signed an open letter – first reported by the Financial Times – that has been sent to the bank’s bosses and widely circulated across its UK offices.The union plans to speak to Barclays about staff concerns in the coming days.A Unite national officer, Rick Coyle, said: “One of the issues that has caused consternation is that most employers in banking and financial services are generally embracing greater flexibility. Our members think that Barclays is trying to fix a problem that doesn’t exist.“Thousands of employees have signed the letter and the figure continues to rise. Unite will be speaking to Barclays about the strength of feeling in the days ahead.”Barclays’ return-to-office order echoes those imposed by other large banks, which tightened their work-from-home policies after the Covid pandemic, particularly for younger staff.That includes JP Morgan, whose chief executive, Jamie Dimon,told Bloomberg last year: “It is an apprenticeship system … you can’t learn working from your basement.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA Barclays spokesperson said: “We recognise the benefits of balancing flexibility for colleagues with the importance of working together in our physical locations. Our minimum time-in-office requirements vary by business area, reflecting the nature of the work and the needs of the business.“This means that most of our colleagues who are not already working in the office three days [per week] will align with our broader approach across the bank. Alongside this, our most senior leaders will spend an additional day in the office to support collaboration, decision-making and leadership visibility.”Get in touchContact the Guardian Business teamThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don't already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Scroll down and click onSecure Messaging.When asked who you wish to contact please select the ‘Business (UK & Global)’ team.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsBarclaysBankingWorking from homenewsShareReuse this content

title: Next forecasts bigger profits after hot weather lifts sales | Next | The Guardian
description: FTSE 100 retailer, which owns UK rights to US brands Gap and Victoria’s Secret, says prices could rise in autumn
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: FTSE 100 retailer, which owns UK rights to US brands Gap and Victoria’s Secret, says prices could rise in autumn
Content: Next has more than 500 stores across the UK.Photograph: Paul Gapper/AlamyView image in fullscreenNext has more than 500 stores across the UK.Photograph: Paul Gapper/AlamyNextNext forecasts bigger profits after hot weather lifts salesFTSE 100 retailer, which owns UK rights to US brands Gap and Victoria’s Secret, says prices could rise in autumnBusiness live – latest updatesKalyeena MakortoffandMark SweneyThu 17 Sep 2026 09.14 EDTFirst published on Thu 17 Sep 2026 03.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNext has thanked warmer weather for an “unexpected” boost in sales, leading the clothing retailer to raise its profit forecasts for the fourth time this year.The FTSE 100 company, which owns the UK rights to the US brands Gap and Victoria’s Secret as well as stakes in labels including Reiss and Joules, raised its expectations for full-year profits by £12m to £1.26bn.It is the fourth time Next has raised profit forecasts this year, with the company having lastratcheted up its expectations in early Augustas Europe faced aseries of heatwaves.Leading UK retailers ‘breaking law’ by not refunding customers for returned goods, Which? findsRead moreNext, which has more than 500 stores across the UK, said in a stock market update on Thursday: “The first half was much better than we originally anticipated, both in the UK and overseas.“It is important to acknowledge that part of this overperformance has been the result of two unusually warm summers in the UK. The rest of the overperformance is, we believe, largely the result of fulfilling the aims we outlined at the beginning of the year.”That has included some cost-cutting efforts, particularly across Next’s warehouses.Overall, total sales across the group were up 9% in the six months to July, helping push pre-tax profits for the half-year up by 11% to £566m.Next said the performance over the past six months was “all the more unexpected given the strength of sales last year”. It made £1bn of annual profits for the first time in the year ending January 2025.However, the retailer cautioned on the impact of the rising cost of living and prospects for the jobs market.“Our primary concerns are rising inflation, higher mortgage interest costs and a weak employment market. These worries will only be compounded if they are accompanied by tax increases,” it said, in an apparent reference to John Healey’s first budget as chancellor on 28 October.“It seems likely that it [the government] will have to increase taxes in order to fund its expenditure.”While the group said it was deploying AI across the business, including its tech division, Next said it was ensuring fashion designs were still led by humans.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“In a world where AI is able to do more and more, our experience suggests that consumers prefer the authentic creativity of human beings,” it said. “That means we are putting more emphasis on designers using techniques that connect them directly to the artwork – painting, drawing, screen printing, etc. That is a big investment in time, and requires a higher level of creative talent than is needed to operate CAD [computer aided design] or prompt AI.”Despite the strong results, the company lowered sales growth expectations in the UK, which accounts for three-quarters of total sales, from 2.8% to 2% for the six months to the end of January.“We are looking at what’s ahead and it is sensible to moderate our expectations,” said the Next chief executive, Simon Wolfson. “We are not talking about [consumer spending] falling off a cliff. I think things are likely to get worse rather than better. Unlike in the past when the government has been able to help it doesn’t have any room for manoeuvre. It has a £100bn deficit. That means not only can we not expect the government to necessarily alleviate the problem, but potentially make it worse.”He added that the escalation of hostilities in the Middle East has not triggered a further increase in further potential cost increases for Next.“We are not expecting shipping costs to get higher, there is already a surcharge we are paying,” Wolfson said. “All those cost increases are baked in [since the start of the conflict in February], and if anything are not as bad as March.”Aarin Chiekrie, an equity analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown, said: “Next delivered its first-half results in style, with sales growth accelerating over the period and breezing past the fashion company’s original guidance. In the UK, hotter-than-expected weather and more effective marketing saw customers logging in to refresh their summer wardrobes online, helping offset a small decline in-store.”Explore more on these topicsNextRetail industryConsumer spendingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Beabadoobee: Pylon review – voice of a generation’s surprisingly relatable rampage through rock star rage | Music | The Guardian
description: The Filipino-British songwriter’s fourth album sprinkles 90s alt fuzz with disarmingly sweet melodies and an impressive host of guests including Paramore’s Hayley Williams and Turnstile’s Brendan Yates
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: The Filipino-British songwriter’s fourth album sprinkles 90s alt fuzz with disarmingly sweet melodies and an impressive host of guests including Paramore’s Hayley Williams and Turnstile’s Brendan Yates
Content: ‘New infatuation’ … Beabadoobee.Photograph: Courtesy of Erika KamanoView image in fullscreen‘New infatuation’ … Beabadoobee.Photograph: Courtesy of Erika KamanoAlexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewBeabadoobee: Pylon review – voice of a generation’s surprisingly relatable rampage through rock star rage(Dirty Hit)The Filipino-British songwriter’s fourth album sprinkles 90s alt fuzz with disarmingly sweet melodies and an impressive host of guests including Paramore’s Hayley Williams and Turnstile’s Brendan YatesAlexis PetridisThu 17 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 10.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast month, the Guardian published a feature aboutthe demise of the monoculture. It suggested that streaming services, personalised algorithms and the declining influence of radio and television meant we now live in a world where stardom isn’t as universal as it once was. It used Sam Fender and Olivia Dean’s single Rein Me In as an example: here was a song that spent a record-breaking 23 weeks at No 1 yet hadn’t attained anything like the ubiquity you would once have expected: to judge by social media, plenty of people seemed to have never knowingly heard it.View image in fullscreenBeabadoobee: Pylon album cover.If you were looking to advance this theory, you might alight on the career of Beatrice Laus, the 26-year-old British-Filipinosinger-songwriter better known as Beabadoobee. To a certain cohort, primarily female and in their late teens and early 20s, she is not just a huge star, but a genuinely iconic figure. The latter is an over-used adjective in 2026, but if social media abounds with tutorials advising female fans how to copy your style and imitate your makeup – if you can be personally held partly responsible for the 2021 outbreak of adolescent girls drawing fake freckles on their faces in imitation of your own – then it probably fits, whether it discomfits Laus or not. The lyrics of Satellite, the closing track on her fourth album Pylon, suggests it does: “I give the generation a new infatuation,” she sings. “If only I knew how to cope with the times.”Laus’s sound has always been rooted in 90s alt-rock – grunge and its various US indie offshoots, shoegaze, Elliott Smith – sprinkled with a hefty pinch of pop nous. The latter gives her a distinct point of difference from her source material: Laus is less of straightforwardpasticheusethan you might expect someone who once released a song called I Wish I Was Stephen Malkmus to be. She’s also spun these once-underground influences into mainstream success. Her biggest hit, a collaboration with Canadian rapper Powfu called Death Bed (Coffee for Your Head) has been streamed more than 2bn times. Her last album, 2024’s Rick Rubin-produced This Is How Tomorrow Moves, entered the UK charts at No 1, while its follow-up arrives boasting an impressively starry range of guests: Paramore’s Hayley Williams, Deftones’ Chino Moreno, Matty Healy and George Daniel of labelmates the 1975 and Turnstile’s Brendan Yates among them. Her forthcoming UK tour is housed exclusively in arenas: the O2, Madison Square Garden. And yet, one suspects most people outside said cohort would struggle to name – or hum – a single song by her.Beabadoobee: Sun Has Set – videoSuch is the way of popular culture these days, and Laus is evidently doing very well for herself. So well, in fact, that Pylon’s lyrical themes include those hardy perennials of the successful rock star, the dislocation of life on tour (the title track comes replete with images of endless roads “in a place that I don’t know the name”), and fake friends attracted solely by your celebrity (the Williams feature Nothing to Prove). If that sounds a little remote for an artist whose success is to some extent founded in talking directly to an audience not much younger than she is about stuff that matters to them, then it’s expressed in snappily relatable terms. “Hold me like a screen, disconnected from reality,” she sings on Pylon. And, besides, there’s plenty here that feels more universal to her fanbase’s lived experiences. “Growing up just means to fuck everything up again,” protests Switchblade, a neat fixing of the confusion of early adulthood, while Sun Has Set rounds on a frenemy in brutal style – “we’ll never be friends, I mean we’ll never pretend – fuck that” – over a heaving, strikingly bloody guitar riff.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘We never apologised for our rage or revenge-seeking’: riot grrrl legends Heavens to Betsy reuniteRead moreThe ferocious storm she raises on the latter track is telling. Released in the wake of her support slot on Taylor Swift’s Eras tour, This Is How Tomorrow Moves leaned into her pop side, but Pylon turns in the opposite direction. There are still plenty of bright melodies to be had, not least on the disarmingly pretty Spark, and Laus’s voice naturally tends to cooing charm, but the guitars come drenched in caustic levels of distortion and the riffs they play are brawny or jagged. The album continually deploys a sweet-to-sour pivot that’s impressively well-judged: the dreamy bedroom-pop mood of Despite That is obliterated by sulphurous fuzz; shards of noise and gusts of feedback blow through Powerline, a duet with Yates; Write Me a Letter starts out mistily autumnal and ends up livid. Only the too-toothsome Estranged gets the balance wrong.It’s strikingly confident, as is her treatment of her celebrity guests: you’re aware they’re present, but always in a supporting role, with no doubt who the main star is. But then, why wouldn’t Laus be confident? As has already been established, she’s doing very well for herself, albeit in a very 2020s kind of way. Pylon offers a compelling argument that Beabadoobee’s reach should be broader.This week Alexis listened toThe CJP Band – We Must BelieveA friend’s enthusiasm belatedly alerted me to We Must Believe: dizzily uplifting jazz-infused disco-funk that hails, improbably, from the New Forest.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekIndiereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Robert Macfarlane and Jackie Morris’ guide to 49 threatened British birds wins Wainwright book of the year | Books | The Guardian
description: The Book of Birds is a twist on classic field guides from the creators of bestseller The Lost Words
Author: Ella Creamer
Headline: The Book of Birds is a twist on classic field guides from the creators of bestseller The Lost Words
Content: Robert Macfarlane and Jackie Morris, authors of The Book of Birds.Photograph: Feather & Grain/Urszula SołtysView image in fullscreenRobert Macfarlane and Jackie Morris, authors of The Book of Birds.Photograph: Feather & Grain/Urszula SołtysBooksRobert Macfarlane and Jackie Morris’ guide to 49 threatened British birds wins Wainwright book of the yearThe Book of Birds is a twist on classic field guides from the creators of bestseller The Lost WordsElla CreamerThu 17 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 14.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Book of Birdsby Robert Macfarlane and Jackie Morris, an illustrated guide to Britain’s threatened bird species, has been named as the Wainwright prize book of the year.Meanwhile, the prize’s children’s book of the year award went toOtherlands: An Illustrated Journey Through Earth’s Lost Worldsby Thomas Halliday, illustrated by Gavin Scott.The Book of Birds features 49 species of declining or endangered birds, with text by Macfarlane alongside artwork by Morris. It’s a “twist on the classic field guides that inspired both authors, evoking the spirit and poetry of birds from avocet to yellowhammer”, wrote Patrick Barkham in aGuardian interviewwith the author-illustrator pair in May.“There are three billion fewer birds in North America than 50 years ago; 600 million fewer in Europe,” said Macfarlane at the time. “Our skies are thinner, our springs quieter. This is a savage loss. We wanted, in paint and word, to pull birds back into focus and splendour – and warn against their vanishing.”‘Fear is good’: my scary subterranean journey into Underland, the film of Robert Macfarlane’s dazzling bookRead moreMacfarlane and Morris previously collaborated on the bestselling titleThe Lost Words, which was a response to a group of nature-related words, including acorn and wren, being removed from the Oxford Junior Dictionary because children were using them infrequently. The book was shortlisted for the 2018 prize. The following year, Macfarlane won the prize with his bookUnderland.Along with its two overall winners, the Wainwright prize, which celebrates the best nature and conservation writing published in the UK, announced four further category winners:Ancient: Reviving the Woods That Made Britainby Luke Barley (nature writing),The Savage Landscapeby Cal Flyn (conservation writing),The Danger of Small Thingsby Caryl Lewis (children’s fiction) andThe Great Bearby Annie Booker (picture books). Macfarlane and Morris had topped the illustrative books category, while Halliday and Scott won in the children’s nonfiction category, before both books went on to be named overall winners.Each of the category winners receive £500 each, while the overall winners receive an additional £2,500 each.“As environmental and social challenges grow ever more urgent, it’s inspiring to see writers using their voices to deepen our connection with the natural world,” said prize director Alastair Giles.The prize was founded in 2013 by Frances Lincoln and the Alfred Wainwright estate. Previous winners include James Rebanks, Merlin Sheldrake and Chloe Dalton, who took homelast year’s book of the year awardfor Raising Hare, about rescuing a leveret during the pandemic.Explore more on these topicsBooksAwards and prizesRobert MacfarlaneJackie MorrisScience and nature booksBirdsnewsShareReuse this content

title: 50 Years of Punk review – rock’n’roll rebels fondly recall the filth and fury a half-century on | Movies | The Guardian
description: Glen Matlock, Viv Albertine and Rat Scabies revisit the music, clothes and disgusting spitting in a likable documentary marking half a century of British punk
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Glen Matlock, Viv Albertine and Rat Scabies revisit the music, clothes and disgusting spitting in a likable documentary marking half a century of British punk
Content: Entertaining … Viv Albertine of the Slits in 50 Years of Punk, a film by Mark SloperView image in fullscreenEntertaining … Viv Albertine of the Slits in 50 Years of Punk, a film by Mark SloperMoviesReview50 Years of Punk review – rock’n’roll rebels fondly recall the filth and fury a half-century onGlen Matlock, Viv Albertine and Rat Scabies revisit the music, clothes and disgusting spitting in a likable documentary marking half a century of British punkAndrew PulverThu 17 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 08.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the majority of them ease into their eighth decade, the overlords of British punk rock get yet another celebratory runout, gently reheating material that has become familiar over the years but never loses its appeal. A subculture that passed almost immediately from tabloid-triggering menace to picture-postcard caricature, punk may have passed into legend as a joyless and even squalid diversion in music and fashion history, but its surviving spokespeople recall their participation in it all with no little enthusiasm, even if they’ve clearly said it a thousand times already. No doubt it is the gen alphas among us who will benefit most; you’d expect their jaws to drop and eyes to roll at some of the stuff deemed perfectly acceptable in the late 1970s: women’s-breasts T-shirts, amateurish pancake makeup, and all that disgusting spitting. (“I didn’t mind it going in my mouth,” says the Damned’s Captain Sensible at one point, out-disgusting everyone.)There’s a good spread of voices on offer; at least one member of most of the era’s big acts puts in an appearance with Glen Matlock (the Sex Pistols), Rat Scabies (the Damned), Terry Chimes (the Clash), Steve Severin (Siouxsie and the Banshees), and Hugh Cornwell (the Stranglers) leading the way. (The latter, though affable enough, is easily the least impressed as to punk’s actual achievements, which is a valuable corrective.) The original punk wave had little space for women (despite the sense that blows were being struck for equality) and that’s the case in the film as well: Gaye Advert (the Adverts) and Viv Albertine (the Slits) get a bit of time on camera though inevitably get a bit lost in it all. Due recognition, however, is paid to designer Vivienne Westwood as punk’s true founding spirit; Sex, the King’s Road boutique she ran with Malcolm McLaren, was a crucible of the British punk scene. Don Boyd, who produced the Pistols’ movie The Great Rock ‘n’ Roll Swindle along with the late Jeremy Thomas, says she “was punk and is punk … it came from her”.Some interesting details emerge: how the Sex Pistols’ early gigs coincided with the sweltering heatwave of 1976, which contributed – literally – to their pressure-cooker atmosphere; how early punk mix-and-match style emerged as a result of Westwood and Malcolm McLaren getting stuck with unsold stock from their shop’s previous incarnations; and, as writer Jon Savage explains, how the use of the word “punk” itself was debated. Inevitably, perhaps, it’s the more peripheral figures who offer the freshest takes, particularly David Barbarossa, drummer for Adam and the Ants and Bow Wow Wow, who talks somewhat regretfully about how McLaren winkled him and his bandmates away from the former to form the latter. All in all, this is an entertaining way to mark the half-century, and one to stick the kids in front of too.50 Years ofPunkis in UK cinemas from 18 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmMusic documentaryDocumentary filmsPunkreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Bad Apples review – Saoirse Ronan’s suffering teacher best thing about school horror-satire | Movies | The Guardian
description: Ronan plays a teacher who finds a way to deal with a disruptive pupil in Jonatan Etzler’s implausible satire, but it’s not shocking or funny enough
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Ronan plays a teacher who finds a way to deal with a disruptive pupil in Jonatan Etzler’s implausible satire, but it’s not shocking or funny enough
Content: Ronan is always watchable … L to r, Nia Brown as Pauline and Saoirse Ronan as Maria in Bad Apples.Photograph: Pulse Films/Nea Asphäll. All Rights ReservedView image in fullscreenRonan is always watchable … L to r, Nia Brown as Pauline and Saoirse Ronan as Maria in Bad Apples.Photograph: Pulse Films/Nea Asphäll. All Rights ReservedMoviesReviewBad Apples review – Saoirse Ronan’s suffering teacher best thing about school horror-satireRonan plays a teacher who finds a way to deal with a disruptive pupil in Jonatan Etzler’s implausible film, but it’s not shocking or funny enoughPeter BradshawThu 17 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 12.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is a strange, heavy-handed and unpersuasive black comedy which owes what success it has to the star-power of its lead,Saoirse Ronan, who is incapable of giving an uninteresting performance. Director Jonatan Etzler has adapted it with co-screenwriter Jess O’Kane from a Swedish novel by Rasmus Lindgren called De Oönskade, or The Unwanted, and is a film that asks you to overlook its plot-holes and implausibilities on the grounds that it is a satire – but a satire saying what, exactly?The scene is a primary school in the English West Country where Maria (Ronan) is a hardworking, idealistic teacher – but her class is hopelessly disrupted by a violent boy, Danny (Eddie Waller), obnoxious and out of control. He seriously injures another pupil, the nerdy teacher’s-pet Pauline (Nia Brown) whom Maria privately considers a bit annoying. After a chaotic visit to Danny’s home, Maria winds up causing the boy to lose consciousness with an accidental chokehold, and in a panic smuggles him back to her house where she imprisons him in her basement. And then, slowly but surely, the rest of the class, freed from Danny’s hateful presence, blossom and Maria gets a glowing Ofsted report. She looks and feels on top of the world. But what is to be done about her shameful secret?Perhaps only a pedant would point out that an unventilated basement, in which the prisoner’s bathroom necessities are met with a bucket, would soon look and smell horrendous, not clean and tidy, like this – and the same goes for the prisoner, incidentally. And how exactly has Maria induced Danny to wear an animal-restraint harness without knocking him out or using drugs?The boy-chained-up-in-a-basement movie could almost be a horror/satire sub-genre all on its own, withJan Komasa’s The Good BoyandMarkus Schleinzer’s Michael. But those shockers work because they never make any secret of how monstrous the jailers are, and what the endgame is; they turn the dials up to 11. Bad Apples cautiously turns the dials to four or five, always wanting to keep Ronan’s character relatable and sympathetic evidently because her well-meaning normality is part of the black-comic point. She is only doing what kindly/liberal teachers secretly long to do: ruthlessly eliminate the bad apples. But there isn’t enough comedy or enough shock to distract you from how laborious and unbelievable the whole thing is, particularly in the closing act. At any rate, Ronan is always watchable.Bad Apples is in UK and Irish cinemas from 18 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsHorror filmsSchoolsSaoirse RonanFilm adaptationsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘When you tell people the story, it’s almost too good to be true’: the incredible journey behind The Cycle of Love | Movies | The Guardian
description: Documentary director Orlando von Einsiedel on how the real life tale of a man who cycles 6,000 miles from India to Sweden to find his true love will warm your heart
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Documentary director Orlando von Einsiedel on how the real life tale of a man who cycles 6,000 miles from India to Sweden to find his true love will warm your heart
Content: ‘It’s about joy and human connection’ … Mina Dale and Chirag Lobo in The Cycle of Love.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘It’s about joy and human connection’ … Mina Dale and Chirag Lobo in The Cycle of Love.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockMovies‘When you tell people the story, it’s almost too good to be true’: the incredible journey behind The Cycle of LoveDocumentary director Orlando von Einsiedel on how the real life tale of a man who cycles 6,000 miles from India to Sweden to find his true love will warm your heartCath ClarkeThu 17 Sep 2026 03.03 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 03.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew Delhi, December 1975. It was love at first sight when a Swedish hippy called Lotta von Schedvin sat down to be sketched by an Indian street artist, Pradyumna Kumar Mahanandia, known to everyone as PK. In the 10 minutes it took PK to complete her portrait, everything clicked into place for the pair. They were swept headlong in a whirlwind romance, and PK took Lotta to his village in the east ofIndiato meet his family. But soon after, the time came for Lotta to pack up her VW campervan and head back home with her friends.Heart-stricken PK promised to follow, but a plane ticket to Sweden was an impossible dream. Determined not to lose the love of his life, PK bought a secondhand Raleigh bike, and with $80 sewn into the waistband of his trousers, set off tocycle 6,000 miles to Lotta. He knew the sun set in the west, so that was the direction he took. His plan was to follow the hippy trail, cycling through India, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran and Turkey, crossing Europe, finally arriving in Sweden.Actually, he was heading to Switzerland until a fellow backpacker pointed out that Switzerland andSwedenwere two different countries. In a new Netflix documentary, The Cycle of Love, PK jokes that his strength was his fuzzy grasp of European geography. Watching the film, you wonder if his superpower might have been his smile – warm and joyous, it lights the room. Either way, he made it to Sweden. The journey took 123 days, and ended up involving a flight or two, and a couple of trains. In May 1977, PK knocked on Lotta’s door in Borås, Sweden. They have been together ever since.Documentary-maker Orlando von Einsiedel first heard about the story when he gave a talk in Sweden. “At the end, two young people came up and handed me a book,” he says. “They said: ‘This is about our parents’ story. We know your work. Would you be interested in this as a film?’” The book was The Amazing Story of the Man Who Cycled from India to Europe for Love by Swedish journalist Per J Andersson.View image in fullscreen‘A tale of fate and destiny’ … The Cycle of Love.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockThe two young people were PK and Lotta’s grownup kids Emilie and Karl. Von Einsiedel politely took the book but didn’t think too much about it. “Normally in my experience, when somebody approaches you and says ‘I’ve got a brilliant story’, it doesn’t work out.”A couple of months later, Von Einsiedel picked up the book as a holiday read, opening it on the flight out of London. “The moment I started I thought, ‘Oh my God, you idiot Orlando! This is extraordinary.’” It wasn’t just the against-all-odds, 6,000-mile cycle ride, PK’s story was a tale of fate and destiny. When he was born, the astrologer in his village made four predictions about his future wife: she would be a Taurus, born outside India, musical and own a jungle. So naturally the first question he asked Lotta was: “Are you a Taurus?” Her answer was yes. She was also a gifted musician, and – most bonkers of all – her family owned land with a forest in Sweden.View image in fullscreenDale and Lobo are the only two trained actors in the film.Photograph: Everett/Shutterstock“When you tell people the story, it’s almost too good to be true,” says Von Einsiedel, cheerful and chatty on a video call from New York. The previous night he attended the US premiere of The Cycle of Love with PK and Lotta, who have been happily married for nearly 50 years. The pair have been getting the celebrity treatment wherever they go. “Everybody in the cinema stands up for them, people are weeping when they come on stage.” What do the couple make of the film? He grins. “I know they like it, because whenever they go to a festival, they watch every single screening from beginning to end.” How many times have they seen it? “A lot.”The film tells their story with enormous warmth. It includes a dramatisation of the epic ride, with PK played by the British-based Indian actor Chirag Lobo, and Mina Dale as Lotta. Everybody else is non-professional, explains Von Einsiedel. “Our producers would go out and street-cast people on the morning of filming.”What about the script, I ask? There are gorgeous, heartwarming scenes as PK shares his story with people he meets on the road, who in return tell him about their life and loves. How were those scenes scripted? “No script. Everything is improvised. When PK interacts with everyday people he meets along the way, those are just normal conversations about love and hopes and dreams.”Wasn’t that a bit risky – getting a plane to India with two actors, no script and trusting that deep and meaningful conversations would materialise from conversations with ordinary people? “Massively risky, except I tested if it might work in Lewisham town centre,” Von Einsiedel says, grinning. “I have a friend who’s an actor. We went to Lewisham with a bike.” Armed with a notepad, his friend told people that he was cycling from London to Cape Town for love. “He pretended to draw portraits. What was extraordinary is the first person he sat down to draw turned around and said: ‘I love your story. I’ll buy you a plane ticket immediately.’”View image in fullscreenFilm-maker Orlando von Einsiedel.Photograph: Arturo Holmes/Getty ImagesIt’s the kindness of strangers that makes the documentary so uplifting. When PK cycles out of Kabul, he stops to help an Austrian backpacker, Linea, who crashed her car, knocking out most of her teeth. He stays with her for several days at hospital, even though it means his visa expiring and further delay. Later, when he arrives in Istanbul and checks his post, there is a train ticket to Vienna – a thank you from Linea for his kindness.What struck Von Einsiedel when he met the real-life PK was that his story about love went beyond boy-meets-girl. “For me, it’s not just about romantic love. It’s about self-love and love for all the people that we share this planet with.” PK was born into a dalit family, the marginalised group in India formerly known as “untouchables”. At school, he was made to sit outside during lessons and not allowed to play with the other children. Even after he won a scholarship to study fine art in Delhi, he experienced periods of homelessness and isolation.“From the moment I started talking to PK it became clear what a difficult and traumatic childhood he’d had,” Von Einsiedel says. “He spoke so movingly about being on the journey and how it was the first time that strangers would touch him and hug him. That it was key to him starting to believe in himself and love himself. He said: ‘How can you love anybody if you can’t love yourself?’ I get emotional just saying that.”PK explained how he felt accepted on the journey, hanging out with hippies and locals in the villages and towns he passed through. People with very little offered him hospitality, a meal or a roof for the night. In the documentary, this warm feeling of togetherness thuds to the ground when PK arrives in Europe, grilled by hostile and overtly racist German border officers. “That was his first experience,” says Von Einsiedel. “He travelled through all these countries, Afghanistan and Iran, and everybody treated him with respect. Then as soon as he got to Europe he immediately experienced racism.”Von Einsiedel grew up in south London. At university he studied social anthropology and in his 20s was a professional snowboarder. “I learned the craft of film-making making snowboard films,” he says. “When I knew how to do that, I segued into making films about social issues I believed in.” He started working with Al Jazeera, travelling to conflict zones.In 2015, he was nominated for an Oscar for his first full-length documentary,Virunga, about the battle to save a national park in eastern Congo, home to some of the world’s last mountain gorillas. His documentary short,White Helmets, following Syrian volunteers rescuing civilians, won an Oscar. Next he madeEvelyn, an incredibly moving film in which Von Einsiedel turned the camera on his own family. His brother Evelyn took his own life aged 22 over a decade earlier. In the film, Von Einsiedel and his two surviving siblings hiked the routes their brother loved to walk with friends and family. “I was very emotionally closed for a long time after my brother died,” he says. “I used to think being emotionally open was a sign of weakness. I was terrified of my own emotions. I see the opposite now. I think being emotionally open is a sign of strength.”When it comes to picking a subject for a new documentary, he says he is attracted to people who inspire him. “I’m drawn to stories that show the better side of human beings. That’s a thread that runs through the work I like to make.” The Cycle of Love is by far the sunniest film he has made to date. What’s that all about, I ask? “I wanted to make an optimistic film that’s about joy and human connection. The world is difficult. Love is one of those things that all of us can agree on. This story just felt so important to tell.”The Cycle of Love is released in the UK on 18 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsCycling (Life and style)SwedenIndiaCycling (News)featuresShareReuse this content

title: De Gaulle: Liberté review – biopic of conquering French war hero reaches his imperial era | Movies | The Guardian
description: A shrewd performance by Simon Abkarian leads this blockbuster account of the wartime leader’s career as he ascends to political dominance
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: A shrewd performance by Simon Abkarian leads this blockbuster account of the wartime leader’s career as he ascends to political dominance
Content: Simon Abkarian as De Gaulle (left) and Campbell Scott as Roosevelt (right) in De Gaulle: Liberté.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenSimon Abkarian as De Gaulle (left) and Campbell Scott as Roosevelt (right) in De Gaulle: Liberté.Photograph: PRMoviesReviewDe Gaulle: Liberté review – biopic of conquering French war hero reaches his imperial eraA shrewd performance by Simon Abkarian leads this blockbuster account of the wartime leader’s career as he ascends to political dominancePeter BradshawThu 17 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 12.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe massive and commercially triumphant two-part movie about GeneralCharles de Gaullecomes to end with this second half, which does not, as I half expected it might, go into the complex area of De Gaulle’s postwar career and the issue of French Algeria. Maybe another movie, a part three, can cover this. Liberté takes us from De Gaulle’s growing international celebrity, or indeed notoriety, as the exiled keeper of the Free French flame, the king over the water, in which role his authority is still, however, contested and undermined. It includes the triumph of the D-Day landings and the liberation of France, in the course of which De Gaulle (Simon Abkarian) brings off the miracle of persuading the Americans, in the form of President Roosevelt (Campbell Scott), to back him when they had originally intended to treat postwar France as hardly more than a glorified US dependency, like postwar Japan.De Gaulle’s stormy bromance with Winston Churchill (who is wonderfully played by Simon Russell Beale), continues from the first half, and the film genuinely has something new to say about Churchill’s Francophilia. It shows us De Gaulle’s foxy cunning, appearing to accept joint status in the provisional French government with General Henri Giraud (Thierry Lhermitte), his rival in the Allied leaders’ affections – and then deftly ousting him. But as inRésistance, the first part, it is in the African theatre of conflict that a new French hero arises; that is General Leclerc (Niels Schneider) whose maverick daring and improvisational brilliance is inspired by De Gaulle. Montgomery, incidentally, is shrewdly played by Pip Torrens, and I was wondering until the last moment if there would be a gamey cameo for Rommel, perhaps played byLars Eidinger. But no. Germans are apparently not allowed in this mythic retelling.As before, Abkarian has plenty of scenes where he gets out of military aircraft and haughtily sizes up the reception awaiting him, hyper-alert to tiny slights to his status and thereby toFranceitself. He cannot enter a room in this film without a moment in which he considers who is there and how they might insult him; Abkarian makes the most of this amusing dark comedy. Perhaps Liberté doesn’t quite have the intrigue and the intimate drama of the first half but it is still a rousingly watchable movie, a French production in the spirit of J Lee Thompson or John Sturges.De Gaulle: Liberté is in UK and Irish cinemas from 18 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmBiopicsPeriod and historical filmsCharles de GaulleSecond world warFranceSimon Russell BealereviewsShareReuse this content

title: My Year in Paris With Gertrude Stein by Deborah Levy audiobook review – gripping vision of a fearless writer | Jenni Fagan | The Guardian
description: A fictional British author in Paris sets out to explore Stein through the lens of her own friendships, in this inventive, perfectly paced portrait
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: A fictional British author in Paris sets out to explore Stein through the lens of her own friendships, in this inventive, perfectly paced portrait
Content: Blending fiction and biography … Deborah Levy.Photograph: Kate Peters/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBlending fiction and biography … Deborah Levy.Photograph: Kate Peters/The GuardianAudiobook of the weekJenni FaganReviewMy Year in Paris With Gertrude Stein by Deborah Levy audiobook review – gripping vision of a fearless writerA fictional British author in Paris sets out to explore Stein through the lens of her own friendships, in this inventive, perfectly paced portraitFiona SturgesThu 17 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is late 2024, and an unnamed British author living in Paris is trying to write an essay onGertrude Stein, the modernist writer and art collector. The author has been distracted by her friend Eva’s cat, who is lost and whose name is “it” in lower case, which inevitably leads to confusion – has Eva lost her cat or her mind? (Her other friend, Fanny, has rechristened the cat Bob, to make talking about him easier.)The Pennsylvania-born Stein was painted by Picasso, hung out with Hemingway and wrote strange, stream-of-consciousness prose long before James Joyce embarked on his masterwork Ulysses. Commercial success didn’t come until she was in her 60s with The Autobiography of Alice B Toklas, a biography of her partner and one of her more accessible books. Our narrator is an admirer of Stein’s work, yet she can be exasperated by it. “Sometimes, when I read her baffling and beguiling writing I want to smack it in the chops. [Stein] longed for her readers to find her, yet there was a part of her that could not bear to be found.”A blend of fiction and biography, Deborah Levy’s ninth novel is read by voice actor Kristin Atherton; her narration is cool, precise and perfectly paced. We follow the author as she goes to Père Lachaise cemetery in search of Stein’s grave and where she reflects on the lives of other literary luminaries, and on her own friendships. The Stein who emerges in this unusual and gripping portrait is fearless, innovative and, the author notes, “so forward-looking that she never learned to reverse her Ford Model T”.Available via Penguin, 3hr 54minFurther listeningNonesuchFrancis Spufford, Faber, 15hr 29minSet during the blitz, this genre-bending thriller finds Iris Hawkins, a smart young office clerk, navigating a chance encounter which propels her into a world of necromancy, time-travelling Nazis and a plot to assassinate Winston Churchill.The DelusionsJenni Fagan, Penguin, 8hr 19minFagan’s satirical novel about the afterlife centres on Edi, who works in “the largest soul terminus in existence” where she processes the newly dead and decides where they should go based on how they lived their lives. Read by the author.Explore more on these topicsJenni FaganAudiobook of the weekFrancis SpuffordDeborah LevyGertrude SteinreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Opus13: Mendelssohn and Grieg album review – an assured and distinctive debut  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The young quartet – winners of the Wigmore Hall String Quartet competition – continue to impress in a recording pairing Mendelssohn and Grieg
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: The young quartet – winners of the Wigmore Hall String Quartet competition – continue to impress in a recording pairing Mendelssohn and Grieg
Content: Distinctive … Opus13.Photograph: Courtesy of Julia WeselyView image in fullscreenDistinctive … Opus13.Photograph: Courtesy of Julia WeselyClassical musicReviewOpus13: Mendelssohn and Grieg album review – an assured and distinctive debutOpus13(Alpha Classics)The young quartet – winners of the Wigmore Hall String Quartet competition – continue to impress in a recording  pairing  Mendelssohn and GriegErica JealThu 17 Sep 2026 09.44 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou would expect good things fromOpus13– current BBC New Generation Artists, and winners at last year’s Wigmore Hall and Bordeaux string quartet competitions – and this assured, distinctive debut lives up to that. The quartet formed in Oslo in 2014 as teenagers, naming themselves after the first piece they played together, and it’s with that work, Mendelssohn’s Op 13 No 2, that they lead off. The brief, soulful introduction breaks into a tense, runaway allegro in which the occasional violin swoop only increases the feeling of urgency. Mendelssohn’s debt to Beethoven in this work is clear, and the quartet play the slow movement with an intense warmth that makes it seem to belong beside that composer’s great adagios.View image in fullscreenOpus13, Mendelssohn and Grieg.Photograph: Courtesy of Julia WeselyThe Mendelssohn is nicely paired with Grieg’s Quartet No 1, a work full of insistent repetition beautifully handled here so as to create momentum rather than sap it. The folksy style hinted at in the second movement blossoms in the third, which gets a touch of Nordic fiddle, exuberant yet elegant. As encore there’s more Grieg, a characterful version of Solveig’s Song. The arrangement is credited not to a single person but to the entire group equally – which comes as no surprise at all.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com.
