title: ‘You think you’re done and you get pigeonholed’: Samantha Morton on raving, Richard Russell and having another shot as a singer | Music | The Guardian
description: The actor and musician spoke at our Guardian Live ‘Honest Playlist’ event at Green Man festival about growing up in Nottingham on the free-party scene, and the healing powers of music
Author: Kate Hutchinson
Headline: The actor and musician spoke at our Guardian Live ‘Honest Playlist’ event at Green Man festival about growing up in Nottingham on the free-party scene, and the healing powers of music
Content: Kate Hutchinson and Samantha Morton dancing to song ‘Original Nuttah’ by Shy FX and UK ApachiPhotograph: Scarlet Pestell/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKate Hutchinson and Samantha Morton dancing to song ‘Original Nuttah’ by Shy FX and UK ApachiPhotograph: Scarlet Pestell/The GuardianMusicInterview‘You think you’re done and you get pigeonholed’: Samantha Morton on raving, Richard Russell and having another shot as a singerKate HutchinsonThe actor and musician spoke at ourGuardian Live‘Honest Playlist’ event at Green Man festival about growing up in Nottingham on the free-party scene, and the healing powers of musicThu 17 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 06.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the Sunday afternoon of Green Man Festival in August,Samantha Mortonjoined me onstage in the Talking Shop tent to discuss her life in music. The celebrated actor and director is currently in cinemas as the scene-stealing Circe inThe Odyssey, but she is also a musician. Later that day, she performed on the main stage later with Everything Is Recorded, the supergroup led by XL label boss Richard Russell, who also collaborated with Morton on her 2024 solo albumDaffodils & Dirt. More recently, she voiced her character’s title song onThe Odysseysoundtrack. “I love talking about music,” she says. “I never really get asked enough to talk about music.”For this in-depth conversation with Guardian Live, Morton took us through herHonest Playlistof songs on various themes that have meant something to her, including the first single she bought, Musical Youth’s reggae-pop hit Pass The Dutchie, the song she’d do at karaoke, Michael Prophet and Ricky Tuffy’s Your Love, and a great song to fall in love to (Moments In Love by Art of Noise). She thinks about playlists often, revealing that she makes them whenever she needs to get into character for a role and used to “carry tapes in my back pocket everywhere I went because I couldn’t have bad music.”Her earliest musical memories are of the record collection belonging to her father, who she lived with as child in Nottingham between foster home placements in the late-70s, early-80s. “My dad had the most beautiful music taste,” she said, though it was selective: “He had all the Beatles albums, Bob Marley, Don McLean, and that was it.” She recalled a hilarious story of watching her older brother and stepbrother getting into hip-hop – and up to mischief. “They cut the lino out of the back of the kitchen floor because they were breakdancing in town,” she said. Of course: they needed a smooth surface for all the “head-spinning”.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Scarlet Pestell/The GuardianReggae factored into her musical upbringing in a big way. “I moved around a lot because we were homeless,” she continued, “so we were either in a hostel or I was in care, or I was back with my dad when he was out of prison. Nottingham is a massive Afro-Caribbean community, it’s a huge Windrush city. We’d be listening to the most beautiful music for the sound clashes, it was everywhere.”In the 90s, her love of soundsystem culture parlayed into a love of rave music. When her favourite party song rings out, jungle classic Original Nuttah by UK Apache and Shy FX, Morton stands up and starts to dance. “I was an original raver,” she said. Her and her foster mother went “travelling with the free party movement,” specifically theDiY Soundsystem, “that went all over the country having parties.”“We did two summers at Breedon on the Hill,” she continued, referencing the legendary Leicestershire spot where festivals would run for days and days. “I was a kid, but this was my world. It’s where I first learned how to make really lovely rice, or talk to people about politics or poetry.” Those formative experiences turned her into “not an original nuttah, perhaps, but an originalthinker,” she said. It’s also where she first heard another transformative track, Papua Nu Guinea by the Future Sound of London. “People talk about things like ayahuasca, or medicinal mushrooms for healing trauma,” she said, but hearing songs like this in the English countryside “was spiritual. I left the field that day and I felt healed. That music took me somewhere that made me feel loved, [like] a child of the universe.”As a musician herself, Morton found her voice gradually. “I’m not a trained singer. I used to do a bit of session singing for Nightmares On Wax and people like that and I used to sing in rave clubs in Nottingham. I wanted to be Dina Carroll so bad. And then Igot into a lot of trouble with the police, things happened, and I ended up acting.” She still “wrote songs constantly” but didn’t think there was a possibility of performing them until she met Richard Russell. The producer helped to “open up a world for me where I can revisit my first love, music,” she said.In 2024, they collaborated on her first solo album under the name Sam Morton,Daffodils And Dirt –an“intoxicating trip-hop debut”. “We started talking, and we had so many connections to do with influences,” Morton explained. “And I said, listen, ‘I’ve been writing songs since I was about 13. Actually, the first song I wrote, I was about seven, and he was like: ‘We’re going to put it on the album’.” She said that working with Russell, both on her debut and with his collective Everything Is Recorded, “is a dream come true, I swear. I’m 49 now. You think you’re done, you think you can’t do the thing that you’ve always wanted to do, and you get pigeonholed, but you can.”New music is on the horizon, though she’s keeping details underwraps, but for now, she ended by saying she took great pleasure in performing with the “incredible musicians” of Everything Is Recorded. “This is how beautiful and spontaneous music can be,” she said. “Don’t overthink it. Don’t worry about it. It’s the act ofdoingthat fills you with joy.”Explore more on these topicsMusicSamantha MortonFestivalsGreen ManMusic festivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: John Farnham’s 20 best songs | John Farnham | The Guardian
description: From soaring ballads to a song that belongs on every road-trip playlist, these are the tracks that underscore why ‘the Voice’ is a national treasure
Author: Cassie Tongue
Headline: From soaring ballads to a song that belongs on every road-trip playlist, these are the tracks that underscore why ‘the Voice’ is a national treasure
Content: John Farnham belts it out at One Electric Day on Cockatoo Island, Sydney, in November 2019.Photograph: Hanna Lassen/WireImageView image in fullscreenJohn Farnham belts it out at One Electric Day on Cockatoo Island, Sydney, in November 2019.Photograph: Hanna Lassen/WireImageSortedJohn FarnhamJohn Farnham’s 20 best songsFrom soaring ballads to a song that belongs on every road-trip playlist, these are the tracks that underscore why ‘the Voice’ is a national treasureCassie TongueandBen NeutzeThu 17 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 20.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the lead-up to a sold-out tribute concert in celebration of the British-born Australian singer’s music, which is being broadcast at Hoyts cinemas around Australia, we rank the songs that sing to Farnsey’s fans in Australia and around the world.20. Two Strong HeartsView image in fullscreenFarnham and Olivia Newton-John perform during a 2020 bushfire relief concert in Sydney.Photograph: Joel Carrett/EPABouncy and bright, this 1988 love song reached No 6 on the Aria charts, fuelled by an effortless lead vocal that takes off in the built-for-singalongs chorus. In the 2010s,John Farnhamand his longtime pal Olivia Newton-John named their hit tour and subsequent live album after the song – their version reimagines the track as a playful duet between good friends.19. Man of the HourThis standout song from Farnham’s underrated 2000 album, 33 ⅓, sees the singer hit his soulful sweet spot. When performing it live, Farnham made a point of sharing the spotlight with his backing singer, Lindsay Field. Farnham’s generous relationships with longstanding members of the Farnham band always made his live shows feel like a family affair.18. Sadie (The Cleaning Lady)Farnham has a love-hate relationship with his 1967 debut. The biggest-selling single by any Australian artist in Australia in the 1960s, Sadie tells the tale of a blue-collar worker struggling with a life of mundane labour. Lyrically? Deeply depressing (“her red detergent hands have for years not held a man’s!”). Musically? A bop.17. ReasonsThe first, but by no means last, song on this list from Whispering Jack (still the highest-selling album by an Australian artist) pairs a sincere pledge to take life into one’s own hands with a synth beat that points like an arrow towards action. The best part is the vocal performance: when Farnham sings that he’ll “climb more than a mountain” and “swim more than an ocean”, you believe him wholeheartedly.16. Looking Through a TearThis sentimental ballad originally recorded by Aretha Franklin is the title track of Farnham’s third studio album, released in 1970. Not every singer could sell “it’s funny how nothing seems clear when you’re looking through a tear”, but Farnham’s sincerity and golden high tenor make this an irresistible early gem.15. Have a Little Faith (In Us)Pop music tends to be the domain of young love and heartbreak but this surprisingly uplifting 1996 hit about a mid-relationship slump was perfectly suited to a 46-year-old Farnham. The chorus ends optimistically: “For all we know, the best is yet to come.”14. Pressure DownIn his memoir, The Voice Inside, Farnham affectionately calls 1986’s Pressure Down a “quirky little song”, especially for its iconic bassline and radio-friendly production. This effervescent track with delightfully off-kilter lyrics about someone turning the pressure up (!) is still one of his most-played songs on Australian radio, ready-made for long drives and summer afternoons.13. Love to ShineYou could make a case for most of the non-single tracks from Whispering Jack to make it on this list but Love to Shine is particularly special. Written by the British musician Harry Bogdanovs and the English pop singer Kiki Dee, Love to Shine has an effortless synth-led groove – and a great, unexpected bridge that turns the chorus’s melody on its head.12. When Something is Wrong With My BabyBarnesy and Farnesy, together at last. When Jimmy Barnes released his fifth album, Soul Deep, it was a smash hit – andJohn Farnhamwas a key ingredient. The grit-and-gravel rock legend and the pure, clean-cut pop star both fell in love with soul, rock and blues growing up, and they give the 1967 Sam & Dave ballad everything they’ve got: heart, soul and guts, too.11. Age of ReasonA ticking clock. An urgent beat. That gorgeous piano. In his memoir, Farnham reflected that he played it too safe on the track, regretting his strained falsetto. But that audible effort, that messy realness in a song begging us to do the work to build a kinder future, feels like exactly the point.10. Comic ConversationA minor hit single released in 1970 but a firm fan favourite, Comic Conversation sees Farnham in storytelling mode, crooning about an unrequited love. It has a fantastic opening line: “I’m going to ask your friends your number, and I’ll call you when your man is out of town.” Colour us intrigued.9. Please Don’t Ask MeWritten and produced by Farnham’s future Little River Band bandmate Graeham Goble, 1980’s Please Don’t Ask Me is the most finely crafted sap. Sure, it’s a tad cloying, but it’s also raw and vulnerable, with a luscious string arrangement that points to the successful live collaborations Farnham would have in future years with Australian orchestras.8. A Touch of ParadiseA Touch of Paradise was the third single from Whispering Jack, and the only true ballad on the album. Originally recorded by the Australian rock band Mondo Rock several years earlier, the song’s pared-back synths and drum machines plant it firmly and satisfyingly in the 1980s. As with many of Farnham’s best, it builds to a thrilling vocal climax.7. Don’t You Know it’s MagicFarnham struggled to find chart success for much of the 1970s but this mid-tempo rock song from the curiously named Hits Magic & Rock ’N Roll album performed pretty well, peaking at No 12 on the Australian national charts and staying there for 15 weeks. Written by the Australian rock statesman Brian Cadd, it really stands up.6. Every Time You CryA retro pastiche filled with wacky aphorisms (“the light at the end of the tunnel doesn’t shine at the end of the day”)andthe obligatory new single on a greatest-hits album? Every Time You Cry has no right being so good. Farnham’s rich and confident vocals were resurrected from sessions for Romeo’s Heart and paired with Human Nature’s lovely four-part harmonies and together they soar. An instant, timeless classic.5. That’s FreedomA song that belongs on every road-trip playlist, That’s Freedom is the sort of tune that propels the listener forward – all the way “from the mountain, to the valley, from the ocean, to the alley, from the highway, to the river”. It just makes you feel good.4. Burn for YouCo-writer and frequent Farnham collaborator Phil Buckle’s delicate and beautiful guitar line on Burn for You helped define Farnham’s evolving sound as he moved away from the Fairlight synths of Whispering Jack and Age of Reason to more stripped-back and roots-inspired sounds. It also features one of Farnham’s most affectingly intimate vocals. It feels as though we’re eavesdropping from the next room while he’s on the phone, begging a lover to not hang up on him again. Like many of the best love songs (and this is one of them) the lyric is straightforward and honest, leaving a singer nowhere to hide. Farnham more than rises to the occasion: he burns.3. Playing to WinFarnham may not have particularly enjoyed his four years fronting Little River Band – he clashed with other members of the band, claiming they had his microphone cable duct-taped to the stage so he couldn’t move around and steal the spotlight – but it inspired him to write one of his best songs, this fiery declaration of tenacity, and the only one from his time in LRB that stayed on his setlist. In many ways, Playing to Win stated Farnham’s intent, setting the stage for one of the most audacious comebacksAustralian musichas ever seen.2. Help!There aren’t many covers that seem to erase all memory of the original, but for the four and a half minutes it takes Farnham to sing Help!, the Beatles feel somehow irrelevant. This slowed-down, beefed-up version was originally performed for Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip at the royal charity concert at Sydney Opera House in 1980. Farnham’s live performances in the decades since are operatic in scale, showcasing everything that made him Australia’s finest pop singer. The final verse is properly staggering. It might be a cover but his is the only voice in the world that could do this.1. You’re the VoiceOn paper, it’s bonkers that a song by four Brits with a bagpipe solo and slamming car-door drums would ever be a hit, let alone an Australian national treasure. Forty years on, it’s easy to take its genius for granted. So close your eyes. Listen again. It’s alchemical, every element contributing to its unstoppable force, but none more so than Farnham himself. The song made him and is made better by him; his power and conviction transforms admittedly vague lyrics about unity and change into something undeniable. It’s a spiritual national anthem, one that imagines us into the Australia we wish we were: equitable and kind, with a fair go for all. Where no one sits in silence, so no one lives with fear.Explore more on these topicsJohn FarnhamSortedAustralian musicPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Feeling overwhelmed by the AI doom loop? Here’s the essential reading list to make sense of it all | Books | The Guardian
description: It’s a chaotic time in an industry that’s reshaping our lives – Guardian reporters and experts recommend the books that help explain how we got here, and where we’re headed
Author: Lois Beckett
Headline: It’s a chaotic time in an industry that’s reshaping our lives – Guardian reporters and experts recommend the books that help explain how we got here, and where we’re headed
Content: The books in our list aim to explain and critique the AI industry and provide deeper political and social context to the AI moment.Illustration: Kittipong Jirasukhanont/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe books in our list aim to explain and critique the AI industry and provide deeper political and social context to the AI moment.Illustration: Kittipong Jirasukhanont/AlamyBooksFeeling overwhelmed by the AI doom loop? Here’s the essential reading list to make sense of it allIt’s a chaotic time in an industry that’s reshaping our lives – Guardian reporters and experts recommend the books that help explain how we got here, and where we’re headingLois BeckettThu 17 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 14.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHave you been feeling trapped in an endless cycle of artificial intelligence hype and panic? You’re not alone.It’s a chaotic time to make sense of the industry that’s reshaping our lives, whether or not we like it. Last week, another AI company employeepublicly resigned, warning the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. Despite these dire warnings, AI companies have seen “otherworldly”surges in revenueand driven the USstock markets to new highsas they continue to push AI tools into everything frompublic school classroomstolaw enforcement agencies, as well as rushing to put up new datacentersacross the country.Thankfully, the Guardian’s tech reporters – and a few other tech experts we respect – are here to help. We’ve compiled an essential reading list of smart books that explain and critique the AI industry; books that, while flawed, illustrate key viewpoints in the AI debates; and a few books that provide deeper political and social context, including some works of speculative fiction.The best books on the AI industryEmpire of AI– Karen HaoThe most intensively reported book on the AI industry so far, Empire of AI covers the rise of OpenAI, as well as the formation of Anthropic and OpenAI chief Sam Altman’s split with Elon Musk. Parts of the book can feel a bit inside baseball, but the reporting is great and shows how the key American AI companies brought us to this point. Some early reviews of the book in 2025 suggested Hao’s take on the industry was overly negative: she has since been entirely vindicated.Project Maven– Katrina MansonAn in-depth look at how the US military and Palantir worked together to build autonomous weapons and surveillance systems that are an actual catastrophic threat – not an imagined one.Hyperscale–Paris MarxFrom the journalist and host of theTech Won’t Save Uspodcast, this is a deep investigation into the physical impact of AI data centers around the world, and the toll they are taking on local communities and the global environment.Your Face Belongs to Us–Kashmir HillA bestselling book on the rise of Clearview AI, the facial recognition company that has provided sweeping surveillance powers to law enforcement, businesses and billionaires, by building a massive database of online images.The AI Con–Emily M Bender and Alex HannaIn response to claims that AI will soon far surpass all human capabilities, and that the technology is advancing so quickly it’s on the verge of becoming a new life form, the authors of The AI Con have a simple response:“LOL” and “they wish”.These two tech critic academics argue that this kind of rhetoric is “AI hype” – lies and exaggerations that are helping rich people make more money “by justifying data theft, motivating surveillance capitalism, and devaluing human creativity”.Flawed books on AI (that still might be worth reading)If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies–Eliezer Yudkowskyand Nate SoaresIf you want to understand the perspective of the people panicking that AI will destroy humanity, this book is a good place to start. It’s a “doomer classic” that has been described as a book-length version ofthe tweet that made everyone freak outthis past week. Unfortunately for readers, its predictions of doom are based more on grand thought experiments than on an engagement with how AI is currently playing out in the world. The book “reads like a Scientology manual”, a New York Times reviewer wrote. For context, Yudkowsky’s other writings include a nearly700,000-word work of Harry Potter fan fictionin which Harry applies the scientific method to magic.Superintelligence– Nick BostromThis 2014 book is one of the foundational AI texts for people like Elon Musk, who, alongside Bill Gates, haspublicly praisedthe bestseller. While the book is useful as a way of understanding the evolution of arguments about how a superintelligent AI might doom society,it’s worth notingthat the author is a controversial Swedish-born philosopher who was forced to apologize in 2023 for a decades-old email in which he claimed “Blacks are more stupid than whites” and used the N-word. In 2024, Oxfordquietly shut downthe academic institute he had run, and Bostrom resigned.Genesis: artificial intelligence, hope, and the human spirit– Henry Kissinger, Eric Schmidt, Craig Mundie and Eleanor RundeAre you looking for AI insights from a man who facedfrequent, wide-ranging and substantial allegations of war crimes? Astonishingly, Henry Kissinger, the former US secretary of state who died in 2023, co-authored a bestselling 2024 book on AI with a billionaire former Google CEO, a less-wealthy former Microsoft executive, and a young lawyer who worked as Kissinger’s researcher. The authors suggest that AI’s ability to provide swift answers without explaining how it got them might end our current “age of reason” and lead humanity back to a “pre-modern acceptance of unexplained authority”. They also raise the possibility that “the companies that own and develop AI will accrue totalizing social, economic, military and political power”, or that AI itself might become an all-powerful “philosopher king”. OpenAI’s ChatGPT listed this as one of thefive best books on artificial intelligence.The Technological Republic– Alex Karp and Nicholas ZamiskaThis manifesto by the CEO of Palantir was described by one Guardian colleague as one of the worst-written books he had ever read. It includes rambling attacks on the Palestinian American academic Edward Said, and goes further than Kissinger and his co-authors by more or less calling for turning tech leaders into philosopher kings. Prose aside, the book provides an important window into what top tech CEOs actually believe, and the way they regard AI and tech as a new nuclear bomb – which, in their view, is a good thing.Deeper context: history, ideology and fictionThe Rise and Fall of the Artificial State– Jill LeporeA historical look at the political and industrial movements that have wanted to cede human agency and democratic rule to automation and authoritarianism. Just published, and a surprisingly fun read!MoreEverything Forever– Adam BeckerWritten by a science journalist, this book provides a good overview of the ideological origins of our current tech leaders. Exploring accelerationism, rationalism, doomerism and more, the book emphasizes how strange and detached from reality these powerful people’s belief systems are.Automating Inequality– Virginia EubanksThis 2018 book predates the generative AI boom, but it provides an essential view into how automated systems and algorithms reinforce social inequality. Modern AI has supercharged these same capabilities and is getting integrated into every critical system, making the book’s insights into the harms of automated inequality even more important.Predatory Data: Eugenics in Big Tech and Our Fight for an Independent Future– Anita Say ChanOur current systems of techno-surveillance and algorithmic discrimination are rooted in 19th-century campaigns against immigration and in favor of eugenics, the practice of selectively breeding humans to improve their intelligence or racial dominance, Chan argues. The book highlights the evolution of “techno-eugenicists” and the persistence of feminist and immigrant activists who have fought against them, and is recommended by Seeta Peña Gangadharan, an associate professor at the London School of Economics who studies the community impact of data-driven technologies.Prophecy: Prediction, Power and the Fight for the Future, from Ancient Oracles to AI– Carissa VélizTracing the parallels between ancient seers, court astrologers, and contemporary algorithms, an Oxford University philosopher argues that “the main promise of prediction is not knowledge of the future but domination over others.” Another recommendation from Peña Gangadharan and her LSE doctoral student, Anna Osterberg, who studies the political dynamics of online communities.I, Robot– Isaac AsimovThough it was first published in 1950, Asimov’s collection of short stories on the ethics of human-robot interactions remains influential, including his “Three Laws of Robotics”, starting with: “A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm.” As humor writerAlex Blechman has pointed out,classic science fiction books and films remain deeply influential in the tech world, even though many tech companies seem set on engineering precisely the kinds of dangerous outcomes that science fictionwarned against.The Lost Books of the Odyssey– Zachary MasonIn 2007, a computer scientist from Palo Alto published a collection of46 retellings of passages from the Odyssey– a book that riffs on the way narratives get revised, fragmented, and reborn. Mason was activelyimagining the prose AI might producelong before the technology was available. Asked for his recommendations on AI-related books, Robin Sloan, a fiction author and media and technology writer, chose this novel, which he called “the first book of the LLM era, even though it was written entirely, and beautifully, by a human”. He says the book “has a lot to say about multiplicity, deep stories and symbols”.Labyrinths– Jorge Luis BorgesSloan also made the case for a classic, Borges’ short story collection Labyrinths, as a book that “gets your head in the right place to think usefully and richly about the deep weirdness and enormity of language models”. The collection includes one of Borges’ most famous stories,The Library of Babel, first published in 1941, which describes and wrestles with a plan for an infinite library.Nick Robins-Early contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsBooksAI (artificial intelligence)US politicsComputingRobotsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The New Dark Ages by James Marriott review – a grandiose but superficial defence of reading | Books | The Guardian
description: What is it that makes books so magical? The Times columnist somehow forgets to tell us in this lofty polemic
Author: Anthony Cummins
Headline: What is it that makes books so magical? The Times columnist somehow forgets to tell us in this lofty polemic
Content: Are we entering a post-literature age?Photograph: Klaus Vedfelt/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAre we entering a post-literature age?Photograph: Klaus Vedfelt/Getty ImagesBooksReviewThe New Dark Ages by James Marriott review – a grandiose but superficial defence of readingWhat is it that makes books so magical? The Times columnist somehow forgets to tell us in this lofty polemicAnthony CumminsThu 17 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile other kids watched cartoons, Times columnist James Marriott would spend his school holidays in bed with piles of books – “a mammoth effort of attention, perhaps the greatest I ever made” – under the spell of his father, a teacher who inculcated in him a literary zeal “not exactly common in the north of England in the early 2000s”.Twenty-five years on, Marriott fears smartphones have all but killed reading for everyone. He had to get rid of his own – “George Eliot is no match” – and now, watching the rest of us scroll, he worries not only that we will lose the ability to appreciate Middlemarch, but that we risk falling prey to tyrants and anti-vaxxers forging “a world very different to the one we have known … mystical, tribal and autocratic”.Such is the gist of Marriott’s first book, The New Dark Ages, a polemical elegy tracing the rise and fall of print from Montaigne to Mr Beast. The point is modest – scroll less, read more – but the tone is grandiose.Literacyturbocharged our capacity for complex argument, he argues, but adds that “conversation is very far from useless”, and says “literate civilisation … has never produced a work of art with quite the same quality of heroic starkness as the Iliad or Beowulf”.double quotation markPunchy quips aren’t enough to keep the book afloat in deep watersThe readerly bicep Marriott likes flashing is rarely as firm as it looks. “The important things Leo Tolstoy [has] to say about life will only be understood if you can pay attention,” he writes, never saying what they are. His advocacy for books relies on browbeating hyperbole: “I believe there is a kind of truth about life which is only accessible through prose fiction with its capacity to show us the inside of other minds … It is the reason that no actor on earth can show with his or her face what Jane Austen can show us about the human heart in half a paragraph.” When he actually articulates a novel’s impact, it’s to tell us that Elena Ferrante taught him “what it is like to be a teenage girl”.Literature isn’t his only focus. “In the early 20th century everyone read a newspaper,” he says, lamenting social media’s impact on politics. He imagines a print report and a TikTok clip from the same war zone: “Even the most simple written article is more likely to offer explanations for events. How did the war start? Why did the war start?” Alternatively, to summon “your rage with an image, I only need to show you a picture of … heaped bodies”; in other words, if you’re angry when “a missile destroys an apartment block in the Middle East” – the clip he envisages – it’s because a journalist hasn’t explained it.The sense grows that lofty proclamations and punchy quips aren’t enough to keep the book afloat in deep waters. “The 21st century’s much-documented epidemic of anxiety, depression and purposelessness is at least partly rooted in the … culture of the screen,” says Marriott, leaving us to wonder if he’s muddled symptom and cause. When the book begins, he calls smartphones the “major culprit” of the drop in reading for pleasure – “factors like inequality” are less to blame – but it ends by warning that “very rich” people have the resources “to keep their children away from addictive screens. Poorer parents who have to work multiple jobs and who lack the money for childcare do not.”It’s the last gasp for a thesis whose apocalyptic urgency fizzles out in equivocating caveats. “Post-literate”, Marriott clarifies, doesn’t mean “incapable of reading and writing”: although there may be “fewer Shakespeares, more Slack messages” – how many Shakespeares does he think there have been? – literacy “still has a future”. Which isn’t “to counsel unthinking optimism”, just to say that “even in the worst-case scenario, reading … will be around for a while yet”. Phew!The New Dark Ages is neatly positioned to appeal to lapsed readers who wince at their weekly screen time report. But there’s a less opportunistic book buried deep between its lines: one about growing up convinced the world begins and ends with literature, only to find that all it took to make you doubt it was a six-inch sliver of black glass.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe New Dark Ages: The End of Reading and the Dawn of a Post-Literate Society by James Marriott is published by Bodley Head (£14.99). title: The Strangers by Naomi Alderman review – where has this odd new species come from? | Fiction | The Guardian
description: A bereavement memoir mingles with speculative fiction, in a wise and ragged examination of grief from the author of The Power
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A bereavement memoir mingles with speculative fiction, in a wise and ragged examination of grief from the author of The Power
Content: Lightness of touch … Naomi Alderman.Photograph: Annabel MoellerView image in fullscreenLightness of touch … Naomi Alderman.Photograph: Annabel MoellerBook of the dayFictionReviewThe Strangers by Naomi Alderman review – where has this odd new species come from?A bereavement memoir mingles with speculative fiction, in a wise and ragged examination of grief from the author of The PowerKeiran GoddardThu 17 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn his Remarks on Frazer’s Golden Bough, Ludwig Wittgenstein alludes to an incident that followed the death of Franz Schubert. He recalls that Schubert’s brother cut several scores into small pieces, each consisting of only a few bars of music, and handed them out to Schubert’s favourite pupils. This, Wittgenstein argues, was a totally understandable act of grief. He goes on to suggest, however, that if, in his grief, Schubert’s brother had left the scores untouched, or even burned them, then that too would be equally legible to us. Such is the disorienting nature of loss – in its wake, anything goes.In The Strangers, Women’s prize-winning author Naomi Alderman tests this thesis to its limits. How about dealing with grief by writing an uneasy memoir/speculative fiction hybrid about the sudden appearance of a new species of quasi-badgers that seem to improve the quality of local soil?Well, it turns out Wittgenstein was right. The Strangers, despite (or perhaps because of) its many ragged idiosyncrasies, is a remarkably successful evocation of loss. Narrated by “the novelist Naomi Alderman”, who is mourning both her recently deceased mother and a series of failed pregnancies, the book ranges incisively across the vast affective terrain bequeathed to those who go on living: despair, disorientation, solipsism, petulance, regret, resignation … the list goes on. After all, grief is not an emotion – it is all the emotions, all at once.And by braiding the memoir within a subtly unnerving tale of eco-horror infestation, Alderman substantially raises the philosophical and symbolic stakes. It is a high-risk, sporadically successful manoeuvre, but one that recognises the gravity of the task at hand. In the same way that a gravestone is an attempt to give form to an absence, Alderman’s structural ingenuity allows the reader to wrangle some of the ineffable aspects of grief into something more coherent and bounded.The plot itself is simple enough, and relatively small fry compared to some of Alderman’s previous work, such as thwarting the techno-apocalypse (The Future) or upending the global gender hierarchy (The Power). A new type of species is discovered, a flat-faced and long-nosed mammal that comes to be known as a mimmoth. They remain largely inscrutable to humans: hard to photograph, even harder to capture, and seemingly responsible for a range of positive ecological changes. Their inscrutability cuts both ways, however, and soon enough the mimmoths are the subject of conspiracy theories and hate campaigns, worship and veneration, floating signifiers swept up into the insatiable polarisation of the present. To some they are harbingers of a better future, sent to teach us how to care for one another and the planet, while to others they are “invaders, genetic freaks, not natural”.double quotation markThe Strangers asserts the painful truth that we do not get to choose the things that we loseOn the whole, Alderman handles the fairly obvious political allegories with a lightness of touch that prevents them from collapsing into polemic, sketching out our political and media environment with the skill of a practised world-builder. The failing institutions of British life are a “Potemkin village” stripped of their engine and replaced with “a clockwork mechanism, slowly running down”. There are occasional moments, however, that seem transplanted from another era entirely; one when people’s political subjectivities were formed by front pages and evening news bulletins, and not by unchecked genocide livestreamed to their phones.Fundamentally, though, The Strangers is a deeply moving and wise book, asserting the painful truth that we simply do not get to choose the things that we lose. When the narrator wonders if she has fallen prey to “mimmoth-psychosis”, the delusion that one has a uniquely intimate relation with the mysterious creatures, I was put in mind of Judith Butler’s observation about grief being a site of temporal reorganisation, a crucible in which our selfhood can be undone and remade. Both Alderman and Butler seem to remind us that while despair may temporarily convince us otherwise, life, in all its terrifying potential, stubbornly persists.That the mimmoths’ arrival coincides with an upsurge in mushroom-like fungus seems particularly telling. Among its many miraculous properties, mycelium contains within it a biological code of deep sociality and connectivity, existing as a network that is constantly reallocating and rebalancing resources, moving nutrients symbiotically between the old and the young, the weak and the strong. The political metaphor contained therein has proved irresistible to many commentators. But in The Strangers, Alderman asks whether there is also a parallel to be drawn in how we allocate our resources of attention and love more proximately. How do we mediate between the existing potential of our own lives, the expired potential of the dead and the unrealised potential of the never or nearly born? It is the type of intractable question one can only ever hope to live alongside. Or, as “the novelist Naomi Alderman” puts it, “I do not wish my ghosts away.”The Strangers by Naomi Alderman is published by Fig Tree (£20). title: Darkling review – Stranger Things’ Linnea Berthelsen confronts a gruesome Indian disaster | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Titas Halder’s coming-of-age monologue is set against the 1984 Bhopal toxic gas leak – but the poetic script doesn’t quite capture the horror
Author: Ammar Kalia
Headline: Titas Halder’s coming-of-age monologue is set against the 1984 Bhopal toxic gas leak – but the poetic script doesn’t quite capture the horror
Content: Tightly wound … Linnea Berthelsen in Darkling at Bush theatre.Photograph: Alex BrennerView image in fullscreenTightly wound … Linnea Berthelsen in Darkling at Bush theatre.Photograph: Alex BrennerTheatreReviewDarkling review – Stranger Things’ Linnea Berthelsen confronts a gruesome Indian disasterBush theatre, LondonTitas Halder’s coming-of-age monologue is set against the 1984 Bhopal toxic gas leak – but the poetic script doesn’t quite capture the horrorAmmar KaliaThu 17 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOminousness permeates Darkling. In Titas Halder’s dramatic monologue, we witness a young girl’s coming of age set against the backdrop of the 1984 toxic gas leak in the Indian city of Bhopal, an environmental catastrophe that remains one of the worst industrial disasters in global history, leading to thousands of deaths.Actor Linnea Berthelsen – best known for her role as Kali in Netflix seriesStranger Things– makes her UK stage debut and gamely takes on the singular role in a tightly wound, physical performance. Leaping across Simon Kenny’s artful, soil-filled set, Berthelsen embodies childlike wonder as she recounts her early years playing in the rain, savouring bowlfuls of plain rice and idolising her older sister.View image in fullscreenChildlike wonder … Linnea Berthelsen in Darkling.Photograph: Alex BrennerSo far so good. Except, alongside her emotional growth, the silhouette of a new factory rises in the background – effectively portrayed by lighting designer Rajiv Pattani’s projection – foreshadowing the calamity to come. When it eventually arrives, we hear of the horrors she witnesses, stepping over maimed bodies, facing blinded relatives and breathing in toxic fumes, all relayed through increasingly frenzied description.Herein lies the main issue with Darkling. By using a monologue format – especially one where our narrator is never dramatically questioned – all the audience receives are streams of poetic description, a barrage of words that never feel emphatic or adequate enough to match the gruesome scale of such a tragedy. Coupled with Halder’s uneven pacing, which lingers in childhood for too long before alighting on trauma and then descending into a hectoring denouement that places the blame for the disaster on individual shoulders, Berthelsen is faced with a gargantuan task to maintain a sense of dramatic tension.As Matthew Xia’s production draws to a close, with a strangely repeated narrative beat that equates female worth to motherhood, you are ultimately left feeling that this is a tragedy told without the requisite horror. Darkling is a worthy reminder of an often-overlooked disaster – but one that may well fail to take root in the mind.AtBush theatre, London, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreBush theatreMatthew XiaIndiaStranger ThingsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Million Dollar Quartet review – jumping jukebox show reignites rock’n’roll classics | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, Carl Perkins and Jerry Lee Lewis’s 1956 get-together is respun with an unsubtle script but some vigorous performances
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, Carl Perkins and Jerry Lee Lewis’s 1956 get-together is respun with an unsubtle script but some vigorous performances
Content: Go, cats, go! … (from left) Christopher Erasmus as Johnny Cash, Joey Bradick as Carl Perkins and Connor Payne as Elvis Presley.Photograph: Alex TabriziView image in fullscreenGo, cats, go! … (from left) Christopher Erasmus as Johnny Cash, Joey Bradick as Carl Perkins and Connor Payne as Elvis Presley.Photograph: Alex TabriziTheatreReviewMillion Dollar Quartet review – jumping jukebox show reignites rock’n’roll classicsThe Arts at Marble Arch, LondonElvis Presley, Johnny Cash, Carl Perkins and Jerry Lee Lewis’s 1956 get-together  is respun with an unsubtle script but some vigorous performancesChris WiegandThu 17 Sep 2026 13.24 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 13.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith the Arts theatre currently closed for major works, it has established a larger base next to Marble Arch. This temporary new home is now given over to some golden oldies with a jukebox musical combining the stories of Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, Carl Perkins andJerry Lee Lewis. It is almost 70 years since they wound up together one December afternoon at Sam Phillips’ Sun Studios in Memphis and recorded 40-odd songs. “Million dollar quartet” ran the caption that accompanied their picture in the newspaper.Did this impromptu supergroup share vocals on Blue Suede Shoes and did Cash and Perkins mash up My Babe and Sixteen Tons as they do here? All the evidence suggests not. They chiefly laid down gospel and spiritual numbers amid some breezy chatter kept on the recordings. Two of those, Down By the Riverside and Peace in the Valley, are kept from the original session – along with Chuck Berry’s Brown Eyed Handsome Man – in a show that uses the occasion to rotate instead through some of their greatest hits including Great Balls of Fire, which wouldn’t be recorded at Sun for another year. Even Libby Watson’s design, which turns the modest studios into a sort of checkerboard-floored rock’n’roll diner cum fairground, has a colourful arch resembling a retro jukebox.View image in fullscreenOwning the room … Jenay Naima as Dyanne in Million Dollar Quartet.Photograph: Alex TabriziThe musical – first staged in 2006 andseen in the West End in 2011, now newly transferred fromCirencester’s Barn theatre– is a curious mix of wildly fanciful and diligently factual. Colin Escott and Floyd Mutrux’s book has some laidback charm and humour but the characters often awkwardly trot out their own and each other’s backstories. Phillips (Darren Day) hosts the evening, adding extra exposition. It can feel like a series of potted histories. Occasionally a song matches the men’s conversation, as when their shared family bereavements inspire Peace in the Valley. Other songs may carry their own stories of danger and passion but the only drama bubbling in the script is Phillips’ proteges being poached by bigger record labels and some rivalry between the foursome.It’s not exactly Stereophonic.View image in fullscreenCockamamie … Joe Bence as Jerry Lee LewisPhotograph: Alex TabriziAnd yet … Jonathan O’Boyle’s production has four actor-musicians so charismatic and combative as these cocky young guns, each playing and singing with such vigour, that the well-worn tunes hit you afresh. Connor Payne’s luxuriously quiffed Presley, Christopher Erasmus’s brooding Cash, Joe Bence’s cockamamie Lewis and Joey Bradick’s driven Perkins are not imitations and instead retain an essence of each musician. Along with drummer Josh Haberfield and double bassist Geraint Downing, they rip through it with an assurance that is irresistible. And in this testosterone-filled studio, Presley’s girlfriend – here called Dyanne – blows them all away with her rendition of Fever then does it again with I Hear You Knocking. Who cares if that really happened either, you may ask, when Jenay Naima owns the room this well.Atthe Arts at Marble Arch, London, until 6 December. Thentouringuntil 17 JulyExplore more on these topicsTheatreMusicalsElvis PresleyJerry Lee LewisJohnny CashRockabillyWest EndreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Thelma & Louise review – musical hoedown is a bland and baffling wrong turn | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Despite a book by the original screenwriter, this stage adaptation doesn’t have the depth – or the songs – worthy of the era-defining feminist parable. And where’s the car?
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Despite a book by the original screenwriter, this stage adaptation doesn’t have the depth – or the songs – worthy of the era-defining feminist parable. And where’s the car?
Content: Southern twang … Amy Lennox and Rachel Tucker in Thelma & Louise at the Young Vic.Photograph: Helen MurrayView image in fullscreenSouthern twang … Amy Lennox and Rachel Tucker in Thelma & Louise at the Young Vic.Photograph: Helen MurrayTheatreReviewThelma & Louise review – musical hoedown is a bland and baffling wrong turnYoung Vic, LondonDespite a book by the original screenwriter, this stage adaptation doesn’t have the depth – or the songs – worthy of the era-defining feminist parable. And where’s the car?Arifa AkbarThu 17 Sep 2026 07.27 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Beware; for I am fearless, and therefore powerful.” These words were written by Mary Shelley two centuries ago but could apply to the two runaways in Ridley Scott’s 1991 film who turn into highway fugitives in their liberating cross-country road trip after a girls’ weekend goes wrong.Thelma & Louise, starring Susan Sarandon and Geena Davis, did not exactly represent Shelley’s “monstrous feminine” but came to be seen as an era-defining feminist parable on freedom from male strictures and abuse. It caught the cultural zeitgeist, the title becoming a byword for sisterhood, with reams written about its feminist layers, spectacular cinematography – and the shock of its un-Hollywood ending.View image in fullscreenUnderpowered … Amy Lennox and Jordan Luke Gage in Thelma & Louise.Photograph: Helen MurraySo it is a brave creative team that decides to adapt the film for the stage. It helps this production’s credentials that the original screenwriter, Callie Khouri, is on board for the book. It also has two capable leads in Rachel Tucker, who plays the tough-cookie Louise, and Amy Lennox as Thelma, the put-upon wife turned fantastically rogue.Beyond that, the intention around this musical adaptation of the road movie is entirely perplexing. Significantly, there is neither road nor car, bar a fleeting glimpse of the latter at the beginning, upturned and static. Streaking neon lights and the sounds of a revving motor denote their journey. “I want the wind in my hair,” sings Thelma at one point. We do too, Thelma.Fans of the film can forget those glorious scenes of the women’s turquoise convertible Thunderbird, and of the magnificently lonely desert, both of which felt like characters in their own right. Instead, the backdrop is a prosaic saloon bar – the fateful one they visit where a drunk man attempts to rape Thelma and is shot dead by Louise.That incident comes early, so the women’s fear of its consequences eclipses their initial joy and release. Their characters remain flatly dichotomous: Thelma is the flirty conventional one, Louise haranguing and hard-bitten. The narrative plays out as two women on the run. You wish for more depth, more bonding between them, which does come in the second half when the show finally fires up, but it still feels like empowerment-lite.‘It’s not good to walk through the world feeling like prey’: Thelma & Louise’s writer on turning a movie classic into a musicalRead moreUnder the direction of Trip Cullman, the characters seem dated and the time-frame wavers uncertainly between the 1980s and now.Bobbi Jene Smithand Or Schraiber’s choreography brings hoedown moves and line dancing men in 10-gallon hats. There are few memorable songs in Neko Case’s country score, although one reprised number takes flight in the heartfelt It Was Worth It. The southern twangs are dialled up to 10, and lyrics offer exposition with plodding lines, although the singing is strong.The sexy young grifter JD – the character that launched the young, incandescent Brad Pitt on film – is patina-thin and played by Jordan Luke Gage. Lead detective Hal (Trevor Dion Nicholas) is also barely there as a character. None of it is powered by enough emotion. When the road trip ends at the mouth of the Grand Canyon, the women’s T-Bird surrounded by police and revving dangerously, you are moved not by what is unravelling before you but by the memory of the unforgettable, defiant ending of the film. Did they really just do that?AtYoung Vic theatre, London, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMusicalsYoung VicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: It’s going to be a blast: why 100 tubas are heading for a garden in Haddington | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Anthony Braxton’s colossal Composition No 19 (for 100 Tubas) has never been performed outside the US so its arrival at the Lammermuir festival merits a mighty fanfare
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Anthony Braxton’s colossal Composition No 19 (for 100 Tubas) has never been performed outside the US so its arrival at the Lammermuir festival merits a mighty fanfare
Content: Diverse in their unity… the world premiere of Anthony Braxton’s Composition No. 19 for 100 Tubas at the World Financial Center Plaza, New York, June 2006.Photograph: Jack Vartoogian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDiverse in their unity… the world premiere of Anthony Braxton’s Composition No. 19 for 100 Tubas at the World Financial Center Plaza, New York, June 2006.Photograph: Jack Vartoogian/Getty ImagesClassical musicIt’s going to be a blast: why 100 tubas are heading for a garden in HaddingtonFaced with a new concert venue – a vast and beautiful walled garden – John Harris and the Lammermuir festival had to decide how to fill it with sound. Anthony Braxton’s colossal composition was the irresistible solution.John HarrisThu 17 Sep 2026 07.12 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 08.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWorking in contemporary music, I am used to eyebrows being raised by friends and family when I answer their seemingly innocent dinnertime question, “What are you up to at the moment?”. My responses over the years have ranged from “staging an opera about alien abductionunderneath Concorde” to “ensuring that a soprano can get a tattoo live on stage while she sings”. However, I’ve never previously experienced anything like the familial spluttering in response to my most recent answer – “putting on a concert with 100 tuba players in a garden outside Edinburgh”.I do understand some of their surprise, but to be honest 100 tubas seemed like such a logical solution to the problem I was given that I’m not sure I understand it entirely! James Waters, artistic director of the Lammermuir festival in East Lothian,Scotland– and regular partner-in-crime for some of Red Note Ensemble’s wilder productions, including the aforementioned opera under Concorde – phoned me one day last year to say “I have found an interesting – and very beautiful – place to put on a concert. I just don’t have a clue what music to do. Come and have a look!”Duly invited out to look atAmisfield Walled Garden– a beautifully laid out space near Haddington, maintained and much cherished by a group of committed volunteers – I was taken not only with how lovely it all was, but also just how big. Originally the kitchen garden for a now vanished stately home, it must have been quite the kitchen. The walls are those of a castle – an intimidating 20 feet high– and the space itself extends over the equivalent of several football pitches. James – face beaming with delight at setting a challenge that he knows I’m not going to turn down – turned to me and said: “Let’s fill the garden with sound!”View image in fullscreen‘The space extends over the equivalent of several football pitches.’ Amisfield Walled Garden, Haddington, Scotland.Photograph: Amazing Aerial/AlamyChallenge duly accepted. But how? To my mind, with something that size, you’ve got three options. Either massive amplification (a little rock’n’roll for Lammermuir, perhaps), a lot of bagpipes (always an option in Scotland, but the contemporary repertoire is sadly limited), or those quintessential outdoor instruments – brass ones. And then the essential question: what on earth are they going to play?I do have some history with large-scale brass performances. I myself don’t play a brass instrument – although my brother was a founder member of the brass band in the town that we grew up in – but I have worked with many brass players over the years, and staged a number of mass-participation brass events in my other job as festival director of New Music Dublin. However, I have no handles at all on the contemporary brass repertoire beyond that, so it was time to call in a second associate from the contemporary music underworld – the celebrated trumpeter Marco Blaauw, well-known for his playing with Ensemble Musikfabrik in Germany to help us work out what everyone was going to perform.double quotation markTubas come in all shapes and sizes, from orchestral ones to over-the-shoulder sousaphones, tenor horns, euphoniums and even the rarely- sighted Wagner tubaMarco breezed into Scotland, trumpet in hand, to “try out the acoustics” of the garden. Those bitingly cold days in Amisfield in December are precious memories, as Marco also brought along John Wallace – fellow trumpeter extraordinaire, former principal of the Royal Conservatoire of Scotland and best known to the general public as the impeccable soloist performing alongside Kiri Te Kanawa at Charles and Diana’s wedding – to have a listen. Very sadly, John died earlier this year, and this year’s Lammermuir festival is dedicated to his memory. I have a very clear memory of John dancing around the garden to Marco’s wild improvisations in the fading winter light, coat flapping, eyes shining with joy. I hope his spirit lives on in what we are about to do.The acoustics in the garden are extraordinary. It’s so large that when we are within it, we are inside an echo chamber, every individual note ricocheting around like an echo off a mountainside. Once Marco had finished his acoustic explorations and we were warming up inside with tea and cake, he turned to me and said, somewhat mischievously: “You do know there’s a piece for 100 tubas? That would be fun and interesting to do!”View image in fullscreenAn aerial view of the 2006 world premiere - at New York’s World Financial Center Plaza –  of Anthony Braxton’s Composition No 19 for 100 Tubas.Photograph: Jack Vartoogian/Getty ImagesAnthony Braxton’sComposition No 19 (for 100 Tubas)(1971) has never had a performance outside the US and this will be only its third performance ever. It was initially written without a first performance in mind, and it was only when the “tubist, composer and improviser” Jay Rozen joined Braxton’s sextet in 2006 and asked the composer about the piece, having seen the score published in an experimental music magazine in the 1970s, that Braxton offered to reconstruct the written music for what would be its premiere in New York in 2006.The venerable composer introduces his score – which consists of four sections of music for four separate bands of 25 tuba players each – with an essay, detailing his extensive thinking and philosophy. He describes the piece as “alternative parade music”, and wonderfully it not only provides this structure, but also allows the players to be “diverse in their unity”. Unity, because everyone is indeed playing a tuba – but diversity, because tubas come in all shapes and sizes, from orchestral tubas to over-the-shoulder sousaphones, tenor horns, euphoniums and even the rarely sightedWagner tuba. There is also unity because everyone is apparently playing the same piece but, as the performance proceeds, it gives spaces and opportunities for every player to diversify and express their own musical personality, acting as an improvising individual within the group. These opportunities become more and more numerous until by the end – in our version, at the hour – it becomes a wild group improvisation, with the players gathered in the centre having paraded their way around the garden in multiple different ways as the light slowly fades into the autumnal dusk.And that small matter of finding 100 tuba players? I don’t want to jinx anything – and it is a phenomenal organisational workout for my colleagues to get everyone to the right place at the right time with the right instruments, right music and right clothes – but it turned out, when the word went out, that tuba players from across the world will come to join in. Performers from the US, Latvia, Estonia and the rest of the UK are bringing their tubas of all shapes and sizes to be a part of what may be the most eyebrow-raising contemporary music event I’ve yet told my family I’m a part of.100 Tubas is at Amisfield Walled Garden, part of theLammermuir festival, on 19 September. John Harris is artistic director and chief executive of theRed Note Ensembleand Festival Director ofNew Music Dublin.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicJazzFestivalsExperimental musicMusic festivalsScotlandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ireland to boycott Eurovision again over Israeli participation and ongoing Gaza deaths | Eurovision | The Guardian
description: Ireland joins joins Dutch broadcaster in refusing to take part in 2027 song contest, in second consecutive year of protests
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Ireland joins joins Dutch broadcaster in refusing to take part in 2027 song contest, in second consecutive year of protests
Content: The Palestinian flag during a protest outside the main gate of the Irish national broadcaster RTÉ in Dublin last year.Photograph: Zuma Press, Inc./Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenThe Palestinian flag during a protest outside the main gate of the Irish national broadcaster RTÉ in Dublin last year.Photograph: Zuma Press, Inc./Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.EurovisionIreland to boycott Eurovision again over Israeli participation and ongoing Gaza deathsIreland joins joins Dutch broadcaster in refusing to take part in 2027 song contest, in second consecutive year of protestsLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentThu 17 Sep 2026 13.32 EDTFirst published on Thu 17 Sep 2026 09.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIreland is to boycottEurovisionfor the second year running over the “appalling” ongoing killing in Gaza, the national broadcaster has said.Ireland wasone of five countries, along with Iceland, the Netherlands, Spain and Slovenia, that refused to take part in the competition this year in protest against Israel’s participation.RTÉ announced on Thursday it would not participate in the 2027 competition. The Dutch broadcaster Avrotrosannounced its own boycottlast month, calling Eurovision a “platform for division”.In a statement, the Irish broadcaster said: “RTÉ feels that Ireland’s participation cannot be justified given ‌the appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis there, which continues to put the lives of so many civilians at risk.”Next year’s Eurovision is to be held in the Bulgarian Black Sea city of Burgas, after the country won for the first time in May.View image in fullscreenNorwegian singer Emmy representing Ireland in the 2025 Eurovision at the St Jakobshalle arena in Basel, Switzerland.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesAvrotros said it would not take part, claiming the competition “can no longer be considered neutral, with a participating country still involved in a large-scale military conflict”.The European Broadcasting Union (EBU), which organises the event, is in talks with other Dutch broadcasters, hoping one of the country’s other public service TV stations will participate.Eurovision’s director, Martin Green, said he regretted but respected RTÉ’s decision. “They remain a valued part of our family and will be missed,” he said.“That power to bring people together is at the heart of what makes the contest so special and is even more important now in an increasingly difficult and divided world,” he added.“All broadcasters decide on an annual basis to participate in the following year’s contest. We will remain in dialogue with RTÉ and hope to welcome them back to the contest in the future.”The EBU has tried twice to address broadcasters’ concerns over the participation ofIsrael.Last year, itreduced the number of votesthat could be entered online or by telephone by one individual, amid allegations Israel had mounted a disproportionate campaign for public votes.Last month, the EBU announced that broadcasters would no longer be eligible to host the Eurovision song contest if their state wasinvolved in an “armed conflict”or in a “sensitive geopolitical situation”.Eurovision has faced protests in and outside the competition venues in recent years over the participation of Israel, a competitor since 1973.In 2024, the European Commission madean unusual interventionafter the organisers banned audience members from waving the EU flag at the grand final in Sweden, describing the decision as “mind-blowing” and “regrettable”.Palestinian authorities report that more than 73,000 people have been killed in ​Israel’s war onGaza, ‌which was launched ​after Hamas-led fighters killed 1,200 ​people in an attack on southern Israel in October 2023.A US-brokered ceasefire agreed last year calls for eventual reconstruction of the territory but Israeli strikes have continued. According to Gaza’s health ministry, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the fragile ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025.Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsEurovisionIrelandIsraelGazaPalestineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Attorneys for Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs drop music mogul, alleging unpaid legal bills | Sean ‘Diddy‘ Combs | The Guardian
description: The musician is serving a 50-month federal prison term for prostitution-related offenses
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: The musician is serving a 50-month federal prison term for prostitution-related offenses
Content: Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs at the Met Gala in New York on 1 May 2017.Photograph: Lucas Jackson/ReutersView image in fullscreenSean ‘Diddy’ Combs at the Met Gala in New York on 1 May 2017.Photograph: Lucas Jackson/ReutersSean ‘Diddy‘ CombsAttorneys for Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs drop music mogul, alleging unpaid legal billsThe musician is serving a 50-month federal prison term for prostitution-related offensesRichard LuscombeThu 17 Sep 2026 09.21 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 12.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAttorneys representing rapperSean “Diddy” Combssay they are no longer acting for the disgraced star in a dispute over months of unpaid legal bills.The musician, who is serving a50-month federal prison termfor prostitution-related offenses, has become increasingly belligerent in recent months, causing “a total breakdown in cooperation and communication” with New York law firm Sher Tremonte, one of its partners, Michael Tremonte, said in a court filing.The firm was representing Combs, 56, in a $100m civil defamation lawsuit stemming from his conviction last year in a sex-trafficking and racketeering case that also saw himacquittedof the most serious charges.‘We live with a big burden’: US sexual abuse survivor hopes priest’s death brings closureRead moreCombs, Tremonte said in the filing seeking to withdraw as counsel as reported byNBC News, “has not paid a substantial balance of attorney’s fees, costs, and expenses” stretching more than six months.“The firm’s representation has been rendered unreasonably difficult by Mr Combs’s lack of cooperation, resulting in a breakdown in attorney-client communications and rendering Sher Tremonte incapable of continuing to provide effective legal services to Mr Combs,” the filing, in US district court in the southern district of New York, said.For four of the months, it said, Combs has “declined to make himself available for timely, substantive and direct communications about his cases”.In a statement provided by his representatives to the news outlet, Combs accused his lawyers of overcharging, and said that he fired them.“I made the decision to switch lawyers because I won’t let anyone take advantage of me by overcharging me and running up bills that were never approved,” he said. “This is strictly a business matter, and any talk about unpaid fees is just part of our dispute over those unapproved charges.”In an email to NBC, Tremonte rejected Combs’s claims and insisted his company had represented its client “zealously and very efficiently”.“As stated in our court filings, we are withdrawing from representing him because he has not paid his long-overdue invoices and has become uncooperative,” Tremonte said.“Any suggestion that we overcharged him is simply false.”Earlier this year, prosecutors in Los Angelessaidthey were mulling filing new sexual assault charges against Combs, who is currently incarcerated at New Jersey’s Fort Dix federal correctional institution.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRecord producer Jonathan Hay has publicly accused Combs of “assault, sexual harassment, false imprisonment and infliction of emotional distress” during a 2020 collaboration relating to the estate of the late songwriter Christopher Wallace, better known as the rapper Notorious BIG.Combs sued Hay for defamation, separate from the action that gave rise to the payment dispute with Sher Tremonte.In those proceedings, Combs is suing Courtney Burgess, a music manager who told a grand jury in 2024 that the hip-hop mogul gave him flash drives containing video of Combs sexually assaulting minors and fellow celebrities.Earlier this month,TMZ reported, a judge allowed Combs’s case to proceed against Burgess, his lawyer Ariel Mitchell, and the media company Nexstar, which featured Mitchell on its NewsNation show vouching for Burgess’s assertions about the videos.Combs has accused the pair of spreading “outlandish claims” and “wild lies” against him.Explore more on these topicsSean ‘Diddy‘ CombsUS crimenewsShareReuse this content
