title: The best resistance bands in the UK to improve mobility and strength on a budget, tested | Fitness | The Guardian
description: Loop and tube bands are cheaper than a gym membership and take up less space than weights – our exercise buff put 18 to the test
Author: Kieran Alger
Headline: Loop and tube bands are cheaper than a gym membership and take up less space than weights – our exercise buff put 18 to the test
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterFitnessReviewThe best resistance bands in the UK to improve mobility and strength on a budget, testedLoop and tube bands are cheaper than a gym membership and take up less space than weights – our exercise buff put 18 to the testThe best treadmills for your homeKieran AlgerThu 17 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMovement breeds motivation, not vice versa. If you want a fast ticket to a regular training habit, you need to remove the friction between you and that first rep. When the sofa looks more appealing than getting a sweat on, it pays to have a simple, quick, convenient way to kick into workout mode. That’s where resistance bands come in.Portable, lightweight, compact and convenient, the right set of bands could be the path of least, er, resistance to easy home workouts and reaching your fitness goals.Cheaper than a pricey gym membership and less clutter than a set of dumbbells, the best resistance bands can be deployed for everything from weights-free workouts to mobility training and physio exercises, then otherwise stashed happily in a drawer.From loop bands that get your glutes firing to full-body training tube bands, here’s my pick of the best resistance bands you can buy right now.At a glanceBest resistance bands overallTechnogymPower bands£95 at TechnogymBest budget resistance bands for beginnersTechnogymLoop bands set£35 at TechnogymBest resistance band set for lower-body workLa PochetteResistance band set£30 at La PochetteBest resistance band for lower bodyMyproteinBooty band£12.99 at MyproteinBest resistance band for yoga and pilatesMirafitResistance band set£74.95 at MirafitWhy you should trust meI’ve spent two decades testing the latestfitness gearand home exercise kit while training for more than 60marathons and ultramarathons. I train most days, sometimes twice, regularly plodding more than 50 miles a week, occasionally runningsolo marathonsand working on general strength. And all the while, I’m testingrunning shoesandother kit.At 47, strength and mobility are increasingly important. I need loose hips and strong glutes to keep running those miles – and tying the laces on those running shoes. If there’s anyone who can benefit from easy at-home resistance band workouts, it’s me.How I testedView image in fullscreenBand practice: the straps were tested across warm-ups, strength work, mobility and home workouts.Photograph: Kieran Alger/The GuardianI spent a solid month testing 18 sets of the latest and most popular resistance bands across different styles, prices and brands, including Les Mills, Technogym, Peloton and Pvolve.I used each set of bands for their intended workouts, working them into my pre-run warm-ups and using them for assisted weights at my gym, plus bodyweight and mobility sessions at home. I even tried a bit of YouTube yoga, workout kryptonite for a tight-hamstring runner who can’t touch his toes.After all that (and a bit of a sit down), I rated the bands on the quality of the materials, resistance range and versatility, while also considering durability, portability and value.After testing, the resistance bands were either returned or donated to local charity shops.The best resistance bandsView image in fullscreenJoin the resistance: the bands put to work for this guide.Photograph: Kieran Alger/The GuardianBest resistance bands overall:Technogym power bandsTechnogymPower bands£95£95 at TechnogymWhat we loveGreat resistance levels; very versatileWhat we don’t loveCould do with a carry bagView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kieran Alger/The Guardian£95 at TechnogymTechnogym’s set of three rubber long-loop bands offers some of the highest resistance levels for this type of band, allowing for a wide – and hard-hitting – variety of strength drills.Why we love itThese heavy-duty resistance bands successfully bridge the gap between simple loop bands and free weights, and bagged the top spot in my test largely for their excellent versatility.The set includes three colour-coded bands with low, medium and high resistance levels. The 31.8kg top-weight band provides resistance towards the higher level for rubber loop bands, while the greater length and stretch make them great for getting stuck into a wide range of workouts.They’ll handle everything from strength training and power development to assisted bodyweight work (such as pull-ups) and advanced resistance exercises (rotations, banded sprints and plyometrics). They also work for activation drills, but they particularly excel when used to add an extra challenge to standard bodyweight drills, such as squats. You can also use them to make gym moves like dips and pull-ups easier.I found them easy to anchor to gym equipment, and the thick rubber is highly robust and durable, with no visible joins or weak spots. I stretched them to the max, and they never looked threatened.They’re a bit chunkier than thinner-style loop bands, but they’re still easy enough to stash in a gym bag. It would have been nice for them to come with a storage bag, but it’s not a deal breaker.It’s a shame that …there are no resistance levels marked on the bands.Suitable for:band-assisted weight training, bodyweight strength buildingMaterial:rubberSize of band(s):1.3/2.1/3.2 x 104cmNumber of bands:3Resistance strength:13.6/20.4/31.8kgTechnogymPower bands£95£95 at TechnogymWhat we loveGreat resistance levels; very versatileWhat we don’t loveCould do with a carry bagBest budget resistance bands for beginners:Technogym loop bandsTechnogymLoop bands set£35£35 at TechnogymWhat we loveAs portable as it gets, and great durabilityWhat we don’t loveSmall-loop style is not great for building strengthView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kieran Alger/The Guardian£35 at TechnogymTechnogym’s triple set of rubber resistance bands offers a range of tension up to 14.5kg, top-quality durability and great versatility for smaller loop bands.Why we love itAlthough it’s tempting to go cheap on loop bands, you still want to make sure you’re prioritising quality. That’s exactly what you get from this trio from Technogym.Made from high-quality natural rubber, they’re conveniently colour-coded by resistance levels. The darker the colour, the more tension they can take. They’re also strong and reliable, with a resistance that’s nicely controlled and smooth. In my tests, they snapped back into shape with no signs of losing that tension.With three levels of resistance and relatively long stretch, they’re surprisingly versatile for a shorter loop. I found them best for pre-run activation drills, simple strength exercises and adding resistance to my bodyweight moves such as lunges, glute bridges and banded walks.The rubber finish is smooth and feels good against the skin – as good as rubber bands can feel, that is. The width is decent, so they didn’t roll up, and the seamless design meant there were no lumps, bumps or snags to cause chafing.They pack up really small, and if you need help with technique and ideas for drills, Technogym’s app has loads of workouts for inspiration.It’s a shame that …they don’t come with a storage pouch.Suitable for:warm-ups and light bodyweight strengthMaterial:natural rubberSize of band(s):29 x 5cmNumber of bands:3Resistance strength:9.1/12.7/14.5kgTechnogymLoop bands set£35£35 at TechnogymWhat we loveAs portable as it gets, and great durabilityWhat we don’t loveSmall-loop style is not great for building strengthBest resistance band set for lower-body work:La Pochette resistance band setLa PochetteResistance band set£30£30 at La PochetteWhat we loveSoft, strong, stylish and great for the lower bodyWhat we don’t loveDoesn’t really work for the upper bodyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kieran Alger/The Guardian£30 at La PochetteLa Pochette specialises in high-end workout accessories, and this trio of short-looped bands brings a bit of style to lower-body band workouts.Why we love itEssentially the same as the Myprotein Booty band below but in a three-piece set, La Pochette covers more of your lower-body prehab, rehab and activation bases with light, medium and heavy resistance options.The bands come in three subtle colours that are more stylish than the majority of garish bands available. And if the muted cashmere, putty and grey tones denoting the weights aren’t immediately distinguishable, they’re also conveniently labelled – not all bands do this.Each band is thick (good for durability), wide (good for staying in place) and soft (great for comfort on bare legs). There’s also a non-slip inner grip that helps them stay put if you’re using them over leggings or other gym gear.Like the Myprotein fabric band, these are robust and reliable. You can give them full force without fear of them snapping under tension. They also hold their shape well.A lightweight mesh carry case is included, making these easy to drop into most gym bags.It’s a shame that …the shorter band length means they’re not suited to upper-body exercises.Suitable for:activation, stability, mobility and low-to-moderate resistance workMaterial:fabricSize of band:38 x 8cmNumber of bands:3Resistance strength:not specifiedLa PochetteResistance band set£30£30 at La PochetteWhat we loveSoft, strong, stylish and great for the lower bodyWhat we don’t loveDoesn’t really work for the upper bodyBest resistance band for lower body:Myprotein Booty bandMyproteinBooty band£12.99£12.99 at MyproteinWhat we loveDurable; wide; good resistance for the lower bodyWhat we don’t loveNot as versatile for full body workoutsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kieran Alger/The Guardian£12.99‎ at MyproteinThe Myprotein fabric “booty band” comes in three levels of resistance and is made for lower-body strength, mobility and recovery.Why we love itIf, like me, you’re not the biggest fan of rubber against the skin, Myprotein’s fabric booty band will bring welcome comfort to your warm-up and mobility work.The wide fabric band is wonderfully soft and much gentler on bare skin than its rubber rivals. Hairier-legged folks will also get fewer painful pulls. There’s a textured inside that helps it grip when you’re wearing leggings, and the wide fabric construction improves stability. Of all the bands I tested, this one had the least unwanted movement, and there was much less roll than with rubber loops.It’s also nicely durable, stretching well beyond what you’d normally need during regular drills with no risk of snapping. This gave me plenty of confidence when using it.The band is sold in three resistance gradations (light, medium and heavy),and the resistance level was excellent. In my testing, I found it a great option for glute bridges, clamshells, lateral walks and hip thrusts, as well as for waking up muscles before my faster running sessions. It comes with a convenient small net pouch, too.It’s a shame that …the shorter length is less well-suited to upper-body drills.Suitable for:activation, stability, mobility and low-to-moderate resistance workMaterial:fabricSize of band:43 x 7.5cmNumber of bands:1Resistance strength:24.9kgMyproteinBooty band£12.99£12.99 at MyproteinWhat we loveDurable; wide; good resistance for the lower bodyWhat we don’t loveNot as versatile for full body workoutsBest resistance band for yoga and pilates:Mirafit resistance band setMirafitResistance band set£74.95£74.95 at MirafitWhat we loveLots of resistance levels to stretch your fitnessWhat we don’t loveLong bands can be harder for beginners to controlView image in fullscreen£74.95 at MirafitMirafit’s resistance loops offer a huge variety of resistance levels, making them well-suited to both upper- and lower-body workouts.Why we love itIn an excellent multipurpose set of six bands, Mirafit’s long-band resistance loops cater for a wide range of workout needs across your upper and lower body. They will suit beginners, intermediates and experts alike, although total newbies may find the longer band length requires a little extra control. They add extra resistance or assistance to weighted drills and bodyweight work, and you can also whip them out for prehab and rehab.I found the variety of resistance levels and thicknesses provided a lot of flexibility, working well for my flailing yoga and mobility work. There’s a good range of resistance, and the toughest band was among the strongest on test.They’re clearly marked for easy identification, highly durable and a great tool for finessing your fitness routine. You canbuy them individually, or as a set which comes in a handy carry bag.It’s a shame that …absolute beginners may struggle with the longer bands, which require some controlSuitable for:assisted weight training, bodyweight strength buildingMaterial:natural latexSize of band:1.3/2.1/3.2/4.5/6.4/8.3 x 208cmNumber of bands:6Resistance strength:11.3/22.7/45.4/54.4/79.4/104.3kgMirafitResistance band set£74.95£74.95 at MirafitWhat we loveLots of resistance levels to stretch your fitnessWhat we don’t loveLong bands can be harder for beginners to controlThe best of the restView image in fullscreenComfortable and great on the go: the Les Mills Sculpt bands.Photograph: Kieran Alger/The GuardianLes Mills Sculpt bandsLes MillsSculpt bands£49.99£49.99 at Les MillsWhat we loveSuperbly stashable; good for gym bags and carry-onWhat we don’t loveBig, scratchy patch where the loop joinsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kieran Alger/The Guardian£49.99 at Les MillsBest for:travelThe most travel-friendly fabric bands on test, this short-loop trio offers light, medium and heavy resistance that’s best suited to warm-ups, mobility drills and controlled time under tension across the upper and lower body. That covers everything from reverse lunges and hip openers to banded rows.Silicone waves on the underside offer good grip, although I found they weren’t quite as stable as some wider fabric bands. The soft finish is a big comfort boost over regular rubber bands, though, and handy labels make it easy to see the resistance levels. The smaller, thinner bands also pack neatly into a mesh pouch.It didn’t make the final cut because …they’re a little pricier than the rivals.Suitable for:toning, mobility, stability and activation;material:fabric;size of band:31 x 5/6/7cm;number of bands:3;resistance strength:12.7/15/18.1kgLes MillsSculpt bands£49.99£49.99 at Les MillsWhat we loveSuperbly stashable; good for gym bags and carry-onWhat we don’t loveBig, scratchy patch where the loop joinsPeloton resistance bandsPelotonResistance bandsfrom£60£60 at Peloton£60.78 at AmazonWhat we loveVideo routines make these great for beginnersWhat we don’t loveHigher resistance would suit the more experiencedView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kieran Alger/The Guardian£60 at Peloton£60.78 at AmazonBest for:a full-body workoutThese tube-handle bands offer light, medium and heavy resistance levels. The colour-coding system makes them easy to use with the small but useful selection of band workouts on the Peloton app. The video routines cover upper-body, lower-body, full-body and core work and are great for newcomers who need a little guidance, though you’ll need a £12.99 per month subscription to unlock them.The bands’ resistance levels cater for light to moderate strength and mobility work, but they don’t quite hit the levels needed for harder strength work. Easy-grip aluminium handles add a durable, premium touch, though, and each band comes with its own travel- and storage-friendly pouch.It didn’t make the final cut because …we would have liked a higher top resistance level.Suitable for:light to moderate resistance workouts, warm-ups and mobility;material:natural rubber latex band, aluminium handles, nylon and rubber grip;size of band:150cm;number of bands:3;resistance strength:not listedPelotonResistance bandsfrom£60£60 at Peloton£60.78 at AmazonWhat we loveVideo routines make these great for beginnersWhat we don’t loveHigher resistance would suit the more experiencedPvolve P BandPvolvePBandfrom£43.32£43.32 at Healf£43.82 at AmazonWhat we loveFingerless gloves offer great comfort levelsWhat we don’t loveOnly good for upper-body workoutsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kieran Alger/The Guardian£43.32 at Healf£43.82 at AmazonBest for:upper-body conditioningPvolve’s unique tube band replaces regular handles with built-in fingerless gloves, a setup that feels a bit more comfortable – or at least easier – than gripping handles as you curl, row and stretch. That frees you up nicely to focus on controlling your movement and engaging your muscles, while cutting the callus risk that comes with some handle bands.The moderate resistance level is effective for targeting arms, shoulders, back and some core, although you can’t use it for lower-body drills. The band also comes with trial access to Pvolve’s on-demand classes and live virtual studio – handy if you’ve never flexed a rubber band in anger before. However, full membership after the trial costs $24.99 (£18.56) a month or $224.91 (£167) a year.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s only good for the upper body.Suitable for:strength and mobility for upper body and core;material:latex band, woven polyester, neoprene and cotton gloves;size of band:35cm;number of bands:1;resistance strength:15.9kgPvolvePBandfrom£43.32£43.32 at Healf£43.82 at AmazonWhat we loveFingerless gloves offer great comfort levelsWhat we don’t loveOnly good for upper-body workoutsWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenFlexible thinking: different bands suit different types of strength, mobility and activation work.Photograph: Nanci Santos/GettyWhat are the different types of resistance bands, and what do they do?Some bands are more versatile than others, but there isn’t a single type of resistance band that will cover all your training needs. It’s important to identify your workout goals before you invest. Are you aiming to add extra resistance to your drills, work on flexibility and mobility, or replace bulky free weights?Loopbands:these are flat, closed-loop bands that come in varying levels of thickness and grades of resistance. They’re light, compact, brilliantly portable and can be used for warm-ups and muscle activation (great for glutes), as well as adding an extra challenge to regular bodyweight or weighted drills and mobility exercises such as lateral walks. They’re good at targeting muscles with controlled movement. Longer loop bands can be used for assisted pull-ups, too.Mini bands:these are smaller continuous-loop bands with resistance ranging from light and easy to very difficult. These work best for muscle activation, stability and control rather than heavy strength. They’re good for glute firing, hip stability, rehab and warm-ups.Tube bands:these are rubber tubes with handles on both ends. They’re great for full-body workouts, often coming colour-coded by resistance level. The handles make them better for rows, presses and pulls, too.Therapy bands:unlike loop bands or tube bands, these flat, elastic resistance strips are mainly used for rehab, mobility and light strength work. They provide progressive tension for controlled movements and are good aids for yoga and pilates.What are the benefits of resistance bands?“Resistance bands are a useful tool for increasing muscle awareness during exercise,” says Caroline Bragg, master pilates trainer at Third Space. “They add tension to a movement, helping people develop better proprioception, coordination and understanding of how their body moves.”“One of their biggest strengths is improving alignment and movement quality. For example, placing a mini band around the knees during a squat can encourage the knees to track correctly and help recruit the appropriate muscles throughout the movement.”Resistance bands help us to work concentrically and eccentrically: concentric work builds our ability to create force, while eccentric work teaches us to control and absorb it, says Marie Grujicic, founder of virtual yoga studio Awespire by MG. “Training both creates stronger, more resilient and adaptable muscles. As I often say, we don’t just want strong muscles, we want ‘smart’ muscles that can respond to the way we move, and bands are the perfect tool to support it.”They also play a significant role in rehab from injury. “The key difference between free weights and resistance bands is that bands provide variable resistance,” says James Stirling, personal trainer, running coach and a Technogym wellness ambassador. “That can be good for beginners or those coming back from injury. The user has full control of how much resistance they apply to the movement being performed – as the band stretches, the tension increases.”How effective are resistance bands?“Very effective!” says Grujicic. “It’s remarkable how such a simple, travel-friendly piece of equipment can develop strength and stability without placing heavy loads on the joints.”Bands can work both slow-twitch muscle fibres, which support endurance and posture control, and fast-twitch fibres, which are important for strength, power and quick reactions.“They’re incredibly versatile because by changing the way you use them: resistance, tempo, range or direction, you can train strength, power, stability and mobility. That versatility is why they’re one of my favourite tools for overall wellness,” adds Grujicic.Provided they’re used correctly, resistance bands can be an effective alternative to moving heavy metal at the gym.Studies show resistance band training canhelp to improve lower-limb strength, balanceandflexibility, andto build explosive power, sprinting prowess and agilityin athletes. But you need to get your reps in.“Bands can also create muscle fatigue when used with higher repetitions, which may contribute to somemuscle growth and endurance adaptations,” says Bragg.“However, for developing significant strength or muscle, traditional resistance training with equipment such as dumbbells, kettlebells or machines will produce better results because greater loads can be applied.”For more ways to get fit with the Filter:The best home exercise kit, chosen by personal trainersThe best treadmills for your homeThe best cross trainers and ellipticalsKieran Alger is arunning, fitness and health journalist who splits his time between testing, training and tapping out reviews. You’ll regularly find him in the gym testing training equipment or running down lofty challenges while wearing three watches, brand new running shoes and a whole host of kit that needs thorough investigationExplore more on these topicsFitnessThe FilterHealth & wellbeingHobbiesTraining programmesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Are you washing your sportswear wrong? An expert guide to making it last longer | Fitness | The Guardian
description: From sweaty kit to grubby trainers, here’s how to wash, repair and care for activewear more sustainably
Author: Charlie Allenby
Headline: From sweaty kit to grubby trainers, here’s how to wash, repair and care for activewear more sustainably
Content: No sweat: the right care can help sportswear cope with hard workouts and repeated wear.Composite: GettyView image in fullscreenNo sweat: the right care can help sportswear cope with hard workouts and repeated wear.Composite: GettyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterFitnessAre you washing your sportswear wrong? An expert guide to making it last longerFrom sweaty kit to grubby trainers, here’s how to wash, repair and care for activewear more sustainablyThe best moisture-wicking underwear, socks and base layersCharlie AllenbyThu 17 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs a running and cycling journalist, I spend a lot of time in sportswear. Lycra is my leg coverage of choice, polyester or merino wool my base layer, and I reach for technical materials like Gore-Tex if the weather isn’t playing ball.A near-daily workout schedule means my washing machine’s sportswear setting takes a hammering to avoid having a laundry basket overflowing with sweaty, salty, sour-scented clothes. But even then, tops can develop hard-to-shift smells in sweat-prone areas, synthetic materials can start to bobbleand lose shape, and my sportswear occasionally gets a foamy detergent residue that hasn’t been properly rinsed out, particularly during wet or intensive training sessions.To find out how to resolve my washing woes, I’ve consulted experts on more sustainable ways to care for your sportswear and how to dispose of kit when it’s ready to go to the big gym in the sky.How to make your sportswear last longerSort it straight awayView image in fullscreenDon’t let it linger: clean and air dirty kit as soon as you can after a workout.Photograph: vorDa/Getty“Don’t leave your dirty exercise clothes in the corner of your room or wardrobe, where they can stay damp and develop mould. You may not notice it, especially with darker sportswear, as mould spores aren’t visible untilthey grow to about half a centimetre in size,” says David Lambert, managing director at the laundry serviceLaundry Republic.“If you’re unable to wash your sportswear straight away, keep it aired out as much as possible on a hanger or airer so that it doesn’t start creating a smell or damp. The first chance you get, put it in the washing machine inside out, as most of the sweat sits on the inside of clothes. If you can, especially during the summer, hang it on a line to air-dry after washing. Don’t put it on your radiators – the direct heat can damage synthetic fibres in sportswear, causing them to change shape. It can also lead to mould growth due to extra humidity, which can cause respiratory issues.”Choose the right detergent“I once heard that some standard detergents only really mask smells and don’t actually tackle the source of what causes odour to build up – bacteria,” saysWill Renwick, professional outdoor gear tester and author ofPeak Bagging Wales. “With some laundry liquids and fabric conditioner, there’s also the risk of them degrading elastane or synthetic fibres and clogging wicking channels, meaning the fabric can hold moisture and smells instead of pulling sweat away from the skin. To counter this, there are specialist detergents designed specifically for cleaning waterproof or performance clothing, including those from Grangers,Stormand Nikwax – the latter tends to be my go-to and has greatsustainability credentialstoo.”View image in fullscreenGrangers Active Wash, 750ml£9 at Millets£8.95 at AmazonView image in fullscreenNikwax BaseWash, 1l£5.50 at Millets£11 at Go OutdoorsWash sportswear separately from day-to-day clothingView image in fullscreenA lighter load: keep technical kit away from towels and heavier fabrics in the wash.Photograph: Helin Loik-Tomson/Getty“You shouldn’t be using fabric softener on any of your sportswear as it will start to damage and prematurely wear your clothes by clogging the synthetic fibres with a waxy residue, which can build up over time,” says Lambert.“Also the fibres that make up sportswear garments are woven to be stretchable, but if you overstretch them it’s an irreversible situation,” he adds. “When your machine is on its final spin cycle, the clothes get spread out into the drum to take out as much of the water as it can. If you’ve got heavier or stronger fabrics, such as other clothes or towels, in the drum at the same time, they can damage sportswear. You might not notice immediately, but after six months of washing sportswear with day-to-day clothes, you’ll probably find the fabric has become too stretchy, and you’ll have to replace it.”Bag it up“I often use the Guppyfriend washing bag,” says Renwick. “It reduces and captures some of the microplastic fibres shed during washing, which matters because synthetic clothing is one of the biggest sources of microfibre pollution in wastewater.”View image in fullscreenGuppyfriend washing bag£25 at Chelsea Peers£25 at DryrobeTackle stubborn smellsView image in fullscreenFresh start: a soak can help shift lingering odours in well-used kit.Photograph: Vasyl Mykhailenko/Getty“Even after washing, a fusty smell can linger on sportswear and towels, especially if sports kit was left in a bag in the car, or a towel was dropped on the floor in the shower room,” says Nancy Birtwhistle, author ofClean Magic: Essential New Tricks for a Sparkling Green Home. “Washing alone or dousing with lots of false perfume may not remove the odour, but an environmentally friendly washing soda soak can.”Washing soda crystals (sodium carbonate) are a naturally occurring chemical compound that dissolve in water, making them a green alternative to other, polluting cleaning products. “They help neutralise odours in fabrics,but avoid using them with wool and silk because it can weaken the natural fibres. For a large sink full, add five to six tablespoons of washing soda, pour over hot water to cover the sink base and stir using a wooden spoon until the soda has dissolved and the solution is cloudy. Then add enough cold water to produce a tepid, deep bath and soak the items overnight. The next day, squeeze out excess solution, then wash in the machine.”For natural fibres such as merino wool, Birtwhistle recommends soaking in one part white vinegar and two parts tepid water instead. “This solution is kinder to wool and can dissolve some stains, neutralise odours and prevent colour runs.”View image in fullscreenWashing soda crystals, 1kg£2.35 at Big Green Smile£1.99 at AmazonView image in fullscreenMiniml white vinegar, 5l£6.60 at Ocado£7.01 at Big Green SmileChoose sustainable sportswear“Merino wool is a miracle material in my eyes – it has such a long list of performance benefits,” says Renwick. “One big advantage is the wool fibres are naturally odour resistant. I do a lot of long-distance hiking where I can’t carry many spare clothes and have few opportunities to wash my kit, so I really rely on merino. Generally,brands like Patagoniasay it’s best to wash a merino base layer after three to five wears, though I’ve pushed mine much further than that in the past. Good brands that make merino sportswear includeSmartwool,Icebreaker,DevoldandBrynje.”View image in fullscreenWomen’s Smartwool hike crew socksskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion£22.99 at Smartwool£24.95 at Cotswold OutdoorView image in fullscreenMen’s Icebreaker base layer top£85 at Cotswold Outdoor£85 at Snow + RockReproof waterproof layersView image in fullscreenBead test: when water stops rolling off, it may be time to reproof your waterproofs.Photograph: Mensent Photography/GettyThe move away from Pfas – synthetic “forever chemicals” historically used in some waterproofing treatments – has environmental benefits, but Paul Smith, equipment officer atMountain Rescue England and Wales, says Pfas-free waterproofs require more maintenance to keep out the water.“I’ll usually wash my waterproof jacket withNikwax Tech Washafter a month of heavy use,” says Renwick. “This safely cleans the fabrics without removing any of the existing water-repellent coating. When my rain gear stops beading water and starts saturating easily, it’s a sign the outer fabric’s water repellency has worn off. Once that happens, the fabric can’t shed moisture properly, so it holds it on the surface instead – this stops the membrane from breathing, traps the moisture vapour my body is generating, and I end up wet from the inside instead of outside. That’s my cue to reproof withNikwax TX Direct, which restores a fresh water-repellent layer to the outer fabric.”Smith recommends tumble drying reproofed clothing on a low, gentle heat because the warmth “reactivates” the durable water repellent (DWR) – a thin chemical coating on a garment’s outer layer that can be renewed by reproofing. “You can also use ahair dryeror put your jacket near a radiator – lay it over a towel or hang it close to protect it from direct heat. When I’ve done mine, I always test it in the bathroom by sticking it under running water to see if it’s beading again.” But it’s always wise to check the manufacturer’s guidance for your items before tumble drying, placing near a heat source or warming with a hair dryer.View image in fullscreenNikwaxTech Wash, 300ml£6 at Millets£8 at Go OutdoorsView image in fullscreenNikwax TXDirect, 300ml£9 at Millets£10 at Go OutdoorsRepair tears and cutsView image in fullscreenMend and make do: small repairs can keep well-used kit going for longer.Photograph: Richard Clark/Getty“As part of our Zero to Landfill initiative at Mountain Rescue, we’ve got together withScottish Mountain Gearto repair any [of our] kit that is damaged during callouts,” says Smith. “I sent in one of my own jackets after all the badges had come off, and it came back like a brand new jacket.” Some outdoor brands, includingAlpkitandMontane, have in-house repair services, whilePatagonia’s website shows how to repair a garment yourself.Find a new use for old newsView image in fullscreenBoots off: clean mud and dirt away before storing footwear.Photograph: vorDa/Getty“I try to avoid putting my walking boots or shoes in a washing machine. To me, there’s too much risk of damaging the shoes and the machine,” says Renwick. “Instead, I hand-clean my gear. I love the Nikwax boot cleaning kit, which comes with a scrubbing brush.“With walking boots, the crucial thing is to ensure you don’t store them away with mud on them; mud can draw moisture from leather, causing it to dry out and crack easily, and it creates a fertile environment for the materials to degrade, affecting synthetic footwear too.“Waterproof footwear also needs help with drying out to prevent odours. Newspaper is surprisingly effective when stuffed into a pair of boots for a night.”Dry boots naturally somewhere warm, but away fromstrong heat sources, which can crack leather and weaken glue, with the insoles removed and laces loosened to keep airflow moving; avoid resting them directly on any heat source.“If you find you’re still struggling to get rid of bad odours from boots or running shoes, I often find it helps to swap in some new insoles. Superfeet makes some useful replacement ones,” says Renwick.View image in fullscreenNikwaxfootwear care kit£8.95 at Cotswold Outdoor£9.99 at DecathlonView image in fullscreenSuperfeet replacement solesFrom £31.89 at Cotswold OutdoorFrom £40 at MilletsDonate or recycle“If you’re getting rid of jackets, give them to charities – lots want to get people out into the countryside,” says Smith.Kitsquadtakes preloved outdoor clothing and passes it on to people with low incomes, whileEllis Brigham’s 2nd Life initiativeredirects unwanted outdoor gear to charities supporting homeless people across the UK. “Failing that, if a garment is beyond repair, companies likeScottish Mountain Gearwill recycle it.”Follow manufacturers’ guidelinesView image in fullscreenRead the label: technical fabrics often need different care from everyday clothes.Photograph: Kwangmoozaa/Getty/iStockphoto“Most technical and outdoor garments come with specific washing guidelines on the label or the brand’s website, covering things such as temperature, spin speed and whether tumble drying or ironing is safe,” says Renwick. “Performance fabrics can be damaged by the wrong treatment in ways that aren’t obvious until the garment stops performing, so it’s always worth checking the label or manufacturer guidance first rather than assuming standard laundry rules apply.“My base layer clothing for hiking and camping will usually either be merino wool or a synthetic blend, and I generally try to ensure I wash them both at a low temperature – 30C is fine for me. This helps prevent shrinkage in wool clothing and reduces stress on technical synthetic fabrics, especially when they have a high elastane content. Mid and outer layers can all be different, so I’ll always consult the labels. If in doubt, though, I’ll stick to that 30C temperature – if you don’t know, go low and slow.”For more fitness inspiration from the Filter:Personal trainers on the best home gym kitThe best treadmills for your home – testedThe best fitness tech and gadgets, according to expertsThe fitness gear that made you fitterThe best resistance bandsCharlie Allenby is a health and fitness journalist whose near-daily running and cycling training regime means his washing machine is spinning almost as much as he isExplore more on these topicsFitnessThe FilterHealth & wellbeingHobbiesSustainable fashionEthical and green livingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sick of sandwiches? Perfect packed lunches – from savoury muffins to bento boxes | Food | The Guardian
description: After the endless road trip of summer, I’m enjoying September’s back-to-school vibes – and the excuse to create delicious lunches to take to work
Author: Georgina Hayden
Headline: After the endless road trip of summer, I’m enjoying September’s back-to-school vibes – and the excuse to create delicious lunches to take to work
Content: Nena Foster's kids' packed lunches.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNena Foster's kids' packed lunches.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.FeastFoodSick of sandwiches? Perfect packed lunches – from savoury muffins to bento boxesAfter the long hot summer, I’m enjoying September’s back-to-school vibes – and the excuse to create delicious lunches to take to workSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastGeorgina HaydenThu 17 Sep 2026 09.02 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter an August spent mostly on the road, I’ve found myself unexpectedly enjoying the back-to-school feeling that arrives with September. Usually, I greet it with the sort of enthusiasm reserved for a tax return, but, having been away for so long, it’s actually been rather nice coming home. Of course, there are all the usual inevitable resolutions and to-do lists: go to bed earlier, eat better, take lunch to work. Admirable stuff, although I suspect a summer of one too many honeycomb ice-creams and an irresponsible amount ofIrish brown breadand salty butter may also have something to do with it. Taking a packed lunch is, in any case, an all-round win, because eating out is increasingly expensive, and food bought in cafes and restaurants tends to be richer and saltier than a homemade equivalent. Depressingly, school and college canteens don’t fare much better, either.But a packed lunch needn’t mean a sad sandwich or last night’s tubbed-up leftovers. Nena Foster’scourgette, olive and halloumi muffinsare a very good argument for taking your lunch with you: nutrient-dense without being remotely worthy, they work just as well in an adult’s lunchbox as in a child’s, and they freeze brilliantly, too. Add a flask ofpumpkin soupor Tom Hunt’ssweetcorn chowderfor an excellent autumn lunch.View image in fullscreenFun for all ages … Shuko Oda’s onigiri bento box.Photograph: Jean Cazals/The ObserverShuko Oda’sonigiri bento boxis another winner, and pleases pretty much every age group, which is no mean feat.Bento boxesare such a hit, in fact, that I have gone one step farther and bought Japanese egg moulds. There are few things more unnecessary than a hard-boiled egg shaped like a rabbit or bear, but they do make lunchtime more exciting. And, really, that is the point. You can fill those little compartments with whatever you fancy: Caroline Craig and Sophie Missingbreak it down here, with a little guidance on what to pop in those small compartments. Another option isJeremy Lee’s ploughman’s, which would be a particularly fine arrangement: thick slices of ham, nuggets of cheese, dollops of chutney, sliced apple. A tiny pub lunch, minus the pub.On days when I crave something more warming, I’m very happy to dust off the Thermos. There is something deeply pleasing about taking a little pot of hot food to work. Meera Sodha’spav bhajiis perfect for this. Keep it warm in the flask until lunchtime, then spoon into a pre-toasted, buttered roll. The butter melts into the warm spiced vegetables and you wonder if there has ever been a more perfect use for a flask. I feel the same about Rachel Roddy’sreal minestroneand Felicity Cloake’spasta e fagioli, and I’m sure they could be premade and reheated in a microwave, if you have access to one. But you might not and, besides, I think dishes such as these are best when they’re nottoohot, and when that rich broth is starchy and thickened. Which, perhaps, is what I like most about September lunches: they don’t have to be virtuous, elaborate or even particularly organised; they just need to be something you’ll actually look forward to eating at 1pm. And that is a resolution I can get behind.My week in foodView image in fullscreenCounty Galway on the west coast of Ireland.Photograph: Robert Harding/AlamySweet like chocolate|A road trip from Ireland’s east to west coast this summer was a useful reminder that the country is full of quietly brilliant food-makers. Among them isGrá chocolates, founded by Gráinne Mullins, an award-winning, Michelin-trained chef – and now, finally, shipping to the UK. Her hand-painted chocolates are made with Irish milk, butter and cream, use seasonal ingredients wherever possible, and their fillings are cooked from scratch. As a result, they are, inevitably, rather hard to resist. My family’s current favourite is thepumpkin spice hot chocolate, made with caramelised white chocolate and warming autumnal spices. Forget about the pumpkin spiced latte; this is amuchmore convincing way to drink the season.Curry heaven|Emma Basic’s Japanese-style curry cubesare the sort of supermarket shortcut that makes everyone’s life better: loved by all ages, and accommodating all palates and dietaries, you really can have dinner on the table in 20 minutes. Make up the sauce as per the packet instructions, maybe add a few veggies for nutritional purposes, then simply add something crisp – chicken, tofu, aubergine, whatever you like – and serve with rice. No preservatives, no colourings, all good stuff and unapologetically convenient.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBeen around the world|Ruby Bhogal’s new book,Around the World in 80 Cakes, is part baking odyssey, part history lesson and part love letter to the humble cake. The former Great British Bake Off finalist has spent three years baking her way around the globe, and I have been following her rollercoaster journey on social media intently. The result? A book filled with thoroughly tested and much-loved bakes: there is everything from Germany’s honey-rich bienenstich to Thailand’s dense, butter khanom badin, and from an Italian torta caprese to a classic British lemon drizzle cake.Explore more on these topicsFoodFeastLeftoversSandwichesBreadSoupPastanewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Welcome to the age of the grown-up soft drink | Food | The Guardian
description: There is now a wealth of less sugary, more sophisticated nonalcoholic options out there, with flavours clearly aimed at an adult market
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: There is now a wealth of less sugary, more sophisticated nonalcoholic options out there, with flavours clearly aimed at an adult market
Content: Quite gron-up: Botivo, a UK-made nonalcoholic botanical.Photograph: Steven Joyce/BotivoView image in fullscreenQuite gron-up: Botivo, a UK-made nonalcoholic botanical.Photograph: Steven Joyce/BotivoGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.FoodWelcome to the age of the grown-up soft drinkThere is now a wealth of less sugary, more sophisticated nonalcoholic options out there, with flavours clearly aimed at an adult marketMina HollandThu 17 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 08.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhave written recently about several families of nonalcoholic drinks that are having a moment:tonic water,flavoured sparkling waterandwine substitutes. It stands to reason that soft drinks are enjoying their time in the sun. Quite literally, too: the heat of 2026 has demanded some serious refreshments and UK booze consumption isat a record low. But it has dawned on me that there is a broader trend in alcohol-free beverages beyond individual categories, namely that we are living in the age of the grown-up soft drink.By that I mean those with less sugar and more complexity than post-mix drinks, or “soda pop” (as my daughter now calls them, thanks to theKPop Demon Hunters songof the same name), which are clearly aimed at adults. One example is the tribe of “functional” drinks that have hit the market in the past year or so and that have supposed health benefits or performance-enhancing qualities, such as improving focus or helping you to slow down. Sonic Tonics’ CBD-infused 0% drink, for example, promises to shift your mood, and it certainly quenches thirst with a really original flavour profile of bitter hemp root with sweet and floral fig and violet. And while usually sceptical of celebrity-backed products with wellness claims,Gillian Anderson’s G Spot drinksare genuinely delicious. The passion fruit and habanero chilli is my favourite; I can’t support its aphrodisiac claims (allegedly due to its ingredients including butterfly pea and L-arginine, both of which are said to increase blood flow to the sexual organs), but, at £6.50 for four from Ocado, it’s cheaper than trying Gwyneth Paltrow’ssex oil.There are also several low-sugar “premium” soft drinks that are worth writing home about, such as deli favouriteSomething & Nothing, which contains no sweeteners and only natural sugars; the yuzu and the mango and Thai basil flavours are both perfect.Rapscallion Sodawas developed to make satisfying soft drinks without a sugar crash; raw fruit is extracted and mixed with citrus, spices and carbonated water: think burnt lemon with cracked black pepper and dry lime with makrut lime leaves.Then there are drinks designed to be consumed on occasions when you might otherwise drink alcohol. Botivo has created a sparkling, premixed version of its nonalcoholic botanical aperitivo – if you don’t like shrubs or drinking vinegars, it may not be for you, but I find it a wonderful alternative to amaro-based cocktails such as the negroni. Fever-Tree, meanwhile, has launchedits own “non-alcoholic spritz”, which is sweeter and not very bitter. Perhaps my favourite discovery of the week, however, is Non, an Australian wine alternative that blends verjus (unripe grape juice) with the likes of raspberry, chamomile and salt. That’smykind of soda pop.Five new drinks to tickle your tastebudsRapscallion Burnt Lemon£3.60 (250ml) Gail’s. The edgiest, tartest lemon meringue pie of your life – in liquid form.Botivo£3.50 (250ml) Waitrose. The bittersweet botanical aperitivo can now be enjoyed on the hoof – cheers!G SpotAwaken£6.50 (4 x 250ml) Ocado. This “may improve libido”, but it will definitely titillate your taste buds with its chilli kick.Non 1£19.99 (750ml) Sous Chef. A blend of tart verjus, chamomile and salted raspberry that’s super for sipping or supper.Sonic TonicsHemp Root Fig & Violet£36 (6 x 240ml) Sonic Tonics. A really unique, florally bitter soft drink with CBD – buzz without fuzz.Explore more on these topicsFoodSoft drinksBritish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Can fish and chip shops survive? ‘We made more money by closing than staying open’ | Food & drink industry | The Guardian
description: Soaring fish prices, labour costs and changing tastes all spell bad news for Britain’s chippies. Is this the end for the seaside staple – or will a few innovators succeed in keeping them alive?
Author: Steve Rose
Headline: Soaring fish prices, labour costs and changing tastes all spell bad news for Britain’s chippies. Is this the end for the seaside staple – or will a few innovators succeed in keeping them alive?
Content: ‘It’s a hard business’ … Kieran Sudlow (right) with Louis Skinner, a colleague at his shop.Photograph: Florence Law/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘It’s a hard business’ … Kieran Sudlow (right) with Louis Skinner, a colleague at his shop.Photograph: Florence Law/The GuardianFood & drink industryCan fish and chip shops survive? ‘We made more money by closing than staying open’Soaring fish prices, labour costs and changing tastes all spell bad news for Britain’s chippies. Is this the end for the seaside staple – or will a few innovators succeed in keeping them alive?Steve RoseThu 17 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 10.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne day in 2007, Darren Sudlow drove past the old stationmaster’s house at Padgate station, in Cheshire, noticed it was empty and decided to lease it. “He just fell in love with the place,” says his son, Kieran, who was 11 at the time. “He said he always wanted a fish and chip shop, for some reason.” Despite having worked as a joiner up to that point, Darren made a go of it, and the Plaice Station, as he named it, was a success from day one. “He worked like mad to get it open and then realised that the hard work hadn’t even started, and he had a queue out the door,” says the younger Sudlow.The family lived nearby. Kieran Sudlow, who is now 30, worked at the Plaice Station as a boy, peeling potatoes, washing dishes after school, then cooking at the range when he was 16. He went on to become a chef, working in Australia for a few years, then returning to help out at the chippy part-time when needed. Business had always been pretty good. They won local awards and had a loyal customer base. But one day in March, Kieran remembers, his father came in and told him: “‘I think the fish and chip shop’s going to go.’ He said, ‘It’s not making money. I can’t see it carrying on.’”In April, after 19 years, the Plaice Station served its last customer. In a Facebook post, Darren Sudlow explained that the closure was the result of multiple pressures: “Soaring fish prices, reduced fishing quotas and political issues around the world, relentless demands on VAT among other ever-increasing expenses, effectively destroying any profit margins remaining. Truth is, the product of fish and chips itself is facing its toughest battle.”View image in fullscreenKieran (left) and Darren Sudlow at their fish and chip shop, which closed earlier this year.Chippies across the UK are feeling similarly pessimistic. According to research carried out in May by the National Federation of Fish Friers (NFFF), 47% of them were “extremely worried” about the future of their business, and a further 30% were “slightly worried”. About 20% of them planned to quit in the next 12 months. Many have already shut in recent years. There are still 7,000-8,000 chippies in Britain, down from a peak of 25,000 in the 1930s, but the number of outlets, and the number of servings, are shrinking weekly. The big chains are also feeling the pressure: Deep Blue, which owns the historic Harry Ramsden’s brand,shut down nine of its restaurantslast summer.12:51Battered: why half of UK’s fish and chip shops face closure – videoCustomers cannot have failed to notice the problem. The average price of takeaway fish and chips has gone up more than 60% in the past five years, from about £7 to £11.43 – a faster rise than other takeaway foods. A family of four would now pay nearly £50 for their meal. “It’s a fair chunk of money and I think it’s shocked people a little bit,” says Andrew Crook, president of the NFFF. “So they cut back on the number of visits, so volumes are going down as well.”Crook has been feeling it himself; he runs two chippies in Lancashire, and has been in the trade for 27 years. The recent hot weather has been good for coastal outlets, but “if you’re inland, nobody wants fish and chips”, he says. It’s been a hard summer for shops like his. “It’s not a very pleasant place to be when it’s hot, and it’s quiet as well. The night drags, and it can be 40-50C in the shop.”View image in fullscreenA new frying range can cost more than £10,000.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThese are difficult times for UK hospitality across the board, but chippy owners have it particularly tough, Crook explains. For starters, they’re beholden to the costs of a very small set of basic ingredients.Fishprices have risen astronomically in recent years, especially cod and haddock. The cod quota in the Barents Sea, where most of the fish comes from, has gone down from about 1m tonnes in 2020 to just 285,000 tonnes this year, according to Undercurrent, a seafood industry data company. Inevitably, this has pushed up prices. “For an 18kg case of cod [fillets], I was paying something like £160 three years ago, and I’m now paying £330,” says Crook. Haddock quotas are slightly less affected, but the scarcity of cod has created a knock-on demand, again affecting prices.The Ukraine war has also had an impact on the industry (hence the “political issues” Darren Sudlow was referring to). The Barents Sea is jointly managed by Norway and Russia, but in May 2025,the EU sanctioned two Russian fishing companies, Murman SeaFood and the giant Norebo JSC, over alleged surveillance and sabotage activities. That has disrupted the whole supply chain, again raising prices.Potato prices are also likely to rise: after the heatwaves and droughts, this year’s European harvest will be one of the worst on record. Even cooking oil prices are going up. Then there are energy costs: the range has to be kept hot, and a lot of freezing and refrigeration is required. And the equipment is not cheap: a new frying range can cost upwards of £10,000.On the administrative side, chippies have been hit hard by recentrises in VAT(it returned to 20% in April 2022, after a temporary reduction during the pandemic to 5% and then 12.5%), business rates, the minimum wage and mandatory sick pay. The government has been putting in relief measures – lowering business ratesfor pubs and clubsin England, capping VAT on children’s meals over the summer – but none of this benefits chippies, says Crook. “So it does feel like we’re being run by our business now, rather than running the business. It’s taken a lot of the fun out of it for many.”View image in fullscreen‘We made more money by closing for three weeks than if we’d just stayed open’ … Kieran Sudlow.Photograph: Florence Law/The GuardianAll of these factors hit the Plaice Station, says Kieran Sudlow, squeezing margins tighter and tighter. VAT was the last straw. Like many small businesses, the firm was paying a flat rate of 12.5% to the government, but in 2025 its accountant warned it was approaching a limit: if the business’s annual turnover exceeded £230,000, the flat rate would no longer apply. “So it was going to cost us tens of thousands of pounds.”The only option was to earnlessmoney. The Sudlows made the painful decision to temporarily close. “As strange as it sounds, we made more money by closing for three weeks than if we’d just stayed open,” Kieran says. In order to justify leaving the flat rate scheme, they would have had to turn over an extra £2,000 a week. “After 19 years, you know where you are with your business. You can’t just find an extra two grand a week.”Closing down was a demoralising experience. “I felt we were doing everything we could to make the products as good as possible. But then all that work that you’ve done to grow your business is ripped out from under your feet.”There’s another factor at play here: changing tastes. Fish and chips has been facing stiff competition from other takeaway options: pizzas, burgers, fried chicken, Indian, Chinese, Korean – most of which use much cheaper ingredients. Deep-fried foods are also losing popularity for health reasons, since they contribute to obesity; the governmentrecently banned themfrom schools in England.View image in fullscreenA great British institution that is not, in fact, terribly British in origin.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianFish and chips is a great British institution, but the origins of the dish are not all that deep, or that British. The technique of coating fish in flour and deep-frying it is thought to have been introduced by Jewish immigrants from Spain and Portugal in the 17th century, but fish and chips only caught on commercially in the mid-19th century (starting in either London or Lancashire – it’s disputed). In the days before British cuisine opened up to international influences, it was one of the few convenience foods. It was also one of the few meals not rationed during the second world war, further cementing its patriotic connotations.One chip shop owner in his 80s (who did not wish to be named, as he is in the process of selling up) recalls starting out in the business in his 20s, in a small town in the north of England. “It was pretty busy, because in those days there was only your chip shop and your butcher’s and your pie shop,” he says. For most of his career it was a good way to make a living. His wife and children helped out in his shops and they often lived above the premises. But it has been tougher in recent years, he agrees, and he’s struggling to find a buyer for his business. Today’s establishments don’t look that different from the ones he started out in: “They’re more modern and very good-looking, but other than that, they haven’t changed. They can’t, because you can’t change the way you cook fish and chips.”The unchanging nature of fish and chips is both its strength and its weakness. Kieran Sudlow had begun to notice the dish falling out of fashion: “You’ve got a very ageing market – your traditionalists, your mums, your dads, your nans, they grew up on fish and chips. But we could see clear as day, and especially now with online orders and social media posts, your 18- to 35-year-olds, that younger bracket that’s your next generation of customers, they’re not interacting. They’re not coming through the doors.”A lot of chippies have tried using different, cheaper fish, such as hake, plaice, rock or spurdog (types of dogfish), or even tilapia, a freshwater fish farmed in southeast Asia. Many chippies claim customers would not be able to tell the difference, but we’re wedded to cod and haddock. Other chippies have expanded their menus to include items such as calamari, fishcakes, fried chicken, sausages, kebabs or loaded chips.View image in fullscreenOn offer at the Sudlows’ Between Bread.Photograph: Florence Law/The GuardianSudlow decided to change tack entirely. Three months after the Plaice Station closed, he reopened asBetween Bread, a high-end sandwich shop. The fare is a cut above: he uses locally sourced “shokupan”, or Japanese milk bread; fillings include braised beef with chipotle sauce, and spicy tuna and avocado; prices are between £8 and £12. He did his homework, researching food trends and visiting similar establishments around the country. Business is great, he says – turnover is “much higher” than when it was a chippy (justifying that VAT change), and the shop is popular on social media and with young people. He also gets to be a bit more creative as a chef. Does he miss the chippy days?“Personally, no,” he says. “It got to a point at the end where it really was like fighting. It’s an expensive product to buy in nowadays and even harder to sell. Staff training is a nightmare: how many people do you know that go, ‘When I grow up I want to cook fish and chips’? It’s a part-time job; staff turnover’s horrendous. It’s a hard business to have.”But the great British chippy is not to be written off just yet. Cod and haddock quotas are expected to increase 10% next year, says Undercurrent, which could help reduce prices, and the UK government is facing increasing pressure to deal with the VAT problems plaguing the hospitality industry.View image in fullscreen‘We need to hark back to just how pure a dish it is’ … Gavin Dhesi at his chippie, the Scrap Box.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianMost importantly, perhaps, a new generation is embracing the chippy tradition and breathing new life into it – not necessarily by totally transforming it, but by doing it simply and well.The Scrap Box, outside York, is one such example: it won best takeaway this year at the NFFF’sNational Fish & Chip awards.The Scrap Box was founded 12 years ago by brothers Aman and Gavin Dhesi, aged 37 and 33. Sons of a local off-licence keeper, they studied politics and economics at university, respectively, but then decided to open a chippy together. “It was pretty much on a whim, to be honest,” says Aman. “I was never proud to be doing fish and chips and never felt like it was really me.” After Covid, the brothers reached a crossroads, he continues. “It was like – do we do something else, do we sell out, or do we really double down and go on a journey to try to make sure we can improve every single aspect of the business?”They went on the journey, researching every aspect of the trade and its history, carefully sourcing their supplies and “letting our ingredients do the talking”: their fish comes from Iceland and is Marine Stewardship Council-certified; they fry in beef dripping from Ireland. There’s no secret formula, Aman says. The fish is lightly seasoned; the batter is just flour and water and a bit of natural colouring, applied as thinly as possible. Nothing artificial is added. “The main thing is, it needs to be made often, as opposed to just all done in the morning, so that it retains its bubbles and you still get your spikiness. And it wants to be cold, so that when it hits the oil, it has a bigger reaction – you get a nicer texture.”View image in fullscreenFriday teatime customers at the Scrap Box.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianWhen I visit on a Friday night, the Scrap Box – a roadside hut on a layby that used to be a council toilet block – is buzzing: six or seven people cooking at a huge range; a constant bustle of customers. The menu is classic: haddock and chips for £11.95, cod and chips a pound more, sides like curry sauce and mushy peas, a few non-fish options. And the food is everything you’d want it to be: the fish fresh and succulent, the batter crisp and light, the chips hot and sog-free.At the end of the shift, Gavin tells me they’ve done about 650 portions that night. The award has raised their profile. They’ve just returned from a trip to see the fishing in Iceland, he says, and they’re about to go to Japan, where they’re doing pop-up stores in three cities. “There’s been so many opportunities – that’s kept us stimulated and excited.” They’re also looking at opening a branch in London, Aman says: “We want to bring the best of the north to the south.”Curb the cod, park the prawns: top chefs on how to swap out the ‘big five’ seafoodRead moreDespite the union-jack-waving seaside cliches, what makes fish and chips quintessentially British is that it’s interwoven with our history of immigration and internationalism, says Aman, whose family has Punjabi roots. It is often immigrants who have run British chippies, he points out: Italians in Scotland, Chinese in Liverpool and the north-west of England, Indians and Pakistanis, Greeks and Turks. The fish recipe came from Sephardic Jews in Portugal; the potatoes often come from central Europe (via South America); the fish comes from Iceland and Norway.There are other outlets doing similar things to the Scrap Box around the UK. In Nottinghamshirethe Cod’s Scallops(corny names come with the territory) includes fresh fish counters in its outlets; in OxfordHarrisons’s Fish & Chip Cohas been diversifying its menu with a range of British fish. There are new young proprietors of established family chippies trying new things, and there are food trucks and mobile chippies such asFrosty’s in Northumberlandkeeping prices down by minimising their premises.So maybe there’s life in the old chippy yet. “I do think the better shops will survive and prosper,” says Aman Dhesi. “But it’s never going to die out.” Gavin agrees: “I think we need to hark back to just how pure a dish it is, how great it is. And when you think about it, for where it’s come from and the work that’s gone into it, it’s still a bargain.”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
