title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for rice, aubergine and mozzarella bake | Food | The Guardian
description: A 1950s cookbook classic – eat it hot and stringy or firm and flavoursome
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: A 1950s cookbook classic – eat it hot and stringy or firm and flavoursome
Content: Rachel Roddy’s rice, aubergine and mozzarella bake.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRachel Roddy’s rice, aubergine and mozzarella bake.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianA kitchen in RomeFoodRachel Roddy’s recipe for rice, aubergine and mozzarella bakeA 1950s cookbook classic – eat it hot and stringy or firm and flavoursomeRachel RoddyThu 17 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYesterday’s lunch and this week’s recipe is thanks to my friend, the designerJake Tilson, who gave me a pristine 1977 edition ofThe Talisman Italian Cook Book. With a cover of red, white and green stripes cover that makes me think as much of seaside rock as Italy’s national colours, the edition was part of the 24th printing of the US translation ofIl Talismano della Felicità(The Talisman of Happiness), by Ada Boni. First published in 1950, the abridged translation was sold as a complete guide to Italian cookery, covering all notable dishes. Well, on the cover at least; inside, the introduction is more realistic, warning the reader that, “to criticise the writer [Boni] or translator [Mrs Matilde La Rosa] for failing to include certain dishes is useless”, because no living man or woman can be acquainted with all the variety of dishes of a such variegated country.The introduction, by a man called Mario A Pei, goes on to explain that the variety of dishes mirrors the wide dialectical array in Italy at the time (1950); its diversity of speech, customs, costumes, psychology and general world outlook. In the next sentence, he notes that this variety was undoubtedly a very bad thing from the standpoint of national unity and progress (the professor and polyglot was an ardent supporter of European fascism and uniting humans under one language). Not that you would guess that from his following sentence: “Variety is the spice of life.” I regretted reading his introduction, and also telling an Italian friend, who said, laughing: “You don’t know the half of it”, in reference to my romanticism about the originalTalismano, which may be great, but also (in her opinion) endorses a Stepford Wives fantasy of womanhood; a journey with Boni as patient guide.I don’t regret making the recipe from page 161 for rice with aubergine, however, which I have adapted for variety’s sake. This bake is good when made with tinned tomatoes, but fresh ones bring a brighter burst of flavour. Ideally, try to get a mix of varieties – a few sweet cherries, a couple of plums, a big fleshy one – that have been peeled and cooked into a sweet-savoury sauce; if necessary, add a pinch of sugar.A reason for eating this pretty much straight out of the oven and while it’s still steaming hot is the mozzarella, because the cheese is molten and pulls into those long strings that make serving it and eating it so entertaining. The benefit of waiting half an hour or longer is that the flavours develop, while the bake itself (and the mozzarella inside and on top) firms up. Or serve at whatever stage or temperature you like, with whatever variety of salad or vegetable.Rice, aubergine and mozzarella bakeServes4-62 medium auberginesOlive oilSalt500g fresh, ripe tomatoes– tinned as a last resort1 onion, peeled and thinly slicedA few red chilli flakes1 handfulbasil leavesSugar(optional)400g long-grain rice80ggrana padano, parmesan, or cheddar400g mozzarella, well-drainedUsing a peeler, pare strips of skin from the aubergines so they are striped, then cut into 1cm-thick slices. Arrange these on an oiled baking tray, zigzag with more oil, sprinkle with salt, then bake at 180C (160C)/350F/gas 4 for 30-40 minutes, until tender and a little golden.Peel the tomatoes by plunging them first into boiling water for four minutes, then cold water, then pulling away the skins. Roughly chop the flesh.In a pan on a medium-low heat, soften the onion in olive oil, then add the tomatoes, some salt, chilli, most of the basil leaves (reserve a few for constructing the bake) and some sugar, if necessary, and simmer until rich and saucy, mashing as you go to break up any lumps; you can also pass the sauce through a food mill.Boil the rice in salted water until al dente and a minute shy of the recommended cooking time. Drain and mix the rice with two tablespoons of olive oil, four tablespoons of the tomato sauce, 30g grated parmesan and salt, if needed; it should be well seasoned.Thinly slice or tear the mozzarella, then construct the bake. Spoon half the rice mix in the base of a round 22cm metal tin or 20cm x 30cm ceramic lasagne-type dish, then use half the aubergine to make a layer on top. Top that with half the sauce, followed by half the mozzarella and a few basil leaves, then repeat this process with the remaining ingredients, ending with a layer of the remaining 50g parmesan. Bake for 20 minutes at 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6, until bubbling.Explore more on these topicsFoodA kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkRiceVegetablesCheeseMain courserecipesShareReuse this content

title: You be the judge: should my brother have told me the money I lent him was for his holiday? | Siblings | The Guardian
description: Ayaan thought she was lending money for something essential. Ahmed says the lender doesn’t get to dictate what it’s spent on. You decide who is on the money
Author: Georgina Lawton
Headline: Ayaan thought she was lending money for something essential. Ahmed says the lender doesn’t get to dictate what it’s spent on. You decide who is on the money
Content: Illustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianYou be the judgeSiblingsYou be the judge: should my brother have told me the money I lent him was for his holiday?Ayaan thought she was lending money for something essential. Ahmed says the lender doesn’t get to dictate what it’s spent on. You decide who is on the moneyFind out how to get a disagreement settled or become a jurorInterviews byGeorgina LawtonThu 17 Sep 2026 03.15 EDTFirst published on Thu 17 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheprosecution: Ayaandouble quotation markI thought I was lending Ahmed money for something vital, not a trip to GreeceMy brother Ahmed and I both live at home – he’s 27 and I’m 25. I look up to him, but he’s much more disorganised than me, and over the years has asked me to keep secrets from our parents when he’s messed up. I lent him money recently, which he then used to go on holiday with his friends. It annoyed me, but I didn’t tell our parents.Ahmed is between jobs right now. I am doing a journalism internship, but at least I have a wage. When Ahmed asked me for the money he didn’t say what it was for, but I assumed it was living expenses or something essential. Our parents work but send money home to family in Somalia, so we try to help out with the rent. Ahmed hasn’t been paying much recently but my parents don’t mind as they want him to find work. Also, I think that as the eldest son, he gets away with more.double quotation markI felt like a mug when he was away while I was workingAhmed and I are close but we don’t talk in detail about our finances. I assumed that for him to have to ask me for money, it was vital. I lent him £400 a month or so ago, which is a lot out of my monthly internship pay of £1,500. We didn’t discuss terms or when he would repay me, but I thought it would be sooner rather than later.But two weeks later, he tells me he is going away with his friends to Greece for five days. I thought: “Am I a mug?” It doesn’t seem reasonable to say you’re hard up and then go on holiday abroad. Ahmed said: “Just because you lent me money doesn’t mean you can dictate what I spend it on.” I wasn’t trying to dictate. And I don’t expect Ahmed to live like a monk until he repays me.Luckily, I don’t need the money back urgently, but I felt stupid when he was away while I was working. I think that if you’ve borrowed a significant amount of money from someone, you should make an effort to pay them back before spending hundreds on non-essentials.Our parents noticed some tension between us, but I didn’t tell them why, as I knew Ahmed would be embarrassed. He said he will pay me back “soon” but it’s going to be a long time after his holiday, I’m sure.You be the judge – send us your domestic disputesRead moreThedefence: Ahmeddouble quotation markI got a cheap flight to cheer myself up – so what? The lender doesn’t get to dictate how the money is spentObviously I’m appreciative of my sister lending me money. Times are tough right now as I was made redundant from my recruitment job a while ago and I haven’t been able to help our parents out as much as I’d like. I don’t enjoy being in this position, but I’d rather borrow from my family than take out a loan or get into credit card debt.When my sister gave me the £400, she literally said: “Pay me back whenever you can.” I didn’t realise there was an unspoken deadline. If you lend someone money in good faith, you cannot tell them what to spend it on. That was never part of the deal. If it had been, I wouldn’t have agreed to it.double quotation markAyaan acts as if I was gallivanting across the world, waving her cash aroundI spent some of the £400 on food, going out and a Ryanair flight. I don’t think I should be demonised for that. The trip was already being discussed with my friends and I did it as cheaply as possible. Ayaan acts as if I was gallivanting across the world, waving her cash around as I went. It wasn’t like that. I’m between jobs, which means I’ve already had to cut back on loads of things and that knocks your confidence. I don’t think owing somebody money means you have to put your entire life on hold until you’re employed again.Ayaan says she doesn’t need the money urgently, so I don’t really understand why me going away has suddenly changed the agreement. If she’d said: “I need this back next month”, that would be different and I would have prioritised it, but she didn’t. Of course I will pay her back and I’m applying for jobs. I just don’t think lending someone money gives you the right to monitor everything they spend it on in the meantime.I appreciate Ayaan not telling our parents. They are fairly strict and want to know what we are doing all the time, especially Ayaan. I don’t think it’s true that I get an easier ride as the eldest son, though. They are always on my case about getting back into work, but thankfully haven’t asked me for rent since I was laid off. I don’t want to be in this position, but I’m happy Ayaan has helped me out. I’d do the same for her.Names have been changedskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe jury of Guardian readersAyaan should have asked what the money was for before agreeing to lend it. But it seems wrong that Ahmed didn’t tell her if he was already planning the holiday. I wouldn’t have been able to relax on my sunbed knowing I’d hoodwinked my sister.David, 45If you’re lending money to someone because they’re in a tight spot, them using it to go on holiday is very cheeky. It sounds as if Ahmed knows that – if not, why didn’t he tell Ayaan what it was for before he borrowed it?Christy, 50Ayaan can chill on this one. Ahmed needed to blow off some steam and go away with his friends. They sound like a family that looks after each other and pay back debts, so I think Ahmed should be cut some slack.Grace, 33Ahmed is right to say “the lender doesn’t get to dictate how the money is spent”, but not telling his sister that it was for a holiday and letting her assume it was for living expenses is bang out of order. I’m with Ayaan.Kofi, 25It’s not Ahmed’s fault that he’s out of work at the moment, but if he wanted to borrow money for a holiday, he should have been upfront with Ayaan from the start. She’s lent her brother a big chunk of her monthly earnings, and he should make more of an effort to pay it back.Jessie, 38Now you be the judgeIn our online poll, tell us: is Ahmed on borrowed time?The poll closes on Wednesday 23 September at 9am BSTLast week’s resultsWe asked whetherJasper should finishold bottles and packets before opening new ones.99% of you said yes –Jasper is guilty1% of you said no –Jasper is innocentExplore more on these topicsSiblingsYou be the judgefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I feel invisible’: over-50s reveal harsh realities of trying to get a job | Work & careers | The Guardian
description: Candidates describe feelings of rejection after submitting hundreds of applications but getting a handful of interviews
Author: Jane Clinton
Headline: Candidates describe feelings of rejection after submitting hundreds of applications but getting a handful of interviews
Content: Some over-50s have sent off hundreds of job applications but have had little success.Photograph: MoMo Productions/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSome over-50s have sent off hundreds of job applications but have had little success.Photograph: MoMo Productions/Getty ImagesWork & careers‘I feel invisible’: over-50s reveal harsh realities of trying to get a jobCandidates describe feelings of rejection after submitting hundreds of applications but getting a handful of interviewsJane ClintonThu 17 Sep 2026 11.49 EDTFirst published on Thu 17 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of job applications, exhausting searches and relentless rejection – the experience of attempting to get back into the workforce after losing their jobs in their 50s and 60s has proved an ordeal for some Britons.For some, those efforts prove fruitless and lead jobseekers to reluctantly take early retirement. Others may have to rely on benefits to pay the bills while they continue to job hunt.Recentresearchby the Centre for Ageing Better found that the number of people between 50 and state pension age having difficulty finding work was 918,000 – akin to the number ofyoung people not in education, employment or training– at the end of last year, the highest since 2020. The count was 2.9 million when including those with long-term health conditions and caring responsibilities.The Guardian asked people over 50 to get in touch and share their experiences of trying to return to work.‘I can’t find a way out of this situation’James, 59, who lives in south-west England, lost his job two years ago and, since then, has had “eight interviews from 598 job applications”.“It has been horrible … and very stressful,” he says. “I have every application listed in an Excel file, none of which were successful for the roles advertised, though I did manage to get some other items of work as a result of them. Overall I have been barely employed, perhaps severely underemployed, for two years, and I can’t find a way out of this situation.”James, who has worked in international development, says when he was applying for jobs in the early 2020s he was getting “an interview every 15 or 20 applications” but now “it’s about one per 80 applications”.At the moment, he is scraping by with occasional editing for organisations in his sector and a bit of freelance writing for a magazine.“It’s tiny, but it’s something,” he says. “I’ve also been living at a relative’s house, who very kindly has said I don’t need to contribute to costs there at the moment, but I rely on my savings when I need them.”He says job application feedback is “never shared, so I’ve no grasp of why I fail”.He adds: “I do wonder if age is an issue. Perhaps companies think a younger person will be more flexible, more capable, and they can mould them into their particular way of working. The only thing to do is to persevere and hope.”‘Looking for a job is at times harder than actually doing a job’Sally*, 52, who has worked in the charity sector and lives in Birmingham, says she has applied for “more than 100 roles” but “still no bites”.She has had 17 interviews in the past 10 months and has been perplexed by immediate rejections for jobs for which she seemed well suited.“I’ve applied for lower and higher level roles, for temp and part-time ones, some outside my field but where I feel my skills can bring value, and some roles that I don’t really want but am desperate,” she said. “I’ve had immediate noes for roles that appear to be written for me and have had interviews for roles which I applied for as a long shot. It’s tough out there.”Sally, who is in receipt of jobseeker’s allowance, adds: “Looking for a job is at times harder than actually doing a job – not to mention the impact on your self-esteem, pocket, and relationships.”She is not sure if age is a factor but feels it could be “part of the mix”.“I’ve wondered if assumptions are made, if there’s perhaps a bias at play, is there an underlying feeling of threat? But I have to stop myself from going down that road. It won’t help my sense of self, as it’s something I cannot change.”View image in fullscreenOne over-50 applicant says they faced ‘clear bias’ at job interviews.Photograph: insta_photos/Getty Images/iStockphoto‘After three years of looking, I abandoned my search and retired’David*, 66, who has worked in IT for 35 years, says he had hoped to find work after he was made redundant in early 2020, but after three years of looking he just could not find a job.“After redundancy I used the Covid-19 period to plan my retirement and move house,” he says. “In 2021 I started to look for a new job.”While David, who lives in the north-east of England, knew his IT experience was “out of date”, he says he was content to look for “part-time or temporary or minimum-wage jobs or zero-hours contracts”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I partly expected I could get a job stacking shelves in a supermarket,” he says.However, he found the job market much tougher than expected.“In 2024, I abandoned the attempt and retired,” he says. “I had applied to all the supermarkets and never got a response.”He says he applied to one well-known store only to see its chair on TV “complaining about how difficult it was to find employees due to the Brexit deal”.‘As a fiftysomething woman, I feel invisible in the workplace and in public life’In 2022, Liz, 51, took a six-month career break to care for her dying father.She returned to the workplace in 2023; first, she took a part-time interim leadership role which was maternity cover. After that, she took a “quite junior role”, thinking it would “tide her over” until she secured a more senior position.But now, more than two years on, she is still in the same job despite applying for other roles.“I have applied for more than 100 jobs and only received a handful of interviews,” says Liz, who works in education and lives in London. “I think it is my age but also my gender. My worry is that I won’t be able to return to a senior position. I feel exhausted and deflated by the whole job-hunting experience.“I feel like I’m being deskilled. But I’m not alone – many of my female friends who are around the same age as me are experiencing similar issues, and I also realise there are people not able to find any employment at all.”She says that initially she thought her lack of success in interviews was solely down to her own shortcomings.“I thought, well, there must be something wrong with me, with my profile, with what I’m saying, with how I’m interviewing. You do the soul searching.”She recalls how just before one interview with a charity she was approached by an interview panel member who asked her: “Do you always dress so formally?”“I felt it was a very personal reference to my age, and this clear bias made its way as the reason not to hire me,” she says. “I have worked with young people my entire career. At another charity, the feedback was that I lacked ‘presence’. What can I do with that?”She adds: “There are lots of people like me in the sector I am applying for, so it means that employers have the pick. I feel invisible in the workplace and in public life as a fiftysomething woman. I just feel like experience isn’t valued any more.”* Names have been changedExplore more on these topicsWork & careersJob huntingUnemploymentEconomicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: English Heritage trains new generation of scythers to maintain meadows and craft | English Heritage | The Guardian
description: Initiative aims to keep alive age-old skill, and at Muchelney Abbey in Somerset improve habitat for the shrill carder bee
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Initiative aims to keep alive age-old skill, and at Muchelney Abbey in Somerset improve habitat for the shrill carder bee
Content: English Heritage volunteer coordinator James Adams scything meadows at Muchelney Abbey, in Somerset.Photograph: Andre Pattenden/English Heritage/PAView image in fullscreenEnglish Heritage volunteer coordinator James Adams scything meadows at Muchelney Abbey, in Somerset.Photograph: Andre Pattenden/English Heritage/PAEnglish HeritageEnglish Heritage trains new generation of scythers to maintain meadows and craftInitiative aims to keep alive age-old skill, and at Muchelney Abbey in Somerset improve habitat for rare shrill carder beeSteven MorrisThu 17 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt sounds like something out of a Thomas Hardy novel: a merry band of men and women roaming the West Country cutting meadows by hand in exchange for hunks of bread and cheese.But the conservation charityEnglish Heritageis recruiting a team of volunteer scythers to maintain 21st-century meadowland in the old-fashioned way.The first scythers have been trained and will use their new skills in the meadows around an abbey inSomerset, where it is hoped that as well as helping to keep the age-old practice alive, they will protect a rare type of bumblebee.View image in fullscreenJames Adams scything at Muchelney Abbey, which will be the focus of the first English Heritage scything project.Photograph: Andre Pattenden/English Heritage/PAGinny Slade, who has completed the training, said she found there was something therapeutic about scything.“You need a level of physical fitness but it’s also about enthusiasm and the passion to learn heritage skills,” she said. “It’s a repetitive movement. You find your rhythm and zone into it. You can really connect with the meadow, the landscape.”The first volunteers have also found that using the scythe is something of a sensual treat – the sound of the blade cutting, the scent of the meadow.Slade said: “Scything is a wonderful example of how traditional skills can still have a role in addressing modern challenges. We hope to help create the diverse, flower-rich habitats that pollinators need while also preserving knowledge and skills that have shaped our landscapes.”Slade, a volunteer and community engagement manager withEnglish Heritage, is one of the first to be trained by professionals at the Exmoor National Park Authority in the art of using and maintaining a scythe. “You want a really good scythe,” said Slade. “If you look after them, they can last generations.”EnglishHeritagerewards volunteers with bread and cheese (it also thought about providing West Country cider but thought this was not a good idea on health and safety grounds).The first group of scythers will help care for the meadow atMuchelney Abbey, in Somerset, which was once a wealthy and important monastery with features including a thatched two-storey monks’ lavatory, which is unique in Britain.They will work on a three-year project with the Bumblebee Conservation Trust to improve habitat for theshrill carder bee,a species that has declined significantly because of the loss of flower-rich grasslands.View image in fullscreenA shrill carder bee.Photograph: Kevin Rushby/The GuardianAs part of the project, English Heritage volunteers have been trained by the bumblebee trust to carry out wildlife surveys.Rather than simply recording numbers, volunteers will monitor the relationship between bees and the meadow ecosystem, including which flowers are in bloom, which plants they are using, how far bees travel from their nests and how the habitat changes over time.Hardy wrote about scything in prose and poetry: in Far From the Madding Crowd, Bathsheba Everdene watches haymaking, and the farm hand Mark Clark is described as “humming a tune to the strokes of his scythe”.In his poem Four in the Morning, Hardy wrote about the “to-and-fro/Wheezed whettings of a scythe apace”.The meadow at Muchelney is one of 100 that English Heritage pledged to create and enhance to mark the coronation of King Charles in 2023.Slade said Muchelney was the pilot site but the idea was for the volunteers to travel to other English Heritage sites to use their skills. “We’re really at the beginning of this journey, but we’re very excited about it.”Explore more on these topicsEnglish HeritageSomersetRural affairsEnglandBeesWildlifeInsectsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hard parties, cheap rents and horrible flats: how 90s art and fashion redefined British culture | Culture | The Guardian
description: An evocative new Tate Britain show captures an era when the UK’s newly flush creative industries teamed up with a generation of skint dreamers to bring the decade into vivid colour
Author: Miranda Sawyer
Headline: An evocative new Tate Britain show captures an era when the UK’s newly flush creative industries teamed up with a generation of skint dreamers to bring the decade into vivid colour
Content: Pretty in pink … Kate Moss, photographed by Juergen Teller.Photograph: Juergen TellerView image in fullscreenPretty in pink … Kate Moss, photographed by Juergen Teller.Photograph: Juergen TellerGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.CultureHard parties, cheap rents and horrible flats: how 90s art and fashion redefined British cultureAn evocative new Tate Britain show captures an era when the UK’s newly flush creative industries teamed up with a generation of skint dreamers to bring the decade into vivid colourIntroduction byMiranda SawyerThu 17 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere isKate Moss, with pink hair splayed across a pillow, her face scrubbed of makeup, her smile sweet and wonky. Sarah Lucas’s Pauline Bunny artwork with its confrontational hosiery on a charity shop chair. Sean Ellis’s collaborative knights-in-grubby-armour shoot with Alexander McQueen. Here are happy ravers, in a club, or saluting the sun as it stretches and yawns over a litter-strewn hill.These photos are old. They were taken a long time ago. But they’re young, too. They are curated by Edward Enninful for the Tate’s exhibition The 90s:Artand Fashion (Enninful worked at i-D in the 90s) and almost everyone involved is shiny and fresh. The models, whether professional or not, are mostly in their 20s, and the photographers are early in their careers. It gives the photos a youthful fizz, a verve. But the energy also comes from an understanding between photographer and subject. In many of the pictures you can feel the shared mischief, a “yes we’re serious about our ideas” but also a “look, we’re getting away with it!” delight.At the time these photos were taken I was writing for magazines such as Select, the Face and Smash Hits. I know some of the subjects in the pictures, as well as some of the photographers. No surprise: I was out a lot, and so were a lot of people in what we now call the creative industries. We were excited: we had just moved to London, or Manchester, had recently left art college or school or university, managed to wangle our ways into occasional, seemingly glamorous jobs that hadn’t yet blossomed into careers. As every generation must, we were elbowing our way in from the edges to the mainstream, finding space for ourselves and people like us. Some of the people in these pictures eventually became very rich, and so moved into different circles. But at the time, everyone was on a level. Skint, hard-working and up for a good night out.double quotation markAs every generation must, we were elbowing our way in from the edges to the mainstreamParties were plentiful. Aside from the club scene, magazines threw them, art galleries threw them, some random person that you met in a late-night drinking den said, “I know this place”, so you went. When you were out, you met artists, photographers, musicians, actors, writers, promoters, dealers, “entrepreneurs”. Often you had no idea what they did: I once walked into an office and realised that the esteemed head of design was the character with whom I’d spent a full-on all-nighter at Glastonbury a month before.Of the three, art parties were the best, often held for impoverished artists by very rich people who wanted to invest in work that would, eventually, make them even richer. I went to a party for an artist at a west London house that was so gorgeous I thought it was a restaurant when I first arrived. The woman who owned the house showed me and others the swimming pool in the basement, and informed us she’d insisted on it when her husband had said they were moving to London. The artist the woman was throwing the party for lived in a tiny housing association flat. Fashion parties were wild, but with a darker edge (rich older men have always been interested in young, insecure models), and more self-conscious. Music ones were cheaper, boozier and scuzzier. There were also parties thrown just because a venue was found: an empty lido, a disused warehouse, film studios vacated between shoots – inner-city spaces that today have almost all been repurposed into flash new apartments.double quotation markParty venues were easy to find. The flats were horrible, but they were plentiful and central, and rent was cheapSuch times were documented, of course, or these images would not exist. But in everyday life, we were less visually obsessed. When you went on a night out, one of your friends might have a camera with them, but they’d forget to use it or leave it in a pile of coats in a darkened corner, never to be seen again. You would embark on whatever adventure the evening might bring and afterwards there wouldn’t be much evidence of it; the sweat and grime washed off by a barely functioning shower. No wonder the good photographers capturing this era had a specialness, a status.Now the 90s are far enough away for us to understand them, it’s clear that there was a hidden architecture to those times, one that supported this burst of creativity. It wasn’t just the party venues that were easy to find. The flats were horrible, but they were plentiful and central, and rent was cheap. I never paid more than £60 a week for a room in a flatshare. And if you couldn’t afford that, you could squat, or claim housing benefit until someone official caught on that you were working, too. So we had places to live, but there was no internet to keep us there: if we wanted food or drink or sex, we couldn’t magic them up on our phones. To get those, you had to leave the house, and we did, often not returning for days at a time. Some friends of mine had what they called “going home fear”. They’d only return to their flat for an hour, to wash and get changed before going straight back out again.Another factor that propped up that time was that the music industry was flush with money from the invention of CDs. Such riches meant that major labels could afford to fund indie labels, indie labels could pay independent PRs to promote their bands, and music magazines could pay journalists to write about them. There were enough jobs in that industry, and in fashion and photography and art, for the people in power to take a punt on the enthusiastic newbie, someone who’d come from nowhere, who knew no one but who had interesting ideas and who kept on coming back. A whole generation of cocky, idea-fuelled kids trying their hands at modelling, writing, presenting, art. Or photography. These pictures are some of the results.Miranda Sawyer is the presenter of the podcastTalk 90s to Me. The 90s: Fashion and Art is at Tate Britain, London, 8 October to 14 February.Bright young things: photographers and curators on works in the showYoung Pink Kate by Juergen Teller, 1998 (main image)Teller: “I first photographed Kate when she was 18, her first fashion campaign, for Katharine Hamnett. Since then we worked together a lot and became friends. She called me up one day, explained she dyed her hair pink for a Versace fashion show in Milan and wanted to dye it back, and asked whether I wanted to come over before and photograph her with pink hair.”View image in fullscreenSarah Lucas, Pauline Bunny, 1997.Photograph: Lucy Dawkins/Sarah Lucas/ TatePauline Bunny by Sarah Lucas, 1997Dominique Heyse-Moore, senior curator: “Sarah had been stuffing tights with different kinds of materials, making spiders and all sorts of many-limbed creatures. But her “bunnies” are really the first time that women’s bodies began to be represented through this method. Her bunnies are named after Bunny Girls, the waitresses who worked in clubs earlier in the 20th century, though still around at this point. But the way she is slumped over a chair perhaps suggests that she is a sex worker. She’s also so slight: it’s a girl’s body in many ways. Sarah has continued to make bunnies. The recent ones have more folds, more flesh: older women’s bodies, but also more assertive, more confident in their sexuality.”View image in fullscreenSam Taylor-Johnson, Fuck, Suck, Spank, Wank, 1993.Photograph: Sam Taylor-Johnson/All Rights Reserved/DACS ImagesFuck Suck Spank Wank by Sam Taylor-Johnson, 1993Heyse-Moore: “A lot of these images are about girlhood, womanhood and youth; the experience of photographing and being photographed. All those themes are beautifully brought together here. There’s this way in which Taylor-Johnson is overtly and explicitly challenging the idea of how a woman is supposed to appear or behave in the making of her art. In the classic kind of 90s way, it’s poking at gender norms, not to mention the idea of the badly behaved artist.”View image in fullscreenJon Shard, Flesh at the Hacienda, 1994.Photograph: Jon ShardFlesh at Haçienda by Jon Shard, 1994Shard: “I took this at Flesh in the early 90s. This guy had created this incredible headdress from silver wire, combined with the long chain around his neck. He was moving around the club like a piece of performance art. Flesh had a different feel from regular Haçienda nights. It was a gay night with its own look and energy, with people experimenting much more with how they presented themselves. I think this was what made the 90s so interesting: people creating things for themselves.”View image in fullscreenFergus Greer, Leigh Bowery, Session VIII, Look 38, 1994.Photograph: Fergus GreerLeigh Bowery, Session VII, Look 38 by Fergus Greer, 1994Greer: “This image of Leigh in a full-length rubber bodysuit, shot on large format, was made just before his sudden death from an Aids-related illness brought our six-year collaboration to an end. Leigh would spend hours preparing in the dressing room with his wife Nicola. When he finally emerged, the studio would fall into a pause of pure incredulity. My part was to find the magic that turned that moment into a photograph that would outlast us both. These are images people still want to reproduce, that 100 years on will hang on gallery walls and run in the media.”View image in fullscreenElle von Unwerth, Naomi Campbell, Babywoman album cover, 1994.Photograph: Ellen von UnwerthNaomi Campbell Babywoman album cover by Ellen von Unwerth, 1994Heyse-Moore: “Naomi Campbell was a symbol of international Black beauty. But what we know now is that she often didn’t get booked in the UK. There was a persistent idea about what British style was: Kate Moss’s more androgynous, indie look. The Babywoman artwork is playing with the idea of her as a girl or a woman. Even the title speaks to questions around Black girlhood: research suggests that Black girls are not seen to be children. We hear so much about what it was like to be a vulnerable young white model but don’t really hear about that with Campbell.”View image in fullscreenSean Ellis, The Dark Knight Returns, styled by Isabella Blow, 1998.Photograph: Sean EllisThe Dark Knight Returns by Sean Ellis, styled by Isabella Blow, 1998Ellis: “I was a huge fan of John Boorman’s film Excalibur and Isabella Blow was very good at mixing not only people but ideas. We spent a lot of time studying 16th-century battle paintings to work out the light and poses. I had a good relationship with Lee [Alexander McQueen, pictured centre]. You could tell he was on a collision course: he almost hated the industry he worked in. Here, he is outnumbered: there is a lowering of the sword as he faces his death. We did ones of him fighting back and another where all the knights are dead but this one, where he was fighting until he couldn’t fight any more, felt the strongest.”View image in fullscreenEileen Perrier, Untitled, Afro Hair and Beauty Show, 1998.Photograph: Eileen Perrier/All rights reserved/DACS 2026Untitled, Afro Hair and Beauty Show by Eileen Perrier, 1998Heyse-Moore: “The Afro Hair and Beauty exhibition filled London’s Alexandra Palace every year. It was an amazing celebration and affirmation of the art of Black hair and makeup. One of the things that is wonderful about this image and the project [Perrier photographed the exhibition over five years] is it’s Black female photographer to Black female subject: there’s a really direct ‘looking at each other’ that takes place; an empowerment and agency for both. We don’t know how old the woman here is exactly, but we know she didn’t go to the show knowing that she and the other women pictured were going to be photographed that day. They’re getting dressed for themselves and for entering into that Black space. It’s a glimpse into this gigantic, quite private world, but with a performative element to it.”View image in fullscreenVinca Petersen, Paula Sunrise 1997.Photograph: Vinca Petersen. Courtesy of Edel Assanti Art.Paula Sunrise by Vinca Petersen, 1997Petersen: “After the 1994 Criminal Justice Act outlawed raves in the UK, I spent a decade travelling around Europe in a van trying to recreate that way of living. This shot captures that feeling of having spent the whole night dancing in the dark in a huge crowd. There is something special about that moment when the sun slowly appears and you start to see the faces of all the people you’ve been surrounded by, and inevitably often sit down and end up talking about the big stuff in life. Nowadays I do kitchen discos. But that sense of freedom and creativity has stayed with us all. The last time I spoke to Paula she was working in the Houses of Parliament.”View image in fullscreenTony Davis, Ravers at the Eclipse, Coventry, 1991Photograph: Tony DavisRavers at the Eclipse, Coventry, by Tony Davis, 1991Edward Enninful, curator: “The 90s were all about a shared energy, where fashion, art and music collided in the same spaces; a moment when a generation of outsiders rejected old hierarchies and for ever changed who gets to be seen. It’s a decade that established conditions that are still with us: the merging of high and low culture, the politicisation of fashion and image, and the emergence of diversity as a creative force.”Explore more on these topicsCultureArtPhotographyTate BritainKate MossfeaturesShareReuse this content
