title: ‘Like a Disney movie’: Three wild dog brothers make Africa’s longest journey | Endangered species | The Guardian
description: As three siblings came of age and had to leave their pack, scientists tracked the dogs’ perilous 2,500-mile odyssey to find their own territory
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: As three siblings came of age and had to leave their pack, scientists tracked the dogs’ perilous 2,500-mile odyssey to find their own territory
Content: Researchers used GPS collars to track 19 groups of wild dogs and monitor their dispersals, including a group of sisters to the brothers who were less successful at finding a new range.Photograph: MSU Department of EcologyView image in fullscreenResearchers used GPS collars to track 19 groups of wild dogs and monitor their dispersals, including a group of sisters to the brothers who were less successful at finding a new range.Photograph: MSU Department of EcologyThe age of extinctionEndangered species‘Like a Disney movie’: Three wild dog brothers make Africa’s longest journeyAs three siblings came of age and had to leave their pack, scientists tracked the dogs’ perilous 2,500-mile odyssey to find their own territoryThe age of extinction is supported byAbout this contentPatrick Greenfield. Photographs by Scott CreelThu 17 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 09.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt sounds like a Disney movie: three wild dogs, all brothers, on an epic journey to find a home of their own after their family tells them to leave. They dodge cars and hunters in search of a new life, navigating bushmeat snares and the hostility of a human-dominated landscape until they find a new haven on the African savannah.But this is exactly what happened inZambialast year, when three endangered African wild dogs made the longest-ever recorded single journey of any mammal from the continent. The brothers travelled more than 2,500 miles (4,100km) over eight months in their “dispersal” – when a young dog comes of age and must establish new territory to find a mate and start a family of their own.View image in fullscreenTwo months after they set out, the brothers and sisters met again, spending a day together before separating.Photograph: MSUFrom point to point, starting in Kafue national park in western Zambia to their final destination in the Luangwa valley in the east of the country, the brothers covered 340 miles (546km), which is also a record.The epic single journey is almost equivalent to travelling the length of Chile by foot and farther than the famouswildebeest and zebra migrationacross the Serengeti in east Africa. The previous record was 2,418 miles, also made by African wild dogs, which moved between Loliondo, in northern Tanzania’s Ngorongoro district, and Tsavo West national park in southern Kenya in 2012.Dr Matt Becker, chief executive of the Zambian Carnivore Programme (ZCP), whose scientists were monitoring the wild dogs and have published theirfindings in the journal Ecology, says: “These extraordinary journeys show that natural connections between Africa’s wildlife strongholds still exist. But they also reveal how difficult and dangerous those journeys have become.“Rather than relying solely on fenced protected areas, these findings reinforce the value of investing in connected landscapes. The dogs are showing us that connectivity still works; now we need to do more to protect and strengthen it.”The researchers tracked 19 separate groups of wild dogs to monitor their dispersals, including a group of sisters to the three brothers who were far less successful at finding a new range. Two of the sisters died, probably caught in snares, but not before they had a touching final encounter with their siblings.LocatorTwo months into their journey, the group of brothers and sisters came across each other deep in Zambia’s copper-belt mining region, spending the day together before going their separate ways again. Related dogs do not form new family packs, and typically have to travel long distances through the landscape to find prospective mates.‘Bringing the boys back home’: how mountain bongos Maue, Fitz, Kudu and Bon64 made their way back to KenyaRead moreOnly 6,600 or so adults remain of 39 distinct populations of African wild dogs, and the species is classified asendangeredon the International Union for Conservation of Nature’sred list. Habitat loss, declining numbers of natural prey, bushmeat hunters’ snares and human conflict are among the biggest threats to their survival.But researchers say the three brothers’ epic journey shows the wild dogs can still survive in a human-dominated landscape despite the enormous challenges they face. Alongside African savannah elephants, whoseancient migration routesare increasingly being blocked by human development, African wild dogs need to be able to make long journeys to find new homes.“These long-term studies provide key evidence that connectivity between large landscapes is still there,” says Dr Nyambe Nyambe, director of the Kavango-Zambezi transfrontier area secretariat, a key conservation region that spans five countries, including Zambia, where governments are trying to keep space for wildlife to move through the landscape.View image in fullscreenAfrican wild dogs have been endangered for decades, with only 6,600 or so adults remaining of 39 populations across the continent.Photograph: MSU“If we conserve and continue to improve these connections – spanning the range of national parks, community areas, nations and regions – a lot of species like wild dogs can make the rest happen,” Nyambe says.Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverage.Explore more on these topicsEndangered speciesThe age of extinctionAnimalsWildlifeAfricaConservationIUCN red list of endangered speciesMammalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: New cat species identified for first time in more than a century in Bolivia | Bolivia | The Guardian
description: New species of wild cat was discovered in Bolivia’s Yungas forest and is smaller than the average domestic ⁠cat
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: New species of wild cat was discovered in Bolivia’s Yungas forest and is smaller than the average domestic ⁠cat
Content: Researcher Paola Nogales Ascarrunz observes the cat at an animal refuge in the Yungas region in Bolivia on 1 September 2026.Photograph: Fernando Faciole/National Geographic/ReutersView image in fullscreenResearcher Paola Nogales Ascarrunz observes the cat at an animal refuge in the Yungas region in Bolivia on 1 September 2026.Photograph: Fernando Faciole/National Geographic/ReutersBoliviaNew cat species identified for first time in more than a century in BoliviaNew species of wild feline was discovered in Bolivia’s Yungas forest that is smaller than the average domestic ⁠catReutersThu 17 Sep 2026 16.43 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 18.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia’s ⁠cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living feline species has been formally named and described in more than a century.The cat, called tilcayo by local communities, is part of a group called tiger ⁠cats found across much of South ⁠America. It was found in Bolivia’s ​lush Yungas forest, a mountainous region where forests are often covered by clouds and surrounded by high humidity, according to researchers. It measures about 18in (46cm) long and weighs about 3lb (1.4kg), making it smaller than the average domestic ⁠cat.Researchers used genetic data to confirm that the cat is a new species, and gave it the scientific nameLeopardus tilcayo, retaining its local name.View image in fullscreenALeopardus tilcayocat at the Senda Verde animal refuge in the Yungas region of Bolivia on 1 September 2026.Photograph: Fernando Faciole/National Geographic/Reuters“Its fur is light brown … with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body,” said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer and one of the authors ⁠of the study describing the newly identified species published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology.Little is yet known about the cat’s biology and lifestyle. Remains of small rodents in scat ​samples suggest they may form part of its diet, while camera-trap evidence indicates it ‌could be more active at night, Nogales-Ascarrunz said.Tiger ‌cats are so-called cryptic species, meaning they cannot easily be distinguished merely by appearance, said evolutionary biologist and study co-lead author Jonas Lescroart of the University of Antwerp in Belgium.Tiger ‌cats previously had been considered a single species, but genetic studies decades ago suggested the existence of multiple species.View image in fullscreenA tilcayo cat, the only known individual of the newly identified species living in protective captivity.Photograph: Fernando Faciole/National Geographic/ReutersReferring to the new species, Lescroart said: “Our information at this moment is limited to the two live individuals that we examined, and a small number of camera-trap records.”One of the live cats is a 10-year-old male that now lives in the Senda Verde wildlife sanctuary in Bolivia after being kept by a local family in their home.Observing the Bolivian cat drew interest because “its characteristics did not match the descriptions, most of them based on Brazilian cats”, Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “This made us wonder: what tiger cat do we actually have in Bolivia?”The team analysed DNA from 38 cats sampled across several South ‌American countries, including eight museum specimens. The study found that tiger cats are in fact five genetically distinct species.“We never expected this Bolivian tiger cat to be a separate species, and no one had ever proposed it as a different animal, subspecies or otherwise,” Lescroart said.Genetic analysis suggested ​that the tilcayo lineage separated from other tiger cats about 1.4m years ago.“The more differences in their DNA, the longer the time that we estimate those lineages to have been physically separated,” Lescroart said, adding that such a gap is generally considered a species-level divide in cats.The research team also described a new tiger cat subspecies in Peru’s Yungas region, naming itLeopardus tigrinus antisuyoafter Antisuyu, the region of the old Inca empire that included the area it inhabits.The International Union forConservationof Nature (IUCN) red list tracking the status of species currently treats ⁠tiger cats as two “vulnerable” species with declining populations.The researchers have shared their findings with the IUCN, whose upcoming review will assess ​the five lineages separately. That could give a more accurate picture ​of risk, Lescroart said, and species such as the tilcayo ​could be considered endangered when assessed on their own.The need for a clearer assessment is particularly acute in the Yungas, one of the ​region’s most threatened ecosystems.The mountain forests ‌face growing pressure from deforestation, agricultural ​expansion, human-caused fires and mining, Nogales-Ascarrunz said. ​Restoring forest patches damaged by fires, protecting remaining native forest and maintaining connections between habitats are urgent priorities, she added.“Showing the general public that even in a flagship group such as cats … there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message,” said Eduardo Eizirik, an evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil and senior author of the study. “There are many undiscovered species out there in the world, and they are at risk of disappearing before we even discover them.”Explore more on these topicsBoliviaWildlifeEndangered speciesIUCN red list of endangered speciesPeruBiodiversityConservationnewsShareReuse this content

title: All smiles in Strasbourg but uncertainty clouds Canada’s EU membership plan | European Union | The Guardian
description: Although Mark Carney welcomed offer to become bloc’s first associate member, no one seems to know what that means
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Although Mark Carney welcomed offer to become bloc’s first associate member, no one seems to know what that means
Content: (From left, front) The president of the European parliament, Roberta Metsola, with Mark Carney and Ursula von der Leyen in Strasbourg.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersView image in fullscreen(From left, front) The president of the European parliament, Roberta Metsola, with Mark Carney and Ursula von der Leyen in Strasbourg.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersEuropean UnionAnalysisAll smiles in Strasbourg but uncertainty clouds Canada’s EU membership planJennifer Rankinin BrusselsAlthough Mark Carney welcomed offer to become bloc’s first associate member, no one seems to know what that meansEurope live – latest updatesThu 17 Sep 2026 11.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareMark Carney received a rapturous reception in the European parliament when he gave his speech on Thursday welcoming a proposal for Canada to become the EU’s first-ever associate member.Politicians queued to shake his hand and take selfies. One described the speech as a historic moment. “Europe has extended a hand, and Canada has taken it,” said the German Green MEP Terry Reintke, who borrowed a Canadian ice hockey shirt for the occasion.Mark Carney calls for ‘deep cooperation’ between Canada and EU in Strasbourg speechRead moreOne day earlier, in the same debating chamber, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, issued theunprecedented invitation to Canada– an idea quickly derided by Donald Trump, whothreatened Europe with “heavy tariffs”if it became a reality.But the prospect of Canada’s associate membership is uncertain, not least because no one is sure what it means. “I’m not quite sure why she [von der Leyen] used that term because there’s simply no legal definition,” said one senior politician. “This has just raised lots of questions. So people are talking more about what an associate membership means instead of … this unique partnership and alliance for the future that EU-Canada relations should be about.”The German chancellor Friedrich Merz’s spokesperson welcomed the initiative for a close partnership with Canada and said Germany was “open to discussing new models that reflect the special significance of the relationship”, but called for the associate membership label to be “reconsidered”.0:35Trump calls EU’s offer of associate membership to Canada ‘laughable’ – videoMerz himself has floated “associate membership” for Ukraine, as a stepping stone to joining the bloc, but this was quickly dismissed by other member states.One EU diplomat said von der Leyen “seemed a bit far out in floating this” and that even before Wednesday’s speech member states had worried that she was overpromising on Canada. A second diplomat said it was “an empty phrase” and it would be up to member states to define the substance.Any new trading and cooperation relationship with a foreign country would need to be approved by the EU’s 27 member states.There is a lot of common ground: both sides want to deepen cooperation on AI, energy security, critical raw materials, quantum computing and work together in the Arctic – Carney noted that Canada shared an Arctic border with Denmark, referring to the maritime border with Greenland.But difficulties went unspoken. Carney described the 2016 EU-Canada comprehensive economic and trade agreement as “one of the world’s most successful trade agreements”, but 10 EU member states have yet to ratify it, including France, Italy and Poland. With all three countries heading into an election year, that looks unlikely to change.While both sides extol the virtues of deeper trade between allies, they are also pursuing policies that appear to contradict that goal. Last year Canada introduced a buy Canadian policy, to ensure Canadian suppliers get priority in public contracts. The EU is debating its own buy European law, known formally as the Industrial Accelerator Act. The IAA, now being debated in the EU,would oblige member statesto meet “made in Europe” content requirements when spending public money on green technologies and electric cars.Associate membership also raises questions about integration into the EU’s tightly guarded single market. Carney proposed “seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services”. But the EU has long insisted that the four freedoms of its internal market – free movement of goods, services, labour and capital – are one package that cannot be split and require alignment with EU rules.Now the applause has died down, there are plenty of tricky issues to work out, even for the closest of allies.Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionCanadaMark CarneyUrsula von der LeyenInternational tradeEuropeAmericasanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Fiji declares national HIV emergency as Pacific nation grapples with surge in cases | Fiji | The Guardian
description: Government estimates that one in 60 adults in Fiji now living with HIV, as escalating use of methamphetamine fuels ‘epidemic’
Author: Kate Lamb
Headline: Government estimates that one in 60 adults in Fiji now living with HIV, as escalating use of methamphetamine fuels ‘epidemic’
Content: The Fiji government estimates one in 50 pregnant women has HIV. Home to less than one million people, the Pacific nation is facing one of the sharpest increases in new HIV infections globally.Photograph: Viniana Bau/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Fiji government estimates one in 50 pregnant women has HIV. Home to less than one million people, the Pacific nation is facing one of the sharpest increases in new HIV infections globally.Photograph: Viniana Bau/The GuardianFijiFiji declares national HIV emergency as Pacific nation grapples with surge in casesGovernment estimates that one in 60 adults in Fiji now living with HIV, as escalating use of methamphetamine fuels ‘epidemic’Kate LambWed 16 Sep 2026 21.43 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFiji has declared a national HIV emergency amid a spike in infections as the Pacific nation grapples with a correlating rise in methamphetamine use.The country’s health and medical services minister, Dr Ratu Atonio Lalabalavu, saidin a statementon social media that an outbreak-level response was no longer sufficient to address what he described an “epidemic”.“Today I am formally declaring a national health emergency in Fiji,” he said. “This decision recognises the seriousness of the epidemic and the urgent coordinated response our country now needs.”The health minister said the government estimates that one in every 60 adults in Fiji is now living with HIV.“Five years ago, the estimate was one in 167. In 2025, we recorded 2,060 new HIV diagnoses,” he said, adding that one in 50 pregnant women has HIV.The emergency declaration followed on from a cabinet decision on 9 September and would require a coordinated response, he added.Home to less than one million people, the Pacific nation is facing one of the sharpest increases in new HIV infections globally, according to UNAIDS, which said that new infections spiked 12-fold between 2010 and 2025.13:14Inside the world’s fastest-growing HIV epidemic – videoFiji’s location asa drug-running hubcoupled with the escalating use of methamphetamine locally has fuelled the rapid spread of HIV, a situation worsened by unsafe injecting and a lack of access to clean needles.Low health awareness, cultural stigma and inadequate testingand treatment have exacerbated the crisis.Drugs, denial and stigma: the babies and children swept up in Fiji’s HIV nightmareRead moreAmong HIV cases in Fiji with a known mode of transmission, over half were linked to sexual transmission and more than 42% to injecting drug use, according to UNAIDS.Of an estimated 9,100 people living with HIV in Fiji in 2025, only 39% were aware of their HIV status and only 22% were accessing antiretroviral treatment, the UN said.Responding to the emergency declaration, UNAIDS executive director Winnie Byanyimasaid in a statementon Wednesday that the situation was a “a stark reminder to the world that AIDS is not over”.“HIV epidemics can change quickly, and countries need health and community systems that are ready to respond urgently,” said Byanyima. “Fiji has recognised the urgency of the moment and is stepping up its response.”The UN agency said it welcomed plans to introduce a needle and syringe programme, with legislative amendments expected to go before parliament, as well as efforts to expand prevention, testing and access to treatment.Explore more on these topicsFijiAids and HIVPacific islandsDrugs tradeDrugsSexual healthEpidemicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m genuinely sorry’: Australian Hyrox athlete who soiled herself apologises to China and rivals | Australia sport | The Guardian
description: Joanna Wietrzyk posts that she regrets her decision to keep racing but has decided to forfeit her win in the Beijing race
Author: Martin Farrer
Headline: Joanna Wietrzyk posts that she regrets her decision to keep racing but has decided to forfeit her win in the Beijing race
Content: Joanna Wietrzyk of Australia competes in the Hyrox event in Beijing.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJoanna Wietrzyk of Australia competes in the Hyrox event in Beijing.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesAustralia sport‘I’m genuinely sorry’: Australian Hyrox athlete who soiled herself apologises to China and rivalsJoanna Wietrzyk ‘regrets’ decision to keep racingShe forfeits points from her win in the Beijing raceMartin FarrerThu 17 Sep 2026 14.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 18.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Australian athlete who caused a storm by winning a Hyrox event in China despite soiling herself during the race has apologised to the “people of China” and rival athletes in a statement online.Posting on Instagram, Joanna Wietrzyk offered a “sincere apology” to the “people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the Hyrox organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing”.Footage of Wietrzyk, a world record-holder,went viralafter it showed her competing in – and winning – Saturday’s event with demanding exercises and using communal equipment, despite having faecal matter running down her legs.But she admitted in her post on Thursday night that she should have “stepped off the track” and that there was “more to life than racing”.Hyrox changes rules and apologises for allowing Australian athlete who soiled herself to continueRead more“I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness,” Wietrzyk wrote.“Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognise that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused.”She said she would forfeit the points from winning the event.“I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected. I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away. On reflection, I have decided to retroactively withdraw from the race and forfeit the points I earned.”Hyrox, an increasingly popular fitness competition launched in Germany in 2017, is now held in locations across the world. It made its debut in mainland China in late 2024.In each race, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises at shared high-intensity stations – including a rowing machine, sled pushes, burpee jumps, medicine ball throws and lunges while carrying a sandbag.Hyrox earlier this week apologised and pledged immediate rule changes after Wietrzyk was allowed to finish and win the Beijing event.Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste apologised in astatementon Instagram to everyone affected “directly or indirectly”.“Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race. In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents – and I did not,” Fürste said.He added that Hyrox had made “rulebook changes immediately”.“As of this moment, there are new rules and procedures in place to prevent situations like this from happening again.”Before the weekend’s incident, event rules penalised athletes for minor infractions such as littering on the course, or spitting or clearing their nose on the floor. But they contained no immediate protocol for faecal matter.Ending her Thursday statement, Wietrzyk said: “Thank you to those standing by me, both as an athlete and as a person, during this time, and to everyone who has reached out with kindness and support. It means more to me than I can properly express right now. I will be taking some time to recover, reflect and look after myself and my family away from the noise.”Explore more on these topicsAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Amid claims of ‘mass migration’, Labor hopes a measured approach will take the hot air out of the debate | Australia news | The Guardian
description: The country’s migration settings have become a source of discontent – but will Tony Burke’s approach be seen as the right mix?
Author: Patrick Commins
Headline: The country’s migration settings have become a source of discontent – but will Tony Burke’s approach be seen as the right mix?
Content: With business groups already suffering from skills shortages even with high immigration, Tony Burke articulated why he believed Labor can win the argument against those competing to announce the lowest targeted Nom.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenWith business groups already suffering from skills shortages even with high immigration, Tony Burke articulated why he believed Labor can win the argument against those competing to announce the lowest targeted Nom.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPAustralia newsAnalysisAmid claims of ‘mass migration’, Labor hopes a measured approach will take the hot air out of the debatePatrick ComminsThe country’s migration settings have become a source of discontent – but will Tony Burke’s approach be seen as the right mix?Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastThu 17 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 20.24 EDTShareTony Burke has promised to make Labor’s existing migration policy work better rather than announcing a dramatic cut in numbers, arguing that populist promises to slash net overseas migration will “trash Australian services and trash the Australian economy”.The home affairs minister’s message was immediately endorsed by employer groups, who over recent days have made it clear that steps to arbitrarily slash migrant numbers would compound already severe skills shortages and hurt businesses, especially those in the regions.“We need immigration. We just need to make sure that it is targeted for the needs of Australia in numbers and across the different categories that work for our economy,” Burke said in his long-awaited address to the National Press Club on Thursday.“We talk about the need for extra housing. It’s pretty hard to get a house built without having a plasterer involved. In both Sydney and Melbourne, close to two-thirds of the plasterers we have were born overseas.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailBran Black, the chief executive of the Business Council in Australia, welcomed thegovernment’s effortsto “restore integrity to the migration system”, even as he argued against new rules that would limit the length of stay for most backpackers.“The starting point for migration policy should not be a number to cut to, but what our economy genuinely needs,” Black said.“Almost one in three occupations in this country are short of workers right now. That translates to not enough workers building homes, caring for us in hospitals and aged care homes, delivering infrastructure and powering the energy transition. That is the challenge that any migration policy should be looking to solve.”Labor has taken a long time to come up with its policy prescription to fix the country’s migration settings which, after the post-pandemic surge in new arrivals, have become a source of growing popular discontent.Spurious claims of “mass migration” have fanned the flames of this discontent, but few would argue that our system is working well and in the best interests of the country – or in the best interests of a ballooning number of people trapped in a kind of temporary visa limbo that has strained public infrastructure and patience.Backpacker ballot and detention centre for visa overstayers: what we know about Australia’s new migration planRead moreAlan Gamlen, the director of the Australian National University’s migration hub, said Burke appeared to have announced the right mix of measures that would give the government the capacity to regulate an out-of-control temporary visa system without damaging the economy.“They don’t seem to have fallen into the trap of chasing a net migration number,” Gamlen said.“Burke made it pretty clear, and in a convincing way, that this is the result of a well-considered process that has been going on for a while and which addresses long-term structural issues, rather than just a kneejerk response to One Nation.”One Nation has committed to lowering net overseas migration (Nom) to 130,000 a year, and the Coalition somewhere between 150,000 and 170,000.In comparison, Burke stuck to the government’s forecast of 225,000 people by 2027-28.He did, however, acknowledge that there was now a public expectation that the government would pull the levers necessary to get there.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Net overseas migration has been viewed as a budget forecast. Last couple of years, people have talked about it as a budget target,” he said.“That is a very different way of looking at it. But given that we have the challenges we have with housing in Australia at the moment, I do think we need to be able to have these additional tools to make sure that what is published and forecast is reached.”With business groups already suffering from skills shortages even at a time of high immigration, the home affairs minister articulated why he believed the government can win the political argument against those competing to announce the lowest targeted Nom.“The lower [Nom] levels will trash Australian services and trash the Australian economy,” he said.Burke pointed out that denying skilled foreign workers the opportunity to bring in family members – as proposed by One Nation – would not free up more visas for more workers.Instead, that approach would slash the number of foreign doctors, tradies, nurses and aged care workers willing to come to our country.“The proportion of doctors who come to Australia with family attached to their application? 50%. How many construction workers come with family attached to their application? 50%. How many nurses and aged care workers come with family attached to their application? Two-thirds.”Whether Burke and the Albanese government can convince the public its measured approach is enough is an open question.“Let’s see if this lets out some of the hot air in the migration debate,” Gamlen said.Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsAustralian immigration and asylumTony BurkeBusiness (Australia news)Australian economyanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Tony Burke rejects farmers’ claims that immigration changes will increase food prices | Australian immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Farming lobby says shoppers will see emptier shelves and higher prices because of restrictions on backpackers
Author: Tom McIlroy
Headline: Farming lobby says shoppers will see emptier shelves and higher prices because of restrictions on backpackers
Content: The farming lobby says supermarkets could run out of food due to a lack of workers to pick produce.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe farming lobby says supermarkets could run out of food due to a lack of workers to pick produce.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersAustralian immigration and asylumTony Burke rejects farmers’ claims that immigration changes will increase food pricesFarming lobby says shoppers will see emptier shelves and higher prices because of restrictions on backpackersFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastTom McIlroyandLuca IttimaniThu 17 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 17.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe farming lobby’s claim that immigration rule changes will increase food prices for households is wrong,Tony Burkehas said, describing moves to speed up processing of backpacker visas as a positive step for agriculture.Burke revealedLabor’s long-awaited reformsat the National Press Club on Thursday, flagging that the plan was more limited than the government would like, due to a lack of support for wider legislation from the Coalition.But the package has received mixed reviews, with business groups and the Coalition saying it did not do enough to lower net overseas migration levels, while refugee advocates said it showed migrants remained “political punching bags”.The National Farmers’ Federation’s chief executive, Mike Guerin, said farmers would see an immediate economic impact from restrictions on working holidaymakers and other temporary migrants. He warned producers were already struggling to get workers for the harvesting season.Backpacker ballot and detention centre for visa overstayers: what we know about Australia’s new migration planRead moreBackpackers seeking to stay in Australia for more than a year will be subject to a new ballot, with places severely restricted for years two and three.“We will see a lift in the price of food,” Guerin said.“We will see emptier supermarkets ... And while it’s yet to play out directly for consumers, for people in the cities, it’s very close. We will not be able to finish the harvest this year, before Christmas.”But Burke told Guardian Australia the plan was carefully formulated, reducing demand driven settings and giving the government great control, while not damaging the economy.He said healthcare, construction and aged care all relied on overseas workers, and broader cuts would hurt essential services.“The economic contribution matters in terms of services that people rely on.“The announcement we made today is about getting the processing moving again for those backpacker visas that have an obligation, if you want the extra years, to work in the regions. That’s a significant advantage … the department getting moving on the processing of those again at a faster pace.”Burke said the agriculture sector could utilise workers from the Pacific Australia labour mobility scheme, and producers had legal responsibilities to pay staff adequately.“I don’t think consumers believe their pathway to paying less should rely on worker exploitation.”View image in fullscreenTony Burke says the changes are not like hardline immigration enforcement in other countries.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPThe government’s changes include new compliance measures to deal with people overstaying their visa, but Burke said enforcement would be measured and sensible.About 100 new additional compliance officers will be added, along with 250 additional beds in immigration detention.Burke said the changes were not like hardline immigration enforcement in countries overseas, such as the approach used byDonald Trump’s administration.But the Asylum Seeker Resource Centre said the planned increase in enforcement would leave Australia “smaller, meaner and more divided”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“How much of its soul is theLabor partyprepared to sacrifice chasing people who will never be satisfied,” founder Kon Karapanagiotidis said.The Greens deputy leader, Mehreen Faruqi, criticised the increased immigration detention and bar on foreign students bringing family members to Australia.“Labor’s move to force people to choose between their family and a chance to study in Australia is soulless mimicry ofOne Nation tactics,” Faruqi said.“Pauline Hanson and her billionaire backers might as well be ghostwriting Labor’s immigration policy.”Major employers welcomed the reforms, with the Minerals Council of Australia praising the government’s prioritisation of mining workers.Big business lobby group the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry said the government had avoided a damaging overcorrection and the plan would help rebuild public confidence. But its CEO, Andrew McKellar, warned its execution via ministerial directives meant policy was being held together by “the stroke of a pen”.The Nationals’ leader, Matt Canavan, accused the government of using farmers and regional industries as “whipping boys for their failure to bring down migration”.Cuts to the working holidaymaker program would lead to staff shortages, the Australian Restaurant and Cafe Association chief, Wes Lambert, warned.“A chef, cook or hospitality manager filling a genuine shortage is valuable too,” Lambert said.“Australia absolutely needs a sustainable migration system. But migration policy cannot simply be a numbers exercise. It must recognise where the workers are actually needed.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian immigration and asylumTony BurkeAustralian politicsLabor partynewsShareReuse this content

title: Albanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildings  | Wearable technology | The Guardian
description: Minister for public service says the devices pose ‘legitimate privacy and security concerns’ in commonwealth-run workplaces
Author: Luca Ittimani
Headline: Minister for public service says the devices pose ‘legitimate privacy and security concerns’ in commonwealth-run workplaces
Content: Meta smart glasses. Schools and hospitals run by state governments will be left to set their own rules over the technology.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreenMeta smart glasses. Schools and hospitals run by state governments will be left to set their own rules over the technology.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersWearable technologyAlbanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildingsMinister for public service says the devices pose ‘legitimate privacy and security concerns’ in commonwealth-run workplacesFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastLuca IttimaniThu 17 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 17.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Albanese government is considering a “world-leading”ban on smart glasses in its offices and service centres as councils around Australia push the technology out of public spaces over privacy fears.The government has avoided a sweeping ban on the import of the camera-equipped technology and encouraged individual workplaces to set their own rules.The public service minister, Katy Gallagher, said on Thursday she had asked the Australian public service for advice on whether the glasses should be prohibited.“We need clear and consistent guidance for public servants,” Gallagher said.“Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information.”Commonwealth-run workplaces range from bureaucrats’ offices to Centrelink service centres and CSIRO laboratories.Smartglasses should automatically blur people’s faces while filming, Australia’s online safety regulator saysRead moreSchools and hospitals run by state governments would be left to set their own rules over the technology, which have grown increasingly popular but raised public outcry.A University of Sydney study of smart glasses-filmed videos posted on Instagram found 60% of a sample could beclassified as potential harassment.The Albanese government said it was seeking to set a world-leading standard. So far, no national government has banned the glasses’ use across their agencies.Courts inEngland and Walesin the UK andNew York state inthe US have banned the technology, while the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency reportedlyclassified them as body-worn camerasand barred them from the “federal workspace”.A local council in Sydneyon Tuesdaybecame the latest to issue a targeted bans on the use of the technology. Canterbury-Bankstown’s mayor, Bilal El-Hayek, decried what he called“pervert glasses”as the council barred the wearable tech from public pools.In August, Brisbane city council became the first to ban the glasses from pools and Melbourne’s Yarra city council has banned them from playgrounds, childcare centres and gyms.The City of Sydney and the Blacktown city councils have prohibited pool patrons from using smart glasses to record.Speaking to Channel Seven earlier this month, the federal attorney general,Michelle Rowland, praised councils’ decisionsand said she would consult businesses on their approach.“Businesses know that good privacy is good business,” Rowland said.“But … we want to make sure we get the balance right and we don’t unfairly discriminate against people who are using this technology to better participate in society.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionVision Australia and some people living with disabilities have praised the technology as a support for people who are blind or have low vision. Rowland said the government was not pursuing a ban but had not “ruled anything out”.8:34Could Meta’s ‘pervert glasses’ be banned across the UK? - The LatestGallagher said she wanted the Australian public service to set the national standard as a “model employer”.“Technology is changing rapidly and as a major employer the Commonwealth needs to make sure our workplace policies keep pace,” Gallagher said.Pending restrictions on smart glasses would be the federal government’s latest workplace technology reform after it issued guidance on the use of AI in the public service last week.The guidelines indicate employees would not need to be consulted on every new tool but should be consulted for major initiatives or changes to how they carry out work.Major businesses will contribute to new national guidelines on AI in workplaces, with Commonwealth Bank, Microsoft, AGL, Telstra, Kmart, Blackmores Group and Ramsay Health Care to attend a roundtable on Friday.Amanda Rishworth, the employment minister, said the government wanted to use the roundtable to take on the lessons of businesses already using AI.“Workers and businesses need the capability to adopt new technologies with confidence that appropriate safeguards are in place,” Rishworth said.Additional reporting from Caitlin CassidyExplore more on these topicsWearable technologyAustralian politicsMetaLabor partyAnthony AlbanesenewsShareReuse this content

title: Ireland to boycott Eurovision again over Israeli participation and ongoing Gaza deaths | Eurovision | The Guardian
description: Ireland joins joins Dutch broadcaster in refusing to take part in 2027 song contest, in second consecutive year of protests
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Ireland joins joins Dutch broadcaster in refusing to take part in 2027 song contest, in second consecutive year of protests
Content: The Palestinian flag during a protest outside the main gate of the Irish national broadcaster RTÉ in Dublin last year.Photograph: Zuma Press, Inc./Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenThe Palestinian flag during a protest outside the main gate of the Irish national broadcaster RTÉ in Dublin last year.Photograph: Zuma Press, Inc./Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.EurovisionIreland to boycott Eurovision again over Israeli participation and ongoing Gaza deathsIreland joins joins Dutch broadcaster in refusing to take part in 2027 song contest, in second consecutive year of protestsLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentThu 17 Sep 2026 13.32 EDTFirst published on Thu 17 Sep 2026 09.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIreland is to boycottEurovisionfor the second year running over the “appalling” ongoing killing in Gaza, the national broadcaster has said.Ireland wasone of five countries, along with Iceland, the Netherlands, Spain and Slovenia, that refused to take part in the competition this year in protest against Israel’s participation.RTÉ announced on Thursday it would not participate in the 2027 competition. The Dutch broadcaster Avrotrosannounced its own boycottlast month, calling Eurovision a “platform for division”.In a statement, the Irish broadcaster said: “RTÉ feels that Ireland’s participation cannot be justified given ‌the appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis there, which continues to put the lives of so many civilians at risk.”Next year’s Eurovision is to be held in the Bulgarian Black Sea city of Burgas, after the country won for the first time in May.View image in fullscreenNorwegian singer Emmy representing Ireland in the 2025 Eurovision at the St Jakobshalle arena in Basel, Switzerland.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesAvrotros said it would not take part, claiming the competition “can no longer be considered neutral, with a participating country still involved in a large-scale military conflict”.The European Broadcasting Union (EBU), which organises the event, is in talks with other Dutch broadcasters, hoping one of the country’s other public service TV stations will participate.Eurovision’s director, Martin Green, said he regretted but respected RTÉ’s decision. “They remain a valued part of our family and will be missed,” he said.“That power to bring people together is at the heart of what makes the contest so special and is even more important now in an increasingly difficult and divided world,” he added.“All broadcasters decide on an annual basis to participate in the following year’s contest. We will remain in dialogue with RTÉ and hope to welcome them back to the contest in the future.”The EBU has tried twice to address broadcasters’ concerns over the participation ofIsrael.Last year, itreduced the number of votesthat could be entered online or by telephone by one individual, amid allegations Israel had mounted a disproportionate campaign for public votes.Last month, the EBU announced that broadcasters would no longer be eligible to host the Eurovision song contest if their state wasinvolved in an “armed conflict”or in a “sensitive geopolitical situation”.Eurovision has faced protests in and outside the competition venues in recent years over the participation of Israel, a competitor since 1973.In 2024, the European Commission madean unusual interventionafter the organisers banned audience members from waving the EU flag at the grand final in Sweden, describing the decision as “mind-blowing” and “regrettable”.Palestinian authorities report that more than 73,000 people have been killed in ​Israel’s war onGaza, ‌which was launched ​after Hamas-led fighters killed 1,200 ​people in an attack on southern Israel in October 2023.A US-brokered ceasefire agreed last year calls for eventual reconstruction of the territory but Israeli strikes have continued. According to Gaza’s health ministry, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the fragile ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025.Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsEurovisionIrelandIsraelGazaPalestineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Poland warns Russia planning ‘hybrid strikes’ against countries supporting Ukraine – as it happened | World news | The Guardian
description: Donald Tusk says ‘very consistent and convincing’ intelligence assessment point towards Russian plans for strikes
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Donald Tusk says ‘very consistent and convincing’ intelligence assessment point towards Russian plans for strikes
Content: 11.23 EDTIntelligence shows Russian 'plans for hybrid strikes ... against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland,' Tusk saysTusk says that intelligence assessments show “plans for hybrid strikes using drones and missiles against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland”.He says the latest intelligence on this is “very consistent and convincing”.He says thatRussia is expected to pretend that any incidents are “accidental” in a bid to “paralyse or at least weaken Nato’s resolveto invoke the relevant provisions” of the Nato treaty.“There is a real risk that drones or other types of projectiles could be launched into the territory of one or more Nato countries on the eastern flank, and could even cause damage, andthe official narrative will be that this is an accident and that there is no reason for anyone to consider any response from Nato.The aim … will be to weaken Nato’s integrity in general and, above all, to convince … member states that Article 5 is more theoretical than practical– that is, the assumption that no one will want to die for Latvia or Lithuania, given that we are dealing with incidents rather than a declaration of war.”He says he expects Russia to use “recurrent” incidents to use them as “an increasingly stark illustration of Nato’s helplessness” to respond in a united manner.ShareUpdated at11.30 EDT

title: Sweden’s PM resigns after centre-left bloc wins slim majority in election | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Ulf Kristersson has stood down from his post, paving way for Social Democrats leader to form a government
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Ulf Kristersson has stood down from his post, paving way for Social Democrats leader to form a government
Content: Ulf Kristersson has stood down as prime minister after four years.Photograph: János Kummer/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUlf Kristersson has stood down as prime minister after four years.Photograph: János Kummer/Getty ImagesSwedenSweden’s PM resigns after centre-left bloc wins slim majority in electionUlf Kristersson has stood down from his post, paving way for Social Democrats leader to form a governmentMiranda BryantNordic correspondentThu 17 Sep 2026 11.28 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSweden’s centre-right prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, has stood down, clearing the way for Magdalena Andersson, the Social Democrats leader, to attempt to form a government.In a victory speech on Thursday, Andersson said the Swedish people had “voted for a new direction for our country, voted for unity and against division”.She added: “The Swedish people have voted to takeSwedenforward and I will realise the new direction that you have voted for.”Among the priorities she named were the climate crisis, schools, healthcare, elderly care and immigration policy.Andersson spoke as the preliminary count for Sunday’s election was finally completed, with 176 seats for the left-leaning opposition parties – a narrow three-seat majority over the right-leaning ruling Tidö coalition supported by the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD). There were 50,359 votes between the two blocs.Earlier on Thursday, Andersson, who was Kristersson’s predecessor as prime minister, sent an invitation to the other left-leaning parties – Left, Centre and Green – for initial coalition talks.Soon after, Kristersson, the Moderates leader, announced his resignation after four years as prime minister.Before the election, some had feared that the vote would mark a turning point for the far right after Kristersson promised key ministerial posts for the SD if his coalition took power. Instead, the SD lost support for the first time in a general election since its foundation, falling from Sweden’s second biggest party to third.In his resignation letter, Kristersson wrote: “Now it is the speaker who will lead the next steps towards forming a new government. In order for that work to begin immediately, I hereby request to be relieved of my duties as prime minister.”The speaker, Andreas Norlén, will now start working on proposals for a new prime minister after talks with representatives of each of the parties.View image in fullscreenMagdalena Andersson claps on stage as the general election results are released in Stockholm, Sweden.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersFour celebration cakes decorated with red roses were brought into the Social Democrats’ headquarters amid cheers from inside.The result will be a considerable relief among Social Democrats, who remain Sweden’s biggest party but received record low support. However, the result marks only the beginning for Andersson of what is expected to be weeks of complicated coalition talks.One of the trickiest negotiations is expected to be between the Centre and Left parties. The Centre party has ruled out being in government with the Left, while the Left has demanded a place in government in return for its cooperation.Other difficult areas are expected to be the Left’s support for a billionaire tax, the Green party’s opposition to nuclear energy and differences of opinion on taxation. The Greens, Social Democrats and the Left are all in favour of tax increases, but the Centre party wants to cut taxes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSweden voted against more power for the far right – but are centrists listening?Read moreNooshi Dadgostar, the leader of the Left party, said: “The Swedish people have voted away Tidö and given us a clear mandate for change.” She added: “This is one of the proudest days of my life.”Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist, the Centre party leader, thanked Kristersson for his work as prime minister but said Sweden was now “entering a new political phase”. She added: “The Centre party will be a constructive force for Sweden to have a functioning government, with policies anchored in the middle.”Andersson, who was prime minister between November 2021 and October 2022, is understood to be reaching out to all the opposition parties, with the exception of the SD. The Liberals and the Christian Democrats have ruled out working with the left, but in his resignation letter Kristersson appeared to leave the door open. However, given Swedish tradition, it is extremely unlikely the Moderates and the Social Democrats would form a coalition.Kristersson wrote that the election had left a “complicated situation” for building a government and called for “constructive openness” from all parties to find a way to form a stable government.In the nervous days since the election, the Social Democrats are understood to have been using the time to prepare for coalition negotiations, where they are understood to be seeking broad cooperation with one or multiple parties.Minority-run governments are common within Swedish politics and it is commonplace for governments to form agreements outside of coalitions. In the last government, the SD were not officially in government, but they held considerable sway over the budget and policies.The Social Democrats are understood to be planning to prioritise making changes to the immigration, integration and climate policies of the last government. But with their policies having moved to the right in recent years, particularly on immigration and crime, much of the legacy of the previous government is likely to remain.Explore more on these topicsSwedenEuropeThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jürgen Klopp wants his Germany team to reclaim national pride from ‘the wrong people’ | Germany | The Guardian
description: Jürgen Klopp has said Germany’s football team can help ensure ‘national pride is not entrusted to the wrong people’ after a recent far-right AfD election victory
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Jürgen Klopp has said Germany’s football team can help ensure ‘national pride is not entrusted to the wrong people’ after a recent far-right AfD election victory
Content: Jürgen Klopp has named a 44-player squad for his first four matches as Germany’s manager.Photograph: Christopher Neundorf/EPAView image in fullscreenJürgen Klopp has named a 44-player squad for his first four matches as Germany’s manager.Photograph: Christopher Neundorf/EPAGermanyJürgen Klopp wants his Germany team to reclaim national pride from ‘the wrong people’Comments follow far-right election win in Saxony-Anhalt‘I’d like to reclaim the flag for myself and for us,’ he saysAgenciesThu 17 Sep 2026 06.42 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJürgen Klopp has said Germany’s football team can help ensure “national pride is not entrusted to the wrong people” after a recentfar-right AfD election victory.In a Frankfurt press conference announcing his firstGermanysquad, the former Liverpool manager referenced a recent state election win by the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany party.‘My scar, not your scar’: Tuchel stands by England semi-final subs but admits wrong timingRead moreThe AfD won almost44% of the vote in the former East German state of Saxony-Anhalton 6 September and expects strong results in elections on Sunday in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.Klopp took the Germany job in July after the four-time World Cup winners experienced a third straight early elimination at the tournament. The 59-year-old has oftenspoken out about social issuesduring his time as manager of Liverpool, Borussia Dortmund and Mainz.While not mentioning the AfD by name, Klopp advocated for adopting “positive patriotism”, while saying: “I don’t want to entrust national pride to the wrong people. A crazy amount of things have happened not that long ago. There was a vote which some people probably found OK, but others would have thought: ‘Good heavens, what’s going on here?’“From the perspective of someone in sport, I’d like to reclaim the flag for myself and for us. When we wave it, I don’t want that someone thinks: ‘What’s going on with you?’ I want that they think you’re happy and you understand how lucky you are to be born in this wonderful country or to have moved here and live here.”Speaking of national pride, Klopp said he was “not even sure if one can – or is allowed to – use that term any more without it being misunderstood”. He said: “I can be proud of being German and still be open, diverse, kind and friendly.”Klopp said it was more important that the country had enough doctors and caregivers but said football can “foster a sense of community here, allowing us to truly feel the power of sport”.He took the unusual step of naming a 44-man squad for four upcoming Nations League matches, despite matchday lists being restricted to 23 players. “It’s very unusual that you’ve got four games in two weeks with the national team,” Klopp said. “I want to get to know as many players as possible in that time.”Germany start away to the Netherlands, then play Greece home and away either side of hosting Serbia.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFlorian Wirtz and Kai Havertz will probably be limited to a maximum of two of the games as Klopp looks to fit in more new faces and reduce the workload on players. Karim Adeyemi returns for the first time in 11 months after a positive start at Barcelona and Ajax’s Marc-André ter Stegen is the first-choice goalkeeper after Manuel Neuer’s international retirement.View image in fullscreenElversberg’s Felix Keidel is among the players called up to Germany’s squad for the first time.Photograph: David Inderlied/DPA/APMany of the players called up have never played for Germany. Some, such as the Elversberg midfielder Felix Keidel and the Eintracht Frankfurt forward Younes Ebnoutalib, have played a handful of top-division games. Celtic’s Mika Baur, Brentford’s Vitaly Janelt and the Cologne youngster Said El Mala are among more new faces.The striker Deniz Undav and winger Leroy Sané were not selected.Explore more on these topicsGermanyJürgen KloppAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)EuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran school bombing: grounds to believe US was behind atrocity, UN finds | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Fact-finding mission says military strikes on school in Minab and sports facility in ⁠February constitute war ⁠crimes
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Fact-finding mission says military strikes on school in Minab and sports facility in ⁠February constitute war ⁠crimes
Content: A man who lost his son in the school strike in February at the site of the atrocity in Minab, Iran, in August.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersView image in fullscreenA man who lost his son in the school strike in February at the site of the atrocity in Minab, Iran, in August.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersUS-Israel war on IranIran school bombing: grounds to believe US was behind atrocity, UN findsFact-finding mission says military strikes on school and sports facility in ⁠February constitute war ⁠crimesPeter Beaumontand agenciesThu 17 Sep 2026 09.22 EDTFirst published on Thu 17 Sep 2026 05.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA UN fact-finding mission has determined there are reasonable grounds to believe the US was behind military strikes on a school and a sports facility inIranin ⁠February that killed 120 children, and that these constituted war ⁠crimes.The school strike, which killed 156 civilians including 120 children, involved a US Tomahawk missile that collapsed the roof of the Shajareh Tayyebehprimary school, which the UN said was “clearly identifiable”, in Minab, Hormozgan province, on 28 February.The Pentagon’s own secretive investigation into the incident is understood to have concluded several months ago. There have been reports that senior US commanders had been warned that targeting data used during the war – including for the Minab strike – was dangerously outdated.The second cited strike, on the same date, targeted a “clearly identifiable sports complex and residential area” in the southern city of Lamerd with a weapon that scattered tungsten pellets.The UN fact-finding team said in a statement: “Following the United States and Israeli attacks on 28 February, the mission found reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed the war crime of launching indiscriminate attacks resulting in the loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects.”The mission also found Iranian ​authorities had committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests.The findings by the independent international fact-finding mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN human rights council in Geneva, examined the ⁠US’s conduct during the Iran war that began in February and the Iranian government’s response tonationwide unrest that began in late December.US officials have previously said military ⁠operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations.The UN mission concluded that the strike on Shajareh Tayyebeh primary school constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to ‌civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law.View image in fullscreenA rubble-strewn classroom at Shajareh Tayyebeh school.Photograph: Vahid Salemi/APAccording to the report, the US relied on intelligence suggesting a senior Iranian military commander was present at the site but failed to adequately verify the information before launching the strike.Investigators said the failure to update targeting intelligence and confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence.“Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen.”In June the US president, Donald Trump, said ‌“nobody” had purposely attacked a girls’ school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident. The Pentagon has since elevated ​the inquiry, but it has not published any preliminary findings.Four months after the horrific Iran school bombing, fears grow that Trump and Hegseth will bury the truthRead moreUN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found no evidence it was being used for military purposes.The experts reached a similar conclusion over the strike on the sports centre in Lamerd. The report said the attack had damaged nearby residential buildings and a school and killed and injured 22 civilians. It concluded that the strike had been indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.US Central Command said in a statement in March that ⁠US forces had not launched any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day.The UN mission also found ​that the Iranian authorities had carried out a widespread and systematic ​attack against civilians duringprotests that eruptedin late ​December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.Rights groups say bystanders were among ​those killed during the biggest crackdown ‌since Shia Muslim clerics took ​power in the 1979 revolution. Tehran blamed “terrorists ​and rioters” backed by exiled opponents and the US and Israel.The investigation said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the number of dead and injured was probably far higher than official figures, which say 3,038 people were killed and 25,000 people injured.The government’s response to the protests, including violence and killings, cutting off the internet and use of the death penalty, marked a significant escalation from previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranIranMiddle East and north AfricaUS militaryUnited NationsWar crimesUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Thursday briefing: Yemen’s war continues to threaten oil supplies– but what about its people? | Yemen | The Guardian
description: In today’s newsletter: The Houthi advance along the Red Sea coast raised fears for global trade and energy supplies, while more than 100,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the fighting
Author: Libby Brooks
Headline: In today’s newsletter: The Houthi advance along the Red Sea coast raised fears for global trade and energy supplies, while more than 100,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the fighting
Content: The latest escalation has displaced at least 100,000 people in Yemen, adding to a humanitarian crisis that has already lasted a decade.Photograph: Eunavfor Aspides Handout/EPAView image in fullscreenThe latest escalation has displaced at least 100,000 people in Yemen, adding to a humanitarian crisis that has already lasted a decade.Photograph: Eunavfor Aspides Handout/EPAFirst Edition newsletterYemenThursday briefing: Yemen’s war continues to threaten oil supplies– but what about its people?In today’s newsletter: The Houthi advance along the Red Sea coast raised fears for global trade and energy supplies, while more than 100,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the fightingLibby BrooksThu 17 Sep 2026 01.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 01.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGood morning. The lightning advance of Houthi militants along the west coast ofYemenover the past week has prompted fears of a spiralling conflict in the region and a new oil supply crisis.For families living in the Middle East’s poorest country, the most significant fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces in years is a crisis upon a catastrophe, with escalating civilian casualties and at least100,000 displacedin recent days.Houthi fighters have captured strategic islands across a critical Red Sea trade route, the Bab al-Mandab strait, one of the most important shipping routes in the world – almost15% of global sea tradepasses through it. The strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas transited in peacetime, has remained largely blocked since the US and Israel launched airstrikes in February, so the prospect of Iran and its allies exerting pressure on two maritime choke points has global implications. The price of crude oil hasalready begun to spike.For today’s newsletter,I spoke toFareaAl-Muslimi, a research fellow at Chatham House, about this new and dangerous dimension to the ongoing war in Yemen, and why fears over oil and global trade must not overshadow the plight of ordinary Yemenis. First, this morning’s headlines.Five big storiesUK politics| Key allies of Andy Burnham have warned the prime minister not to back down over his promises to put water companies under public control,after details emergedabout the prime minister’s plan to give mayors more oversight of the industry.Environment| Climate breakdownprobably weakened the glacierthat collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing hundreds of people in Nepal and Tibet last month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found.Health| Women with the same medical condition as men are less likely to be offered treatment such as surgery, a stent or a strong painkiller,research has found.Europe| The UK government’s EU reset summitwill be delayed againunless the bloc agrees to discuss legislation that could lock British business out of parts of EU industry, government sources have said.UK news| Police searching for a three-year-old boy who went missing from a playground on the Suffolk-Essex borderhave found a body.In depth: The fight for Yemen’s Red Sea coastView image in fullscreenYemen refugees arrive in Djibouti as intensified fighting drives displacement.Photograph: International Organization for Migration/ReutersThe current escalation of violence in Yemen has its roots in a civil war that broke out in 2014 between the Yemeni army and the Houthi movement, which champions Yemen’s Shia Muslim minority. A year later, theHouthis– part of Iran’s “axis of resistance”, a loose coalition of armed groups that includes Hamas and Hezbollah – toppled the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.Al-Muslimi grew up in a remote mountain village in Yemen, where his family made honey, one of the country’s most lucrative and popular exports. His mother used to tease him because the bees didn’t recognise him after he spent long periods studying away from home – he was the only person in his family who had to wear a beekeeping suit.Al-Musliminow writesabout how the years-long internecine conflict has had a devastating impact on the honey trade and the farmers who tend Yemeni bees. At least 150,000 people have been killed since 2014, mainly through aerial bombardment by the Saudi-backed coalition that supports the Yemeni government, which has resumed this week. About 4.5 million people – the population of Birmingham and Greater Manchester combined – have already been displaced by fighting over the past decade, while the UN estimates thatmore than 18.2 million– twice the population of London – are in dire need of humanitarian assistance.The situation now is “worse than 2015”, says Al-Muslimi, with global attention diverted to crises in Syria, Sudan, and Ukraine and now focused on oil prices and regional consequences. “There is even less willingness to help civilians.”After the Houthiscaptured the port cityof Mocha, birthplace of the global coffee trade, last week, Al-Muslimi heard local media reports of more than 240 pregnant women ready to give birth without accessible healthcare.“It’s absolutely nuts,” he says. “This is a country that was already suffering so many things, including indifference.”How has the conflict escalated in the past week?It has been plain for months to Yemen-watchers that the Houthis were preparing for a significant offensive, says al-Muslimi. This erupted about a week ago with the militants seizing control of parts of the west coast and gaining a hold over the Bab al-Mandab strait, including the strategic port of Mocha and key islands of Perim, Greater and Lesser Hanish in the 20-mile stretch of water that forms a natural chokepoint on the trade route connecting Asia with Europe.With government supporters in disarray, the degree of division among anti-Houthi forces is complicating the fight back. The Houthis have achieved what Al-Muslimi calls “the most consequential change in territorial control in Yemen for years”.Since then, the Houthis have claimed responsibility for missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, including the bombing of a critical east-west oil pipeline. On Wednesday a military spokesperson for the Houthisdenied attempting to fly a droneclose to the holy city of Mecca, and claimed that Saudi Arabia has carried out as many as 450 airstrikes in Yemen ‌this week in retaliation. The ongoing aggression is driving fears that more Muslim nations could be drawn into the conflict.What does it mean for global oil supply?If ​the Houthis were to close the Bab al-Mandab strait, vessels would be forced to reroute all the way around the southern tip of Africa. The consequences for the global economy could be dire, particularly when taken along with the ongoing blockade of Hormuz.With Iran and its Houthi allies controlling potentially a third of energy trade globally, “it’s more dangerous than a nuclear bomb,” says Al-Muslimi bluntly, “especially at a time when the world still depends massively on this type of energy”.Attacks on Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline – which is now closed for repairs and has been crucial for moving oil from the strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea export hub of Yanbu – will add further pressure to global supplies.Al-Muslimi advises caution over Houthi claims that they don’t intend to impose transit fees on vessels passing through Bab al-Mandab. The UN security councilhas seen evidencethat, since the militants started attacks on Red Sea shipping in 2023, in response to Israel’s decimation of Gaza, the Houthis have been extracting informal payments from some shipping agencies in return for safe passage.Meanwhile, Saudi anger with Iran for assisting Houthi attacks saw thecancellation of a meetingwith Gulf states about the future of the strait of Hormuz on Monday. Reports in the early hours today that Saudi Arabia may be offering more crude cargoes through Oman saw the price of Brent crude drop to $104.59 a barrel after hitting $108 earlier this week. But for perspective, it was trading at $80 a barrel in early July.This comes as the average price of diesel in the US hit$6 per gallonfor the first time last week, with theIran war, combined with Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, continuing to squeeze supply.What does it mean for the region?The UN security council held an emergency meeting in New York on Tuesday to discuss the escalating violence in Yemen and threats to maritime security, with members urging maximum restraint to avoid the situation devolving into a wider regional war. The conflict is the first test of a mutual defence pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, announced in August – but Saudi has yet to publicly call on either for assistance.Meanwhile, Al-Muslimi says the US, a close Saudi ally, faces a dilemma. The States reached a truce with the Houthis in May 2025, after conducting airstrikes against the group after attacks on Red Sea shipping. “The existing truce gives both sides reasons for restraint,” he says. “For Trump, preserving that arrangement helps keep the US away from another costly Middle Eastern military confrontation while it remains engaged in the strait of Hormuz. The Houthis have equally strong incentives to not be drawn into conflict with the US, which caused them serious damage in the 2025 bombing campaign.”Yesterdaythe Guardian confirmedthat officials from the US had met Houthi leaders over the weekend in Oman, where they received assurances that the ceasefire still held and that the movement had no intention of attacking US shipping in the Red Sea. While Trump condemned the Houthi advance for threatening freedom of navigation, he has far rejected any military response in support of Riyadh.Al-Muslimi calls for a more coherent international approach to his country, which he considers one of the least understood in the region. Yemen analysts have frequently criticised the US and allies for approaching Yemen’s challenges with a focus on security rather than diplomacy or development, while internal instability has been exploited by larger regional powers to fight their own proxy battles.Most importantly, he says: “While this new international dimension of Yemen’s war makes the country strategically more important to the world, it should not overshadow the plight of ordinary Yemenis”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat else we’ve been enjoyingView image in fullscreenDawn Butler writes: ‘We know Diane Abbott has received extraordinary levels of abuse, while I often feel specifically targeted because I am a Black woman.’Photograph: UK Parliament/Jessica Taylor/PAFollowing the release of a report into the significant abuse faced by those who run for office, Labour MP Dawn Butlerwrites hereabout how politics is becoming a “no-go zone” for too many.Charlie Lindlar, newsletters teamWho doteenage girlsdream of becoming? I loved seeing the variety of items significant to young women inthis picture galleryby Belgian photographer Eva Verbeeck.Sundus Abdi, newsletters teamWe may be hurtling toward autumn, but don’t let that stop you from reading our Filter team’s rundown ofthe best ice-cream makersfor every budget. (Kudos to Danielle Amatofor bravely taking on the assignment.)CharlieI lovedthis piece in the Atlanticthat boils down to being an ode tobeing silly. “Few social situations encourage or even allow unadulterated loopiness,” Lily Mayer writes. “In general, art made for adults tends to abide by this taboo.
