We get satire, scatological jokes, imitations, and absurdity, but rarely do we get silliness.”CharlieSportView image in fullscreenMaxim De Cuyper scored what proved to be Brighton’s winner three minutes after coming on.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Nigel French/Apl/SportsphotoFootball| Manchester Unitedscored two early goals but lost 3-2to Brighton in the Carabao Cup, while Tammy Abrahamscored his first goalsof the season in Aston Villa’s 3-1 win at Coventry.Formula One| Formula Onehas announced its calendarfor 2027, with an increase in sprint races to 10 events, including at Monaco, and the addition of meetings in Portugal and Turkey.Rugby union| The inaugural women’s British & Irish Lions tour of New Zealand next year is expected to be broadcast live on Sky Sportsin a significant boostfor the women’s game.The front pagesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: The Guardian“Prisoners to ‘double up’ in single prefab jail cell units”, is theGuardian’s front page today.TheMailsplashes on “‘Rest assured, we will forget her soon enough’”, theTimeshas “King: Grief has coloured earl’s claims over Diana”, theTelegraphwrites “Palace hits back at Diana’s brother”, and theSun’s take is “Recollections may vary … again”.TheMirror’s front page is “Heartbreak”, thei Paper’s splash is “Burnham warns of ‘challenging’ budget after 3.1% inflation”, and theExpresssays “We are ‘paying the price’ for Labour’s economy failure”. TheFTleads on “Fed raises rates despite Trump pressure in bid to tame prices”. Lastly,Metroruns with “‘Putney pusher’ suspect dead”.Today in Focus: The LatestPhotograph: The GuardianEd Sheeran support acts quit after Macklemore ‘Free Palestine’ rowAll four supporting acts for the upcoming dates of Ed Sheeran’s tour have withdrawn in solidarity with fellow opener Macklemore. The American rapper was removed from Sheeran’s tour after comments made onstage in support of Palestine. Sheeran responded that venue owners – including Robert Kraft who owns the New England Patriots and its home stadium – had objected to Macklemore’s appearance on the tour. But after he had tried to negotiate with the venue owners ‘at length to build bridges’, ultimately the promoters made the decision to pull the plug. Artists who have pulled out include Finneas, Aaron Rowe and Beoga. Lucy Houghspeaks to Guardian assistant opinion editorJason Okundaye.Cartoon of the day | Nicola JenningsView image in fullscreenIllustration: Nicola Jennings/The GuardianThe UpsideA bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all badView image in fullscreenPrincessan Glittergull, Tove Jansson (1922).Photograph: ©️Tove Jansson EstateThe Moomin books about lovable trolls with hippopotamus snouts arecoming to lifein a new London exhibition, featuring previously unseen drawings by their creator, Tove Jansson.Opening in November, the show will include more than 100 works, from early Moomin sketches to photographs and films, celebrating Jansson’s enduring themes of nature, friendship, tolerance and being yourself.Sign up herefor a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every SundayBored at work?And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.Quick crosswordCryptic crosswordWordiplyExplore more on these topicsYemenFirst Edition newsletterHouthisStrait of HormuzMiddle East and north AfricanewslettersShareReuse this content

title: IS member sentenced to 20 years in prison for role in 2021 Kabul airport bombing  | Islamic State | The Guardian
description: Mohammad Sharifullah, 28, was convicted of aiding the terrorist group that took credit for the suicide bombing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Mohammad Sharifullah, 28, was convicted of aiding the terrorist group that took credit for the suicide bombing
Content: Funeral services are held for marine L/Cpl Kareem Grant Nikoui on 18 September 2021 in Riverside, California.Photograph: Barbara Davidson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFuneral services are held for marine L/Cpl Kareem Grant Nikoui on 18 September 2021 in Riverside, California.Photograph: Barbara Davidson/Getty ImagesIslamic StateIS member sentenced to 20 years in prison for role in 2021 Kabul airport bombingMohammad Sharifullah, 28, was convicted of aiding the terrorist group that took credit for the suicide bombingAssociated PressThu 17 Sep 2026 09.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 11.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnIslamic Stategroup member was sentenced on Wednesday to 20 years in prison for aiding the terrorist organization that took credit for a suicide bombing that killed 13 US service members and about 160 Afghans at the Kabul airport five years ago during the US military’s chaotic withdrawal from the country.A federal jury in Virginia had convicted Mohammad Sharifullah in April of providing material support to the IS affiliate known as Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP). But jurors could not agree whether he bore some responsibility for the airport bombing on 26 August 2021.US troops were conducting an evacuation operation at the airport when a suicide bomber detonated an improvised explosive device near an entry point known as Abbey Gate. Sharifullah’s role in the attack was scouting a route to Hamid Karzai international airport, prosecutors said.Al-Qaida and IS-linked violence in Africa’s Sahel belt set to hit record levels this yearRead moreSharifullah, 28, received the maximum sentence for his one-count conviction in an international terrorism case that Donald Trump heralded last year during a speech to a joint session of Congress.Sharifullah did not testify at his trial and declined to address the court before the US district judge Anthony Trenga imposed the sentence. The judge said the defendant was a “dedicated terrorist” who expressed no remorse for the “unfathomable” grief and suffering that he had caused.Trenga heard victim impact statements from several parents of US service members. From a podium only a few feet from where Sharifullah sat, they took turns paying tribute to their children’s sacrifices and describing how the attack has shattered their families.Mark Schmitz of Missouri asked Sharifullah to turn and look at him as he spoke about the life and death of his 20-year-old son, Marine Corps L/Cpl Jared Schmitz.“They may have taken his life, but they’ll never take his legacy,” Mark Schmitz said. “A bomb killed my son. It did not kill what he stood for.”Paula Knauss-Selph, whose son, army SSgt Ryan Knauss, was killed in the Abbey Gate bombing, said the family was “forever changed” by the attack.“No justice will ever be enough to mend my broken heart,” she said.Sharifullah requested a 17-year prison sentence, while prosecutors sought 20 years. His lawyers said he was never an ISKP leader and had not been convicted of any conduct related to the airport suicide bombing.“He was brought here because the government believed he participated in the Abbey Gate attack, a theory which it was unable to prove at trial,” defense attorneys wrote.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionProsecutors said in their sentencing memo that “from his teenage years, when he pledged an oath of allegiance to [ISKP], Sharifullah’s carnage was driven by hate. Hate towards Americans.”Jurors convicted Sharifullah of providing material support to ISKP. They deadlocked on whether any deaths at the airport “resulted from” that conspiracy. Sharifullah could have faced a possible life sentence if the jury had unanimously decided that question.According to prosecutors, Sharifullah told a journalist that he wanted to “catch and kill the crusaders” from the United States for invading his country afterthe attacks of September 11. They said Sharifullah was involved in dozens of other attacks, including a March 2024 assault on a Moscow concert hall that killed roughly 140 people.Defense lawyers argued that prosecutors failed to present any evidence tying Sharifullah to the Kabul bombing besides his own words during hours of FBI questioning. His team said Sharifullah told FBI agents what he thought they wanted to hear, possibly because he was afraid of being tortured in Pakistani custody before he was brought to the US.A review by US Central Command found that the Abbey Gate bomber was Abdul Rahman al-Logari, an IS member who had been released from an Afghan prison by the Taliban. According to an FBI affidavit, Sharifullah recognized the alleged bomber as an operative he had known while incarcerated.Explore more on these topicsIslamic StateAfghanistanUS militaryUS justice systemSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Outright racist’ activist Daniel Thomas will face ‘full force of law’ over any crimes, says home secretary | Far right | The Guardian
description: Shabana Mahmood says she wants to distinguish between far-right extremism and legitimate local concerns over asylum sites
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Shabana Mahmood says she wants to distinguish between far-right extremism and legitimate local concerns over asylum sites
Content: Shabana Mahmood referred to ‘the far right and outright racists like Danny Thomas’ (above) whose behaviour was ‘completely unacceptable’.Photograph: Theo Shaw/PAView image in fullscreenShabana Mahmood referred to ‘the far right and outright racists like Danny Thomas’ (above) whose behaviour was ‘completely unacceptable’.Photograph: Theo Shaw/PAFar right‘Outright racist’ activist Daniel Thomas will face ‘full force of law’ over any crimes, says home secretaryShabana Mahmood says she wants to distinguish between far-right extremism and legitimate local concerns over asylum sitesRajeev SyalHome affairs editorThu 17 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShabana Mahmood has described the anti-asylum activist Daniel Thomas as “a far-right and outright racist” who will feel “the full force of the law” if his organisation commits crimes near contested asylum sites such as Piddington.In an interview with the Guardian, the home secretary also “wanted to reassure” concerned villagers that asylum seekers due to move in to a neighbouring former defence site would not “put pressure” on local resources because they would be given “self-contained facilities”.Her intervention came after Thomas, a convicted criminal known as “Danny Tommo” and the co-founder ofthe Patriot Platform, said thousands of his masked followers could descend “for days” on to the Oxfordshire village to prevent male asylum seekers being moved in.At the launch of a crackdown on knife crime inBirminghamon Thursday, Mahmood said she wanted to distinguish between legitimate concerns felt by Piddington residents over a large-scale asylum centre and extremists who were “hijacking” community concerns.“I understand the anxiety of local people when they’re about to see a change to their community. But it is important to distinguish that anxiety, where reasonable people can have a conversation, and the far right and outright racists like Danny Thomas walking into town, hijacking an issue and then using that to divide our communities,” she said.“Their behaviour is completely unacceptable. And where they break the law, they will face the full force of the law.”View image in fullscreenResidents of Piddington, Oxfordshire, voted overwhelmingly to become an independent state in a symbolic ‘referendum’.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAPiddington’s local populationregistered their oppositionto the proposed asylum facility on Wednesday, casting 285 votes against 26 in a symbolic ballot to leave the UK and seek self-determination.The parish has been approached by hundreds of other town and village councillors and residents for advice on replicating the campaign, which was backed by the Conservatives, Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats.Thomas visited Piddington the day after the vote. He was dressed in a grey suit and white shirt and was not accompanied by people wearing balaclavas.Joe Marshall, a parish councillor, said it was a private visit and Thomas was due to be given a tour of the village and a cup of tea by a resident.“It is a closed meeting. We will engage with them and walk them around the village and have a cup of tea,” he said. “We have also had an open invitation to Reform, Labour, Conservatives and Restore to visit.”Marshall said it was not clear that villagers would want security assistance from men in balaclavas, if it were offered. “This is a mild-mannered place,” he said.View image in fullscreenPiddington, Oxfordshire; MoD Bicester, the proposed site for the asylum camp, can be seen in the background.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAThomas visited the village hall briefly and later visited the entrance to the Ministry of Justice camp where the asylum seekers are scheduled to be housed. In an interview broadcast on YouTube with Dan Wootton, he said he had spoken to three residents.“The people we are meeting are just normal mothers, normal grandmothers, normal men,” Thomas said. “We have to start somewhere. Right now there are no men in that camp. We are going to put a legal, lawful plan in place to help this community in a way that has never been done before.”Asked how she would respond to Piddington residents after the vote, Mahmood said: “I want to reassure the residents of Piddington that actually our experience from other large sites where we already have, asylum seekers accommodated, whether that’s inWethersfieldorCrowborough, is that putting all facilities on to one site is actually the best way to manage pressures for local communities.“Our experience of other large sites where we are housing asylum seekers is that we’re able to put on that site more of the facilities that asylum seekers need. It’s a relatively self-contained facility, and the knock-on pressure to those local areas, I don’t think we’re going to see.”Mahmood said she understood the anxiety of people in the countryside towards large groups of asylum seekers, but she pointed out that many people in inner-city areas such as her Birmingham constituency had similar concerns.“I do understand the anxiety that people feel, when they’re about to see a change in their community or they are reading misinformation on the internet, or when they’re just concerned that a village is about to have a facility nearby that maybe they think may pose them some challenges,” she said.“I also hear that concern from communities such as mine, where there are large numbers of HMOs [houses of multiple occupation] and accommodation in which asylum seekers are held as well. There is concern across every type of community. Not just in the countryside or in those sorts of areas, but in inner-city areas as well.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenShabana Mahmood said she understood ‘the anxiety of local people when they’re about to see a change to their community’.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAWhat is Patriot Platform, the far-right group that descended on Dover and Portsmouth?Read moreThomas and his supportersrecently coordinateddisruptive protests in Dover and Portsmouth, where masked supporters blocked roads and attempted to intercept newly arrived people.On Thursday, Mahmood summoned police chiefs and urged them to improve their intelligence gathering and use all powers at their disposal, including new laws that allow for a blanket ban on face coverings at a designated location.Hampshire police then sought to impose the ban on Saturday asan anti-asylum demonstrationtook place in Thomas’s home town of Portsmouth. Thomas urged his supporters to stay away.A former bodyguard for Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known asTommy Robinson, Thomas established his anti-immigration movement after serving a prison sentence for attempted kidnapping.In an interview with Robinson, broadcast on Friday night, he said: “How powerful would it be if 5,000 men … surround the [Piddington] camp. We take tents. We sit there for days and we don’t let them [the asylum seekers] get in. And then we reinforce [the blockade] with members from the north, from Scotland, from Ireland.”In the interview, Thomas said he was not racist and welcomed people of other nationalities into his organisation. “Racism within our organisation is just not acceptable. That is the stance we have. We are not a white nationalist movement. I have friends that are black.”Thomas has been approached for comment.Mahmood made her comments as she launched an anti-knife crime programme. More than 230 areas affected by knife crime will share £26.25m to pay for police patrols, CCTV and early-prevention work as part of a knife-crime crackdown across 27 police forces in England and Wales.Each area, roughly the size of 10 football pitches, will receive more police patrols, alongside programmes designed for young people most at risk of being a victim or a perpetrator of knife crime. Action in small, targeted areas was the most effective way of driving down knife crime, the Home Office said.Mahmood launched the initiative at the Acocks Green boxing gym in south Birmingham, which plays a role in the local area in supporting vulnerable young people to stay away from crime. She was joined by the anti-knife campaignersLynne Baird, Lorraine Jones Burrell andPooja Kanda. Each has lost a child to knife crime.Additional reporting byAmelia GentlemanExplore more on these topicsFar rightShabana MahmoodImmigration and asylumOxfordshireBirminghamTommy RobinsonKnife crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Find a credible plan for British Steel, ministers told as ‘startling’ costs soar | British Steel | The Guardian
description: Government spending watchdog warns of ‘startling’ price of keeping publicly owned firm in business
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Government spending watchdog warns of ‘startling’ price of keeping publicly owned firm in business
Content: British Steel was taken into public ownership in July.Photograph: Darren Staples/ReutersView image in fullscreenBritish Steel was taken into public ownership in July.Photograph: Darren Staples/ReutersBritish SteelFind a credible plan for British Steel, ministers told as ‘startling’ costs soarGovernment spending watchdog warns of price of keeping publicly owned firm in businessAlex DanielThu 17 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLabour has been urged to lay out a credible plan for the future ofBritish Steel, as the government spending watchdog warned of the “startling” costs of keeping the struggling manufacturer in business with no end in sight.British Steel was taken into public ownership in July to protect “the future of steel production”, 15 months after the government stepped in to prevent the closure of its steelworks in Scunthorpe and the loss of 4,000 jobs.But it is costing £1.3m a day to keep the company running, with the total estimated cost reaching as much as £1.5bn by 2028. By mid-June, the government had spent £555m paying workers’ salaries and buying raw materials, excluding the cost of external advisers.The public accounts committee of MPs said on Friday that ministers were still “unable to articulate what business model” would put the company on a sustainable footing, nearly ayear and a half after taking control at Scunthorpe.It added that the Department for Business and Trade had not given “even indicative estimates” of how much British Steel would ultimately cost taxpayers or how long the situation would continue.Afternationalising British Steel,the government appointed new bosses to focus on stabilising the business.Clive Betts, the committee’s deputy chair, said the move to save the company was “all well and good”, but added: “This was just the beginning. Having brought British Steel onto the taxpayers’ books, it is now up to government to explain its plan for its future.“Unfortunately, beyond simply propping up the company with public money, the government was not able to outline such a plan to our inquiry. The reality is that British Steel is unable to wash its own face, and government is now in charge of making sure it gets on to a sustainable financial footing for the future.“We also require assurances that the startling levels of funding British Steel is currently receiving do not come at the expense of the wider sector.”The criticism came days after Labour alsonationalised Britain’s third-biggest producer of the metal,the Yorkshire-based Speciality Steel UK, in an attempt to protect 1,300 jobs.Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said at the time that the government did not “intervene in private companies lightly” but that the move was important to safeguard heavy industry.The public accounts committee said it showed the government could not “spend all its money supporting British Steel, when clearly there will be a need to support other parts of the industry”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt added: “[Taxpayers] remain exposed to significant and growing costs and uncertainty – it is not clear whether the money will ever be recovered.”The government should publish a plan for the company that included “options and analysis for the intended future production model and the role of British Steel in the UK economy; the preferred decarbonisation pathway; how the company will become financially sustainable; and the expected costs, funding sources and timetable”, the committee’s report said.The former owner Jingye has separately argued that British Steel owed it almost £1bn when it was nationalised and has started a formal process under an international treaty to win compensation from the government.The move has also put pressure on UK-Chinese relations, with China’s governmentsaying it is “strongly dissatisfied”with the situation.Explore more on these topicsBritish SteelSteel industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Addison Lee founder owes £20.5m in tax after UK tribunal ruling | HMRC | The Guardian
description: HMRC wins challenge over John Griffin’s claim to be non-dom despite having lived in England since childhood
Author: Patrick Daly
Headline: HMRC wins challenge over John Griffin’s claim to be non-dom despite having lived in England since childhood
Content: John Griffin pictured in 2012. He was born to Irish parents in 1942 and briefly lived there until he moved to London at the age of nine.Photograph: Felix ClayView image in fullscreenJohn Griffin pictured in 2012. He was born to Irish parents in 1942 and briefly lived there until he moved to London at the age of nine.Photograph: Felix ClayHMRCAddison Lee founder owes £20.5m in tax after UK tribunal rulingHMRC wins challenge over John Griffin’s claim to be non-dom despite having lived in England since childhoodPatrick DalyThu 17 Sep 2026 17.04 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 17.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe founder of Addison Lee owes £20.5m in tax after a tribunal dismissed a claim that he should be treated as a nom-dom despite living in the UK since childhood.John Griffin had argued he should be treated as a nom-dom due to his connection toIreland, saying: “I was and am besotted with Ireland, infatuated with Ireland. I believe that I have always been and am Irish.”HM Revenue and Customs challenged the domicile status on Griffin’s self-assessment tax returns from 2013 to 2020, which would have allowed the 84-year-old to not pay UK tax rates on foreign earnings kept outside the country.This week, a London tribunal ruled in the tax authority’s favour.Billionaire Chris Rokos, who paid £330m in tax last year, to quit UKRead moreGriffin was born to Irish parents in 1942 and briefly lived there until he moved to London at the age of nine, according to tribunal documents.HMRC argued thatEnglandshould be considered Griffin’s home, with the businessman raising a family in Hertfordshire and building his London-based taxi empire, having founded Addison Lee in 1975.Tribunal judge Michaela Snelders and tribunal member Gill Hunter said: “We are satisfied that by 5 April 2013, Sir John had settled in England in every meaningful sense.”“England was where he had established his home, raised his family, built his business, accumulated his wealth and organised his personal, social and professional life.“Although he retained a powerful emotional attachment to Ireland and a genuine hope that he might one day spend more time there, those sentiments never crystallised into a sufficiently definite intention to make Ireland his permanent home.”View image in fullscreenThe ruling reflects the period after John Griffin sold Addison Lee to a private equity firm in 2013. The business was reported to be worth £300m at the time.Photograph: Felix ClayThe tax chamber tribunal was told Griffin spent eight nights in Ireland in 2015, one of the years he claimed to be domiciled there, which the chamber ruled was “inconsistent with someone seriously preparing for permanent relocation”.As part of his appeal against HMRC’s stance, Griffin had argued that his domicile should be the same as his father, Jack, who had come to England from Ireland in search of work in 1935. Under UK law, a child’s domicile is the same as their father’s if the parents were married at the time of their birth.Legal counsel for HMRC, however, said Griffin’s domicile status under UK law would have changed when his father’s domicile of choice became England. They argued it had done so some time before Griffin reached adulthood at the age of 21 in 1963. The tribunal agreed with HMRC’s stance.The ruling caps off a long-running inquiry into Griffin’s tax affairs and reflects the period after hesold Addison Leeto private equity firm the Carlyle Group in 2013. The business was reported to be worth £300m at the time.Having Irish domicile would have potentially allowed Griffin to avoid being taxed on earnings made outside the UK, a legal benefit of being classified as a nom-dom. The tribunal’s ruling makes his worldwide income from the period subject to UK tax rules, with HMRC calculating that he owes an additional £20.5m covering the seven-year period.Nom-dom status was scrapped by the Labour UK government in April 2025, after a promise a year earlier by Rishi Sunak’s Conservative administration to do the same.Griffin, knighted in 2024 for services to business and charity, did not give evidence in person to the tribunal after HMRC accepted he was not medically fit to do so due to “cognitive decline”.Explore more on these topicsHMRCIrelandSelf-assessment taxEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Suspect in ‘Putney pusher’ case told family that investigation was ‘murdering him’ | London | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Sisters of Nicholas Brandram recount 44-year-old’s deteriorating mental health in days before he took his life
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Exclusive: Sisters of Nicholas Brandram recount 44-year-old’s deteriorating mental health in days before he took his life
Content: Brandram was arrested in June on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm, nine years after a jogger shoved a woman into the path of a bus in London.Photograph: Family handout/PAView image in fullscreenBrandram was arrested in June on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm, nine years after a jogger shoved a woman into the path of a bus in London.Photograph: Family handout/PALondonSuspect in ‘Putney pusher’ case told family that investigation was ‘murdering him’Exclusive: Sisters of Nicholas Brandram recount 44-year-old’s deteriorating mental health in days before he took his lifeEmine SinmazThu 17 Sep 2026 16.33 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 18.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDays before Nicholas Brandram, the man suspected of being the “Putney pusher”, killed himself, he told his family that the police investigation was “murdering him”.He had “no fight left” in him, he told his sisters, Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker, and could not see an end to the Metropolitan police investigation, or the online abuse.Brandram’s lawyers warned the Met last week that his mental health had deteriorated and he was receiving treatment in a psychiatric hospital after renewed press reporting that he had been released under investigation.“He said a couple of days ago that this investigation was murdering him. Day by day, he was slowly being murdered,” Hicks, 40, said through tears.“He saw no end to this investigation,” added Voelcker, 45. “My sister and I were keeping a close eye on him because he was telling us he couldn’t go on. He said it more than once in the week before, that he couldn’t keep going. All we could do was just reassure him. We had faith in the system, we had faith in the police, and they neglected him. They failed in their duty of care to him, to the wider family, and we do not want to see another family going through this.”The pair insisted that Brandram, 44,was not the “Putney pusher”and that he died thinking no one would believe in his innocence.He was arrested on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm on 15 June, nine years after a jogger shoved a woman headfirst into the path of an oncoming bus on Putney Bridge in south-west London.The case attracted considerable media attention but appeared to elude detectives, who wound down their investigation in 2018, after interviewing 50 men and arresting three suspects.But there was renewed interest in the case after Brandram’s arrest, which his family described as heavy-handed and disproportionate. A number of officers in body armour reportedly swooped on his home address, his sisters said, while a reporter who had been tipped off about the arrest filmed the ordeal.Although Brandram’s name was not published in the media because he had not been charged, his family said that biographical information in reports made him easily identifiable. He was described as a wealthy banker who lived in a £1.4m west London home and an army veteran with links to royalty. Brandram was the grandson of Princess Katherine of Greece, who was a great-granddaughter of Queen Victoria.View image in fullscreenFrom left to right: Nicholas Brandram, Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker as children.Photograph: Family handoutWhile in police custody in June over the Putney Bridge incident, he was also arrested on suspicion of possession of class A and class B drugs.His sisters said there was no forensic evidence linking Brandram to the Putney incident and that he had a prominent military tattoo and a withered calf which, they said, distinguished him from the man in footage of the attack on 5 May 2017.That morning, Brandram had walked from his home in Notting Hill Gate to his office in Bond Street and sent his sisters an email from his work account, which they said he could only access from his workplace. They said that evidence was passed on to the police.They added that Brandram had volunteered to take part in an identification parade and provided his DNA for comparison with a sample recovered at the time of the incident. Hicks said detectives told Brandram just days ago that they still did not know when the DNA analysis would be completed.“Our brother willingly provided DNA in an attempt to obviously help clear his name and to complete the investigation, and for weeks now we’ve been asking the police just to complete the DNA test,” Voelcker said.“We’ve always maintained that he’s innocent. He always maintained he was innocent. We just needed the police to complete their inquiry, and it just felt particularly egregious that they were just hanging this DNA test over him.”Hicks said as details of the case kept being reported in the press, her brother became preoccupied by online abuse on forums such as Reddit.“His reputation within a couple of days was in tatters. People saying he’s the alleged pusher, and you can imagine the vitriol that was coming out online,” Voelcker said.“You can imagine what people might say about somebody they think tried to push a woman in front of a bus. There was a lot of people had a lot of views about our brother, about his background, about where he worked.”“And the problem was he was reading it all every day,” Hicks said. “The vitriol is still there and that’s what’s so heartbreaking for us, is that when he took his own life he died thinking that effectively everyone hated him and thought he’d done something awful and that no one would see that he was innocent and he knew that his family were behind him but it wasn’t enough.”The sisters said Brandram had stayed with them in recent days after his mental health deteriorated following the publication of an update about the case that said he had been released under investigation.“He was really talking about ending his life and ending things. And he was very low and said he felt like he had no fight left in him. He couldn’t see the end,” Voelcker said.Brandram was admitted to a psychiatric hospital for six days before being discharged on Sunday.His family insisted the Met police were warned about his mental health.Voelcker tried to boost his mood on Tuesday by telling him it was a beautiful day and that he had many friends and his family supporting him. He wasfound dead at his home in Chiswick, west London,later that day.The family said their priority was to clear their brother’s name and “to ensure another family does not have to go through what we have as a result of the police delays and leaks to the media”.Hicks said: “Nick was really very loving, enthusiastic. He had an infectious character to be around, very funny. He was an extrovert, so he loved people. He was a much-loved father and uncle.”Voelcker added: “He spent a long time in the army before going into the city. And his reputation was important. He was a proud man. I think that’s the thing and even the fact that he needed to seek help from a psychiatric hospital was a big deal for him.”Ch Supt Dan Knowles, in charge of policing for south-west London, said: “Our thoughts are with Mr Brandram’s family and friends at this deeply distressing time. We recognise the significant impact his death will have on those who knew and loved him. We also understand the strain that being subject to a police investigation can place on individuals and their families.“The investigation remains ongoing. Following Mr Brandram’s release under investigation, it was made clear that inquiries would continue while officers progressed outstanding lines of inquiry and forensic examinations. This remains the position, and further investigative work is ongoing.“Investigations of this nature, particularly those involving complex evidential and forensic work, can take a number of months to complete as officers gather and assess all available evidence.”He added that the force had made a mandatory referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct on 16 September.In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsLondonMetropolitan policePolicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Nato head: Britain must show ‘credible path’ of annual defence budget increases | Nato | The Guardian
description: Mark Rutte said Britain will need to steadily increase defence spending to meet Nato target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Mark Rutte said Britain will need to steadily increase defence spending to meet Nato target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035
Content: Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, spoke with the Press Association following meetings with Ed Miliband and Wes StreetingPhotograph: The Ditchley Foundation/PAView image in fullscreenNato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, spoke with the Press Association following meetings with Ed Miliband and Wes StreetingPhotograph: The Ditchley Foundation/PANatoNato head: Britain must show ‘credible path’ of annual defence budget increasesMark Rutte said Britain will need to steadily increase defence spending to meet Nato target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035Dan SabbaghDefence and security editorThu 17 Sep 2026 15.29 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain needs to show “a credible path” of annual increases in its defence budgets to meet aNatotarget of spending nearly £30bn more on the military by the middle of the next decade, the head of the alliance said on Thursday.Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, said that Britain could not wait until just before 2035 to lift defence spending to 3.5% of GDP, in an unusually pointed intervention a day after he met prime ministerAndy Burnham.In an interview with the Press Association, he said: “And that is why you need a credible path towards that 3.5%, and yearly increments.”The alliance’s secretary general, a former Dutch prime minister, made similar remarks to the BBC, where he said that the UK understood that the target could not be met “in one go in 2034” and that it would have to be achieved gradually.Earlier on Thursday, Rutte met withWes Streeting, the defence secretary, and Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary. He saw Burnham on Wednesday, at a business park in Didcot, and also met representatives from the defence industry.Keir Starmer signed the UK up to a Nato-wide target of increasing defence spending to 3.5% of GDP in the summer of 2025, under pressure from the US president, Donald Trump. The figure has since been endorsed by Burnham and his chancellor, former defence secretary John Healey.Current spending plans, covering until 2028/9, show defence spending levelling off at 2.7%, nearly £30bn below the ultimate target, raising the question of how it would be achieved after the next general election. It is unclear if taxes or borrowing would have to rise, or other government spending cuts.Healey resigned as defence minister in June because Starmer would not commit to lifting defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. At the time Healey said Labour needed to set “a clear path” to meet the Nato commitment, similar language to that used by Rutte in his interviews.But since then Healey and Burnham have avoided committing to the 3% by the end of the decade. Decisions on future spending are likely to be left to the next government spending review due next year, prompting the Nato leader to engage in public lobbying on his trip to Britain.Rutte said he was certain the Burnham government remained behind the ultimate goal and the need to increase defence spending gradually. “I am absolutely confident that when it comes to the yearly increments, they totally take it and accept it, that they have to be there,” he told the BBC.“There has to be a credible path. What that credible path exactly will be, we will see with the spending review next year,” Rutte added.A day earlier, Rutte gave a speech toat Ditchley Park in Oxfordshire, in which he warned that the 32 country military alliance faced “the most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation” with wars in Ukraine, the Middle East coming at time of rising state competition.Nato needed “more UK and more Europe”, he added, to take up the slack as the US reduces its military commitment to the alliance. Trump has long argued that the UK and Europe should match US levels of defence spending and take the lead in defending the continent from Russia aggression.Explore more on these topicsNatoMark RutteAndy BurnhamEd MilibandWes StreetingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Man who sprayed Ilhan Omar with vinegar sentenced to 14 months | Ilhan Omar | The Guardian
description: Anthony Kazmierczak agreed plea deal over January town-hall attack that came amid Minneapolis ICE crackdown
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Anthony Kazmierczak agreed plea deal over January town-hall attack that came amid Minneapolis ICE crackdown
Content: Kazmierczak was tackled by security officers and turned over to police after the 27 January 2026 assault.Photograph: Steven Garcia/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenKazmierczak was tackled by security officers and turned over to police after the 27 January 2026 assault.Photograph: Steven Garcia/NurPhoto/ShutterstockIlhan OmarMan who sprayed Ilhan Omar with vinegar sentenced to 14 monthsAnthony Kazmierczak agreed plea deal over January town-hall attack that came amid Minneapolis ICE crackdownAssociated PressThu 17 Sep 2026 18.48 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 18.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe man whosprayed vinegar at the Democratic US House member Ilhan Omarduring aMinneapolistown hall was sentenced Thursday to 14 months in prison after reaching a deal with prosecutors.The sentencing of 56-year-old Anthony Kazmierczak came nearly eight months after the 27 January assault. At the time,Minneapoliswas facing an immigration crackdown that led to angry protests, arrests and the killing of two US citizens by federal officers.Kazmierczak was also sentenced to three years of supervised release, which includes no contact withOmar. US marshals escorted him from the courtroom after he was sentenced.Ilhan Omar brings bill to make ICE ‘pay the price’ for terrorizing communitiesRead more“This wasn’t a spur-of-the-moment act,” the US district judge Joan N Ericksen said before handing down the sentence, noting that Kazmierczak had secured tickets for the town hall weeks in advance.“An attack on a public figure is not a political statement. It is misguided, selfish and inconsistent with any concept of a free or democratic society,” Ericksen added. She also said spraying anything at an elected official “is a terrifying thing. And you knew that when you did it.”Kazmierczak, who has been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease, shook visibly at times as he sat at the defense table. He spoke quietly and haltingly, occasionally wiping away tears as he stood before Ericksen.He spoke about being a good neighbor – and how his troubles with insurance companies as well as prison had exacerbated his ailments. His attorney, John Fossum, argued that Kazmierczak had not been taking his mental health medications before the attack, lowering his inhibitions and contributing to what happened.“I’ve spent enough time in jail thinking,” Kazmierczak said, his voice barely audible. “I really apologize to her for having put her through that,” he said, referring to Omar.In an earlier hearing, Kazmierczak was unable to explain his actions, saying only “it’s fuzzy” when Ericksen asked what he remembered.“I’m sorry if I scared you,” he wrote to Omar after the attack.During the town hall, witnesses saw Kazmierczak jump up from the audience, spraying liquid from a syringe at Omar and saying she was “splittingMinnesotaapart”. Omar’s security officers tackled Kazmierczak and turned him over to police, who arrested him.Omar was not injured and continued with the town hall after the arrest.Authorities later determined he had sprayed her with a mixture of water and apple cider vinegar. He pleaded guilty to assaulting a US officer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe government sentencing memorandum, submitted to the court by prosecutors, said he had texted at least three people indicating he planned to do something at the meeting involving Omar “but would not answer their questions about his intent”.He also sent messages to a neighbor to arrange for dog care and asking for bail bond company contact information.The sentencing memo said Kazmierczak had long struggled with alcohol abuse and had “a history of mental and emotional health concerns” and a string of health issues tied to his 2022 Parkinson’s disease diagnosis.Omar, a refugee from Somalia, has long been a target ofDonald Trump’s anti-immigrant rhetoric across his two presidencies. In 2019, after Omar’s election to Congress, Trump said she should “go back” to her country of birth. He has described her as “garbage” and said she should be investigated.In social media posts, Kazmierczak had criticizedJoe Biden– who was president between Trump’s two Oval Office terms – and referred to Democrats as “angry and liars”. He wrote that Trump wants the US to be “stronger and more prosperous”.His attack came as the Minneapolis area was on edge due to the crackdown, with protesters often facing off against convoys of immigration officers and conservatives criticizing protesters.Explore more on these topicsIlhan OmarHouse of RepresentativesMinneapolisUS crimeUS CongressUS politicsMinnesotanewsShareReuse this content

title: RFK Jr promises anti-vaxxers a ‘friend at the White House’ amid deadly measles outbreak | Robert F Kennedy Jr | The Guardian
description: The US health secretary added that he would’ve made sweeping changes ‘on day one’ but he had to follow the law
Author: Melody Schreiber
Headline: The US health secretary added that he would’ve made sweeping changes ‘on day one’ but he had to follow the law
Content: Robert F Kennedy Jr speaks during the second day of the Republican National Committee midterm convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas on 10 September 2026.Photograph: Blake Fagan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRobert F Kennedy Jr speaks during the second day of the Republican National Committee midterm convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas on 10 September 2026.Photograph: Blake Fagan/AFP/Getty ImagesRobert F Kennedy JrRFK Jr promises anti-vaxxers a ‘friend at the White House’ amid deadly measles outbreakThe US health secretary added that he would’ve made sweeping changes ‘on day one’ but he had to follow the lawMelody SchreiberThu 17 Sep 2026 15.59 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 21.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the death toll from the worst measles outbreak in decades rises,Robert F Kennedy Jrheadlined the Washington DC conference of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense, which he led for nearly a decade.“Let me be clear. You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House,” Kennedy, now serving as secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), told anti-vaccine activists at the conference in a nearly hour-and-a-half-long speech. He urged patience, saying that he would’ve made sweeping changes “on day one” but that he had to follow the law in order to make permanent change.With US measles deaths on the rise, local officials are stepping in where RFK Jr won’tRead more“But as I said, you have friends in the White House, and we are doing this one day at a time,” Kennedy said.He only addressed the measles outbreak, which recently killed four people in Pennsylvania, once.“In our country we care about rare illnesses and deaths. We care about every child who dies from measles. They get headlines,” he said. “I’d ask you to care about children who are dying or suffering or being injured by vaccine injuries.”Recentpollingsuggests that one quarter of Americans now have doubts about the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccines following a years-long campaign against immunizations by once-fringe actors. But the majority of Americans also disapprove of the Trump administration’s handling of the widening measles outbreak, which killed three people in Texas and Arizona last year in addition to those inPennsylvania.Kennedy described “vaccine-injured children” as “damaged” because of diagnoses of allergies, asthma, ADHD and autism, among other conditions. He also claimed that diabetes, sudden infant death syndrome, and anorexia can be side effects of routine vaccines, and he said that the system to track such effects is “broken”.RFK Jr challenges vaccine safety and promotes chemtrail skepticismThere is little daylight between Kennedy and his former organization. “I spent 40 years in these battles,” Kennedy said. “I intend to stay in this fight as long as I am able.” He thanked his friends who are still at CHD.Longtime anti-vaccine activists celebrated their unprecedented role in the national conversation, at times expressing astonishment over the ways anti-vaccine sentiment has been elevated to thehighest levelsof the US government.“We have an opportunity today to speak to our colleagues and our friends in mainstream media,” the CEO of the Children’s Health Defense, Mary Holland, said at the event on Thursday.Andrew Wakefield, a former gastroenterologist whose medical license was revoked after he was found to have fabricated research indicating a link between vaccines and autism, spoke before and immediately after Kennedy.“I could not have imagined two years ago that Bobby [Kennedy] would be in the White House and that President Trump would be saying ‘divide up theMMRinto three different’,” said Wakefield, who proposed the same strategy years earlier when he attempted to patent his own single measles shot to compete with the MMR. He stopped to laugh. “What drug was I on that morning?”Anti-vaccine activists had become nervous earlier this year after the White House reportedlyput the kiboshon speaking about vaccines before the US midterm elections. “February, March, April, May, vaccine reform got a little quiet, a little scary. You know, behind the scenes, we’re like, “Yeah, what happened?” said Michael Kane, CHD’s director of advocacy.But recent months have shifted vaccines back into the spotlight.“Just a few years ago, we were the, you know, hated stepchild in the corner,” Kane said. “Now we are a national movement that isn’t going anywhere.”The organization laid out its policy agenda, including plans to challenge state-level immunization requirements for school attendance, to recruit younger people to the aging organization, and to combat the installation of cell phone towers for fears of 5G and 6G. Several speakers explicitly linked vaccination to autism, despite decades of research showing no connection.Meanwhile, Kennedy also focused on the role of food systems in health, and touched on efforts to study electromagnetic fields and chem trails.He praised researchers at the University of Southern Denmark, who are now underinvestigationby their institution, as “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy attempted to fund their project in Guinea-Bissau looking at mortality after hepatitis B vaccination before local authoritiescancelledthe project. Their prior work on vaccines has been called “a house of cards” by other researchers.Mark Gorton, president of the Maha Institute, referred to himself as “the boldest anti-vaxxer in the anti-vax conference”, adding that “only anti-vaxxers can speak clearly enough to raise awareness.”Being called the “largest anti-vaccine conference, probably in the world” is “a red badge of courage”, said sen Ron Johnson, a Republican from Wisconsin. Johnson and Sen Rand Paul, a Republican and physician from Kentucky, both rehashed grievances over the Covid pandemic and the immunizations that were rapidly deployed to stem the tide of illness and death.Republican congressman Thomas Massie said he called Donald Trump soon after the election to ask for the agriculture secretary position. Trump asked, “Are you friends with Bobby? Is he too much for HHS? Don’t you think we need some vaccines?” Massie recounted. Kennedy was nominated to HHS the next day, he said.Massie offered two pieces of advice to the anti-vaccine activists: Instead of trying to get rid of “clowns”, he said, “get the clowns who are here to do what you want. Get them to get in the clown car you want. And use pressure. Treat them like cattle.”Coverage of the measles outbreak is a “psy op” that is “meant to control what I think, what I do, what I believe, and what my attitude towards Bobby Kennedy ought to be,” said Tony Lyons, the publisher of books from Kennedy who now heads Maha Action.Kennedy was frequently invoked as a hero of the movement at the conference. “The truth is, he really is dangerous,” Lyons said, invoking the common refrain from scientists and experts. “I think Bobby Kennedy is the most dangerous individual to this system who’s come along in a generation,” he said to a burst of applause.This article was amended on 17 September 2026 to clarify that Kennedy led Children’s Health Defense for nearly a decade.Explore more on these topicsRobert F Kennedy JrMMRUS healthcarenewsShareReuse this content

title: Accused Oregon serial killer indicted in connection with death of sixth woman | Oregon | The Guardian
description: Grand jury indicts Jesse Calhoun on a charge of first-degree manslaughter in the death of Elizabeth Gibson
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: Grand jury indicts Jesse Calhoun on a charge of first-degree manslaughter in the death of Elizabeth Gibson
Content: Jesse Lee Calhoun in Multnomah county circuit court for his arraignment on 6 June 2024 in Portland, Oregon.Photograph: Dave Killen/APView image in fullscreenJesse Lee Calhoun in Multnomah county circuit court for his arraignment on 6 June 2024 in Portland, Oregon.Photograph: Dave Killen/APOregonAccused Oregon serial killer indicted in connection with death of sixth womanGrand jury indicts Jesse Calhoun, 41, on charge of first-degree manslaughter in the death of Elizabeth GibsonDani AnguianoThu 17 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 20.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnOregonman accused of killing five women has been indicted in connection with the death of a sixth woman, officials announced this week.Jesse Calhoun was indicted by a grand jury on a charge of first-degree manslaughter in the death of Elizabeth “Libby” Gibson, said the Multnomah county district attorney on Wednesday. Calhoun is accused of causing Gibson’s death and acting “unlawfully and recklessly under circumstances manifesting extreme indifference to the value of human life”.Gibson, who lived inPortland, was 32 when she was last seen in 2022 and reported missing the following year. Officials believe she was killed on or around 18 November 2022 but have not found her body.Ohio mother of 16 children rescued from ‘deplorable’ conditions pleads not guilty to child neglectRead moreCalhoun, 41, hasalready been chargedin the killings of Ashley Real, 22; Kristin Smith, 22; Charity Perry, 24; Bridget Webster, 31; and Joanna Speaks, 32, between 2022 and 2023. He has pleaded not guilty to five counts of second-degree murder and four counts of abuse of a corpse.“We will not stop. We will do everything in our power to hold him accountable and see that justice is done for each and every one of these victims. We remain committed to these families for as long as it takes,” Nathan Vasquez, the Multnomah county district attorney, said in a statement.Prosecutors said earlier this year that they plan to try Calhoun for all murders in one trial rather than holding separate proceedings.Calhoun was previously incarcerated for assaulting a police officer, trying to strangle a police dog, burglary and other charges. He was released early in 2021 for helping fight wildfires through a prison program, but Oregon’s governor’s reversed the decision in 2023 when he came under investigation for the deaths.Gibson’s family said in a statement that they were “grateful that a definitive step toward justice is finally being taken”.“Libby was kind, creative, and silly. She welcomed everyone with love and acceptance. Her future was tragically taken from her way too soon,” her siblings said in the statement.“We are deeply appreciative of the tireless work and dedication of the law enforcement officers and the district attorney’s office whose efforts have helped bring us to this point.”Melissa Marrero, the senior deputy district attorney, said the scope of the investigation had been “enormous”.“But all information is useful. And to the extent that individuals have been willing to come forward in the past and provide information to us, no matter how small, that information has led us to where we are here today,” she said in a statement.Explore more on these topicsOregonUS crimePortlandWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump and Rubio allies are vying for control of Cuba’s assets if regime falls | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Washington and Florida insiders are exploring lucrative deals for a post-communist Cuba crushed by ever-increasing US sanctions
Author: Ed Augustin
Headline: Washington and Florida insiders are exploring lucrative deals for a post-communist Cuba crushed by ever-increasing US sanctions
Content: Marco Rubio and Donald Trump at a cabinet meeting at Camp David in Maryland, on 31 July 2026.Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMarco Rubio and Donald Trump at a cabinet meeting at Camp David in Maryland, on 31 July 2026.Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/AFP/Getty ImagesTrump administrationTrump and Rubio allies are vying for control of Cuba’s assets if regime fallsWashington and Florida insiders are exploring lucrative deals for a post-communist Cuba crushed by ever-increasing US sanctionsLee Schlenker andEd AugustinThu 17 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 17.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpanish hotelchains. A Canadian miningfirm. European shippinggiants.Visa and Mastercard.Scoresof foreign companies have been driven out of Cuba this summer over fear of being hit with potent, newsecondary sanctions. Marco Rubio, the secretary of state,toldAxios last month there are “no escape valves” from his unprecedented pressure campaign against the island.But not everybody is losing out. Agrowing cast of Washington and Florida insiders – from billionaire Trump allies and Rubio-linked lobbyists to Cuban exiles – are jockeying for control of the communist-ruled island-nation’s key assets, charging top dollar to help clients navigate the ever-expanding web of sanctions, and positioning themselves for lucrative business opportunities in the case of regime collapse.Since an executiveordersigned by Donald Trump on 1 May drove Canada’s Sherritt International from its nickel and cobalt miningjoint venturewith the Cuban state, two rival US bids to buy out its stake have been presented to US authorities.As the lights go out, Cuba’s true believers vow to resist US interventionRead moreRay Washburne,the vice-chair of Trump’s 2016 Victory Committee whoorganizedlast week’s Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas, is clashing withAlbert Huddleston, another Texas oil tycoon withclose tiesto the White House. Both are hoping to swoop in,despitenine-figure claims on Sherritt’s Cuba holdings by Citigroup and Office Depot – Fortune 500 corporations. Washburne did not respond to the Guardian and the consortium group including Huddleston declined to comment.View image in fullscreenRay Washburne, co-chair of the host committee, during an interview ahead of the first day of the Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, US, on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026. Washburne said President Donald Trump and the GOP will have no problems generating enthusiasm at the party’s midterm event by stressing the strength of the economy.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesA similarapproachis being pursued by Australia’s Antilles Gold Ltd, which after beingblacklistedover its Cuba operations in June received thegreen lightfrom the Trump administration to negotiate thetransferof its stake in a Cuban copper-gold mine to the New York-based, multibillion-dollar investment fund,Global Emerging Markets.“If I had done during the Biden administration what Trump’s friends have done now, I’d have been put in jail,” said a person with several decades of experience in Cuba policy who requested anonymity.Sources tell the Guardian that several Trump Organization executives who had previouslytraveledto the island to explore real estate deals and who evenregisteredthe Trump trademark there in 2008 have in recent months returned to Cuba under the aegis ofDominari Holdingsfor meetings. The executives are said to have met with Raúl Guillermo Rodríguez Castro, thegrandsonof former Cuban president Raúl Castro, dubbed “the Crab”, to explore opportunities amid thedepartureof Spanish hotel giants Meliá and Iberostar, which had been operating on the island since the 1990s.View image in fullscreenCuba’s Colonel Raul Guillermo Rodriguez Castro, grandson of Raul Castro, attends the funeral of the 32 Cuban soldiers killed during the US incursion in Venezuela at Colon cemetery in Havana on January 16, 2026. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has held secret talks with a scion of Cuba’s communist Castro leadership as he intensifies pressure on the island, a report said. Axios, quoting unnamed sources, said Rubio has been speaking with Raul Guillermo Rodriguez, the grandson of former leader Raul Castro, who succeeded his brother Fidel Castro.Photograph: Yamil Lage/AFP/Getty ImagesNeither Antilles nor Dominari returned calls for comment.But American investors aren’t the only ones sensing opportunity in Rubio’seffortto coerce the sanctions-battered country of his parents’ birth intobecomingeconomicallydependenton the US.Cubans have been living under an effective fuel blockade since January 2026: the Trump administration cut oil shipments to the island from the island’s main ally after abducting Nicolás Maduro, the Venezuelan president; it then nixed oil deliveries from Mexico bythreateningtariffs on any country sending petroleum to the island.‘We count every litre’: how Cuba’s energy crisis sparked a daily struggle for waterRead moreTreasury department-authorised oil exportsfromFlorida and Texas to the island’s private sector, however – all but non-existent last year – have shot up to over$160mso far this year.Meanwhile, Florida shipping lines such as Crowley, adonorto Cuban-American Republican lawmakers from Florida, Mario Díaz-BalartandMaría Elvira-Salazar, seem to be beneficiaries of fresh sanctions that havehitforeign shippers and forced Cuba-bound commerce to reroute through Florida, according to informed sources who spoke with the Guardian. Crowley declined to comment.And as UN human rights expertswarnthat Washington’s latest measures “knowingly deprive a population of the means to survive”, Franklin Graham, theTrump-alliedCEO of evangelical aid organization Samaritan’s Purse recentlysecureda $40m federal contract to distribute humanitarian aid in Cuba – despite lacking the capacity to effectively implement such a contract on the island, according to sources familiar with the matter. A spokesperson for Samaritan’s Purse said: “Details about aid for Cuba are still being developed and are not yet finalized.”Ironically, some of those who have called most vociferously for harsher sanctions are also cashing in.In July, Madrid-based Vima World SL, a leading player in the island’s food industry whichpartnerswith GAESA, the Cuban military conglomerate that controls large swathes of the island’s economy and has become the maintargetof the US squeeze,hiredtop Washington lobbying firm Continental Strategy – led by Cuban-American allies of Rubio whooversawthe maximum pressure Cuba policy asofficialsin the first Trump administration – for matters related to trade, foreign relations and the food industry.View image in fullscreenCaptured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores are escorted, as they heads towards the Daniel Patrick Moynihan United States Courthouse in Manhattan for an initial appearance to face U.S. federal charges including narco-terrorism, conspiracy, drug trafficking, money laundering and others, at Downtown Manhattan Heliport, in New York City, U.S., January 5, 2026.Photograph: Adam Gray/ReutersContinental’sexecutivesinclude Carlos Trujillo, Trump’s former ambassador to the Organization of American States John Barsa, Trump’s former acting USAID administrator and Alberto Martinez, Rubio’s former chief of staff. The firm, whichterminatedits contract with Vima this month after netting nearly $40,000 according to corporate disclosures, has been known for providing lobbying and government relations services to clients staunchly opposed to the one-party state, includingMasTec, the telecom company owned by Rubio’sfriendJorge Mas Santos;American Sugar Refineries, owned by Trump-ballroomdonorandRubio patronPepe Fanjul; andGeneral Cigar Co, which is fighting Cuba’s state-owned tobacco enterprise in US court for therightsto the Cohiba cigar trademark.“It’s been interesting to watch how quickly some hardline ideologues become pragmatists once there’s money on the table,” one person familiar with the contract told the Guardian, noting that Continental has taken on other Spanish firms with Cuban business interests “trying to get on the right side of sanctions, like banks and hotel chains”.Other organizations that for years have won seven-figure grants from US federal agencies are capitalizing on the Trump administration’s push to force sweeping political and economic change on the island.Lobbying disclosureformsfiled in July by a newly formedgroupmade up of former employees at the UStaxpayer-fundedFoundation for Human Rights in Cuba (FHRC), alongside longtime Republican lobbyistOtto Reichand thehusbandof top Rubio state department aideViviana Bovo, indicate it is “advising [the] State Department on [an] economic development plan for a future free and democratic Cuba, including energy-sector development and compensation for owners of property/business expropriated by the Cuban government”.Reich and Tony Costa, the Foundation for Human Rights chairman, areinvolvedin efforts tomobilizebillions of dollars in private investment from wealthy Cuban exiles for a post-communist Cuba through the newly created Cuban-American National Chamber of Commerce (CANCC).To get their priorities heard by lawmakers and officials in Washington, FHRC and another attendee of the CANCC gatherings, Armando Labrador, a Miami-based plastic surgeon who regularlymeetswith state department officials andwantsto become Cuba’s next leader, havepaidDC lobbying firm The Cormac Group acombined$100,000 since December.For another UStaxpayer-fundednon-profit that had been the subject of an internal Biden administration inquiry that was quickly shut down by powerful House appropriators, the administration’s unprecedented economic siege could not have come at a better time.Just before the Julyreleaseof aheavilycriticizedstate department report referring to Cuba as a nearby terror hub plotting to conquer the US, Digital News Association Inc received a fresh $250,000contractfrom the US government’s office of Cuba broadcasting for “investigative journalism, research and media production”, after which its main sitelaunchedan online interview series repeating Trump administrationclaimsof Cuba’s purported threat to US national security.Vima, Continental, Cormac and Digital News did not return calls for comment.“The cause is regime change,” said Erik Cartelle, a consultant working to connect prominent exiles with Rubio’s state department. “I have clients that want to do a lot of business in Cuba, and the administration is banking on Cuban-Americans going to Cuba and investing, but if there’s a deal that’s going to be had with the regime, it needs to take into account the diaspora’s wishes. You’ve got to listen to this community.”Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationCubaMarco RubioUS politicsUS foreign policyDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump threatens to stop trading with EU over ‘laughable’ membership offer to Canada | Canada | The Guardian
description: US president responds as Mark Carney seeks to move closer to Europe and diversify defence ties
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: US president responds as Mark Carney seeks to move closer to Europe and diversify defence ties
Content: 0:35Trump calls EU's offer of associate membership to Canada 'laughable' – videoCanadaTrump threatens to stop trading with EU over ‘laughable’ membership offer to CanadaUS president responds as Mark Carney seeks to move closer to Europe and diversify defence tiesEurope live – latest updatesJennifer Rankinand agenciesThu 17 Sep 2026 04.25 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has threatened the EU with “serious tariffs” and a halt to trade after the bloc proposed making Canada its first ever associate member – an idea he derided as “laughable”.The US president said that if the EU moved forward with the plan, Washington could impose “very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe”. He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs onEurope.”Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, is due to address the European parliament on Thursday, a day after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen,invited his country to become the EU’s first “associate member”.11:56Taking on Trump?: Canada and EU forge closer ties - The LatestVon der Leyen pitched closer cooperation on tech, defence and energy to Carney, telling the European parliament that, as democracies faced a “fracture in the international rules-based system”, Brussels and Ottawa needed to pull closer together.She said: “This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength. In short, we want to bring the relationship withCanadato the highest level possible.”In response to Trump’s comments, France’s Europe minister Benjamin Haddad said on Thursday that Washington had no power to veto EU decisions.“It is not up to the United States, or ‌anyone else, to choose the political and geopolitical direction of the Europeans. Once again, we have a relationship ⁠with Canada, and we are fully entitled to seek to deepen it,” Haddad ‌told Public Sénat TV channel.Is EU’s offer to Canada a blueprint for Britain – or a reminder it is out in the cold?Read moreA European Commission spokesperson said: “As our president made clear yesterday, the proposed strengthening of the relationship with Canada is not against anyone else, but for our common strength.”View image in fullscreenMark Carney and Andy Burnham, both Everton fans, watch Everton v Wolverhampton Wanderers in Liverpool on Wednesday.Photograph: Paul Cooper/ReutersCarney has called fora “unique alliance” with the EUas Canada seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on US trade. After meeting EU leaders in Strasbourg on Wednesday, he described the EU and Canada as “natural partners, united by shared values” and said that both sides were focused on “a deeper partnership that reinforces our mutual sovereignty to create more opportunities and prosperity for our peoples”.An associate membership agreement would have to be approved by the EU’s 27 member states, who generally support closer ties with Canada, but were taken by surprise by the term.Canada and the EU already have a trade deal and numerous bilateral agreements, but have been moving closer since Donald Trump returned to the White House and raised tariffs on both old allies, while repeatedlytalking about Canada becoming the 51st US stateand lambasting the EU.In a sign that Canada was seeking to further diversify its defence ties ⁠away from ⁠the ​US, Carney’s office announced on Wednesday that the country had formally applied to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force military ⁠coalition.The force is ​a rapid response ‌military partnership comprising 10 North Atlantic Nato member states including Denmark, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden.On Wednesday, Carney and the British prime minister,Andy Burnham, held a bilateral meeting at the ground of Everton football club. The leaders, who are both fans of the premiership club, then attended the team’s game against Wolves.The two discussed deepening defence cooperation and the opportunities and ⁠challenges presented by ⁠artificial ​intelligence. Downing Street said both prime ministers emphasised the importance ​of building close ties with European partners, particularly on trade and defence.The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, although it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, allowing deep economic integration with these countries, who follow many EU rules. However, it remains to be seen what associate membership means, including for Canada’s relationship with the EU single market.Von der Leyen said on Wednesday that it was time to move from cooperation based on trade to a broader “alliance for the future” and bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.“We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project,” she said.She listed energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, cyber and economic security as other fields of cooperation. “This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said.With Agence France-Presse and ReutersExplore more on these topicsCanadaEuropean UnionEuropeDonald TrumpMark CarneyAndy BurnhamUrsula von der LeyennewsShareReuse this content

title: Albanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildings  | Wearable technology | The Guardian
description: Minister for public service says the devices pose ‘legitimate privacy and security concerns’ in commonwealth-run workplaces
Author: Luca Ittimani
Headline: Minister for public service says the devices pose ‘legitimate privacy and security concerns’ in commonwealth-run workplaces
Content: Meta smart glasses. Schools and hospitals run by state governments will be left to set their own rules over the technology.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreenMeta smart glasses. Schools and hospitals run by state governments will be left to set their own rules over the technology.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersWearable technologyAlbanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildingsMinister for public service says the devices pose ‘legitimate privacy and security concerns’ in commonwealth-run workplacesFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastLuca IttimaniThu 17 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 17.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Albanese government is considering a “world-leading”ban on smart glasses in its offices and service centres as councils around Australia push the technology out of public spaces over privacy fears.The government has avoided a sweeping ban on the import of the camera-equipped technology and encouraged individual workplaces to set their own rules.The public service minister, Katy Gallagher, said on Thursday she had asked the Australian public service for advice on whether the glasses should be prohibited.“We need clear and consistent guidance for public servants,” Gallagher said.“Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information.”Commonwealth-run workplaces range from bureaucrats’ offices to Centrelink service centres and CSIRO laboratories.Smartglasses should automatically blur people’s faces while filming, Australia’s online safety regulator saysRead moreSchools and hospitals run by state governments would be left to set their own rules over the technology, which have grown increasingly popular but raised public outcry.A University of Sydney study of smart glasses-filmed videos posted on Instagram found 60% of a sample could beclassified as potential harassment.The Albanese government said it was seeking to set a world-leading standard. So far, no national government has banned the glasses’ use across their agencies.Courts inEngland and Walesin the UK andNew York state inthe US have banned the technology, while the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency reportedlyclassified them as body-worn camerasand barred them from the “federal workspace”.A local council in Sydneyon Tuesdaybecame the latest to issue a targeted bans on the use of the technology. Canterbury-Bankstown’s mayor, Bilal El-Hayek, decried what he called“pervert glasses”as the council barred the wearable tech from public pools.In August, Brisbane city council became the first to ban the glasses from pools and Melbourne’s Yarra city council has banned them from playgrounds, childcare centres and gyms.The City of Sydney and the Blacktown city councils have prohibited pool patrons from using smart glasses to record.Speaking to Channel Seven earlier this month, the federal attorney general,Michelle Rowland, praised councils’ decisionsand said she would consult businesses on their approach.“Businesses know that good privacy is good business,” Rowland said.“But … we want to make sure we get the balance right and we don’t unfairly discriminate against people who are using this technology to better participate in society.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionVision Australia and some people living with disabilities have praised the technology as a support for people who are blind or have low vision. Rowland said the government was not pursuing a ban but had not “ruled anything out”.8:34Could Meta’s ‘pervert glasses’ be banned across the UK? - The LatestGallagher said she wanted the Australian public service to set the national standard as a “model employer”.“Technology is changing rapidly and as a major employer the Commonwealth needs to make sure our workplace policies keep pace,” Gallagher said.Pending restrictions on smart glasses would be the federal government’s latest workplace technology reform after it issued guidance on the use of AI in the public service last week.The guidelines indicate employees would not need to be consulted on every new tool but should be consulted for major initiatives or changes to how they carry out work.Major businesses will contribute to new national guidelines on AI in workplaces, with Commonwealth Bank, Microsoft, AGL, Telstra, Kmart, Blackmores Group and Ramsay Health Care to attend a roundtable on Friday.Amanda Rishworth, the employment minister, said the government wanted to use the roundtable to take on the lessons of businesses already using AI.“Workers and businesses need the capability to adopt new technologies with confidence that appropriate safeguards are in place,” Rishworth said.Additional reporting from Caitlin CassidyExplore more on these topicsWearable technologyAustralian politicsMetaLabor partyAnthony AlbanesenewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Spurs and Villa meet in desperation derby and Andoni Iraola faces test on south-coast return
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Spurs and Villa meet in desperation derby and Andoni Iraola faces test on south-coast return
