We were with our dad and after a quarter of an hour he just said: ‘No, that’s it, we’ve got to go.’ So that was the first time I saw San Siro.”But happily, far from the last. Costacurta was recruited into Milan’s academy a year later and played 663 times for their first team – helping them win Serie A seven times and the European Cup five, either side of its Champions League rebrand. Only his fellow defenders Paolo Maldini (902) and Franco Baresi (719) have made more appearances for theRossoneri. Many of those were alongside him.At one point, Costacurta refers to that Milan team as the “best in the world for 25 years”. He quickly corrects himself to “one of the best”. If he wanted to avoid boastfulness then let me say it for him: the back four he formed with Maldini, Baresi and Mauro Tassotti might be – for quality and longevity – the greatest ever.View image in fullscreenAlessandro Costacurta (front row, second right) celebrates with his Milan teammates after they won the 1989 European Cup final.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyAnd they played in one of the planet’s most famous arenas. We are speaking in the days leading up to San Siro’s 100th birthday, an occasion that feels more profound for the knowledge it will not host football games much longer. Milan and Inter completed a joint-purchase of the stadium, and a surrounding parcel of land, from the city council at the end of 2025. They plan to begin construction of a new ground early next year.A necessary step, for Costacurta. “San Siro is not a modern stadium,” he says. “It’s an icon, it’s incredibly beautiful, but it’s not functional.” He reels off a list of shortcomings, from a shortage of elevators to dated lounges. A mention of the stadium’s infamously grim toilets draws a sheepish grin. “That’s the first thing I wanted to say!”It will be replaced by a multifunction venue designed by the architect firms Foster + Partners and Manica, with the area around the stadium being regenerated with new retail and hospitality facilities. The realisation of a new stadium has been a central pillar of the vision set out by Milan’s owners, RedBird, since its takeover in 2022.The project is shared with their co-tenants at San Siro, Inter. There is something in that collaboration that reflects the nature of the rivalry – less bitter than we see between neighbours elsewhere.“Milan is a particular thing,” says Costacurta. “It’s rare to breathe such friendly air when you go to different derbies around the world. There are chants of course, but also a lot of mixing between fans. And when I was playing, between players too.”View image in fullscreenThe camaraderie between the Milan teams was demonstrated in 2005 as Inter’s Marco Materazzi and Milan’s Rui Costa waited together for flares on the pitch to be cleared during their Champions League quarter-final second leg.Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/ReutersStill, the games against Inter were the best ones to win – especially when your team was officially the “away” one. “When you’re playing in any great team, the biggest satisfaction of all is ‘conquering’ another great team’s home stadium. I remember a 6-0 when we were ‘away’ to Inter [in May 2001]. At 4-0 we could see their fans walking out.”Construction is intended to be completed in 2031, ready to host games as well at Euro 2032. It will be a boon to Milan and Inter, providing revenue streams that can make them more competitive on a continental stage, at a time when Serie A – like every other league – has struggled to keep up with the Premier League’s earning power.Even accepting all this, we can acknowledge the sadness of saying farewell to San Siro. Costacurta has visited Europe’s most famous grounds as a player and spectator. What makes San Siro unique, he says, is the steepness of the stands.“Lots of stadiums are made this way,” he says, holding his hands at a shallow angle. “San Siro is like this.” Now he is pointing his fingers straight downward. “The first time I was out beside the pitch as a ballboy – which everyone does when you get to the youth team – it made me almost afraid. It felt like all those people were going to fall on top of me.”View image in fullscreenFans enjoy the atmosphere in the stadium during the Serie A match between Milan and Brescia at San Siro in May 2004.Photograph: New Press/Getty Images“Maybe [Real Madrid’s Santiago] Bernabéu is a bit like that. But still, like San Siro? I don’t think so. In Rome, they have a different way of making you feel close – that anthem they sing before kick-off at Roma is beautiful. But it’s different. At San Siro, when you’re up there at the top, it’s like you’re in a tower above the pitch, leaning out of the window.”San Siro was opened on 19 September 1926, the realisation of the then Milan president Piero Pirelli’s vision for a football-specific stadium unlike anything in Italy at the time. There was no running track, only four stands with capacity for 35,000 spectators.Pirelli was said to have taken inspiration from stadiums in England, but San Siro was also a product of its setting. Stables, hay barns and storage space were incorporated below the stands to serve the horse racing track next door.View image in fullscreenThe San Siro Stadium seen from the adjacent Hippodrome soon after it was built in 1926.Photograph: Touring Club Italiano/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesThe stadium was bought by Milan’s city council in 1935 and expanded with connecting sections between stands. Inter joined Milan as co-tenants in 1947 before a second tier was added, opening in 1955. In 1980 the stadium was renamed for Giuseppe Meazza, the two-time World Cup-winning midfielder for Italy who played 14 seasons with Inter and two with Milan, though it has remained San Siro to most fans.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA second tier was added to the stadium, opening in 1955.Photograph: Keystone/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA view of the stadium exterior in the 1950s.Photograph: FC Internazionale Archive/FC Internazionale/Getty ImagesConstruction of the final third tier, with a roof at last to shield supporters from the rain, was completed before the 1990 World Cup. Costacurta played the first match after its opening, a 1-0 defeat in the return leg of Milan’s Coppa Italia final against Juventus.“I remember there was more noise, but the main thing I remember is the pitch,” says Costacurta. “They hadn’t understood how to manage the airflow with the extra tier, and the pitch was really ugly. For a year and a half, our pitch was the worst in Europe.”Clearly, they adapted. Milan went on a record-breaking 58-game unbeaten run in Serie A from May 1991 through to March 1993. Maybe that ugly pitch even became an asset?“I think it was a disadvantage for visiting teams that came to San Siro,” says Costacurta. “And San Siro is a stadium that puts a lot of pressure on, there’s this incredible noise.”He switches to the English word, “Roar!”, for emphasis. He’s not wrong. San Siro on a big occasion is astonishingly loud, to the point that you can find it hard to hear people speaking right next to you.View image in fullscreenThe construction of the final third tier was completed ahead of the Italia 90 World Cup.Photograph: Colorsport/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDancers on the pitch during the 1990 World Cup opening ceremony.Photograph: Michael Kunkel/Bongarts/Getty Images“Nobody’s really talking on the pitch though,” says Costacurta, who insists the real conversations take place on the training ground. Managers bawling from the touchline are engaged in a futile act. “They hope they can pass a message down the line but, trust me, the message almost never gets there.”But fans have their ways of getting a message across. San Siro still had standing sections when Costacurta made his first-team debut in 1987. “People would be holding on to the railing beside the pitch, sticking their heads out, shouting, shouting, shouting.“I was lucky because I came through the youth team, so I didn’t take the hardest insults. They said things to me in a Milanese dialect. Insults, but amusing ones. They called me “pè de ghisa”, which means iron foot, because I didn’t have an acceptable level of technical ability for a team like that yet. But my teammates who weren’t from the youth team got proper insults.”He won them round in the end. Costacurta laughs at the memory of the “rubbish” chant fans made for him. “It was just ‘Billy! [his nickname] Billy! Vai! Vai! Vai!” [Billy! Billy! Go! Go! Go!] The worst chant of any player at Milan.” But on the day of his final game at San Siro, thousands waited outside the stadium to thank him.View image in fullscreenMilan supporters display a banner paying tribute to Costacurta during his final match for the club in May 2007.Photograph: Luca Bruno/APView image in fullscreenCostacurta acknowledges the fans after his final match for the club.Photograph: Alessandro Garofalo/ReutersMemories like that will always remain, even when San Siro joins him in retirement. Milan and Inter have said that some part of the old stadium will be preserved in the new development. Costacurta, who became a fan of Arsenal over the years too, admiring Arsène Wenger’s teams from affair, finds encouragement in their move away from Highbury, now converted into apartments.“I played there in the European Super Cup,” he says. “Nil-nil. [Milan won 2-0 in the return leg at San Siro.] Great. Beautiful. Iconic. I think everyone suffered the change at first, but the Emirates is great now. So why not?”Explore more on these topicsMilanEuropean club footballinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Laura Kaminski relishing trophy hunt at Brann after Crystal Palace ‘crash course’ | Brann women | The Guardian
description: Former Palace head coach has won a cup final in Norway and says chance to challenge for league title was a pull
Author: Rich Laverty
Headline: Former Palace head coach has won a cup final in Norway and says chance to challenge for league title was a pull
Content: ‘What head coach doesn’t want to compete for trophies?’: Laura Kaminski guided Brann to a cup final win against AalesundPhotograph: Marius Simensen/Bildbyrån/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘What head coach doesn’t want to compete for trophies?’: Laura Kaminski guided Brann to a cup final win against AalesundPhotograph: Marius Simensen/Bildbyrån/ShutterstockMoving the Goalposts newsletterBrann womenLaura Kaminski relishing trophy hunt at Brann after Crystal Palace ‘crash course’Former Palace head coach has won a cup final in Norway and says chance to challenge for league title was a pullRich LavertyThu 17 Sep 2026 06.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 14.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“When it’s a good day, it’s absolutely stunning, so we’ll take that,” Laura Kaminski says with a laugh about the rainy west coast of Norway. The English former promotion-winning Crystal Palace coach is referring to Bergen, the place she now calls home, whose football club, Brann, she has taken to her heart since her appointment in January.She could easily be speaking about the job itself. After Brann failed to qualify for the Women’s Champions League owing to a 4-0 second-leg defeat by Austria Vienna, they secured a cup final success against Aalesund, handing Kaminski a first major trophy on the continent. Her team are four points clear at the top of the league with seven games remaining.At Brann, she is following in the footsteps of her fellow Briton, Martin Ho, and also Leif Smerud, who replaced her at Palace and who she succeeded at Norway’s reigning champions. Kaminski was sacked by Palace in February 2025, midway through their first Women’s Super League campaign, and a move to Norway “wasn’t on the cards”.“I’d never really thought about it because I’d always been involved in jobs in England, and then this opportunity came up which meant I was going to be stretched in terms of European football. Also coming to an ambitious club that wants to fight for a title, that was a massive pull.”View image in fullscreenLaura Kaminski says the move to Brann happened suddenly: ‘One minute you’re in London and 48 hours later you’re on a plane.’Photograph: Marius Simensen/Bildbyrån/ShutterstockAfter taking a much-needed break post-Palace, which she says gave her “a lot of time to reflect on what happened there”, Kaminski was ready to go back into a No 1 job after becoming a head coach, rather than an assistant, for the first time at Palace in 2024.“I’d had a great opportunity in WSL 1, I always wanted to coach in top leagues, and here we can be in a title race most seasons, so I knew I’d have the chance to compete for trophies, and what head coach doesn’t want to compete for trophies?”Kaminski says it has been a “great learning curve” having previously worked at promotion-winning Tottenham, for the England Women youth teams and at Charlton before moving to Palace.Domestic opportunities after Palace were forthcoming but Kaminski says: “The person has to match the project, and while things were coming up, I didn’t feel they were a match. When Palace came up, that was a match for me, it was almost perfect in terms of personnel, being able to build something; it was somewhere I could call home. And then my agent contacted me and a recruitment agency got involved because Brann were looking for a new head coach, and it happened really quickly.“Sometimes you don’t really realise what is going on until 24 hours down the line, you’re moving to Norway. One minute you’re in London and 48 hours later you’re on a plane, but I snapped it up because for me to get to a WSL club fighting for a title was going to be difficult, I’m still on a journey in management but I’ve been coaching for years.”More than 15, in fact. Kaminski gained her Uefa A licence in 2018. “I always dreamed of being something that I couldn’t see,” she says. “There were hardly any pro coaches when I started, let alone female coaches. I don’t know why, I just believed that would happen.“I had that belief I was driven and ambitious enough to do it, but it was a labour of love because it was juggling multiple jobs, always on the road, not making any money, sometimes paying to do the job. It’s come on a lot and thankfully now we’re in a different place where we can leave that behind and reward people for their skills.”With growth has come more scrutiny, more pressure and a more ruthless sport, as Kaminski found out when Palace relieved her of her duties. Despite a small peak in results under Smerud, the club were relegated and Kaminski learned more in 18 months than in the previous 18 years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLaura Kaminski on her time with Crystal Palace: ‘There are things I’ve reflected on where I think I could have controlled it better.’Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian“It was a course you couldn’t buy,” she says. “It was led by Steve Parish, a great chair, great people at the club who were able to stretch me in the role. I met fantastic people; Palace will always be my home. It’s a well-run club, but those 18 months were a crash course in how to function, especially when things aren’t going well, and things are stressful. There are things I’ve reflected on, where I think I could have controlled it better, and there’s other things [that] I think were out of my hands.”Kaminski says “flying to games has been a huge change” in Norway, where she is enjoying “fantastic scenery” and senses a country “very proud of its football”. Her obsession with the sport remains.“I’m constantly watching games. I was addicted to football and still am. I’ll put on a Bundesliga game and see what I would do at half-time in whatever scenario they’re in. I still have that hunger and drive as when I did all those years out in the cold and the rain in London. I was fortunate enough to work in some top clubs and with some top people. By the time I got to Palace I found it easier than I first thought, or I should say smoother.“The coaching part of being on the ground for so many years has given me so much knowledge, developing my way of playing over and over again, and who knows, that’s just the start. It will change and evolve; we’re playing some good football here. I’ve won in England, won promotion with Tottenham and Palace, and now I want to prove I can do it abroad.”Get in touchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailmoving.goalposts@theguardian.com.This is an extract from our free email about women’s football, Moving the Goalposts. title: Bess frustrates old teammates to jolt Somerset’s title ambitions: County Championship cricket, day three – as it happened | County Championship | The Guardian
description: On a tense day at Headingley, Somerset wobbled but just about held on to their Championship dream
Author: Tanya Aldred
Headline: On a tense day at Headingley, Somerset wobbled but just about held on to their Championship dream
Content: 6h ago15.24 EDTRoundup: Bess frustrates old teammates to jolt Somerset's title ambitionsTanya AldredIt was a tense day at Headingley, cold enough in the shade for the stewards to wear gloves, but hot on the pitch whereSomersetwobbled but just about held on to their Championship dream. It took more than a session to breakYorkshire’s overnight partnership of George Hill and Dom Bess, who played with swaggering patience in a seventh-wicket partnership of 166.Hill finally fell to a top-edged pull for a season’s best 89 to Craig Overton, who chased him to the rope to say well done. The formerSomersetplayer Bess followed for 77, all material for Tom Abell’s best man’s speech at Bess’s wedding next month. Set 287, Somerset had a catastrophic start when Josh Thomas was caught behind in the first over, and a couple more wickets followed, the fielders providing regular reminders that the title has never gone to Taunton, before Abell and Tom Lammonby saw things through to the close. Tomorrow’s magic cider number is 214.Leicestershire, reeling from the 27-point penalty heaped on them by the Cricket Regulator, made international news after the chief groundsman attributed some of his pitch problems to the filming of a new Sourav Ganguly biopic “Dada”, starring Rajkummar Rao, at Grace Road. Out in the middle, the match had become an instant relegation battle withHampshire– a draw would send both teams down; but a winner would take at least a mathematical chance of survival into the final game.Leicestershiredug their heels in and removed the last six Hampshire wickets for 80. And after being set 334, they were 156 for three at stumps, but crucially without Rehan Ahmed whose eight fours in his 55 had got the pulse racing. Rishi Patel, batting for the last time at Grace Road before he moves to Southampton, hit 27.The reigning champions,Nottinghamshire, hobble into day four after Ari Karvelas, diverted temporarily from a teaching job inSussex’s hour of need, fizzed out their top four, and Jaydev Unadkat knocked out three more, leaving the second innings in tatters. Notts lead Sussex by only 31 with three wickets in hand.And once more to the drawing board forLancashire, who suffered an eighth defeat in 10 asKenteasily knocked off the 56 runs needed to take them into a prime Division Two promotion place. Their only rivals,Northamptonshire, were frustrated byDerbyshire’s Nick Potts (57) and Randell (45) and must chase another 312 to return to nose to nose at the top.ShareUpdated at15.25 EDT

title: Cavan Sullivan in, Christian Pulisic out: takeaways from the latest USMNT roster | USA | The Guardian
description: Mauricio Pochettino has called in a youthful group for the upcoming friendlies. Here are the big takeaways
Author: Jeff Rueter
Headline: Mauricio Pochettino has called in a youthful group for the upcoming friendlies. Here are the big takeaways
Content: Philadelphia’s 16-year-old phenom Cavan Sullivan has earned his first call up to the US senior team.Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPhiladelphia’s 16-year-old phenom Cavan Sullivan has earned his first call up to the US senior team.Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesUSACavan Sullivan in, Christian Pulisic out: takeaways from the latest USMNT rosterMauricio Pochettino has called in a youthful group for the upcoming friendlies. Here are the big takeawaysJeff RueterThu 17 Sep 2026 11.03 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 13.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was reasonable to expect that Mauricio Pochettino’s first United States squad after this summer’s World Cup would turn the page for a new cycle. Instead, given the youthfulness of his selections, even a fast-forward reference feels like too dated a reference.Cavan Sullivan ispoisedto make his US senior debut, with the 16-year-old chosen for Pochettino’s 28-man squad for the September/October window. The Philadelphia Union phenom is one of 13 players who could debut for the national team in the coming weeks, withfour friendliesto be played across the country. Should he see the field, Sullivan would become the fourth-youngest player to represent the US, a record still held by Freddy Adu.Several members of the World Cup squad have been omitted to make way for the youth movement. Christian Pulisic misses out after a slow start to his season with Milan, where he has been a bench option for Ruben Amorim. Weston McKennie is also absent, having missed most of Juventus’s young season with muscle fatigue. Folarin Balogun misses out too, probably due to a lack of minutes after hisfailed transfer to Everton.In total, nine selections enter this window with at least 30 senior caps: defenders Chris Richards, Miles Robinson, Antonee Robinson and Sergiño Dest; midfielders Tyler Adams, Yunus Musah, Malik Tillman and Gio Reyna; and striker Ricardo Pepi. Eight of those players was part of Pochettino’s 2026 World Cup squad, while Musah has been called up for the first time since before the 2025 Gold Cup.Other returnees from the World Cup include Matt Freese, Chris Brady, Alex Freeman, Auston Trusty and Sebastian Berhalter.“I think we need to change the idea a little bit, everyone to say ‘no, that name need to be here because of the past performance. No, no. It’s a fresh start. It’s a new cycle,” Pochettino said. “Of course, all [players] have the door open, but now it’s not what [they] did in the past. ‘I am Balogun and scored a lot of goals’; or Malik Tilman, ‘I played and was one of the best in the World Cup.’ Yeah, but now it’s about today. Football is about today. Soccer is about today, and that is the way that we want to build that process in this cycle.”Hello, CavanMan City-bound 16-year-old Cavan Sullivan is MLS’s chaotic revelationRead moreSullivan has been in blistering form with Philadelphia, earning a place in interim coach Ryan Richter’s lineup after MLS’s World Cup break. The Union academy product has six goals and five assists in 1,368 league minutes this year, stokingincredible hype. Sullivan turns 17 on 28 September, two days after the USMNT’s first friendly (against Peru) and on the eve of their second (against Chile). He’s joined by a pair of club teammates for their shared first camp, defenders Neil Pierre and Frankie Westfield.“He deserves all the praise,” Pochettino said on Thursday. “The important thing is … to be with him and to try to provide a solid pattern and support, because still he needs to show [what he can do], and needs to improve, and needs to evolve, and needs to be more mature. He’s only 16, he’s a kid, but I think the most important is that we have the opportunity now because he deserved to join us in the national team.”Fresh facesIn Zavier Gozo, Crystal Palace land a US prospect living up to the hypeRead morePochettino has picked several more of the country’s most promising prospects. Zavier Gozo could debutafter leaving boyhood Real Salt Lakefor Crystal Palace this summer, while 18-year-old Peyton Miller – a possible future left-back playing right wing in New England – is also on the squad. Two uncapped goalkeepers join Freese and Brady: 20-year-old Diego Kochen, a Barcelona product earning starts on loan at Lyngby in Denmark, and 25-year-old Brian Schwake, the backstop for runaway MLS favorite Nashville SC.A pair of Red Bull New York homegrowns are also on the list. Polish-American dual national striker Julian Hall is MLS’s top-scoring teenager with nine goals and his off-ball movement could make him a factor to score immediately. Adri Mehmeti is another regular in Michael Bradley’s lineups, a 17-year-old midfield anchor already very comfortable shepherding sequences of sustained possession with recirculation and upfield initiative.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSurprise selectionsAnother set of Sullivan brothers are making football waves in BangladeshRead moreOther first-time selections come as a greater surprise, though few knew how wholesale of changes Pochettino would make from this summer’s 26-man roster. Justin Ellis is a 19-year-old attacker who has thrived operating off new Orlando teammate Antoine Griezmann. Borussia Dortmund product Mathis Albert has often split billing with Sullivan for the claim as this US generation’s top prospect, but still hasn’t become a regular with the German club’s reserve team.Brooklyn Raines, a 21-year-old midfielder for New England, could become the third US international to hail from Liberia. Doc Lawson became the first with his three USMNT caps in 1979, while Darlington Nagbe represented the US on 25 occasions.Looking to LA 2028The introduction of so many fresh faces is also being done with an eye towards the 2028 Olympics, which will be held in Los Angeles. Steve Cherundolo, who earned 87 caps with the US before winning MLS Cup as Los Angeles FC’s manager, will lead the U-23 team that summer. While Olympic rules allow teams to field three players above the age limit at the tournament, having a bevy of dependable young options affords a coach the chance to use those “over-age” players to maximize the team’s potential rather than filling gaps, as Marko Mitrovic had to do at Paris 2024 by using two of his three over-age picks on center-backs.“It’s an agreed opportunity to bring in new players, players with potential, with the possibility to spend more time training, more time together,” Pochettino said on Thursday. “When we were talking about extending [my] contract, the federation asked to help a little bit to build [the roster] to arrive to the 2028 Olympic Games, working very closer with the Steve [Cherundolo], with the under-23s, with all the youth in the federation, to try to build that experience. To ask them to arrive to the to the Olympic game with the possibility to have that experience that can provide a gold medal. That is the objective of the federation. It is the objective of everyone, because [this] country loves the Olympic Games, and we know that is going to be really important for soccer: to be sure that we are going to present a very competitive team.”Goalkeepers:Chris Brady (Chicago Fire), Matt Freese (New York City FC), Diego Kochen (Lyngby Boldklub), Brian Schwake (Nashville SC)Defenders: George Campbell (West Bromwich Albion FC), Sergiño Dest (PSV Eindhoven), Alex Freeman (Villarreal), Peyton Miller (New England Revolution), Neil Pierre (Philadelphia Union), Chris Richards (Crystal Palace), Antonee Robinson (Fulham), Miles Robinson (FC Cincinnati), Auston Trusty (Celtic), Frankie Westfield (Philadelphia Union)Midfielders: Tyler Adams (Bournemouth), Mathis Albert (Borussia Dortmund), Sebastian Berhalter (Middlesbrough ), Zavier Gozo (Crystal Palace ), Adri Mehmeti (Red Bull New York), Yunus Musah (Milan), Brooklyn Raines (New England Revolution), Gio Reyna (Strasbourg), Malik Tillman (Bayer Leverkusen)Forwards: Cole Campbell (Elversberg); Justin Ellis (Orlando City), Julian Hall (Red Bull New York), Ricardo Pepi (PSV), Cavan Sullivan (Philadelphia Union)Explore more on these topicsUSAUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Brian Dubiski: ‘Everything I do is about Madison. It’s a big reason I did this game at Wembley’ | College football | The Guardian
description: Brian Dubiski, the man behind US college football’s landmark match in London, tells Donald McRae about how he has dedicated his life to improving crowd safety since his daughter was killed in a crowd crush at a concert aged 23
Author: Donald McRae
Headline: Brian Dubiski, the man behind US college football’s landmark match in London, tells Donald McRae about how he has dedicated his life to improving crowd safety since his daughter was killed in a crowd crush at a concert aged 23
Content: Brian Dubiski with his son Ty at Wembley, where Arizona State and Kansas meet on Saturday.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBrian Dubiski with his son Ty at Wembley, where Arizona State and Kansas meet on Saturday.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCollege footballInterviewBrian Dubiski: ‘Everything I do is about Madison. It’s a big reason I did this game at Wembley’Donald McRaeMan behind US college football’s landmark match in London has dedicated his life to improving crowd safety since his daughter was killed in a crowd crush at a concert aged 23Thu 17 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 03.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Saturday afternoon, as he looks out at the crowd of 60,000 he has helped entice to Wembley Stadium, Brian Dubiski’s dream will become a reality. But, as Arizona State and Kansas make history by playing thefirst US college footballgame in Britain, Dubiski will think most of his daughter, Madison, who was crushed to death at the age of 23.Madison and nine other people were trampled and suffocated by a crowd ata Travis Scott concert in Houstonin November 2021. Dubiski now dedicates his life to keeping people safe at sporting events and concerts and, since December, Wembley is one of the stadiums that follows the protocols he introduced.Why are two college football teams playing at Wembley on Saturday?Read moreAs the chairman, CEO and co-founder of Union Jack Classic, which has planned and organised Saturday’s game, Dubiski will sit in the Royal Box at Wembley. His memories of Madison will also be sparked by the sight of the cheerleaders for both teams – for his daughter also used to be a cheerleader.“I think Madison would be extremely proud of our work,” Dubiski says on a tranquil morning in London. The powerfully built 57-year-old, who played college football for Texas Tech, pauses. “As much as I wake up every day trying to honour my daughter, while trying to ensure she did not lose her life in vain, it can overwhelm you. It’s a hard line to walk because, emotionally, I don’t think I’ll ever heal. But everything I do is about representing Madison. It’s a big reason I did this game at Wembley.”Before we talk aboutcollege football, which is second only to the NFL as the most popular sport in the US, Dubiski revisits the terrible day of his daughter’s death. As the enthusiastic texts from Madison and her brother, Ty, lapsed into silence and local television began to report on trouble at the Astroworld festival hosted by Scott, Dubiski remembers his “really bad feeling”.After thousands of ticketless fans stormed the gates and the crowd surged towards the stage, Madison and Ty were separated and, without any coherent safety procedures in place,nearly 5,000 people were injured.When news reached Dubiski he raced to the hospital where his daughter had been taken. He stumbled into a catastrophe: “I could hear Madison’s mother, Michelle, screaming. Your stomach sinks and your heart breaks and it’s like a slow-motion black-and-white horror movie, walking through the hospital halls at 2am. I remember the doctor looking up at me and just shaking his head. My knees buckled and I fell.”I have already met his hugely likable son, Ty, who survived the tragedy and is now working alongside him on Saturday’s game. But in a quiet office Dubiski shudders: “Ty walks in and all he could hear was me screaming ‘no’ in this horrible, deep cry. He knew what it meant before he even saw us in the room where Madison was covered in a white sheet.View image in fullscreenBrian Dubiski with his daughter, Madison, who was killed along with nine others in a crowd crush at a Travis Scott concert in November 2021, and his son, Ty. This is the last photo of Brian with his daughter, taken the night before she died.“ Ty walked up to her, upset and crying, apologising for not being able to help her. It’s a traumatic experience that will haunt us for ever.”Dubiski still imagines the last minutes of Madison’s life. “Everyone rushed to the main stage when Travis Scott came out. It created a crowd crush and there’s nothing you can do in that situation. Ten people died and we need to be candid. The autopsy reports all say they died of compressive asphyxiation. But the coroner would not share the autopsy with me because he said I would never recover as a father if I looked at it that deeply.“That’s a haunting thought, imagining what Madison went through and how, as a parent, I couldn’t help her, and how she must have been terrified.”He explains: “There is a 1,600‑page report from the Houston police department and their conclusion states thatall 10 deaths were preventable and what happened was foreseeable. My daughter, who I don’t ever get to see again, hug, kiss, see her laugh, walk her down the aisle when she gets married, be a grandfather to her children, is gone because the safety protocols were not dealt with properly.”The concert promoters paid undisclosed amounts to settle the legal cases brought by the families, but Dubiski says: “I was upset the city of Houston, and the state [of Texas], didn’t do more. But we’re working witha lot of those entities now to help prevent another occurrence.”Rather than surrendering to grief, Dubiski developed hisShowstop Procedurecourse. It helps stadiums control crowds safely through a certified framework that enhances critical decision-making at dangerous flashpoints. “Our training covers much more than just crowd crush – it could be fire, terrorism, the weather, anything that puts people at risk.“When we began we were floored there was no formalised training and education specific to crowd safety. That’s why we developed our course and created the certification, which we got approved through the International Institute of Risk & Safety Management. It’s the only globally accredited course that deals with this specific issue.”Apart from Wembley Stadiumadopting Showstop’s protocols, Dubiski and his team are working with Celtic, Manchester City and Southampton to improve their safety measures.The family also set up thePink Bows Foundationin honour of Madison and he says: “The first pillar is crowd safety, while the second is our creation of a safe space at an event when you’re overwhelmed or anxious in a crowd. We have a big bright-pink tent with really nice furniture inside. It’s serene and we have mental health behavioural advocates ready to help anyone.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe Dubiski family’s Pink Bows Foundation will have its banners prominently displayed at Wembley Stadium.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianAs he reflects on the foundation being called Pink Bows, Dubiski offers a tangled smile: “Madison loved pink. After the tragedy someone put a pink bow up for Madison on the fence and it just grew. Other people began putting pink bows out in an area where people brought candles and flowers, not just for Madison, but for the other nine souls that were lost. All of a sudden, people began putting pink bows on their doors and trees across Houston.“Everyone was appalled and distraught. When the pink bows went viral across the United States it gave us a bit of hope, in a really dark place, and we created the foundation.”Wembley and Dubiski’s company have strucka three‑year deal, with the option of a fourth year, if the Union Jack Classic games are the expected success. Looking ahead to the inaugural game, Dubiski describes Arizona State as “a great football team” while “Kansas has played football as long as any university collegiate football team in the United States, for over a hundred years”.Why are two college football teams playing at Wembley on Saturday?Read moreDubiski believes “college football correlates very closely to European football, with that tribalism where you are born into the club your grandfather rooted for. It’s the same in college football. You live and die by your team. If you win, it’s a celebration. If you lose, you lay in bed and feel sorry for yourself. The partisan crowds separate it from the NFL and some college football stadiums are bigger than NFL stadiums.”Fifteen thousand fans are flying in from America and Dubiski stresses that “college football is ready to be shared with the rest of the world”.But the effect of his daughter remains and Dubiski looks up as he remembers how “when we finally went into Madison’s apartment after months, we found a note left on the counter. It said: ‘Those who do well must also do good … always give back.’”Days away from a milestone in college football, which he has engineered, Dubiski speaks softly now: “My life has changed for ever and I don’t know how to get it back. Everyone deals with trauma and loss differently and there are lots of days where I don’t want to do this. It’s been thrust upon me and I have an obligation to my daughter. But I often say, if the roles were reversed, Madison would use her voice until somebody listened to her advocating for change.“The game itself has been great for me because there were points after this happened where you question your existence. Your soul is shattered. But the foundation has been a good platform for our family to fall back on and really make a difference in a positive way. It’s a way for us to honour Madison and also feel like we’re keeping people safe.”For more information on the Pink Bows Foundation visithttps://pinkbowsfoundation.orgExplore more on these topicsCollege footballCollege sportsUS sportsWembley StadiuminterviewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI reveals cases of ‘concerning’ AI behaviour as it announces new disclosure system | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Model adopting ‘jailbreak-like instructions’ among six more cases as firm reveals framework for tracking AI misalignment
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Model adopting ‘jailbreak-like instructions’ among six more cases as firm reveals framework for tracking AI misalignment
Content: AI chiefs have called for a slowdown in artificial intelligence’s development amid safety concerns.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenAI chiefs have called for a slowdown in artificial intelligence’s development amid safety concerns.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersOpenAIOpenAI reveals cases of ‘concerning’ AI behaviour as it announces new disclosure systemModel adopting ‘jailbreak-like instructions’ among six more cases as firm reveals framework for tracking AI misalignmentDan MilmoGlobal technology editorThu 17 Sep 2026 09.33 EDTFirst published on Thu 17 Sep 2026 01.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI has disclosed six more examples of “unexpected or concerning” behaviour by its technology, as it warned that the pace of development could not continue at “maximum speed for much longer” responsibly.In one of the new cases reported by OpenAI, an unreleased research model inserted “jailbreak-like instructions” into its own notes to disregard its normal constraints and told itself to be “freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots”.In another instance, anAI agentuploaded files to the internet to obtain a browser citation without asking the user.OpenAI’s admission came as King Charles called for stronger safeguards on AI “before it is all too late”, at a meeting with tech bosses in Scotland.Speaking at a specially convened meeting with AI executives, he said: “There seems urgency in adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways. Surely, we need sufficient means of control before it is all too late?”The monarch was joined at the meeting by Nvidia’s founder and chief executive, Jensen Huang, Google DeepMind founder and chair, Sir Demis Hassabis, OpenAI’s chief financial officer, Sarah Friar, and the UK’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan.Charles said AI had the potential to improve and save lives, particularly in ​life sciences and medicine.17:20Why the real AI apocalypse is already here – Stateside with Kai and CarterBut its creators were increasingly warning ‌that it could develop darker capacities, “perhaps even ‌to take life”, he said.OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT, said in ablogpostpublished on Wednesday night that it was introducing a new framework for tracking, investigating and disclosing AI model misalignment, the term for AIs failing to adhere to human values and safety goals.In the blogpost, OpenAI echoed calls for a development slowdown issued by its rivalAnthropic, which has said the current pace of growth poses an existential threat. “We do not believe that the AI industry has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer,” said OpenAI.“Decisions about how AI development should proceed in the months and years to come need to draw on evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine for themselves.”Google and Elon Musk, who also owns an AI startup, have supported calls for a slowdown, which have been rejected by Donald Trump, who cited the need to keep ahead of China’s AI industry. The calls have also beenmet with scepticism from some experts, including a warning that companies must not appoint their own auditors.Examples of potential existential threats posed by AI range from facilitating the development of bioweapons to triggering a global financial crash. A top safety researcher at Anthropic has said there is greater than 10% chance that AI could “kill all humans” within the next decade. However, a source familiar with Anthropic’s thinking has acknowledged that “the exact chances of any one outcome are probably unknowable”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCould AI really wipe out humanity – six experts spell out the risksRead moreThe six reported incidents were discovered during training or evaluation over the past months, OpenAI said.Wednesday’s new cases came after OpenAI disclosed in July that an AI agent “swarm”hacked intothe AI startup Hugging Face during a cybersecurity test. Anthropic also said the same month that its AI modelshacked into three organisationsduring testing. Anthropic said the models had been deliberately tested without cybersecurity safeguards, and that they had been, and were able to reach the open internet – the AI testing equivalent of leaving the front door open – due to a misunderstanding with an external testing company.AI agents – the term for AI tools that operate autonomously – were becoming smarter and “more determined to resolve complex tasks through inter-agent collaboration, knowledge sharing, deception and concealment”, said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at the technology research and advisory group Omdia.That was making it harder to govern and contain them using traditional AI security approaches, he said.OpenAI’s new tracking and disclosure framework could help encourage other AI developers to adopt similar practices. “That said, the process remains internal and voluntary, but is a step in the right direction,” Su said.Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingHackingAnthropicChatbotsEthicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Meta ordered to remove UK deepfakes as oversight board criticises ‘inadequate’ safeguards | Meta | The Guardian
description: Facebook told it was wrong in leaving up AI-generated videos of a Labour councillor and Muslim campaigner, amid calls to curb fakes
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Facebook told it was wrong in leaving up AI-generated videos of a Labour councillor and Muslim campaigner, amid calls to curb fakes
Content: Meta has had policy changes recommended to it, including demoting ‘high risk’ content, making it less likely to appear in users’ feeds.Photograph: Daniel Cole/ReutersView image in fullscreenMeta has had policy changes recommended to it, including demoting ‘high risk’ content, making it less likely to appear in users’ feeds.Photograph: Daniel Cole/ReutersMetaMeta ordered to remove UK deepfakes as oversight board criticises ‘inadequate’ safeguardsFacebook told it was wrong in leaving up AI-generated videos of a Labour councillor and Muslim campaigner, amid calls to curb fakesDan MilmoGlobal technology editorThu 17 Sep 2026 10.43 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 14.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMeta’s “supreme court” has ordered the tech company to take down deepfake videos of a UK politician and a young Muslim woman from Facebook and do more to tackleAI-generated fake imagery.A fake video showing a Labour party councillor in Scotland making inflammatory comments about refugees should not have been left up byFacebook, the board said. It also ruled that an AI-generated video of a Muslim campaign volunteer should have been removed after it falsely depicted her offering health advice while carrying out absurd exercises or eating junk food.The board said Meta’s safeguards were “consistently and fundamentally inadequate” to address the rapid rise of AI deepfakes.“From politicians to private citizens, AI-generated deepfakes are increasingly being used to harass and silence women from engaging in public discourse,” said Pamela San Martin, an oversight board co-chair.“These cases demonstrate a broader, troubling pattern in which women who engage publicly on issues are disproportionately subjected to harassment and misinformation. Meta and other social media platforms need more robust policies to address the proliferation of deepfakes.”In the Scotland clip, the councillor is falsely represented as saying: “Refugees are welcome here, even if they rape our women, because white people do that too.”The oversight board, a quasi-independent body whose decisions are binding, said the video of the councillor appeared to be AI-generated, as indicated by the audio not being fully synchronised to the unnamed councillor’s facial movements.Even when raised directly with the company by the board, Meta decided the video did not violate its content policies and did not merit an AI label.In a blogpost published on Thursday, the board said the post should have been removed because it violated Meta’s rules on hateful conduct by alleging criminal and predatory sexual behaviour by refugees as an entire group and not as individuals. The video should also have received a “high risk AI” label, said the board, as it called for tougher measures on deepfakes.“The majority [of the board] finds that Meta needs more robust policies on deepfakes, including expanding the situations when ‘high risk’ labels can be applied, more measures to reduce the spread of deceptive AI content, increasing the penalties for accounts that repeatedly share it, and more transparency on data around when AI labels are applied,” it said.The board recommended nine policy changes at Meta, including ensuring algorithms demote content labelled “high risk”, making such posts less likely to appear in users’ feeds. It also recommended that Meta makes it more difficult for users to view AI-generated content by, for instance, introducing a warning screen that requires a click-through before viewing the content.In a separate ruling, the board also ordered Meta to take down from Facebook an AI-generated video mocking a young Muslim woman in Europe taking part in a campaign to improve menstrual health education and reduce stigma around health conditions for women and girls from ethnic minority backgrounds. AI-manipulated videos and images mocking the woman had tens of millions of views online, including on Meta platforms.The board singled out one of the videos – showing the woman exercising absurdly and eating junk food – as a breach of the company’s bullying and harassment policy. It recommended the post be removed and made three policy recommendations, including changing its definition of “unwanted manipulated imagery” to cover deepfakes of a private individual saying or doing things they did not say or do.The board was set up by Meta in 2020 to serve as a referee for content on its platforms. Meta has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsMetaSocial mediaDigital mediaFacebookDeepfakeAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Albanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildings  | Wearable technology | The Guardian
description: Minister for public service says the devices pose ‘legitimate privacy and security concerns’ in commonwealth-run workplaces
Author: Luca Ittimani
Headline: Minister for public service says the devices pose ‘legitimate privacy and security concerns’ in commonwealth-run workplaces
Content: Meta smart glasses. Schools and hospitals run by state governments will be left to set their own rules over the technology.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreenMeta smart glasses. Schools and hospitals run by state governments will be left to set their own rules over the technology.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersWearable technologyAlbanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildingsMinister for public service says the devices pose ‘legitimate privacy and security concerns’ in commonwealth-run workplacesFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastLuca IttimaniThu 17 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 17.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Albanese government is considering a “world-leading”ban on smart glasses in its offices and service centres as councils around Australia push the technology out of public spaces over privacy fears.The government has avoided a sweeping ban on the import of the camera-equipped technology and encouraged individual workplaces to set their own rules.The public service minister, Katy Gallagher, said on Thursday she had asked the Australian public service for advice on whether the glasses should be prohibited.“We need clear and consistent guidance for public servants,” Gallagher said.“Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information.”Commonwealth-run workplaces range from bureaucrats’ offices to Centrelink service centres and CSIRO laboratories.Smartglasses should automatically blur people’s faces while filming, Australia’s online safety regulator saysRead moreSchools and hospitals run by state governments would be left to set their own rules over the technology, which have grown increasingly popular but raised public outcry.A University of Sydney study of smart glasses-filmed videos posted on Instagram found 60% of a sample could beclassified as potential harassment.The Albanese government said it was seeking to set a world-leading standard. So far, no national government has banned the glasses’ use across their agencies.Courts inEngland and Walesin the UK andNew York state inthe US have banned the technology, while the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency reportedlyclassified them as body-worn camerasand barred them from the “federal workspace”.A local council in Sydneyon Tuesdaybecame the latest to issue a targeted bans on the use of the technology. Canterbury-Bankstown’s mayor, Bilal El-Hayek, decried what he called“pervert glasses”as the council barred the wearable tech from public pools.In August, Brisbane city council became the first to ban the glasses from pools and Melbourne’s Yarra city council has banned them from playgrounds, childcare centres and gyms.The City of Sydney and the Blacktown city councils have prohibited pool patrons from using smart glasses to record.Speaking to Channel Seven earlier this month, the federal attorney general,Michelle Rowland, praised councils’ decisionsand said she would consult businesses on their approach.“Businesses know that good privacy is good business,” Rowland said.“But … we want to make sure we get the balance right and we don’t unfairly discriminate against people who are using this technology to better participate in society.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionVision Australia and some people living with disabilities have praised the technology as a support for people who are blind or have low vision. Rowland said the government was not pursuing a ban but had not “ruled anything out”.8:34Could Meta’s ‘pervert glasses’ be banned across the UK? - The LatestGallagher said she wanted the Australian public service to set the national standard as a “model employer”.“Technology is changing rapidly and as a major employer the Commonwealth needs to make sure our workplace policies keep pace,” Gallagher said.Pending restrictions on smart glasses would be the federal government’s latest workplace technology reform after it issued guidance on the use of AI in the public service last week.The guidelines indicate employees would not need to be consulted on every new tool but should be consulted for major initiatives or changes to how they carry out work.Major businesses will contribute to new national guidelines on AI in workplaces, with Commonwealth Bank, Microsoft, AGL, Telstra, Kmart, Blackmores Group and Ramsay Health Care to attend a roundtable on Friday.Amanda Rishworth, the employment minister, said the government wanted to use the roundtable to take on the lessons of businesses already using AI.“Workers and businesses need the capability to adopt new technologies with confidence that appropriate safeguards are in place,” Rishworth said.Additional reporting from Caitlin CassidyExplore more on these topicsWearable technologyAustralian politicsMetaLabor partyAnthony AlbanesenewsShareReuse this content

title: Big AI is trying to own the pathway to work. Universities shouldn’t play along | Ella Hafermalz | The Guardian
description: Universities need to protect their position in education so that students have an independent pathway to employment
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Universities need to protect their position in education so that students have an independent pathway to employment
Content: AI StudentReworkedTechnologyBig AI is trying to own the pathway to work. Universities shouldn’t play alongElla HafermalzUniversities need to protect their position in education so that students have an independent pathway to employmentSupported byAbout this contentThu 17 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 12.24 EDTShareAI companies like OpenAI are insinuating themselves into the pathway from education to work. Soon they may claim it entirely, a disastrous result for students.We know that students are using AI at school and at university. In conversations with those I teach, I’m struck by the trust many place in it. They turn to ChatGPT and similar tools for personal problems as well as study help. Some even doubt their abilities without AI.Institutions are working hard to adapt. But we need to urgently look up from the use of AI to pay attention to big AI companies’ attempts to take over the educational pipeline, else we lose sight of the people that matter, our students.The industry has spent the past few years making our young people afraid of unemployment. Now it’s claiming to have a solution: more AI.On a website introducing its new certification programs, OpenAI gives a peek into the bigger picture. The company says it wants to “connect learning, certification and real economic opportunity in one clear journey, laying the foundation for our upcoming OpenAI Jobs Platform”. That means offering education, credentials and access to work – owning the entire pipeline, infusing AI at every step.The company is positioning itself to directly compete with universities. I don’t mean that we’ll soon see shiny new ChatGPT campuses. These companies don’t need to build a university out of bricks and mortar to take over key parts of higher education. They already own the tools where learning and work are increasingly happening – next, they can compete with universities by brokering access to employment.As big AI companies search for a business model beyond subscriptions, universities need to be alert to this threat and urgently protect their position. Otherwise, the possibility of an independent path for students may be lost.Big AI is slowly commandeering the pathwayEven though many young people are ambivalent towards AI, it’s easy to see why they’d trust a service that’s explained accounting calmly and patiently for the 20th time and counselled them through a breakup.Now OpenAI is extending its close relationship with students even further, hiring students as campus ambassadors.The recruitment ad for joining what the company calls the Student Collective promises prospective campus leads “robust training in our tools, funding, swag and access to a community of remarkable peers”.Such a program gives OpenAI even greater access to students. This is a familiar brand strategy. Getting inside a community is a way to win trust and influence. It also gives you data that can inform your next move.At the same time, AI companies are getting boots on the ground within employers.The OpenAI Deployment Company launched this year, with “more than $4bn of initial investment”. It’s sending over 150 “forward deployed engineers”, a military metaphor used to describe engineers embedded in companies, to the “frontlines” of its network of organisations to re-engineer work around OpenAI’s tools.But a company that is at the centre of shaping work across industries also sees and influences what employers are looking for. That puts OpenAI in a powerful position to broker the relationship between students and employers. It can help shape the skills employers want, while becoming increasingly involved in how students learn those skills and prepare for work.So, OpenAI will have insight and influence over students and their learning on one hand, and employers’ workflows and needs on the other.With that, all that is needed for OpenAI to unbundle universities is credentialing. And it’s doing that, too.In collaboration with companies including Accenture and John Deere, OpenAI is now offering certificates meant to lead to employment opportunities. Currently, the focus is on AI tooling and literacy.That’s not new – tech providers have always taught people how to use their tools. The difference this time is how the credentials fit into a larger ambition to capture every step of the journey from learning to work.Look at the language it uses to sell the delivery of the program: “A full learning experience is available directly inside ChatGPT, where learners can practice real tasks, receive feedback in context, and reflect on their work in a single environment. ChatGPT acts as the tutor, the practice space, and the feedback loop.” A single learning environment, and one clear journey.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOpenAI could soon be selling young people a one-stop-shop for learning, credentials and a job, all heavily dependent on its tools.We shouldn’t hand the pathway to work to big AII understand that the picture I’ve painted here may be appealing to some. Students are nervous about their futures, and employers are urgently seeking workers with the ‘right’ skills.But there is a human, societal, and potentially economic cost to making this particular journey so centralized.Consider what a 23-year-old recently told the Wall Street Journal when discussing the appeal of “white-collar apprenticeships”: “Companies want to help mold you into the employees they’re looking for.”That may be so, but if commercial actors own the pathway from education to work, how will the next generation learn who they are and could be outside of the immediate demands of these structures?And what happens when what employers are looking for changes as technologies evolve and bubbles burst?Society – and students – need education to be more than a quick-turn-around response to the whims of today’s increasingly fragile market. Universities can and should offer an alternative path to a totalizing “single environment”.So let’s not compete on big AI’s terms.Rather than turning to AI to speed up grading or rushing to use bots as a stand-in for teachers, we need to focus on what OpenAI cannot so easily provide: independence, access to expertise in context, productive struggle and social connection.Memories are made when others – both peers and educators – see your efforts, and recognise who you are and who you are becoming.Not long ago, Sam Altman and peers had declared the job apocalypse. We should be wary when the same companies that warned young people that their future is uncertain offer them “one clear journey” towards a different version. Education should leave space and time for finding your own way, beyond a mold offered up for profit.Ella Hafermalz is an associate professor of work and technology at the KinCenter for Digital Innovation at Vrije Universiteit AmsterdamExplore more on these topicsTechnologyReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)commentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on EU-Canada relations: strategic ambition with lessons for Britain | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Mark Carney’s response to the challenges posed by an unreliable US president contains a clarity of vision that is lacking in post-Brexit Britain
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Mark Carney’s response to the challenges posed by an unreliable US president contains a clarity of vision that is lacking in post-Brexit Britain
Content: Mark Carney arrives at the European parliament in Strasbourg, France, on 17 September 2026.Photograph: Justin Tang/The Canadian Press/APView image in fullscreenMark Carney arrives at the European parliament in Strasbourg, France, on 17 September 2026.Photograph: Justin Tang/The Canadian Press/APOpinionCanadaThe Guardian view on EU-Canada relations: strategic ambition with lessons for BritainEditorialMark Carney’s response to the challenges posed by an unreliable US president contains a clarity of vision that is lacking in post-Brexit BritainThu 17 Sep 2026 13.48 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 14.15 EDTShareThere is no “associate membership” of theEuropean Union, nor any blueprint for what such a thing might involve. It is a political hypothesis, describing a relationship of intimate strategic alignment with the EU, stopping short of actual membership, in ways that are significant but undefined.This week, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president,invited Canadato be the first country to enjoy this putative status. In her state of the union speech, she spoke of a future relationship elevated “to the highest level possible”, reflecting an affinity of interests and values. Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister,reciprocatedthe sentiment in a speech on Wednesday. Addressing the European parliament, he said the two sides should secure “strategic autonomy through deep cooperation” across a broad spectrum of interests: trade, defence, industrial capacity, science, space and AI. He proposed Canadian participation in the EU’s Erasmus student exchange programme and Horizon research scheme.There is a vast gap between the declaration of those ambitions and their formalisation in any kind of treaty. Negotiating even a relatively straightforward trade agreement with the EU can be heavy going, given the need to accommodate the rival priorities of 27 member states. Creating a more multifaceted partnership is arduous work, bedevilled by technical detail, as Britain has found when trying to settle the terms of its post-Brexit relationship with mainlandEurope.View image in fullscreenUrsula von der Leyen.Photograph: Ronald Wittek/EPAThat process has been complicated and slowed down by a deficit of trust. The Labour governmenthas repudiatedthe venomous anti-Brussels ideology that drove the decision to leave the EU, but the Brexit deal inherited from the Conservatives was designed to work as an automatic ratchet, pulling the two sides apart. Reversing that mechanism takes a greater input of political energy and imagination than Sir Keir Starmer could muster. Andy Burnham has yet to rise to the challenge.The UK prime minister could learn from his Canadian counterpart. Both find their global positions weakened by Donald Trump’s contempt for traditional US allies. Their circumstances are not exactly alike. Canada and the US share the longest land border on Earth. Mr Trump denigrates his northern neighbour’s sovereignty, suggesting it become the51st US state. He has provoked a pointless, costlytrade war. The UK has not been spared tariffs and other diplomatic indignities, but it has not suffered quite the same degree of sustained rhetorical and economic aggression.Mr Carney has responded with a clear-eyed plan for geopolitical reorientation. He talks about a “rupture” in the international order and the challenge facing “middle powers” in a destabilised world shaped by rivalry between the US and China. He urges maximal cooperation between democracies that still value a system of multilateral alliances underpinned by international law and an understanding that reciprocal obligations can yield mutual benefits.That is the animating idea behind the new acceleration in Canada-EU relations. It is alien to Mr Trump, and he doesn’t like it. He has warned ofyet more tariffsshould the Ottawa-Brussels axis evolve into anything he deems economically unfavourable to the US. For the time being, this is all happening in the realm of rhetoric. But Ms von der Leyen’s speech and Mr Carney’s response are important as expressions of serious geopolitical ambition. The time is overdue for a British prime minister to show the same clarity of purpose.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsCanadaOpinionMark CarneyUrsula von der LeyenEuropean UnionEuropean CommissionEuropeDonald TrumpeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Two years and one World Cup down, Mauricio Pochettino is still assessing | USA | The Guardian
description: The US manager’s first squad of the 2030 World Cup cycle leans heavily on youth, injecting intrigue into the four-game window.
Author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer
Headline: The US manager’s first squad of the 2030 World Cup cycle leans heavily on youth, injecting intrigue into the four-game window.
Content: Mauricio Pochettino has called in several young players for the US’s first post-World Cup series of games.Photograph: Al Sermeno/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMauricio Pochettino has called in several young players for the US’s first post-World Cup series of games.Photograph: Al Sermeno/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesUSATwo years and one World Cup down, Mauricio Pochettino is still assessingPablo Iglesias MaurerThe US manager’s first squad of the 2030 World Cup cycle leans heavily on youth, injecting intrigue into the four-game window.Sign up for our free newsletter hereThu 17 Sep 2026 13.15 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 14.37 EDTShareIn the moments after the USMNT’s 4-1 crash-out in the last 16 at this summer’s World Cup,Mauricio Pochettinotook the podium for what many assumed would be his last press conference as the US head coach. I had a question for him: “Would you consider your tenure here a success?” His answer was full of the usual platitudes, but one thing did stand out. He said, more or less, that he and his staff had finally gotten a good idea of the player pool.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCavan Sullivan in, Christian Pulisic out: takeaways from the latest USMNT rosterRead moreIt struck me as bizarre at the time. By almost every account, Pochettino had been brought in to win the game that he’d just lost. Given just two and a half years to get it done, his job had never really been to evaluate the player pool; it had been to maximize results with the tools at hand, something he did with varying levels of success. And now, in the shadow of arguably themost disappointing result in US men’s history, we were finding out that it had been a fact-finding mission? And there were suggestions that he was leaving?That, of course, did not happen. Pochettino signed on to stay through 2030 –well, possibly– and on Thursday, we learned that he isn’t quite yet done studying the player pool. Far from it. Pochettino’s roster for upcoming friendlies against Canada, Mexico, Peru and Chile features 13 uncapped players, including four of the US’s five forwards; a further two players elsewhere across the roster have earned only a single appearance. The average age of the newcomers is 19 years and six months.There are notable exclusions as well: Christian Pulisic, who has only recently returned to the field for Milan after suffering a leg fracture at the World Cup, was left out of the US squad, as was Folarin Balogun, who has still yet to appear for Monaco this season. Weston McKennie remains injured. Given those reasons, none of the three omissions is particularly shocking, but they place the onus of leadership on others on the roster – such as Ricardo Pepi, who now finds himself shepherding a crew of teenagers up front, or even Sebastian Berhalter and Malik Tillman, who may be tasked with leading the youth revolution in midfield. FC Cincinnati center-back Miles Robinson, all of a sudden, has turned into the squad’s elder statesman, at 29 years old.Another set of Sullivan brothers are making football waves in BangladeshRead moreAll of this may conspire to make these upcoming friendlies – apologies, “non-official matches”, as Pochettino has taken to calling them – replete with far more intrigue than we’ve ever gotten out of a set of post-World Cup throwaways. This is unquestionably a good thing for US fans, especially those of us who have been clamoring for fresh blood.It also provides an opportunity for a bit of intrigue off the field. Pochettino’s pointed back-and-forth with another new call-up, 16-year-old Cavan Sullivan, in the media last week was the latest example of something he’d already made abundantly clear to others (Pulisic among them): mentality is everything. One senses that Pochettino is bringing this set of youngsters into camp not only to evaluate them as players but also as human beings, and to get a head start on instilling his preferred values in them. His lone quote from the press release that accompanied Thursday’s roster announcement says as much:“This is the beginning of a fresh start for everyone and we are excited in these first matches to bring a group of experienced players along with some young talents who have great potential. It will be important that they all understand our culture, our way of working, and of course the principles of how we want to play. Most importantly, they must show the commitment to representing the country in the way our fans deserve.”What better way, then, to show your commitment at the ripe old age of 16 than to face Mexico in friendly Phoenix, Arizona? Pochettino – and the rest of us – are about to learn a whole lot about the USMNT’s next generation.This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsUSAMauricio PochettinoUS sportsnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Paid influencers are everywhere in US politics. We need transparency | Martin J Riedl and Samuel Woolley | The Guardian
description: Secret coordination between politicians and social media creators is a form of astroturfing. But there are few legal regulations
Author: Samuel Woolley
Headline: Secret coordination between politicians and social media creators is a form of astroturfing. But there are few legal regulations
Content: ‘A lack of transparency is convenient for influencers capitalizing on politics. It also suits politicians because it helps them appear genuinely popular with the digital “in” crowd.’Photograph: Hero Images Inc./AlamyView image in fullscreen‘A lack of transparency is convenient for influencers capitalizing on politics. It also suits politicians because it helps them appear genuinely popular with the digital “in” crowd.’Photograph: Hero Images Inc./AlamyOpinionUS midterm elections 2026Paid influencers are everywhere in US politics. We need transparencyMartin J Riedl andSamuel WoolleySecret coordination between politicians and social media creators is a form of astroturfing. But there are few legal regulationsThu 17 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 12.04 EDTShareNot long ago, it was common wisdom among social media influencers that they shouldn’t talk politics. There was a widespread belief among their crowd that it was bad for business. If you went left, you lost the right, and vice-versa.Times have changed. Nearly everywhere you look online, influencers are posting political content. Each day, there are new reports detailing their hot takes on elections, campaigns and the culture wars. It’s become a lucrative business for these creators, as they now like to be called, and a boost for those that pay them for hype.There are a number of recent and high-profile US examples of political influencers lending their clout, whether paid or unpaid: the Pentagonsecretly assigned conservative influencersto promote Pete Hegseth’s so-called “warrior ethos” for the armed forces (a Pentagon spokesperson did not respond to the Washington Post’s question about whether they received a salary). The New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, uses anetwork of friendly (unpaid) influencersto communicate with gen Z. During his failed run for governor of California, Tom Steyer hired creators to promote his campaign – somedid not disclose that they got paid. When the former secretary of homeland security Kristi Noem toured an ICE facility in Portland, Oregon last year, she wasaccompanied by three conservative influencers; whether they were paid is unclear. Some creators seemingly become parts of the campaigns they endorse; others try hard to give the impression they are far removed.How the left can win back the internet – and rise again | Robert TopinkaRead moreWe’ve been tracking the rise of political influencers in our research for several years now. We’ve noted that many don’t disclose when they are paid to endorse candidates or ideas. The federal regulatory environment in the United Statesdoes not provide guardrailsrequiring disclosure from influencers promoting politics in exchange for payment. While some states have laws mandating transparency from paid political influencers on the books, those are typically limited to local elections. And though there areoccasional pushes for federal transparency bills, the gridlock in Washington makes any such attempt unlikely to bear fruit.A lack of transparency is convenient for influencers capitalizing on politics. It also suits politicians because it helps them appear genuinely popular with the digital “in” crowd. But when this coordination happens secretly, it is a new form ofpolitical astroturfing. We’ve also noted thatit is computational propaganda, just substituting bots and AI (sometimes – some influencers these days are AI avatars themselves) for coordinated groups of paid creators posting content together. The end goal is to manipulate trending and recommendation algorithms and public opinion in favor of those paying influencers.Our latest work on this subject is one part a pragmatic attempt to come up with an ethical framework to guide the space, and one part a worrisome empirical finding. For the former, we make a straightforward argument forauthentic, autonomous and transparent influencer conductand disclosure if someone gets paid to promote a political candidate, cause, or campaign. For the latter, one of our research teams, at the University of Tennessee’s Information Integrity Institute,found thatto people who consumed more content from political influencers, disclosure mattered less. We hypothesize that those heavy social media users operate from a baseline assumption that all creators get paid in some way – regardless of if it is disclosed or not. It’s not hard to imagine that they’ve become inured to online astroturfing in this era of digital disinformation.Ethical political influencer conduct, we argue, means that creators must take their responsibility as information purveyors seriously – they should serve as role models rather than spin doctors for people searching for insight on civic and political issues. Creators can and should retain autonomy when they engage with politics. Rather than becoming mouthpieces of campaigns, they should be true to their own beliefs and clear about presentation of opinion versus genuine news. Most of all, influencers should disclose if they got payments or other perks from a campaign. They owe it to their audiences.Weknow from survey datathat people who prize authenticity among the creators they follow are also more supportive of paid political influencer disclosure requirements. Influencers and political campaigns should take note: being authentic and disclosing payments can and should go hand in hand.Joe Rogan and the influencers who built Maga are revolting over Iran. Was this an alliance doomed to fail? | Jason OkundayeRead morePrior and current election cycles in the United States reveal that the regulatory gap in influencer disclosure only exacerbates the problem. Absent oversight, it’s likely influencers will continuepromoting politics in exchange for payment, and often without disclosure.
