Creators are vital in today’s media ecology in shaping public opinion on political issues, candidates and campaigns – but when they covertly work as paid propagandists, they degrade an already struggling information ecosystem rather than build it up. This might yield short-term financial gain, but it’s a poor long-term approach to business. People are already overwhelmed by AI slop and falsehoods online. If even some influencers continue along this current path, all risk becoming lumped in with these other forms of junk content – they lose the impact of the carefully constructed candor and inventiveness that drew people to them in the first place.If Congress won’t act to preserve democratic communication and election integrity, what’s left is to directly appeal to those who bankroll political influencer operations or have sway over the online ecology – campaigns, influencer marketing companies, social media platforms, and creators themselves. Some may be willing to change, but others helped to create the current state of affairs in the first place.That said, influencers who make a good-faith effort to pick up and follow the principles of authenticity, autonomy and acknowledging payment could do a lot to improve the integrity of political communication, especially around elections, crises and other significant events. Such action would help voters understand if those who speak loudest online do so because they genuinely care, or because they are getting paid to do so.Martin J Riedl is an assistant professor at the University of Tennessee’s School of Journalism and Media and a senior fellow at theInformation Integrity Institute. He researches political influencers, journalism, and platform governanceSamuel C Woolley is the author ofManufacturing Consensus: Understanding Propaganda in the Era of Automation and Anonymityand several other books on computational propaganda. He is an associate professor at the University of Pittsburgh and directsPitt CTRLExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionSocial mediaUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Robert Kraft, once the NFL’s good guy, is just another billionaire silencing Macklemore | NFL | The Guardian
description: The Patriots owner’s decision to ban the rapper from performing at the team’s stadium brings back memories of the blackballing of Colin Kaepernick
Author: Howard Bryant
Headline: The Patriots owner’s decision to ban the rapper from performing at the team’s stadium brings back memories of the blackballing of Colin Kaepernick
Content: Robert Kraft stands next to Donald Trump at the Kennedy Center.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersView image in fullscreenRobert Kraft stands next to Donald Trump at the Kennedy Center.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersNFLRobert Kraft, once the NFL’s good guy, is just another billionaire silencing MacklemoreHoward BryantThe Patriots owner’s decision to ban the rapper from performing at the team’s stadium brings back memories of the blackballing of Colin KaepernickThu 17 Sep 2026 09.14 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 11.02 EDTShareSix years ago, in the middle of a “racial reckoning” that never was, a White House that had begun out of control reached its chaotic apex. Federal officials were sweeping citizens off American streetsin unmarked vehicles, surrounding the Lincoln Memorialwith armed guardsand rolling military vehiclesthrough residential neighborhoodsin a fascist reaction to protests against the murder of George Floyd. It was at this point that NFL commissioner Roger Goodell, realizing it had all gone too far, appeared on a Zoom andadmitted his league was “wrong”for not listening to its players when they had protested against police brutality.The implication was clear: more than any other sports league, the NFL was harshest in its reaction tothe proteststhat began with Trayvon Martin in 2012 and continued with Ferguson, Baltimore and Colin Kaepernick. By blackballing Kaepernick, sitting by while broadcast partnersrefused to air the national anthemto undermine the protests, and, most embarrassingly, Goodell’s draconian announcement that teamswould be subject to finesif players showed dissent, the NFL had proven itself to act in the most un-American of ways.Colin Kaepernick knelt 10 years ago. America responded with a clear warning to Black people | Howard BryantRead moreThis week, New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft showed he has learned nothing from those years.He banned Macklemorefrom supporting Ed Sheeran at the Patriots’ Gillette Stadium over the rapper’s vocal support for Palestine – something that has become a career-threatening political position as dangerous as kneeling during the national anthem. Kraft imposed his own version of authoritarianism:Macklemore claimsthat Kraft not only banned him from his stadium, but appeared to influence other NFL owners to stop the rapper from appearing at most of Sheeran’s other stadium dates. For his part, Kraft says his decision to stop Macklemore from performing at Gillette was due to both Macklemore’s “recent actions” and “a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community”. In 2014, Macklemoreapologizedafter he wore a wig, beard and hooked nose at a Seattle concert, which critics said was an anti-semitic caricature.No NFL owner has worked harder to be seen as reasonable and socially conscious as Kraft. He has appeared on the surface as a shrewd businessman, power-neutral, making political donations to Republicans and Democrats alike. New Englanders recall him fondly as the man who rescued the Patriots from the misogyny and vile incompetence of the Victor Kiam years; from the threat of the team relocating to St Louis when he bought the Patriots from James Orthwein in 1994; and, of course, the man whosaved them from all the losing.Kraft was eventually given the benefit of the doubt as the hero in his stadium battle againstdisgracedformer Massachusetts legislature speaker Thomas Finneran that nearly led to Kraft moving the Patriots out of the Commonwealth. He did so by buildingthe only 100% privately financedstadium in the NFL – even though in 1998 Kraft himself had agreed to take a lucrative offer of public money from the Connecticut legislature and move the Patriots to Hartford. It was under Kraft’s ownership – led by his late wife Myra – that the Patriots took a stand for women, renouncing the rights to Christian Peter a week after drafting him, when multiple domestic violence accusations and convictions against the player surfaced.As the NFL collectively destroyed Kaepernick’s career (the former quarterback saysthe same tactics of collusion are now being used against Macklemore), it was Kraft who tried to appear sympathetic to those who suffered under systemic racial injustices. HesupportedPatriots Devin and Jason McCourty in their advocacy of criminal justice reform,helped the releasefrom prison of rapper Meek Mill, and following the deadly 2018 school shooting in Parkland, Florida,loaned the Patriots’ planeto students traveling to Washington to protest gun violence. Despite a president whocalled the pandemic a hoaxand encouraged citizensto inject bleachto immunize themselves against the coronavirus, Kraft sent his private plane to Chinato help transport shipmentsof N-95 masks to the United States. Bob Kraft has always believed he’s one of the good guys.In theMacklemoresituation, he is not. While he has been lauded by his supporters, all Kraft has done is follow a familiar script of a rich man applying power. He has undermined his everyman persona as a guy who sat on the cold metal seats at Schaefer Stadium alongside his fellow Patriots fan but was fortunate enough to eventually buy the team. Now he is just another billionaire using his power to stifle words – to do exactly what his fellow owners did to Kaepernick a decade ago. Nor should it be forgotten that no matter how many rappers treat Kraft like the cool old white dude, Bob Kraft, hater of hate speech, lover of peace, is a prominent part of a league that conspired to ban a player from playing football for telling the truth:cops are getting paid leave for killing people. That’s not right.Hardly hate speech.The end result is an old man threatened, unable to maintain the facade that he is any different, any better, than the moral rot around him. While truth often belongs to those who get to tell the tale, who control the airwaves, who get to do the blackballing and destroy the careers, it also belongs to the silenced. Both the overstepping Kraft and the tattered Sheeran – whose supporting actshave resigned from the tourin solidarity with Macklemore – know that now. One looks like a dictator, the other a wimp.Kraft is also displaying a perverse, pervasive strain of American exceptionalism normalized by Donald Trump where might makes right. His supporters have attempted to argue that Kraft hasn’t violated the first amendment over Macklemore because he owns Gillette Stadium, the land under it and paid for it with his money rather than with public funds that would be better spent on potholes, bridges and better schools. Along those narrow grounds, Kraft can certainly decide who gets to say what on his property – although even that argument is a specious one if he cares about community and not oligarchy. By then extending his influence from his private bubble of Foxborough to allegedly use that influence to blackball Macklemore from the rest of Sheeran’s tour by calling ahead to Philadelphia, Dallas, Tampa, Charlotte, Indianapolis and Atlanta, Kraft engaged in yet another collusion, for each of those venues are largely publicly financed. They do not belong privately to Kraft, or the rest of the football oligarchy, but to the taxpaying public. Public space is protected by the first amendment. Kraft has either forgotten what the pregame flags and flyovers are supposed to be about, or like so many other foundations in this country, has simply decided to stop caring.Where does Kraft stand today? The lover of peace and hater of hate speech is now backpedaling, remembering his position as one of the good guys, offering to throw money at the bad publicity –he suggested he would pledge $2m to unspecified charitiesin the Middle East without reinstating Macklemore – but he really stands with Trump, that most seasoned practitioner of hate speech,who once calledKaepernick and the NFL players who smash their bodies into a million pieces every Sunday “sons of bitches”.Kraft gave Trump $1m for his first inaugurationthen said in 2024that he hadn’t spoken to the presidentsince the January 6 attack on the Capitol.But there he satthis January in the Kennedy Center presidential box next to Trump for a screening of the Amazon Studios bomb Melania. As Trump petulantly destroys the arts, Kraft’s wife Dana Blumbergsits on the Kennedy Center board, part of the unanimous voteto close the centerunless Trump’s name is added to the building. Kraft has his name on another blackballing, but he’s headlining the marquee this time. For people who decry anti-democratic behavior, the Krafts seem comfortable in its company and quick studies at mastering it themselves. They’ve had a lot of practice.Howard Bryant is the author of 11 books, including Full Dissidence: Notes from an Uneven Playing Field, and Kings and Pawns: Jackie Robinson and Paul Robeson in America.He also writes on SubstackExplore more on these topicsNFLNew England PatriotsMacklemoreEd SheeranUS sportscommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump says the US doesn’t need Canada. But it’s the source of key minerals for the military | Vince Beiser | The Guardian
description: Trump himself has acknowledged the US need for Canadian aluminum – and has largely exempted metals from tariffs
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Trump himself has acknowledged the US need for Canadian aluminum – and has largely exempted metals from tariffs
Content: ‘It’s not only the US military that depends on Canada’s minerals.’Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘It’s not only the US military that depends on Canada’s minerals.’Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersOpinionCanadaTrump says the US doesn’t need Canada. But it’s the source of key minerals for the militaryVince BeiserTrump himself has acknowledged the US need for Canadian aluminum – and has largely exempted metals from new tariffsThu 17 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 14.35 EDTShareAs trade talks with Canada shambled toward collapse in late August,Donald Trumpbrayed on Truth Social: “WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!” But in fact, Canada, like China, has something the US needs badly: critical metals that undergird modern military technology.Canada is the United States’s biggest foreign source of minerals, supplying about$47binworth each year.Sixty per centof all the aluminum the US uses each year, for instance, comes from Canada, where mighty, remote rivers provide smelting plants vast quantities of cheap,low-carbonelectricity. The US military uses the lightweight metal foreverything fromshell casings to ship hulls and aircraft fuselage. The Pentagon’s cutting-edge F-35 fighter jet’s airframe is about40%aluminum. “This country desperately needs aluminum,” Trump complainedlast month. “We get it all from Canada for the most part, and we need it badly.”Trump’s clash with Canada is his latest imperialistic embarrassment | Sidney BlumenthalRead moreThat dependence explains why the USquietly exemptedalmost all metals from the list of Canadian products subject to the new 50% import levies. But just because Americans want to keep buying Canadian metals doesn’t mean Canada will keep selling them.Shortly after trade talks collapsed last month, the Ontario premier, Doug Ford, threatened to cut offnickel exportsif the tensions heat up further. Nickel is a vital ingredient in the steel alloys that go into jet engines and armor plating for vehicles and ships, not to mention a wide range of industrial products. The US gets about half of its supply from Canada. The US has only a single nickel mine, but no refineries – so even the raw ore from that one lonely mine gets sent to Canada to be refined, and then sold back to US companies.Thepremier of British Columbiahas also suggested that his province could ban exports to the US of germanium, which is used to make military equipment such asnight-vision goggles and laser rangefinders, as well as solar panels and fiber optics. That would present a real problem to US manufacturers, since China, which produces the bulk of the world’s germanium, has already largely stopped selling that metal to the US.China has alsorestricted exportsto the US of gallium, an ingredient in high-performance computer chips that power missile defense and radar systems. The US doesn’t produceany primary galliumat all. But anew gallium plantis slated to open next year in, yes,Canada.And it’s not only the US military that depends on Canada’s minerals. Canada also supplies US nuclear reactors with much of theuraniumthey use to generate nearly a fifth of the country’s electricity. Even the US’s food supply is propped up with Canadian minerals. Almost90% ofthe potash, a crucial fertilizer, that US farmers spread on their fields comes from their northern neighbor. (It’s a similar story withpeat, another agricultural input.)Of course,Canadaisn’t the only place that has these materials. The US has deposits of many of them, too, and is trying to rebuild its once-mighty domestic critical metal industries. But getting the financing and regulatory approvals needed to open a single new mine in the US takes years, and the metals that come out are often more expensive than those produced elsewhere.The US could also turn to non-Canadian foreign suppliers. But that would require a hugely expensive project of unravelling cross-border supply chains that have been built up over decades and support countless US jobs, and rebuilding them to more distant countries. In any case, the alternatives aren’t all that appealing. The US’s second-biggest source of potash is Russia – not exactly a trading partner most countries would choose to rely on. And the world’s biggest producer of most of the critical metals the US needs happens to also be its biggest rival: China. This is precisely why the US has for the last several years been pushing to build up a supply chain of critical metals that isn’t under Beijing’s control.Trump’s ridiculous bullying of Canada is backfiring | Robert ReichRead moreClearly, someone has explained all of this to Trump since last year, when he was threatening to tariffeverythingcoming from Canada. He’s learned that the US can’t afford to lose its supply of Canadian critical metals – especially at a time when China is already throttling exports of those badly needed commodities. That’s why they’ve been exempted this time around.But Canada knows it too. Cutting off metal supplies would seriously escalate the trade war, and would be a painful punch to Canada’s economy. But it has been proven to be a very effective weapon. Among many other commodities, China produces approximately 90% of the world’s refined rare earths, another set of minerals vital to military and other technologies. When Trump threatened China with tariffs last year, Beijing responded by threatening to ban exports of rare earths and the magnets and other products made from them. The US quickly backed down. Canada’s leaders took note. As Ontario’s Ford warned recently: “Everything’s on the table.”Vince Beiser is the author ofPower Metal: The Race for the Resources That Will Shape the Futureand thePower Metal newsletter.Explore more on these topicsCanadaOpinionTrump tariffsCritical mineralsDonald TrumpTariffsUS foreign policyTrump administrationcommentShareReuse this content

title: Bad news this week for Trump – but Fox viewers might have missed it | Margaret Sullivan | The Guardian
description: The network continues to cater to its presidential ‘audience of one’, downplaying his supreme court loss and more
Author: Margaret Sullivan
Headline: The network continues to cater to its presidential ‘audience of one’, downplaying his supreme court loss and more
Content: ‘The network often looks the other way when news comes along that might disturb its viewers.’Photograph: Yuki Iwamura/APView image in fullscreen‘The network often looks the other way when news comes along that might disturb its viewers.’Photograph: Yuki Iwamura/APOpinionFox NewsBad news this week for Trump – but Fox viewers might have missed itMargaret SullivanThe network continues to cater to its presidential ‘audience of one’, downplaying his supreme court loss and moreThu 17 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 13.59 EDTShareTwo breaking stories roiled US politics this week and immediately got big play on most news sites.The supreme court surprisingly rejected – for now – Donald Trump’s attempted restrictions on mail-in ballots, a blow to Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections.And the investigative site ProPublicarevealedthat a Russian oligarch had helped to bankroll the Bahamas wedding of Trump’s son Donald Jr, to the tune of hundreds of thousands of dollars. The blockbuster story quickly became ProPublica’s most-read article this year and was covered heavily elsewhere.“There’s no looking away from this Trump scoop,”wroteCNN’s Brian Stelter.Unless you watchedFox News, of course. There, it was business as usual.No conspiracy, no mystery, just a gift from a Russian oligarchRead moreThe wedding blockbuster got barely a nod on Monday night: a mere minute on the rightwing network’s evening programming, as the progressive non-profit watchdog Media Mattersreported.It was much the same for the vote-by-mail story.“The news broke during the 7 p.m. hour, but Laura Ingraham, a law school grad, didn’t bother to tell viewers,” Stelter noted. Neither did the other big-name Fox opinion hosts, Jesse Watters and Sean Hannity.You would have had to wait until 11.30pm for that 45-second report, Stelter wrote, even as it was a leading story in many other places.In subsequent days, Fox paid more attention to both stories, but mostly to hand the megaphone to Trump’s trashing of the justices who didn’t give him what he demanded.double quotation markFox News often looks the other way when news comes along that might disturb its viewersFox News has long billed itself as the more balanced alternative to mainstream media, an antidote to what Trump constantly slams as “fake news”.But in fact, the network often looks the other way when news comes along that might disturb its viewers, who still number in the millions during primetime hours.“This is the ‘negative space’ of Fox News coverage, in which they pretend something is simply not happening,” Matt Gertz, who tracks Fox News at Media Matters, told me.“Trumpian corruption is the biggest part of this,” Gertz said. Thus the endless self-dealing and self-enrichment of Trump, his family and his allies are subjects left to others.Don Jr’s wedding falls squarely into this category.Normal news outlets are concerned withinformingtheir audience.Fox’s network stars and executives have a different priority.“They are concerned with coddling their audience and maintaining the GOP’s political power,” as Gertz put it.They are also concerned with how Trump views the network and what he says about individual hosts or pieces.This is the well-known “audience of one” syndrome. Trump sometimes complains about Fox, but there’s little doubt that he’s watching closely, as he posts segments and praises individual hosts.The Fox News viewer, to some extent, is in a bubble and happy to stay there.This shows up in polls like a new one fromAxios, in which 53% of respondents said the word “corrupt” describes Trump more than any other quality. (That’s followed by “dangerous”, “out of touch” and “cruel” – not exactly a rave review by the American public.)But an astonishing 23% said “corrupt” doesnotdescribe him. These people don’t seem to know about the cryptocurrency schemes, the insider trading, the pay-to-play pardons and the lavish gifts such as a $400m jet from Qatar.Or, of course, the Russian oligarch, close to Putin, who was somehow moved to finance a Trump son’s wedding.Why is Trump’s $5,000 offer to voters ‘like a woman’? Ask Fox News | Arwa MahdawiRead moreHow could theynotknow? They could simply have their heads in the sand.Or they couldthinkthey’re staying informed while watching Fox as it once again explores its favorite primetime topics – race and gender in the WNBA, panic over commie Democrats, the evils of socialism and the troubles that come with illegal immigration.But some subjects do fall out of favor.Fox’s primetime hosts, who egged on Trump’s Iran war months ago and made it a favorite topic, have now added that quagmire to their “ignore it and maybe it will go away” list.Why?Because it’s unpopular and upsetting.Of course, so is Trump himself, which raises the vexing question of Fox’s exit strategy from the president the network has supported so diligently and helped at nearly every turn.No Fox, no President Trump, one might argue.But now, Trump, with his bottom-dwelling approval ratings and waning power, looks more and more like a problem for the network.So far, though, he’s one problem that Fox refuses to ignore.Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and cultureExplore more on these topicsFox NewsOpinionDonald TrumpDonald Trump JrUS supreme courtUS television industryTV newscommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s love of fossil fuels is about more than money | Moira Donegan | The Guardian
description: The US decision to remove limits on coal and gas plant emissions is rooted in a perception of manliness in these industries
Author: Moira Donegan
Headline: The US decision to remove limits on coal and gas plant emissions is rooted in a perception of manliness in these industries
Content: ‘If there is a single throughline in Trump’s actions and priorities, it is his reverence for the most brutish and regressive form of masculinity.’Photograph: Carolyn Kaster/APView image in fullscreen‘If there is a single throughline in Trump’s actions and priorities, it is his reverence for the most brutish and regressive form of masculinity.’Photograph: Carolyn Kaster/APOpinionTrump administrationTrump’s love of fossil fuels is about more than moneyMoira DoneganThe US decision to remove limits on coal and gas plant emissions is rooted in a perception of manliness in these industriesThu 17 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 09.14 EDTShareYou can impress a certain kind of person at a party by reciting the fact that there are more yoga instructors in the US than there are coalminers. In fact, the disparity is greater than this catchy phrasing suggests: there are actually more yoga instructors in the US than there are people employed in the entirety of the coalmining industry, miners and otherwise. It’s not even especially close: about 38,000 people in the US work in coal, according to theBureau of Labor Statistics, compared to about 100,000 yoga instructors who areregisteredwith the Yoga Alliance, an industry group.If you looked only at the numbers, you might think a politician would be incentivized to talk about the interests of the yoga industry, about the dignity that yoga jobs give to American families, or about the need to foster growth in the yoga industry, more than they talk about these things for coal; after all, yoga, not coal, is putting food on the table in more American households. But no politician would ever talk about the interests of yoga teachers, or wax poetic about their role in the American dream, the way they do with coal miners; if they did, they’d be laughed out of the room. And we all know why: yoga is thought of as decadent, cosmopolitan and feminine, while coal mining is imagined as hardscrabble, honorable and masculine.The Iran war reminds us: we’ll never be energy-independent with fossil fuels | Lloyd Doggett and Michael ShankRead moreThis was at the forefront of my mind this past weekend when the EPAannounced that it would lift limitson carbon emissions from coal- and gas-burning power plants, a reversal of Biden and Obama era climate policies. It’s just the latest in a long line of energy industryderegulation effortsby the Trump administration, which has also loosened or removed limits on carbon emissions fromvehiclesandhousehold appliances; in 2022, the Republican-dominatedsupreme court ruled, in a six to three decision along party lines, that the EPA lacks the independent authority to regulate carbon at all.Some of the motivations for the Trump administration’s pro-carbon, anti-green policy postures have to do with cold, hard cash. Fossil fuel companies have given a staggering amount to Trump over the past several years, with energy companiesdonating at least $75mto his campaign, in addition to large personal donations from executives. They’ve kept the money flowing since. Oil and gas companies donatednearly $12mto Trump’s 2025 inauguration fund, and have continued making large contributions to Trump affiliated Pacs. At least $25m hascome just fromone oil firm, Energy Transfer Partners, and its CEO. The industry and its major power brokers may see these contributions as a way to purchase a favorable regulatory environment; when he solicited contributions from the energy industry during his 2024 campaign, Trumpcharacterized their donationsas part of a “deal”.But part of Trump’s love of fossil fuels – and his accompanying hostility to climate change mitigation, green initiatives, and nature conservation – might be less transactional than libidinal. Because to him, part of the appeal of climate-destroying, future-inhibiting, polluting energy industries is not merely that their executives are writing him checks. It’s that he sees these industries, and these forms of energy consumption, as more manly.This is the theory put forth by the Virginia Tech professor Cara Daggett, whose2018 paper“Petro-Masculinity: Fossil Fuels and Authoritarian Desire” has become something of a cipher for political observers, eager to understand the Trump administration’s commitment to dirty energy even at the cost of the country’s competitive advantage (China, for instance, hassurpassed the US in solar panel productionat an alarming rate). For Daggett, much of the American right’s energy policy posture is not explainable by recourse to strictly material measures: it requires a psychological explanation. To them, she argues, oil, gas and the lifestyle markers and forms of consumption that they enable – think cowboy hats, broad asphalt highways, and big trucks parked before a field of swinging pumpjacks – represent an ideal of American manliness and dominance whose symbolic power has become a meaningful obstacle to a US energy transition. In other words, the Trump administration isn’t just committed to doubling down on America’s reliance on oil and gas because those are the industries that enrich their donorsand friends. They’re also committed to fossil fuels because they see them as manly, and understand green energy, by contrast, as effeminate.If this sounds too stupid to be plausible, remember that this is Donald Trump we’re talking about. His policy decisions are not the result of a complex weighing of benefits and liabilities, or a sober assessment of competing interests: they are decisions based on gut feelings and often motivated by obscure resentments. Trying to articulate ideological coherence in the man is a bit of a fool’s errand: he has no discrete ideological worldview and seems to operate largely on impulse and id. But if Trump has no ideology, he most certainly has a psyche. If there is a single throughline in Trump’s actions and priorities, it is his reverence for the most brutish and regressive form of masculinity: his admiration for those who dominate and humiliate their rivals, his desire to punish those he sees as weak, his contempt for responsibility, his ostentatious recklessness towards the wellbeing of others or the prospects for the future. It might sound childish, but that’s by design; Trump, after all, is the man who sat inthe cab of a semitruckon the White House lawn, blowing the horn like a sugared-up kindergartener. Responsibility is for grown-ups, which, in his mind, means it is for wimps.Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionUS Environmental Protection AgencyClimate crisisUS politicsFossil fuelsOilOil and gas companiescommentShareReuse this content

title: Big AI is trying to own the pathway to work. Universities shouldn’t play along | Ella Hafermalz | The Guardian
description: Universities need to protect their position in education so that students have an independent pathway to employment
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Universities need to protect their position in education so that students have an independent pathway to employment
Content: AI StudentReworkedTechnologyBig AI is trying to own the pathway to work. Universities shouldn’t play alongElla HafermalzUniversities need to protect their position in education so that students have an independent pathway to employmentSupported byAbout this contentThu 17 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 12.24 EDTShareAI companies like OpenAI are insinuating themselves into the pathway from education to work. Soon they may claim it entirely, a disastrous result for students.We know that students are using AI at school and at university. In conversations with those I teach, I’m struck by the trust many place in it. They turn to ChatGPT and similar tools for personal problems as well as study help. Some even doubt their abilities without AI.Institutions are working hard to adapt. But we need to urgently look up from the use of AI to pay attention to big AI companies’ attempts to take over the educational pipeline, else we lose sight of the people that matter, our students.The industry has spent the past few years making our young people afraid of unemployment. Now it’s claiming to have a solution: more AI.On a website introducing its new certification programs, OpenAI gives a peek into the bigger picture. The company says it wants to “connect learning, certification and real economic opportunity in one clear journey, laying the foundation for our upcoming OpenAI Jobs Platform”. That means offering education, credentials and access to work – owning the entire pipeline, infusing AI at every step.The company is positioning itself to directly compete with universities. I don’t mean that we’ll soon see shiny new ChatGPT campuses. These companies don’t need to build a university out of bricks and mortar to take over key parts of higher education. They already own the tools where learning and work are increasingly happening – next, they can compete with universities by brokering access to employment.As big AI companies search for a business model beyond subscriptions, universities need to be alert to this threat and urgently protect their position. Otherwise, the possibility of an independent path for students may be lost.Big AI is slowly commandeering the pathwayEven though many young people are ambivalent towards AI, it’s easy to see why they’d trust a service that’s explained accounting calmly and patiently for the 20th time and counselled them through a breakup.Now OpenAI is extending its close relationship with students even further, hiring students as campus ambassadors.The recruitment ad for joining what the company calls the Student Collective promises prospective campus leads “robust training in our tools, funding, swag and access to a community of remarkable peers”.Such a program gives OpenAI even greater access to students. This is a familiar brand strategy. Getting inside a community is a way to win trust and influence. It also gives you data that can inform your next move.At the same time, AI companies are getting boots on the ground within employers.The OpenAI Deployment Company launched this year, with “more than $4bn of initial investment”. It’s sending over 150 “forward deployed engineers”, a military metaphor used to describe engineers embedded in companies, to the “frontlines” of its network of organisations to re-engineer work around OpenAI’s tools.But a company that is at the centre of shaping work across industries also sees and influences what employers are looking for. That puts OpenAI in a powerful position to broker the relationship between students and employers. It can help shape the skills employers want, while becoming increasingly involved in how students learn those skills and prepare for work.So, OpenAI will have insight and influence over students and their learning on one hand, and employers’ workflows and needs on the other.With that, all that is needed for OpenAI to unbundle universities is credentialing. And it’s doing that, too.In collaboration with companies including Accenture and John Deere, OpenAI is now offering certificates meant to lead to employment opportunities. Currently, the focus is on AI tooling and literacy.That’s not new – tech providers have always taught people how to use their tools. The difference this time is how the credentials fit into a larger ambition to capture every step of the journey from learning to work.Look at the language it uses to sell the delivery of the program: “A full learning experience is available directly inside ChatGPT, where learners can practice real tasks, receive feedback in context, and reflect on their work in a single environment. ChatGPT acts as the tutor, the practice space, and the feedback loop.” A single learning environment, and one clear journey.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOpenAI could soon be selling young people a one-stop-shop for learning, credentials and a job, all heavily dependent on its tools.We shouldn’t hand the pathway to work to big AII understand that the picture I’ve painted here may be appealing to some. Students are nervous about their futures, and employers are urgently seeking workers with the ‘right’ skills.But there is a human, societal, and potentially economic cost to making this particular journey so centralized.Consider what a 23-year-old recently told the Wall Street Journal when discussing the appeal of “white-collar apprenticeships”: “Companies want to help mold you into the employees they’re looking for.”That may be so, but if commercial actors own the pathway from education to work, how will the next generation learn who they are and could be outside of the immediate demands of these structures?And what happens when what employers are looking for changes as technologies evolve and bubbles burst?Society – and students – need education to be more than a quick-turn-around response to the whims of today’s increasingly fragile market. Universities can and should offer an alternative path to a totalizing “single environment”.So let’s not compete on big AI’s terms.Rather than turning to AI to speed up grading or rushing to use bots as a stand-in for teachers, we need to focus on what OpenAI cannot so easily provide: independence, access to expertise in context, productive struggle and social connection.Memories are made when others – both peers and educators – see your efforts, and recognise who you are and who you are becoming.Not long ago, Sam Altman and peers had declared the job apocalypse. We should be wary when the same companies that warned young people that their future is uncertain offer them “one clear journey” towards a different version. Education should leave space and time for finding your own way, beyond a mold offered up for profit.Ella Hafermalz is an associate professor of work and technology at the KinCenter for Digital Innovation at Vrije Universiteit AmsterdamExplore more on these topicsTechnologyReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)commentShareReuse this content

title: We terminated a pregnancy so our daughter never had to suffer. It cannot be the right of One Nation to choose for us | Anonymous | The Guardian
description: We must defend – ardently, passionately, implacably – the right of parents to decide, in whatever circumstances they find themselves
Author: Anonymous
Headline: We must defend – ardently, passionately, implacably – the right of parents to decide, in whatever circumstances they find themselves
Content: ‘Our daughter was real. We knew she was there; we saw her moving in the ultrasounds; we dreamed of meeting her.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Our daughter was real. We knew she was there; we saw her moving in the ultrasounds; we dreamed of meeting her.’Photograph: AlamyOpinionAbortionWe terminated a pregnancy so our daughter never had to suffer. It cannot be the right of One Nation to choose for usAnonymousWe must defend – ardently, passionately, implacably – the right of parents to decide, in whatever circumstances they find themselvesThu 17 Sep 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 18.34 EDTShareIt felt like a cliche out of a medical drama. We huddled together in the ultrasound room, marvelling at the shadow of our baby moving on the screen in the darkness; behind us, the technician quietly left the room “just to check some numbers”. The wait stretched out; five, 10 minutes. When she finally returned, a more senior doctor in tow, we knew something was horribly wrong.Several sleepless nights and tear-filled days later, we had our diagnosis. Our daughter had a genetic syndrome – not inherited from either of us but a completely random genetic error that occurred during cell division – that put her chance of living until birth at something close to 1%. Even if she were safely born, she could never have children of her own without drastic intervention and would require medical care throughout her life – care we could not afford to provide.The choice that was presented to us was horrendous.Those words are insufficient. We stared at the walls and moved through our days in a daze, in a fog of confusion and fear. The bright sun and beautiful weather became mocking, cruel. After fighting so long to become pregnant, we had been struck by a curse, a one-in-a-thousand fluke of nature, a bolt from the blue that destroyed our lives. But we had to face the reality of the situation: a week after the diagnosis, tearful and worn out, we terminated the pregnancy.One Nation’s lurking attachment to the fringe anti-abortion movement sounds like the start of a horror movie | Van BadhamRead moreNow imagine all of that but you cannot even begin to find and centre yourself, to begin to breathe again, let alone heal; all of that but now you have no control over your own body – thanks to One Nation and anti-abortion activists. Perhaps you will have to outrun yet another time limit – this time with criminal penalties attached – or jump states or even countries to regain some small semblance of control over your own lives, your own fates. (In the US, where such activists are ascendant, these are not mere hypotheticals but very real situationsmany families find themselves in.)The likes of Barnaby Joyce and Pauline Hanson want to pretend their stances – as extreme as they already are – are the conciliatory, reasonable, measured options. Certainly, our circumstances (a termination for medical reasons made before 20 weeks) would not have been affected by One Nation’sofficialpolicy on restricting abortion access.On Wednesday the party’s New South Wales leader,Mike Newman, saidits policy on abortion was “clear” and he had “made a mistake” when he told a rally that he wanted abortions to “stop”. But his initial comments and the presence of Malcolm Robertsat a gathering this yearwhere a preacher called women who have had terminations “murderers” are telling.One Nation’s stance more broadly is alreadyemboldening anti-abortion activistswhose explicit goal is to outlaw abortion entirely. And if Roberts is merely a loose cannon, or Newman simply misstated and obfuscated what One Nation’s “clear” policies actually are, then party discipline is so weak it doesn’t matter what the leader says – only what its most extreme elements desire.And it’s not just One Nation: the Libertarian John Ruddick introduced legislation in the NSW upper house to criminalise sex-selective abortions.Newman saidhe would support the bill’s principles in parliament. Thankfully it was voted down in the Legislative Council on Wednesday.At a time like this, those policies don’t offer compassion, warmth or empathy; instead, they call us killers and would have forced us to carry our baby until she died. We are infuriated by the re-emergence of this issue, ofour pain, of our grief and suffering, as a political football. This is not a game; this is our reality.So-called “pro-life” advocates are anything but. For those born in circumstances incompatible with the living of a good life, will they be there to offer a helping hand? Or does their devotion to the sanctity of life begin and end with taking control of the lives of others and forcing them to live a hell not of their own making?No parents should have to make the decision that we had to make. But nor should their ability to choose be stripped from them.There is an unjust perception that those who choose termination are monsters, or unfeeling robots, who don’t think of foetuses as children or potential people. But our daughter was real. We knew she was there; we saw her moving in the ultrasounds; we dreamed of meeting her, discovering her smile, her joys and her fears and laughter and good days and bad, and of guiding her to experience all that is good and wonderful in this world.We take on this suffering so she never has to suffer.We must defend – ardently, passionately, implacably – the right of parents to choose, in whatever circumstances they find themselves.At the heart of every decision to terminate a pregnancy is this simple recognition: the family has judged themselves unable or unwilling to devote the time, care, resources and attention to keep a child healthy and happy. And that is theirs to judge and to feel the crushing weight of. It cannot be the right of Hanson, of Joyce, of Roberts, of Newman or any anti-abortion activist to choose for us. It belongs to those closest to the pain.In Australia, support is available atBeyond Blueon 1300 22 4636,Lifelineon 13 11 14, and atMensLineon 1300 789 978The author lives in SydneyExplore more on these topicsAbortionOpinionOne NationAustralian politicsHealthNew South WalesNew South Wales politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Australia’s approaching summer fills me with dread. I’m not equipped to battle 40C  | Rebecca Shaw | The Guardian
description: When people say they love the heat, I presume they either have air conditioning or are lying
Author: Rebecca Shaw
Headline: When people say they love the heat, I presume they either have air conditioning or are lying
Content: ‘If you’re a summer lover (slight slur), someone who doesn’t sweat or who likes feeling overheated and burned and dehydrated, good for you.’Photograph: Glenn Campbell/AAPView image in fullscreen‘If you’re a summer lover (slight slur), someone who doesn’t sweat or who likes feeling overheated and burned and dehydrated, good for you.’Photograph: Glenn Campbell/AAPOpinionAustralia weatherAustralia’s approaching summer fills me with dread. I’m not equipped to battle 40CRebecca ShawWhen people say they love the heat, I presume they either have air conditioning or are lyingThu 17 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 20.24 EDTShareAs a cultured citizen of the globe (social media), I am witness to a lot of different opinions about the weather throughout the year. I will soon be sharing my own, as Sydney weather begins to warm, triggering my dread of the hot months to come.As the cold mornings start to ease, and everyone and their hot mothers start to post from the beach, I see friends overseas shivering in fear at the fast-approaching winter, when they will then shiver from the cold. Anytime and anywhere cold months happen, people post about having Sad. Not having sad, which is what I call my depression, but Sad – seasonal affective disorder.For some of these people it is a genuine mood disorder, and some are being hyperbolic (in the way that a portion of people who just like their things to be neat claim to have OCD) – but the point is that there is a common language for people who get miserable in winter. There are products that cater to the winter-haters. There are special lamps and alarm clocks that mimic outdoor light (not to mention heaters), and I’m glad people have the support to get through it.Europe’s summer emergency was a dire warning for Australia. What can be learned before it’s too late? | Nick RowleyRead moreBut you almost never hear about the reverse – the people whose spirits, not just skins, shrivel in the hot sun.When I complain about the heat, which I do often and loudly, people occasionally comment that I should be used to it, being from Queensland. This might be true for most Queenslanders, however I am from Toowoomba, a place that sits 700 metres above sea level, remaining cooler than most.It’s not that I don’t enjoy warm weather, or get sick of cold weather. I’m normal. My perfect weather is 26C, blue sky with a few clouds and a slight cooling breeze. But in Sydney, on this ever-hotter planet, I experience this perfect weather for approximately two weeks of the year. Then it tips into uncomfortably hot, then unbearably hot, and finally into maybe I want to die hot. Sure, there are fun parts in there. There are happy friends, being outside, beers, being outside with friends having beers, and most importantly, stone fruit. A perfectly ripe peach offsets approximately three hours of doom feelings.But the fun things about summer are really only fun if you can get some relief, and if you can get some sleep.This is where air conditioner privilege comes in. I have never lived in a house with air conditioning. When people say they love summer, I presume they either have air conditioning or are lying. If you sleep in air conditioning, wake up in air conditioning, drive your air-conditioned car to your air-conditioned workplace and then to the beach and then back to your air-conditioned home, of course you bloody love summer. You get to dip in and out of it, while people like me are sticking to every surface, draping wet towels over fans that blow warm air around, gilding ourselves with frozen peas, lying in cold baths, lurking extensively in bottle-o cold rooms, going to movies we would never otherwise pay to see, mopping our brows and boobs and various crevices, and generally debasing ourselves in various ways to feel a sliver of coolness on our disgusting sweaty skins.The heat affects my mood, and not in a good way. The second I wake up in smothering heat, I dread the day. I am not built for this. I am from Scottish and Irish stock; I shouldn’t be under the Australian sun, getting burned in places I didn’t even know the sun could see. I should be shivering in a shawl in the mud with some sheep. I should be in the pouring rain getting inspiration for my sad and yearning folk songs. Colonisation isn’t just a violent blight on humanity, it’s also just really stupid of us.Admittedly, I have never experienced a winter anywhere but Australia. I am sure my distaste and anguish over 40C days would be slightly mitigated if I experienced long stretches of 5C days. I’m sure I would start to feel a bit gloomy and yearn for the Australian heat. But in my current reality, it’s much easier to get warm than cold. I can live in my badly insulated rotting house, not built to withstand any weather at all, and put on socks and jackets and get into bed with my hot-water bottle (girlfriend). But I am not equipped to battle the heat that is coming, and certainly not the worse heat that is coming after that, and the worse heat after that (climate crisis).If you’re a summer lover (slight slur), someone who doesn’t sweat or who likes feeling overheated and burned and dehydrated, good for you. But spare a thought for those of us that will be Sad about it.Rebecca Shaw is a writer based in SydneyExplore more on these topicsAustralia weatherOpinionClimate crisiscommentShareReuse this content

title: Watching NAZA was like peering through a window – and seeing the machinery of killing in Gaza  | Mahmoud Mushtaha | The Guardian
description: I now know that the only difference between life and death may have been an AI algorithm, says Mahmoud Mushtaha, a Palestinian journalist from Gaza
Author: Mahmoud Mushtaha
Headline: I now know that the only difference between life and death may have been an AI algorithm, says Mahmoud Mushtaha, a Palestinian journalist from Gaza
Content: Palestinians search for missing people under the rubble of a destroyed house following Israeli air strikes on Deir Al Balah, 22 February 2024.Photograph: Mohammed Saber/EPAView image in fullscreenPalestinians search for missing people under the rubble of a destroyed house following Israeli air strikes on Deir Al Balah, 22 February 2024.Photograph: Mohammed Saber/EPAOpinionNAZAWatching NAZA was like peering through a window – and seeing the machinery of killing in GazaMahmoud MushtahaFor so long I wondered why I survived while family and friends were killed. Now I know the only difference between life and death may have been an AI algorithmThu 17 Sep 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 14.15 EDTShareThe lights go down, and for a moment I forget I’m watching a screen. It fills with a rooftop in Tel Aviv at night, black and grey. The camera pans down. Through windows, we see people watching screens of their own – couples holding each other close, following the news, eating food. They appear absorbed in their own worlds, and why wouldn’t they be?That’s the thing I can’t get past as a Palestinian journalist fromGaza, watching this apparent tranquillity: this must be it – this must be what safety actually looks like. Just an evening uninterrupted, with no military aircraft flying overhead or drones buzzing incessantly. Meanwhile, men and women on the rooftop above them calmly talk about how they decided how many Palestinian civilians would die on any given night.These are the soldiers, mostly intelligence officers, who helped Israel carry out its destruction of Gaza. Theirtestimonies form the basis of NAZA, a documentary whose title comes from an Israeli military acronym used to indicatehow many civilians are likely to die in an airstrike on the territory.What surprised me in the film wasn’t the massive scale of the killing, or even the coldness of it, but the proficiency of the soldiers who coolly described destroying people’s lives as if they were discussing a routine errand. One described the work simply as a “mission”, while another compared it to a “video game”.One soldier described knowing exactly what some of the people were doing in the moments before he killed them. He recalled hearing a man talking to his wife in bed. A baby crying. The sound of the TV. Despite taking all that humanity in, he quickly gave permission to drop the bomb.The soldier explained how he would then go out with friends in the evening, and come back the next morning to do it all over again. For these Israeli soldiers, killing Palestinians was simply a task that could be paused and repeated.There was no hesitation in their voices, no sense that they were describing something that should be difficult to say aloud. They spoke with the ease of people who had learned how to do this, how to talk about it and how to carry on afterward – as one of them put it, with “zero” consideration for the lives they annihilated.NAZA makes visible the targeting systems and planning decisions that precede a strike. But this is only part of the story.Some of the perpetrators were on the ground in Gaza, where the same violence became much more immediate as they moved through Palestinian neighbourhoods, entering homes, setting them on fire and enforcing “kill zones”.Yet for every act shown on film, there are many others that were never recorded and so will never be reckoned with – the constant surveillance, the restrictions on movement, the displacement of entire populations. NAZA opens a small window into the machinery of killing in Gaza, but it is something much larger than any film can capture.View image in fullscreenA scene from NAZA, a documentary produced by the Guardian and directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.Photograph: The GuardianThroughout the screening, I could not stop myself from putting names back into the places where the film placed numbers. When one soldier described how Israeli forces massacred Palestinians at aid distribution sites, I thought of my cousin, 35-year-old Raed Majed Mushtaha, killed in the “Flour Massacre” in early 2024 as he searched for food for his family. I remembered my friend Youssef Maher Dawas, killed in the first week of the genocide, whose body was later found beneath rubble.Other soldiers described how the army authorised the killing of 20 civilians in pursuit of a single junior target, and as many as 500 in pursuit of a senior target. These targets, however, had predominantly been “incriminated” by an AI system that, the soldiers admit, was known to err in about 15% of cases – yet they killed them anyway, along with their whole families.I felt stuck on that. I thought about my uncle, Hisham Zafer Mushtaha, his wife, Hanan, their sons, Basel and Mohammed, and their four grandchildren, Raged, Hisham, Lana and Abdrahman, aged between three and 12 years old. I imagined them being killed because an AI algorithm assumed there might be a target there.For the soldiers, these moments are merely part of a daily “mission”. But Raed, Youssef, Hisham, Hanan, Basel, Mohammed, Raged, Hisham, Lana and Abdrahman were people I knew and loved, whose calls I waited for, whose absence will for ever be felt.For so long, I had asked how these people I knew were killed. Watching the film, my mind kept returning to the opposite question: how did I survive? I had spent so much of my life in Gaza thinking that, because I did not belong to any faction, I would be safe. I believed that if Israel was justifying its killings to the world by portraying those it killed as military targets, then I would make it out alive, because I was not one of them.But the difference between me and the people I’ve lost may have been nothing more than what an AI algorithm flagged, and what someone decided, through a screen in Tel Aviv, would be an acceptable amount of NAZA. I realised, perhaps for the first time, that there was no precaution that I could have taken that would have guaranteed my survival. The fact that I did survive was completely random. And when I think about that, my heart sinks.What I want, watching this, is not catharsis. I have had enough of that. I want to attach names to the soldiers themselves – the ones who said it was “fun” to destroy Gaza, who viewed Palestinians in Gaza as mere data points. This is the only way that the “systematic” nature of Israel’s killing machine stops functioning as a shield, one that allows those responsible to feel as if they were mere cogs.When the film ended, I called my family in Gaza, as I do every night. I have rung them often to tell them where to move and which road to avoid, hoping to keep them safe amid the ongoing senseless destruction. But having watched the film, I kept thinking about surveillance and systems that track their movements and could turn them into targets.But sitting there after the film, a new thought took over: what if the soldiers watching them know more about where my family are than I do? What if they can see what I cannot? My family might be sitting together, drinking tea, laughing at something one of my brothers said, while, somewhere far away, those same moments could already be data on a screen.And as I spoke to them that night, for a moment I forgot everything I had seen in the film. I did not hear coordinates, or surveillance, or AI. I heard my family. A familiar voice. A breath. And I understood, in that moment, what these systems can never account for: that each person on the screen is an entire world unto themselves.After its screening at the Venice film festival,the film received a 25-minute standing ovation– an indictment, I couldn’t help thinking, of a western media that spent three years treating Palestinian journalists as unreliable narrators of our own deaths. A room rose to its feet, but that has not stopped the machine: the bombing hasn’t stopped, the machine on screen is still running even as the credits roll.I’m glad the testimony exists; glad it’s believed now. But belief this late, costing us this much, is not safety. My people do not feel safer because a film about their killers received applause in a theatre they will never sit in.Mahmoud Mushtaha is a Palestinian journalist from Gaza, and the author of Sobrevivir al genocidio en Gaza (Surviving the Genocide in Gaza). title: British people understand the climate crisis threat. Today I’m empowering them to tackle it  | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: With nearly £30m of funding, I’m giving communities power over local energy. They know the gravity of global heating, and they want to be part of the solution, says UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Author: Andy Burnham
Headline: With nearly £30m of funding, I’m giving communities power over local energy. They know the gravity of global heating, and they want to be part of the solution, says UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Content: Solar panels being fitted on a roof in Wales.Photograph: Chris Howes/Wild Places Photography/AlamyView image in fullscreenSolar panels being fitted on a roof in Wales.Photograph: Chris Howes/Wild Places Photography/AlamyOpinionEnergyBritish people understand the climate crisis threat. Today I’m empowering them to tackle itAndy BurnhamWith nearly £30m of funding, I’m giving communities power over local energy. They know the gravity of global heating, and they want to be part of the solutionAndy Burnham: UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050Thu 17 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 15.59 EDTShareOn the day I became prime minister,I pledged to bring power to every postcode. Today, we begin to make good on that promise in the most literal sense. With nearly £30m of funding for People’s Power projects, communities across every nation of the UK will soon have the chance to build and control their own clean energy supply.This investment means villages, towns and cities can harness the natural resources around them with solar panels on libraries, publicly owned windfarms, hydro schemes in their rivers, or whatever else works for them. The purpose is to put money back in people’s pockets while giving them a direct role in tackling the climate crisis.Every council and community group awarded funding will have at least part-ownership in its renewable energy projects. That means, in the years ahead, more and more communities in Britain will do more than simply host solar panels and wind turbines. They will own a stake in them and retain a share of the wealth they create.Today’s announcement is part of this government’s sustained effort to make energy more affordable. In my first week in office,I said I would remove VAT from household electricity bills. From the beginning of October, that policy kicks in, giving families some much-needed breathing room. But the only lasting way to bring down bills is to produce more of our own clean, renewable energy at home, which People’s Power will achieve.I am acutely aware that our changing climate is a major concern for many Britons, not least because we have just emerged fromour hottest summer on record. Punishing heatwaves left nurses collapsing on hospital wards and bus drivers working in 40C cabs.Wildfires destroyed homes, leaving families with nothing. Andmore extreme weatheris forecast in the months ahead. The climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is here and with us now. The British people are no longer insulated from the consequences, and they do not want to be excluded from the solutions. They are looking for ways to do their bit. Community energy gives them that chance.Across Britain, people are taking back control of the things that matter to them: their pubs, their libraries, their leisure centres. Some have already done the same with energy. There are fine examples across the UK of community energy schemes that keep the lights on, the local economy moving and the benefits close to home.These projects work and we want to take them nationwide. Today’s investment is the first down payment on a £1bn Great BritishEnergyprogramme, the biggest investment in community energy ever, which will eventually fund more than 1,000 People’s Power projects.The climate crisis presents us with an enormous challenge and possibility. In the coming years, we need to change the way we travel, build homes and produce energy. I have long seen the green transition as the best chance we will ever have to reindustrialise Britain.With this in mind, I believe there are two routes we can follow. There’s the traditional Whitehall way: make people pay for the change with more regulation and higher costs, and allow private companies to reap the rewards. Or we can pursue a different route: help people make the change by creating jobs, lowering bills and bringing power back to them.That is the approach I took as mayor of Greater Manchester. When we brought the buses back under public control, we capped fares and made the fleet cleaner. The result was a transport system designed around the needs of the people who pay for it and rely on it. We are applying the same principle to community energy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI am determined that we meet the commitment on which Labour was elected and reach net zero by 2050. I want Britain to believe in itself again. That will not happen by asking people to stand still while the world spins around them. Everyone should have a say and a stake in their future. That is whatNo 10 Northis all about. It is what today is about – it is community power in every sense. Power owned by local people, power generated by local projects and power returned to every postcode.Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United KingdomExplore more on these topicsEnergyOpinionClimate crisisLabourCommunitiesRenewable energySolar powerWind powercommentShareReuse this content

title: Dear Ed Sheeran, fence-sitting is so last century: musicians can no longer opt out of politics | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: It’s all very 2026: with a stadium owner on one side and angry support acts on the other, the cornered star will have to pick a side, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: It’s all very 2026: with a stadium owner on one side and angry support acts on the other, the cornered star will have to pick a side, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Content: Ed Sheeran performing at BBC1’s Big Weekend festival in Sefton Park, Liverpool, 24 May 2025.Photograph: Andy Von Pip/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEd Sheeran performing at BBC1’s Big Weekend festival in Sefton Park, Liverpool, 24 May 2025.Photograph: Andy Von Pip/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionEd SheeranDear Ed Sheeran, fence-sitting is so last century: musicians can no longer opt out of politicsZoe WilliamsIt’s all very 2026: with a stadium owner on one side and angry support acts on the other, the cornered star will have to pick a sideThu 17 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 08.18 EDTShareEd Sheeran, seeking to stay out of politics, has become, in this moment, the most political artist in the world. And in trying to leave himself room to manoeuvre, he has backed himself into a corner. Since the rapper Macklemore was dropped as a support act on Sheeran’s Loop tour on Monday,every other opening acthas pulled out. Finneas O’Connellkept it briefon Tuesday: “Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed. I stand with Palestine and its people.” Aaron Rowewas already out, saying: “I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence … rightful voices.”Beoga, Sheeran’s actual backing band,then pulled out, along with the Danish band Lukas Graham, who probably made the mildest statement, managing to not even mention any countries: “We should be able to speak about war, about civilians being killed, about children who deserve to grow up. Wherever they live. Whatever flag flies over them.”Sheeran said thedecision to dropMacklemore was entirely down to venue owners and promoters, adding that there was a reason he didn’t talk about politics on stage: “My audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds.” Both statements sound weak, but more importantly, it is not true that Sheeran doesn’t take political stances. He hastaken part in a fundraising gigfor Ukrainians, telling them, “I love you, I stand with you”; in 2017 he outed himself as a “Corbynista fanboy” (TM the Sun), and has been a vocal supporter of LGBTQI+ rights, on stage and off, throughout his career. More specifically, it seems unlikely he didn’t know the views of his support acts when he chose them: Macklemore had asong about Hind Rajab, the five-year-old killed by the IDF in 2024, on his set list; Beoga arefounding membersof Irish Artists for Palestine.To try to psychoanalyse Sheeran, and say definitively whether he was trying to borrow the spirit of these artists while distancing himself from their beliefs, or in fact shares their views, would be premature; ultimately, he’s bound to declare himself. So far hehas simply saidhe was “appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine” and that the “suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy”. Just because he didn’t choose to speak publicly, he said, “doesn’t mean I don’t care”.This omertà won’t hold. But what we can say for certain now is that the idea of keeping politics out of entertainment, music, or art, is last century’s fantasy. Censorship is swift – but often not as overt as in this case. It is simply a fact that if artists don’t studiously avoid voicing certain opinions, they will get caught up in politics. It’s unclear whether it’s possible to create art – at least art that will be seen by a mass public – in those conditions.At thevanguard of the moveto jettison Macklemore from the tour was the Israeli-American Council, whose chief executive, Elan Carr,told the Today programmeon Wednesday that the rapper had “put forth a blood libel against the state of Israel and, by connection, the Jewish people”. He was pressed by Justin Webb on what Macklemore actually said: “The words free Palestine don’t necessarily mean … that anything awful should happen to Jewish people or indeed to the state of Israel.” “Free Palestine absolutely is a call for the extermination of the state of Israel and the Jewish people,” Carr replied.So what kind ofPalestineis it acceptable to want? The other difficult strand of Carr’s argument was that a concert audience was “captive … people have paid to be there”. If you’ve paid money to be somewhere, the logic runs, you shouldn’t be subjected to politics of any kind. Yet billionaires have no qualms about having a political agenda. Macklemore, both onstage and in his own statement, has rebuffed the argument that voicing support for Palestinians and criticising Israel and its actions in Gaza and the West Bank is antisemitic. (In 2014, he apologised for a costume he wore on stage, which critics said was antisemitic, saying: “I respect all cultures and all people.”)The concern of many of the artists was that they were facing not justcensorship, but censorship by billionaires: specifically Robert Kraft, who demanded Macklemore’s removal withthe threat of axingthe whole show from his Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts. Kraft has so far not commented onAlexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s chargethat he put pressure on other stadiums to follow suit. In his own statement, he insisted his decision to ban Macklemore from Gillette was “not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf”, but that such advocacy,“should not … obscure the responsibility of Hamas”.What next,Ocasio-Cortezasked an interviewer, rhetorically: “It could be speaking out about AI … you can now just get a handful of stadium owners to ensure that an entire person’s career can be jeopardised.”Ultimately, now, the only acceptable thing to say is nothing: there is no statement mild enough aboutIsraeland Palestine that can be made on a stage to a general audience. Even to wish for a world in which children aren’t killed is too political, and even the Sheeran fix – that there’s a lot of pain on both sides – which might or might not have been devised to soothe billionaire interests, does not meet their preference. They would simply prefer that everyone pretend the situation doesn’t exist, that they’ve never heard of it, that nothing has happened, and if anything ever had, they wouldn’t be able to find it on a map. The slippery slope argument, that an enforced public silence could spread to protests against datacentres next, is plausible but unnecessary: we don’t need this censorship to get worse before we take it seriously.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionZoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
