title: How’s your apocalypse stockpiling coming on? Three weeks in, mine has hit a few snags | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: Cans of tuna, sparkling water and an old torch – if the end of the world came for me now I’d struggle, but it’s hard to know how to prepare for an unknown threat, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: Cans of tuna, sparkling water and an old torch – if the end of the world came for me now I’d struggle, but it’s hard to know how to prepare for an unknown threat, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Content: ‘I’m not really prepared, and the biggest deficit in my unpreparedness is, evidently, my attitude.’Photograph: Lucy Ray/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘I’m not really prepared, and the biggest deficit in my unpreparedness is, evidently, my attitude.’Photograph: Lucy Ray/AlamyOpinionEmergency planningHow’s your apocalypse stockpiling coming on? Three weeks in, mine has hit a few snagsEmma BrockesCans of tuna, sparkling water and an old torch – if the end of the world came for me now I’d struggle, but it’s hard to know how to prepare for an unknown threatThu 17 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 10.46 EDTShareIt’s been three weeks since the government advisory urging us to startstockpiling in case of emergency– how’s your prep coming along? The Prepare campaign, backed by Wes Streeting, who one imagines gliding through the apocalypse, quiff undisturbed, listed nine essential items, among them wet wipes, first-aid kits and batteries. The World Health Organization, meanwhile, suggests budgeting for15 litres of waterper person per day, so a family of four will need to store upwards of 180 litres to cover the recommended period of three days. The chances of this actually happening seem to me, intuitively, to be considerably lower than the disaster they’re supposed to forestall. But hope springs, so let’s see.The first step towards stockpiling is stocktaking. This is where I’m at: one mega-torch (uncharged), which I bought in prepper mode after surviving the terrifying New York blackout of 2019 when for about an hour we couldn’t charge our phones; lots of very large sticking plasters and a handful of small round ones, the normal sizes having long been used up; two cans of tuna, which will go down to one after lunch; two litres of sparkling water, so for the first hour or so after a nuclear strike, assuming it happens this afternoon, we’ll at least be able to enjoy some bubbles; and three OxyContin saved from my c-section almost 12 years ago, which are probably less powerful than homeopathy at this point but I retain a vague hope I can use for barter when money breaks down.In other words, I’m not really prepared and the biggest deficit in my unpreparedness is, evidently, my attitude. On the evidence of what appeared to be a collective shrug, recently, when we wereinformed of the threats posed by AI, it’s an attitude problem that’s widely shared. It’s not that we don’t care, perhaps, but that it is hard to know what to do. By which I mean, it’s hard to know what to do that doesn’t involve giving over precious closet space to 40 two-litre bottles of water or disrupting our thought patterns to accommodate large, uncomfortable truths.In other words, if this is a collective failure of imagination, then what’s needed is some rigorous thought experiments that address our inability to imagine the worst. It’s wild that this should be necessary six years after a global pandemic, but of course, if there’s one thing to be said about humankind, it’s our ability to go scorched earth on recent trauma and pretend like nothing ever happened. This is called resilience – and there are, I’m sure, good evolutionary reasons for it, yet in this case it’s unhelpful. From scratch, then, we must develop what the government calls “household resilience”, which in my house means learning not to go into meltdown when someone can’t find their favourite hoodie or we run out of Nutella, or the Russians aim a missile towards our area.With this in mind, I would recommend browsing something called thelocal resilience forum, made up of regional lists of potential threats starting with “nuclear attack by a state on the UK mainland”, working down through pandemics, biblical droughts, floods, and the collapse of the National Grid, all the way to the threat posed by “space weather”. It’s very When the Wind Blows, and if it’s hard to square with real world scenarios, I suspect it’s because when you put something in local government language and stick it in a table, any sense of threat collapses beneath the sheer weight of boredom.For real imaginative engagement, we must turn to the fiction writers. The scene I go to in my head is the opening pages of Emily St John Mandel’s Station Eleven, in which a character called Jeevan, tipped off by a doctor friend that a pandemic is coming that will kill 99% of the world’s population, runs to a supermarket, shackles seven big shopping carts together and buys enough food and water to barricade himself in his apartment for 58 days, until the first panic has passed.So, as long as Tesco is open and I can beat the rush, perhaps things will work out just fine? I know there are some walnuts at the back of the cupboard. We could take the batteries out of the remote to use in the torch. Per The Day After Tomorrow, I have plenty of books for firewood, and worst-case scenario, can wear the cats for extra warmth. And while water is a problem, I think about that couple whosurvived in a tiny boatin the middle of the Pacific for 118 days, and imagine we will figure it out. I can catch the drips from the freezer as it defrosts and suck the gel from the aloe vera. See? Already thinking like a survivor. We’ve got this!skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEmma Brockes is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsEmergency planningOpinionFoodcommentShareReuse this content

title: Driving that’s too fast, too dangerous and utterly lawless: why do we tolerate this petro-masculinity? | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: In towns and in the countryside, I see 4x4s and pick up trucks driven without care or conscience. It’s a Magafication of transport, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: In towns and in the countryside, I see 4x4s and pick up trucks driven without care or conscience. It’s a Magafication of transport, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: Illustration: Sébastien Thibault/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Sébastien Thibault/The GuardianOpinionRoad safetyDriving that’s too fast, too dangerous and utterly lawless: why do we tolerate this petro-masculinity?George MonbiotIn towns and in the countryside, I see SUVs and pickup trucks driven without care or conscience. It’s the Magafication of transportThu 17 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 11.16 EDTShareWhere is lawbreaking not just visible, but designed to be seen? Where is antisocial behaviour worn as a badge of honour? Where is pleasure gained directly from causing distress? And where is reckless endangerment often ignored by the police or treated with the mildest of punishments? The answer is on the roads.Last month, three men in the West Midlandswere convictedof street racing. Two were driving at over 80mph in a 40mph zone. The third clocked over 90mph in a 30mph zone. The West Midlands has long been blighted byorganised racing, sometimes involving 200 cars or more and hundreds of spectators. The result is a long catalogue of deaths and life-changing injuries, including some caused when racers have left the road andploughed into onlookers or pedestrians. And there are plenty more accidents where the police have little idea whether racing is to blame, for as soon as they happen, the drivers disperse.The West Midlands is one of the few places in the UK where the police are actively trying to stop antisocial driving. Aninjunction bans street racingand dangerous tricks such as “drifting” (long sideways skids) and “doughnutting” (making the car spin on the spot). The local police commissioner has warned that reckless drivers “will face the full force of the law … including seizure of your vehicle and imprisonment”. But are the courts listening?Of the three men convicted at Birmingham magistrates court,one receiveda suspended sentence, a £272 fine, 150 hours of community work and a two-year driving ban. Another was handed a £1,275 fine and seven penalty points: in other words, he could step out of the court and back into his car. The man who did over 90mph in a 30mph zone got a £253 fine and a 56-day driving ban. He’ll be back on the roads in November. All appear to have kept their cars.If these men had caused the same level of endangerment by any other means, it’s hard to believe they would have got off so lightly. But in dozens of ways,driving gets special treatment.There’s a similar racing culture in mid-Wales, where I lived until 2012. Night after night, a convoy of cars with exhausts modified to be as loud as possible would race past, at 50mph or more in a 30mph zone. They would start at around 10pm and continue some nights until 2am, going round the nearby roads in a loop. As soon as I’d got my infant daughter to sleep, they’d roar past and wake her up again.Calls to the police were useless: they told me to take down the number plates and “report the incident”. When I did so, they explained, in effect, that I was wasting my time, as I couldn’t prove the drivers were breaking the speed limit. In fact, their advice was counterproductive: when I went outside to take down the number plates, the young men jeered, gave me the finger and accelerated. It seemed that shock and disgust was what they craved. And this was before TikTok, where drivers can achievemuch wider notoriety.The first young man to “do a ton” (100mph) down my high street in Wales on his motorbike became a local hero. Soon afterwards, he rode into a wall and died. Other drivers killed their passengers, hit pedestrians or forced other cars off the road. When people were killed or injured, the drivers were prosecuted and lightly punished, but there was little effort to address the underlying culture. Some men went straight back into the convoys when they regained their licences. I’m told that nothing has changed, despite thedefault 20mph speed limitnow applied to residential areas across Wales, and that every year a new cohort of young men joins the local urban racetrack.Now I live in Devon, where there’s a different culture of antisocial driving. Here it’s mostly middle-aged men in“lifted” pickup trucks, which have been modified to be as loud and smoky as possible. Two local SUVs have been refitted to “roll coal” from twin exhaust towers mounted behind the cab, releasing a dense black cloud of soot when the driver hits the “smoke switch”. Adapting your truck for this purpose means buying a “delete kit” to bypass the vehicle’s emissions control system, retuning the engine andfitting bigger injectors. The practice emerged in the US, both as ananti-environmental protestand as aform of amusement. It is largely deployed against cyclists, pedestrians and electric vehicles. I’ve seen these two trucks doing it, blinding the drivers behind and choking everyone around. Of courseit’s illegal. But it doesn’t seem to be a priority for the police in my area.What we see here are manifestations ofpetro-masculinity: a violent, misogynistic, climate-denying version of manhood, expressed through an antisocial driving culture. Some of the modified trucks have decals saying “Stop the Boats” or “Save Our Children” (who are apparently being brainwashed byLGBTQ+ cultural Marxists). This is the Magafication of transport – a vehicle that carries some of the worst aspects of US culture and politics into the UK.It’s the extreme end of a much wider trend. In the UK last year, 52% of the new cars on sale wereSUVs. Not only do the ever-rising bonnets of these trucks make it harder for drivers to see pedestrians and cyclists,especially children, but higher and heavier cars are also more likely to cause deaths or serious injuries when they hit people: children under nine are three timesmore likely to be killedif they’re hit by an SUV than by a regular car.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd what are they for? On narrow country lanes round here, tourists in these “off-road” vehicles won’t back up if it means touching a hedge, in case the high-gloss finish on their Wankpanzer Childkiller SUV gets scratched. In one of the poshest parts of London, theChelsea Truck Company advertises“iconic urban 4x4s”. “Iconic” appears to mean huge. But what the hell is an “urban 4x4”? And why is it legal?Isn’t it obvious that selfishness on the road changes us as a society? The belief that a driver should be allowed to do whatever they please, regardless of the impact on others, mounts the pavement and travels deep into our lives. If this is to be a decent, inclusive country that values human life, then the law and its enforcement should match that aspiration. But when the roads are used to amplify and celebrate a dangerous, antisocial culture, we are driven towards a very dark place.George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsRoad safetyOpinionCrimeMotoringWest MidlandsTransportWalesDevoncommentShareReuse this content

title: Opening the EU door for Canada is a harmless gesture. But it won’t fix Europe’s security crisis | Paul Taylor | The Guardian
description: Beyond the morale boost and Mark Carney’s stardust, ‘associate membership’  means little, says Paul Taylor of the European Policy Centre
Author: Paul Taylor
Headline: Beyond the morale boost and Mark Carney’s stardust, ‘associate membership’ means little, says Paul Taylor of the European Policy Centre
Content: ‘Carney’s presence in Strasbourg made the EU look more desirable globally than it sometimes appears to angry European electorates.’Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Carney’s presence in Strasbourg made the EU look more desirable globally than it sometimes appears to angry European electorates.’Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockOpinionEuropean UnionOpening the EU door for Canada is a harmless gesture. But it won’t fix Europe’s security crisisPaul TaylorBeyond the morale boost and Mark Carney’s stardust, ‘associate membership’  means littleThu 17 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 11.05 EDTShareUrsula von der Leyen brought a new mascot to her annual State of the Union address to the European parliament: the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney.The leader of a plucky, like-minded liberal democracy, locked in an unsought trade war with its much bigger bully of a neighbour, Carney crossed the Atlantic and attended this flagship event of Europe’s political calendar to demonstrate his country’s shared values and desire to get closer to the EU. He was rewarded with a standing ovation and the first ever offer of an (invented) status of “associate member” of the EU.The grand-sounding title is more a gesture of political support and reciprocal affection than any sort of binding engagement. The EU doesn’t have associate membership in its founding treaties. It does make association agreements with close countries, some of which eventually join the bloc. It also has partnership, trade and cooperation agreements with more distant friends – it had one with Russia, in happier times.But using the “m” word in connection withCanada, which fails the geographical test for membership, may create an ambivalent precedent for the many Balkan and eastern European countries that are actually negotiating to join the bloc – and for the UK, which stormed out a decade ago but is now eager to get closer again.Ukraine railed against any such “associate” status in May, when the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz,floated the ideaas a stepping stone towards eventual full EU membership. Western Balkan states that have been waiting more than two decades for accession want nothing to do with such a halfway house.For Canada, though, the honorific title conveys a sense of European solidarity in its struggle with Donald Trump’s US, and a degree of closeness on fundamental values that responds to Carney’s seminal call at Davos in January for an alliance of like-minded “middle powers” to uphold as much as possible of the rules-based international order.Carney’s presence in Strasbourg, and his applause for EU free trade, tech regulation and defence initiatives, made the EU look more desirable globally than it sometimes appears to angry European electorates tempted to vote for Eurosceptic populists in national elections next year. Von der Leyen must be hoping that a little of the Canadian prime minister’s stardust will rub off on the embattled European integration project, which faces headwinds not only from predatory great powers and hostile big tech but also from recalcitrant governments loth to share power and pool sovereignty in sensitive fields such as defence.Closer cooperation with Canada and other like-minded powers such as India, Japan, Australia and New Zealand can amplify the EU’s global influence and help build alliances in defence of democracy, open rules-based trade and security of supply for critical raw materials. However, it cannot mitigate the urgent threats that Europe faces from increasingly reckless Russian aggression, nor be a substitute for a vengeful US that under Trump seems hell-bent on disengagement from European security.View image in fullscreenUrsula von der Leyen delivers the annual State of the European Union speech in Strasbourg, 16 September, 2026.Photograph: Pascal Bastien/APVon der Leyen offered three initiatives to address these challenges. She proposed a new EU mechanism, aligned with Nato’s article 4 security consultations, to enable countries to trigger urgent EU consultations if they fall victim to so-called hybrid warfare – cyber-attacks, drone incursions, undersea cable cutting, railway sabotage, energy grid disruption and disinformation campaigns. It was time for a “counter-hybrid playbook”, she said, in which the EU moved beyond just boosting resilience and took a more robust approach to responding to covert warfare.Whether all member states have the stomach to risk escalation by hitting back at Russia, even if such hybrid attacks start causing casualties, remains to be seen. EU and Nato members that have offensive cyberwarfare capabilities could and should be striking back now to set red lines for Moscow, for instance by putting Russian energy grids or airports out of action as a warning. But these are national measures unlikely to be aired or jointly approved in Nato or EU councils.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEuropean countries have gone beyond sanctions to put Russia’s shadow fleet of rust-bucket oil tankers out of action – impounding them on safety or insurance grounds, as France and the UKhave done episodically, and denying them passage through sensitive straits. But each action must be thought through, to achieve a deterrent effect rather than inviting ever bolder defiance by Vladimir Putin that could spiral into a wider war.Von der Leyen’s other initiative, to be detailed in an updated European security strategy due next month, was to call for a European security council – including Ukraine, the UK and Canada alongside EU powers – to steer the continent’s expanding defence effort. Such a coalition of the willing,as I have advocated, could indeed provide top-level leadership and a crisis-management forum. The challenge will be to give it real levers of power, and avoid it becoming a talking shop.Von der Leyen’s Canadian caper is welcome because it shows we have friends willing to link their destiny to ours in troubled times. But it is not in itself a solution to the continent’s urgent security problems.Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy CentreExplore more on these topicsEuropean UnionOpinionUrsula von der LeyenMark CarneyEuropeCanadaAmericascommentShareReuse this content

title: Do whales grieve? Rare footage of humpback alongside stillborn calf suggests they might | Olaf Meynecke for the Conversation | The Guardian
description: The behaviours we observed could represent grief, but they could also reflect maternal attachment, confusion or instinctive caregiving
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The behaviours we observed could represent grief, but they could also reflect maternal attachment, confusion or instinctive caregiving
Content: ‘Humpback whales are remarkable for the way they respond to other animals in distress,’ writes Olaf Meynecke.Photograph: By Wildestanimal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Humpback whales are remarkable for the way they respond to other animals in distress,’ writes Olaf Meynecke.Photograph: By Wildestanimal/Getty ImagesThe ConversationMarine lifeDo whales grieve? Rare footage of humpback alongside stillborn calf suggests they mightOlaf Meynecke for the ConversationThe behaviours we observed could represent grief, but they could also reflect maternal attachment, confusion or instinctive caregivingWed 16 Sep 2026 22.22 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 02.46 EDTShareIt was a tragic sight.One day last July, a newborn humpback whale calf lay motionless on the seafloor, just a kilometre off Australia’s Gold Coast. The encounter was captured through underwater video.For more than an hour, the mother repeatedly returned to the same spot, gently touching the calf with her head and pectoral fin and resting beside it eye-to-eye. Ournew researchsuggests this is the first described case of a humpback whale mother caring for her deceased newborn calf.1:13Humpback whale filmed apparently grieving its stillborn calf – videoThe encounter offers a rare window into one of the least understood aspects of whale behaviour: how these highly social animals respond to death.And it raises the question: do whales, and other highly social animals such as elephants, grieve?Caring creaturesHumpback whales are known for their spectacular migrations and acrobatic breaches. However, they are equally remarkable for the way they respond to other animals in distress.Iceland to submit bill that could ban whaling in its watersRead moreHumpback whales often defend their calves from killer whales. Researchers havealso observedthem remaining alongside whales thatare injuredorentangled in nets, circling them, resting nearby and attempting to assist. Humpback whales mayeven intervenewhen killer whales attack seals, sea lions and grey whale calves.These responses of care and attention are known asepimeletic behaviourand are common amongcetaceans, a group of marine mammals including whales, dolphins and porpoises.Dolphinsandkiller whalesoften remain close to distressed companions, evidence of their strong social bonds. These animals may even risk their own lives for others. This happened in April off Scotland’s north-west coast, when multiple pilot whalesbecame strandedafter following a birthing female.When a whale loses a calfKiller whale mothers have repeatedly been observed carrying their dead calves for hours, days and, in exceptional cases, weeks. The most famous example is thekiller whale Tahlequah, who in 2018 carried her dead calf for 17 days over more than 1,500 kilometres. Scientists have observedsimilar behaviourin pilot whales and dolphins.Such prolonged responses illustrate the strength of the bond between mother and calf.Maternal instinctsandhormonal changesafter birth may contribute to mothers remaining with their deceased offspring. But exactly what the animals understand about death remains unknown.Until now, scientists have almost exclusively documented these epimeletic behaviours towards deceased calves intoothed whales. The research on baleen whales, including humpback whales, is scarce. This is likely because dead newborn baleen whales often sink quickly, making it extremely difficult to observe such cases.Twenty-two years and 15,000km later: fluke discovery sets new record for humpback whale journeyRead moreHumpback whale mothers give birth after almost ayear of pregnancyand spend the next few months feeding their calf with nutrient-rich milk. Right after the delivery, mothers often lift their calf to the surface to help it take itsfirst breath. During the first months of its life, a calfrelies entirelyon its mother for nourishment, protection and guidance during migration.Tragically, some calves don’t survive. This may be due to disease, pollutants or a mother’s lack offat reservesthat help female whales cope better with pregnancy and better care for their calves.A first for humpback whalesOurnew studyaimed to help fill this research gap.We observed two adult whales off the Gold Coast of north-east Australia. The two whales stayed in the same area for several hours, after what appeared to have been a stillbirth. The female humpback whale released an ammoniac membrane shortly after the birth, but a placenta was not seen.Underwater footage revealed the calf resting motionless on the seafloor while the presumed mother repeatedly approached it. She remained close to the calf, continuing to touch it with her head and pectoral fin. A second adult whale, likely an escort, also stayed nearby.The humpback mother did not try to lift the calf to the ocean’s surface. This may indicate that she recognised the calf had died or was unable to carry it up from the seabed.Members of the public reported two adult humpback whales remaining in the area over the next two days. However, our research team could not confirm they were the same animals.Do whales grieve?To our knowledge, this is the first detailed scientific study of a humpback whale mother attending her deceased newborn calf. It provides crucial insight into how baleen whales cope with death.Could humans ever communicate with whales? - videoMany of the behaviours we observed – including remaining close to the calf and suspending normal behaviours such as travelling or socialising with other whales – resemble how other species respond to death.Elephants,great apesand sometoothed whalespecies care for dead offspring in similar ways.However, we can’t directly measure the emotional state of whales. The behaviours we observed could represent grief, but they could also reflect maternal attachment, confusion orinstinctive caregiving. For this reason, researchers use broader terms – such aspostmortem attentive behaviour– rather than concluding that whales grieve in the human sense.Nevertheless, these behaviours reveal that humpback whales maintain strong maternal bonds even after the death of a calf. Our study suggests similar cases may have gone unnoticed because scientistsrarely observewhale births at sea.In good news, researchers are increasingly able to observe these animals aswhale populations recoverand scientific equipment makes at-sea studiesmore feasible.So while there’s much more to learn about whales, their emotional lives may be infinitely more complex than we once imagined.Olaf Meynecke is a research fellow in marine science and manager of the whales and climate program at Griffith University.
