title: Beck: ‘What does a devil’s haircut look like? Anything with a lot of architecture and wild flights of fancy’ | Beck | The Guardian
description: The genre-fluid singer answers your questions on being funky v lonesome, his infamous MTV interview with Thurston Moore and why he said yes to performing with a chain-smoking alcoholic robot
Author: Kate Solomon
Headline: The genre-fluid singer answers your questions on being funky v lonesome, his infamous MTV interview with Thurston Moore and why he said yes to performing with a chain-smoking alcoholic robot
Content: ‘I don’t think anybody’s mentioned Odelay to me in years’ … Beck.Photograph: Autumn De WildeView image in fullscreen‘I don’t think anybody’s mentioned Odelay to me in years’ … Beck.Photograph: Autumn De WildeFilm & Music reader interviewBeckInterviewBeck: ‘What does a devil’s haircut look like? Anything with a lot of architecture and wild flights of fancy’As told toKate SolomonThe genre-fluid singer answers your questions on being funky v lonesome, his infamous MTV interview with Thurston Moore and why he said yes to performing with a chain-smoking alcoholic robotRead Alexis Petridis’s 5* review of new album Ride LonesomeThu 17 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 13.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou’ve been performing since the late 80s. What keeps you going?AmongstTheWavesIt’s a good question. I don’t really know any other life. I’ve spent a lot of my time trying to create a body of work, and out of that, maybe there’s a few songs at the end that are not bad. So I just keep going down into the mine, trying to come back with a couple of things worth keeping. It’s a lot of digging. If I had to stop and get a job painting houses or something, I would still make songs just for myself, because that’s how it started.You tend to alternate between styles from album to album. What do you feel is closer to your intrinsic self, funky Beck orlonesome Beck?MazziniProbably lonesome. But the other side of things gets me out of my shell, stops me from being a little too ponderous, which I’m apt to do. The other side of what I do – Loser or Odelay – was more of a fluke. At the time that was what people liked. Now it’s kind of reversed – they prefer the more introspective, quiet songs, and stuff that’s a little more genreless. I don’t have any songs that they play at weddings, like Uptown Funk. I remember telling Mark Ronson, “Hey, you made a wedding song.” He was like, “Yeah, finally.” That’s a very elite category of song.Your interview withThurston Moore on MTV in 1994is one of the most gloriously ramshackle interviews ever. Were you both doing a bit?LoftyDogWe filmed a bunch of things they wouldn’t air because they thought they would get in trouble or get sued by people. I’d brought an old-fashioned telephone and at one point we pulled out some baseball bats and destroyed the phone. I don’t remember what the bit was – who was calling us? Whatever it was, we decided to smash the phone in reaction to a call. We were kind of doing performance art. I met a lot of resistance and ridicule for being like that on my first album. I would do interviews and say wild things because so much of it was boring, just rote questions – and I thought if my friends are reading this, they’d be bored to death.A lot of the things on TV were just going through the motions. As a kid, every once in a while I’d see something that jarred me. Like, wow, there was a glitch in the system and something real broke through. Something genuine that reminded us that this is all a construct, this smooth oiled machine that provides content for us. It was a very youthfully exuberant attempt to try to disrupt everything that was very pre-programmed and uninteresting. Thurston and I both came from underground art backgrounds, so it was preposterous to be allowed on mainstream TV. We were like, let’s seize the moment and do something.View image in fullscreen‘Let’s seize the moment’ … Beck at the Troubadour in West Hollywood in 1994.Photograph: Lindsay Brice/Getty ImagesGiven how productive you were right from the start of your career, how did you feel about being tagged with the “slacker rock” label?SalfordianBlueI thought it was a reductive term. There was this influx of all this underground music that had been bubbling through the 80s and early 90s, and it all hit the mainstream at once. One day it was Vanilla Ice and hair metal and Whitney Houston, and then the next day it was Nirvana and all the stuff that you would see at your local dive bar. The 80s had been very curated and airbrushed and brightly coloured – I remember the first time I went to a record label, they told me I looked messy and rough, and it would never work. Whoever that was missed the point. We were reacting to how cleaned up everything was, and going back to something a little more raw and real.To many, Loser felt like a classic one-hit wonder. Did you always have faith that you’d have a long career in music?StayPositiveI never had any expectations. I think the thing that supersedes everything is whether you are writing good songs. The people I came up with who wrote good songs – they’re the ones that are still around and playing arenas and stadiums. And it was tricky when I was coming up, writing a catchy song was frowned upon. If you had anything that was too poppy or catchy, you were selling out, it wasn’t real art. What’s funny is the catchiest, poppiest songs from that time are the ones that everybody loves now.What would a devil’s haircut look like, and have you ever seen someone sporting one?StayPositiveBeck: Devils Haircut – ideoIt’d probably have a little bit of a rockabilly edge. Somebody showed me a video once of these proto-punk type people in Australia called sharpies, and they had a bizarre version of a mullet. It was really short bangs and kind of draped in the back. Something like that, maybe. I have a book of hairstyle photos that they would use in 80s hair salons – there are a lot of devil’s haircuts. I think any haircut that has a lot of architecture to it, with wild flights of fancy.In their1998hitYou Get What You Give the New Radicalsthreatened tokick the asses of Hanson, Courtney Love, Marilyn Manson – and Beck. Did they ever catch up with you?Dave_RowlinsonI ran into [New Radicals songwriter Gregg Alexander] in an Erewhon [health food supermarket] at the time, and he said: “I’m a big fan. We should write together.” And I just looked at him like, “What do you …? What’s happening here?” I thought the song was a little corny at the time, but it’s probably a classic now. It’s pretty catchy. I think the chords, to me, were a little too fancy for the aesthetic of the time.View image in fullscreen‘If you had anything that was too poppy or catchy, you were selling out’ … performing at the John Anson Ford Amphitheatre, LA in 2017.Photograph: Chris Pizzello/Invision/APAre you still in touch with [producer duo]the Dust Brothers? You’re one of the last artistswho worked with them, onGueroin2005, before they vanished into thin air. I genuinely wonder what happened to them!CoopertapesI did actually see them about a year ago. I see them from time to time. We have unfinished records that were never put out, so who knows? Maybe there’ll be something down the road. I’ve never asked, but I’m guessing they don’t really need to work in music, they’re doing other things. They worked with Hanson right after Odelay – people thought we were related [Beck’s surname is Hansen]. I remember they were working on that, the Rolling Stones and the Fight Club soundtrack. So that’s why my next two albums were not fully produced by the Dust Brothers, after the success of Odelay they became too busy.View image in fullscreen‘You have to do it!’ … Beck in Futurama.Photograph: 20th Century FoxLooking to the future, do you see yourself sharing the stage with a chain-smoking alcoholic robot? AKA how did you come to be a guest star on Futurama?vammypThey wrote a script and sent it to me, and I said no. Through that whole era, I said no to pretty much everything. I was asked to do the theme for Austin Powers 2 and 3, and Shrek, and I was even saying no to, like, Amores Perros and Y Tu Mamá También and Run Lola Run, all these classic movies. They wanted me to act in High Fidelity and Ghost World, and I just decided that I didn’t want to “go Hollywood”.They sent me this cartoon and I thought, well, if I did something like this it would be The Simpsons – a lot of people have done that, Sonic Youth have done that. The script was sitting on the tour bus, and my band got a hold of it on a long drive and said, “What is this?” And I said, “Oh, it’s this show, Futurama. I’ve never heard of it, but they want me to do this ridiculous thing.” And they said, “You have to do it!” They all ganged up on me so I did it.‘Our computer sampler cost more than a house!’: how the Korgis made Everybody’s Got to Learn SometimeRead moreBeercanis my go-to “shake your ass” number. What is yours?TeeDubyaBeeI would say anything from the early 80s funk era. Anything Sly Stone, James Brown – and early 80s Prince era, Talking Heads. Classics.Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mindis one of my favourite films, and your recording ofEverybody’s Got toLearn Sometimeis a sublime part of it. How did you get involved with the film, and why that song in particular?CybillserviceI did a music video withMichel Gondry, the director, and we became pals. I was having dinner over at his house one night, and he described this convoluted plot that I couldn’t quite follow. I said, “I don’t totally understand what this is, but when you make it, I want to see it.” Three or four years later, he called me up and said, “I made the movie.” My buddy Jon Brion was doing the score. It’s one of the only things, again, that I said yes to. But it was because it was a personal relationship. It’s become one of my songs that people love the most. I had just done Sea Change, which I think is one of the reasons they called me. That album had met so much shock from my fans that I swore to never make a record like that again. And now it’s beloved. It’s probably the main thing that people care about. I don’t think anybody’s mentioned Odelay to me in years, it’s all Sea Change and Midnite Vultures.Beck’s new album Ride Lonesome is released 18 September via Iliad/CapitolExplore more on these topicsBeckFilm & Music reader interviewPop and rockMichel GondryThurston MoorefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I thank God for killing me and bringing me back’: Nicolas Winding Refn on the heart surgery that inspired his new sci-fi horror | Movies | The Guardian
description: Notorious for ultra-violent movies like Drive and The Neon Demon, the Dane had lost the will to direct until ‘the Tom Cruise of surgeons’ saved his life – and triggered an astonishing creative rebirth
Author: Tim Jonze
Headline: Notorious for ultra-violent movies like Drive and The Neon Demon, the Dane had lost the will to direct until ‘the Tom Cruise of surgeons’ saved his life – and triggered an astonishing creative rebirth
Content: ‘I didn’t make a fuss about it because I’m like a superhero’ … Refn, whose new film is called Her Private Hell.Photograph: Suki Dhanda/the GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I didn’t make a fuss about it because I’m like a superhero’ … Refn, whose new film is called Her Private Hell.Photograph: Suki Dhanda/the GuardianMoviesInterview‘I thank God for killing me and bringing me back’: Nicolas Winding Refn on the heart surgery that inspired his new sci-fi horrorTim JonzeNotorious for ultra-violent movies like Drive and The Neon Demon, the Dane had lost the will to direct until ‘the Tom Cruise of surgeons’ saved his life – and triggered an astonishing creative rebirthThu 17 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 10.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNicolas Winding Refn has his phone out, showing me one of the goriest scenes he’s ever been involved in. Given that the Danish director’s movies have involved hands getting sliced off, eyeballs being gouged out and a son reaching deep inside his mother’s womb, that’s certainly saying something. In this video, the camera is fixed upon a beating heart when suddenly – slash! – it gets sliced open with a knife. We travel into the open chamber, as needles arrive to pierce through the muscle. Unsettling and compelling, could this be a future Palme d’Or winner?Unlikely. You see, Refn isn’t the director of this footage; he’s actually the guy lying conked out in the operating room while a surgeon attends to him. Requesting that someone films your own heart surgery is a very Nicolas Winding Refn thing to do. “At first they said no,” says the film-maker known for Drive, Bronson andThe Neon Demon. “But then they said, ‘As it’s you, we’ll record it.’”double quotation markSomeone who’d had a similar op looked like they’d boxed Mike TysonSitting in a swanky London hotel bar, drinking espressos and wearing a smart blue polo shirt under a skinny suit, Refn is here to talk about his latest movie, Her Private Hell, a ludicrously camp dream-collage of sci-fi, horror, spoof and revenge set in neon-lit Tokyo. But for the first 40 minutes of our chat, he recounts – with precious little interruption from me – the story of the 2023 operation that saved his life. Without it, he says, Her Private Hell would never have been made – not so much on health grounds, but because, before he was given this second chance at life, he had lost the passion for making movies.“When you’re young, your creative flame is bright red,” he says. “But my own flame had vanished, like tears in the rain. I had fallen into a form of abyss. I was 50 years old and had no idea what to do with my remaining years.”View image in fullscreen‘A movie AI could never make’ … Sophie Thatcher in Her Private HellPhotograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyThe story begins in summer 2023, when Refn was working on a Prada campaign in Italy. He was feeling increasingly tired, and his daughter mentioned how pale he appeared, but he put it down to overwork. It was only after he returned to his home in Copenhagen that a doctor examined him and discovered that a valve in his heart was broken, and filling his lungs with blood. “I was essentially dying,” says Refn. They told him to come back in two weeks for open heart surgery, and gave him a choice of replacement valve: metal or pig.Her Private Hell stars Sophie Thatcher as Elle, an actor hoping to rebuild her relationship with her film mogul father by making her own Barberella-style sci-fi film: throughout the movie, you’re never quite sure if what you’re watching is the actual plot, or scenes from the fictional movie, or one of the characters’ fever dreams. That’s pretty much how I feel listening to Refn’s tale of heart surgery, which he has transformed into some kind of epic cinematic quest.He mentions the quality of the light, the long silences (both features of his movies), and describes himself pleading to a higher power like George Bailey in It’s A Wonderful Life (his favourite film of all time): “Like, please God, just give me five more minutes, man!”Refn was told to write a will and says he “made peace” with his wife: “I said, it’s been 30 years, we had a good run at it, but like tears in the rain, everything has an end.” (He really does love that Blade Runner quote.) He says he went through all the typical emotions: fear, anger, sadness, desperation. Not that anyone would have known.“I didn’t make a fuss about it,” he says, “because I’m like a superhero.”The lowest point came when he met a man who was fresh from similar open heart surgery. “He looked like he’d been in a boxing match with Mike Tyson,” says the director, who wasn’t keen on ageing a decade overnight.View image in fullscreen‘I love femininity, flamboyance and camp’ … Bella Heathcote and Abbey Lee in The Neon Demon.Photograph: Album/AlamyBut just as all heroes suffer setbacks, they eventually rise to conquer them. Just before the operation, Refn received a phone call from his surgeon that would change everything. “He was the Tom Cruise of surgeons,” says Refn, somewhat lustily. “He rode a motorbike, he had rings, he was very sexy. All the nurses said, ‘Oh my God, you’re gettinghim. You’re so lucky!’”Sexy Tom Cruise told Refn that he could fix him in a way no other doctor in Copenhagen could – through telescopic surgery, which meant not needing to open up his ribcage. Refn believes it was divine intervention. “I think God was trying to tell me something. He’s saying, ‘You’re not ready to go yet, kid. But you’re going to go through a challenging process to reignite whatever that is inside of you.’”By the time his operation came around, Refn says he was already a different person: “I was a champ, a winner. The nurses prepare you for how your life will probably change afterwards. But I remember telling them that, actually, this was the best thing ever in my life. And that they were not to worry because my sex drive was going to be times a thousand when I was back.” Er, was that an issue before? He pauses and smiles. “No. It actually ended the conversation. But it was a way to show how [the operation] was about rebirth, regeneration.”double quotation markPrivate K’s story was a narrative I could cling to, my fantasy version of what happened to meWhen Refn was washed and shaved for the operation, he saw it in quasi-religious terms: he was rinsing his past away. In the eerily empty hospital, he remembers feeling full of cinematic emotion when someone from LA, who had no idea what Refn was going through, called to ask “a random question”. They ruined a key scene in your movie! “Yeah, it was kind of like somebody getting up to buy more popcorn in the final farewell scene,” he says.Refn may have avoided fighting Tyson but his operation was no walk in the park: he remembers “incredible physical pain”, and it took three months to rebuild himself. He says he was like an infant, learning to do things for the first time again. But when it came to film-making, that proved to be an advantage.View image in fullscreenEngine trouble … Ryan Gosling in Drive.Photograph: Filmdistrict/Sportsphoto/AllstarIn Her Private Hell – which is chiefly about the protective relationship between father and daughter – we meet Private K, played by Charles Melton, an American GI in postwar Japan searching for his lost daughter. Private K believes she was taken by a mythical figure known as the Leatherman, who is said to roam Tokyo ripping open girls’ chests with his diamond-studded gloved hands (no prizes for guessing what inspired that particular method of execution).The character of Private K came from Refn realising that, while his eldest daughter, Lola, had recently left home, his youngest, Lizzielou, was only 12 and still needed him around. “Private K’s story was a cinematic narrative I could cling on to, my fantasy version of what happened to me.”Refn’s films often contain echoes from his previous movies, and Her Private Hell is no different, in particular sharing a line from Only God Forgives, in which a father is told: “You should have protected her.” This clearly taps into a fear of Refn’s: that he won’t be able to. “I call it ‘dadsploitation’,” he says, with a hint of a smile. “It’s a form of fetish that appeals to men, that you are basically allowed to indulge in extreme biblical violence to protect innocence, especially when it comes to your daughter. Every father’s worst nightmare is something happening to their daughter of a sexual nature, and it gives a kind of permission: it gives me the authority to tear you to pieces in a biblical way, and I will enjoy every minute of it. Lots of films do it.”I did wonder if this message taps into current rightwing tropes: from Trump’s fetishisation of muscle-bound “real men” to the anti-immigrant activists who claim they want to “save our girls”. But Refn says he’s not a politician selling a message. “All I know is that all humans want a hero. And I believe that for fathers, whether you’re left or right, we all have the same primal instinct inside us.”View image in fullscreen‘A Sex Pistol of cinema’ … Mads Mikkelsen in Pusher.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyHe doesn’t seem like a macho guy, though. “I’m a very unmacho guy,” he says. “I love femininity. I love flamboyance. I love camp. I love colour. Her Private Hell is my version of playing with dolls. Everyone’s dressed up in uniforms, I get to move these girls around in fabulous clothes, and I get to take Charles Melton’s shirt off and show his ripped body like an action figure.”It’s certainly outrageously camp at times. Elle’s movie mogul father is a ridiculous figure named Johnny Thunders (yes, he’s a Heartbreakers fan) who wears leather trousers and lights matches on his neck stubble. Throughout the film we hear leather garments stretch and bodily joints crack. “I love fetish,” says Refn. “Those sounds are incredibly erotic.”Back in the 90s, when Refn was an enfant terrible making the gritty Danish drug drama Pusher, he considered himself “a Sex Pistol of cinema, there to fight for teenagers against the system, making things that would piss off their parents. But you grow out of that because everyone my age starts doing their gardening.” He smiles, then adds. “Except me, because I don’t garden.”Now, he says, the “system” has been replaced with new enemies: social media, AI, tech overlords. Her Private Hell, Refn says with confidence, is “a movie that AI could never do. It’s the enemy of the algorithm. Because it’s not one movie, it’s five movies in one.”“Most entertainment today is like this,” he adds, holding a white napkin up to his face. “A white sheet with codes on it. You don’t even need to pay attention, you can do a lot of other things at the same time. I don’t think that’s particularly healthy for the mind or the soul.”View image in fullscreen‘There is no afterlife. I can say that. I didn’t see the light’ … Refn.Photograph: Suki Dhanda/The GuardianHis films, he says, are more like fairytales: simplistic enough to read to a child, yet bottomless in interpretation. “That’s why people still examine Hans Christian Andersen. But we’ve forgotten this because our entertainment is based on just giving and receiving information.”Not everyone agrees with his assessment: reviews for Her Private Hell have been wildly mixed. In fact, it’s hard to think of a film-maker who splits opinion so consistently. Depending on who you listen to, Refn movies are either gorgeously shot, hypnotic meditations on the human psyche, or tedious borefests full of style and zero substance.Refn claims not to care. In fact, he says he wouldhateit if everyone loved his movies. “It would be devastating. I would be very depressed,” he says. “If we like something and we all agree on it in this room, it’s as if we don’t like it. But if one likes it and one doesn’t and we end up arguing about it, that’s passion. That means that we have been penetrated.”He points to Raging Bull: “Commercially bad. Very divisive at the time. Now you would say, ‘How can you make anything better?’ Opinions disappear, like tears in the rain, but passion will still exist.”He sighs, reflecting on the reaction to his film’s Cannes premiere. “A lot of people had a meltdown again. It’s like, here we go again, ‘There’s no storyline!’ And I’m like, ‘You’re so wrong! There’s so much going on, you’re just looking in the wrong places.’”Her Private Hell review – Nicolas Winding Refn’s shapeshifting fantasia is a dreamy swirl of strangenessRead moreThe kids are far smarter than critics, he says. “They feel things. Because they’ve been sold artificial whatever on social media and screens. So they will love it or they will hate it. But they do it with such a passion.”Critics notwithstanding, Refn seems in a content place right now. Is he actually glad his heart packed in? “I’m so happy, I can’t tell you,” he says. “Every day I thank God for killing me and bringing me back. Because why make me go through all this if I don’t have a purpose? Now I have a mission.”If he gets another 25 years, he says, he will use them to make art, to forge new films from the furnace of his roaring creative fire. After all, he says, there’s nothing else out there. “There is no afterlife. I can say that. I didn’t see the light. So whatever time you have left, live it now, man.”What about all the people who’ve had near-death experiences and claim to have seen the heavenly gates? Refn sniffs and, with no visible irony, says: “They’ve seen too many movies.”Her Private Hell is in cinemas on 25 SeptemberThis article was amended on 17 September 2026. In a previous version, a still from the film The Neon Demon was incorrectly captioned as showing Elle Fanning.Explore more on these topicsFilmNicolas Winding RefnScience fiction and fantasy filmsThrillersDriveBronsonThe Neon DemoninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hard parties, cheap rents and horrible flats: how 90s art and fashion redefined British culture | Culture | The Guardian
description: An evocative new Tate Britain show captures an era when the UK’s newly flush creative industries teamed up with a generation of skint dreamers to bring the decade into vivid colour
Author: Miranda Sawyer
Headline: An evocative new Tate Britain show captures an era when the UK’s newly flush creative industries teamed up with a generation of skint dreamers to bring the decade into vivid colour
Content: Pretty in pink … Kate Moss, photographed by Juergen Teller.Photograph: Juergen TellerView image in fullscreenPretty in pink … Kate Moss, photographed by Juergen Teller.Photograph: Juergen TellerGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.CultureHard parties, cheap rents and horrible flats: how 90s art and fashion redefined British cultureAn evocative new Tate Britain show captures an era when the UK’s newly flush creative industries teamed up with a generation of skint dreamers to bring the decade into vivid colourIntroduction byMiranda SawyerThu 17 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere isKate Moss, with pink hair splayed across a pillow, her face scrubbed of makeup, her smile sweet and wonky. Sarah Lucas’s Pauline Bunny artwork with its confrontational hosiery on a charity shop chair. Sean Ellis’s collaborative knights-in-grubby-armour shoot with Alexander McQueen. Here are happy ravers, in a club, or saluting the sun as it stretches and yawns over a litter-strewn hill.These photos are old. They were taken a long time ago. But they’re young, too. They are curated by Edward Enninful for the Tate’s exhibition The 90s:Artand Fashion (Enninful worked at i-D in the 90s) and almost everyone involved is shiny and fresh. The models, whether professional or not, are mostly in their 20s, and the photographers are early in their careers. It gives the photos a youthful fizz, a verve. But the energy also comes from an understanding between photographer and subject. In many of the pictures you can feel the shared mischief, a “yes we’re serious about our ideas” but also a “look, we’re getting away with it!” delight.At the time these photos were taken I was writing for magazines such as Select, the Face and Smash Hits. I know some of the subjects in the pictures, as well as some of the photographers. No surprise: I was out a lot, and so were a lot of people in what we now call the creative industries. We were excited: we had just moved to London, or Manchester, had recently left art college or school or university, managed to wangle our ways into occasional, seemingly glamorous jobs that hadn’t yet blossomed into careers. As every generation must, we were elbowing our way in from the edges to the mainstream, finding space for ourselves and people like us. Some of the people in these pictures eventually became very rich, and so moved into different circles. But at the time, everyone was on a level. Skint, hard-working and up for a good night out.double quotation markAs every generation must, we were elbowing our way in from the edges to the mainstreamParties were plentiful. Aside from the club scene, magazines threw them, art galleries threw them, some random person that you met in a late-night drinking den said, “I know this place”, so you went. When you were out, you met artists, photographers, musicians, actors, writers, promoters, dealers, “entrepreneurs”. Often you had no idea what they did: I once walked into an office and realised that the esteemed head of design was the character with whom I’d spent a full-on all-nighter at Glastonbury a month before.Of the three, art parties were the best, often held for impoverished artists by very rich people who wanted to invest in work that would, eventually, make them even richer. I went to a party for an artist at a west London house that was so gorgeous I thought it was a restaurant when I first arrived. The woman who owned the house showed me and others the swimming pool in the basement, and informed us she’d insisted on it when her husband had said they were moving to London. The artist the woman was throwing the party for lived in a tiny housing association flat. Fashion parties were wild, but with a darker edge (rich older men have always been interested in young, insecure models), and more self-conscious. Music ones were cheaper, boozier and scuzzier. There were also parties thrown just because a venue was found: an empty lido, a disused warehouse, film studios vacated between shoots – inner-city spaces that today have almost all been repurposed into flash new apartments.double quotation markParty venues were easy to find. The flats were horrible, but they were plentiful and central, and rent was cheapSuch times were documented, of course, or these images would not exist. But in everyday life, we were less visually obsessed. When you went on a night out, one of your friends might have a camera with them, but they’d forget to use it or leave it in a pile of coats in a darkened corner, never to be seen again. You would embark on whatever adventure the evening might bring and afterwards there wouldn’t be much evidence of it; the sweat and grime washed off by a barely functioning shower. No wonder the good photographers capturing this era had a specialness, a status.Now the 90s are far enough away for us to understand them, it’s clear that there was a hidden architecture to those times, one that supported this burst of creativity. It wasn’t just the party venues that were easy to find. The flats were horrible, but they were plentiful and central, and rent was cheap. I never paid more than £60 a week for a room in a flatshare. And if you couldn’t afford that, you could squat, or claim housing benefit until someone official caught on that you were working, too. So we had places to live, but there was no internet to keep us there: if we wanted food or drink or sex, we couldn’t magic them up on our phones. To get those, you had to leave the house, and we did, often not returning for days at a time. Some friends of mine had what they called “going home fear”. They’d only return to their flat for an hour, to wash and get changed before going straight back out again.Another factor that propped up that time was that the music industry was flush with money from the invention of CDs. Such riches meant that major labels could afford to fund indie labels, indie labels could pay independent PRs to promote their bands, and music magazines could pay journalists to write about them. There were enough jobs in that industry, and in fashion and photography and art, for the people in power to take a punt on the enthusiastic newbie, someone who’d come from nowhere, who knew no one but who had interesting ideas and who kept on coming back. A whole generation of cocky, idea-fuelled kids trying their hands at modelling, writing, presenting, art. Or photography. These pictures are some of the results.Miranda Sawyer is the presenter of the podcastTalk 90s to Me. The 90s: Fashion and Art is at Tate Britain, London, 8 October to 14 February.Bright young things: photographers and curators on works in the showYoung Pink Kate by Juergen Teller, 1998 (main image)Teller: “I first photographed Kate when she was 18, her first fashion campaign, for Katharine Hamnett. Since then we worked together a lot and became friends. She called me up one day, explained she dyed her hair pink for a Versace fashion show in Milan and wanted to dye it back, and asked whether I wanted to come over before and photograph her with pink hair.”View image in fullscreenSarah Lucas, Pauline Bunny, 1997.Photograph: Lucy Dawkins/Sarah Lucas/ TatePauline Bunny by Sarah Lucas, 1997Dominique Heyse-Moore, senior curator: “Sarah had been stuffing tights with different kinds of materials, making spiders and all sorts of many-limbed creatures. But her “bunnies” are really the first time that women’s bodies began to be represented through this method. Her bunnies are named after Bunny Girls, the waitresses who worked in clubs earlier in the 20th century, though still around at this point. But the way she is slumped over a chair perhaps suggests that she is a sex worker. She’s also so slight: it’s a girl’s body in many ways. Sarah has continued to make bunnies. The recent ones have more folds, more flesh: older women’s bodies, but also more assertive, more confident in their sexuality.”View image in fullscreenSam Taylor-Johnson, Fuck, Suck, Spank, Wank, 1993.Photograph: Sam Taylor-Johnson/All Rights Reserved/DACS ImagesFuck Suck Spank Wank by Sam Taylor-Johnson, 1993Heyse-Moore: “A lot of these images are about girlhood, womanhood and youth; the experience of photographing and being photographed. All those themes are beautifully brought together here. There’s this way in which Taylor-Johnson is overtly and explicitly challenging the idea of how a woman is supposed to appear or behave in the making of her art. In the classic kind of 90s way, it’s poking at gender norms, not to mention the idea of the badly behaved artist.”View image in fullscreenJon Shard, Flesh at the Hacienda, 1994.Photograph: Jon ShardFlesh at Haçienda by Jon Shard, 1994Shard: “I took this at Flesh in the early 90s. This guy had created this incredible headdress from silver wire, combined with the long chain around his neck. He was moving around the club like a piece of performance art. Flesh had a different feel from regular Haçienda nights. It was a gay night with its own look and energy, with people experimenting much more with how they presented themselves. I think this was what made the 90s so interesting: people creating things for themselves.”View image in fullscreenFergus Greer, Leigh Bowery, Session VIII, Look 38, 1994.Photograph: Fergus GreerLeigh Bowery, Session VII, Look 38 by Fergus Greer, 1994Greer: “This image of Leigh in a full-length rubber bodysuit, shot on large format, was made just before his sudden death from an Aids-related illness brought our six-year collaboration to an end. Leigh would spend hours preparing in the dressing room with his wife Nicola. When he finally emerged, the studio would fall into a pause of pure incredulity. My part was to find the magic that turned that moment into a photograph that would outlast us both. These are images people still want to reproduce, that 100 years on will hang on gallery walls and run in the media.”View image in fullscreenElle von Unwerth, Naomi Campbell, Babywoman album cover, 1994.Photograph: Ellen von UnwerthNaomi Campbell Babywoman album cover by Ellen von Unwerth, 1994Heyse-Moore: “Naomi Campbell was a symbol of international Black beauty. But what we know now is that she often didn’t get booked in the UK. There was a persistent idea about what British style was: Kate Moss’s more androgynous, indie look. The Babywoman artwork is playing with the idea of her as a girl or a woman. Even the title speaks to questions around Black girlhood: research suggests that Black girls are not seen to be children. We hear so much about what it was like to be a vulnerable young white model but don’t really hear about that with Campbell.”View image in fullscreenSean Ellis, The Dark Knight Returns, styled by Isabella Blow, 1998.Photograph: Sean EllisThe Dark Knight Returns by Sean Ellis, styled by Isabella Blow, 1998Ellis: “I was a huge fan of John Boorman’s film Excalibur and Isabella Blow was very good at mixing not only people but ideas. We spent a lot of time studying 16th-century battle paintings to work out the light and poses. I had a good relationship with Lee [Alexander McQueen, pictured centre]. You could tell he was on a collision course: he almost hated the industry he worked in. Here, he is outnumbered: there is a lowering of the sword as he faces his death. We did ones of him fighting back and another where all the knights are dead but this one, where he was fighting until he couldn’t fight any more, felt the strongest.”View image in fullscreenEileen Perrier, Untitled, Afro Hair and Beauty Show, 1998.Photograph: Eileen Perrier/All rights reserved/DACS 2026Untitled, Afro Hair and Beauty Show by Eileen Perrier, 1998Heyse-Moore: “The Afro Hair and Beauty exhibition filled London’s Alexandra Palace every year. It was an amazing celebration and affirmation of the art of Black hair and makeup. One of the things that is wonderful about this image and the project [Perrier photographed the exhibition over five years] is it’s Black female photographer to Black female subject: there’s a really direct ‘looking at each other’ that takes place; an empowerment and agency for both. We don’t know how old the woman here is exactly, but we know she didn’t go to the show knowing that she and the other women pictured were going to be photographed that day. They’re getting dressed for themselves and for entering into that Black space. It’s a glimpse into this gigantic, quite private world, but with a performative element to it.”View image in fullscreenVinca Petersen, Paula Sunrise 1997.Photograph: Vinca Petersen. Courtesy of Edel Assanti Art.Paula Sunrise by Vinca Petersen, 1997Petersen: “After the 1994 Criminal Justice Act outlawed raves in the UK, I spent a decade travelling around Europe in a van trying to recreate that way of living. This shot captures that feeling of having spent the whole night dancing in the dark in a huge crowd. There is something special about that moment when the sun slowly appears and you start to see the faces of all the people you’ve been surrounded by, and inevitably often sit down and end up talking about the big stuff in life. Nowadays I do kitchen discos. But that sense of freedom and creativity has stayed with us all. The last time I spoke to Paula she was working in the Houses of Parliament.”View image in fullscreenTony Davis, Ravers at the Eclipse, Coventry, 1991Photograph: Tony DavisRavers at the Eclipse, Coventry, by Tony Davis, 1991Edward Enninful, curator: “The 90s were all about a shared energy, where fashion, art and music collided in the same spaces; a moment when a generation of outsiders rejected old hierarchies and for ever changed who gets to be seen. It’s a decade that established conditions that are still with us: the merging of high and low culture, the politicisation of fashion and image, and the emergence of diversity as a creative force.”Explore more on these topicsCultureArtPhotographyTate BritainKate MossfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Queen at Sea review – crushingly sad dementia drama offers a startling portrait of intimacy  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Driven by fine performances from Tom Courtenay and Anna Calder-Marshall, Lance Hammer’s comeback is unbearable in its tragic candour and essential in its moral questioning
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Driven by fine performances from Tom Courtenay and Anna Calder-Marshall, Lance Hammer’s comeback is unbearable in its tragic candour and essential in its moral questioning
Content: Tom Courtenay and Anna Calder-Marshall in Lance Hammer’s Queen at Sea.Photograph: © Seafaring LLCView image in fullscreenTom Courtenay and Anna Calder-Marshall in Lance Hammer’s Queen at Sea.Photograph: © Seafaring LLCPeter Bradshaw's film of the weekMoviesReviewQueen at Sea review – crushingly sad dementia drama offers a startling portrait of intimacyDriven by fine performances from Tom Courtenay and Anna Calder-Marshall, Lance Hammer’s comeback is unbearable in its tragic candour and essential in its moral questioningPeter BradshawThu 17 Sep 2026 09.05 EDTFirst published on Wed 18 Feb 2026 10.29 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis inexpressibly painful and sad story – featuring angry, complex, brilliant late-career performances fromTom Courtenayand Anna Calder-Marshall – is about dementia, the endgame of care and the decisions that need to be made when the spouse-carer is as vulnerable as the patient (and whose right it is to take those decisions). It is about the nature of intimacy between the two; and about the moment this becomes a problem for the grownup children with a conflicting sense of their own responsibilities.Queen at Sea is directed by indie US film-maker Lance Hammer, absent sincehis 2008 Sundance winner, Ballast. This is an almighty comeback, a lacerating movie bearing comparison withMichael Haneke’s AmourorGaspar Noé’s Vortex. It concludes with a heartbreakingly ironic and enigmatic final sequence refusing the traditional final cadence; a diptych of love, contrasting the pleasures and expectations of intimacy across the generations.The setting is a gloomy and wintry London, with porridge-grey cloud cover.Juliette Binocheplays Amanda, a recently divorced academic. She has taken a sabbatical with her teen daughter, Sara (Florence Hunt), to be closer to her elderly mother, Leslie (Calder-Marshall) – who has dementia – and her stepfather, Martin (Courtenay).One dull weekday morning, she looks in on Martin and Leslie, catching them having sex, with a mask of incomprehension on her mother’s face. Furiously, she accuses him of raping Leslie. The shock and disgust clearly stem at one level from the fact that he is her stepfather, not her father; and also because they have already received the GP’s advice that Leslie can no longer give meaningful consent.Yet Martin has done his own research on the internet contradicting this, claiming that marital sex comforts dementia patients just as much as all the other things that are done for them without meaningful consent: food, shelter, medical care. Crucially, it comforts the carer, too. He loves his wife and this is a vital way to keep this alive.Icily livid, Amanda calls the police, which sets in train events that she almost instantly regrets. Martin is prevented from seeing Leslie, who is terrified by the rape exam and whimperingly baffled as to why her husband is not there. The only way to suspend the legal action is for Leslie to go into a care home, which has long been Amanda’s demand. This is furiously resisted by Martin, who now sees all this as a malicious, dishonest way of forcing the situation on them both – it’s a care home, or it’s the cops – and a permanent stain on his character whatever the outcome. Meanwhile, Sara is developing a relationship with a boy at her new London school that her mother knows nothing about.The story moves from one agonisingly difficult and ambiguous situation to the next – each a terrifying point of no return, each the awful occasion of things seen and said that can’t be unseen or unsaid. Is Amanda right to take the view that she has – or has she, in some crucial way, mishandled things? Is Martin an abuser of the most sinister and hateful kind, or misunderstood? Is the care home itself such a bad place? Even the crisis that this entails, connected to the unmentionable truths about older people’s sexuality and propensity to abuse, doesn’t exactly solve the question. Everything that happens, each station of the cross, each unbearable ordeal, is just a function of the overall situation, which can only be managed up to a point.The crux of the film is a four-way conversation between a social worker, Amanda, Martin and Leslie. This involves Martin’s tearful, passionate declaration of love for his wife and best friend; a virtual reaffirmation of vows, which Leslie poignantly returns. Has dementia made her affirmation valueless? Queen at Sea is a film with a tragic, wintry candour.Queen at Sea screened at theBerlin film festivaland is in UK and Irish cinemas from 18 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmPeter Bradshaw's film of the weekDrama filmsDementiaJuliette BinocheTom CourtenayMental healthHealthreviewsShareReuse this content

title: It’s going to be a blast: why 100 tubas are heading for a garden in Haddington | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Anthony Braxton’s colossal Composition No 19 (for 100 Tubas) has never been performed outside the US so its arrival at the Lammermuir festival merits a mighty fanfare
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Anthony Braxton’s colossal Composition No 19 (for 100 Tubas) has never been performed outside the US so its arrival at the Lammermuir festival merits a mighty fanfare
Content: Diverse in their unity… the world premiere of Anthony Braxton’s Composition No. 19 for 100 Tubas at the World Financial Center Plaza, New York, June 2006.Photograph: Jack Vartoogian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDiverse in their unity… the world premiere of Anthony Braxton’s Composition No. 19 for 100 Tubas at the World Financial Center Plaza, New York, June 2006.Photograph: Jack Vartoogian/Getty ImagesClassical musicIt’s going to be a blast: why 100 tubas are heading for a garden in HaddingtonFaced with a new concert venue – a vast and beautiful walled garden – John Harris and the Lammermuir festival had to decide how to fill it with sound. Anthony Braxton’s colossal composition was the irresistible solution.John HarrisThu 17 Sep 2026 07.12 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 08.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWorking in contemporary music, I am used to eyebrows being raised by friends and family when I answer their seemingly innocent dinnertime question, “What are you up to at the moment?”. My responses over the years have ranged from “staging an opera about alien abductionunderneath Concorde” to “ensuring that a soprano can get a tattoo live on stage while she sings”. However, I’ve never previously experienced anything like the familial spluttering in response to my most recent answer – “putting on a concert with 100 tuba players in a garden outside Edinburgh”.I do understand some of their surprise, but to be honest 100 tubas seemed like such a logical solution to the problem I was given that I’m not sure I understand it entirely! James Waters, artistic director of the Lammermuir festival in East Lothian,Scotland– and regular partner-in-crime for some of Red Note Ensemble’s wilder productions, including the aforementioned opera under Concorde – phoned me one day last year to say “I have found an interesting – and very beautiful – place to put on a concert. I just don’t have a clue what music to do. Come and have a look!”Duly invited out to look atAmisfield Walled Garden– a beautifully laid out space near Haddington, maintained and much cherished by a group of committed volunteers – I was taken not only with how lovely it all was, but also just how big. Originally the kitchen garden for a now vanished stately home, it must have been quite the kitchen. The walls are those of a castle – an intimidating 20 feet high– and the space itself extends over the equivalent of several football pitches. James – face beaming with delight at setting a challenge that he knows I’m not going to turn down – turned to me and said: “Let’s fill the garden with sound!”View image in fullscreen‘The space extends over the equivalent of several football pitches.’ Amisfield Walled Garden, Haddington, Scotland.Photograph: Amazing Aerial/AlamyChallenge duly accepted. But how? To my mind, with something that size, you’ve got three options. Either massive amplification (a little rock’n’roll for Lammermuir, perhaps), a lot of bagpipes (always an option in Scotland, but the contemporary repertoire is sadly limited), or those quintessential outdoor instruments – brass ones. And then the essential question: what on earth are they going to play?I do have some history with large-scale brass performances. I myself don’t play a brass instrument – although my brother was a founder member of the brass band in the town that we grew up in – but I have worked with many brass players over the years, and staged a number of mass-participation brass events in my other job as festival director of New Music Dublin. However, I have no handles at all on the contemporary brass repertoire beyond that, so it was time to call in a second associate from the contemporary music underworld – the celebrated trumpeter Marco Blaauw, well-known for his playing with Ensemble Musikfabrik in Germany to help us work out what everyone was going to perform.double quotation markTubas come in all shapes and sizes, from orchestral ones to over-the-shoulder sousaphones, tenor horns, euphoniums and even the rarely- sighted Wagner tubaMarco breezed into Scotland, trumpet in hand, to “try out the acoustics” of the garden. Those bitingly cold days in Amisfield in December are precious memories, as Marco also brought along John Wallace – fellow trumpeter extraordinaire, former principal of the Royal Conservatoire of Scotland and best known to the general public as the impeccable soloist performing alongside Kiri Te Kanawa at Charles and Diana’s wedding – to have a listen. Very sadly, John died earlier this year, and this year’s Lammermuir festival is dedicated to his memory. I have a very clear memory of John dancing around the garden to Marco’s wild improvisations in the fading winter light, coat flapping, eyes shining with joy. I hope his spirit lives on in what we are about to do.The acoustics in the garden are extraordinary. It’s so large that when we are within it, we are inside an echo chamber, every individual note ricocheting around like an echo off a mountainside. Once Marco had finished his acoustic explorations and we were warming up inside with tea and cake, he turned to me and said, somewhat mischievously: “You do know there’s a piece for 100 tubas? That would be fun and interesting to do!”View image in fullscreenAn aerial view of the 2006 world premiere - at New York’s World Financial Center Plaza –  of Anthony Braxton’s Composition No 19 for 100 Tubas.Photograph: Jack Vartoogian/Getty ImagesAnthony Braxton’sComposition No 19 (for 100 Tubas)(1971) has never had a performance outside the US and this will be only its third performance ever. It was initially written without a first performance in mind, and it was only when the “tubist, composer and improviser” Jay Rozen joined Braxton’s sextet in 2006 and asked the composer about the piece, having seen the score published in an experimental music magazine in the 1970s, that Braxton offered to reconstruct the written music for what would be its premiere in New York in 2006.The venerable composer introduces his score – which consists of four sections of music for four separate bands of 25 tuba players each – with an essay, detailing his extensive thinking and philosophy. He describes the piece as “alternative parade music”, and wonderfully it not only provides this structure, but also allows the players to be “diverse in their unity”. Unity, because everyone is indeed playing a tuba – but diversity, because tubas come in all shapes and sizes, from orchestral tubas to over-the-shoulder sousaphones, tenor horns, euphoniums and even the rarely sightedWagner tuba. There is also unity because everyone is apparently playing the same piece but, as the performance proceeds, it gives spaces and opportunities for every player to diversify and express their own musical personality, acting as an improvising individual within the group. These opportunities become more and more numerous until by the end – in our version, at the hour – it becomes a wild group improvisation, with the players gathered in the centre having paraded their way around the garden in multiple different ways as the light slowly fades into the autumnal dusk.And that small matter of finding 100 tuba players? I don’t want to jinx anything – and it is a phenomenal organisational workout for my colleagues to get everyone to the right place at the right time with the right instruments, right music and right clothes – but it turned out, when the word went out, that tuba players from across the world will come to join in. Performers from the US, Latvia, Estonia and the rest of the UK are bringing their tubas of all shapes and sizes to be a part of what may be the most eyebrow-raising contemporary music event I’ve yet told my family I’m a part of.100 Tubas is at Amisfield Walled Garden, part of theLammermuir festival, on 19 September. John Harris is artistic director and chief executive of theRed Note Ensembleand Festival Director ofNew Music Dublin.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicJazzFestivalsExperimental musicMusic festivalsScotlandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Beabadoobee: Pylon review – voice of a generation’s surprisingly relatable rampage through rock star rage | Music | The Guardian
description: The Filipino-British songwriter’s fourth album sprinkles 90s alt fuzz with disarmingly sweet melodies and an impressive host of guests including Paramore’s Hayley Williams and Turnstile’s Brendan Yates
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: The Filipino-British songwriter’s fourth album sprinkles 90s alt fuzz with disarmingly sweet melodies and an impressive host of guests including Paramore’s Hayley Williams and Turnstile’s Brendan Yates
Content: ‘New infatuation’ … Beabadoobee.Photograph: Courtesy of Erika KamanoView image in fullscreen‘New infatuation’ … Beabadoobee.Photograph: Courtesy of Erika KamanoAlexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewBeabadoobee: Pylon review – voice of a generation’s surprisingly relatable rampage through rock star rage(Dirty Hit)The Filipino-British songwriter’s fourth album sprinkles 90s alt fuzz with disarmingly sweet melodies and an impressive host of guests including Paramore’s Hayley Williams and Turnstile’s Brendan YatesAlexis PetridisThu 17 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 10.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast month, the Guardian published a feature aboutthe demise of the monoculture. It suggested that streaming services, personalised algorithms and the declining influence of radio and television meant we now live in a world where stardom isn’t as universal as it once was. It used Sam Fender and Olivia Dean’s single Rein Me In as an example: here was a song that spent a record-breaking 23 weeks at No 1 yet hadn’t attained anything like the ubiquity you would once have expected: to judge by social media, plenty of people seemed to have never knowingly heard it.View image in fullscreenBeabadoobee: Pylon album cover.If you were looking to advance this theory, you might alight on the career of Beatrice Laus, the 26-year-old British-Filipinosinger-songwriter better known as Beabadoobee. To a certain cohort, primarily female and in their late teens and early 20s, she is not just a huge star, but a genuinely iconic figure. The latter is an over-used adjective in 2026, but if social media abounds with tutorials advising female fans how to copy your style and imitate your makeup – if you can be personally held partly responsible for the 2021 outbreak of adolescent girls drawing fake freckles on their faces in imitation of your own – then it probably fits, whether it discomfits Laus or not. The lyrics of Satellite, the closing track on her fourth album Pylon, suggests it does: “I give the generation a new infatuation,” she sings. “If only I knew how to cope with the times.”Laus’s sound has always been rooted in 90s alt-rock – grunge and its various US indie offshoots, shoegaze, Elliott Smith – sprinkled with a hefty pinch of pop nous. The latter gives her a distinct point of difference from her source material: Laus is less of straightforwardpasticheusethan you might expect someone who once released a song called I Wish I Was Stephen Malkmus to be. She’s also spun these once-underground influences into mainstream success. Her biggest hit, a collaboration with Canadian rapper Powfu called Death Bed (Coffee for Your Head) has been streamed more than 2bn times. Her last album, 2024’s Rick Rubin-produced This Is How Tomorrow Moves, entered the UK charts at No 1, while its follow-up arrives boasting an impressively starry range of guests: Paramore’s Hayley Williams, Deftones’ Chino Moreno, Matty Healy and George Daniel of labelmates the 1975 and Turnstile’s Brendan Yates among them. Her forthcoming UK tour is housed exclusively in arenas: the O2, Madison Square Garden. And yet, one suspects most people outside said cohort would struggle to name – or hum – a single song by her.Beabadoobee: Sun Has Set – videoSuch is the way of popular culture these days, and Laus is evidently doing very well for herself. So well, in fact, that Pylon’s lyrical themes include those hardy perennials of the successful rock star, the dislocation of life on tour (the title track comes replete with images of endless roads “in a place that I don’t know the name”), and fake friends attracted solely by your celebrity (the Williams feature Nothing to Prove). If that sounds a little remote for an artist whose success is to some extent founded in talking directly to an audience not much younger than she is about stuff that matters to them, then it’s expressed in snappily relatable terms. “Hold me like a screen, disconnected from reality,” she sings on Pylon. And, besides, there’s plenty here that feels more universal to her fanbase’s lived experiences. “Growing up just means to fuck everything up again,” protests Switchblade, a neat fixing of the confusion of early adulthood, while Sun Has Set rounds on a frenemy in brutal style – “we’ll never be friends, I mean we’ll never pretend – fuck that” – over a heaving, strikingly bloody guitar riff.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘We never apologised for our rage or revenge-seeking’: riot grrrl legends Heavens to Betsy reuniteRead moreThe ferocious storm she raises on the latter track is telling. Released in the wake of her support slot on Taylor Swift’s Eras tour, This Is How Tomorrow Moves leaned into her pop side, but Pylon turns in the opposite direction. There are still plenty of bright melodies to be had, not least on the disarmingly pretty Spark, and Laus’s voice naturally tends to cooing charm, but the guitars come drenched in caustic levels of distortion and the riffs they play are brawny or jagged. The album continually deploys a sweet-to-sour pivot that’s impressively well-judged: the dreamy bedroom-pop mood of Despite That is obliterated by sulphurous fuzz; shards of noise and gusts of feedback blow through Powerline, a duet with Yates; Write Me a Letter starts out mistily autumnal and ends up livid. Only the too-toothsome Estranged gets the balance wrong.It’s strikingly confident, as is her treatment of her celebrity guests: you’re aware they’re present, but always in a supporting role, with no doubt who the main star is. But then, why wouldn’t Laus be confident? As has already been established, she’s doing very well for herself, albeit in a very 2020s kind of way. Pylon offers a compelling argument that Beabadoobee’s reach should be broader.This week Alexis listened toThe CJP Band – We Must BelieveA friend’s enthusiasm belatedly alerted me to We Must Believe: dizzily uplifting jazz-infused disco-funk that hails, improbably, from the New Forest.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekIndiereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Human harps, massive bananas and dogging: the 20 best Busby Berkeley dance routines – ranked! | Movies | The Guardian
description: To mark 50 years since the director and choreographer’s death, we count down his best fantastical, kaleidoscopic numbers, from erotic silhouettes to sinister tap dancers
Author: Anne Billson
Headline: To mark 50 years since the director and choreographer’s death, we count down his best fantastical, kaleidoscopic numbers, from erotic silhouettes to sinister tap dancers
Content: On the hoof … The Gang’s All Here, 1943.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreenOn the hoof … The Gang’s All Here, 1943.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyRankedMoviesHuman harps, massive bananas and dogging: the 20 best Busby Berkeley dance routines – ranked!To mark 50 years since the director and choreographer’s death, we count down his best fantastical, kaleidoscopic numbers, from erotic silhouettes to sinister tap dancersAnne BillsonThu 17 Sep 2026 07.48 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 14.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. Sittin’ on a Back Yard Fence from Footlight Parade (1933)So you thought Cats (2019) was tacky? Wait until you see Ruby Keeler (AKA Mrs Al Jolson) gambolling around as a fluffy white feline, being wooed by an ogling tomcat, or chasing Billy Barty, a child actor with dwarfism, costumed as a mouse.19.The Girl at the Ironing Boardfrom Dames (1934)Joan Blondell (seven months pregnant during filming) livens up workaday laundry tasks by fantasising about the men whose underwear she hangs out to dry. And the underwear flirts right back. Who cares if you can see the wires?18.Fascinating Rhythmfrom Lady Be Good (1941)If this were a tap dancing Top 20, Eleanor Powell would be at No 1, but Berkeley wisely stands back and showcases her epic skills with minimal fuss. All the tricksiness took place out of frame, where stagehands were pushing grand pianos out of her way.17.The Lady in the Tutti Frutti Hatfrom The Gang’s All Here (1943)View image in fullscreen‘Some people say I dress too gay, but every day I feel so gay!’Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyBerkeley’s first colour film as both director and choreographer stars “Brazilian Bombshell” Carmen Miranda in her signature fruit-laden headdress. The fruity motif continues in a musical number set on a fake tropical island where chorus girls wield giant bananas. Nothing salacious to see here, move along.16.Young and Healthyfrom 42nd Street (1933)This quintessential backstage musical was a huge hit and established Berkeley’s approach to choreography. An initially stagebound song with innuendo-laden lyrics, belted out by lecherous Dick Powell, blossoms into revolving geometric formations of young women shot from every conceivable angle, culminating in a travelling shot through their spread legs. This is cinema!15. Spin a Little Web of Dreams from Fashions of 1934 (1934)“Mr Berkeley, I’m not raising my daughter to be a human harp!” was one critic’s reaction to a vision of chorus girls plucking at harps fashioned from other chorus girls. Just before theHays Codebanished navels from Hollywood, blond-wigged beauties flaunt their belly buttons while performing the ultimate ostrich feather fan dance.14. Honeymoon Hotel from Footlight Parade (1933)Before Dick Powell went all film noir as Philip Marlowe in Farewell, My Lovely (1944), he and Keeler regularly played sweethearts in Berkeley’s musicals. The camera glides around what is essentially a sex hotel, as attempts to consummate their hasty marriage are hampered by other guests, interfering relatives and an unnaturally precocious child.13. Oh, Lady Be Good! from Lady Be Good (1941)Once again, Berkeley the choreographer stands back and lets Eleanor Powell work her magic. MGM failed to come up with a suitable dog to partner her for this number, so Powell bought a terrier mix called Buttons and trained it herself.12. Dames from Dames (1934)“What do you go for, go see a show for?” The answer is dames (male gaze, sorry) and here they are, not as scantily clad as in pre-code days, but forming a wide range of pleasing kaleidoscopic configurations and Bridget Riley-esque patterns until Dick Powell’s head bursts through their tableaux.11.Shuffle Off to Buffalofrom 42nd Street (1933)Keeler once again tries to consummate a marriage (to Clarence Nordstrom), this time on a sleeper train to Niagara Falls. Other passengers leer salaciously out of their curtained compartments, while worldly Una Merkel and Ginger Rogers predict the ingenue will soon be on a train to Reno for a quickie divorce.10. Shadow Waltz from Gold Diggers of 1933 (1933)Chorus girls, wired up to neon-tubed violins, twirl around on vertiginous walkways. Then the lights go out so all you can see are the violins, which rearrange themselves into the shape of one massive violin. So many ways this could have gone horribly wrong – and indeed, a 6.4 earthquake hit Los Angeles during filming, and some of the violins short-circuited.9.The Polka Dot Polkafrom The Gang’s All Here (1943)One minute Alice Faye is singing as normal, surrounded by dancing children who are only marginally weird. The next, we are plunged into a Technicolor hallucination of neon hoops, more dots than DC’s Polka-Dot Man could dream of, and psychedelic effects that will have you wondering if you accidentally ingested LSD.8.We’re in the Moneyfrom Gold Diggers of 1933 (1933)Before teaming up with Fred Astaire in the first of their 10 musical collaborations, Ginger Rogers played a golden-hearted broad in Berkeley’s first two backstage musicals. Heading a chorus line draped in silver dollars, she belts out an upbeat ode to capitalism, including one verse inPig Latin.7.42nd Streetfrom 42nd Street (1933)View image in fullscreenJust an ordinary day in NYC … 42nd Street.Photograph: Moviestore Collection/AlamyOnce again, a musical number opens out into an entire panorama that could not possibly be physically contained in a theatre. Keeler’s effortful hoofing (she’s no Eleanor Powell, but we love her anyway) gives way to rhythmic travelling shots of New Yorkers going about their business: traffic, newspaper sellers, hairdressers and, adding a touch of dirty realism, a murder.6.Pettin’ in the Parkfrom Gold Diggers of 1933 (1933)Dick Powell is trying to get into Keeler’s knickers in an outrageously nudge-nudge number featuring snowball fights, erotic silhouettes, roller-skating cops and stocking tops galore, before she finally stymies her beau with a onesie made of metal. Enter leering child actor Billy Barty, with a can opener.5. I Only Have Eyes for You from Dames (1934)Powell loves Keeler so much he keeps seeing her everywhere. And so do we, thanks to lookalike chorus girls in Keeler masks, holding up cut-outs of her face, or pulling their skirts over their heads to form one gigantic Keelertifo, all set to a Harry Warren-Al Dubin earworm that quickly became a standard.4. Shanghai Lil from Footlight Parade (1933)After The Public Enemy, James Cagney was keen to avoid being typecast as a gangster and draws on his vaudeville roots to give us a tap dance that almost makes up for Keeler in yellowface. Get an eyeful of Hollywood orientalism in all its pre-code horror, complete with sex workers, opium smokers and half the US Navy on manoeuvres.3.Remember My Forgotten Manfrom Gold Diggers of 1933 (1933)Audiences of the 1930s went to the cinema to escape the Great Depression, but numbers like this assured them that their pain wasn’t being ignored. Joan Blondell, with a sort ofsprechgesang, and contralto Etta Moten lament the treatment of poverty-stricken veterans of the first world war. As the chorus swells, the number segues from a theatrical street into montages of men marching to war and limping home to the breadline and a treadmill of silhouettes. Lump in throat time.2.By a Waterfallfrom Footlight Parade (1933)Dick Powell and Keeler celebrate “love in a natural setting”. Berkeley illustrates this early 1930s ode to dogging with an astonishing aquatic ballet of 100 synchronised swimmers forming flowers, snake shapes and a human fountain, shot from all angles in a glass-walled pool that filled an entire soundstage. None of this, of course, would be visible to the theatre audience glimpsed at the start of the number.1. Lullaby of Broadway from Gold Diggers of 1935 (1935)You ain’t heard nothing until you’ve heard 200 feet stomping out a time step in unison. Of all the musical numbers he directed, Berkeley’s personal favourite was this 13-minute expressionist nightmare in which a young woman’s nightclubbing gets out of hand. From Wini Shaw’s disembodied head turning into the Manhattan skyline, to the most sinister phalanx of tap-dancers this side of Leni Riefenstahl, to the frankly rather shocking ending, it’s an intoxicating masterpiece. “Come and dance!”Explore more on these topicsFilmRankedDancefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Strangers by Naomi Alderman review – where has this odd new species come from? | Fiction | The Guardian
description: A bereavement memoir mingles with speculative fiction, in a wise and ragged examination of grief from the author of The Power
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A bereavement memoir mingles with speculative fiction, in a wise and ragged examination of grief from the author of The Power
Content: Lightness of touch … Naomi Alderman.Photograph: Annabel MoellerView image in fullscreenLightness of touch … Naomi Alderman.Photograph: Annabel MoellerBook of the dayFictionReviewThe Strangers by Naomi Alderman review – where has this odd new species come from?A bereavement memoir mingles with speculative fiction, in a wise and ragged examination of grief from the author of The PowerKeiran GoddardThu 17 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn his Remarks on Frazer’s Golden Bough, Ludwig Wittgenstein alludes to an incident that followed the death of Franz Schubert. He recalls that Schubert’s brother cut several scores into small pieces, each consisting of only a few bars of music, and handed them out to Schubert’s favourite pupils. This, Wittgenstein argues, was a totally understandable act of grief. He goes on to suggest, however, that if, in his grief, Schubert’s brother had left the scores untouched, or even burned them, then that too would be equally legible to us. Such is the disorienting nature of loss – in its wake, anything goes.In The Strangers, Women’s prize-winning author Naomi Alderman tests this thesis to its limits. How about dealing with grief by writing an uneasy memoir/speculative fiction hybrid about the sudden appearance of a new species of quasi-badgers that seem to improve the quality of local soil?Well, it turns out Wittgenstein was right. The Strangers, despite (or perhaps because of) its many ragged idiosyncrasies, is a remarkably successful evocation of loss. Narrated by “the novelist Naomi Alderman”, who is mourning both her recently deceased mother and a series of failed pregnancies, the book ranges incisively across the vast affective terrain bequeathed to those who go on living: despair, disorientation, solipsism, petulance, regret, resignation … the list goes on. After all, grief is not an emotion – it is all the emotions, all at once.And by braiding the memoir within a subtly unnerving tale of eco-horror infestation, Alderman substantially raises the philosophical and symbolic stakes. It is a high-risk, sporadically successful manoeuvre, but one that recognises the gravity of the task at hand. In the same way that a gravestone is an attempt to give form to an absence, Alderman’s structural ingenuity allows the reader to wrangle some of the ineffable aspects of grief into something more coherent and bounded.The plot itself is simple enough, and relatively small fry compared to some of Alderman’s previous work, such as thwarting the techno-apocalypse (The Future) or upending the global gender hierarchy (The Power). A new type of species is discovered, a flat-faced and long-nosed mammal that comes to be known as a mimmoth. They remain largely inscrutable to humans: hard to photograph, even harder to capture, and seemingly responsible for a range of positive ecological changes. Their inscrutability cuts both ways, however, and soon enough the mimmoths are the subject of conspiracy theories and hate campaigns, worship and veneration, floating signifiers swept up into the insatiable polarisation of the present. To some they are harbingers of a better future, sent to teach us how to care for one another and the planet, while to others they are “invaders, genetic freaks, not natural”.double quotation markThe Strangers asserts the painful truth that we do not get to choose the things that we loseOn the whole, Alderman handles the fairly obvious political allegories with a lightness of touch that prevents them from collapsing into polemic, sketching out our political and media environment with the skill of a practised world-builder. The failing institutions of British life are a “Potemkin village” stripped of their engine and replaced with “a clockwork mechanism, slowly running down”. There are occasional moments, however, that seem transplanted from another era entirely; one when people’s political subjectivities were formed by front pages and evening news bulletins, and not by unchecked genocide livestreamed to their phones.Fundamentally, though, The Strangers is a deeply moving and wise book, asserting the painful truth that we simply do not get to choose the things that we lose. When the narrator wonders if she has fallen prey to “mimmoth-psychosis”, the delusion that one has a uniquely intimate relation with the mysterious creatures, I was put in mind of Judith Butler’s observation about grief being a site of temporal reorganisation, a crucible in which our selfhood can be undone and remade. Both Alderman and Butler seem to remind us that while despair may temporarily convince us otherwise, life, in all its terrifying potential, stubbornly persists.That the mimmoths’ arrival coincides with an upsurge in mushroom-like fungus seems particularly telling. Among its many miraculous properties, mycelium contains within it a biological code of deep sociality and connectivity, existing as a network that is constantly reallocating and rebalancing resources, moving nutrients symbiotically between the old and the young, the weak and the strong. The political metaphor contained therein has proved irresistible to many commentators. But in The Strangers, Alderman asks whether there is also a parallel to be drawn in how we allocate our resources of attention and love more proximately. How do we mediate between the existing potential of our own lives, the expired potential of the dead and the unrealised potential of the never or nearly born? It is the type of intractable question one can only ever hope to live alongside. Or, as “the novelist Naomi Alderman” puts it, “I do not wish my ghosts away.”The Strangers by Naomi Alderman is published by Fig Tree (£20).
