title: Ireland to boycott Eurovision again over Israeli participation and ongoing Gaza deaths | Eurovision | The Guardian
description: Ireland joins joins Dutch broadcaster in refusing to take part in 2027 song contest, in second consecutive year of protests
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Ireland joins joins Dutch broadcaster in refusing to take part in 2027 song contest, in second consecutive year of protests
Content: The Palestinian flag during a protest outside the main gate of the Irish national broadcaster RTÉ in Dublin last year.Photograph: Zuma Press, Inc./Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenThe Palestinian flag during a protest outside the main gate of the Irish national broadcaster RTÉ in Dublin last year.Photograph: Zuma Press, Inc./Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.EurovisionIreland to boycott Eurovision again over Israeli participation and ongoing Gaza deathsIreland joins joins Dutch broadcaster in refusing to take part in 2027 song contest, in second consecutive year of protestsLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentThu 17 Sep 2026 13.32 EDTFirst published on Thu 17 Sep 2026 09.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIreland is to boycottEurovisionfor the second year running over the “appalling” ongoing killing in Gaza, the national broadcaster has said.Ireland wasone of five countries, along with Iceland, the Netherlands, Spain and Slovenia, that refused to take part in the competition this year in protest against Israel’s participation.RTÉ announced on Thursday it would not participate in the 2027 competition. The Dutch broadcaster Avrotrosannounced its own boycottlast month, calling Eurovision a “platform for division”.In a statement, the Irish broadcaster said: “RTÉ feels that Ireland’s participation cannot be justified given ‌the appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis there, which continues to put the lives of so many civilians at risk.”Next year’s Eurovision is to be held in the Bulgarian Black Sea city of Burgas, after the country won for the first time in May.View image in fullscreenNorwegian singer Emmy representing Ireland in the 2025 Eurovision at the St Jakobshalle arena in Basel, Switzerland.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesAvrotros said it would not take part, claiming the competition “can no longer be considered neutral, with a participating country still involved in a large-scale military conflict”.The European Broadcasting Union (EBU), which organises the event, is in talks with other Dutch broadcasters, hoping one of the country’s other public service TV stations will participate.Eurovision’s director, Martin Green, said he regretted but respected RTÉ’s decision. “They remain a valued part of our family and will be missed,” he said.“That power to bring people together is at the heart of what makes the contest so special and is even more important now in an increasingly difficult and divided world,” he added.“All broadcasters decide on an annual basis to participate in the following year’s contest. We will remain in dialogue with RTÉ and hope to welcome them back to the contest in the future.”The EBU has tried twice to address broadcasters’ concerns over the participation ofIsrael.Last year, itreduced the number of votesthat could be entered online or by telephone by one individual, amid allegations Israel had mounted a disproportionate campaign for public votes.Last month, the EBU announced that broadcasters would no longer be eligible to host the Eurovision song contest if their state wasinvolved in an “armed conflict”or in a “sensitive geopolitical situation”.Eurovision has faced protests in and outside the competition venues in recent years over the participation of Israel, a competitor since 1973.In 2024, the European Commission madean unusual interventionafter the organisers banned audience members from waving the EU flag at the grand final in Sweden, describing the decision as “mind-blowing” and “regrettable”.Palestinian authorities report that more than 73,000 people have been killed in ​Israel’s war onGaza, ‌which was launched ​after Hamas-led fighters killed 1,200 ​people in an attack on southern Israel in October 2023.A US-brokered ceasefire agreed last year calls for eventual reconstruction of the territory but Israeli strikes have continued. According to Gaza’s health ministry, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the fragile ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025.Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsEurovisionIrelandIsraelGazaPalestineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Bonnie Greer obituary | Bonnie Greer | The Guardian
description: Writer and critic who became known for her sharp, composed appearances on TV shows such as Late Review and Question Time
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: Writer and critic who became known for her sharp, composed appearances on TV shows such as Late Review and Question Time
Content: Greer at the Edinburgh International Book festival in 2014. ‘She was particularly proud of Entropy, a 2009 experimental novel on which she worked for many years.’Photograph: Lorenzo Dalberto/AlamyView image in fullscreenGreer at the Edinburgh International Book festival in 2014. ‘She was particularly proud of Entropy, a 2009 experimental novel on which she worked for many years.’Photograph: Lorenzo Dalberto/AlamyBonnie GreerObituaryBonnie Greer obituaryWriter and critic who became known for her sharp, composed appearances on TV shows such as Late Review and Question TimeMark LawsonThu 17 Sep 2026 09.43 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 12.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe writing and broadcasting ofBonnie Greer, who has died aged 77, were driven by divided perspectives. Her technical experience across an unusual range of genres – drama, fiction, biography, memoir, documentary – informed her work as a wry and lively critic, especially on the late-night BBC2 cultural programmes Late Review and Newsnight Review from the 1990s onwards.And, having spent the first half of her life in the US and the second in the UK, she was also perfectly positioned – in an era when British writers, movie-makers and artists were making much work about and for America – to adjudicate on such creative duality, as well as the escalating Americanisation of British politics. Another asset was her connections: reviewing a David Mamet play or a Madonna album, she had worked with the former in Chicago theatre andmet the latteras a young music wannabe in a Manhattan apartment share.Bonnie’s most successful play,Marilyn and Ella(2008), emblematically explored black and white culture through a dramatised encounter between Ella Fitzgerald and Marilyn Monroe.The television persona that brought Bonnie a niche, but serious, celebrity had two essential elements: a sharp, inquisitive, generous brain – never outweighed on discussion shows that often became rhetorical boxing contests – and a warm, throaty laugh that charmed those who were drawn to her, and disarmed the suspicious or resistant. Having heard that signature sound for years next to me on BBC studio sofas, and before and afterwards in hospitality rooms, it came immediately to my mind on hearing of her death. One of her declared aims was to “bring people together”, and her inclusive, empathetic personality greatly helped.Bonnie’s ability to mix and thrive in what might have been hostile environments – reflecting this, her 2014 memoir was called A Parallel Life – was shaped by her early years. She was born in Chicago, one of seven children of Ben Greer, a sharecropper turned factory hand, and Willie Mae (nee Randolph). Her father was a teenage GI at the end of the second world war. Later, though a committed cinephile, Bonnie struggled to watch Saving Private Ryan, Steven Spielberg’s film about the terrible death toll among young men in that conflict.Ben was stationed in England as part of the D-day landing forces and, having grown up in then segregated Mississippi, was astonished by a society in which discrimination was tacit rather than mandated. His love of Britain passed by osmosis to his daughter. Her unusual first name was, in different accounts, either a tribute to Bonnie Prince Charlie, seen by her parents as a heroic resister to the status quo, or a reference to the now King Charles III, born two days before Bonnie and dubbed in newspaper headlines at the time Bonnie Prince Charlie. She became a British citizen in 1997 and when she was appointed OBE in 2010, she dedicated it to her father.Bonnie described her childhood as “quiet and sheltered”, which was exactly what her Roman Catholic parents would have wanted. But her life became notably noisier from 19 when, while she was a student at DePaul University, a gay friend introduced her to a bohemian group of Chicago actors and writers who unlocked another self: “They would put me in vintage dresses and take me to parties. They made me see life another way.”Through them she met Ivan, who worked at the UN in New York, and cajoled Bonnie to move there in 1978 to live with him and his boyfriend in Manhattan’s West Village. She loved their careless lives there, and began to write plays until the Aids epidemic brutally reduced the group. After nursing Ivan until his death, she moved to London in 1986.View image in fullscreenGreer on BBC Two’s Newsnight Review in 2001, with, from left, Philip Hensher, presenter Mark Lawson and Tom Paulin.Photograph: Richard Kendal/BBCThere she was introduced to a person, David Hutchins, and an institution, the BBC, who would change and shape her adult life. Although she was surprised to find herself in love with a “British white public schoolboy”, her marriage in 1993 to David, a solicitor turned teacher, proved to be the most successful of her many cross-cultural encounters. As well as her great love, he was her amanuensis, chauffeur and a huge encourager of her writing and developing broadcasting career.Critics risk their opinions becoming predictable, although the format of those arts “shout shows” reduced this risk by asking the panel to judge, in a brisk 10 minutes each, a subtitled movie, a sitcom, a Broadway musical and the latest novel by a Nobel literary laureate. It was impossible to guess what Bonnie’s take on any of these would be. She loved Fight Club for its unflinching realism about masculinity, but Amélie for its whimsical artificiality, because she loved “fairytales”.And, while what critics fear is acclaiming a critical disaster as a masterpiece, or vice versa, Bonnie immediately identified Sean Penn’sThe Pledge(2001), in which Jack Nicholson’s retired detective takes an appalling risk to catch a child killer, as a great American movie. I think she had even read the German novella that was the obscure source material. She was also movingly acute on Aids stories such as the film Philadelphia and the novels of Edmund White.When Bonnie’s TV career began in the 90s, her surname was already taken by Germaine, one of the world’s best-known cultural figures. I called them on air “the Greer sisters” and, generally seated next to each other by a canny studio director, they played up to this, becoming a double act, eyes widening in not completely mock surprise at what the other had just said, and continuing their arguments over wine and nibbles afterwards. It is a very modern compliment to say that they should have had a podcast.‘Newsnight’s kindest critic’: Bonnie Greer was always effortlessly in commandRead moreBonnie had wrecking-ball energy – among her listed recreations was “the gym” – and an enduringly youthful enthusiasm. At a time when people of colour were shamefully rare on arts and news programmes – largely because contributors were drawn from monochrome political and cultural establishments – she was of a black generation forced to be pioneers and role models.Live TV shows like to get guests there early for makeup and to mitigate erratic city traffic. In those pre-digital days, we would be handed, on arrival at BBCTelevisionCentre, our fan and hate letters. For Bonnie, the first quickly formed by far the bigger stack, but the second were disgracefully, often frankly, racist. She would crease her face in unsurprised dismay, and focus on the positive correspondence. To my naive shock, this was often from young black women who had never before seen someone who resembled them given such television prominence. Dry-eyed at what the bigots wrote, Bonnie would sometimes well up then.Increasingly, as British institutions began to address their lack of diversity, the mail included invitations of trusteeships. Bonnie served diligently and with familiar sparkle at the British Museum (as deputy chair 2005-13), the Serpentine Gallery, the Royal Opera House and the London Film School. From 2013, she was chancellor of Kingston University. In 2015, though, shesuddenly resignedas president of the Brontë Society, exhausted by the egotistical squabbles that can afflict volunteer cultural bodies, after an ill-tempered public meeting in which she used the heel of her Jimmy Choo shoe as an impromptu gavel.Bonnie’s long experience of racial politics in two nations – one of her later books, Obama Music (2009), anatomised a transformative presidency – informed the biggest non-arts moment of her TV career when, in 2009, she was chosen asa panellist on BBC One’s Question Timealongside the British National party leader, Nick Griffin. The broadcast prompted protests. Because Bonnie was so naturally charming on air, it was clear that she was withholding her charm from Griffin, though, crucially, without losing her temper or being openly rude in a way that might have justified his supporters in their views. After another Question Time appearance, opposing Brexit, Bonnie was offered the freedom of numerous Irish villages.Bonnie’s one regret about her broadcasting success was that it overshadowed her writing, and she was particularly proud of Entropy, a 2009 experimental novel on which she worked for many years.She is survived by David.Bonnie Greer, writer and broadcaster, born 16 November 1948; died 15 September 2026Explore more on these topicsBonnie GreerTelevisionQuestion TimeNewsnightTheatreobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Attorneys for Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs drop music mogul, alleging unpaid legal bills | Sean ‘Diddy‘ Combs | The Guardian
description: The musician is serving a 50-month federal prison term for prostitution-related offenses
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: The musician is serving a 50-month federal prison term for prostitution-related offenses
Content: Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs at the Met Gala in New York on 1 May 2017.Photograph: Lucas Jackson/ReutersView image in fullscreenSean ‘Diddy’ Combs at the Met Gala in New York on 1 May 2017.Photograph: Lucas Jackson/ReutersSean ‘Diddy‘ CombsAttorneys for Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs drop music mogul, alleging unpaid legal billsThe musician is serving a 50-month federal prison term for prostitution-related offensesRichard LuscombeThu 17 Sep 2026 09.21 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 12.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAttorneys representing rapperSean “Diddy” Combssay they are no longer acting for the disgraced star in a dispute over months of unpaid legal bills.The musician, who is serving a50-month federal prison termfor prostitution-related offenses, has become increasingly belligerent in recent months, causing “a total breakdown in cooperation and communication” with New York law firm Sher Tremonte, one of its partners, Michael Tremonte, said in a court filing.The firm was representing Combs, 56, in a $100m civil defamation lawsuit stemming from his conviction last year in a sex-trafficking and racketeering case that also saw himacquittedof the most serious charges.‘We live with a big burden’: US sexual abuse survivor hopes priest’s death brings closureRead moreCombs, Tremonte said in the filing seeking to withdraw as counsel as reported byNBC News, “has not paid a substantial balance of attorney’s fees, costs, and expenses” stretching more than six months.“The firm’s representation has been rendered unreasonably difficult by Mr Combs’s lack of cooperation, resulting in a breakdown in attorney-client communications and rendering Sher Tremonte incapable of continuing to provide effective legal services to Mr Combs,” the filing, in US district court in the southern district of New York, said.For four of the months, it said, Combs has “declined to make himself available for timely, substantive and direct communications about his cases”.In a statement provided by his representatives to the news outlet, Combs accused his lawyers of overcharging, and said that he fired them.“I made the decision to switch lawyers because I won’t let anyone take advantage of me by overcharging me and running up bills that were never approved,” he said. “This is strictly a business matter, and any talk about unpaid fees is just part of our dispute over those unapproved charges.”In an email to NBC, Tremonte rejected Combs’s claims and insisted his company had represented its client “zealously and very efficiently”.“As stated in our court filings, we are withdrawing from representing him because he has not paid his long-overdue invoices and has become uncooperative,” Tremonte said.“Any suggestion that we overcharged him is simply false.”Earlier this year, prosecutors in Los Angelessaidthey were mulling filing new sexual assault charges against Combs, who is currently incarcerated at New Jersey’s Fort Dix federal correctional institution.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRecord producer Jonathan Hay has publicly accused Combs of “assault, sexual harassment, false imprisonment and infliction of emotional distress” during a 2020 collaboration relating to the estate of the late songwriter Christopher Wallace, better known as the rapper Notorious BIG.Combs sued Hay for defamation, separate from the action that gave rise to the payment dispute with Sher Tremonte.In those proceedings, Combs is suing Courtney Burgess, a music manager who told a grand jury in 2024 that the hip-hop mogul gave him flash drives containing video of Combs sexually assaulting minors and fellow celebrities.Earlier this month,TMZ reported, a judge allowed Combs’s case to proceed against Burgess, his lawyer Ariel Mitchell, and the media company Nexstar, which featured Mitchell on its NewsNation show vouching for Burgess’s assertions about the videos.Combs has accused the pair of spreading “outlandish claims” and “wild lies” against him.Explore more on these topicsSean ‘Diddy‘ CombsUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Peter Max, psychedelic pop artist who epitomized flower power, dies aged 88 | Art and design | The Guardian
description: The US artist, whose swirly, colorful, instantly recognizable designs became hugely commercially successful, died on Monday
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The US artist, whose swirly, colorful, instantly recognizable designs became hugely commercially successful, died on Monday
Content: Peter Max in his studio in New York, with a series of portraits of Paul McCartney on the musician’s birthday, in 2012. Max has died aged 88.Photograph: Erik Pendzich/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPeter Max in his studio in New York, with a series of portraits of Paul McCartney on the musician’s birthday, in 2012. Max has died aged 88.Photograph: Erik Pendzich/ShutterstockArt and designPeter Max, psychedelic pop artist who epitomized flower power, dies aged 88The US artist, whose swirly, colorful, instantly recognizable designs became hugely commercially successful, died on MondayAssociated PressWed 16 Sep 2026 20.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeter Max, whose colorful, psychedelic pop art expressed the optimism of the “flower power” movement of the 1960s and graced everything from postage stamps to a cruise ship, has died at 88.Max died on Monday, his son, Adam Max, said in a written statement on Wednesday. No cause was given.“We will remember his extraordinary creativity, his warmth, his curiosity, and the way he saw beauty and possibility everywhere,” Adam Max wrote in the statement. “His art became part of American culture, but the man behind that art – the father we knew and loved – is the person we will miss most.”Max began his career in graphic design in the 1960s and his swirly, colorful, instantly recognizable designs epitomized the era’s “flower power” art. But thanks to his prolific output and fun, accessible style, Max’s work remained well known and popular well into the 21st century.He described his own work as “always on the side of the peaceful nature. I don’t discuss in my paintings negative things, I don’t dwell on it in my mind and don’t dwell on it in my canvasses.”Max was the official artist for the Olympics, the Super Bowl, the Indianapolis 500, the World Cup, the World Series and many other events. His art appeared on a Boeing 777 airplane and a Norwegian Cruise Line ship. His portrait subjects ranged from US presidents to Taylor Swift.But in his first flush of success in the late 1960s and early 1970s, his mural-like tableaus of flowers, the cosmos and cartoonish figures – all in vivid colors such as turquoise, orange and neon green – seemed to be everywhere. Dorm room walls were plastered with his posters. Household furnishings such as clocks and bedspreads sported his designs.He even created covers for the Manhattan Yellow Pages, a business phone directory distributed to millions of people. Max himself was featured on the cover of Life magazine in 1969, his trademark dark, bushy mustache framing a hearty grin.View image in fullscreenPeter Max among some of his creations in his New York studio in 1973.Photograph: Dave Pickoff/APMax was born Peter Max Finkelstein in 1937 to a Jewish family in Berlin. They fled Nazi Germany for Shanghai when he was a baby and later spent time in Tibet, Israel and Paris before settling inNew YorkCity when Max was 16. By then, he said in an interview, he was already “a huge fan of American culture”: comics, movies and “all the jazz music.”By the 1960s, Max’s bold, unique style was a hit with ad agencies, publications, the corporate world and in pop culture, leading to a booming commercial business. “My work was really, I would say, almost exploited,” he said. “It was on mugs, it was on bedsheets, it was on dresses, it was on silks and scarves and ties – 70 product lines.”Max shut the business down for a time in the early 1970s to reconnect with his art. One of his biggest projects after returning to public life was a series of portraits of the Statue of Liberty, painted at the White House at the invitation of first lady Nancy Reagan in 1981.View image in fullscreenPeter Max in 2012.Photograph: Erik Pendzich/ShutterstockMax weathered various controversies in his personal and professional life. He pleaded guilty to tax fraud in 1997 after the IRS alleged he concealed more than $1m in income from his art. He was originally sentenced to two months in prison but was allowed to serve the time in a work-release program, pay the back taxes and a $30,000 fine, and perform 800 hours of community service teaching art in Harlem schools.‘Kafka would blush’: artist Peter Max caught in legal guardianship lawsuitRead moreIn 2015, his family life became tabloid fodder in a back-and-forth between his second wife, Mary, and Adam, his son from a previous marriage. The son and a guardian alleged that Mary Max had depleted his finances and browbeat him. She in turn claimed that they had kept him from her against his will and stolen paintings that belonged to her.Mary Max died in 2019.The art for the Beatles’ Yellow Submarine was sometimes mistakenly attributed to Max, but the design for the album cover and Yellow Submarine movie are officially credited to the late Heinz Edelmann. Max was friends with the Beatles and many other celebrities. He also had a deep interest in Eastern spiritualty, bringing “Swami” Satchidananda Saraswati to the US and helping him popularize yoga in the country.Max’s first marriage to Elizabeth Nance ended in divorce. He is survived by Adam and his daughter, Libra.Explore more on these topicsArt and designArtNew YorkPaintingnewsShareReuse this content

title: South Park – I mean, South America – is back, with no Donald Trump in sight (yet) | South Park | The Guardian
description: After adopting the president’s fondness for renaming things America, the season 29 premiere sees Trey Parker and Matt Stone use e-bikes to critique the ruination of the US
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: After adopting the president’s fondness for renaming things America, the season 29 premiere sees Trey Parker and Matt Stone use e-bikes to critique the ruination of the US
Content: South Park’s season 29 premier follows the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario in being renamed ‘America’.Photograph: ParamountView image in fullscreenSouth Park’s season 29 premier follows the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario in being renamed ‘America’.Photograph: ParamountSouth ParkSouth Park – I mean, South America – is back, with no Donald Trump in sight (yet)After adopting the president’s fondness for renaming things ‘America’, the season 29 premiere sees Trey Parker and Matt Stone use e-bikes to critique the ruination of the USJesse HassengerThu 17 Sep 2026 03.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 11.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSouth Park has been renamed South America.That was the main newsahead of Trey Parker and Matt Stone’s animated series returning for its 29th season, which seemed like it could be a one-off promotional gag – oranother Trump-related storyline after last year’s scorchingimitation of the US president’s “renaming” ofthe Gulf of Mexicoand more recentlyLake Ontario.South Park changes name to South America in response to Trump changesRead moreIt turns out that neither is exactly the case, at least not so far. The season premiere doesn’t see theSouth Parksign scribbled over by the president’s dumb-guy sharpie pen. But it’s not just a passing sight gag, either. The six-episode season opens with the renaming already a fait accompli, not even commented on.Initially, the episode focuses on the desire of every kid in South America for a class-three e-bike that can reach speeds of up to 25 miles per hour.Cartman agitates for one most connivingly, as is his way, tearfully insisting to his mother that he needs a bike to get in shape to avoid bullying over his weight. Instead, he winds up with a motorised bike that’s the envy of Stan, Kyle and Kenny (as he informs them by doing doughnuts on their lawns and telling them to – well, you’ll hear the phrase enough times in the episode itself).Soon the jealous boys, unable to afford their own top-of-the-line bikes, are visiting Mr Kim to buy cheaper, faster knockoff e-bikes,creating an opportunity for the show to indulge in some more “ironic” Chinese-accent gags, some of which involve an appropriately profane-sounding pronunciation of “city e-bikes”. (Yes, Mr Kim is canonically a white guy with dissociative identity disorder, but … are these hacky jokes really that worthwhile?) At three for $200, they’re a steal, and soon the streets of South America are even more crowded with kids having fun.This proliferation of noisier and less effortful e-bikes sends Stan’s bicycle-riding dad, Randy, into full Calvin’s Dad mode, recalling the occasional cycling-centric strips from Bill Watterson’s Calvin & Hobbes. Randy recruits more grown-ups to his cause, and they complain about gangs of bandana-wearing, wheelie-popping, and (they assume) drug-doing bikers – while, of course, forming an actual biker gang.View image in fullscreenRandy Marsh is unhappy about the proliferation of e-bikes in South Park, ahem, America.Photograph: ParamountAccordingly, the cyclists amass members, block traffic, demand protein packets and, eventually, much worse stuff (while still demanding protein). After Googling how to change laws in South America, they attempt to ban e-bikes by bribing the cops with cash and cigars. When that doesn’t work, they escalate to full-on violence. The townsfolk can only lament that they hope things improve in November (“That’s when Grand Theft Auto 6 comes out”).These references to the hopelessness of South America are a few of the many big winks at what it really means whenlarge companies roll overand let the president rename geographic features like a cartoon supervillain.Though Stan, Kyle and Kenny protest that the actions of a few (cough, Cartman) are being ascribed to every e-bike-riding kid in town, their sensible analysis cannot avert tragedy. After a hopeful agreement to talk with their parents, Kenny’s bike is blown to smithereens, taking its perpetually killed owner with it. Was it the cheap construction of the bike itself, which had them signing away Mr Kim’s liability? Or was it a gang killing? Either way, it was a more impactful death for Kenny than the show’s early days, with the three remaining core boys visibly grieving. The biker gang, meanwhile, uses Kenny’s death as an opportunity to bring everyone together … to ban e-bikes from South America. Ineffectual rules are made through a combination of minority-view brute force and exploitation.South Park has become the most important TV show of the Trump 2.0 era | Jesse HassengerRead moreThe episode brings the renaming joke to a crescendo with a patriotic song boasting that “we will always be South America” while, as per usual, the children must suffer the whims of hair-trigger, selfish adults who either behave rashly or shrug at the idea of actually finding a solution to problems.It’s typical of Parker and Stone to critique the ruination of the US by comparing it to another area of the world that, by their implication, their country should stand above.In fact, it’s kind of hard to picture them having much quarrel with Trump’s designation of “shithole countries” – except, crucially, his repeated insistence that the US isn’t down in the hole with everyone else. South (Park) America argues otherwise. It is this point in this season’s premiere that cuts the deepest: that to roll over and accept a nonsensical rebranding by a dim-witted maniac is a kind of cultural graffiti that isn’t easy to wash off. It looks like the town, and the show’s new moniker, will stick for a while.Explore more on these topicsSouth ParkAnimation on TVTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: romance scams to make your blood boil  | Television | The Guardian
description: Hey Beautiful: Anatomy of a Romance Scam picks apart an especially galling emotional grift. Plus: a rival vet arrives in the Dales in All Creatures Great and Small. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Hey Beautiful: Anatomy of a Romance Scam picks apart an especially galling emotional grift. Plus: a rival vet arrives in the Dales in All Creatures Great and Small. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Gaby in Hey Beautiful: Anatomy of a Romance Scam.Photograph: BBC/American Broadcasting Companies, Inc.View image in fullscreenGaby in Hey Beautiful: Anatomy of a Romance Scam.Photograph: BBC/American Broadcasting Companies, Inc.TV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: romance scams to make your blood boilA new series picks apart some shocking cases. Plus: a rival vet arrives in the Dales in All Creatures Great and Small. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Hannah Verdier,Jack SealeandHannah J DaviesThu 17 Sep 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHey Beautiful: Anatomy of a Romance Scam9pm, BBC TwoGiven that romance scam documentaries have become a regular fixture in the schedules, you would think they would have lost the power to shock. But blood will boil in viewers of the first of this three-parter, where three women in middle life recall what happened when they were lonely and started talking to a handsome man online. It turned out, of course, that the same man was dating them all – and he was finding new ways of getting them to send him money.Hollie RichardsonLudwig9pm, BBC OneA foreboding sushi conveyor belt signals a crime this week, when a diner keels over in the middle of a team lunch. John (David Mitchell) thinks he’s on to something when he spots a vital piece of discarded evidence. “People write important things on napkins,” he advises. “Pac-Man was created on a napkin.”Hannah VerdierTaskmaster9pm, Channel 4Chloe Petts enjoys a strong start this week, with an outstanding show-and-tell object – the best ones always bully host Greg Davies in some way – followed by a task where her knowledge of the word “gleek” might be useful. Not all the episode’s tasks work brilliantly, but it’s still more than funny enough.Jack SealeAll Creatures Great and Small9pm, Channel 5View image in fullscreenPet problems … All Creatures Great and Small.Photograph: 5 Broadcasting LimitedIt’s easy to see why this rural reboot has been a hit at home and away, with its wholesome vision of the English countryside and, of course, a steady stream of charming animals. As series seven begins, James (Nicholas Ralph) has an ailing cat as his patient and there’s a new rival vet, Granville Bennett (Caolan McCarthy), in town.Hannah J DaviesThe Paper9pm, Sky OneThe journalism-themed US Office spin-off seems unlikely to become as ubiquitous as that show, but there are still moments of Office-ish, Parks and Rec-esque mockumentary gold. As season two carries on, Oscar (Oscar Nuñez) negotiates with the Truth Teller’s corporate overlords, while newly minted investigative journalist Mare (Chelsea Frei) sinks her teeth into a new story.HJDFightland9pm, Sky AtlanticThe silly boxing/gangland drama staggers on, led by Howard Charles as wronged former heavyweight champion Maduka “Duke” Kilroy. It’s finally time for Duke to put his grand plan for revenge against the Marshall boxing and crime clan into action, but when others around him start pursuing their own selfish agendas, chaos reigns once more.JSExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My Year in Paris With Gertrude Stein by Deborah Levy audiobook review – gripping vision of a fearless writer | Jenni Fagan | The Guardian
description: A fictional British author in Paris sets out to explore Stein through the lens of her own friendships, in this inventive, perfectly paced portrait
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: A fictional British author in Paris sets out to explore Stein through the lens of her own friendships, in this inventive, perfectly paced portrait
Content: Blending fiction and biography … Deborah Levy.Photograph: Kate Peters/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBlending fiction and biography … Deborah Levy.Photograph: Kate Peters/The GuardianAudiobook of the weekJenni FaganReviewMy Year in Paris With Gertrude Stein by Deborah Levy audiobook review – gripping vision of a fearless writerA fictional British author in Paris sets out to explore Stein through the lens of her own friendships, in this inventive, perfectly paced portraitFiona SturgesThu 17 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is late 2024, and an unnamed British author living in Paris is trying to write an essay onGertrude Stein, the modernist writer and art collector. The author has been distracted by her friend Eva’s cat, who is lost and whose name is “it” in lower case, which inevitably leads to confusion – has Eva lost her cat or her mind? (Her other friend, Fanny, has rechristened the cat Bob, to make talking about him easier.)The Pennsylvania-born Stein was painted by Picasso, hung out with Hemingway and wrote strange, stream-of-consciousness prose long before James Joyce embarked on his masterwork Ulysses. Commercial success didn’t come until she was in her 60s with The Autobiography of Alice B Toklas, a biography of her partner and one of her more accessible books. Our narrator is an admirer of Stein’s work, yet she can be exasperated by it. “Sometimes, when I read her baffling and beguiling writing I want to smack it in the chops. [Stein] longed for her readers to find her, yet there was a part of her that could not bear to be found.”A blend of fiction and biography, Deborah Levy’s ninth novel is read by voice actor Kristin Atherton; her narration is cool, precise and perfectly paced. We follow the author as she goes to Père Lachaise cemetery in search of Stein’s grave and where she reflects on the lives of other literary luminaries, and on her own friendships. The Stein who emerges in this unusual and gripping portrait is fearless, innovative and, the author notes, “so forward-looking that she never learned to reverse her Ford Model T”.Available via Penguin, 3hr 54minFurther listeningNonesuchFrancis Spufford, Faber, 15hr 29minSet during the blitz, this genre-bending thriller finds Iris Hawkins, a smart young office clerk, navigating a chance encounter which propels her into a world of necromancy, time-travelling Nazis and a plot to assassinate Winston Churchill.The DelusionsJenni Fagan, Penguin, 8hr 19minFagan’s satirical novel about the afterlife centres on Edi, who works in “the largest soul terminus in existence” where she processes the newly dead and decides where they should go based on how they lived their lives. title: The New Dark Ages by James Marriott review – a grandiose but superficial defence of reading | Books | The Guardian
description: What is it that makes books so magical? The Times columnist somehow forgets to tell us in this lofty polemic
Author: Anthony Cummins
Headline: What is it that makes books so magical? The Times columnist somehow forgets to tell us in this lofty polemic
Content: Are we entering a post-literature age?Photograph: Klaus Vedfelt/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAre we entering a post-literature age?Photograph: Klaus Vedfelt/Getty ImagesBooksReviewThe New Dark Ages by James Marriott review – a grandiose but superficial defence of readingWhat is it that makes books so magical? The Times columnist somehow forgets to tell us in this lofty polemicAnthony CumminsThu 17 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile other kids watched cartoons, Times columnist James Marriott would spend his school holidays in bed with piles of books – “a mammoth effort of attention, perhaps the greatest I ever made” – under the spell of his father, a teacher who inculcated in him a literary zeal “not exactly common in the north of England in the early 2000s”.Twenty-five years on, Marriott fears smartphones have all but killed reading for everyone. He had to get rid of his own – “George Eliot is no match” – and now, watching the rest of us scroll, he worries not only that we will lose the ability to appreciate Middlemarch, but that we risk falling prey to tyrants and anti-vaxxers forging “a world very different to the one we have known … mystical, tribal and autocratic”.Such is the gist of Marriott’s first book, The New Dark Ages, a polemical elegy tracing the rise and fall of print from Montaigne to Mr Beast. The point is modest – scroll less, read more – but the tone is grandiose.Literacyturbocharged our capacity for complex argument, he argues, but adds that “conversation is very far from useless”, and says “literate civilisation … has never produced a work of art with quite the same quality of heroic starkness as the Iliad or Beowulf”.double quotation markPunchy quips aren’t enough to keep the book afloat in deep watersThe readerly bicep Marriott likes flashing is rarely as firm as it looks. “The important things Leo Tolstoy [has] to say about life will only be understood if you can pay attention,” he writes, never saying what they are. His advocacy for books relies on browbeating hyperbole: “I believe there is a kind of truth about life which is only accessible through prose fiction with its capacity to show us the inside of other minds … It is the reason that no actor on earth can show with his or her face what Jane Austen can show us about the human heart in half a paragraph.” When he actually articulates a novel’s impact, it’s to tell us that Elena Ferrante taught him “what it is like to be a teenage girl”.Literature isn’t his only focus. “In the early 20th century everyone read a newspaper,” he says, lamenting social media’s impact on politics. He imagines a print report and a TikTok clip from the same war zone: “Even the most simple written article is more likely to offer explanations for events. How did the war start? Why did the war start?” Alternatively, to summon “your rage with an image, I only need to show you a picture of … heaped bodies”; in other words, if you’re angry when “a missile destroys an apartment block in the Middle East” – the clip he envisages – it’s because a journalist hasn’t explained it.The sense grows that lofty proclamations and punchy quips aren’t enough to keep the book afloat in deep waters. “The 21st century’s much-documented epidemic of anxiety, depression and purposelessness is at least partly rooted in the … culture of the screen,” says Marriott, leaving us to wonder if he’s muddled symptom and cause. When the book begins, he calls smartphones the “major culprit” of the drop in reading for pleasure – “factors like inequality” are less to blame – but it ends by warning that “very rich” people have the resources “to keep their children away from addictive screens. Poorer parents who have to work multiple jobs and who lack the money for childcare do not.”It’s the last gasp for a thesis whose apocalyptic urgency fizzles out in equivocating caveats. “Post-literate”, Marriott clarifies, doesn’t mean “incapable of reading and writing”: although there may be “fewer Shakespeares, more Slack messages” – how many Shakespeares does he think there have been? – literacy “still has a future”. Which isn’t “to counsel unthinking optimism”, just to say that “even in the worst-case scenario, reading … will be around for a while yet”. Phew!The New Dark Ages is neatly positioned to appeal to lapsed readers who wince at their weekly screen time report. But there’s a less opportunistic book buried deep between its lines: one about growing up convinced the world begins and ends with literature, only to find that all it took to make you doubt it was a six-inch sliver of black glass.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe New Dark Ages: The End of Reading and the Dawn of a Post-Literate Society by James Marriott is published by Bodley Head (£14.99).
