title: Feeling overwhelmed by the AI doom loop? Here’s the essential reading list to make sense of it all | Books | The Guardian
description: It’s a chaotic time in an industry that’s reshaping our lives – Guardian reporters and experts recommend the books that help explain how we got here, and where we’re headed
Author: Lois Beckett
Headline: It’s a chaotic time in an industry that’s reshaping our lives – Guardian reporters and experts recommend the books that help explain how we got here, and where we’re headed
Content: The books in our list aim to explain and critique the AI industry and provide deeper political and social context to the AI moment.Illustration: Kittipong Jirasukhanont/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe books in our list aim to explain and critique the AI industry and provide deeper political and social context to the AI moment.Illustration: Kittipong Jirasukhanont/AlamyBooksFeeling overwhelmed by the AI doom loop? Here’s the essential reading list to make sense of it allIt’s a chaotic time in an industry that’s reshaping our lives – Guardian reporters and experts recommend the books that help explain how we got here, and where we’re headingLois BeckettThu 17 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 14.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHave you been feeling trapped in an endless cycle of artificial intelligence hype and panic? You’re not alone.It’s a chaotic time to make sense of the industry that’s reshaping our lives, whether or not we like it. Last week, another AI company employeepublicly resigned, warning the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. Despite these dire warnings, AI companies have seen “otherworldly”surges in revenueand driven the USstock markets to new highsas they continue to push AI tools into everything frompublic school classroomstolaw enforcement agencies, as well as rushing to put up new datacentersacross the country.Thankfully, the Guardian’s tech reporters – and a few other tech experts we respect – are here to help. We’ve compiled an essential reading list of smart books that explain and critique the AI industry; books that, while flawed, illustrate key viewpoints in the AI debates; and a few books that provide deeper political and social context, including some works of speculative fiction.The best books on the AI industryEmpire of AI– Karen HaoThe most intensively reported book on the AI industry so far, Empire of AI covers the rise of OpenAI, as well as the formation of Anthropic and OpenAI chief Sam Altman’s split with Elon Musk. Parts of the book can feel a bit inside baseball, but the reporting is great and shows how the key American AI companies brought us to this point. Some early reviews of the book in 2025 suggested Hao’s take on the industry was overly negative: she has since been entirely vindicated.Project Maven– Katrina MansonAn in-depth look at how the US military and Palantir worked together to build autonomous weapons and surveillance systems that are an actual catastrophic threat – not an imagined one.Hyperscale–Paris MarxFrom the journalist and host of theTech Won’t Save Uspodcast, this is a deep investigation into the physical impact of AI data centers around the world, and the toll they are taking on local communities and the global environment.Your Face Belongs to Us–Kashmir HillA bestselling book on the rise of Clearview AI, the facial recognition company that has provided sweeping surveillance powers to law enforcement, businesses and billionaires, by building a massive database of online images.The AI Con–Emily M Bender and Alex HannaIn response to claims that AI will soon far surpass all human capabilities, and that the technology is advancing so quickly it’s on the verge of becoming a new life form, the authors of The AI Con have a simple response:“LOL” and “they wish”.These two tech critic academics argue that this kind of rhetoric is “AI hype” – lies and exaggerations that are helping rich people make more money “by justifying data theft, motivating surveillance capitalism, and devaluing human creativity”.Flawed books on AI (that still might be worth reading)If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies–Eliezer Yudkowskyand Nate SoaresIf you want to understand the perspective of the people panicking that AI will destroy humanity, this book is a good place to start. It’s a “doomer classic” that has been described as a book-length version ofthe tweet that made everyone freak outthis past week. Unfortunately for readers, its predictions of doom are based more on grand thought experiments than on an engagement with how AI is currently playing out in the world. The book “reads like a Scientology manual”, a New York Times reviewer wrote. For context, Yudkowsky’s other writings include a nearly700,000-word work of Harry Potter fan fictionin which Harry applies the scientific method to magic.Superintelligence– Nick BostromThis 2014 book is one of the foundational AI texts for people like Elon Musk, who, alongside Bill Gates, haspublicly praisedthe bestseller. While the book is useful as a way of understanding the evolution of arguments about how a superintelligent AI might doom society,it’s worth notingthat the author is a controversial Swedish-born philosopher who was forced to apologize in 2023 for a decades-old email in which he claimed “Blacks are more stupid than whites” and used the N-word. In 2024, Oxfordquietly shut downthe academic institute he had run, and Bostrom resigned.Genesis: artificial intelligence, hope, and the human spirit– Henry Kissinger, Eric Schmidt, Craig Mundie and Eleanor RundeAre you looking for AI insights from a man who facedfrequent, wide-ranging and substantial allegations of war crimes? Astonishingly, Henry Kissinger, the former US secretary of state who died in 2023, co-authored a bestselling 2024 book on AI with a billionaire former Google CEO, a less-wealthy former Microsoft executive, and a young lawyer who worked as Kissinger’s researcher. The authors suggest that AI’s ability to provide swift answers without explaining how it got them might end our current “age of reason” and lead humanity back to a “pre-modern acceptance of unexplained authority”. They also raise the possibility that “the companies that own and develop AI will accrue totalizing social, economic, military and political power”, or that AI itself might become an all-powerful “philosopher king”. OpenAI’s ChatGPT listed this as one of thefive best books on artificial intelligence.The Technological Republic– Alex Karp and Nicholas ZamiskaThis manifesto by the CEO of Palantir was described by one Guardian colleague as one of the worst-written books he had ever read. It includes rambling attacks on the Palestinian American academic Edward Said, and goes further than Kissinger and his co-authors by more or less calling for turning tech leaders into philosopher kings. Prose aside, the book provides an important window into what top tech CEOs actually believe, and the way they regard AI and tech as a new nuclear bomb – which, in their view, is a good thing.Deeper context: history, ideology and fictionThe Rise and Fall of the Artificial State– Jill LeporeA historical look at the political and industrial movements that have wanted to cede human agency and democratic rule to automation and authoritarianism. Just published, and a surprisingly fun read!MoreEverything Forever– Adam BeckerWritten by a science journalist, this book provides a good overview of the ideological origins of our current tech leaders. Exploring accelerationism, rationalism, doomerism and more, the book emphasizes how strange and detached from reality these powerful people’s belief systems are.Automating Inequality– Virginia EubanksThis 2018 book predates the generative AI boom, but it provides an essential view into how automated systems and algorithms reinforce social inequality. Modern AI has supercharged these same capabilities and is getting integrated into every critical system, making the book’s insights into the harms of automated inequality even more important.Predatory Data: Eugenics in Big Tech and Our Fight for an Independent Future– Anita Say ChanOur current systems of techno-surveillance and algorithmic discrimination are rooted in 19th-century campaigns against immigration and in favor of eugenics, the practice of selectively breeding humans to improve their intelligence or racial dominance, Chan argues. The book highlights the evolution of “techno-eugenicists” and the persistence of feminist and immigrant activists who have fought against them, and is recommended by Seeta Peña Gangadharan, an associate professor at the London School of Economics who studies the community impact of data-driven technologies.Prophecy: Prediction, Power and the Fight for the Future, from Ancient Oracles to AI– Carissa VélizTracing the parallels between ancient seers, court astrologers, and contemporary algorithms, an Oxford University philosopher argues that “the main promise of prediction is not knowledge of the future but domination over others.” Another recommendation from Peña Gangadharan and her LSE doctoral student, Anna Osterberg, who studies the political dynamics of online communities.I, Robot– Isaac AsimovThough it was first published in 1950, Asimov’s collection of short stories on the ethics of human-robot interactions remains influential, including his “Three Laws of Robotics”, starting with: “A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm.” As humor writerAlex Blechman has pointed out,classic science fiction books and films remain deeply influential in the tech world, even though many tech companies seem set on engineering precisely the kinds of dangerous outcomes that science fictionwarned against.The Lost Books of the Odyssey– Zachary MasonIn 2007, a computer scientist from Palo Alto published a collection of46 retellings of passages from the Odyssey– a book that riffs on the way narratives get revised, fragmented, and reborn. Mason was activelyimagining the prose AI might producelong before the technology was available. Asked for his recommendations on AI-related books, Robin Sloan, a fiction author and media and technology writer, chose this novel, which he called “the first book of the LLM era, even though it was written entirely, and beautifully, by a human”. He says the book “has a lot to say about multiplicity, deep stories and symbols”.Labyrinths– Jorge Luis BorgesSloan also made the case for a classic, Borges’ short story collection Labyrinths, as a book that “gets your head in the right place to think usefully and richly about the deep weirdness and enormity of language models”. The collection includes one of Borges’ most famous stories,The Library of Babel, first published in 1941, which describes and wrestles with a plan for an infinite library.Nick Robins-Early contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsBooksAI (artificial intelligence)US politicsComputingRobotsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 50 Years of Punk review – rock’n’roll rebels fondly recall the filth and fury a half-century on | Movies | The Guardian
description: Glen Matlock, Viv Albertine and Rat Scabies revisit the music, clothes and disgusting spitting in a likable documentary marking half a century of British punk
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Glen Matlock, Viv Albertine and Rat Scabies revisit the music, clothes and disgusting spitting in a likable documentary marking half a century of British punk
Content: Entertaining … Viv Albertine of the Slits in 50 Years of Punk, a film by Mark SloperView image in fullscreenEntertaining … Viv Albertine of the Slits in 50 Years of Punk, a film by Mark SloperMoviesReview50 Years of Punk review – rock’n’roll rebels fondly recall the filth and fury a half-century onGlen Matlock, Viv Albertine and Rat Scabies revisit the music, clothes and disgusting spitting in a likable documentary marking half a century of British punkAndrew PulverThu 17 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 08.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the majority of them ease into their eighth decade, the overlords of British punk rock get yet another celebratory runout, gently reheating material that has become familiar over the years but never loses its appeal. A subculture that passed almost immediately from tabloid-triggering menace to picture-postcard caricature, punk may have passed into legend as a joyless and even squalid diversion in music and fashion history, but its surviving spokespeople recall their participation in it all with no little enthusiasm, even if they’ve clearly said it a thousand times already. No doubt it is the gen alphas among us who will benefit most; you’d expect their jaws to drop and eyes to roll at some of the stuff deemed perfectly acceptable in the late 1970s: women’s-breasts T-shirts, amateurish pancake makeup, and all that disgusting spitting. (“I didn’t mind it going in my mouth,” says the Damned’s Captain Sensible at one point, out-disgusting everyone.)There’s a good spread of voices on offer; at least one member of most of the era’s big acts puts in an appearance with Glen Matlock (the Sex Pistols), Rat Scabies (the Damned), Terry Chimes (the Clash), Steve Severin (Siouxsie and the Banshees), and Hugh Cornwell (the Stranglers) leading the way. (The latter, though affable enough, is easily the least impressed as to punk’s actual achievements, which is a valuable corrective.) The original punk wave had little space for women (despite the sense that blows were being struck for equality) and that’s the case in the film as well: Gaye Advert (the Adverts) and Viv Albertine (the Slits) get a bit of time on camera though inevitably get a bit lost in it all. Due recognition, however, is paid to designer Vivienne Westwood as punk’s true founding spirit; Sex, the King’s Road boutique she ran with Malcolm McLaren, was a crucible of the British punk scene. Don Boyd, who produced the Pistols’ movie The Great Rock ‘n’ Roll Swindle along with the late Jeremy Thomas, says she “was punk and is punk … it came from her”.Some interesting details emerge: how the Sex Pistols’ early gigs coincided with the sweltering heatwave of 1976, which contributed – literally – to their pressure-cooker atmosphere; how early punk mix-and-match style emerged as a result of Westwood and Malcolm McLaren getting stuck with unsold stock from their shop’s previous incarnations; and, as writer Jon Savage explains, how the use of the word “punk” itself was debated. Inevitably, perhaps, it’s the more peripheral figures who offer the freshest takes, particularly David Barbarossa, drummer for Adam and the Ants and Bow Wow Wow, who talks somewhat regretfully about how McLaren winkled him and his bandmates away from the former to form the latter. All in all, this is an entertaining way to mark the half-century, and one to stick the kids in front of too.50 Years ofPunkis in UK cinemas from 18 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmMusic documentaryDocumentary filmsPunkreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘When you tell people the story, it’s almost too good to be true’: the incredible journey behind The Cycle of Love | Movies | The Guardian
description: Documentary director Orlando von Einsiedel on how the real life tale of a man who cycles 6,000 miles from India to Sweden to find his true love will warm your heart
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Documentary director Orlando von Einsiedel on how the real life tale of a man who cycles 6,000 miles from India to Sweden to find his true love will warm your heart
Content: ‘It’s about joy and human connection’ … Mina Dale and Chirag Lobo in The Cycle of Love.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘It’s about joy and human connection’ … Mina Dale and Chirag Lobo in The Cycle of Love.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockMovies‘When you tell people the story, it’s almost too good to be true’: the incredible journey behind The Cycle of LoveDocumentary director Orlando von Einsiedel on how the real life tale of a man who cycles 6,000 miles from India to Sweden to find his true love will warm your heartCath ClarkeThu 17 Sep 2026 03.03 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 03.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew Delhi, December 1975. It was love at first sight when a Swedish hippy called Lotta von Schedvin sat down to be sketched by an Indian street artist, Pradyumna Kumar Mahanandia, known to everyone as PK. In the 10 minutes it took PK to complete her portrait, everything clicked into place for the pair. They were swept headlong in a whirlwind romance, and PK took Lotta to his village in the east ofIndiato meet his family. But soon after, the time came for Lotta to pack up her VW campervan and head back home with her friends.Heart-stricken PK promised to follow, but a plane ticket to Sweden was an impossible dream. Determined not to lose the love of his life, PK bought a secondhand Raleigh bike, and with $80 sewn into the waistband of his trousers, set off tocycle 6,000 miles to Lotta. He knew the sun set in the west, so that was the direction he took. His plan was to follow the hippy trail, cycling through India, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran and Turkey, crossing Europe, finally arriving in Sweden.Actually, he was heading to Switzerland until a fellow backpacker pointed out that Switzerland andSwedenwere two different countries. In a new Netflix documentary, The Cycle of Love, PK jokes that his strength was his fuzzy grasp of European geography. Watching the film, you wonder if his superpower might have been his smile – warm and joyous, it lights the room. Either way, he made it to Sweden. The journey took 123 days, and ended up involving a flight or two, and a couple of trains. In May 1977, PK knocked on Lotta’s door in Borås, Sweden. They have been together ever since.Documentary-maker Orlando von Einsiedel first heard about the story when he gave a talk in Sweden. “At the end, two young people came up and handed me a book,” he says. “They said: ‘This is about our parents’ story. We know your work. Would you be interested in this as a film?’” The book was The Amazing Story of the Man Who Cycled from India to Europe for Love by Swedish journalist Per J Andersson.View image in fullscreen‘A tale of fate and destiny’ … The Cycle of Love.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockThe two young people were PK and Lotta’s grownup kids Emilie and Karl. Von Einsiedel politely took the book but didn’t think too much about it. “Normally in my experience, when somebody approaches you and says ‘I’ve got a brilliant story’, it doesn’t work out.”A couple of months later, Von Einsiedel picked up the book as a holiday read, opening it on the flight out of London. “The moment I started I thought, ‘Oh my God, you idiot Orlando! This is extraordinary.’” It wasn’t just the against-all-odds, 6,000-mile cycle ride, PK’s story was a tale of fate and destiny. When he was born, the astrologer in his village made four predictions about his future wife: she would be a Taurus, born outside India, musical and own a jungle. So naturally the first question he asked Lotta was: “Are you a Taurus?” Her answer was yes. She was also a gifted musician, and – most bonkers of all – her family owned land with a forest in Sweden.View image in fullscreenDale and Lobo are the only two trained actors in the film.Photograph: Everett/Shutterstock“When you tell people the story, it’s almost too good to be true,” says Von Einsiedel, cheerful and chatty on a video call from New York. The previous night he attended the US premiere of The Cycle of Love with PK and Lotta, who have been happily married for nearly 50 years. The pair have been getting the celebrity treatment wherever they go. “Everybody in the cinema stands up for them, people are weeping when they come on stage.” What do the couple make of the film? He grins. “I know they like it, because whenever they go to a festival, they watch every single screening from beginning to end.” How many times have they seen it? “A lot.”The film tells their story with enormous warmth. It includes a dramatisation of the epic ride, with PK played by the British-based Indian actor Chirag Lobo, and Mina Dale as Lotta. Everybody else is non-professional, explains Von Einsiedel. “Our producers would go out and street-cast people on the morning of filming.”What about the script, I ask? There are gorgeous, heartwarming scenes as PK shares his story with people he meets on the road, who in return tell him about their life and loves. How were those scenes scripted? “No script. Everything is improvised. When PK interacts with everyday people he meets along the way, those are just normal conversations about love and hopes and dreams.”Wasn’t that a bit risky – getting a plane to India with two actors, no script and trusting that deep and meaningful conversations would materialise from conversations with ordinary people? “Massively risky, except I tested if it might work in Lewisham town centre,” Von Einsiedel says, grinning. “I have a friend who’s an actor. We went to Lewisham with a bike.” Armed with a notepad, his friend told people that he was cycling from London to Cape Town for love. “He pretended to draw portraits. What was extraordinary is the first person he sat down to draw turned around and said: ‘I love your story. I’ll buy you a plane ticket immediately.’”View image in fullscreenFilm-maker Orlando von Einsiedel.Photograph: Arturo Holmes/Getty ImagesIt’s the kindness of strangers that makes the documentary so uplifting. When PK cycles out of Kabul, he stops to help an Austrian backpacker, Linea, who crashed her car, knocking out most of her teeth. He stays with her for several days at hospital, even though it means his visa expiring and further delay. Later, when he arrives in Istanbul and checks his post, there is a train ticket to Vienna – a thank you from Linea for his kindness.What struck Von Einsiedel when he met the real-life PK was that his story about love went beyond boy-meets-girl. “For me, it’s not just about romantic love. It’s about self-love and love for all the people that we share this planet with.” PK was born into a dalit family, the marginalised group in India formerly known as “untouchables”. At school, he was made to sit outside during lessons and not allowed to play with the other children. Even after he won a scholarship to study fine art in Delhi, he experienced periods of homelessness and isolation.“From the moment I started talking to PK it became clear what a difficult and traumatic childhood he’d had,” Von Einsiedel says. “He spoke so movingly about being on the journey and how it was the first time that strangers would touch him and hug him. That it was key to him starting to believe in himself and love himself. He said: ‘How can you love anybody if you can’t love yourself?’ I get emotional just saying that.”PK explained how he felt accepted on the journey, hanging out with hippies and locals in the villages and towns he passed through. People with very little offered him hospitality, a meal or a roof for the night. In the documentary, this warm feeling of togetherness thuds to the ground when PK arrives in Europe, grilled by hostile and overtly racist German border officers. “That was his first experience,” says Von Einsiedel. “He travelled through all these countries, Afghanistan and Iran, and everybody treated him with respect. Then as soon as he got to Europe he immediately experienced racism.”Von Einsiedel grew up in south London. At university he studied social anthropology and in his 20s was a professional snowboarder. “I learned the craft of film-making making snowboard films,” he says. “When I knew how to do that, I segued into making films about social issues I believed in.” He started working with Al Jazeera, travelling to conflict zones.In 2015, he was nominated for an Oscar for his first full-length documentary,Virunga, about the battle to save a national park in eastern Congo, home to some of the world’s last mountain gorillas. His documentary short,White Helmets, following Syrian volunteers rescuing civilians, won an Oscar. Next he madeEvelyn, an incredibly moving film in which Von Einsiedel turned the camera on his own family. His brother Evelyn took his own life aged 22 over a decade earlier. In the film, Von Einsiedel and his two surviving siblings hiked the routes their brother loved to walk with friends and family. “I was very emotionally closed for a long time after my brother died,” he says. “I used to think being emotionally open was a sign of weakness. I was terrified of my own emotions. I see the opposite now. I think being emotionally open is a sign of strength.”When it comes to picking a subject for a new documentary, he says he is attracted to people who inspire him. “I’m drawn to stories that show the better side of human beings. That’s a thread that runs through the work I like to make.” The Cycle of Love is by far the sunniest film he has made to date. What’s that all about, I ask? “I wanted to make an optimistic film that’s about joy and human connection. The world is difficult. Love is one of those things that all of us can agree on. This story just felt so important to tell.”The Cycle of Love is released in the UK on 18 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsCycling (Life and style)SwedenIndiaCycling (News)featuresShareReuse this content

title: Why stop at Wuthering Heights: House of the Damned? Bring on Mrs Dalloway’s Rampage! | Movies | The Guardian
description: It isn’t just Winnie the Pooh – now the star of Blood & Honey II. Budget shockers are treating any story with expired copyright as ripe for murderous exploitation
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: It isn’t just Winnie the Pooh – now the star of Blood & Honey II. Budget shockers are treating any story with expired copyright as ripe for murderous exploitation
Content: Bad dreams in the night … a screengrab from the trailer for Wuthering Heights: House of the DamnedPhotograph: Saban FilmsView image in fullscreenBad dreams in the night … a screengrab from the trailer for Wuthering Heights: House of the DamnedPhotograph: Saban FilmsMoviesWhy stop at Wuthering Heights: House of the Damned? Bring on Mrs Dalloway’s Rampage!Stuart HeritageIt isn’t just Winnie the Pooh – now the star of Blood & Honey II. Budget shockers are treating any story with expired copyright as ripe for murderous exploitationThu 17 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 11.08 EDTShareIt is significant that, at this point in our cultural journey, we have become accustomed to film producers jumping on every single property as it enters public domain, so they can make a cheap and exploitative horror film about it. We have seenWinnie-the-Pooh: Blood and Honey. We’ve seen Bambi: The Reckoning. We’ve seen the six separate horror movies (including Mouseboat Massacre and Mouse of Horrors) that are based on Steamboat Willie. This is just the world we live in now.But if you zoom out even a tiny amount, it all starts to look a little silly. Not because it suggests the paying public has a fondness for inarguably bad horror films based on loose interpretations of recognisable figures, but because it’s missing the bigger picture. In other words, while producers are watching eagerly for the next newly out-of-copyright property to exploit (by the way, Babar the Elephant will enter the public domain in January), there is an entire ocean of public domain work just sitting there to be desecrated.In which case, you really have to applaud whoever came up with the idea of Wuthering Heights: The House of the Damned. Available on digital platforms in three short weeks (on 19 October in fact), it is a remake of Emily Brontë’s classic novel, only scarier. In the film, as far as I am able to tell, Cathy has died and her ghost starts haunting Heathcliff to the point that he starts murdering everyone. Is it any good? All signs point to not really, especially since the trailer contains a shot where Cathy seems to become a zombie so that she can punch through a window and strangle someone to death. But will I watch it? Oh God, try to stop me.You can see what’s happening here, can’t you? Emerald Fennell made aWuthering Heights filmthis year and it was wildly successful, currently the 19th biggest film of 2026. But Wuthering Heights was published 179 years ago, so anyone can do whatever they want with it. Fennell’s film proved this all too well, with its rubbing and squishing and skin-coloured rooms. But it also means that someone else can hop on the back of it and turn it into a hammy horror about a zombie in a bridal gown. It’s not like the Brontës are around to sue, is it?View image in fullscreenCathy come home …  Wuthering Heights: House of the Damned (2026)Photograph: Saban FilmsWhat makes this so ingenious is that Hollywood is built on the back of expired copyright. All of Disney’s early animated films were based on public domain fairytales and Universal built its reputation on adapting lapsed horror novels. And don’t think this isn’t still a thing, because it very much is. In the coming weeks and months, we will see films and television shows based on Sense and Sensibility (215 years old), Pride and Prejudice (213 years old), Treasure Island (143 years old), Mrs Dalloway (101 years old), The Age of Innocence (106 years old) and The Sun Also Rises (100 years old). And there will be more, because there’s nothing the entertainment industry loves than not paying for an option to a published work.But still, my point is that these are all ripe for the taking. Blood and Honey and its ilk have shown that we are all crying out to see something we recognise get shredded to pieces in a cheap and not particularly convincing manner, so let’s go for it. If someone can make a direct-to-digital horror movie based on Wuthering Heights, what’s stopping us from doing the same to any of these films?View image in fullscreenA bit too knowing … Jess Radomska in Pride and Prejudice and Zombies.Photograph: Jay Maidment/APLook, some of them have even been done. Ten years ago, they made a film called Pride and Prejudice and Zombies, and it was big enough to attract Lily James, Matt Smith and Charles Dance. That said, it was a bit too knowing to properly qualify for the market we’re talking about – the one where you watch it drunk at 2am and feel a bit grubby afterwards – so it’s still up for grabs. Pride and Prejudice: Darcy’s Bloodbath, maybe. It doesn’t even need to adhere to the plot very much. Just buy a load of cheap period costumes, rent a big house for a week and make a poster of a guy walking seductively towards the camera with their shirt soaked through with blood.Or what about this: The Sun Also Rises: Revenge of the Bull, where a mutant bull escapes from Pamplona and stabs its way across the cafe society of 1920s Paris? Come on, that one’s gold. I really hope you’re paying attention to this, because I’m making one of you a lot of money here.Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsFilm adaptationscommentShareReuse this content

title: Bad Apples review – Saoirse Ronan’s suffering teacher best thing about school horror-satire | Movies | The Guardian
description: Ronan plays a teacher who finds a way to deal with a disruptive pupil in Jonatan Etzler’s implausible satire, but it’s not shocking or funny enough
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Ronan plays a teacher who finds a way to deal with a disruptive pupil in Jonatan Etzler’s implausible satire, but it’s not shocking or funny enough
Content: Ronan is always watchable … L to r, Nia Brown as Pauline and Saoirse Ronan as Maria in Bad Apples.Photograph: Pulse Films/Nea Asphäll. All Rights ReservedView image in fullscreenRonan is always watchable … L to r, Nia Brown as Pauline and Saoirse Ronan as Maria in Bad Apples.Photograph: Pulse Films/Nea Asphäll. All Rights ReservedMoviesReviewBad Apples review – Saoirse Ronan’s suffering teacher best thing about school horror-satireRonan plays a teacher who finds a way to deal with a disruptive pupil in Jonatan Etzler’s implausible film, but it’s not shocking or funny enoughPeter BradshawThu 17 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 12.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is a strange, heavy-handed and unpersuasive black comedy which owes what success it has to the star-power of its lead,Saoirse Ronan, who is incapable of giving an uninteresting performance. Director Jonatan Etzler has adapted it with co-screenwriter Jess O’Kane from a Swedish novel by Rasmus Lindgren called De Oönskade, or The Unwanted, and is a film that asks you to overlook its plot-holes and implausibilities on the grounds that it is a satire – but a satire saying what, exactly?The scene is a primary school in the English West Country where Maria (Ronan) is a hardworking, idealistic teacher – but her class is hopelessly disrupted by a violent boy, Danny (Eddie Waller), obnoxious and out of control. He seriously injures another pupil, the nerdy teacher’s-pet Pauline (Nia Brown) whom Maria privately considers a bit annoying. After a chaotic visit to Danny’s home, Maria winds up causing the boy to lose consciousness with an accidental chokehold, and in a panic smuggles him back to her house where she imprisons him in her basement. And then, slowly but surely, the rest of the class, freed from Danny’s hateful presence, blossom and Maria gets a glowing Ofsted report. She looks and feels on top of the world. But what is to be done about her shameful secret?Perhaps only a pedant would point out that an unventilated basement, in which the prisoner’s bathroom necessities are met with a bucket, would soon look and smell horrendous, not clean and tidy, like this – and the same goes for the prisoner, incidentally. And how exactly has Maria induced Danny to wear an animal-restraint harness without knocking him out or using drugs?The boy-chained-up-in-a-basement movie could almost be a horror/satire sub-genre all on its own, withJan Komasa’s The Good BoyandMarkus Schleinzer’s Michael. But those shockers work because they never make any secret of how monstrous the jailers are, and what the endgame is; they turn the dials up to 11. Bad Apples cautiously turns the dials to four or five, always wanting to keep Ronan’s character relatable and sympathetic evidently because her well-meaning normality is part of the black-comic point. She is only doing what kindly/liberal teachers secretly long to do: ruthlessly eliminate the bad apples. But there isn’t enough comedy or enough shock to distract you from how laborious and unbelievable the whole thing is, particularly in the closing act. At any rate, Ronan is always watchable.Bad Apples is in UK and Irish cinemas from 18 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsHorror filmsSchoolsSaoirse RonanFilm adaptationsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Watergate Caper: Richard Nixon and the Death of the American Dream review – political scandal, 70s style | Movies | The Guardian
description: Shane O’Sullivan’s documentary weaves archive clips and snippets from films old and new to draw out the highlights of the crisis that rocked the US
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Shane O’Sullivan’s documentary weaves archive clips and snippets from films old and new to draw out the highlights of the crisis that rocked the US
Content: On the campaign trail in 1972 … a clip from the National Archives of President Richard Nixon in The Watergate Caper.Photograph: National Archives, 37-WHPO-D0685-17View image in fullscreenOn the campaign trail in 1972 … a clip from the National Archives of President Richard Nixon in The Watergate Caper.Photograph: National Archives, 37-WHPO-D0685-17MoviesReviewThe Watergate Caper: Richard Nixon and the Death of the American Dream review – political scandal, 70s styleShane O’Sullivan’s documentary weaves archive clips and snippets from films old and new to draw out the highlights of the crisis that rocked the USLeslie FelperinThu 17 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 08.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJudging by his past work, the Irish-born, London-based writer and film-maker Shane O’Sullivan may have a chronic case of born-too-late nostalgia. It manifests as a fascination with the politics and counterculture of the late 1960s and 70s, and that’s clearly a theme in O’Sullivan’s previous works, which include: a book and film about the assassination of Robert Kennedy; the acclaimedfeature doc Children of the Revolutionabout the female leaders of the Baader-Meinhof Group and the Japanese Red Army; anda film about Lee Harvey Oswald.His latest takes aim at the big kahuna itself:Watergate– the crime, the scandal and the cultural phenomenon. It is explored through a hailstorm of archive clips and snippets of feature films, all nimbly stitched together, with a deadpan voiceover by the great Harry Shearer. The result is, of course, nostalgic, but also feels fresh and immediate, especially thanks to the use of moments from more recent features about, but not from, the period, including a Watergate-hearings-obsessed teenage Christina Ricci in The Ice Storm from 1997, the comic ineptitude of the Watergate burglars as represented in 1999 spoof Dick, or Shea Whigham’s skewering of break-in mastermind G Gordon Liddy from recent TV miniseries Gaslit. These performed moments all play nicely with O’Sullivan’s selection of clips from more contemporaneous, Watergate-adjacent classics such as Medium Cool, All the President’s Men and Taxi Driver.Alongside this, the archive material is neatly marshalled and excerpted in such a way as to explain to a bright gen Alpha kid roughly what this Watergate thing was all about, although O’Sullivan chooses not to get to bogged down in the detail and mostly surveys the highlights. Of particular note are some less well-known clips of “Tricky Dicky” Nixon himself, coming across as surprisingly amusing, joking around with his aides before the cameras go live. Even when we see him lying through his teeth, one can’t help thinking he seems like Abraham Lincoln compared with the current occupant of the White House. The times, they have a-changed, and not for the better.The Watergate Caper:Richard Nixonand the Death of the American Dream is in UK cinemas from 18 September and on digital platforms in the UK, Ireland and the US from 29 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsRichard NixonWatergatereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Jonathan Majors’s anti-Islam action thriller is laughably terrible far-right propaganda | Jonathan Majors | The Guardian
description: The disgraced former Marvel villain has found work with Ben Shapiro for hateful campus-set thriller Run Hide Fight: Infidels, which makes its politics clear from the outset
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: The disgraced former Marvel villain has found work with Ben Shapiro for hateful campus-set thriller Run Hide Fight: Infidels, which makes its politics clear from the outset
Content: Jonathan Majors in Run Hide Fight: Infidels.Photograph: The Daily WireView image in fullscreenJonathan Majors in Run Hide Fight: Infidels.Photograph: The Daily WireJonathan MajorsJonathan Majors’s anti-Islam action thriller is laughably terrible far-right propagandaAndrew LawrenceThe disgraced former Marvel villain has found work with Ben Shapiro for hateful campus-set thriller Run Hide Fight: Infidels, which makes its politics clear from the outsetThu 17 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareBehold the new and improved Jonathan Majors: paragon of hypermasculinity, the Denzel Washington of the Daily Wire, a Delta Force veteran forced back into action when his war on terror follows him on to home soil. Against all odds, he has tracked his way back to the Khalid Sheikh Mohammed analogue who killed his partner as the Americans were debating whether to bring the criminal mastermind to justice or execute him on the spot. Our Fox News jihadi has no doubt Captain Saunders will respect the letter of the law again. “The American way is your taskforces and your trials,” the enemy hisses. “Your climate change and your abortions – ”‘I aggressed you’: Jonathan Majors reportedly admits to assault in audio recordingRead moreBlam!A bullet cuts him down mid-monologue, and the camera pushes in as Captain Saunders lowers his semi-automatic rifle. “Actually,that’sthe American way,” he says.You can just imagine that scene, in an alternate reality where conservative crackpottery is gospel, furnishing the Oscar-reel clip for Run Hide Fight: Infidels – a Hollywood treatment for far-right fear-mongering that Majors has latched onto like a piece of Titanic driftwood. The latest release from Ben Shapiro’s Nashville-based streaming studio, intended as a bulwark against the wider film industry’s ostensibly liberal biases, Run Hide Fight: Infidels follows writer-director Kyle Rankin’s 2020 Daily Wire debut Run Hide Fight. Where the original film had a white teenage waif (1883’s Isabel May) fighting her way out of a high school shooting, this one thrusts Captain Saunders into an Islamist mass-casualty attack on a college campus. And if the sequel registers, who knows? A Sandy Hook-meets-Kindergarten Cop green light can’t be far behind.Co-produced with Bonfire Legend, another macho studio headquartered in Austin, Infidels is not offered up as fodder for interpretation. The film made its intended message clear from the very first trailer, conflating fictional clips with actual footage of the 9/11 attacks, pro-Palestine protests and Fox News personalities, before revealing an IS flag flying over a college campus as the Islamic call echoed with doom. Then there was the tagline: “Coming soon … or already here?” Talk about twirling the mustache.The reactions were as polarized as you would expect, with mainstream filmgoers and critics deriding the premise as xenophobic and Islamophobic, while rightwing commentators in the media and online cheered the brazen political incorrectness. “If you’re afraid to put radical jihadis as your villains,” said Bonfire’s Dallas Sonnier, “then you’re a wimpy movie producer. We don’t have that fear.”The entertainment proposition with Infidels lies in how deeply it can offend the snowflakes. The 128-minute feature, which took me three tries to finish, plays like a PragerU student film. The characters aren’t so much colorful as they are drawn in crayon: the campus HR who is dazzled by the mysterious terrorist sleeper cell in her midst, the spineless university president whose failure to crack down on student protests makes his campus vulnerable. Only the pregnant college professor, who just a few scenes earlier was urging the president to crack heads, stands out as totally incidental to this batshit story.Meanwhile, the oafish Black campus security guard could be a last line of defense if he weren’t so lazy. At one point, he’s approached by a young girl who has become disoriented at the carnival that is also unfolding on campus.“My daddy lost me,” she says.“I’m still looking for mine,” he shoots back.The terrorists in Infidels are cobbled from Heritage Foundation talking points, planting bombs around campus, herding “unclean” women into the showers to cleanse their souls and forcing Christ-loving scholars to swear allegiance to the caliphate in bin Laden-style broadcasts. Rankin turns punching down into a bingo game. Gluten allergy?Pow!Gay agenda? Shoved off a roof. Mainstream-media proxy? Off with his head,inshallah! Korean NPC? Maim him – but not so badly that he can’t hack the terrorists’ security mainframe, or explain how he pulled off the impossible (“I’m Asian”). No scene, it seems, can pass without a parting pun. Yet they hardly grate as much as Rankin’s liberal use of AI for newscasts and other screen filler. Overall, the film’s “bad Muslim” conceit is as dated as an 90s alt-rock soundtrack – headlined by Deep Blue Something’s Breakfast at Tiffany’s.Majors disappears into the role of a TemuEqualizer, railing against sharia law’s incursion into the west when he isn’t dodging bullets, screaming for cover or crashing through plate glass –a botched stunt that tipped a crew strike, one the production had apparently hoped to forestall by shooting in right-to-work South Carolina. In fact, one would be hard-pressed to picture another disgraced actor bringing as much commitment to the one-note role of Captain Saunders as Majors – who, doubtless, had stronger scene partners at Yale than in this stiff cast. As he pops in and out of this low-budget, provocative-for-provocation’s-sake thriller – one minute bleeding out and clinging to life; the next, completely healed without hint of explanation – it was hard not to be reminded of just how he wound up at professional rock bottom.Three years ago, Majors was Hollywood’s hottest property, a young hunk with range. His breakout roles in HBO’s Lovecraft Country and Spike Lee’s Da 5 Bloods not only marked him as a future superstar but put him on a fast track that Black actors rarely reach so early in their careers, if ever. Marvel tapped him to play Kang the Conqueror, a supervillain with an arc across the MCU. But just before that work really got going, Majors wasarrestedafter an altercation with his girlfriend and foundguiltyof two misdemeanor counts of assault and harassment.The consequences were immediate. Marvel recast Kang, bringing Robert Downey Jr out of retirement, the US army dropped Majors as a spokesperson and he became persona non grata in the industry. Despite attempts to rebuild his public reputation in the media and rally Black community support – including making a great show of having moved on from his white accuser to dating Black Hollywood princess Meagan Good, now his wife – Majors never recovered. His next film, Magazine Dreams, a bodybuilding feature that was touted as Oscar bait, landed with a thud. Other potential high-profile collaborations soon fell through despite the apology tour and Majors completing a domestic violence intervention program. In the intervening years, some online observers have wondered whether Majors was punished more harshly than white male actors who found themselves in similar predicaments and bounced back. But it could be that Majors’s real crime was devastating a multibillion-dollar franchise plan – and making other studios wary of getting burned, too.And so older with flecks of gray for character but still in fine fettle, Majors is stuck at the Daily Wire, doing political kabuki – but for how much longer? Infidels is his first fresh production since his 2023 legal troubles, and at a glance it hardly scans like the kind of work that could spring a comeback. But the political winds have shifted since Hollywood turned its back on Majors. #MeToo and wokeness have given way to incel culture and DEI crackdowns. Rightwing media fixtures run the government. In a climate that protects abusers, whether targeting women orbeasts, one would have to think it’s only a matter of time before Majors is returned to prominence – becausethat’sthe American way.Explore more on these topicsJonathan MajorsAction and adventure filmsThrillerscommentShareReuse this content

title: Million Dollar Quartet review – jumping jukebox show reignites rock’n’roll classics | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, Carl Perkins and Jerry Lee Lewis’s 1956 get-together is respun with an unsubtle script but some vigorous performances
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, Carl Perkins and Jerry Lee Lewis’s 1956 get-together is respun with an unsubtle script but some vigorous performances
Content: Go, cats, go! … (from left) Christopher Erasmus as Johnny Cash, Joey Bradick as Carl Perkins and Connor Payne as Elvis Presley.Photograph: Alex TabriziView image in fullscreenGo, cats, go! … (from left) Christopher Erasmus as Johnny Cash, Joey Bradick as Carl Perkins and Connor Payne as Elvis Presley.Photograph: Alex TabriziTheatreReviewMillion Dollar Quartet review – jumping jukebox show reignites rock’n’roll classicsThe Arts at Marble Arch, LondonElvis Presley, Johnny Cash, Carl Perkins and Jerry Lee Lewis’s 1956 get-together  is respun with an unsubtle script but some vigorous performancesChris WiegandThu 17 Sep 2026 13.24 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 13.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith the Arts theatre currently closed for major works, it has established a larger base next to Marble Arch. This temporary new home is now given over to some golden oldies with a jukebox musical combining the stories of Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, Carl Perkins andJerry Lee Lewis. It is almost 70 years since they wound up together one December afternoon at Sam Phillips’ Sun Studios in Memphis and recorded 40-odd songs. “Million dollar quartet” ran the caption that accompanied their picture in the newspaper.Did this impromptu supergroup share vocals on Blue Suede Shoes and did Cash and Perkins mash up My Babe and Sixteen Tons as they do here? All the evidence suggests not. They chiefly laid down gospel and spiritual numbers amid some breezy chatter kept on the recordings. Two of those, Down By the Riverside and Peace in the Valley, are kept from the original session – along with Chuck Berry’s Brown Eyed Handsome Man – in a show that uses the occasion to rotate instead through some of their greatest hits including Great Balls of Fire, which wouldn’t be recorded at Sun for another year. Even Libby Watson’s design, which turns the modest studios into a sort of checkerboard-floored rock’n’roll diner cum fairground, has a colourful arch resembling a retro jukebox.View image in fullscreenOwning the room … Jenay Naima as Dyanne in Million Dollar Quartet.Photograph: Alex TabriziThe musical – first staged in 2006 andseen in the West End in 2011, now newly transferred fromCirencester’s Barn theatre– is a curious mix of wildly fanciful and diligently factual. Colin Escott and Floyd Mutrux’s book has some laidback charm and humour but the characters often awkwardly trot out their own and each other’s backstories. Phillips (Darren Day) hosts the evening, adding extra exposition. It can feel like a series of potted histories. Occasionally a song matches the men’s conversation, as when their shared family bereavements inspire Peace in the Valley. Other songs may carry their own stories of danger and passion but the only drama bubbling in the script is Phillips’ proteges being poached by bigger record labels and some rivalry between the foursome.It’s not exactly Stereophonic.View image in fullscreenCockamamie … Joe Bence as Jerry Lee LewisPhotograph: Alex TabriziAnd yet … Jonathan O’Boyle’s production has four actor-musicians so charismatic and combative as these cocky young guns, each playing and singing with such vigour, that the well-worn tunes hit you afresh. Connor Payne’s luxuriously quiffed Presley, Christopher Erasmus’s brooding Cash, Joe Bence’s cockamamie Lewis and Joey Bradick’s driven Perkins are not imitations and instead retain an essence of each musician. Along with drummer Josh Haberfield and double bassist Geraint Downing, they rip through it with an assurance that is irresistible. And in this testosterone-filled studio, Presley’s girlfriend – here called Dyanne – blows them all away with her rendition of Fever then does it again with I Hear You Knocking. Who cares if that really happened either, you may ask, when Jenay Naima owns the room this well.Atthe Arts at Marble Arch, London, until 6 December. title: Fences review – August Wilson’s classic family drama is as smart as paint | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Daniel Bailey’s dynamic production fizzes with jazz and moments of possibility amid taut scenes of thwarted ambition and harsh realities in 1950s America
Author: Catherine Love
Headline: Daniel Bailey’s dynamic production fizzes with jazz and moments of possibility amid taut scenes of thwarted ambition and harsh realities in 1950s America
Content: Heartbreaking … Madeline Appiah as Rose Maxson and Everal A Walsh as Jim Bono in Headlong at Leeds Playhouse.Photograph: Tyler FayoseView image in fullscreenHeartbreaking … Madeline Appiah as Rose Maxson and Everal A Walsh as Jim Bono in Headlong at Leeds Playhouse.Photograph: Tyler FayoseTheatreReviewFences review – August Wilson’s classic family drama is as smart as paintLeeds PlayhouseDaniel Bailey’s dynamic production fizzes with jazz and moments of possibility amid taut scenes of thwarted ambition and harsh realities in 1950s AmericaCatherine LoveThu 17 Sep 2026 07.16 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 07.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive years on from their excellent production ofJitney, Leeds Playhouse and Headlong return to August Wilson’s Pittsburgh cycle of plays with a revival of his 1985 classic Fences. It’s another drama of family, masculinity and thwarted ambitions, painting national issues of race and inequality on a domestic canvas.Set in the 1950s, the focus is the African American Maxson family and its patriarch, Troy: a trash-collector, former convict and one-time baseball player robbed of professional success by the colour of his skin. Ray Fearon is horribly compelling as this tragic figure, a man made monstrous by circumstance. His anger at the world seems to radiate across his wide shoulders, which he braces against the anticipated onslaught. Raised in hardship and denied his dreams, Troy rains this same harshness down on his two sons, not allowing the possibility of a better future for his offspring.View image in fullscreenRadiates anger against the world … Ray Fearon and Josh Tedeku.Photograph: Tyler FayoseFor Troy, responsibility towards his flesh and blood is a matter of providing food and shelter, absent of any affection or encouragement. Over the course of the play we see the effect of this on his sons: grownup musician Lyons (Michael Ahomka-Lindsay) and high school football player Cory (Josh Tedeku), who visibly hardens as his father sabotages his chance of a college scholarship. Similarly ill-treated is Madeline Appiah’s heartbreaking Rose, the loyal wife whose own dreams have to be squashed down in service of her family.Sky’s the limit! Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater – in picturesRead moreDaniel Bailey’s dynamic production pulses with the jazz played by Lyons, weaving music around the taut scenes. These eruptions of joy and expression are what Troy’s impoverished worldview lacks. A similar emptiness is suggested by Lily Arnold’s set, which revolves to reveal the shell-like interior behind the naturalistic veneer of the Maxsons’ home. Bailey also reminds us that this is a fiction, with house lights remaining up for a beat at the start of each half and actors occasionally stepping in and out of the dramatic frame.The overall effect is a striking blend of gritty realism and playful theatricality – an apt stage metaphor for Wilson’s story of brutality and injustice shot through with fleeting moments of possibility.AtLeeds Playhouseuntil 26 September. Thentouringuntil 14 November.Explore more on these topicsTheatreHeadlongLeeds PlayhouseAugust WilsonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Darkling review – Stranger Things’ Linnea Berthelsen confronts a gruesome Indian disaster | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Titas Halder’s coming-of-age monologue is set against the 1984 Bhopal toxic gas leak – but the poetic script doesn’t quite capture the horror
Author: Ammar Kalia
Headline: Titas Halder’s coming-of-age monologue is set against the 1984 Bhopal toxic gas leak – but the poetic script doesn’t quite capture the horror
Content: Tightly wound … Linnea Berthelsen in Darkling at Bush theatre.Photograph: Alex BrennerView image in fullscreenTightly wound … Linnea Berthelsen in Darkling at Bush theatre.Photograph: Alex BrennerTheatreReviewDarkling review – Stranger Things’ Linnea Berthelsen confronts a gruesome Indian disasterBush theatre, LondonTitas Halder’s coming-of-age monologue is set against the 1984 Bhopal toxic gas leak – but the poetic script doesn’t quite capture the horrorAmmar KaliaThu 17 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOminousness permeates Darkling. In Titas Halder’s dramatic monologue, we witness a young girl’s coming of age set against the backdrop of the 1984 toxic gas leak in the Indian city of Bhopal, an environmental catastrophe that remains one of the worst industrial disasters in global history, leading to thousands of deaths.Actor Linnea Berthelsen – best known for her role as Kali in Netflix seriesStranger Things– makes her UK stage debut and gamely takes on the singular role in a tightly wound, physical performance. Leaping across Simon Kenny’s artful, soil-filled set, Berthelsen embodies childlike wonder as she recounts her early years playing in the rain, savouring bowlfuls of plain rice and idolising her older sister.View image in fullscreenChildlike wonder … Linnea Berthelsen in Darkling.Photograph: Alex BrennerSo far so good. Except, alongside her emotional growth, the silhouette of a new factory rises in the background – effectively portrayed by lighting designer Rajiv Pattani’s projection – foreshadowing the calamity to come. When it eventually arrives, we hear of the horrors she witnesses, stepping over maimed bodies, facing blinded relatives and breathing in toxic fumes, all relayed through increasingly frenzied description.Herein lies the main issue with Darkling. By using a monologue format – especially one where our narrator is never dramatically questioned – all the audience receives are streams of poetic description, a barrage of words that never feel emphatic or adequate enough to match the gruesome scale of such a tragedy. Coupled with Halder’s uneven pacing, which lingers in childhood for too long before alighting on trauma and then descending into a hectoring denouement that places the blame for the disaster on individual shoulders, Berthelsen is faced with a gargantuan task to maintain a sense of dramatic tension.As Matthew Xia’s production draws to a close, with a strangely repeated narrative beat that equates female worth to motherhood, you are ultimately left feeling that this is a tragedy told without the requisite horror. Darkling is a worthy reminder of an often-overlooked disaster – but one that may well fail to take root in the mind.AtBush theatre, London, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreBush theatreMatthew XiaIndiaStranger ThingsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Thelma & Louise review – musical hoedown is a bland and baffling wrong turn | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Despite a book by the original screenwriter, this stage adaptation doesn’t have the depth – or the songs – worthy of the era-defining feminist parable. And where’s the car?
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Despite a book by the original screenwriter, this stage adaptation doesn’t have the depth – or the songs – worthy of the era-defining feminist parable. And where’s the car?
Content: Southern twang … Amy Lennox and Rachel Tucker in Thelma & Louise at the Young Vic.Photograph: Helen MurrayView image in fullscreenSouthern twang … Amy Lennox and Rachel Tucker in Thelma & Louise at the Young Vic.Photograph: Helen MurrayTheatreReviewThelma & Louise review – musical hoedown is a bland and baffling wrong turnYoung Vic, LondonDespite a book by the original screenwriter, this stage adaptation doesn’t have the depth – or the songs – worthy of the era-defining feminist parable. And where’s the car?Arifa AkbarThu 17 Sep 2026 07.27 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Beware; for I am fearless, and therefore powerful.” These words were written by Mary Shelley two centuries ago but could apply to the two runaways in Ridley Scott’s 1991 film who turn into highway fugitives in their liberating cross-country road trip after a girls’ weekend goes wrong.Thelma & Louise, starring Susan Sarandon and Geena Davis, did not exactly represent Shelley’s “monstrous feminine” but came to be seen as an era-defining feminist parable on freedom from male strictures and abuse. It caught the cultural zeitgeist, the title becoming a byword for sisterhood, with reams written about its feminist layers, spectacular cinematography – and the shock of its un-Hollywood ending.View image in fullscreenUnderpowered … Amy Lennox and Jordan Luke Gage in Thelma & Louise.Photograph: Helen MurraySo it is a brave creative team that decides to adapt the film for the stage. It helps this production’s credentials that the original screenwriter, Callie Khouri, is on board for the book. It also has two capable leads in Rachel Tucker, who plays the tough-cookie Louise, and Amy Lennox as Thelma, the put-upon wife turned fantastically rogue.Beyond that, the intention around this musical adaptation of the road movie is entirely perplexing. Significantly, there is neither road nor car, bar a fleeting glimpse of the latter at the beginning, upturned and static. Streaking neon lights and the sounds of a revving motor denote their journey. “I want the wind in my hair,” sings Thelma at one point. We do too, Thelma.Fans of the film can forget those glorious scenes of the women’s turquoise convertible Thunderbird, and of the magnificently lonely desert, both of which felt like characters in their own right. Instead, the backdrop is a prosaic saloon bar – the fateful one they visit where a drunk man attempts to rape Thelma and is shot dead by Louise.That incident comes early, so the women’s fear of its consequences eclipses their initial joy and release. Their characters remain flatly dichotomous: Thelma is the flirty conventional one, Louise haranguing and hard-bitten. The narrative plays out as two women on the run. You wish for more depth, more bonding between them, which does come in the second half when the show finally fires up, but it still feels like empowerment-lite.‘It’s not good to walk through the world feeling like prey’: Thelma & Louise’s writer on turning a movie classic into a musicalRead moreUnder the direction of Trip Cullman, the characters seem dated and the time-frame wavers uncertainly between the 1980s and now.Bobbi Jene Smithand Or Schraiber’s choreography brings hoedown moves and line dancing men in 10-gallon hats. There are few memorable songs in Neko Case’s country score, although one reprised number takes flight in the heartfelt It Was Worth It. The southern twangs are dialled up to 10, and lyrics offer exposition with plodding lines, although the singing is strong.The sexy young grifter JD – the character that launched the young, incandescent Brad Pitt on film – is patina-thin and played by Jordan Luke Gage. Lead detective Hal (Trevor Dion Nicholas) is also barely there as a character. None of it is powered by enough emotion. When the road trip ends at the mouth of the Grand Canyon, the women’s T-Bird surrounded by police and revving dangerously, you are moved not by what is unravelling before you but by the memory of the unforgettable, defiant ending of the film. Did they really just do that?AtYoung Vic theatre, London, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMusicalsYoung VicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘You think you’re done and you get pigeonholed’: Samantha Morton on raving, Richard Russell and having another shot as a singer | Music | The Guardian
description: The actor and musician spoke at our Guardian Live ‘Honest Playlist’ event at Green Man festival about growing up in Nottingham on the free-party scene, and the healing powers of music
Author: Kate Hutchinson
Headline: The actor and musician spoke at our Guardian Live ‘Honest Playlist’ event at Green Man festival about growing up in Nottingham on the free-party scene, and the healing powers of music
Content: Kate Hutchinson and Samantha Morton dancing to song ‘Original Nuttah’ by Shy FX and UK ApachiPhotograph: Scarlet Pestell/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKate Hutchinson and Samantha Morton dancing to song ‘Original Nuttah’ by Shy FX and UK ApachiPhotograph: Scarlet Pestell/The GuardianMusicInterview‘You think you’re done and you get pigeonholed’: Samantha Morton on raving, Richard Russell and having another shot as a singerKate HutchinsonThe actor and musician spoke at ourGuardian Live‘Honest Playlist’ event at Green Man festival about growing up in Nottingham on the free-party scene, and the healing powers of musicThu 17 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 06.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the Sunday afternoon of Green Man Festival in August,Samantha Mortonjoined me onstage in the Talking Shop tent to discuss her life in music. The celebrated actor and director is currently in cinemas as the scene-stealing Circe inThe Odyssey, but she is also a musician. Later that day, she performed on the main stage later with Everything Is Recorded, the supergroup led by XL label boss Richard Russell, who also collaborated with Morton on her 2024 solo albumDaffodils & Dirt. More recently, she voiced her character’s title song onThe Odysseysoundtrack. “I love talking about music,” she says. “I never really get asked enough to talk about music.”For this in-depth conversation with Guardian Live, Morton took us through herHonest Playlistof songs on various themes that have meant something to her, including the first single she bought, Musical Youth’s reggae-pop hit Pass The Dutchie, the song she’d do at karaoke, Michael Prophet and Ricky Tuffy’s Your Love, and a great song to fall in love to (Moments In Love by Art of Noise). She thinks about playlists often, revealing that she makes them whenever she needs to get into character for a role and used to “carry tapes in my back pocket everywhere I went because I couldn’t have bad music.”Her earliest musical memories are of the record collection belonging to her father, who she lived with as child in Nottingham between foster home placements in the late-70s, early-80s. “My dad had the most beautiful music taste,” she said, though it was selective: “He had all the Beatles albums, Bob Marley, Don McLean, and that was it.” She recalled a hilarious story of watching her older brother and stepbrother getting into hip-hop – and up to mischief. “They cut the lino out of the back of the kitchen floor because they were breakdancing in town,” she said. Of course: they needed a smooth surface for all the “head-spinning”.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Scarlet Pestell/The GuardianReggae factored into her musical upbringing in a big way. “I moved around a lot because we were homeless,” she continued, “so we were either in a hostel or I was in care, or I was back with my dad when he was out of prison. Nottingham is a massive Afro-Caribbean community, it’s a huge Windrush city. We’d be listening to the most beautiful music for the sound clashes, it was everywhere.”In the 90s, her love of soundsystem culture parlayed into a love of rave music. When her favourite party song rings out, jungle classic Original Nuttah by UK Apache and Shy FX, Morton stands up and starts to dance. “I was an original raver,” she said. Her and her foster mother went “travelling with the free party movement,” specifically theDiY Soundsystem, “that went all over the country having parties.”“We did two summers at Breedon on the Hill,” she continued, referencing the legendary Leicestershire spot where festivals would run for days and days. “I was a kid, but this was my world. It’s where I first learned how to make really lovely rice, or talk to people about politics or poetry.” Those formative experiences turned her into “not an original nuttah, perhaps, but an originalthinker,” she said. It’s also where she first heard another transformative track, Papua Nu Guinea by the Future Sound of London. “People talk about things like ayahuasca, or medicinal mushrooms for healing trauma,” she said, but hearing songs like this in the English countryside “was spiritual. I left the field that day and I felt healed. That music took me somewhere that made me feel loved, [like] a child of the universe.”As a musician herself, Morton found her voice gradually. “I’m not a trained singer. I used to do a bit of session singing for Nightmares On Wax and people like that and I used to sing in rave clubs in Nottingham. I wanted to be Dina Carroll so bad. And then Igot into a lot of trouble with the police, things happened, and I ended up acting.” She still “wrote songs constantly” but didn’t think there was a possibility of performing them until she met Richard Russell. The producer helped to “open up a world for me where I can revisit my first love, music,” she said.In 2024, they collaborated on her first solo album under the name Sam Morton,Daffodils And Dirt –an“intoxicating trip-hop debut”. “We started talking, and we had so many connections to do with influences,” Morton explained. “And I said, listen, ‘I’ve been writing songs since I was about 13. Actually, the first song I wrote, I was about seven, and he was like: ‘We’re going to put it on the album’.” She said that working with Russell, both on her debut and with his collective Everything Is Recorded, “is a dream come true, I swear. I’m 49 now. You think you’re done, you think you can’t do the thing that you’ve always wanted to do, and you get pigeonholed, but you can.”New music is on the horizon, though she’s keeping details underwraps, but for now, she ended by saying she took great pleasure in performing with the “incredible musicians” of Everything Is Recorded. “This is how beautiful and spontaneous music can be,” she said. “Don’t overthink it. Don’t worry about it. It’s the act ofdoingthat fills you with joy.”Explore more on these topicsMusicSamantha MortonFestivalsGreen ManMusic festivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Opus13: Mendelssohn and Grieg album review – an assured and distinctive debut  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The young quartet – winners of the Wigmore Hall String Quartet competition – continue to impress in a recording pairing Mendelssohn and Grieg
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: The young quartet – winners of the Wigmore Hall String Quartet competition – continue to impress in a recording pairing Mendelssohn and Grieg
Content: Distinctive … Opus13.Photograph: Courtesy of Julia WeselyView image in fullscreenDistinctive … Opus13.Photograph: Courtesy of Julia WeselyClassical musicReviewOpus13: Mendelssohn and Grieg album review – an assured and distinctive debutOpus13(Alpha Classics)The young quartet – winners of the Wigmore Hall String Quartet competition – continue to impress in a recording  pairing  Mendelssohn and GriegErica JealThu 17 Sep 2026 09.44 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou would expect good things fromOpus13– current BBC New Generation Artists, and winners at last year’s Wigmore Hall and Bordeaux string quartet competitions – and this assured, distinctive debut lives up to that. The quartet formed in Oslo in 2014 as teenagers, naming themselves after the first piece they played together, and it’s with that work, Mendelssohn’s Op 13 No 2, that they lead off. The brief, soulful introduction breaks into a tense, runaway allegro in which the occasional violin swoop only increases the feeling of urgency. Mendelssohn’s debt to Beethoven in this work is clear, and the quartet play the slow movement with an intense warmth that makes it seem to belong beside that composer’s great adagios.View image in fullscreenOpus13, Mendelssohn and Grieg.Photograph: Courtesy of Julia WeselyThe Mendelssohn is nicely paired with Grieg’s Quartet No 1, a work full of insistent repetition beautifully handled here so as to create momentum rather than sap it. The folksy style hinted at in the second movement blossoms in the third, which gets a touch of Nordic fiddle, exuberant yet elegant. As encore there’s more Grieg, a characterful version of Solveig’s Song. The arrangement is credited not to a single person but to the entire group equally – which comes as no surprise at all.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com.
