title: Is this world-class, free gallery Cambridge’s best-kept secret? | Art | The Guardian
description: Maggi Hambling, Paula Rego, Bridget Riley … Murray Edwards College houses the Women’s Art Collection, featuring some of the industry’s biggest names from the last 40 years
Author: Chloë Ashby
Headline: Maggi Hambling, Paula Rego, Bridget Riley … Murray Edwards College houses the Women’s Art Collection, featuring some of the industry’s biggest names from the last 40 years
Content: ‘We’ve got the materials. We’ve got the ambition’ … The Women's Art Collection at Murray Edwards College, Cambridge.Photograph: Wilf SpellerView image in fullscreen‘We’ve got the materials. We’ve got the ambition’ … The Women's Art Collection at Murray Edwards College, Cambridge.Photograph: Wilf SpellerArtIs this world-class, free gallery Cambridge’s best-kept secret?Maggi Hambling, Paula Rego, Bridget Riley … Murray Edwards College houses the Women’s Art Collection, featuring some of the industry’s biggest names from the last 40 yearsChloë AshbyThu 17 Sep 2026 05.39 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 05.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMuseum shows can be expensive. Commercial galleries intimidating. And as forCambridgecolleges? They’re usually marked with signs saying things like “Closed to visitors” and “Keep off the grass”. Murray Edwards College, though, has a magnificent art collection that’s free to visit and open to the public all year round. And Harriet Loffler says you can do whatever you like on the lawn.View image in fullscreenWelcome sign … Guerrilla Girls, The Advantages of Being a Woman Artist, 1988.Photograph: Stephen Bond/The Women’s Art CollectionShe’s the director of the Women’sArtCollection, a permanent fixture of modern and contemporary works by female artists at Murray Edwards, and one of the best-kept secrets in Cambridge. By the time she’s greeting me in the porter’s lodge of the college, I’ve already clocked two Tracey Emin lithographs. In the cafe is a screen print by the Guerrilla Girls and a charmingly clumsy canvas by Rose Wylie. In the corridors and rooms in between we pass pictures by Leonora Carrington, Faith Ringgold, Barbara Walker – and, astonishingly, we’re the only ones around.It all began, Loffler tells me, with Mary Kelly, the first artist in residence at the college, which was established by a group of strong-minded women as New Hall over on Silver Street in 1954. (Women may have been admitted to the University of Cambridge towards the end of the 19th century, but they weren’t issued with degrees until the middle of the 20th century; when they were finally allowed into Magdalene College in 1988, apparently a bunch of the male fellows wore black armbands.) In 1965, New Hall moved to its current location off Huntingdon Road, a landmark building designed by Chamberlin, Powell and Bon. Commissioned by the college’s founding president Rosemary Murray, the architects, who designed the Barbican, envisioned it as a manifesto for women’s education, with open walkways, an altar-like staircase in the library, and a soaring dome.View image in fullscreenShe said yes … Paula Rego’s  Inês de Castro, 2014.Photograph: Courtesy The Women’s Art CollectionDuring her time at New Hall (the name changed to Murray Edwards in 2008), Kelly created Extase (1986), a series of screen-printed images of her clothes in disarray, which she paired with snippets of conversation she’d overheard from women involved in 1970s feminism – an exploration into the components that make up modern womanhood, the things we wear and the words we say. It was acquired by the college and displayed in the dining hall, where it planted the seed of having other art by women on the walls.So, a few years later, the college president Valerie Pearl, with the curator Ann Jones, reached out to others and invited them to donate works of their own – works, they wrote, that would not be sold but “remain on view as a source of inspiration to students, researchers and visitors”. Among those who received that letter were Maggi Hambling, Paula Rego, Bridget Riley and Eileen Cooper, all of whom said yes (Sonia Boyce’s letter got lost in the post, but happily a piece she made in the early 1990s is about to join the fold). Within two years, the college had been sent more than 70 artworks, and the collection was well on its way.“There are lots of artists you might recognise, but there are also lots you won’t have heard of,” Loffler tells me. It’s a level playing field – in the spirit of learning, as much space is given to lesser-known names as art world elite. “The other thing we always think about is reciprocity,” she says. “We never want a donation to be an empty gesture. We want it to be part of a relationship.”View image in fullscreenNew acquisitions … Bambou Gili, Legally Stev, 2024.Photograph: The Women’s Art CollectionToday, it’s Europe’s largest publicly accessible collection of modern and contemporary art by women, with over 600 works by more than 300 artists. New acquisitions occur sporadically, as and when artists are prepared to donate works, or the college has the funds to buy them. Unlike nearby Kettle’s Yard and the Fitzwilliam Museum, which are part of the university and therefore eligible for university funding, the Women’s Art Collection is run by the college, so has to find money elsewhere. In 2024 it partnered with the art philanthropists Spirit Now London to acquire three works by young female artists from China, South Africa and the US. At this year’s Frieze London it’s working with Female Artists of the Mougins Museum to buy a piece by a female artist not yet in a UK public collection.It’s been four decades since the college acquired Extase; to celebrate, a new exhibition, What Remains, will bring together archival materials (including Kelly’s application for the artist residency) and works by contemporary artists who are engaged with similar feminist concerns. Just as her predecessors wrote to Hambling, Rego and Riley all those years ago, Laura Moseley, the curator, has invited women from outside the Women’s Art Collection to take part. Among them are Ellen Lesperance, who pays homage to female activism through painted knitting patterns, and Sadé Mica, who’s making a new embroidered chest binder in response to Extase.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenFour decades on … Mary Kelly’s Extase installation at The Women’s Art Collection.Photograph: Jo Underhill/© Mary Kelly. The Women’s Art Collection.After a stroll through the garden – keep your eyes peeled for Emma Darwin’s greenhouse (Emma was Charles Darwin’s wife) – we head back to the porter’s lodge, and Loffler tells me that the “long-term, blue-sky thinking” is to create a new gallery space right here at the entrance. The existing rooms within the college aren’t environmentally controlled, so there are limits when it comes to museum loans. “But we’ve got the materials. We’ve got the ambition.” All they need is the backing. “What really motivates me is trying to unlock something of the university for a general public,” says Loffler with a smile. “I love the idea that local residents walking down Huntington Road could just pop in.”What Remainsis at the Women’s Art Collection, Cambridge, from 23 September until 28 FebruaryExplore more on these topicsArtCambridgeExhibitionsMuseumsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Welcome to the age of the grown-up soft drink | Food | The Guardian
description: There is now a wealth of less sugary, more sophisticated nonalcoholic options out there, with flavours clearly aimed at an adult market
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: There is now a wealth of less sugary, more sophisticated nonalcoholic options out there, with flavours clearly aimed at an adult market
Content: Quite gron-up: Botivo, a UK-made nonalcoholic botanical.Photograph: Steven Joyce/BotivoView image in fullscreenQuite gron-up: Botivo, a UK-made nonalcoholic botanical.Photograph: Steven Joyce/BotivoGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.FoodWelcome to the age of the grown-up soft drinkThere is now a wealth of less sugary, more sophisticated nonalcoholic options out there, with flavours clearly aimed at an adult marketMina HollandThu 17 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 08.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhave written recently about several families of nonalcoholic drinks that are having a moment:tonic water,flavoured sparkling waterandwine substitutes. It stands to reason that soft drinks are enjoying their time in the sun. Quite literally, too: the heat of 2026 has demanded some serious refreshments and UK booze consumption isat a record low. But it has dawned on me that there is a broader trend in alcohol-free beverages beyond individual categories, namely that we are living in the age of the grown-up soft drink.By that I mean those with less sugar and more complexity than post-mix drinks, or “soda pop” (as my daughter now calls them, thanks to theKPop Demon Hunters songof the same name), which are clearly aimed at adults. One example is the tribe of “functional” drinks that have hit the market in the past year or so and that have supposed health benefits or performance-enhancing qualities, such as improving focus or helping you to slow down. Sonic Tonics’ CBD-infused 0% drink, for example, promises to shift your mood, and it certainly quenches thirst with a really original flavour profile of bitter hemp root with sweet and floral fig and violet. And while usually sceptical of celebrity-backed products with wellness claims,Gillian Anderson’s G Spot drinksare genuinely delicious. The passion fruit and habanero chilli is my favourite; I can’t support its aphrodisiac claims (allegedly due to its ingredients including butterfly pea and L-arginine, both of which are said to increase blood flow to the sexual organs), but, at £6.50 for four from Ocado, it’s cheaper than trying Gwyneth Paltrow’ssex oil.There are also several low-sugar “premium” soft drinks that are worth writing home about, such as deli favouriteSomething & Nothing, which contains no sweeteners and only natural sugars; the yuzu and the mango and Thai basil flavours are both perfect.Rapscallion Sodawas developed to make satisfying soft drinks without a sugar crash; raw fruit is extracted and mixed with citrus, spices and carbonated water: think burnt lemon with cracked black pepper and dry lime with makrut lime leaves.Then there are drinks designed to be consumed on occasions when you might otherwise drink alcohol. Botivo has created a sparkling, premixed version of its nonalcoholic botanical aperitivo – if you don’t like shrubs or drinking vinegars, it may not be for you, but I find it a wonderful alternative to amaro-based cocktails such as the negroni. Fever-Tree, meanwhile, has launchedits own “non-alcoholic spritz”, which is sweeter and not very bitter. Perhaps my favourite discovery of the week, however, is Non, an Australian wine alternative that blends verjus (unripe grape juice) with the likes of raspberry, chamomile and salt. That’smykind of soda pop.Five new drinks to tickle your tastebudsRapscallion Burnt Lemon£3.60 (250ml) Gail’s. The edgiest, tartest lemon meringue pie of your life – in liquid form.Botivo£3.50 (250ml) Waitrose. The bittersweet botanical aperitivo can now be enjoyed on the hoof – cheers!G SpotAwaken£6.50 (4 x 250ml) Ocado. This “may improve libido”, but it will definitely titillate your taste buds with its chilli kick.Non 1£19.99 (750ml) Sous Chef. A blend of tart verjus, chamomile and salted raspberry that’s super for sipping or supper.Sonic TonicsHemp Root Fig & Violet£36 (6 x 240ml) Sonic Tonics. A really unique, florally bitter soft drink with CBD – buzz without fuzz.Explore more on these topicsFoodSoft drinksBritish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sick of sandwiches? Perfect packed lunches – from savoury muffins to bento boxes | Food | The Guardian
description: After the endless road trip of summer, I’m enjoying September’s back-to-school vibes – and the excuse to create delicious lunches to take to work
Author: Georgina Hayden
Headline: After the endless road trip of summer, I’m enjoying September’s back-to-school vibes – and the excuse to create delicious lunches to take to work
Content: Nena Foster's kids' packed lunches.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNena Foster's kids' packed lunches.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.FeastFoodSick of sandwiches? Perfect packed lunches – from savoury muffins to bento boxesAfter the long hot summer, I’m enjoying September’s back-to-school vibes – and the excuse to create delicious lunches to take to workSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastGeorgina HaydenThu 17 Sep 2026 09.02 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter an August spent mostly on the road, I’ve found myself unexpectedly enjoying the back-to-school feeling that arrives with September. Usually, I greet it with the sort of enthusiasm reserved for a tax return, but, having been away for so long, it’s actually been rather nice coming home. Of course, there are all the usual inevitable resolutions and to-do lists: go to bed earlier, eat better, take lunch to work. Admirable stuff, although I suspect a summer of one too many honeycomb ice-creams and an irresponsible amount ofIrish brown breadand salty butter may also have something to do with it. Taking a packed lunch is, in any case, an all-round win, because eating out is increasingly expensive, and food bought in cafes and restaurants tends to be richer and saltier than a homemade equivalent. Depressingly, school and college canteens don’t fare much better, either.But a packed lunch needn’t mean a sad sandwich or last night’s tubbed-up leftovers. Nena Foster’scourgette, olive and halloumi muffinsare a very good argument for taking your lunch with you: nutrient-dense without being remotely worthy, they work just as well in an adult’s lunchbox as in a child’s, and they freeze brilliantly, too. Add a flask ofpumpkin soupor Tom Hunt’ssweetcorn chowderfor an excellent autumn lunch.View image in fullscreenFun for all ages … Shuko Oda’s onigiri bento box.Photograph: Jean Cazals/The ObserverShuko Oda’sonigiri bento boxis another winner, and pleases pretty much every age group, which is no mean feat.Bento boxesare such a hit, in fact, that I have gone one step farther and bought Japanese egg moulds. There are few things more unnecessary than a hard-boiled egg shaped like a rabbit or bear, but they do make lunchtime more exciting. And, really, that is the point. You can fill those little compartments with whatever you fancy: Caroline Craig and Sophie Missingbreak it down here, with a little guidance on what to pop in those small compartments. Another option isJeremy Lee’s ploughman’s, which would be a particularly fine arrangement: thick slices of ham, nuggets of cheese, dollops of chutney, sliced apple. A tiny pub lunch, minus the pub.On days when I crave something more warming, I’m very happy to dust off the Thermos. There is something deeply pleasing about taking a little pot of hot food to work. Meera Sodha’spav bhajiis perfect for this. Keep it warm in the flask until lunchtime, then spoon into a pre-toasted, buttered roll. The butter melts into the warm spiced vegetables and you wonder if there has ever been a more perfect use for a flask. I feel the same about Rachel Roddy’sreal minestroneand Felicity Cloake’spasta e fagioli, and I’m sure they could be premade and reheated in a microwave, if you have access to one. But you might not and, besides, I think dishes such as these are best when they’re nottoohot, and when that rich broth is starchy and thickened. Which, perhaps, is what I like most about September lunches: they don’t have to be virtuous, elaborate or even particularly organised; they just need to be something you’ll actually look forward to eating at 1pm. And that is a resolution I can get behind.My week in foodView image in fullscreenCounty Galway on the west coast of Ireland.Photograph: Robert Harding/AlamySweet like chocolate|A road trip from Ireland’s east to west coast this summer was a useful reminder that the country is full of quietly brilliant food-makers. Among them isGrá chocolates, founded by Gráinne Mullins, an award-winning, Michelin-trained chef – and now, finally, shipping to the UK. Her hand-painted chocolates are made with Irish milk, butter and cream, use seasonal ingredients wherever possible, and their fillings are cooked from scratch. As a result, they are, inevitably, rather hard to resist. My family’s current favourite is thepumpkin spice hot chocolate, made with caramelised white chocolate and warming autumnal spices. Forget about the pumpkin spiced latte; this is amuchmore convincing way to drink the season.Curry heaven|Emma Basic’s Japanese-style curry cubesare the sort of supermarket shortcut that makes everyone’s life better: loved by all ages, and accommodating all palates and dietaries, you really can have dinner on the table in 20 minutes. Make up the sauce as per the packet instructions, maybe add a few veggies for nutritional purposes, then simply add something crisp – chicken, tofu, aubergine, whatever you like – and serve with rice. No preservatives, no colourings, all good stuff and unapologetically convenient.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBeen around the world|Ruby Bhogal’s new book,Around the World in 80 Cakes, is part baking odyssey, part history lesson and part love letter to the humble cake. The former Great British Bake Off finalist has spent three years baking her way around the globe, and I have been following her rollercoaster journey on social media intently. The result? A book filled with thoroughly tested and much-loved bakes: there is everything from Germany’s honey-rich bienenstich to Thailand’s dense, butter khanom badin, and from an Italian torta caprese to a classic British lemon drizzle cake.Explore more on these topicsFoodFeastLeftoversSandwichesBreadSoupPastanewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for rice, aubergine and mozzarella bake | Food | The Guardian
description: A 1950s cookbook classic – eat it hot and stringy or firm and flavoursome
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: A 1950s cookbook classic – eat it hot and stringy or firm and flavoursome
Content: Rachel Roddy’s rice, aubergine and mozzarella bake.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRachel Roddy’s rice, aubergine and mozzarella bake.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianA kitchen in RomeFoodRachel Roddy’s recipe for rice, aubergine and mozzarella bakeA 1950s cookbook classic – eat it hot and stringy or firm and flavoursomeRachel RoddyThu 17 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYesterday’s lunch and this week’s recipe is thanks to my friend, the designerJake Tilson, who gave me a pristine 1977 edition ofThe Talisman Italian Cook Book. With a cover of red, white and green stripes cover that makes me think as much of seaside rock as Italy’s national colours, the edition was part of the 24th printing of the US translation ofIl Talismano della Felicità(The Talisman of Happiness), by Ada Boni. First published in 1950, the abridged translation was sold as a complete guide to Italian cookery, covering all notable dishes. Well, on the cover at least; inside, the introduction is more realistic, warning the reader that, “to criticise the writer [Boni] or translator [Mrs Matilde La Rosa] for failing to include certain dishes is useless”, because no living man or woman can be acquainted with all the variety of dishes of a such variegated country.The introduction, by a man called Mario A Pei, goes on to explain that the variety of dishes mirrors the wide dialectical array in Italy at the time (1950); its diversity of speech, customs, costumes, psychology and general world outlook. In the next sentence, he notes that this variety was undoubtedly a very bad thing from the standpoint of national unity and progress (the professor and polyglot was an ardent supporter of European fascism and uniting humans under one language). Not that you would guess that from his following sentence: “Variety is the spice of life.” I regretted reading his introduction, and also telling an Italian friend, who said, laughing: “You don’t know the half of it”, in reference to my romanticism about the originalTalismano, which may be great, but also (in her opinion) endorses a Stepford Wives fantasy of womanhood; a journey with Boni as patient guide.I don’t regret making the recipe from page 161 for rice with aubergine, however, which I have adapted for variety’s sake. This bake is good when made with tinned tomatoes, but fresh ones bring a brighter burst of flavour. Ideally, try to get a mix of varieties – a few sweet cherries, a couple of plums, a big fleshy one – that have been peeled and cooked into a sweet-savoury sauce; if necessary, add a pinch of sugar.A reason for eating this pretty much straight out of the oven and while it’s still steaming hot is the mozzarella, because the cheese is molten and pulls into those long strings that make serving it and eating it so entertaining. The benefit of waiting half an hour or longer is that the flavours develop, while the bake itself (and the mozzarella inside and on top) firms up. Or serve at whatever stage or temperature you like, with whatever variety of salad or vegetable.Rice, aubergine and mozzarella bakeServes4-62 medium auberginesOlive oilSalt500g fresh, ripe tomatoes– tinned as a last resort1 onion, peeled and thinly slicedA few red chilli flakes1 handfulbasil leavesSugar(optional)400g long-grain rice80ggrana padano, parmesan, or cheddar400g mozzarella, well-drainedUsing a peeler, pare strips of skin from the aubergines so they are striped, then cut into 1cm-thick slices. Arrange these on an oiled baking tray, zigzag with more oil, sprinkle with salt, then bake at 180C (160C)/350F/gas 4 for 30-40 minutes, until tender and a little golden.Peel the tomatoes by plunging them first into boiling water for four minutes, then cold water, then pulling away the skins. Roughly chop the flesh.In a pan on a medium-low heat, soften the onion in olive oil, then add the tomatoes, some salt, chilli, most of the basil leaves (reserve a few for constructing the bake) and some sugar, if necessary, and simmer until rich and saucy, mashing as you go to break up any lumps; you can also pass the sauce through a food mill.Boil the rice in salted water until al dente and a minute shy of the recommended cooking time. Drain and mix the rice with two tablespoons of olive oil, four tablespoons of the tomato sauce, 30g grated parmesan and salt, if needed; it should be well seasoned.Thinly slice or tear the mozzarella, then construct the bake. Spoon half the rice mix in the base of a round 22cm metal tin or 20cm x 30cm ceramic lasagne-type dish, then use half the aubergine to make a layer on top. Top that with half the sauce, followed by half the mozzarella and a few basil leaves, then repeat this process with the remaining ingredients, ending with a layer of the remaining 50g parmesan. Bake for 20 minutes at 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6, until bubbling.Explore more on these topicsFoodA kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkRiceVegetablesCheeseMain courserecipesShareReuse this content
